_childDocuments_.review: /* ==== *//* Pros */Omg it's so cute I wanna dieeee also the music is so GOODAny low-level monstie you have on your team gets an extreme EXP boost. Power-leveling is extremely easy and encourages putting new monsties on your team.Being able to retake certain subquests for EXP is helpful while power leveling.Put any gene on any monster! Base stats don't fluctuate between monsters too much, so usually the only limitation is the element the monster normally uses. Your team can be whatever you want! Don't let your dreams be dreams!! Make that world-ending Aptonoth!Layered armor is super easy to obtain and I looove being able to recolor the main material of each set. I wish Rise had these options instead of usually small accents.I rank the difficulty between "playing Pokemon solo" and "actual Pokemon meta". It's a lot of memorizing rock-paper-scissors patterns, but there's a deal of coordination and monstie gene-building needed for the endgame.Flying and swimming on monsties is extremely satisfying!There's an actual endgame?! And it's good? You bet! There's also an update roadmap!Coop is simple and efficient. I can't really speak much on it, though.I put Anjanath's fire blast on a Great Baggi because I COULD.Being able to pick my partner endgame instead of being stuck alone is very thoughtful on the dev's part./* ==== *//* Cons */This game needs evolution to be lore-accurate to mainline Monster Hunter. Certain Deviants and Variants are just normal monsters that had something done to them- example: hatching a Black Diablos is weird. Weirder than hatching a dog Pokemon-style.Every monster in the game except the really big bad Elders should be rideable. Tetsucabra and Agnaktor my beloveds :c The land traversal abilities are too scarce. IMO anything that flies should have the Fly ability etc.Your mileage may vary, but I found the story terrible. Like, even bad by Monster Hunter standards. A bunch of characters are forgettable or unlikable, Navirou is intolerable, and the plot features (as far as I remember) an unexplained Chekov's Gun at the end to tie all the absurdly weird plot devices together. I'm happy I'm in endgame and don't have to deal with that.The game wants you to connect to and care for Ratha but I used him in 2 whole hunts??? I didn't even fly with him- I used my own Astalos. _childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a considerebly story rich game with a very soulful spectacle and charming artstyle. It does the Pokemon esque kind of gameplay better than Pokemon does in my opinion especially in this day and age. Riding and befriending monsters is fun, leveling them into killing machines you fight by and commanding then in battle is fun. The story is heartwarming and the supporting cast is likeable. It makes for a solid monster catching JRPG and the turn based combat is honestly one of the better ones I've ever played through. For Monster Hunter fans at large I'd say it really captures the Monster Hunter style of gameplay really well despite being a completely different kind of game, game lets you use 3 weapon types and switch between them mid battle which is super convenient as well as your monsters. Getting stronger monsters and min maxing is addictive. Don't expect too much of a gripping story but it is very serviceable and the soundtrack is great.I've mainly played the game singleplayer only. From what I know you can co op through quests with friends but beware of the region restrictions making it so you can't play cross region online. Also co op is for non story quests only. Having figured that I only played singleplayer and, funnily enough the co op quests can be played with bots so I saw no real reason to engage in co op since the bot is always the same level as you and does a good job at fighting. A solid and very joyful turn based JRPG for Monster Hunter fans and those that are new to the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories was charming, but after how much I enjoyed Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate and how excited I was for the already announced Monster Hunter World, a spin-off limited to handheld devices just didn't appeal to me. I even bought the game on 3DS and mobile to support the franchise, but could never actually work up the will to play. Fortunately Capcom decided to give the series another chance on much better hardware, and because of this I not only got to enjoy Monster Hunter Stories, I actually kind of regret not giving it a fair chance sooner.✪ The Rite of Channeling allows you to keep your favorite Monsties with you for as long as you'd like without ever worrying about them becoming obsolete.✪ The tale it tells makes it a great example of family friendly entertainment that doesn't focus too much on the kids in the room.✪ Monster Hunter Stories 2 has no difficulty scaling, but it still does a great job making me feel as if my time going above and beyond was well-spent.✪ It's carried by an excellent take on turn-based combat.✪ It does an excellent job translating just about everything that makes them special into a fantastic JRPG.✪ For those into the competitive side of things, you can host your own lobbies with overrides that ensure you and your opponent are balanced, which doubles as a nice way to counter anyone who didn't acquire their monsties, skills or levels legitimately.✪ Those interested in co-op have three different quest types to enjoy with a buddy, random, or AI.✪ There's a whole lot to do after the credits, properly called "Post-Game Content", and a  highlighting new activities to do in co-op and Monsties to collect for those itching for more content. ✘ Much like Monster Hunter World and Monster Hunter Rise, you'd better make darn sure you're satisfied with the way your character looks, because changing it is gonna cost you actual money again. ✘ Though you can change just about every keybind and the general feeling of mouse and keyboard was great, there are a few things that didn't make sense or could have been done better. • It's a shame this game has no kind of photo mode, because even in its most repetitious biomes, it is full of so many vibrant visuals and delightful characters that I'd love to run around taking pictures without the game's permanently fixated menu getting in the way. • You can sort your Monsties by Level, Rarity and when you Acquired them, but there's no way to organize your Monsties beyond these means.• Waiting for Monster Hunter Rise to release on PC became a much bigger struggle than I thought it would.Monster Hunter Stories 2 is among the most delightful games I've ever played. With so many ways to play, so much to do and even more on the way at no extra cost, not only do we have a new standard for turn-based RPGs, but what was already a fantastic franchise—which doubles as my favorite franchise—has become even better. It's a really good time to be a Monster Hunter fan.[𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗼]■ Post-Story Free Roam: Yes■ Chapter Select: No■ New Game+: No (at time of writing) ■ DLC: Yes; strictly cosmetic.■ Optional Content: Immense; side quests aplenty, with post-game content and even a post-game to the post-game. There's a whole lot to do beyond the main story.■ Update Frequency: Steady; Capcom is doing a decent job handling patches and fan feedback, with the Roadmap providing several incentives to return.■ Accessibility Options: None, from what I could gather in the Options via the Main Menu and in-game.■ Plan to 100%: Yes, but slowly because of how grindy Genes are.■ Replay Worthy : The story? Yes. The 100%? No chance.For more information and a much longer review, !

Prantic (my Pukei-Pukei) and I have been getting rid of the stragglers and letting the others escape.Log #181: Apparently, this migration wasn't just an attempt to regroup and survive... it was to increase their numbers. This shall prove more fruitful then I thought.Log #205: Barroth kill count was only 43 today, down from yesterday's 49. Either I'm getting rusty, or the population's thinning. Let's hope it's the latter.Log #220: Against my better judgement, Prantic convinced me to keep a Barroth egg we found in one of their dens. Perhaps making a bond with it when it hatches and convincing it to kill it's brethren will be more useful then simply making the mother of all omelets, Jack. As for Jack, if you somehow find this... good on you, you finally stopped drinking those so-called "electrolytes.")Log #256: Klepoth (the Barroth that hatched from the egg) has been incredibly helpful in finding Barroths in hiding. _childDocuments_.review: Aloha,This is my reivew for Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin, a JRPG that puts you in the role of a monster rider instead of a hunter unlike the other games in the series. You follow the story of the wings of ruin, where a terrible prophecy fortells doom to the world. The game delivers the standard JRPG tropes [friendship is power] and the usual play cycle [fight, get xp, level up, repeat] and you travel from one area to the next solving mysteries regarding the legendary wings of ruin.The Good: probably the best JRPG I've played in recent memory, colourful well crafted cell shaded graphics and fun environments, cool monster designs, a memorable cast of characters, wonderful orchestral music, the story while having some predictable plot points [see if you can spot Lysanderoth in the first hour of the game], it is a fun romp with great game play mechanics. Also, it should be a design document for making a good RPG, it has lots of quality of life improvements which will make the next JRPG I play seem antiquated [quick finish battles, teleport to checkpoints, fastmode, skip cut scenes, and more]. The Bad: the sidekick character is pretty annoying, but the game is designed for children, so I can see how they would have enjoyed him; that being said, despite being made for children, it doesn't feel like a kids game, except for the light tone, and I authentically enjoyed the game, despite it being far outside what I usually play [rogue-likes, dark souls, h-games].The Ugly: the Lysanderoth character reveal was only lacking a "I would have gotten away with it if it wasn't for you meddling kids!" line because I guessed it after he first appeared with his mask.The Last Word: this is one of the funnest and most comfy JRPG's I've played since Cyberdimension Neptunia; and after two years of pandemic, my life becoming an unrecognisable mess, this whimsical romp filled my heart with joy and gave much needed relief during one of the darkest winters of my life, and I hope you consider purchasing it, and hope you will enjoy it too.

_childDocuments_.review: Pokemon for Monster Hunter fans. Monsters from multiple generations on display along with weapons and armor. Combat is based around a rock-paper-scissors system with each monster specializing in a single type but with the ability to use multiple. Damage elements and affinities are also in the game adding an extra layer of strategy. The player has access to 6 weapons (SnS, GS, HH, Ham, Bow, GL) and skills to go with them to supplement their monster (monstie) in battle along with various staple items from Monster Hunter. The art style and story is not exactly breaking new ground but visually it is a vast improvement over its predecessor. If you enjoy Mon games and like Monster Hunter this game can be very enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: It is pretty good if you like creature collectors. It mainly works on a rock-paper-scissors basis with power/speed/technical attacks. You can pick which one you use but each monster has one that they heavily favour over the others. Most special attacks also work the same way.Monsters have 9 gene slots, which hold all their abilities, including all their attacks and passive bonuses. You can upgrade them by transferring a gene from one monster to another, deleting the one you're taking the genes from. This means that even if they start with different genes, you can just keep upgrading the same monster without having to replace it if you don't want to. The only non-gene differences are species-wide stats, finishers and overworld abilities.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is coming from the perspective of someone who has played all the mainline Monster Hunter games and also the first Monster Hunter Stories game both on the Nintendo 3DS and the mobile port. MH Stories 2 evokes a whole wide range of emotions that ultimately is an enjoyable experience. Well atleast after getting through the very slow start.Negatives first, this game has starts okay but then really drags in the snow region. Both storywise and gameplaywise, the snow region is the worst time I ever had playing through the game. I was considering dropping the game, but I somehow didn't. The snow region does not reflect the whole quality of the game as a whole and for newcomers, just hold on til the next region where the story and gameplay ramps up in quality.  Still on the negatives section, there is no value in exploring the world. The world you venture in ultimately is split into three types of places, which is the towns, the big wide regional map, and the sub-areas that connects the big maps. The big wide regional maps are the highlights and are very beautiful with its artstyle and elevation in heights. But ultimately its all just very generic that kinda doesn't look like a Monster Hunter world other than the monsters roaming in it. Sub-areas connecting the big region maps have repetitive designs that gets old very, very fast, and are also reused in monster dens that will make it even more repetitive and a chore to go through, ultimately feeling like going through the same maps over and over again.About the snow region being worse storywise and gameplaywise, this region have alot of sub-areas, or can be called dungeons, that are very bland and are needed to go through to progress the main story. Storywise, the narrative suddenly treats you like a toddler in the snow region. It's not just family friendly now, its a kids show all of a sudden. Lorewise, there are alot of inconsistencies with how the MH world works. There are alot of monsters roaming that don't belong there, like Tobi Kadachi and Barroth. This ultimately just gave me a bad time playing through the snow region.All of these negatives are mainly personal because I am a fan of open world games so I expected some semblances of reward in exploration. Also, admittedly, I am comparing MH Stories 2 world map and design to its predescessor, to me is very much superior and unique design. That's pretty much my very personal rant that I hope MH Stories 3 can avoid.With the negatives out of the way, I really love this game. Despite some missteps, this game is pretty much a very solid followup from MH Stories 1. Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a Turn Based RPG, monster collecting game where you collect monsters from the Monster Hunter franchise. A pretty great alternative if you never play a Pokemon game. Unlike the mainline MH games, the story takes center stage and gameplay is turn-based, unlike the mainline real time combat and gameplay focus.The story is okay and takes a more light-hearted tone but sometimes can get dark in places like the great old Pixar films. The story is also very simple and not a whole lot of twists and depth. Kinda like the usual mainline MH foray, monster goes bad, fight gets bad, but our friendship can beat it, letter A goes to the letter B. Very simple story that gets the job done. Ultimately I like MH Stories 1 more with more memorable characters. The characters in MH Stories 2 do feel like they are there just because they are there.Monster collecting is where the gameplay is at. Combat is played with turn-based where attacks are executed in a rock-papper-scissors kind of manner. Each monsters have a type and you can collect them by harvesting eggs from the dens. After hatching the eggs, you can assemble a six monster team called Monsties. This is pretty much the gameplay. I have a very enjoyable time assembling a team of the mainline flagships like Tigrex and Zinogre. Hell, Nergigante is in this game too.The combat is simple and can get repetitive if you memorise what type the monster is. For example, the Velocidrome is Speed Type, which is weak to Technical Types. That means Velocidrome will always use Speed Type attacks that can be countered by Technical Types. It ultimately boils down to how well you can memorise the monsters moveset since the monsters attacks can change depends on their state like raging or flying. I do think it is a bit of a downgrade from MH Stories 1's combat where its more unpredictable and monsters only mostly use their type attacks. MH Stories 2 omits the unpredictability aspect of MH Stories 1 and uses more AOE attacks or double attacks per turn in difficulty. For me, I much prefer MH Stories 1 unpredictability used for difficulty since that reflects some qualities of the mainline MH games.Other positives, the soundtrack is great. Hunting with NPCs are fun too. I finished the main campaign in 50 hours, and as per usual Monster Hunter tradition, the real game starts after beating the story. There's whole bunch of things unlocked after the main campaign, adding my playtime until 70 hours.Overall, an amazing Monster Hunter experience.4/5

_childDocuments_.review: This one's difficult. The game has improved in some aspects from the first one, but it also makes some baffling changes in others. This will mostly be a list of the changes I can remember, in the order I remember them. TL;DR: I had fun for the whole playthrough but I feel they didn't try their hardest to make the best game possible.1. They added two new weapon types, gunlance and bow, and made each weapon except the sword & shield have a bit of a gimmick in how they work. That's a good way of spicing it up a bit. 2. Most big monsters always have parts that you can break instead of that being limited to certain boss fights, and each part has separate weaknesses to the three weapon types (blunt, slash, pierce). This is also neat but it's always unclear what effect breaking a part has unless it makes the monster fall down or something.3. The buddies are neat but are often just straight better than you, especially near the beginning.4. The amount of time until the second speed type monstie is way too long. Like 15-20 hours in I think, it's been too long to remember fully.5. They removed the multiple patterns on eggs so that each monster has only one to worry about. This is fantastic, no more Dovan Volcano stupidity with basarios/gravios/brute tigrex all looking basically the same.6. They removed the battle pouch. I'm sorta mixed on this one. On the one hand we no longer have unnecessary status healers that we can't use in combat because we always have them, on the other we can now use 15 ancient potions in the same battle if we need to.7. Ena is more important for everything than you are. This is fine, in a vacuum, but in my opinion they didn't use the silent protagonist in a good way AT ALL. Navirou is literally just your mouth and I would've enjoyed it more if he wasn't there and the protagonist wasn't silent. 8. Several scenes are just animated awkwardly. Not the prerendered ones, the ones where they stand around talking. Movement in these are sometimes very mechanical.9. They, for some stupid reason, destroyed sorting in the quest log. You can ONLY sort them by difficulty, or put the ones ready to turn in first. There is no way to set the active-but-not-done quests in front so you will have to search through the entire list if there's one you've missed somewhere.10. Speaking of quests, the named monsters are stupid hard. I enjoy a challenge but if the optional boss I'm expected to take on ONESHOTS me even when I win a Head-to-Head we have got a problem.11. The eggs with rare genes now not only smell more to Navirou but also shine when you pick them up, letting you know much more quickly if it's worth keeping.12. I played through Stories again last year, and I can confidently say that it was A LOT more challenging. I actually lost to several bosses in that one. The buddies and removal of the battle pouch just destroy any sense of challenge unless you try to limit yourself.13. SPOILERS: The ending is basically a rehash of the first one. They could've at least TRY to make something new. SPOILERSOverall, decent game. I never felt bored during my playthrough at least, but it could've been MUCH better.What I wish they'd done is to make Kyle and Ena the playable protagonists, maybe have Kyle be unlocked as an extra thing after you finish the main story and have them both play differently (rider/hunter after all) and their storylines be different (they're on opposing ends of a conflict for a large chunk of the game after all).

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a monster collecting game that actually had effort put into it then this game is for you.Monster Hunter Stories 2 takes aspects from the main games and turns it into a turn-based RPG and mostly succeeds in this. Unlike Pokémon, battles aren't braindead and actually challenge you. You have quite a lot of options in battle and the game does a good job easing you into this. My main issue in the gameplay is more in the endgame department where I sometimes just get 1-shotted by normal attacks by the hardest monsters, even at level 90. While it is possible to prevent this, it is a bit too punishing for getting hit once.The story of the game is fine, nothing too noteworthy but not bad. The pacing around the 2nd and 3rd town isn't great though, the 3rd town honestly bored me a bit 'cus it really didn't add anything to the story for so long. AT LEAST unlike Pokémon, if you don't care about the story or do a repeated playthrough, you can actually skip cutscenes with a button. I'm very surprised the highest-grossing media franchise can't even make a skip button after 25 years.While the music can be nice, the lack of overworld music really hurts exploration as it's mostly just silence. I also wish you could choose your battle theme as hearing the same big monster theme in co-op quests gets a bit tiring. This is probably the only time I'm gonna give Pokémon a point as those games always have awesome music.I'm not a graphics guy but I really like this game's art style. Seeing the monsters in a more stylized art style is pretty charming to me and I would love a mainline game in this art style. Also high quality animations, this game has them. Fire breath attacks actually come out of the mouth and not thin air.In conclusion, pretty good game and I recommend it to RPG fans, even if you don't play the normal MH games.

_childDocuments_.review: MHST2 takes the great foundation laid down by the 3DS title Monster Hunter Stories and builds upon it. The graphics have been massively updated and while the cell-shading, colorful palettes stuck around, the character, armor, and monster designs are a little less cutesy and closer to the main series in proportion, although still with significantly less detail. This is a massive boon to the game as the design work of Monster Hunter has always been one of its (or, in my opinion, *the*) best assets to bring it above the competition.        The turn-based combat in this game uses the attack patterns in the Monster Hunter franchise as its inspiration to prevent it from becoming too predictable and dull. While the predecessor had an element of strict memorization and even randomness to spice up combat and make it challenging, this game tries to broadcast each set of moves an enemy will make clearly which looses a lot of the difficulty and can make combat a bit boring for skilled players. I don't mind this as I enjoy turn-based monster taming games primarily as a lower-effort engagement brightened by strong creature designs and longer-term goals, which MHST2 is perfect for, but if your main complaint about monster taming games is that few are as high engagement and challenging as Shin Megami Tensei you're looking in the wrong place.       Fans of franchises like Digimon, Pokemon, or Yokai-Watch will find that the beautiful and varied monsters and their interesting and unique animations, the wide and varied selection of armors and weaponry, and easier gameplay feeds their needs very well. In fact, if your main gripe about those games is that you can't explore the colorful and interesting worlds flying on the back of a Birdramon or leaping up cliffs on a Gogoat, this is exactly the game for that itch. Pokemon Let's Go Pikachu and Eevee took a lot of inspiration from the first game in this series to implement their own follow/ride mechanics and this still stands as the strongest representation of that.  If you love games that let you feel like you can really get attatched to your mounts or pets, this is for you.TL;DR breakdownGameplay - CasualCompletionist suitability - A lot of RNG grind for eggs, will be time consumingGraphics - Beautiful and consistent but not particularly resource intensiveStory - Nothing special, but cute enoughMusic - FantasticReplayablility - High

The controls are decent enough given this was ported from switch, and the player handbook in game still has the switch buttons in the images, but the controls are easy enough to get, and after about 2 hours of playing you won't even have to think about them anymore.Pros: Fun and challenging enough combat systemlots of monstersvaried scenerybeautiful graphics and  landscapesCons:This game is fully voice acted, and I'll be damned if navirou doesn't make me want to hurl him off of a cliff after about three conversations.Things that could be cons or pros, based on your personal preferencesThe plot is exceedingly japanese. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game for anybody that enjoys monster collection games or even just turn-based RPGs in general. There's a lot of content, good enemy variety, and a large selection of monsters. The mechanics are simple enough that a kid could probably pick it up, but there is still some depth to engage with in predicting enemy behavior and memorizing what monsters do, much like the mainline games. The game does a good job of translating mechanics from the mainline Monster Hunter games into a new format, so fans of the series will have fun with that. In an era where Pokemon is frequently criticized for being phoned-in, this game shows love, care, and respect for the genre and series. If you've ever wanted to ride around on your monsters or fight alongside them in battles, this game's the chance to do it.Beyond gameplay, the music is good, the story is fun, and the visuals are nice, especially if you're fond of cute baby monsters. The controls for keyboard take some fiddling to get comfortable, but they can be set up so they're not too clunky and the game has controller support.The game is clearly made for kids, but, like all good children's media, it can still be enjoyed by adults. So long as you like cheesy cat puns and the fact that they're called 'monsties'. Even the annoying sidekick critter grows on you.

_childDocuments_.review: In most ways, this is an improvement over Pokemon. The monster design is better, combat is more interesting, and customizing monsters is more intuitive and fun. One of the main ways Monster Hunter Stories 2 falls short is in its length. You probably won't play it much longer than it takes to complete the main story, and obtain your former team in high rank. The last bit feels like an unnecessary grind. The game could really use an expansion that adds a few more areas and activities. So it might be worth waiting for a sale.The main story is aimed at younger teenagers, at most. So adults will find the dialogue a bit grating with its childishness. Otherwise, the voice acting is good. Combat is complex with having to factor in elemental weaknesses, physical damage type, attack technique, and syncing up attacks with your "monstie" in order to be most effective. Each weapon type has different combos and strategies. Armor is equipped as a set, and each set has a unique selection of skills that change how effective various combat strategies are. Armor and weapons can then be upgraded, in order to keep using them, or to maximize their effectiveness in the late game. Monsters can have several skills equipped, but mostly act on their own. Players may spend kinship points to direct them to use specific attacks. Outside of combat, monsters can help the player with mobility, utility, and detection skills.Overall, this is a surprisingly deep monster battler, but it could be fleshed out to make it a top-notch game.

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom did a good job on this game, I play Monster Hunter games, and occasionally RPGs like this, and in my opinion Stories 2 is a better turn-based RPG game than Monster Hunter Rise is a Monster Hunter game.Some people draw similarities between this and Pokemon, I can't comment because I don't play Pokemon, but I think it's more like Dragon Quest meets Monster Hunter.  I say that because you actually fight with your main character in this, and in some of the Dragon Quest games you could recruit and use monsters in combat as regular party members (5 for example).  Pokemon is also a kid's game that you can faceroll I'm told, but this game has a semblance of a challenge to it, so there's a lot of strategy involved in the combat in this.  You got rock/paper/scissors with 3 types of attacks, you got double attacks that cancel a monster's attack if you use rock/paper/scissors correctly, you got monsters with multiple states where they change their attack types, you got element and status vulnerabilities, a robust selection of items you can use in combat to counter specific monster attacks, like flash bombs on fliers, and sonic bombs on stuff that burrows into the ground, healing items, buffing items, items to inflict status effects (including traps).  The monster genes (passive buffs and attacks) can be fully customized once you reach a certain point in the game, so there's builds for monsters and player characters.  So it's a pretty robust selection of options you got here, and you'll need to use them wisely.  Don't buy this for the multiplayer, I can tell you straight up it's garbo.  Buy this as a single player RPG game, and forget that multiplayer exists.  If you liked Dragon Quest XI, you'll probably like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic turn based monster battler! Might be best in the genre-interesting and engaging battle system (you'd never get tired of it since you can speed battles up to times 3 and skip battles you are engaged in if you are higher level than the enemies)-NO GRIND (other than skipping battles, exp share is on and there's a system that allows you to passively level a group of monsters up; you can also find monster with better stats easier as the game will indicate it to you)-extremely malleable monsters (can basically give a Ratata Charizard moves)-cool monsters, armor and weapons (as expected from Monster Hunter)-cool landscapes (open areas you can fly in on your favorite monster)-aesthetically pleasing graphics (great color pallette at all times, very dynamic animations)-stand-alone game (despite its title, you do not need to play the first game to enjoy this one)RAMBLE BELOWTL;DR 80% perfect Pokemon gameNitpicks I have with the game:-cut features from the original (mini games, even more customization with the monsters via changing their colors up to 6 variantions, monster saddles changing colors according to bingos, character specific side quests that gives them more depth, easier to use side quest tracker)-no true relation to the first game (story doesn't follow up the previous; with all the returning characters and a similar story it's basically a reboot, would of worked better that way) -characters are nolonger endearing nor memorable (for example the Pikachu of the series went from dorky and lovable in the original to simply obnoxious)-not every large monster is ridable (cannot hip check my enemies :c)-terrible story in a game with "Stories" in the title (the story is stereotypical and boring; where the first at least kept you hooked with its characters, this game just drags on with you feeling inferior as no one would shut up about someone better than you)-isn't entirely polished (UI at the stables, the PC of this game, has very basic designs and functions compared to the first game, missing ability to skip pages with 1 click for example, nor does your cursor and button prompts have customized overlay unlike other PC Monster Hunter games, where the first game has monster special attack animations match the area you are in this game doesn't, some cut scenes are slideshows)Wishful thinking for probably unrealistic things that can be added in the next entry:-selection of starters (Ratha has run his course being the default for these 2 titles; wished he would turn into a Silver Rathalos in the end of the first game)-return of the color changing system (more personalized monsters)-monsters are born according to their ecology  (e.g. Great Jaggi would be born as a Jaggi or at least without scars)-add a "evolution system" (putting subspecies and deviants in the same tree; e.g. Dreadqueen Rathian needs a regular Rathian use the default poison move a number of times; Great Jaggi needs to defeat a number of Jaggis to "grow up"; giving a Yian Kut-Ku the Rathian "poison tail gene" yields a Yian Garuga)-a better story (please either make it completely seperated to everything else to attract more new comers or make it coherently related to the previous, at least add a Red in Pokemon Gold thing; maybe even have multiple endings so players actually have a choice in the story)-full multiplayer  (can play the story in multiplayer)-monster interaction minigames (e.g. Pokemon Amie; the "Pet" ability is a nice touch already though)-monster dress up (very small things like decorating the saddle, give the monsters a small head dress like a bow, could just be within a minigame)-story boss monster loot (equipment made from them)-ridable version of previous final bosses (just something cool to have)In any case still highly recommend anyone who likes turn based RPG and Pokemon games!!

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you're a monster hunter and JRPG fan this is one of the best games everStory: 6.5/10Nothing spectacular here, the story is serviceable enough but there's nothing that really made it stand out too much, with it being a kid's game and all. It goes more or less the way you would expect a game like this to go. It actually sort of feels like a rehash of the first game, and if you did not play the first one you might be a little bit confused on who some of the later characters introduced are. Not too big of a worry though as it has minimal impact on the actual story of the game itselfGraphics: 9/10It's no Monster Hunter World, but the graphics fit the game quite nicely and every monster looks more or less the same as their counterpart in the mainline games (with a bit of differences here and there - I don't remember Azure Rathalos being this bright blue)Animations are superbly done - each monster follows the exact same animations as they would in the mainline game for idle / attacking animations and moreKinship skills are also a big plus and a joy to look at just for the sheer spectacle of being anything between a super cheesy ham attack to launching what is essentially a nuke at your opponent and possibly leaving a crater where they standMusic: 9/10The BGMs are all amazingly done, you can hear the actual monster's theme mixed into the boss battle theme during their boss intro cutscenes, each area has day / night music that plays when you first enter them and it is, in general, very fitting and a joy to listen toGameplay: 9.5/10Rock, paper, scissors with a few twists here and there, each monster you fight have fixed patterns they follow and it's up to you the player to figure it out and play around them. This is emphasized to the extreme when it comes to the hard mode bosses which more or less instantly or heavily punish you if you don't know how to counter their patterns properly to cancel their attacks every round. Surprisingly addicting even in the post game.Certain monster mechanics from the mainline series remain in the game as well, such as monsters falling over when you break their legs or other specific parts, or even them toppling themselves over if certain parts are broken upon performing certain attacks.My only gripe is that the post game more or less dictates that you MUST play online / co-op rooms in order to find the end game monsties, as the other option of trying to spawn a super rare high rank monster den is extremely tedious and can take hours to pay offFinal Score: 34/40Story may not be anything special and drags the game down a little, but everything else makes up for it and creates what is in essence a very enjoyable game, particularly for monster hunter fans.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying the game but I don't think I could recommend it to anyone. I literally can't use the monsters I want because I'm stuck balancing types and "movement abilities" and only have so many slots. Velocidrome is the only damn thing that has jump until mid-late game and it's replaced with just another one of the great jaggi types. If I want my beefy tigrex, I can't make room for the nercylla I want because they both have climb. It's so stupid, my team is full of monsters I don't care about. I thought it would all be fixed when I unlocked fly but it's not even usable once you enter a dungeon area. It's the exact same with the weapons. If I use hammer, I can't have hunting horn because I have to cover the three damage types. And each weapon only does one damage type it's assigned. You know what's cool about great sword in the actual monster hunter games? It can do slash AND BLUNT damage depending on what combos you use. You even learn the charge rush maneuver WHICH IS A BLUNT ATTACK. But in this game it still does slash despite that. And then since each individual part has different weapon type resistances that also change depending on what state the monster is in, you gotta constantly swap what weapon your using. It would be a cool system honestly if it didn't completely gimp weapons that rely on stockpiling to use their abilities. The gunlance generally gets one bullet loaded with each attack, two on a won head-to-head I think. But you know what happens by the time I get it fully charged for it's ultimate ability? The part breaks or the monster becomes enraged or what have you and now I have to switch weapons or do no damage. That sucks.And to top it off, a lot of the cooler monsters, you can't actually have on your team for what seems like no real reason. I can have Nercylla (bug) but not Seltas or Seltas Queen (also bugs). I can have Popo or Anklyo (trash mob) but I can't have Hermitaur (cool crab).The gameplay is pretty much the same as the first game. Rock-paper-scissors with memorization. The buddy system is cool, there are more monsties, still forced to have Rathalos in your party, etc. The UI and the game as a whole feels extremely un-polished. There aren't simple things like being able to sort your quests by ONES YOU HAVEN'T ALREADY COMPLETED. Why would I want to even look at un-repeatable quests I've finished? Much less have them randomly mixed together with the ones I'm actively tracking. The quick travel map is just kind of a list of names without any indicator of where exactly they take you. The villages aren't marked with anything different to indicate that they are villages. You can't mark your own map for things to come back to or view areas you aren't in to figure out where you want to go. The villages are designed to make it take as long as possible to get to everything. But by far, the most infuriating thing in this entire game is Navirou. There are no options to tell him to shut the heck up and every single damn time he pops up dialogue, you have to click a button to dismiss it. Which of course leads to stuff like not picking up items because dismissing the dialogue ate your button click as you were walking by. Not getting back on your monstie to run away in time. Not being able to click the catstand to activate it as you walk by because FOR SOME GOD FORSAKEN REASON, HE WAITS UNTIL YOU ARE ALREADY ON TOP OF IT TO TELL YOU IT'S NEARBY. Not to mention EVERYTHING HE SAYS IS INSANELY BASIC AND UNHELPFUL. "The monster is asleep! Here's your chance!"I CAN SEE IT. THERE ARE GIANT BUBBLES COMING OUT ITS NOSE AND EVERYTHING."There's a catstand nearby"YES AND I MISSED IT THANKS TO YOU, STUPID. "I think you've collected all the bottle caps buddy"Yeah that's great, I'm currently next to an egg running from a monster and you've prevented me from picking it up and now I'm stuck in a fight thanks.And he repeats all of this dialogue, every. single. time. without fail. I hate him, I wish he would die.*ahem* So to summarize, the game is fun and a good addition to the monster hunter franchise generally but it misses the mark on creature collecting, gameplay, quality/polish and is just generally annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has never played turn based games aside from Pokemon, I've found this game to be pleasantly enjoyable so far. When I started the trial I thought to myself that this wouldn't be a game for me, but pushed through to give it a proper shot. Now the trial itself is actually enjoyable, however it doesn't even scratch the surface of what all you can do. I am currently in post game play, so without giving spoilers I can say the story is about the same as any other Monster Hunter game. However, it still sucked me in and gave me chills at some points due to being so invested.Pros:- Graphics are perfect for my preference, I love the cartoony aspect.- Open world is one of the best features of the game, the exploration is just enough to make the grind worth it.- The fight/gear mechanic is over-all well balanced.- The game has a lot of content to play through, even after the story.Cons:- The multiplayer system wasn't what I expected it to be, you're only allowed to do certain missions with your friend. And even those missions are practically limited till you complete the story. Which by that point you've already invested practically 30hrs into the game if you played through without rushing. Post game would have been better if they implemented co-op with a friend for the Lair at least, given the fact you can choose to take an NPC. But why take an NPC when you can play with friends?- I turned on japanese audio because I was tired of hearing the word monstie ( why did you choose this term Capcom ).- It is a grindy game if you are looking to create perfect monsters, it's not for everyone. So be aware that you're in for a RNG grind.The game is brand new, and there's going to be plenty of updates to the game to make it even more inviting. That being said I would recommend this game to anyone. Highly suggest trying out the demo, you're basically getting 8hrs of gameplay for free that transfers over! I personally would recommend PC over Switch, I played the demo on both and over all the PC handles far better.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a cat in this game called Navirou...dude is a whole trip. Everything he does is hilarious. All his scenes make me laugh, heck I smile just seeing his face on-screen lmao. He has some of the funniest run scenes ever, rivaling run scenes of legends such as Tom Cruise and Steven Seagal. The game itself is alright, but he makes everything better by a long shot. He's one of the main reasons I kept booting this game back up, cuz it has its share of problems, but my boy Navirou made it bearable. I'll get into some of the issues below:- There's a game breaking bug regarding multiplayer, you'll see several people explaining what it is in other reviews- The game randomly bugs out of full screen mode into windowed mode & becomes choppy & you need to reboot the game to fix it. It's extremely annoying and shocking knowing Capcom's record for solid PC ports.- The battle system was not well thought out. The flow of battle is ridiculously slow, and the slightest attacks have the biggest, coolest animations. It's amazing at first but gets very old, very quickly. They tried to help by letting you speed up battles by X3 speed but honestly, that doesn't help. You can beat far weaker enemies by pressing a single button to end the fight quickly, but in the grand scheme of things it doesn't help either. Battles become a BORING slog through the mud after some time, and the game is long. If they could have figured out a way to make battles flow better it'd be perfect. The way it is now, you can tell they knew how bad it was with all these patchwork features like speed ups that come after the fact.In the end I wouldn't pay full price for this game. At $19.99 it's pretty solid if you like JRPGS, Monster Breeding, or Monster Hunter. _childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a great sequel and a great game on it's own. Everybody compares the gameplay to Pokemon, and that's probably the best comparison i can think of. So, the game has you playing as a "Rider," and as a Rider, you form bonds with monsters as opposed to slaying them. Near the beginning, you are given a Rathalos egg, and this Rathalos is known as Razewing Ratha; the Wings of Ruin. Ratha is a permanent party member for the entire story and then you can switch him out of your party in post game. So the combat is not too complex, and not too simple, the main battle mechanic is sort of a "rock, paper, scissors" game; you have Power Attacks which are colored red, Technical Attacks which are colored green, and Speed Attacks which are colored blue. Now to get the advantage, Red Power Attacks beat Green Technical Attacks, Green Technical Attacks beat Blue Speed Attacks, and Blue Speed Attacks beat Red Power Attacks. Now, when attacking monsters, most monsters have different body parts that you can target, and each body part may resist the 3 different types of weapons, Slash, Pierce, and Blunt. at the end of the day, Monster Hunter Stories 2; Wings of Ruin is a great game for fans who already have knowledge of the Monster Hunter universe, and great to help players who don't know Monster Hunter get some knowledge about the universe.

_childDocuments_.review: MHS2 is a great addition to a wonderful series of games. It may not attract the same audience as Monster Hunter: World did, but it’s still a great game on its own. If you can look past the childish story and characters, subpar graphics and lack of returning monsters, you’ll still have lots of fun here. As others have said, Pokémon can take some notes here, this game makes taking eggs and hatching them fun, almost addicting. The combat system is your typical turn-based combat but with a rock, paper scissor-esque system. I liked it but I can see why others prefer combat in games like Ni No Kuni or the other monster hunter games. In combat you can switch out your weapons and your “monsties” to gain an edge on your opponent or break objects the opposing enemy is holding. The exploration is also a little less exciting than World and very typical of other JRPG’s. Exploring caves, taking down the monster, then it runs away to a cave where you can go in and kill them for good or take their eggs whilst they sleep.Gathering ingredients makes a comeback as well. You can create potions, bring items to a smithy to make weapons and armour or bring Bottle Caps to a felyne to get special weapons, armour and upgrades that increase the amount of monsties you can hold at one time in your farm. I don’t recommend this game to everyone but it you enjoy Ni No Kuni mixed with Pokémon and Monster Hunter all rolled into one, you’ll get some good fun out of this!

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up as I have an interest in Monster Hunter, and am a fan of creature collectors, and having put 140 hours into this game I can easily say it's one of my favourite games. The story is ok, with some cool/emotional moments, and the characters are decent, despite getting a lot of flak I actually quite like Navirou. The start is a little slow and the initial pool of available monsters is small, but it eventually speeds up quite a lot.The game plays similarly to other creature collectors, you travel the world conscripting the local wildlife into your merry band and command them to destroy your enemies, but rather than defeating them in battle and then capturing them, you instead channel your inner loot goblin and steal the eggs right out of the nest, have the newborn imprint on you, and then have dragon junior fight alongside you, and you can ride them as mounts. There are over a hundred different monsters to collect, and many of them have useful abilities when exploring the world, like breaking boulders, leaping across chasms, turning invisible to sneak past unwanted fights etc.Once you and your monsters reach a high enough level, most fights in that area become significantly faster as you get the option to instantly win, which makes leveling up new monsters much faster. The game eventually gives you access to special missions you can send inactive monsters on so they still gain experience and level up when not in your party, so you can do less grinding with them.All monsters have 9 geneslots, which is where their abilities, both passive and active, can be found, and partway through the game you gain the ability to take genes from monsters and put them in other ones, enabling you to customise and tailor your party exactly the way you want, so you can specialise certain monsters for particular fights etc, and its quite fun trying to come up with your own builds and test them out.Combat in this game is a mix of both Monster Hunter and the typical creature collector turn based gameplay. Both you and your monsters fight, with your monsters having a selection of moves pokemon style, whereas you craft and wield multiple weapon types, from the sword and shield, bows, axes etc, and your moveset changes depending on what you have equipped during that battle. You can have 3 weapons equipped at a time, and can switch between them during a fight, you also have access to various traps, sonic and flash bombs, barrel bombs, paintballs etc.Monsters have both elemental and weapon type weaknesses, and moves both yours and monsters, have one of 3 types: Power, Speed, and Technical, which mostly comes into play during head to head fights during a battle. Power beats Technical, Technical beats Speed, Speed beats Power, so taking advantage of this, in addition to elemental and weapon weaknesses, is important for winning fights. Winning head to heads, using certain moves etc, fill up a special kinship gauge. Once this is full, you get the option to ride your monster, restoring health and enabling you to use a special kinship move which plays a special cutscene and does a lot of damage.Once you beat the main story there is a considerable amount of post story content, such as new quests, new monster variations, and a new zone called the Elders Lair, which is where you will find some of the toughest fights in the game.I cannot say anything about the multiplayer, coop or PvP, as I don't have much interest in those, but if you are a fan of Monster Hunter or creature collectors/turn based combat games in general, or looking to get into them, I highly recommend this game, it's a ton of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I am someone who adores the Monster Hunter setting, but is downright terrible playing any of the mainline games, so Stories was always an interesting game to me. My friend brought it up again recently and showed it to me, so I took a proper try; a week or so later I played barely anything else, and finished its main story.It's a very charming and easy to get into RPG, with a more traditional party and turn-based combat system, except it adds the easy to grasp rock-paper-scissors mechanic to vary it up, and enough wiggle room for you to get used to it thoroughly. You can add a ton of Monsters to your roster, finetune their abilities and skills, and kit yourself out the same way as you always did; crafting your gear from monster materials. Side missions are present to give you things to do, but the general gameplay loop of going out, fighting monsters, and clearing out minidungeons is kept fresh for a long time due to all the variety.Storywise it is nothing out of the ordinary - a pleasant, simple, but endearing tale about companionship and growing as a person.You got arenas, you got multiplayer, you got the real hard-hitting hunts later on that the franchise's always kept around.It was a game well-worth getting, and I am still having a lot of fun with it. If you like Monster Hunter, Pokémon-like monster collecting games and the turn-based RPG gameplay that comes with it, you'll love this - I say this as someone who only really likes the first of those three, and is having a blast with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very satisfied with this adorable roller coaster. A true delight for children, adults, and Monster Hunter fans.It started off not being the sort of turn based rpg I think I would get used to, but it quickly began to grow on me and I ended up getting obsess with it. I'll try to articulate why i've enjoyed this.First off, you start off as a young teen of your creation (Male or Female - For my playthrough I chose Female), and you are a Rider of your tropical tribal village called Mahana, on a small island. You're the grandchild of a legendary rider called Red, who has recently passed. His dragon Guardian Ratha makes residence there, and a mysterious girl has met in secret with him while being persued, and Ratha grants this girl an egg. However, things are not as they seem. A strange red light is driving all these dragons to somewhere unknown, and it's making all the monsters overly aggressive. And once you become a rider? It's your job to help explore these lights and stop whatever is the cause of it. It's only a simple summary as it's not an especially clever story, but it's still fun to go through. Let's get to the main meal of this then, shall we? No, it's not oven ready.Now combat works revolves around a Rock Paper Scissors style. You get 3 main attack types: Power, Speed, and Technical. While you can still attack however you like, you need to choose correctly in order to win a head-to-head clash with your opponent, to deal high damage and take less.Power beats Technical; Technical beats Speed; Speed beats PowerYour monster (referred to as a monstie), if not directly told to used certain skills, will attack at their own discretion. Each monster has their own specified attack type (For example, Speed), however they will still used different ones regardless of their main type. You can have 5 (later 6) accompany you at one time. Each has a different attack type, element, and weakness. You get to switch out a monster once per turn, should the monster you're fighting have an attack type yours has a disadvantage to. You can kind of see the similarities to an extent with Pokemon can't you?  You also have 3 weapon types. You have slashes, pierces, and crushes (basically hammers, bows, and swords) - All big monsters will have different parts you can attack seperately, and breaking them will give you more materials from said monster. These parts are all weak to a different weapon type, so you should be ready to swap out your weapons during combat to maximize damage on these parts, as breaking parts will have the additional benefit of weakening the monster's capabilities.Monsties will also have unique interactions with the big hunchos depending on their traits. You have your charge clashes by default (which involves mashing the space bar. Sorry pal...), but if it's flying monsters they can have an Air Showdown (alternate Q/E), and finally if they both have a elemental breath attack, those will clash (circle strafe your arrow keys, son!).You also have several other factors here. You have a standard health system, but you also have hearts. This is jointly shared between you and your monsite: If one of you reaches 0 HP, a heart is consumed and they are restored to full. You essentially have 3 lives in any given combat, and you will be sent back to the closest town should you, or your ally, lose all 3 hearts in a fight. Next is your Kinship gauge. This is a circle that will fill up overtime during battle, and is how you and your monstie will use skills. You, like hearts, will jointly share this pool, and not both of you will be able to use a skill on occasion due to not have enough points for the task. And speaking of joining, it also applies to attacking: When an ally, or you, is the target of a head to head, and one of your monsites (or your companion's) also targets that monster with the same attack type it's weak to, you will conduct a duel attack which will deal much more damage to the target than normal. You also have unique Kinship Skills to use which are mega flashy attacks (and the double attack mentioned earlier will also apply to these as well, though it will only be unique with specific combinations). Outside of combat you've got open areas to roam (areas can be inaccessible until you have certain monsties in your party, who have unique traversal traits,, such as climbing vines), and in these you'll have monsters, dens, and materials and items scattered everywhere. Next, you have settlements that act as hubs where you can pick up quests from the questboard and npcs, buy/sell items and upgrade and forge armour and weapons. You also get a house in each of these to save and customize the look of yourself and the outfits you and your companions wear. Simple, and gets the job done. Maybe there's something hiding there? I dunno, but you also have a shady felyne (the bipedal cat creatures in the series) selling you equipment in exchange for bottle caps. Har har har, I know. Please leave your Fallout jokes at my desk.Now, let's finish with a brief summarry Monster Dens. Dens are where you'll find monster eggs waiting for you (and mostly, other monsters to fight as well, usually with a sleeping one in the nest area). Though, I will mention that this also means touching on the one MAJOR criticism with the game: You WILL see den layouts repeat (A LOT) due to the nature of the game. I won't hold this too much against the game as they are hand-crafted and no procedural, but you will also see this in the actual areas. Like, the dens I get, but unique zones? The only difference in these areas are the monsters you find there. Limitations for the game don't really matter when it can be labelled lazy that you recycle your Rare Monster Den maps to use for later game areas. It won't be as egregious as i'm making it out, but I definitely remember being at places with the same look as Dens.-----But this is mostly a nitpick and I do have others (including the lack of unique combos for Duel Kinship Skils) that mean nothing in the grand scheme of things. This is an adorable, engaging, Pokemon-like Roleplaying Game that's kept my interest far longer than I ever expected. Well worth the money and then some, and will be a fun time killer as an adult or child. ^.^

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a sequel to the first game by a similar name, and a good iteration on it at that. However, the chances are if you're looking at this game, you probably didn't play the first, so I'll keep this review focused on the game by its own merit.1. You do not need to have played the first Stories to be able to play this game. That said, if you have played the first, you'll see some familiar faces in this game. (And to be fair, it might... make you a little bit angry.)2. Similar to Pokemon, this game is easily accessible and has a low skill floor, but has a higher skill ceiling and a lot of room for customisation and optimisation. (And, unlike Pokemon, you probably won't need to waste hours of your life trying to breed for perfect IVs and special moves just for one single creature.)3. If you're familiar with typical cartoon stories or anime/manga, the story isn't particularly mind-blowing in any regard. It's fairly average at best; good enough to follow along, but not really enough to get you on the edge of your seat.The basic gameplay of Stories involves combat that focuses on a Rock/Paper/Scissors system - or in this case, Power/Speed/Tech. All monsters in the game have a preference for the type of move they like to use, and this preference might change as the battle goes on and the monster becomes enraged, or maybe charges itself up with a special move. The basic goal of the game as you progress is to learn these monsters' different preferences, and then counter them with the corresponding correct type. So, if you're fighting a Power monster, you'll want to use Speed moves.From there the game builds on this system outwards: you can have three weapons equipped at a time, and can swap between those weapons once . There are six weapons in the game, two of which that deal Slash damage, two that deal Pierce, and two that deal Blunt. Like in the mainline game, different monster parts are weak to different kinds of damage, and so the game encourages you to make use of the once-per-turn weapon swap to switch to a strong weapon to break a part off a monster. Similarly, monsters have a variety of elemental defences, in this game all streamlined so that they are resistant to one, and then particularly weak to another. (So, for example, the titular Rathalos of the game is more resistant to Fire, but is weak to Lightning.) Weapons can also deal elemental damage, meaning that you can truly capitalise on monster weaknesses by using the right type of weapon with the right type of element to deal large damage each turn.Throughout all the game, you'll also be playing together alongside your AI monsters, known as Monsties. There are over 100 to choose from, some of them being variants of others, and many all have a unique gene of their own while also potentially carrying several "cross species" genes. The goal is to go out and raid Monster Dens to get eggs, hatch these eggs, and then slowly build up monsters with good gene boards - aiming to align their elemental genes or their move type genes in a row or column of three within the 3x3 gene board to get bingo bonuses. Bingo bonuses will ultimately dictate the strength of your monster, as they can increase the power of an element or a specific type of move (power/speed/tech) by 10% each per the first two bonuses, and then an extra 5% for every bonus after.And... that's it! The game takes a very simple idea, like rock/paper/scissors, and then rather masterfully elaborates on that idea to create a game around it while interweaving more familiar aspects of the mainline Monster Hunter games. The core game isn't particularly challenging, but the post-game challenges in the Elder's Lair can require incredibly specific strategies if you want to beat them. The game is easy to start playing, but offers a lot for those who also want to try and be more optimised in their builds, and unlike similar games such as Pokemon, Stories 2 is respectful of your time and doesn't require hours upon hours of monster breeding just to get decent base stats. (Bingo bonuses make the initial base stats generally irrelevant unless you're looking to be as optimised as physically possible.)• Excellent gameplay that's gotten me to sink in 120+ hours on the Switch and nearly 50+ hours on PC.• Beautiful graphics that, when you think about it, put Sword and Shield to absolute shame.• Great soundtrack with some real bops, though sadly a lot of the overworld doesn't have a soundtrack and I... don't know why. It's actually a huge shame.• Easy to learn combat with a lot of potential for customising builds and monsters, where I've never found grinding for monsters or genes to be unreasonable.• Huge variety of monsters to ride around on and be your friend! That said, the movement skills in this game are a holdover from the first, and kind of a disappointment. The game should really allow you to teach monsters certain viable movement skills that are, within reason, things they could learn to do. As it stands, movement skills can leave you feeling hamstrung on what monsters to take to certain areas, which is a real negative.• The base vanilla game was honestly not too challenging for me even on my first playthrough, outside of a couple of snags. Replaying the base game my second time around was even easier. Thankfully, post-game content is challenging and there's many hours of it to enjoy, much of it that will really push you and your Monsties to the test.

_childDocuments_.review: is the quintessential "Creature Collection" game available to the contemporary PC audience, and arguably the best in the genre to arrive upon any platform since  Best of all, familiarity with the mainline  series is by no means required to jump in here. sees you take on the role of a young Rider who teams up with "Monsties" from Capcom's   series to... fight other Monsters. Despite the nauseatingly cloying name for these friendly creatures, the engaging gameplay, combat and anime artstyle really help lift what could have been just another "turn-based JRPG" to something more, something Gamefreak's Pokémon games should start taking note of.Combat plays out like your standard creature-battling game. Rock-Paper-Scissors move types, elemental damage types and status effects like Poison and Paralysis are all thrown into the mix; in general the higher numbers and levels win. The major draw is the use of the  roster to include iconic and over the top Kinship attacks that are a spectacle to behold, as well as detailed weapons and armour sets for your Rider to wear as in the mainline series.Each monster is unique and worth going out of your way to acquire, even if the "best in slot" choices do point you towards the series'  as you reach the endgame.True to form, Capcom have a roadmap to include new (forgive me) "Monsties" every month or so, and new co-op and solo content. This is not a game you dump 50 hours in and never think of again, as a healthy competitive multiplayer base and the aformentioned updates aim to keep  relevant for at least the rest of 2021.Unlike others within the genre, there is a true endgame here and a deep and detailed gene system with which you can raise your perfect monstrosity or chase the current meta. Of my 77 hours at the time of writing, 40-50 of them were the main storyline, and the rest are mostly endgame farming and grinding.While  might contain spectacular combat and creature-raising, the story is woefully forgettable outside of a few key moments. The characters you meet along the way really help prop up the frustrating use of a silent protagonist, which hampers some of the scenes designed to illicit emotion from the player. There are also a handful of pacing issues around three-quarters of the way through the story which feel like unnecessary padding to prolong the wait until the endgame.In spite of its minor flaws,  is excellent value for money and is a "must buy" if you like Pokémon, Digimon, Shin Megami Tensei, Siralim and other games of that ilk.

_childDocuments_.review: 50 hours in I realized I just could not care about any of it. The repetitive dungeons, the frustrating combat with unavoidable attacks, the absolutely painful storyline with one-note unlikeable characters.What you have to understand about the game is it is 50% shonen nonsense for kids and 50% rock-paper-scissors style combat. You have a monster companion, or monstie - "monster bestie" - who will attack based on its type, or you can spend points to select a specific attack. These attacks counter each other in an RPS style. Fine. Beat the monster and get materials, or cart 3 times and game over.The problem comes when you're saddled with an AI partner and monster, neither of whom you have any control over, and if they cart 3 times you also game over. And they will often make the wrong choice in terms of attacks, which means effectively the game is a series of escort quests over which you have very little control.It's like the story is for kids but the gameplay mechanics are for the most obsessive grognards so I'm not even sure who this is for.So, while not necessarily a bad game, it is definitely not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I kind of forgot that JRPGs can be fun. Maybe I've been playing the wrong stuff most of the time for a long, long time, but most JRPGs don't my attention anymore. Octopath Traveler is an exception; its in-depth battle mechanics held my attention for double-digits of hours - that's more than I can say for most games in this genre that I've played in recent years.But this game helped me remember that turn-based battles don't have to be stale. The rock-paper-scissors mechanics work extremely well. Picking the right monster to fight the monster(s) in the current encounter didn't get old. I know, I know, Pokémon incorporates a lot of RPS mechanics, but this doesn't ask me to remember a slew of sometimes arbitrary strengths and weaknesses. There are three attack types and their opposites are fairly obvious. (Please keep in mind that I haven't gotten to the point that elemental strengths/weaknesses have become very important.)The story so far is… fine. That's it; it's fine.I don't know if I'll return to this game any time soon, but I'm sure I will at some point. Please know that that is not a statement the game’s quality (see above), it's really a statement about adulthood etc., etc.; I get the feeling that this will be a pretty long game and I don't have the time or attention span to play a long JRPG at the moment. Still, if you do have such an attention span and free time, give this a try. You probably won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - Good game.I'm a fan of Monster Hunter franchise, and this is a love-letter from Capcom to the likes of me. Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a great turn based strategy game with a heartwarming yet cruel story, great gameplay that does not feel far from home and many improvements over the previous game especially a multiplayer mode.  You start the game as the grandkid of a legendary rider, who aims to follow the path of your grandfather. The gameplay mechanics are beautifully explained by the tutorial missions and make some things clear so you don't feel like you are mission out on anything. Your companions -Navirou and Ena- can get pretty annnoying or bothersome at times but they're helpful. Monsters are well designed (especially the final boss) and are kept faithful to the mainline Monster Hunter games. This game also includes Elder Dragon monsties as well as Deviant monsties, which were not present in the previous game and considering they're mostly fan favourite monsters, this is an amazing feature. Soundtrack is beautiful and surgically induces you with emotions you were meant to feel during the key moments of the story. It's an overall amazing experience with very generous post-game content, making you want to play for the hours to come.This does not mean it is perfect though. There are some important downsides. Although the music is great, only ambience can be heard whilst exploring the world or a den, this does make exploring feel tedious and boring. The story is also not very adult-like either despite taking some bog steps from the first game, it ultimately falls short of maturity except for some key instances which I cannot spoil for anyone. Yet, in my opinion, the game is amazing and polished enough.Monster Hunter Stories 2 was an amazing experience for me and I would recommend it to anyone that is or willing to be into Monster Hunter. This was the first game I pre-ordered and I was not disappointed in the slightest.

_childDocuments_.review: Wondering if the price tag for this game is worth it? Yes!I've been a Pokemon fan since the old days of red and blue, played a lot of competitive Pokemon in generation 5 only. From generation 6 onwards the series lost its charm (for me).This game gets compared a lot to Pokemon due to a few similarities. The similarities I've seen so far in my 7 hours are mostly coming from battles. The game has the same "rock, paper, scissors" combat system (don't deny it, Pokemon is mostly that) with less RNG factors and takes a more tactical approach to battles.One of the things I love about this game is fighting along side your monster. Your character doesn't feel weak and has a nice selection of weapons. Did I mention you can switch out monsters AND weapons during battle if you feel you don't have an advantage? Each weapons have their strengths and weaknesses, learn to use them wisely.As for the story of the game itself. Pretty cheesy so to say. But to be expected since it seems like this game was aimed towards a younger audience. You have a "guide" like the main franchise and he's a bit on the annoying side, but you learn to love him in the end.Other than that, the graphics are pretty. You don't need a big computer to run this smoothly (compared to the main franchise of course). There is a few slight issues with framedrops if you don't enable steam controller in the options, hopefully this will be fixed in a future update.The music is average at most. Battle music is catchy and changes from area to area. So you are not stuck listening to the same song from start to end. There is no music during hunts, like any Monster hunter game really. Voice acting is top notch. Though some characters don't really match their voices. And some of the lines would of needed a bit more work. I mean... come on duuuuude.Honestly, give the demo a try first. You'll get the feel of the game and from there on out you can judge if this is for you or not. For myself, it's the type of game I've been waiting for from Gamefreak. But knowing Gamefreak, they won't ever change their little "recipe".!

_childDocuments_.review: The initial marketing for this game didn't really pull me in, but the increasing amount of gameplay clips I saw post-release made it look interesting and I ended up picking it up, and I gotta say that I didn't expect to like this game nearly as much as I did. It's actually amazing.Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a turn-based monster collecting rpg in a very similar vein to Pokémon, except that the visuals, world design, story and especially the animations are all set on a much higher level. The battle system is a fun combination of several layers of Rock-Paper-Scissors, effective element strategizing and enemy moveset memorisation (again, like Pokemon). The character customisation is tried and true Monster Hunter style, with many of the favorite sets from the series making a return, and the monster roster is also very respectable with 128 different monsters to fight. Couple of them are colored variants of each other, and you cannot add some of them to your own team, but there are still plenty of amazing creatures to collect.The game is also considerably lengthy at around 60 hours for the main story (at least on my pace, but I did do plenty of side quests as well). The post-game is also implied to be quite robust, so I'm excited to keep going and see what else there is in store.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm fairly new to the Monster Hunter series, but I picked this up as a lover of turn-based JRPGs and I thought the art style was cute. I figured after playing for 200+ hours I should finally leave a review. This game is SO fun and addictive. There's so many different features and things to do. You can really tell that a lot of love and care went into making this game which is something I always appreciate. Every monstie has their own special ultimate ability animation and the armor/weapon designs are so cool. And there's SO. MANY! I love that you can customize the colors of your armor as well and even "layer" it so you can keep your favorite designs on without sacrificing stats. My favorite thing is collecting monster eggs and customizing genes. I wish more games had mechanics like this. This isn't a game where you can just roll your face into the keyboard or controller; you gotta know what you're doing. It has some easy moments, but when faced with tougher monsters, you can't rely on random button mashing. You have to know how to build up your team as each monster, even of the same kind, has their own abilities and effects. You can't just throw together a random team and punch your way through the game without dying a lot, oh no no no. You got to pick the right monsters to help you not only in battle, but in the environment as well, to get to places and things you can't usually get on your own. The game itself is a bit "kiddish" in the sense of having some rather silly moments, but it's really cute in the end. You can equip up to 3 different weapons to take with you so you don't feel stuck with just one.Pros:- Beautiful music and ambiance- Very anime-esque graphics.- Open world- Really cute and touching storyline- Battles aren't quick and you have the option to Run Away!- You get to create your own character the way you want!- Store content isn't mandatory, but you do get a free starter pack! - Not as difficult or frustrating as MHW, but still has its tough moments- Team building is a thing! - You don't have the useless and annoying Handler with you, always getting herself into trouble and danger, forcing you to always save her. - You can change your gear out in the wild!Cons:-  No pet Palico to join you; instead you get an annoying Felyne who won't shut TF up, and you just want to punt him into a Rathalos' mouth. - Your character doesn't talk :( - The battle cut scenes do tend to get annoying and repetitive, but there's a skip button for that!- The talking Felyne won't.
