_childDocuments_.review: Already dropped about 220 or so hours on my Switch version, getting all the best Monsters and maxing out their bingo-sheets fully optimized and 2-stared on every gene. Now I'm finally wrapping up the PC version  and caught up now. I'm basing my review content-wise on what I've already done on the Switch version (pretty much everything bar a few irrelevant subquests) and the performance is based on what I've seen so far with my own eyes starting at launch day (made it to the second Anjanath sighting) and then today (Made it to the end of Rutoh Village so far). Content:The game is, really good! Simple and easy at first but eventually the difficulty doesn't come from playing RPS, but rather kinship management, gene placement (so you can actually WIN those HtHs often and deal damage), and the timing for healing (not healing at the right time if you need another heart or to top off CAN get you wiped). The story I really couldn't personally care for. It's not bad by any measure (the plot "twist" kinda sucked and was unpredictable for bad reasons but, it's not TERRIBLE at least), I'm just saying I didn't care for it since its not why I bought this game. For fans of the first game, the story is probably amazing to you since it's filled with characters from the previous title and a few cheeky references. As much as I can appreciate the love and care done, it's not why I bought this time. For someone taking their time and grinding monsters out, and getting average and acceptable genes for the sake of progress, I finished the main story in about 60 hours (10+ hours were from the demo alone). I bought this game knowing the majority of my time playing this game would be in the post-game and its content. I was correct. I love the gameplay loop, I love the Super Rare tickets I can do with friends, I like the trials MUCH MORE than the Tower from the first game, and the overall gene editing as well. Even if I couldn't appreciate the QoL improvements made in this game coming out of the first game (causing me to NEVER look back), I'd still wind up in love this with game enough to play through it (and pay for it) two separate times. I do miss being able to easily change monster elements, but I don't mind it as much as I was expecting. The monster selection in this game is pretty neat, and the future roadmap is 100% going to keep me coming back monthly to catch up and try out all the new stuff (although I'm expecting one of the things to kinda suck I'm ngl). It's nothing 900IQ or anything but, it's not dumb either. It's just nice casual fun, which I think I've needed after playing a ton of minmaxy and hardcore games I've been diving into for thousands of hours the past few years. The attention to detail and the love put into this game is NOT unnoticed (example: using the Ice Armor move on Velkhana gives it it's ice armor form from Iceborne when it enrages). It's not perfect, and it doesn't actually have to be. It's pretty damn close though.Performance:This game was raided with negative reviews on the launch day this game had. I have zero exaggeration when I say this: none of it was even correct lmao. Like cumon, if you're gonna exaggerate stuff to try and make this game look bad, at least base it in truth to make it LOOK honest. People were claiming they were using top of the line specs and they were encountering stuttering, frame dips, the works. I'm running this game on a Rysen 3600 and a 1660 Super and I can play this game at MAX settings and at 144fps smoothly with zero problems, even when a lot is happening on the screen at once. There's ZERO way people were having this many issues with the game. Really now? Keyboard controls were maybe KINDA awkward? Man, using KBM on a Monster Hunter game? That sounds like a goooood idea. This is like lambasting a Souls game in its entirety for not feeling as good on KBM as it does on controller. And to top it off, it was people complaining about the simple character creation when it came to these controls. You can run this game on a potato, and as long as you know where you W, A, S, and D keys are on your keyboard you can figure out how to play this game. This thing is optimized insanely well, and the controls.... well if you can't afford a controller then you better get used to using right click to rotate that camera, bc it really ain't THAT bad. TLDR: Anyone complaining about performance with GOOD hardware 100% has issues with their PC that are not related to the game, and they should get that stuff checked out ASAP because this game is optimized insanely well. Please check your parts if you claim your 2070 Super cant hit 60 fps because something is VERY wrong and it is NOT on the game's end. TL;DR: Bulldrome rarely drops its own parts in 144fps, good game. Worth at full price, which means on sale it's even more worth getting.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a turn-based RPG set in the Monster Hunter world. To say it draws inspiration from the Pokemon franchise is an understatement - most of its mechanics are taken at least somewhat from Pokemon games.I mean that in no ill intent - if you like Pokemon games, this game will probably be up your alley.This game also uses many classic mechanics and features from the standard Monster Hunter games, which add a nice spice to the game.This is a very chill game all about collecting all the different monsters you can. It's story-driven, sure, but even though the plot is more complex than in standard Monster Hunter games, I won't say it's significantly better. The story in this game isn't mind-shattering, but rather there to get the game moving.The turn-based combat, while fairly simple and not too challenging, is still fun. Just like in Monster Hunter fashion, you need to figure out what the monsters you're fighting are weak to, and preparation for a fight is greatly rewarded. However, this game isn't too hard. You really don't need to grind or stay on your toes, you'll usually win encounters.The graphics are stylized and charming, and the music is nice. In my personal opinion, the anime-esque nature of this game is not a welcome addition, but this is simply a matter of taste.In short, MHS2 is a fun game that has plenty of content for those who want to collect 'em all. It's not really challenging, it's not really interesting in terms of story, but it's harmless fun. If you like Pokemon, you'll probably like this game, but if you're looking for a great story like in other RPGs or challenging gameplay like in regular Monster Hunter, you may be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: MHS2 is a fantastic experience for those seeking a story-driven Pokemon experience in the world of Monster Hunter. Instead of adding an absurd amount of monster designs and attack moves like the Pokemon series, the game points towards refining what it already does by adding additional fun mechanics and quality-of-life features. Unlike Pokemon, you have a method of speeding up battles and combat. You also get rewarded each battle you play based on your performance and how well you do. You also fight alongside your own monsties and unlock special moves for working together. While MHS2 is certainly part of the monster-catching genre, it's not just another clone of Pokemon like other games of the same genre try to be. It stands on its own. For players who come from the world of Monster Hunter, you'll notice settle nods to the series through monster references and more.A lot of the current bad reviews of the game haven't given it much effort. I'm going to try to acknowledge each of the major things said to give you an idea about what's actually going on there and you can see if the game is for you.  - The controls are a little janky at first, but they're pretty easy to understand once you know what you're doing. I'll admit the original key layout is questionable, but it doesn't really affect you too much in a meaningful way because the game is a turn-based RPG. Fortunately, you can rebind every key in the game which remedies any issue you could ever have. - This is far from a bad console port. As stated above you can rebind every key in the game. A controller is not required and the game supports the mouse for camera viewing and clicking. Bad console ports don't offer either of these things. - This is a lie. While I'll admit you can't save while on the go and messing around, there's definitely a manual save found in your "home" which is located in every town. - I'm running a normal 1070 with a i5 6600k and the game works flawlessly for me. I maxed out my graphics too. If you're having issues with something better than this, you should check your end first before mindlessly blaming the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played Monster Hunter, as slow action combat without any real exploration isn't really my thing. Nor are enemy sponges, which Hunting games seem to specialize on. Stories is quite a different game, for starters it's turn-based and you actually have a fairly normal jrpg in your hands. And as far as I played so far, it could be one of the best of recent times.Good music, some really well done cutscenes, and a reasonable enough character creation for you to have fun with designing who you want to go into this world with. On top of that, every armor and weapon is visually seen, and can be quite varied. So in that department, this game is well done. It's also running quite well, so even the biggest toaster can probably play this at 1080p/30fps. That said, visuals and music wouldn't cover bad gameplay. Luckily it's not bad:Generally speaking, the game's battles combine paying attention to your enemies with RNG elements to spice things up. Every enemy has very specific types of attacks they do, but who they aim at is random, just like all actions of party members that are not yourself are random-ish. Your job is to know what type of attacks an enemy does when, and choose your attack types (power, speed or technical) accordingly, as well as your monster. Allied monsters prefer a type of attack, though it's not guaranteed. This generally means, you pay attention to what you fight, and how you fight. That said, this only comes into play, when there's a clash of an ally and an enemy. (as in they attack each other) The winner gets a huge advantage through this, but if there's no confrontation, it doesn't matter what type you use. Buffs, heals and the likes never lead to a confrontation. Typical weaknesses to elements also exist, and those work as you'd think. There's slash, blunt and pierce, as well as several elements like fire or water. Ailments also exist.There's more to the battle system, but I think I wrote enough to make clear: You should pay some attention to things. That said, the game isn't particularly difficult so far, as levels give fairly huge bonuses early on, so bad play can be covered by doing the side-quest and upgrading equipment, as well as actively fighting. At least as far as I've played. That said, bad play will tank your battle rewards, so even though the game is on the easier side, you still are encouraged to play well and use the mechanics given to you. Even if dying is probably not something you will do for quite a bit in this game, you probably don't want to get bad battle ranks, which are actually surprisingly well done given the mechanics of the battles. Often battle ratings are more artificial than anything else, here they feel very accurate.As a final note I'd like to mention the areas. Jrpgs started to have more and more uninteresting areas without much to find around. MHS2  seems to be slightly different, and there's a little more to the world. A good example is that environmental skills exist, that you get as you progress and get different monsters, to reach formerly unreachable points and treasures. I'm very happy about the designers actually caring a little about the world design. I will update again later on how it keeps up.edit: It doesn't. On the surface it's good, but the inner workings aren't. I still had my fun for some hours, and I wouldn't call it a good game, but also not a bad game. The more casual your approach it, the better the game probably performs. For how much mechanics there are, it's really demotivating to realize how little all of it matters. Different weapons? Whatever, you gotta dual attack anyway. Hundreds of different genes? Whatever, only bingos matter. Random stat bonuses for new born monsters? Flat, and not base stats, so they don't matter. A game that truly wasted its immense potential like few other games manage to do.edit august 5th.: Capcom still hasn't fixed the multiplayer bug with corrupted character data because a (usually) non preset skin color being chosen. This is not acceptable, as such I can no longer recommend this game. All things considered, the product has too many issues.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a really tough one to score. This is one of those games where you need to sit down and way the pros and cons before you get into it. So here’s what you need to know:The gameplay is fairly simple, being made up of two parts. The wandering/exploration, and the combat. The exploration part consists of you running around on a miniature monster, usually collecting resources while looking for your next objective.The combat is basically a flashy game of rock-paper-scissors. It's alright, but it does have a long-term problem. In its design, it is not simple enough to just turn your brain off to and enjoy, but it is also not interesting enough to warrant an enjoyable challenge. It exists in this bland middle ground where you can quickly get bored of it, and if bored, it still demands enough attention that you can’t just go into it while multitasking something else.While the two main parts of the gameplay  fairly simple, they are also what’s advertised, and to that extent, they are just fine. A major issue of the game, as well as the main reason for most of its negative reviews is the fact that you can’t play Co-op through the main campagin. This would be tolerable, if it wasn’t for the fact that the main campagin is around 8-20 hours long. There is also PvP, though I can’t say anything about it since I couldn’t find a single person playing it.The Story, is petty much the weakest part of the game. While Munster Hunter games generally don’t have much of a story, I have to say that I expected a game with “Stories” in the title to have at least some semblance of sense. The story is your usual excuse to go fight monsters, most details are overlooked for convenience, and the plot eventually hinges on a random MacGuffin so miniscule that I can freely spoil it knowing that you will never remember it come the point where it's needed.As far as the general appeal of the game goes, it’s a mixed bag. On one side, most people who get this game likely do it because they are fans of the franchise, and are entertaining the idea of having the monsters be on your side for once. On the other hand, this is a game aimed at kids, and that is apparent as some parts of it can make you cringe so hard that it hurts. And I am talking about the Kinship attacks. In my personal case, I came into the game because I liked the idea of getting to control the monsters, and I certainly wasn’t disappointed, even if it was in a turn-based game.Something that is quite worthy of praise in this game is the upgrade system. This game is one that can easily be compared to Pokemon on basic premise alone. To that extent, it is worth praising the fact that this game does not copy some of the major flaws of some Pokemon games. I am specifically talking about the artificial time bloat, that is making every creature spawn with random, unchangeable power levels. In fact, one of the worst things that some Pokemon games do is giving you a starter Pokemon that has horrible stats that you can’t change, making you have to replace it later down the line with the same, better Pokemon. This game doesn’t have that. Your starting monster is as good as any other monster of that species, any skills it lacks, you can later add. There is no bs 0-100% quality system like in games such as Pokemon Go.Now, if you put the upgrade system aside, the gameplay loop is still just wandering around and collecting monsters. BUT, that is what the game advertises, and it does it well enough.Ehhh… $60 is a bit steep for what it is, especially considering the multiplayer issue. Now to be fair, you could pull quite a lot of hours out of it as there is a lengthy end-game after the initial story. However, most of the gameplay can be brushed off by the common definition of being repetitive, so I would probably recommend that you get it at a sale if the general idea of what I listed so far doesn’t seem particularly appealing.======================================================As a whole, this game has enough ups and downs to the point where I wouldn’t normally write a review on it, simply because its too far in the dead center of quality where its not so bad as to be bad, but not so good as to be worth recommending.The gameplay is a slow-burner, though it is decent.The story is, -well, dumb. But it is entertaining enough.The multiplayer is absent throughout the most lengthy and interesting part of the game. Making anyone who bought this to play it with a friend likely feel ripped off for having to go 10+ hours just to unlock proper multiplayer.And the aesthetics are quite nice.Altogether, this game certainly has some shortcomings. But it also has some generally good aspects. Small details such as continued quest board tasks remembering your progress from the previous quest, the fact that your character doesn’t have the turn rate of a buss, the fact that multiplayer is  quite alright if you find a soul interested in playing through the game just to get to it. It has issues, but it strives to deliver a good experience. Also, it didn’t rip off the horrible Pokemon CP system. So props there.So, if you like solo, turn based games that vaguely resemble Pokemon, then you might like this one.======================================================

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game for children. I am complaining regardless.The plot: interesting enough, unfortunately littered with sequences dominated by social ineptitude usually found in *quirky* anime. Example: centuries old wyverian woman trapped in a 14 year-old's body jumps onto your character on-sight, mistaking you for your own grizzled old grandpa. She constantly grabs your hands and follows your character around, making a burden of herself because she's *ahem* "the one who gave you the egg so she should follow you because she gave you an egg once." You can also change her outfit. How great is that. My theory: Capcom has been funding an experimental science program. This program uses a specialized team of shadow operatives to capture and confine wild bonobos, holding them within pens. Taking a look around, the bonobos will find a single control panel with a "cringe dialogue" button. Which, once pressed, sends a string of commands to an advanced A.I., while simultaneously rewarding the bonobo with a fruit, and the power cord to their ipad. On which they may watch one markiplier episode. As you can probably imagine, the button gets pressed very frequently. The gameplay: when you aren't walking around(the ying) the combat(the yang) sits comfortably at above average, but is satisfying to play. It has some similarities to fossil fighters. No real complaints here.The world: empty and without any interest or majesty. An impressive feat for a monster hunter inspired game. When you ride monsters the game plays and feels no differently than when your character walks around on-foot. I would say you move faster while riding but they somehow managed to fine tune that to feel slow as well. Side note: Yian Kut Ku and Yian Garuga cannot fly. This is quite interesting when you consider that they can in fact fly. The cAT.I made the mistake of playing with english dub on, and as a consequence Navirou's voice is an assault on the senses. He constantly repeats information just explained to the main characters in a confused and incessant manner that I can only imagine is a result of his wickedly misshapen brain. He eliminates any possibility of subtlety by idiotically blurting out obvious plot connections, lengthening dialogue sequences as a by-product of his cognitive disfigurement. This would be tolerable if he was a side character played for laughs. But he isn't. He is quite literally the main character of this game. He has no purpose other than be the silent protagonists' "voice," and injecting his cringe anime-tier dialogue between every single sentence spoken by other characters. It is as if the writers were so afraid that their other characters might be compelling enough to illicit some kind of intrigue from the player and they added this fiend in post.Another thing about this cat. His gameplay "purpose" is that he can "sense," with his level 100 myticisim whether a monster egg has a good or average monster within it. He uses the forbidden and arcane magic of "smelling" and "holding" the egg, to see how stinky or heavy the thing is. Incredible I know. It seems our protagonist is not only mute, but was struck by lightning shortly after being born. Like the victim of some Greek tragedy, our hero is unable to experience the smells, tastes, and textures of their world. Overall, disappointing game. Any listing over 10 dollars is overpriced. I enjoy parts of this game, but they wrote Scrappy-do into the main cast of characters, and all the tolerable or fun parts take a backseat to his screeching.

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom’s answer to Pokémon, Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a Turn-Based RPG which allows players to tame and develop many of the most iconic monsters found throughout the franchise. Beneath a candy coated façade is a fleshed out game that far exceeds the sum of its parts, but unlike many games of the genre it takes its time before introducing the full experience.The core gameplay loop tasks players with hunting down Monster Dens to acquire Eggs. Each Den provides a small handful of chances to acquire an egg of varied quality related to the Den of origin; the rarer the egg, the better the “Genes” for a specific monster and type. After a certain point in the story, roughly about level 18, players will be able to sacrifice monsters to transfer their “Genes” to another.In layman’s terms; when hatched, monsters generate a random assortment of traits, abilities, and empty slots. Some of which are level locked. Each is related to the species and type, some of which are even unique. Players can then transfer a single one of these so-called “Genes” to a monster of their choice as many times as they like, therefore gradually creating a fully customized monster to fight with.The combat is the traditional turn-based fair with a Rock, Paper, Scissors twist that is deceptively simple on the surface. However, there is little in the way of randomness. Enemies have a pre-scripted set of potential attack types they’ll favor, which means that they can be easily read and memorized. Later in the game, familiarizing yourself with these patterns is essential to victory.Along the way you can gear up your hunter, but weapons are less about play style in this game and more about exploiting a target’s weaknesses. There are three flavors of weapon: Slashing, Blunt, and Piercing. All of which can be switched out every turn without penalty, which allows the player to adjust for every situation on the fly.Monsters can also be switched out mid combat, and in fact that is the primary flow of the combat system overall. The game rewards the player for having a wide variety of weapons and monsters at their disposal at any time. This can make combat feel very trivial and easy, especially in the early game. This sense of ease is further reinforced by the game providing the player with a number of extremely powerful companions early on.These companions do a high amount of damage and even heal the player and their monster, which may give players the feeling that the game is on autopilot. However, as the game progresses further into the story, the aid provided by the AI companions has far less impact on the outcome of the battle. The difficulty spike is there, and it may come as a surprise for many players who haven’t been properly preparing for it. But that spike rears its head around level 20 or so.Multiplayer features are not unlocked until a certain point in the story; once unlocked, players can team up and take on side quests via the quest board. Since the game provides an Open World that gradually gets bigger the further a player progresses, there is plenty to explore and interact with; not to mention a great many quest boards. Although each region is essentially the same in the overall progression: unlock the region; do a few story quests to unlock Monster Dens; hunt and tame monsters unique to that region; complete the story section and move on. Rinse and repeat.There is plenty to do overall, and like its predecessor the game offers a robust post-game experience once the Story has reached a conclusion. From that point on monsters become a lot tougher, armor gets a variety of upgrades and new abilities, and more Genes become available. Any progression beyond the story's conclusion is often related to the game’s PVP Arena, where players strive to rear the most overpowered monster they can and try to annihilate the competition as swiftly as possible.Do not be fooled, this game has a surprising amount of staying power. After all, it is a Monster Hunter title. So there are a great number of personal challenges you can achieve in this game, especially during the expansive post-game. But that being said, there is no doubt the game’s longevity will vary wildly based on how many people a player has to engage with. At launch there is already a robust community of dedicated fans that congregate on Discord; offering up advice, team mates, and even periodic tournaments for PVP.Yet there is either no, or very little in the way of a solid in-game infrastructure that makes finding friends easy. Worse, there doesn’t appear to be any Crossplay, further fragmenting an already niche community.The game is the polar opposite of grim and gritty: the story is cliché, the characters are cartoonish, the protagonist is silent, and there is a certain level of cuteness to a lot of the designs. Yet that is all just a candy shell concealing a truly deep and engaging RPG. The only real gripe I have is that that the early game is deceptive in its simplicity. There is a lot of hand holding and withholding of core mechanics. Much of which the Trial Version doesn’t even bother to brush on.The game opens up very late into the story and doesn’t truly reveal itself until after the credits have rolled; which is as much a blessing as it is a burden upon the player. Ultimately I recommend this game if you’re already a big fan of the Monster Hunter franchise, it rewards players with foreknowledge of the series by allowing them to translate their experience into this unique combat system. While there is a huge variety of Monsters within the roster, sadly not all are present. But many series favorites are there.This game is especially appealing to those who have a taste for Min-Maxing, allowing for hours upon hours of grinding for the perfect Monster, the perfect Genes, and the perfect team composition. As a fan of JRPGs and Monster Hunter, I find this to be a perfect combination of the two; which isn’t as easy as it sounds._____________

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is not a terribly bad game but it isn't the most appealing one either especially once you get past the initial excitement of capturing monsters. Then again, I'm a 33 year old man and it's probably my fault for attempting to play a game that's targeted at a younger audience.The pros:1) The anime-style graphics are pretty good lookingThe cons:1) The story is pretty dull and if you're one of those who's obsessed with capturing all monsties, it's going to slow down the game play even more. Having a silent protagonist really just drags everything down to a crawl.2) The game is super repetitive - the dungeons are all fairly standard. But what's worse is every time you reach a new chapter, it's all about doing the same stuff again.3) The battle mechanics is too simple (not in terms of difficulty, but the concept of it). The fact that the creators of the game had a quick battle system meant they knew the battles were going to tire gamers out. And while I appreciate the quick battle system, maybe they should have tried creating a more compelling experience in the first place?4) The open world is big but empty. Ends up being very hollow.5) The sound system of the game is quite unbalanced. A lot of the time you;re going to be wondering if there's any BGM at all. (Yes you can tune it yourself in the settings section but the default settings should have worked a lot better to begin with)6) The dialogues are probably the worst aspect of the game. Again, this is from a perspective of a 33 year old man, so I'm probably not the intended audience. But boy does the writing sucks. It's written for a 10 year old with loads of kiddo-type dialogues and humour that annoys the ♥♥♥♥ out of me. It's one thing to try to create an anime-styled game, it's another to create a childish game for kids watching PAW Patrol.Overall, it's a 4/10 but if you're like me who bought the game at full price, it's closer to a 3/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not big on writing reviews, and I may or may not revisit this later to update it with a more comprehensive opinion, but for now I just really want to get the word out there to my friends and everyone else that this is an especially good game if turn based JRPG mechanics and collecting and befriending monsters sounds right up your alley. _childDocuments_.review: (For simplicity's sake, before I start this review, I will say that I am a major fan of both Pokemon, which this game gets compared to quite a bit due to the monster battling aspect, and Monster Hunter as a whole, as I started with Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate. Everyone's perspective of this game might be different due to this slight bias, so reader's discretion and understanding of bias is advised and appreciated. Thank you.)This game's concept and gameplay is really fun, it's like Pokemon's Super/Non/Weak Effective typing, except multilayered through games of rock paper scissors, while also having that typing advantage on top of that (excluding the effects of non-effective things, like Pokemon had, ex. normal can't touch ghost, MHS2 has none of that). I see that a lot of reviews compare to Pokemon, but I'd go as far to say that the only thing this game has to compare to Pokemon is that it's monster battling, that's about it in my opinion. The amount of stuff you can do with your monsties in this (save for, say, a "take care of" minigame like Pokemon had with Pokemon-Amie) greatly outweighs the stuff you can do in even current Pokemon games. I will say tho that the "Trainer" Battles in this are somewhat lackluster as they only appear a handful of times, and are scripted to happen through the story. You can pick up quest versions to make up for this, but they don't feel as natural to me. A small critique, but that was one I wanted to bring up in terms of comparison.As for the actual monsters/monsties, there's honestly a fair bit to fight/use in a party (122 if I remember for both combined). Each of them have their own unique stuff, but you can mix and match moves on any monstie, so it's more about stats/preference for which monstie to use. Lots of returning monsters and fan favorites, like Kecha Wacha (my fav, both varients), Deviljho, and Glavenus, to name a few. The story itself reminds me of Sword and Shield from Pokemon, but it puts it's own spin and uniqueness to it. Razewing Ratha was an interesting concept as a companion and the game's main antagonist/protagonist mystery (up until a certain point, where the "true bad guy appears", without spoilers it reminded me of the Eternatus debacle from SWSH in terms of it's use). There is unfortunately a slight amount of padding in the early game, but I count that as a pro rather than con because it helps build the world slightly better, and helps you get more used to new mechanics as they're introduced, as well as introduce more monsters and areas. The amount of time it took me to complete the campaign while not doing ALL the side stuff/grinding was about 60 hours, so it's fairly long, which to me is a good thing. It does all it wants to do in the time it's given, without feeling too too long in the end.All in all I would say if you like Monster Hunter and want to try something unique and fun, and if you're somewhat of a Pokemon fan as well, pick this game up (on sale preferably, the price is somewhat steep to me. Don't worry about DLC as it is all cosmetic and not too important) and give it a try. You might like it!Game's Scoring:- Gameplay: 8/10- Story: 7/10- Party Members: 9/10- Fandom Tailoring: 6.5/10- Graphics: 8/10Final Score:7.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: With the genre seemingly to have shifted more towards the action oriented variety, the news of a AAA RPG with turn-based combat being released in 2021 caught my attention. While older titles in the genre can feel tedious by current game design metrics, Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin truly modernizes the genre, not just by bringing it to current technical standards, but by renovating the gameplay as well.Combat rewards intuition and memorization, making the battles extremely engaging. Correctly predicting an enemy's attack feels very rewarding, and being able to draw from the knowledge of previous encounters makes hours invested into the game translate into a usable skill. This unique style of gameplay keeps the player thinking (as opposed to spamming X on the most powerful abilities) and keeps the encounters fun. Additionally, the current turn number is displayed during battle, something I found interesting and wish more games did.The game also makes use of various computer controlled allies in a marvelous way. Being able to play off of the computer's choices and spend gauge to influence a Monstie's actions adds a previously unseen level of strategic depth that is both fun and powerful. The truth is, playing alongside a bot generally feels like either a burden or a non-factor. The fact that the developers managed to turn this into a strategic and fun gameplay element is an exemplary game design feat.There are also several convenience features that eliminate some of the annoyances traditionally seen in the genre. Enemies are visible throughout the world, making avoiding unwanted encounters a game in and of itself. In addition, if an encounter is started with a previously faced enemy that is weaker than the player, a quick finish can be used to instantly result in a player victory. Leveling up new Monsties to the player's level is quite quick, making switching between them relatively easy (although the personal attachment to them is another story).Both a minimap and a full-sized map make exploration manageable, but the icing on the cake is a trail on both of these that traces player movement. Fast travel is readily available for previously discovered locations and can be easily accessed not only from the map, but from the quests themselves.With a plethora of content available at all stages of the game (and more steadily added post-launch) and a diverse world crafted in a distinct artistic style, there is a lot to see and do. The soundtrack is especially stunning and there were multiple times I didn't want to leave a zone's music behind, only to discover the next zone's music was just as good. A strong cast of characters backed by surprisingly good English voice acting tell an engaging tale and bring the world to life.The game supports 1440p and other details, such as achievements being viewable in-game and PS4 button prompts being displayed when a PS4 controller is used, create a solid user experience. With Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin, the turn-based RPG is no longer a dated relic of the past, but a modern genre that can rival any other.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool concept (pokemon monster hunter), but the execution is poorly done.The variety of monsties is good, but there's problem with balance, while some monsties are just not appealing at all (herbivores notably).The bingo system with genes make it annoying to "catch" new monsties during the progression of the story and make you not want to bother until endgame, because you're gonna want amazing eggs or else it's costly to unlock the genes slots.Leveling new monsties each time you catch a new one is annoying (always start at level 1).Combat system is OK at best but can be really frustrating, due to monsters barely balanced (in the same zone, some monsters are just punching ball, while others will just one shot you even if you full counter them because they attack twice a turn while angered) and also due to you not having full control on your own team (you can only control you own monsties if you have the "mana" (kinship) for it, so countering is not always possible which is a bit strange if you base the whole system around it). Except if you're overlevel and oversutff (but what's the point then ?)The story is pretty standard but i didn't finish it so can't say too much on that point.Graphics are OK and the art style is nice.Conclusion : I can't recommand this game even to fans of the franchise, overall for me it's clunky and frustating while being grindy (which is ok to an extent, but it's not bearable here)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. I don't know that I could ever recommend this game over any of the (playable) actual Monster Hunter games, but it's a fun romp with surprisingly competent writing. Characters from the first game have surprising depth and nuance (except for Navirou for the most part), with the events of the first game heavily affecting their decisions and character development. In all honesty, I don't know that I would recommend the game at full price, but it's worth it on sale. As far as the combat goes for both Stories games, as I've played both, I do miss the patterns within the triangle system from the first game, even when monsters were not enraged or in other "modes", but I understand the decision in an effort to streamline it. While the combat is a little bit shallow, due to having to control and manage so many variables, despite the lack of immediate depth, decisions get pretty involved later in the game, especially depending on your level.The difficulty, like any RPG, heavily depends on the player's level and the levels of the monsters in their party. The gene system is nice, although a lot of the genes require a bit too much dedication to RNG than I would like. The overall length, not including the endgame, Is about 25-30 hours, which causes the game to not overstay its welcome, but gives it time to flesh out the characters, areas, and mechanics. 7.4/10, good game.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 Best memories playing a game. As a rule of thumb, anything they set out to do, they nailed. But they didn't set out to do everything, or even close to it. I think they understood that too much can often have bad effects on the impact of a game like this, and only chose a specific scope they wanted to pursue, and they crushed it. LOVE this gameStory:- doesn't rely on the first game's stories, but refers to them a good deal and reuses a number of characters. Get the story easily with the anime "Monster Hunter Stories: Ride On", 48 episodes like good Pokemon episodes.- the new story in this game follows a very similar structure to the first, which can make it a little predictable at a glance, but the story still has it's own way of going about it that was very fun to be part of.- the story isn't meant to be overly dramatic, full of deep and convoluted mystery, or anything too groundbreaking. But it's simple focus on love, values, and relationships is perfectly presented in ways you can easily enjoy and appreciate. - the characters are so fun and distinct that you can easily fall in love with any and all of them, though you might not relate so much to your own character till late in the story. Like many games, your character doesn't really talk. - Navirou is your partner felyne who is fundamentally tasked to be your voice. The only problem with this is it takes a while to appreciate Navirou's character and voice acting, I do, and many do, but most don't. Please give my boy a good chance.Gameplay:- I am not a nitpicky person so you may not get the good guide you're looking for from me.- feels a lot like an older gen game because the landscape is not made of complex details and textures, but the monsters are excellently modeled to the style.- some dungeons are specific locations, but the generic randomly generated ones can get repetitive as they use a selection of pre-made layouts and piece them together more or less randomly. I wouldn't ask for more, but it becomes a little obvious shortly into each location what the dungeons will be like.- Battling is a big game of rock-paper-scissors with special abilities, trump cards, and usually multiple opponents and teammates, making for a unique and learnable battle system that is approachable to anyone but rewards those who can crack the codes and form solid strategies. Honestly took me some notable mistakes to really grasp the secondary rules they use, but the game is not punishing for one or two major mistakes in battle till nearly the end of the game. - difficulty wise, you can deliberately chose how difficult you want it to be by giving yourself a set of rules, but the game makes winning almost inevitable for those well-enough prepared. You are given three hearts between you and your monster partner, and any time you or your monster runs out of health you lose a heart (and then get your health back). Losing all three hearts ends the fight in defeat. This difficulty is normal, and actually more than challenging at a few points in the game. However, there are some items that can restore a heart during a battle to basically keep your team in the fight forever (unless you are horribly under leveled, in which monsters can take out multiple hearts at once with multi hit attacks that you cant keep up with. So anyway, not a souls-like, but not impossible to lose like PokemonSw/Sh- Any monster can ultimately learn any move (Nergigante can learn elemental attacks, Velocidromes can learn Nergigante moves) which is honestly really weird to me in the main story but when it comes to PvP its a definite win. If this feature is your focus, look it up to learn all its technicalities from people more qualified.Replayability:- The main story is on set tracks you can't derail, so there aren't second endings to find (that I know of. nothing major at least).- I think the average person could play it twice happily, but its always been fun for me to watch people play the game for the first time to go through the story again that way and see how they take it. - There is end game content I haven't really pursued yet, but there are things to do after the main story- The main reason to keep playing after the story would be PvP and making the perfect team of monsties, if that's what you're into

_childDocuments_.review: A great sequel that improves on everything that made the first game great. It’s basically Pokemon, but in the Monster Hunter World. But here, the monsters can be your friend. While players can’t tame the monsters, they can follow them to their nest and steal their eggs to raise tame so-called Monsties! The game features a connected world that is separated into smaller areas that can be freely explored. Exploration features some very light metroid-vania elements where the player needs certain Monsties to reach new locations. For example you need a Tigrex to climb ranks or a Velicoprey to jump over chasms. Just like in the main series, most of the time is spent on fighting wild monsters. But in Monster Hunter Stories a classic turn based JRPG-battle system takes over. It still features most of the mechanics of the main line series with elemental weaknesses and different weapon types doing different kinds of damages. It also adds a stone, rock, paper like system where fast attacks trump strength attack, strength attacks trump tech attacks and tech attacks again trump fast attacks. Learning the patterns of all the enemies and finding out their weak spots is a big part of the fun.Where there is a JRPG battle system there is also a level up system. Contrary to the mainline series the main character, NPC followers and all Monsties can be leveled up to improve their stats. Later in the game, Monsties can even be fused to transfer skills between them. The system is quite deep and gives a lot of room to build your dream Monstie team. And of course killed monsters drop tons of items and parts that can be crafted into new armors and weapons that can also be improved further. While I’ve only played the single-player, the game also features an extensive online mode where players can go on co-op hunts or even battle each other in an arena. So this can be enjoyed as a single player narrative JRPG and/or as a PvP/Coop game equally. Because it was mainly developed for the Nintendo Switch, Monster Hunter Stories 2 isn’t the most technically advanced game. The graphics are even more stylized then in Monster Hunter Rise. But in my opinion it is still a mighty fine looking game with a strong artstyle. Especially the care and craftsmanship that was put into all the battle animations deserves extra praise. This game looks spectacular in battles and I’d wish Pokemon games could finally keep up with that. It also features nicely rendered and voiced cutscenes that are never too long but also not too sparse. The game is just neatly paced and the mix between exploring, fighting and story segments with funny characters just works. Last but not least a word to Steam Deck compatibility. The game is marked as “not compatible” but it ran without tinkering for me. The game runs pretty good, but not as good as I’d expect from a Switch port. It also makes the Steam Deck fans go “bzzzzzzz!” and the battery drain quickly. So best use some good headphones while playing it and have a power source nearby.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, really good. If you've played the first you know what to expect, as this game builds on the previous game's foundation with a variety of QOL changes and so many new areas/monsters. If you haven't, think Pokemon mixed only your trainer fights too and the Pokemon all want to beat you up. The battles have quite a bit of substance to them; you'll have to learn each enemy's patterns and what damage types they're weak to if you want all the drop rate bonuses, but thankfully the game tracks everything you've learned about enemy weaknesses and stores that information for you permanently. The story's tacky but it works well enough, and the writing has a surprising amount of charm behind it. It's good enough that you won't feel the need to skip it, and that's all it has to be.My only gripes with the game so far are the co-op being locked 10 hours in and the relatively low number of co-op quests so far, but they've already announced more co-op content and the wait to unlock the mode is well worth it.Oh, and the PVP is fantastic - other than the questionable decision to make elder dragons/deviants immune to traps, the item sets are well balanced and let you make just about any playstyle viable in both solo and duo battles. Learning elemental weaknesses and trying to predict bluffs makes it consistently fun and challenging, and the option of automatic level balancing means that you don't have to grind your monster levels up just to compete.

_childDocuments_.review: As soon as I was introduced to the combat system, I thought it was just gonna be a rock-paper-scissors luck based game... Thankfully I was wrong... The first encounter with a new monster is always gonna be the most challenging one because you have no idea of how the monster is going to move... After a while however, you start to recognize the patterns and you end up choosing the right moves to counter the enemy. There are combo attacks and super abilities that allow you to skip your opponent's turn if you manage to execute them properly. Pretty neat. Like other monster hunter games, you have a variety of weapons to choose. There are three categories: Blunt, piercing and slashing weapons. The player can equip all of the three types but can only attack with one type at a time therefore, learning how to use the right type of weapon at the right time is crucial to your success. You can break monster parts, use skills, successfully win head-to-head battles etc etc... to increase your battle rating. The better you perform in a battle, the better the rewards you get.The player can use those rewards to craft/upgrade their weapons. Like other monster hunter games when you equip new gear, you can actually see your character using that equipment... which is a feature that is sadly not present in most games nowadays...You can get new monsters to fight by your side by hatching eggs that you collect from monster dens. The rarity of the eggs seems to vary from... no glow, to gold... to rainbow? The better the glow the better the quality of the egg? Not sure...There is some depth with combining monsters to get better abilities. Which is cool.There's a pvp mode where you can battle other players and there seems to be a co-op mode later in the game as well. I only played for 10 hours but the story so far seems interesting. You create your character, he/she learns how to tame monsters, stuff happens and he/she goes on an adventure. Some of the dialogue isn't voiced but for the most part we get voice acting.If this game is anything like other monster hunter titles... there should be a decent amount of post game content as well. This game seems very solid and if you enjoy story driven, turn-based games... you should definitely consider picking this one up. In case of doubt... there's always the demo version that you can download to try the game out.

_childDocuments_.review: T:L:D:R = Great game with a lot to love for new and old fans. 8/10As a huge MH fan i had to pick this up at launch even if going in I wasn't expecting much. What i found however was a very well made turn based RPG with a classic rock, paper, scissors battle system that was way better than it has any right to be. You can tell almost immediately that this game was made with so much love.Its a very open and accessible RPG to people unfamiliar with the franchise but it also rewards veterans with a lot of subtle nods. A seasoned hunter can make an educated guess what types each monster is based on their move set and ecology within the main line games. While the game is also forgiving enough to allow new players to not be punished so severely for not knowing and messing up an opening attack. _childDocuments_.review: Where do I begin? This was a game I greatly regret sleeping on for so long.I'm a diehard JRPG fan, and among them played many monster collectors like Shin Magami Tensei, Digimon, Symphonia 2, the pokemon franchise, and DQ monsters. I can proudly add this title to my shelf. It stands out to me how much thought was put into the game's combat mechanics, The game's cornerstone, head to heads seems like a simple Rock paper scissors mechanic that ends up expanding into other interwoven game mechanics inspired by the mothership franchise. Rage mode and monster actions change behaviours, part breaking affects their move pools. Status effects can be used offensivsly and defensively to help your party.  All the monhun mechanics are translated over into this head to head system intuitively. Riding is this game's super meter, and building it requires you to actively participate and learn how to make the most of the system.Compared to the juggernaut Franchise pokemon where battles are more of a chore of mashing A through menus to snowplough through the game, you actually activate your neurons and think on what your next move is after reading the field.This is hugely rewarding as your motivated to fight, not just to grind up numbers, but because fights are both really fun and you improve on your own as a player.  This also plays into its monster recruiting, You paintball monsters and raid dens to get a shot at stealing their eggs. The monster pool is best described as quality over quantity. With many monsters from the core franchise up to worlds able to be hatched and raised at your mounts.The monsters all have unique moves and are loaded with personality, each species feeling like their own character with great animations.The monsters field skills as you ride them to get around actively encourage you to build a diverse team for many reasons besides being a bigger bag of stats with an element on it. Getting a swimming or climing monster in your group feels like a big deal with the involved process of getting an egg. Story is a fairly kid-friendly boy becoming a man in their forebearer's footsteps stuff you see a lot of in JRPGs and such, with a healthy seasoning of monster hunter lore and personality. Its engaging, and the game isnt beating you over the head too hard with the usual suspects. (Navirou the Felyne can be a polarizing character however, acting as the comic-releif voice surrigate for the mute protagonist.)Graphically its style focus over technical focus as it was originally a switch title. But never feels like one. And tbe open world areas are typical of a monster hunter franchise, beautiful ecology-scapes. World's endemic life making the area even more lively. Audio is also typical monster hunter affair, great music tracks and meaty sound design. And even the switch version featured fully voiced cutscenes, something neither switch pokemon games could even attempt, but standard for many JROGs in the late playstation 2 era. Lastly the game's combat system also enables co-op through its buddy system. In the story an NPC and their monstie join in battle with you, and the full head to head system cross interacts and compounds. Later on you can invite a friend to join you in fights online to take on the game's bigger targets.This game was the boogeyman under Pokemon Company's bed, and legends arceus tried its best and failed at appropriating ideas from MH Stories.As the old addage goes; imitation is the greatest form of flattery.If you want a fresh take on a monster collector, or want to experience what Pokemon Legends Arceus wished it could be, or a Mon-Hun fan who loves everything Monster Hunter. You will not be dissapointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is probably the most fun I've had in a long time.If you haven't played Stories 1, that's perfectly fine. There are recurring characters in this, but you don't need to know the story of 1 to enjoy the story of 2. That said, I heavily recommend the original Stories as well. I cannot speak enough praise about this series.I had such an enjoyable experience playing this game in every way. Pros:- Monster CollectionCapcom just has this way of taking monster collection and turning it into something that's unique beyond just "hey this is a new monster, catch it :)." Not to bag on pokemon or anything like that, but in most games like pokemon, what makes your team usually comes down to you finding new monsters to put on your team and them overall being stronger just based on progression. There's nothing wrong with that, but Stories takes that concept and while not immediately disregarding it by making every monster do the same thing, it gives you an opportunity to build your monster in any way you want due to the genetics system. While the genes can be frustrating in the sense of you can get screwed over by rng a lot of the time, it's never really a slog to get those genes. By hunting for new genes, you're exploring new dens, finding new items, possibly even discovering new monsters. Every monster is unique in whatever ways you can make it unique, and that's fascinating for me being a long time pokemon player.-CombatWhile there are some frustrations around the combat mechanics such as monsties sometimes being just really stupid (why is my nargacuga just SPIKE BOMBING), overall it's very straightforward and honestly fun. They manage to keep it simple with a RPS style combat, but it's not completely random or based on weapons like in FE (more on weapons later). Kinship skills are a super cool way to have an interaction with your monsties that isn't just directly controlling them like a traditional JRPG, and basically every skill in the game *has a use* which is a complaint I had with a lot of RPGs and JRPGs, as a lot of them just have some moves that just make no sense.-Story and charactersThe characters are phenomenal. Every character has a clear personality. You can tell what they're thinking. You can see how they're meant to be and that's amazing. There's twists that I genuinely didn't expect, and that's just a rarity at this point for me. They put a lot of effort into it.-Animations:My god the attack animations are so good. That's literally all I can say. Watch every kinship skill at least once, you won't regret it.-WeaponsYou have 3 types of weapons, with 2 weapons in each type. Slice, Pierce and Blunt. Weapons do different damage to parts based on that part's weakness to said type of weapon. Classic monster hunter. The weapon pool is limited, but it makes sense for stories and that's fine. They still all have their unique uses and give you the opportunities to use each one whenever you see fit.Con:-DensThe only issue I have with the game is repetitive den layouts. Every den comes down to a random number of rooms, which is fine, and I understand why they made this decision, but after a while you are just going through the same rooms over and over and over again. The random monsters and items in the den definitely make up for it though.Overall, this game is absolutely incredible. I wanted to wait until I had completed the game just to see if my opinion changed at all, but it didn't. I loved it from start to finish. I just started the endgame content, and I haven't messed with multiplayer much so I won't comment on those, but overall this game is a great time. If you're even remotely a fan of either pokemon-esque games or monster hunter. Please try this game.(Redeemed via steam key. Preordered on the 23rd through a different site that I always use, for clarity.)

_childDocuments_.review: + Beautiful open world and overall graphics+ Detailed ability animations+ Lots of Monsties to capture+ Lots of gear+ Decent voice acting+ Option to insta-win encounters when you're over-levelled+/- Combat is simplistic+/- Lots of endgame content, but not much point to play through unless you have someone to play co-op with you- Some Monstie capture requirements are poorly designed as they don't actually work. Eg. Telling you to trap an enraged Monster even though enraged monsters can't be trapped- Combat can get really repetitive thanks to the overall design- Online multiplayer is dead- Several consumables serve little to no purpose, due to how the turn based combat is designed.There are a lot of comparisons to Pokemon. But other than the ability to "capture" monsters and the turn-based combat, there really isn't much of a similarity. MHS2 is mainly story-focused with a simplistic battle system, while Pokemon is focused on "catching em all" and its deep "easy to learn, hard to master" battle system.While the battle system in MHS2 isn't "bad" per se, the biggest problem with it is the rock-paper-scissors system, and how optimal gameplay is centered around not taking damage at all. When your Rider and Monstie use the same type of move and beat a monster at rock-paper-scissors, you attack together, denying the enemy from taking an action. This style of play is essential to get you through the game, as monsters can potentially one shot you or your monstie if they land a blow.And unfortunately, this can also get extremely repetitive, as you'll be doing the same thing for pretty much every monster. Because you don't have a lot of HP, you can't really play any other way. For example, you can't really afford to take a turn to use a whetstone to increase your crit rate, as a monster landing a hit on you or your monstie can potentially one shot either of you. Every turn is valuable and cannot be wasted.But despite the mediocre combat system, I'd say the main strengths of MHS2 are the gorgeous open world and animations, large number of capturable monsters, and its lighthearted story and humour. The colours throughout the game always looked vibrant, and were a treat to look at. Because of that, I enjoyed most of the game.As for the endgame content, MHS2 stays true to the Monster Hunter tradition with the game being packed with endgame content. There is a lot of depth to optimising your gear and Monsties, but because I found the combat system kinda boring, I didn't see any point in going through the trouble of doing all that.Overall, I'd say this is definitely worth a play, but only really worth the buy at half off or more.

_childDocuments_.review: Pokemon Hunter: Wings of Rathalosit's a SOLID rock, paper, scissors style turn based RPG. That rock, paper, scissors game play has additional rock, paper, scissors elements mixed in so you can rock, paper, scissors while you rock, paper, scissors directly into a Tigrex's stupid face.The Story is alright, nothing AMAZING but it is serviceable enough to keep you going, voice acting is great, animations are fantastic.Graphically it is not the most mind blowing game out there but remember this came from the Switch and it does a decent job at beefing up the visuals for PC. Unlocked frame rate, 4k monitor support, controllers or Keyboard and mouse work great and are able to be completely re-bound to any keys(or buttons) you wish.Sound is great, there is even a totally pointless slider to adjust the pitch of monster battle cries. hearing a whiny Tigrex is funny I guess?There is an "endless" endgame here which is basically running randomly generated dungeons with either online cooperative play or an AI partner. The point being to find good "genes" for your "Monsties" to fully kit them out, a system not too dissimilar from Final Fantasy's Materia system only it's like Connect 4, but with nine slots in a grid, so maybe more like Tic-Tac-Toe or "Connect 3x3x3"... anyways, lining up matching elements(colors) and types(symbols) provides exponential gains to that element or skill's buff and some genes can provide your Monstie with new moves to use in combat. Essentially you can make a "Fire Type" Mizutsune for example or a Anjanath that uses water attacks. It's engaging enough and if you enjoy the core loop of collecting monsters, battling monsters and running, somewhat repetitive dungeons to min-max your party then the game will be PERFECT for you!There IS a PvP online element to the game where you battle your friends parties and can test your builds and test your mettle, but It is pretty dead at this point so you might want to consider scheduling that with them instead of hoping to find a match naturally, Maybe check out the game's DISCORD server for other players to party up with and what have you.It's a great game, I spent close to 120 hours with it on Switch and couldn't help but start over on PC (finally) because I just missed that core loop.As a long time Monster Hunter fan and someone who fell off Pokemon at a young age once there was like 500+ monsters to remember this scratches all those itches while being charming, funny and moderately addicting.

_childDocuments_.review: A must play game for fans of Monster Hunter. As a JRPG it stands on its own merits for gameplay and mechanics, and combined with the setting and faithful recreation of monster attacks and unique attributes, it makes for very enjoyable and nostalgic experience. Stories 2 has a mix of light-hearted simplicity and just-enough complexity to make it addicting and make you want to finish it. The main campaign is 30-50 hours long, with a wide range of time you can spend stopping to smell the roses and mess around with the monster breeding system. The actual structured content for post-game is about 10-20 hours long once you have assembled a team capable of taking it on. I won't spoil what the post-game consists of, but I will say that it an interesting and welcome, and thematically consistent PvE challange that is not tacked on as an afterthought. There are potentially hundreds of hours of time you can spend in post-game creating and editing monster genes, and this is a casual gameplay type of activity that is relaxing and simple and goal oriented. The multiplayer has problems right now, but the developers are working on it. I can't comment on that section because I didn't want to risk my save being corrupted.In terms of content, there is good value for your $60 here, though much of it is a bit 'samey' after you figure out the gameplay. It's no MMO, but it's a very strong entry in the single player monster breeding genre, even without taking into account the franchise. Overall 8/10.All the DLC is cosmetic garbage you will never even notice. I don't understand why it exists or what capcom is thinking. I cannot imagine that anybody cares about their stupid mascot navirou character enough to spend money on dressing him up. I will never buy DLC of this type.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are planning to get this game just for the combat, creature collecting and customization, you will probably be satisfied.  Though I feel the game is a bit too expensive for just that.  Maybe wait for a sale.If you want to immerse yourself into this title, forget it.  The story is offensively bad.  The music isn't amazing and is often times completely absent.  Wandering the world or exploring dens with nothing but ambient sounds is far from enjoyable.The story though is really what I hate the most about this.  It was passable for most of the game.  But the final 1/5th of the story is so painfully bad that I would recommend anyone interested in the story to avoid this game completely.  For those that had a passing interest in the story, skip all cutscenes.  It is for the best.  The final bosses, their motivations and all the contrivances around them made me genuinely upset.  It's not that they are simple, it's that they are nonsensical.  This isn't a story made for a child.  This is a story made by a child.I will continue to play the after story game as there is plenty of content there, but if I ever dream to replay this game, I will absolutely turn on my own music and skip as much dialogue as I can.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the Monster Hunter series and never played the first "Stories" entrance.However, I'm almost 9 hours in and can't drop this game, the combat feels unique, every monster has it's own quirks and style which is amazing. Some compare this to a Pokémon-ish game and to a certain extent that's true. But these monsters feel a lot more unique and, unlike Pokémon, I actually give names to these creatures and feel more connected to them, I know it sounds weird. The world is huge, there are so many monsters and the JRPG combat takes me back to when I used to play FF when I was young.Now for cons, the game runs amazingly smooth, never had a crash, but the mouse controls tend to work against you. At many times the mouse is unable to control the camera, which is easily remedied by pressing the right mouse button. The graphics are okay, not amazing, which has it's charm sure, but it's obvious this game is a port. Dungeons may become repetitive for some, if not many, people. One critique, but that's just me. It would be amazing, since it's on pc already, to also be able to play this on xbox. This game deserves to be played on a 65" TV!Capcom, honestly, keep 'em coming. Been a MH fan since I was 13 and it's still one of my most favorite franchises.

_childDocuments_.review: The game shines with its engaging narrative, featuring a compelling plot filled with emotional depth and interesting character arcs. The story of a world threatened by the mysterious Wings of Ruin keeps players hooked and eager to uncover the truth.The game’s charming, anime-inspired art style stands out with its colorful, detailed visuals and expressive character designs, creating an inviting and immersive world.The turn-based combat system is refreshing and strategic, offering a break from the real-time action of mainline Monster Hunter games. The addition of “Kinship” skills and monster alliances adds more depth to battles.The ability to collect, hatch, and train various monsters provides a satisfying yet strategic element to gameplay. With every monster having different skills, advantages and disadvantages. Pick your monsters wisely for battles! The customization options for both the player’s character and their monsters enhance the overall experience.The game features a diverse range of environments and regions to explore, each with its own unique creatures and resources, encouraging thorough exploration and discovery.Players may find the pacing to be slow at times, particularly during the early stages of the game. The story and gameplay can feel a bit drawn-out, with cutscenes, dialogue-heavy sections and frequent back and forth moving.While the combat system is innovative, it can become repetitive very easily. The reliance on similar strategies and tactics for various battles may lead to a sense of monotony for some players.The behavior of AI-controlled allies in battles can sometimes be inconsistent, leading to less effective strategies and occasional frustration during key fights as the AI pulls some random garbage on you.Personally I had a extremely smooth experience from start to finish but there have been reports of occasional performance issues and technical glitches, such as frame rate drops and minor bugs, your mileage may vary here depending on your hardware combination.For players who have completed the main story, the endgame content may feel somewhat lacking. While there are post-game activities, they might not be as engaging or varied as some players would hope for.Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a delightful and engaging RPG that successfully expands the Monster Hunter universe with its unique turn-based combat and rich storytelling. While it may excel in creating an immersive world and offering strategic gameplay, it is not without its challenges. Slow pacing, repetitive elements, and technical issues are aspects to consider before purchasing. Nonetheless, for hardcore fans of the series and newcomers alike, the game provides a memorable and enjoyable adventure that is well worth experiencing.

_childDocuments_.review: First I'd like to say although I'm not new to the Monster Hunter franchise, I have never played the Monster Hunter Stories games before this one.That being said, I'll explain what I felt were good and bad (and ugly) aspects of the game. - Monsters (Called Monsties) are collected through obtaining eggs from Monster Dens. The system is fun albeit repetitive after a while. It appeals to people who like that "RNG Fishing" kind of game and trying to get the best monsters via luck. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: MHS2: Wings of Ruin looks, feels, and plays like the first game. If you liked the first one, you'll love this one too. There's a generous demo/trial version of this game available to anyone on the fence. This game is easily worth $20 on sale.The gameplay loop consists of loot grinding, egg hunting, weapon/armor crafting, and monster collection. The turn-based combat is based off a rock-paper-scissors model with weapon-specific skills and monster-specific kinship skills. The monsters themselves can be customized using the gene system and rite of channeling -- each monster can have up to 9 active or passive skills that can be upgraded or replaced. The story takes place decades after the first game, but because your character is a new Rider, you won't miss out from not recognizing a few of the NPCs. The story is straightforward and centered on the relationship between humans and monsters. You're gonna get a Ratholos, and you WILL love him.Edit: The endgame is satisfying yet repetitive. You can also complete co-op quests by yourself, which I didn't try out until post-story. Still having plenty of fun grinding levels and genes after 150+ hours in game.Because MH:W came out in between the first game and this one, it gets a better roster that includes World-premiers like Legiana, Nergigante, Paolumu, and Tobi-Kadachi.Best part about MHS2 on PC is that it's moddable. If you hate the skimpy nature of most female armor sets, you can grab the Underarmor mod. Someone give Avinia some leggings, please. It's cold in Loloska.
