_childDocuments_.review: was exactly what I was expecting it to be but hoping it wouldn’t! Much like VTM:Bloodlines and Red Embrace: Hollywood (I haven’t played Coteries of New York), you play as a recently turned fledgling whose sire isn’t in the picture. This time you play as Julia, a former investigative journalist who is now the bottom of the barrel in vampire society. Self-loathing, outspoken and a chronic chain smoker. The future doesn’t look bright for this lost soul – well literally because you know, no sun. When a sudden murder needs investigating, Julia is thrown head first into a political game that she is not only unqualified for, but also no one is really willing to help her out. It’s clear she is a pawn and a disposable one but being the type of person she is, she soldiers on in the hopes of busting this case wide open.  Needless to say, this shares a lot of common ground with other vampire games; newly turned. No sire to guide her. Shouldered with responsibilities far above her status and way too much politics; it’s not exactly original. This version also has a heavy side dose of religion. Nether are things I really enjoy reading. I do however, like being the underdog that no one really suspects. The one everyone takes for granted and doesn’t believe will ever succeed. Extra points for being sassy too.  The artwork is beautifully dark and envisions children of the night quite nicely with it’s gritty, stylish and grungy design. Animated backgrounds and atmospheric sounds/music really push this to the next level as well. As someone who can appreciate the beauty in darkness, this was nice eye candy for my twisted little mind. The cast of eccentric characters was the cherry on the top to this delicious ice-cream Sunday!  Considering Vampire: The Masquerade is in it’s own universe I was a little annoyed when there was mentions of a pandemic that originated from China in 2020 – I mean, really? REALLY? I don’t know about other people but I play games to get away from all that chaos outside. I don’t want it to needlessly show up in the thing I’m trying to use to escape mention of the damn virus and when I say “needlessly”, I do mean it. It literally had no effect on the story what so ever apart from a few lines here and there that could quite easily have been replaced with – oh I don’t know – anything else!!  Something that really let me down was the sheer lack of clan traits. For example, I’m a huge fan of Malkavian’s. I adore the insanity that was displayed in VTM:B but there was no crazy to be found here. In fact, only Julia really displayed any clan traits and that was merely necessity to keep the relationship with her human friend for the ending decisions. Completely disappointed! The choice on how you get the good and bad ending was  To get the good ending  To get the bad ending Overall, not a fan of the visual novel version and I’d be very hard pressed to recommend this to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game for what it was, up until the ending, and the way the game ended shifted my vote from a "yes" to a reluctant "no".For most of the game, I was perfectly fine with feeling confused and relatively powerless as I tried to sort out a mystery while the powerful vampire clans who secretly control New York City pursued their own labyrinthine private agendae, and typically got in my way, or blocked my intentions while doing so.From the get-go this story is about being a "small fish" trying to accomplish certain things while large, unseen forces affect the environment around you.Even when you take on the job of solving a mystery on behalf the vampire lords, it quickly becomes clear that certain factions are more interested in blocking your progress than assisting it.The trouble comes toward the end of the game, though. Perhaps it was just a quirk of my particular playthrough, but when answers arrived, they arrived in a sort of "infodump" kind of rush, and there wasn't much context to what I learned.In the end sequence, I was pretty much still silent, and powerless to affect events. Ironically, the game awarded me the "Bad Ending" achievement for an ending that seemed inevitable all along -- an ending which didn't actually seem so bad;  more like, the best resolution one could hope to achieve.From the beginning, the game essentially hammers at you that you are a small creature surrounded by large forces which care nothing for you. Perhaps I missed some crucial branching choice which would've opened up other options, but the game does not allow you to save game-states as you play (i.e. saving automatically exits the game afterward); it doesn't even allow you to backtrack dialogue as you play to perhaps make a different choice.As such, the only way to try for a different ending is to replay the entire game again from the top, and while the game is well-made, once you already know the secret mysteries which lurk behind the central plot, replays lose a lot of what makes the game interesting. I don't think it's worth it, myself.This is a very well-made game in most respects, and it absolutely nails the sort of moody, introspective modern-gothic tone one would expect from a Vampire: The Masquerade game.Unfortunately, to preserve its storytelling, I felt that the game sacrificed too much player agency, and did not make clear when certain actions or reactions by the player might be significant. When every action feels equally important or unimportant as you play, you're basically just guessing your way through events -- and the game's structure doesn't make replays involving enough to warrant the time spent slogging through familiar content again, in the hope of seeing different outcomes.Short Version: A reluctant "no" from me. A well-made story game in so many respects, but certain design decisions genuinely diminish a player's engagement with the tale.

_childDocuments_.review: Fully recommend this game. Liked it even more than the prequel (Coteries), and, to my mind, these two games are best played in succession. Keep in mind, though, that the praise is in no small part due to the personality and overall vibe of the main character, so I'm probably somewhat biased because of my preferences. Julia is written very persuasively, and I could clearly see her motivations and inner turmoil. I would even say she is the farthest character from a 'blank slate' that I've seen for some time now, and definitely very high in my personal 'the MC who has a strong personality in interactive fiction' ranking. Naturally, I couldn't help but be absolutely won over by her.Here, the story is more linear than in the first game: less variety, less impact of your choices of how Julia spends her time, and the same course of overarching events in every playthrough. But, at the same time, this game implements a neat system of Traits that determine how the story concludes, so you get to have an actual influence on the ending you'll get. Shadows of New York calls the options 'good' and 'bad', and it's certainly par for the course - but only from a vampire's perspective. Not going to spoil the plot, so I'll stop my comments on it there.However, I definitely want to take time to sing a few praises to the art, animation, and soundtrack. The backgrounds, the cinematics, and the melodies accompanying your playthrough are all simply amazing and tie into each other nicely to create an atmosphere that, again, has a very clear character that confidently pulls you in. The developers also took note of some complaints directed at the previous game's character sprites (namely, them having almost no variety despite the narrative): here, the events of the plot reflect on the characters where it's important, and Julia in particular has several very striking expressions to depict her attitude to the situation or general mood.Overall, one of the best story- and universe-based VN experiences I've had. Going to go watch some of the mentioned films now, as the game is ripe with cultural references I'm interested in exploring.

_childDocuments_.review: weaves a familiar tale. Yet it is not a tale familiar out of triteness, but rather in its bleak and despairing contemporaneity.  artfully depicts our 2020 hell-scape, holds it up as a mirror and doesn’t so much ask whether or not we’re ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as yell it in our faces.It is a tale of a debauched, grotesquely wealthy elite presiding over a city of broken, desperate people, haunted by an impending apocalypse—climate-induced, technological, viral, pick your horror—precious few seem inclined to curtail, let alone prevent.And this apocalypse cares not a whit for whether you’re human or vampire; after all, Kindred were once human themselves, and its ruling body, the Camarilla—so intent on maintaining the status quo at all costs—a potent metaphor for a global system that refuses to change, adapt, or evolve.Even when everything is at stake (soz). is a game about politics and the way politics is infused into every facet of our beings. The boldness of its narrative impressed and enthralled me, and I want more of it in my games in these oh-so-urgent times of ours.That being said, it’s a difficult prospect writing a story of ‘now’, and one I’ve always been inclined to stay clear of. It runs the risk of trying to capture those defining moments, those shocking turning-points in the historical narrative unfolding in real-time, and rendering them shallow, even cringe-inducing, as some level of distance is always necessary to properly understand it.Somehow  avoids these pitfalls, managing to feel at one with both the lore of the vast world it takes place in  our own fraught, ruptured reality.Sadly, that’s all just texture for the most part. Whilst the writing is solid, demonstrating a strong understanding of the culture wars currently being fought across the digital landscape and gratifyingly skewing towards the inclusive and progressive, it’s the narrative itself that struggles to assert itself.Polish developer Draw Distance’s  is billed a “stand-alone expansion” to their , which was released last year. It’s a visual novel, meaning the story is told purely through text and the captivating backdrops each character scene provides.The expansion takes you back to the Big Apple, but this time you’re playing as a newly-inaugurated member of the Lasombra Clan, one Julia Sowinski. The Lasombra, an aristocratic clan that derive pleasure in exerting power over others, are known for casting no reflections—they are visible only to the naked eye. In an increasingly digital world, that’s quite an interesting wrinkle, especially for someone so self-absorbed as Julia.When a local vampire bigwig is found dead—the ‘Final Death’, as it’s known—Julia is cast into the unenviable role of investigator. Given the deceased was the leader of a rival faction to the ruling elite, well, the investigation is going to be a tricky one. A chain-smoking nobody afflicted with a deeply vampiric form of ennui, Julia isn’t exactly thrilled with the role, but it’s an opportunity to climb the ladder—providing no one kicks it down, first.And you just know they will.As a visual novel, the narrative-driven  offers choices throughout the story, leaving interactions with the city’s inhabitants in your hands, at least to an extent. I don’t feel like there were nearly enough possible routes to take, with conversations mostly being moulded by decisions you had made earlier. That’s fine in the sense that it shows your (sparse) choices are shaping Julia’s traits, but a lot of the time it felt like it was out of my control and the path thoroughly predetermined. The game’s well-written enough to coast on by, but more input would’ve been welcome.See, Julia isn’t a blank slate. It’s about how  want to take Julia forward from where she’s at at the beginning of the game; how will  use those base materials to crack the case?She starts out as a down-on-her luck freelance copywriter barely able to pay rent, her entire life going to ♥♥♥♥ around her. She’s bitter and jaded, tired of seeing the powerful thrive and everyone else rot in the gutter. Social mobility? Forget about it. You’re a cog in a machine, Julia thinks. Hard to disagree with her there.The tragedy is that once she’s inaugurated into vampire society, she finds it’s no different from the world she’d grown to hate, if only because it decided from the outset to hate her. The same hypocrisies, the same greed, and the same self-interested power-brokers. Only with a taste for blood, and lots of it. The game’s about how you choose to navigate this quagmire, but it’s only half successful in its aims. I never felt like I had much of a grip on the Julia I was shaping, which led to the credits rolling without my even realising we’d come to the end of the story.The murder mystery itself is underwhelming and unfulfilling, even if that’s the very point (and I suspect it is). There’s a potent point there and one I will not spoil, but it’s simply not enough to justify itself, which left me feeling pretty disappointed by the whole affair. It may be that’s just a consequence of the path I had taken, but I have my doubts about that: there weren’t enough divergent options to take me to a truly shocking place, as the case is clear from its earliest stages.The journey itself is visually enchanting, at least.The World of Darkness is where the  stories take place, but for all its thematic gloom whenever it takes shape in the video game medium it is rich in colour, mood and texture. Troika Games’ beloved  was a murky, humid, noirish L.A, and next year’s follow-up—forget it, I ain’t typing the title—looks to accomplish something similar with its wet and dreary Seattle., on the other hand, is an enticing mix of pink and blue neon hues—the night illumined by technological interfaces that won’t ever register Julia’s face again. And, every so often, the golden glare of an Upper East Side mansion where she’s never really going to be welcome, not now, and perhaps not ever.A most vampiric form of ennui indeed.Vampirism has seen many critical interpretations over the decades, one of which being infection, disease, something that’s eating away inside of you.  acknowledges this, but at its most audacious it compares it to the growing existential dread that permeates all of us in our divided, fragile twenty-first century. If only it had gone even further with it.I wanted to love . Its atmosphere is intoxicating, its imagery gorgeously seductive, and the writing sharp. I’ve even been listening to the soundtrack by Resina, with its dangerous, moody tunes that bring the imagery to life. The ingredients are all present and accounted for, but it just isn’t able to bring itself to a cohesive statement, which is so frustrating when it’s so,  close to taking hold of something more.Maybe next time.Originally published on the .

_childDocuments_.review: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York is great as a novella, but not much of a game. The sheer amount of clicking to read each new bit of dialog, with so few choices along the way, means I can't bring myself to play again. And even those few choices seem pointless. Its precursor, Coteries, allowed character personalization and a choice of side quests to make it worth replaying, with an introduction that could be clicked through fairly quickly. Shadows feels like a hundred just to get to the embrace, and a thousand to reach the ending, at which point the text leads you to believe you'll be allowed a climactic decision, but there is none. The character has already made it for you. Coteries led me to purchase Shadows; Shadows leaves me unwilling to risk buying any more products from this publisher. I say that with no rancor. It's just a disappointing fact.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played the first game, you have a certain veneer of choice - you have an introductory three clans, and you have a certain amount of choice in which quest threads to pursue.Shadows of New York removes all of that choice - you're one character, you don't form a coterie, and your nightly options are extremely limited.  The story is still very good, but there's no real game to it - purely a visual novel that you click on occasionally.There's certainly no meaningful choices, even though there's a rather arbitrary "bad ending" and "good ending" a la Mass Effect 3.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm new to the Vampire: The Masquerade franchise. I really enjoyed learning about the world and the court intrigue at the heart of the game. I appreciated the glossary, and it made it accessible for me. I understand that a long running vampire franchise must have the experience of becoming a vampire in depth in their various games and media. The moral dilemma at the heart of being a vampire- having to consume human blood to survive- may very well seem trite to the creators at this point. However, it's a question that is absolutely essential if you want to establish a character with some credibility.Because Julia comes off as a huge hypocrite. She detests the media agency she works for because they are unwilling to stand up to a shadowy corporation- only to join a cabal of vampires that is every bit as menacing and controlling the entity they posed as once she has a taste of power. She is set up as a decent person, so the decision to not question her turn is a bizarre one. Yes, she's suffered a lot, but her last human act was fighting for good. This is a character who should be fighting for independence or refusing to work for pretentious elites- even if it ends in her destruction. She mentions her family and girlfriend being used as hostages, but never whether she truly needs hostages to stay in her position. If she's going to change, show us the path of that change. Don't just plop her into the power structure involving some truly detestable characters and show her desire to work her way up. And I found it hard to care about anyone. These are rich, powerful people with superpowers without much emotionally vulnerability to make them interesting. I didn't feel like there was being risked except Julia's place in the hierarchy, which I didn't think she should care about anyway. It felt more like chance to pretend to hang with the rich, cool vampires than any examination into what could be a truly interesting culture. Also, while there were some non-white characters, I have lived in New York and it's far, far more diverse than this, to the point where you wonder what the explanation is. If you're going to set a story in NYC, have it reflect the city. This isn't even a politically motivated point- it just makes the story seem inauthentic. I think this story would have been a lot better if we were able to direct the personality of the character more. That way if she were to engage in hypocrisy, it would be our own. It would make it a lot more engaging and immediate.

_childDocuments_.review: is a visual novel set in the World of Darkness universe. You play as Julia, investigating a murder that disrupts the NYC vampire community. The game's strength lies in its narrative, where choices impact relationships and lead to one of two endings: a "redemptive" one and a ruthless one, each resonating differently from human and vampire perspectives.The dual-ending structure is notable, with a "bad" ending prioritizing human life and a "good" ending focusing on power and clan. This dynamic adds depth, reflecting the complex morality of vampiric existence. Achievements encourage exploring various narrative paths and multiple playthroughs.For players of , this game offers a fresh perspective on familiar characters, enhancing the story's depth and intrigue.

_childDocuments_.review: First hour seems boring, but the crescendo is so worth it. This game is clearly very special, it's bleeding style, and it makes you hungry for more. If it sucks later I'll edit a warning here, but I trust it now, even though I hate VNs.An hour in and this game single-handedly convinced me to unblock the Visual Novel tag. I got it in some bundle, had basically no interest, just wanted to check what it's like and got drawn in by the presentation. That hour seemed too edgy, long-winded, and mundane, but without it I wouldn't have experienced what it led up to so vividly. And the atmosphere kept me there long enough, then elevated the real start of the game beyond what I thought VNs, or any work of fiction in general, could do.I think the emotion or combination of emotions in that moment was the equivalent of seeing a new color. Haven't had the chance to keep playing for a couple days, but the game has stayed on my mind the whole time since. That moment, the music, the whole presentation was just hypnotic. Like a vampire's charisma.It's all about the atmosphere. The realistic (if cringe at points) thoughts and dialogue that paint a person so well, along with a soundtrack that fits scenes perfectly (and from looking up more of it - it echoes shades of itself later like something John Williams would do), and such appropriate animated image backdrops (just inspiring yet abstract enough)... Together they create this beautiful, surreal vibe that fits the setting (World of Darkness) and vampire stories in general better than I've seen from them in anything else. And just different music in a scene you've been at before immediately gives you (and doesn't just set) the right mood, even before you start reading the text.I can't see this atmosphere being achieved on paper or film, because it comes from how you take in the stimuli of what's happening to your own senses, as the protagonist (at least partially). And that's why the intro is slow, and why the combination of senses the game influences multiplies their individual value. I started out not relating to the character at all, to seeing a lot of myself and people I know in her fears/doubts/disappointments, to basically blurring the line between us, just in time to experience a feeling along with her that can't exist in the real world. At least I assume not without mescaline.Getting this surreal, romanticized/horror/noir? vibe, is how you portray a world of vampires. And it doesn't happen unless you're directly involved, immersed, it would come off as too cheesy to be taken seriously. Instead it lulls you into a sort of lucid dream feeling, the kind where style is the substance. The game demonstrates the strengths of interactivity as a way to experience art, and not even by relying on many dialogue choices.So many words, and I think I'm both overhyping it and not doing it justice. Basically, it offered me a very interesting emotion I never imagined, let alone expected to experience something that powerful from a visual novel. And it could be strictly subjective, but there's clearly something to this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: Whoever did not experienced RPG in real life, should throw the stone first. Even right now.But whoever would like to gain knowledge on that matter and start from something simple, Vampire The Masquerade might be a good choice for a starter. Delightful in all of that is a matter of fact, that from this title you cannot expect any fireworks, shocking tales to be told, or action twists in the "dirty harry" style. Instead of that, you receive a casual game, where industrial music, artwork and a simple story about female "goth" protagonist are well balanced. If you're fan of vampire motives, folklore and all blood-sucking topics, congratulations; during the time spend on that title, you might feel relaxed and enjoy it to all the lasts bits of it.[MINI SPOILER ALERT]If I have to complain at this point, I feel like the first part presented more choices and options to interact with. Compared to that, this part - is shortly a continuation of some plots from part one. But clearly in case of main character, there are some gasps, some limitations to the way how things can be narrated. While first part of this game-series was enriched with additional classes of characters, here in the second one, we just focus on a single female persona, which has to follow only one of two possible paths created during the dialogue options. While the 1st game gave us a choice between one female or two male characters, each with different abilities as a vampires, the 2nd gives us Julia - girl that represents only one class, vampire which keeps following one type of an attitude, and does not have much to be told - rather than helping in present bits of the other character lives or attitudes.[MINI SPOILER ALERT OVER]In total, I do not think my time was wasted. Since I need sometimes minimalism and simplicity in games, I have found that exact thing here. I had my coffee, played, made different choices, and in about 6h of chill, managed to finish the whole game with 100% of achievement. If you have to choose between a typical work shift, versus spending it on that game... You can easily find the correct answer yourself. All players looking for very rich story-line in indie games, should not bother with this title. All vampires enthusiasts that tend to play in noir games or something crime related - gonna enjoy it, especially if RPG is not a red flag for them.

_childDocuments_.review: An unfortunate case of a lot of good parts not coming together to form an interesting whole. The art and music, as in Coteries of New York, is fantastic. The amount of unique assets is small, but they're all very well done. However, the engine used is the exact same as Coteries of New York. If you've played any other Visual Novel prepare to be shocked by the lack of QOL features. No rollback, no save slots (only one exit save slot), no hyperlinks to their glossary, it's all very bare bones. There is a trait system tied to the player's response to choices, but it's barely more than a list. Depending on the player's answers, a list of different personality traits will build up over the course of the game. This has minimal impact until the ending, of which there are two. If your answers skew towards ruthlessness, you will get one ending. If your answers skew towards compromise, you will get the other. There are a handful of exclusive choices between who to talk to, but probably not enough to justify a second or third run through the otherwise linear story.That aside, the story is fine. The protagonist is abrasive and self-absorbed but other characters routinely react to her behaviour with disapproval and condescension. There is no character creation or role playing but you are given some chances to work on her behaviour. She's not a Mary Sue but YMMV on this. The weakest point here is her inner monologue.  Prepare for lots and lots of pop culture references, many already tired and dated at the time of this review. It's constant and distracting. The story is less ambitious and smaller in scope than Coteries of New York, playing out more like a side story or second chapter than a totally new game.Shadows of New York is not worth playing without having completed Coteries of New York first and the lack of any meaningful improvement is a shame. If you liked Coteries of New York, you probably won't hate Shadows, but it's the inferior of the two.

_childDocuments_.review: is a visual novel in the World of Darkness setting. While the art is outstanding, the saving system, GUI in general, the choices and the story make it hard to recommend. The writing and music are fine, the VA is not present. The protagonist is predetermined, from the name to the background to the clan. There are some choices that do determine the ending, but I was unable to follow the logic. It is possible to skip to the next choice by holding Ctrl. There is no gallery to view the backgrounds and CG, but there is a dictionary with 1-paragraph descriptions.To elaborate on the saving system, there are 3 auto-saving slots, one per playthrough, and the game just deletes the save after the playthrough is finished. It was the same in the previous game and seeing it not fixed is disappointing. While it is possible to use Windows Explorer, the developers should have implemented manual saving at will as in any technically-decent visual novel.

_childDocuments_.review: Great soundtrack, great art, and mostly great writing. There's some eye-rolly stuff right away in the beginning, but once you are Embraced it finds its stride. I like playing as Julia, and I buy into the relationship and tensions with Dakota. This is a natural sequel to Coteries of New York that I think is better written and more interesting on the whole. I'm partial to Lasombra and familiar with VtM lore, so that helps. Coteries felt like a primer on Vampire the Masquerade, and Shadows feels like "Okay, now here's the type of story you could tell in this world."That said, this lacks replayability (though I played through twice), but I can see myself coming back to it like returning to a comfortable favorite novel. I don't feel that the choices I made as Julia really altered a whole lot in the end though. I think it's interesting that the "good" ending appears to be , but also having a delineation between a Good and Bad ending makes it pretty clear that your story can end in only two ways (three, if you die).I still recommend the game. Maybe grab it on sale if the price seems steep, but I would pay $12 for a decent graphic novel/novella so I think it's worth the price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming back for seconds after not being impressed by Coteries of New York does sound like me, but in this case I was pleasantly surprised by Shadows of New York. I think playing more to its strengths as a Visual Novel was what ended up working in game's favor. Top shelf production for the genre notwithstanding, of course.Following her stint as a very mortal journalist we see Julia Sowinski get embraced into a newly-minted Camarilla clan Lasombra. Provided you have any familiarity with Vampire: the Masquerade this is already a hook beyond belief seeing as clan switched allegiances and narratively you're a solitary Turncoat in New York. What follows is Julia getting assigned a task to resolve a murder mystery of a disliked elder and seemingly set up for failure by the Prince. I wouldn't say playing the previous game is mandatory, but you'll strongly benefit if you have seeing as almost all characters make a return and current crisis is set after Coteries. If anything it's once again a showpiece of Camarilla politics and World of Darkness itself.So what actually sets Shadows of New York above the last game for me? How it really isn't trying to deliver crunch-based mechanics only to half-ass them in the attempt. Protagonist is fixed and has a fleshed out personality of her own. Not that I'm a fan of this whole “alternative, whiny millennial” mindset, but it grounds a character who has a lot to say about the contemporary world. Strawberry jam aka Hunger mechanic is a non-issue here which in turns leads to more liberal use of Disciplines and not worrying about feeding crippling your options. I was surprised by how decisions you make throughout the game actually build up to one of the two endings, though. This time around endings truly ARE meaningfully different.Some surprising callbacks to Redemption of all games perhaps endeared Shadows of New York to me more than it deserves, but in a sense it embodies the new roleplaying edition rather well – an intimate journey with your own shadows.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10: So-So.A direct sequel to Coteries, Shadows of New York dispenses with the protagonist of Coteries and replaces them with an established persona. Gone is your chance to select an origin story and explore a new vampire world, rather you’re already an established member of the political ladder now.There are two endings this time (big woop) and they all focus on your actions (aggregated) over the course of the storyline. I can confirm, whatever actions you choose the story outcome is mostly the same, with changes being superficial. Again, fairly disappointing. Even the optional sections are just there to pad out the story.Really, they should dispense with the pretence of writing a choice driven novel and just make it a generic kinetic novel in my opinion, because this route is fairly mundane, it doesn’t really embrace the strengths of the visual novel genre, which is partially why I’m throwing it in as a choose your own adventure genre.Again, it is very short, clipping in at three and a half hours, which is fairly disappointing. There’s not enough new art, a lot of it is recycled from Coteries – heck, the entire cast is recycled here, so considering they had a lot of assets already in place, I was hoping to see something of a 20-30 hour epic with the resources on hand. I guess for me, having read many visual novels, epics and shorts, I need to be seeing more from this to elevate it beyond being just vanilla.The story is okay, it’s a personal one, a political one with vampires, a few modern references, sometimes it tries far too hard, sometimes it is pompous, unbearably so. But in the end, it is just flat, which is a great shame.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: While my playthrough of Coteries of New York is still fresh in my mind, I feel it is now the best time to review Shadows of New York, its continuation. If not for the fact that my review of the previous game was written well after both of them were published, I'd have exclaimed "Well I'll be damned, somebody actually listened to me!". The main pain of Coteries was that your choices didn't matter and the game streamlined you to the same ending. That is not the case with Shadows. The story is still not exactly branching out, but at least it offers you 2 different endings. The narrative feels much more personal as well, since you play as a preset character, Julia of the Lasombra Clan, whose personality is affected by your decisions. The game is rich in Julia's inner monologue and it is there that those Traits you develop are reflected, offering slightly different dialogues and comments on certain scenes. So storywise - Shadows is a huge improvement from the already good-but-in-the-end-leaving-you-disappointed Coteries.Visually, it's beautiful. The game reuses a few backgrounds from its predecessor, but with updated graphics. The scenes are still hand painted, now with more dynamic elements and animations. The character models are redesigned in case of most returning characters and are not the same cut-and-paste illustrations throughout the whole story. It's a real pretty thing, Shadows. Reaaaally nice on the eyes.Music is great as well. Even as I write this review, Steam is adding another hour to my playtime, because the game is running in the background just so that I can listen to the main menu theme. It really sets the atmosphere and fits the Lasombra Clan I think. Pretty thing. Worth paying extra money for, really.So now that I've painted a picture almost as pretty as Shadows, let's talk about what's not awesome. I did 2 playthroughs, gathering all the achievements, not really skipping any dialogues, and that took me, according to Steam, around 10 hours. The narrative doesn't exactly branch out - you get to make some small decisions that affect your dialogues or minor descriptions, but there are 5 points which do matter. It is at those points that Julia develops Traits. As far as I can tell, you could assign + and - to them and near the end, they are counted. You have more -, you get ending B, and + for ending A. It's a simple system and in that simplicity lies a certain narrative problem for me. The decision you make – or rather, the Traits you develop – are of the same importance. So, without spoiling too much, it could mean that you are a ruthless, aggressive monster lying through your teeth, but end up going down a conformist and pacifistic route. It is probably because of that I found one of the endings just…meh. But that’s subjective.Another thing – being a Vampire in World of Darkness is a lot about controlling your inner Beast. Coteries showed it through the Hunger mechanic. If you went without feeding for too long and kept on using your powers, you WOULD lose control. Whether it was relevant to the plot or not is another matter, but the idea was there. In Shadows, feeding and Hunger are mentioned, but even if I went crazy and used my vampiric powers at every opportunity, nothing happened. So a bit of a step back. Speaking of Vampires and their powers, you play as part of Lasombra Clan. I didn’t know too much about them, being a Gangrel fan and overall more of a Werewolf person, but they are the masters of shadows, with some books describing them manipulating those like physical tendrils and so on. Maybe I’ve picked wrong dialogue options, but I sure wish there were more descriptions of that. Gimme my shadowy tentacle monsters. Well then, to sum it up:PROS:+ beautiful visuals. I’m buying the artbook.+ awesome, atmospheric music. Buying the soundtrack too.+ well written dialogues+ again, believable characters, though maybe a bit less complex than what Coteries showed+ on the other hand, a much more personalised story and more complex protagonist+ your choices matter this time+ it’s a really pretty thing, ok?CONS:- step back when it comes to Hunger and vampiric powers- very simply mechanic for determining the ending- the game is short. Internal monologue hides it, but it’s very short actually.SUBJECTIVE:+/- Game is very focused on main plot, thus offering less optional quests than Coteries and less chances to do them. On one hand I feel that it improves the overall flow of the story and its quality, on the other, some might miss having side quests.+/- In my personal opinion, one of the endings is…anticlimactic would be the best word I think. It makes sense I suppose, but with the traits my Julia developed in that playthrough and her “speech” at the end it was a bit of a let down for me. But the other one was awesome.SPOILER ALERT:I do love how the endings are called the Good and the Bad one. It’s very clever.END OF SPOILER ALERT.Overall, I recommend this one, without a doubt and with clear conscience. It does make you want to come back to it. Which I shall do immediately.

_childDocuments_.review: I surely did make the right choice by waiting for some chill summer nights to play the game. Smoothly flowing story, superb music and Julia- who not just looks hot but also acts hot. 10/10This one turned out to be a lot more enjoyable than Coteries of New York. The events in this game take up after the incidents of Coteries of New York, It was great to see all the familiar faces once again but mostly what hooked me was the main character, Julia. Though Coteries seems as if it's offering 3 different characters to play as ,none of them actually make any significant difference. And what's more is that all of them were dull sounding and looking characters, so I think focusing on only one character and making them so that they're potentially remarkable to the player was a good choice in Shadows of NY. Though writing might seem simpler in this one compared to the previous one, I gotta say that I prefer the recent a lot more. I remember forcing myself through some parts of Coteries to finish and be finally done with but in Shadows I finished the game in just 2 sittings, it went on very smoothly and it was a relief to not being obliged to go through pragaraphs of trivial stuff. I played Bloodlines prior to these two VNs and that's pretty much it for my VTM lore knowledge and this one did introduce me to some lore bits to those I was a total stranger of, which was quite pleasant.  My only negative remark would be about the game's art. Not to the quality of it but the quantity. There were few scenes which were recycled straight from Coteries, why? You are making a new game, New York surely didn't remain the same way as it was back in Coteries. I'd like to also see more of character art, and more variety in general. _childDocuments_.review: Got this as a gift a long time ago and finally got around to playing it.First off if you want to compare this to the first entry 'Coteries of New York' you're probably going to be disappointed. You play as one character throughout the story and there are no chances to form allegiances like you could in the first game. The writing isn't as expansive as in Coteries but we also aren't given 3 characters to choose from this time. There are also only 2 endings and 1 instant death ending you can get. Despite some negative points compared to the first entry I still found this to be an enjoyable experience. The way the Lasombra clan is represented in this iteration is really interesting and engaging as a player. The character can take sometime to grow on you but once you get an idea of her as a person it starts to click and become an enjoyable experience. I will say however, it doesn't feel like there are as many choices in this game but it seems to be built on making 'big choices' throughout the game which applies certain 'traits' to the character. This can mean that sometimes the narrative will keep moving with no input from the player based on what they picked before. What I mean with this is certain personality traits picked up like aggression or impatience may influence the narrative a different way. This is the same with the "good ending" where you will be pressing next a lot and reading along. (I still enjoyed this ending regardless) Overall I think this game really is going to be more enjoyable for fans of the world of darkness universe, particularly fans of VtM. However I also feel you may be left disappointed if you played the first entry and are expecting more choices and different outcomes. My advice is to go in with low expectations and you'll have a good time. Enjoy it for what it is which is essentially a story about someone finding their way within the Vampire world.

_childDocuments_.review: Vampire was my first TTRPG.  From a point of nostalgia, it was an interesting take on the game I used to play.  For that reason alone, I would recommend it for people already familiar with the setting, or who are interested in dipping their toe in the World of Darkness waters.So that you know what you are getting into, here are my criticisms.  Despite their number, I do not regret the time I used in hunting the achievements:1. While the story was interesting, I felt like I was reading too much.  I could have gotten the same experience reading it as a short paperback novella.  It was a fun read; I probably won't read it again.2. As for replayability, once you get the first ending, it makes the rapid clicking through the story just to get to the few choices to influence the outcome a chore.3. Moreover, because of the specific references pop culture references and events of early 2020, I do not foresee this game aging well.4. There is no customization.  For the sake of the story, you are forced to "play" from the perspective of a specific character.  There are a few choices which determine the outcome of the game, but no real sense of investment into the character or her choices.5. I did not like the main character.  Perhaps it was her gratuitous foul language or the fact that I have a completely different worldview than her, she just didn't do it for me as a protagonist.6. It is an exercise in nihilism, with just about every character lacking redeeming qualities to the point that they are caricatures and stereotypes.7. Minor spoiler alert: there is no winning, there are only varying degrees of losing in the World of Darkness.

_childDocuments_.review: If a reader pines for a starry-eyed anime drone who never challenges status quo, they will have to achieve their  rapturous release of eight routes elsewhere.Shadows of New York is an exquisite narrative experience. It is *art*. Not only thanks to the writers’ impressive vocabulary – reaching for both French as well as Latin expressions – but the level of realism it depicts in a fantasy universe. It is engaging, emotionally rich and very personal. In true Toreador fashion, I revere its beauty and profundity.A distinguishing feature of this visual novel is its unapologetic stance towards hideous facets of society. Through Julia, the astute main character, writers depict human ugliness in all its glory – especially its normalised and whitewashed kind. The kind which, when complained about, raises heartbeats of rubes wheezing at the slightest sign of divergence.If there is anything to indignantly point at, it is the story’s powerful pull to depressing reality. The suffocating inescapability of Julia’s situation is accentuated by sombre art style and soundtrack whispering of sorrow, emptiness, and regret. This helplessness can be very upsetting. To this day, disconcerted reviewers ascribe their dissatisfaction to poor writing. It is a vogue explanation that makes sense to them. And that is, ironically, very Shadows of New York.

_childDocuments_.review: !!Spoiler Alert!!I enjoyed it, but I find that it has some logical errors in the scenarioand the interpretation of the characters. _childDocuments_.review: Love this game!  Be aware, its a story game, like a choose your own adventure.  If you liked Vampire the Masquerade: Coteries of New York, you will probably like this one.Its a little different though.  Instead of a choice of three, you only get one.  You HAVE to play Lasombra in this one.  And I'll be honest, you have to power through the opening....  Cause the main character is a self-loathing woke hot mess.  Hey, I'm female, and I had a LOT of trouble identifying with her.  But.... when your choices come up, you don't have to play into the woke thing, and after you get through the opening dialogue (like to the point you get turned), then the wokeness takes a back seat and steps aside for some interesting story, and awesome artwork.The atmosphere, the music, the mystery and the darkness are what kept me going.  Despite that touch of clown-world liberalism which almost none of us can take seriously, the plot is really good.  The game got the mystery down good.  When Katherine appeared, my mind gave her a voice that gave me chills.  Your choices DO actually matter and change the dialogue for many scenes to come, giving you a different experience even though there are only 3 endings.  The game also ties heavily back in to Coteries, so if you haven't yet, I would play Coteries before you play this one for added "OMG" moments.  And, the game is really creative.  I love that there's a bum vampire who keeps rats drunk so that when he sucks on them he can get a buzz.  I dunno.  The atmosphere really got me hooked on this one.  Remember, you're playing as a Lasombra, you aren't necessarily supposed to be a good guy this time............ ......  You can be if you want to though.My only actual complaint is that they did a 180 on Benoit.  (Yes, he's back!)  I always loved VTM because they didn't do the easy thing and just leave religion and vampirism divorced.  In Coteries, Benoit raised interesting things about faith which I loved, and you explore what rare, true faith feels like in the eyes of a vampire and stalk one of the only priests with real faith to learn more.  However in this one, they kinda made a joke of his character and went back to the overplayed dime-store cliched "faith isnt real" shtick which was a huge let down.  They took the cheap way out.  But, once again, you are a Lasombra..........  and Lasombra's used to be Sabbat.......       Anyway, for reals, a game has to have some decent atmosphere and mystery to keep me going with a woke main character and this one just had it.  I shudder to think how dang good it would be if they actually went full dark with the main character.  No whiny "Im emo cause my tendies are cold" but a truly dark person, and delved into the shadows of the Lasombra and made her a REAL monster.... it would've been awesome.  Ditch the woke, VTM, its holding you back from pure genius.  It would be the difference between a spoiled brat with nothing to live for having fun being aggressive, and a failing try hard letting the shadows eat her up and unleashing a void of horror and savagery.  One is okay, and the other would've been memorable.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't particularly like this installment. I just found a lot of the characters and dialogue bland and the story ranging from mildly interesting at best, confusing or bland at worst. I really didn't care (in a good or bad way) about any of the characters in the game (including the MC), neither was I particularly invested in the task I had been given to complete which is not ideal.  It seemed to be overly descriptive and wordy in places. For example "He slowly slinks away looking defeated, deflated, debased." (This did not need this many descriptors to get the point across. I think the character that said that annoyed me as much as it did the MC and not in a good way. There just wasn't much point to it when it even when it into metaphorical and belief systems territory. It kinda seemed like he could have been removed from the story completely without it affecting it except to mean you didn't have to sit through his pointless discussions.)Most choices didn't seem to have a heap of impact and it seems to add up the choices from a select few during the game to determine the ending outcome. The ending I got didn't make as much sense as I'd like, but at least this one did have a proper conclusion unlike the first game. You could probably replay it twice at most to see a couple of events you missed and get the alternative ending if you really wanted to.I really disliked some of the imagery. _childDocuments_.review: After an hour played for my coverage of the Humble Choice January 2021:This may look familiar to long time fans of Humble Choice.  This is a sequel to Vampire the Masquerade - Coteries of New York, or rather a stand-alone expansion.  According to How Long to Beat it’s about half the length at 3 hours instead of 6 hours long. This is a simple visual novel where the main character becomes a vampire, though this time around it skips her joining the Masquerade and instead focuses on her navigating the vast underground.   The main character starts as a reporter and then is turned and the game jumps forward to her being treated as a traitorous outsider of the vampire group, so the player starts from there.   This is the second Vampire the Masquerade game I’ve played, and it’s a strange one.  I think there is a lot of potential in the game world, known as the World of Darkness, but this has the same issue I have with Vampire the Masquerade - Coteries of New York.  It feels like it’s going to mostly appeal to people who already are fans of the World of Darkness.Grab this game if you enjoyed Vampire the Masquerade games, or Coteries of New York from Humble Choice September 2020, or love Visual Novels.  Otherwise, I think this is a safe skip. If you want to see more from me or my coverage of the Humble Choice:

_childDocuments_.review: This is a text-based visual novel. If you do not like those types of games do not play this.This visual novel takes place after Coteries of New York so I recommend playing that first. You play as a newly turned Lasombra called Julia. As a Lasombra you are looked at with suspicion and distrust for your nature. The Lasombra have only recently joined the Camarilla and are not yet allowed a Primogen in most cases. As a new vampire, your sire abandoned you and you had to work hard to make your place in the Camarilla. As a Lasombra you may make questionable decisions but you are the one who chooses your fate in the unlife. Play this as though you were reading a book. Get comfy and be ready to be taken on twists and turns. Your brain will be your limit to the world. The artwork and music will help lead you but it is overall up to you. Good luck surviving in such a cruel world. May the blood of Lasombra guide you.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: I did stay interested long enough to finish the story so I guess this is kind of a qualified "no," but ultimately I'm not sure the 4 hours or so I spent on it were particularly well spent.  I got the "bad" ending though I'm not sure what's so bad about it and I can't imagine being interested enough to ever play... or more accurately read... through the entire thing again to see what the "good" ending was.It's a visual novel, not a game.  You make some choices but they're just minor forks that immediately flow back to the main river.  It's kind of a convoluted story and the truth is I had a hard time staying interested enough to really understand what was going on.  There were vampires and lesbians and the main character is very emo and hates herself and is pissed off about just about everything... just not my scene.  I did like the art and the music, it really set the mood well, and I liked the way the story really introduces you to the world of Vampire: The Masquerade.  As an RPG geek I've been vaguely familiar with the mythos and this game did a nice job of fleshing it all out.  I just found the overall story pretty unsatisfying and dull.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: Main character is very "men writing women"Choices have no direct narrative consequences, they're just five checkpoints that tally up "good" or "bad" ending.Tonally all over the place: strong WoD lore, lots of out of place pop culture references, tons of Polish (and Catholic) cultural references that don't feel very natural in modern NYC.No fun game mechanics (hunger, humanity, etc.) underpinning the narrative like the Werewolf VN's or even the previous Vampire title.The "mystery" you're investigating is unsatisfying- clues go nowhere and the denouement is limp. The investigation only exists to move you from point A to B and introduce you to some fun but ultimately pointless characters. Each time a scene goes nowhere, it ends with "it was supposed to go this way, they set you up to fail", then boom you're railroaded into the next completely unrelated scene to ask a different irrelevant character some different irrelevant questions. And all while you get the privilege of reading the main character's intense self-loathing for not being able to do anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: What a ride. Despite me loving the story and improvements on sound design I had complained about in Coteries of New York, I would say this is a one playthrough ride. These two titles, Coteries and Shadows , discover different scopes of VtM. Coteries focuses more on building your own character, learning the ropes. After I finished the first playthrough of Coteries, I knew I wanted to play it 2 more times with different characters, different mindsets. Shadows, on the other hand, tells a story of character building. Somewhat, you can't just "be yourself". There were moments when you had to break yourself as you see this is the best way to follow the Lasombra way. I had a great emotional ride, but I think I would, of course, see what different paths can offer, but it's kind of hard to imagine huge differences. Somewhat, even some options are always "illusion of choice" (and I'm ok with it) there was more of a narrative, rather than having a lot of illusions. Overall, love the story and especially the polished sound design. For what's next I would love to see in next instalment? Something in between these two scopes of Shadows and Coteries.P.S.Music is absolute fire and immerse you deeply.P.P.S.Finished the second run. Although I could not put myself in different mindset to enjoy it whole as I did with Coteries (full reading, no skips, full dive). I enjoyed the second ending. And I now can see why people argue what ending is actually good or bad. For me, It was all right in the first run.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of New York chronicles Julia Sowinski's climb or descent (?) into becoming a Lasombra, for the ones unfamiliar with the setting they are a Clan who's long been known for its cruelty and is only recently trying to make its way into the more lawful side of the underworld. The story never hides the fact and sets you off with an appropriately put "You are a monster born into a world of monsters", over the course of the plot you'll witness Julia's ever encroaching darkness which culminates into one of the most well crafted endings to a story that I've seen to date.Shadows of New York is a love letter to the setting that it's based on and doesn't pull any punches in delivering the hilariously dark and thought-provoking narrative it's known for, additionally the art is gorgeous and the dynamic CG's breathes some welcomed life into the experience. The music excellently fits the atmosphere that you want in a game of VTM and I found myself immersed as soon as it started playing.The only flaws I could list would be nitpicking but for the sake of fairness I admit that I sometimes found myself making decisions based on the potential trait it might unlock rather than how I felt about the individual choice, and there were a couple of times where my character reacted in a way opposed to me (the player) where I felt player choice would have been appropriate. I appreciate the trait system for being something new and interesting but I ultimately felt like the standard is just that for a reason.I whole heartedly recommend Shadows of New York to anyone and it's a must for those who are fans of the setting already, I suggest reading it's predecessor Coteries of New York first however - while not necessary to understand the plot both stories tie together frequently and reading Coteries first would definitely enhanced your experience. I also feel I should mention that while Coteries is a great story in it's own right it was the weaker of the two and struggled with some bugs at the time of it's release, I had no technical issues whatsoever with Shadows, take from that what you will.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: After the first game this is fresh breath to the idea of story book. Once you start playing you do not want to stop, like a book it grabs you holds you and teases you with multiple nice options to play the game through. I am still I do not know in the middle not in the start but certain that it is not near the end parts of the game. Love it – and if you love Vampire the Masquerade this is in your alley as a game. Also again very new player friendly explaining all the terminology and things, only advice I can tell you if you are considering to buy is – get the first game play it through and continue to this one after that, this way you get the most out from this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: I love VTM and have read several world of darkness books. I really liked coteries of new york and devoured it.This "game" is SO boring. The main character is so uninteresting and I'd go as far as saying she's unbearable. You get so much of that BS, and then they SKIP what could've been interesting like the first interactions with the sire after the embrace. _childDocuments_.review: This is a Vampire WOD visual novel, and in particular a sequel of sorts to coeteries of new york, with an engaging new protaganist, this time from clan lasombra. I had a blast playing this, its obvious the love of the TTRPG the creators of this must have. Overall the prot was interesting, a sort of Jesssica Jones style troubled investigator with with repartay. I liked how the character would acquire traits which later on dictate the actions and course of the plot. As with the prequel I still wish we could customize our vamp more. I rather enjoyed how COVID had a part in the story of the game, though I rather wish it actually had a larger part to play...was a bit of a background character that walked out, did a bow, and nothing more really. Some of the social issues presented in the game seemed to get a bit precchy, at least in my opionion, though that seems to happen all to often in these sorts of games, at least to my experience. I ended up with one of the bad endings as I  gave Julia rather goodly, unlosmbraisk traits...other than one which got me...though not really sure why it was characterized as a bad end. Seemed like more the start of a new, exciting chapter. In conclusion, I think fans of WOD and Vamp will like this game, though there are a few sections that dragged a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: The really good parts: The art is wonderful, the soundtrack is very immersive, and Qadir. Qadir is good. There's a moment in the scenery where you're looking at a distortion of your character and I thought it was presented beautifully. There are quite a few of those, little visually artistic expressions that just draw you in and make you feel right at home. It feels like a VtM universe. The Camarilla representation felt appropriate, and as a longtime VtM enthusiast that was pretty nice to see. Towards the end, especially.The rest of it: I hate Julia and the rest of this review is mostly me just ranting about how much I hate Julia and why.She's out of touch at her best, and insufferable at her worst. Most of Julia's dialogue that's supposed to be quirky falls so flat it lands into cringe territory. Why is this a problem? Because you spend 100% of the game with Julia. Her attitude is one-note, and would be acceptable as a side character but she's the full focus. There are no breaks. There are no cuts away from her perspective or her dialogue, the game is LITERALLY just Julia in some shape, way, or form. I don't want to go on this adventure with her, I don't like her. I want nothing to do with her. There are multiple moments in the game where Julia is flat out aggressively verbally assaulted and I'm cheering from the other side of the monitor. It felt like the writers were being self aware, doing that thing where they go 'lol we know how terrible she is'... That's not cute. It's not quirky. If you know how bad this is, then fix it. It is possible to have an edgy character without this happening. Bloodlines, the groundbreaking rpg released in 2004, had dark and edgy moments GALORE but none of them were so poorly executed that it comes off as the hot garbage Julia is portrayed as. Yes, the two games are different down to their very core mechanics, but this specific issue is a matter of writing competency. Bloodlines managed to take a literal Batman archetype character, grit and edge to the core, and humanized a minor character into a memorable personality you could empathize with. There was none of this with Julia. There was nothing that made her an empathetic character. I think, later in the game, they tried to give her a little bit of a 'power burst' so you'd cheer for her as she 'stuck it to the man' and it just felt so inauthentic and stupid. I was actively rooting for her to fail. There are points in her dialogue with other characters where it feels like the writers have manipulated the dialogue so that she has some sort of superior perspective, and that perspective feels legitimately offensive. Speaking of which, a lot of the dialogue is very stiff and awkward to read. I think maybe instead of just having text, next time it might benefit them to get professional voice actors for the roles. That tends to help. Maybe they can see about getting whatever budget is left over from Bloodlines 2, we all know that's not coming out.Moving on to a minor critique in the gameplay, how come there's no journal log of characters/people you've interacted with? I get that it's a visual novel, not a detective game, and you're not going to have like an Ace Attorney list of evidence. But it would be nice to just have a tab with pictures, names, clans, and a short description. We get a dictionary of VtM terms every time they pop up, so would it really have been so difficult to add a little bit of flavor imagery and text? I don't think it would have ruined/increased my attitude either way, but it just would have been nice.Last words: By the end of the story, I was so pissed off at everything this game put me through with Julia's garbage that I didn't even care about the jaw dropping Easter Egg they threw in there. It was a wonderful little nod at VtM lore and I should have enjoyed it a lot more than I did. I just wanted the game to be over and done with at that point. Honestly, I wouldn't have even completed this game if I didn't plan on leaving a review. I thought it was only fair to play the entire thing through, at least once, if I was going to publicly judge it.I received the 'bad ending' on my first play through. And it feels like unless you play Julia a very specific way, you won't get a 'good ending'. I don't know how much I agree with that. And I don't know if I'm going to play through again to get whatever good ending there was. I understand that this was a sequel to a previous visual novel. Maybe I'll play that, instead.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first this is a visual novel. Really enjoyed Shadows of New York. Playing Coteries of New York may help as there are quite a few threads that run through both.
