_childDocuments_.review: The game is very enjoyable, especially if you like Coteries of New York. It is basically the same type of gameplay, but with a new storyline. The major improvements I can name is that the character you play this time, has herself more of an established personality, that is brought out very well during the entire story. The other is that it has a vastly more interesting and satisfying ending, two actually, so you can chose what kind of person you want to shape into as you play through the game. On the internet it is often mentioned as having a "good" and "bad" ending, but I liked both. It really just comes down to how you envision the character you are playing and where you want her to end up.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: As the game continues the story of Coteries of New York, it is hard to review it without comparing it to that game.Coteries gave players the choice of three interchangeable characters with little to no personality. The choice in Shadows to focus on one character and flesh her out, allowing players to actually care about her, was a step in the right direction then.Coteries only had one ending, which made sense, considering the utter lack of power a fledgling vampire had, but it left players disatisfied seeing none of their choices matter in the least, tiniest bit. Shadows has two endings, not counting the way early on to die and not play the game. Again, a step in the right direction.Yet somehow, the improvements hold the game back.Where Coteries had choices that changed events during the game but ultimately didn't affect the ending, Shadows has very few choices, which add to a hidden counter for which ending is achieved, but do not alter anything during the journey there.Where Coteries had a number of side stories you could advance over the course of the game, and to make each of the three playthroughs give you new events to explore and new choices to make, Shadows has nothing to explore. Each night you choose to read two out of three possible encounters, but none of them have any meaning, any progression. They are one off events that simply allow the writer to showcase some character they came up with.Coteries had a bland protagonist but a very interesting supporting cast. Characters with personality that explored the unlife of vampires and different ways different clans deal with it. The cast of characters in Shadows is the same. Yet those same characters that were so interesting in the first game have lost all personality in the second, being just soulless vessels to give plot information. If even that. As a result, the second "playthrough" comes down to clicking the next button for ten minutes, to skip to the choices, choose the opposite approach in morality, read the one line that differs, then read the changed ending.Should that ending be the "good" ending, it will be grand standing posturing - a fitting end to the self absorbed navel gazing that precedes it. Had this been a novelette, without any illusion of choice or two endings, I would have mostly enjoyed reading through it. Though I would still have rolled my eyes at the ending. It is well written and tries to explore the main character's inner struggle. The different format would not have made the other characters any less flat and lifeless, but it would have felt less like the writer's cry: This is my amazing writing!I did not buy the game for the amazing writing, but for the tale it tells. A story needs both. And Shadows of New York focused so hard on getting the words right, it forgot to have these words mean anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: Three words. Disappointment. Disappointment. Disappointment.Let's start with a bit of history. I played "Coteries" and hopped into "Shadows" immediately after completing. I played "Coteries" with all characters, restarted the game like 20 times to check all the possible ways to piss Qadir and generally enjoyed myself - it has it's flaws (both technical and story-wise), but allows a nice dip in VtM anyway. So I gleefully moved on to get more of alike experience. Well, quoting a phrase the writer of "Shadows" clearly likes, no dice.What I found was walls and walls, and walls... and walls... and walls.... and walls... and walls of text, 50% (or even 80%) of which doesn't bring anythig into the story. In one of my play-throughs of "Coteries" I reached the point when Benoit should be put down, but, unfortunately, the story in "Shadows" doesn't follow this timeline - he's here and he's even more annoying, because here there's no mystery, no arguments. All characters have their minds set and you can just scroll through walls and walls, and walls... well, you get it. I started fast-forwarding his dialogues in the middle of second encounter. The apartment scenes did a little better - I managed to read about 2,5 nights of meaningless "oh I love you so much", then it was fast-forward as well...Ok, so what about side quests, these brought a lot of replayability to "Coteries" - to check NPCs reactions to your actions and decisions, solve issues one way or another to see different outcomes in part II/III/IV? Yes, you guessed it - no dice. All "side quests" are now one-night-stands and bring ABSOLUTELY NOTHING to the story - no achievements, no companions. N-O-T-H-I-N-G.Main quest line? The idea was good. There even were a few moments I liked (the moment we learn the cause for the future investigation, reading the diary, meeting an old "gumshoe"), but they were scarce. Other than that it was 80% a pity party for the protagonist. And overwhelming feeling of having absoultely no influence on the story. People say that "Coteries" plot is on rails. True, but there you can PRETEND to have impact on the events. At one point you can even try to abandon the main quest line. Here? Well, I'd say the plot is not on rails. It's squeezed into tight, claustrofobic pipeline filled with... I don't really know what that was, as I fast-forwarded throught it, afraid to die of boredom before learning the story outcome. One moment I really liked was the "good ending" - if only the whole story had this climate, the game would be awesome...At one point I really got hopeful - I got "prepare for action" call. First thought: "Finally! Let the show begin!". In "Coteries" "action" was looking along the SI assault rifle's barrel from the wrong end and deciding if you prefer to fight (and risk wounds/Hunger increase) or flee for your unlife. Or which NPC to shield. Or other kind of "action stuff". And no one was warning you it's coming. What was "action" in "Shadows"? Going through the doors and speaking (walls and walls, and walls...) with people on the other side.Speaking of Hunger mechanics. Not present. So feeding is meaningless. Are we still playing a vampire here?Ok, so both strorytelling and mechanics suck. Last chance. Characters. There were some distinctive ones in "Coteries", so maybe they'll save the day. Yup. No dice.Let's start with the protagonist. Most of the time she's throwing herself a pity party. Engaging as hell... And when she does not, she seems more lost than a 14th gen Thin-blood on a moonless night (no offense to ppl who enjoy playing Duskborns). For crying out loud - she's Lasombra! One of the LEADING clans (I'd say second only to Ventrue in Camarilla). I expected her to be cunning, sleek and shady. Instead I found something closer to Brujah mentality, unable to control her tongue and relaying on brutal force more than intelligence. But even there she does no good work - even my scared and highly-emotional Toreador from "Coteries" was showing more guts than she. And my Brujah boy was acting with more caution and reason than she does. And I say it despite he got staked at the very beginning of his road. Twice. At one point I came to conclusion that compared to her, even Arturo seems fine (and he was one of the most annoying NPCs to me in "Coteries", second only to Benoit, so it's bad... really bad...).So maybe side characters? Yeah, there was a potential here. Past tense. Each of the "old companions" stories got reduced to one-night-stand, so there's no time to get engaged (again if someone played "Coteries"). Then there's one particularly mean and cold vampire that somehow got his fangs filed and started showing parental instincts (traded his Presence/Intelligence/Wits for Humanity?). But what hit me the hardest (huehue) was an old vampire, who's dealing in all the kinds of shady trades on nightly basis and who's unable to fend off or even flee from a few-months-old neonate. Really? I mean REALLY?So to sum-up my rant: I wanted to like this game. I was desperate to like it until the very end. But this game killed the mood. Final Death. End of story.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: This is to Sheridan le Fanu's 'Carmilla', what Carmilla was to Coleridge's 'Christabel'. Not the game I expected to find over 200 years of intertextuality between various bits of vampire (and proto-vampire for Coleridge) literature, but here we are. It's good. Really good. Coteries of New York will get you to know what the setting is about, Shadows of New York will make you understand what a rich tapestry the Vampire: the Masquerade and broader World of Darkness is for storytelling. Beautiful art and a soundtrack I cannot praise enough. Absolutely worth the purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: This is a small scale visual novel with great art, and some genuinely interesting side stories. The mystery is fun to unravel, and as a newcomer to the series I thought the game did a great job of bringing me into the lore at my own pace. But with only two possible endings and dialogue that tries too hard to be edgy in the way a Netflix teen drama does, this ultimately didn't have the replayability or writing quality I had hoped for.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this brief but entertaining story an awful lot more than I did Coteries of New York. The latter I was having fun with until I had the ending forced on me before I was able to properly explore the side line stories - in a few years, when I have another look at it I'll surely do things differently, so I can conclude at least a few of those sidelines but for now the game doesn't inspire me enough for another try just yet. That said though, I would strongly recomend you play through before trying Shadows of New York because without knowledge of the events in Coteries, Shadows will seem rather empty.I got the 'Good Ending' on my first playthrough by playing the narrator true to her clan, one of the traditionally power hungry Lasombre and that's one of the things I like about Shadows of New York: it's true to the source material. For me this was revisiting old territory and lore and a warm fuzzy feeling in finding that all the backstory I know is not only being put to good use but that it also adds to the enjoyment of the story. I would have been very disappointed if it had just been 'based upon' but no, this was pleasantly the real deal.Still, lets be honest, there's not much to it - 5 hours tops. For me Shadows of New York and Coteries are a taster while I wait for the more substantial games related to this franchise, namely Bloodlines 2 and Swansong. However, even a taste is nice given how sadly starved the gaming world has been of 'The World of Darkness' since the original Bloodlines messy release - yes, I know its all down to who had the rights when and various failed projects but nearly 20 years is an overly long wait as far as I'm concerned.Anyway, if you're a fan and perhaps know a bit of the lore then this game is at least a place to sate your hunger until something juicier comes along.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: DNF. I really liked the previous game and had hopes for this one, but I couldn't even get through the first hour. The facts that we have to creepily stare at the protagonist every now and then while she sits in sexually suggestive poses, and the fact that the writing is so edgy I basically cut myself on it, are bad enough, but not my main problem with the game. My main problem with the game is that this is no visual novel, it is a novel with pictures. During one hour of play, partly spent skipping conversations, I got to make maybe ten dialog choices, and only one of them had any impact on the game whatsoever. The team making this should have written a book, not made a game. And don't creep on your own characters, it's noticable, and wierd. Play Cotieries of New York instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: If you like visual novels, and don't mind them being extremely light on gameplay (even for the genre), this may be for you - especially if you're at least casual fan of the setting. Otherwise, it's not worth a play-through or your time unless there's nothing else engaging, as a time-sink, AND you get it for free or next-to-nothing. I played through Coteries, and after about two or so hours into this one, decided it wasn't worth seeing through.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: While visual novels aren't usually my cup of tea, I found myself quite enjoying this story. The background art was amazing, and the music worked quite well. I am not familiar with the World of Darkness that this story takes place in, but the glossary the game provides is a nice way to learn more. There is also the function to quickly skip through dialog which makes exploring the different decisions and their outcomes super simple. As for the story itself, I enjoyed it, even if I got the bad ending my first playthrough =)
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: This Game... actually more: this storyAs its predecessor VTM CoNY this is more of a "interactive" novel than your usual videogame. And a novel that is. The character Julia, whose mental state and development we are experiencing, is incredibly well written, compelling, and relatable. Rarely have I ever enjoyed a story set in our times as much as I have enjoyed this.I might later add to this review. As of now I am still in awe, with how well thought out this story was.Play time for experiencing the story in the available ways is at about 6-7 hours, if you're a quick reader.Normally I'd call this overpriced.... but in this case, I won't. It's worth every single cent.Enjoy, fellow kindred, enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly funny to see the negative views being 50% "this story based game is based in a story" and 50% "they won't let me be racist".Like, the character is created for you. She has her own morals and you are playing as her, not your self insert right wing loser. If that's not the type of game you like, then you probably won't like this game. As for my personal opinion, I was promised "SJW fan fiction", "leftist garbage", and a "pc lgbt party pamphlet" from the negative reviews (the reading of which was what prompted me to move the game from my wishlist to my library), and from the steam description "Shadows presents a more personal and unique tale." While the game certainly delivered on the latter with a very on rails and biased (not necessarily in a bad way but from like one character's point of view), it honestly seemed very centre liberal to me. Not a huge deal, because most supposedly left wing media isn't really very left at all, but something to bear in mind. Lots of the typical centrist delusional/psychopathic/pyscho ableist insults. The art, as with the previous game, is very good. The dynamic backgrounds really help engage you, but can be turned off if your pc or eyes are having a hard time. The music is also very well created and helps make a really good atmosphere. The, like, layout? of the text itself has a few little bits that weren't how they should be (like going" quote" instead of "quote"), and the way the character speaks, likely on purpose, is very hashtag edgy. Some of the way they introduce new terms (e.g. kindred, childe, embraced etc) seems a bit forced, but that might just be because I was aware of them before the game and for someone who didn't know what they were it'd seem much more casual and natural.The gameplay mechanics of night time and the passing of time is the same as the first game; At night you have a set number of tasks you have enough time to do, and you pick which ones you do. The story itself seems engaging enough, though I have only just gotten to what seems to be the main plotline (though as with any vtm story there's guaranteed to be a lot of twists and turns so I can't say for sure about anything without spoilers). I've played enough, though, to be introduced to quite a few people in conversation, and it portrays the different characters personalities well.10/10 for the line "I think the only good Englishman is a dead Englishman"

_childDocuments_.review: Not including the early change in the main character's circumstances by , it takes more than an hour to introduce the real conflict to the game. The overall plot has some interesting ideas, but even after the murder mystery is introduced there is a ton of bloat. Conversations run on for too long, pop culture references feel forced and out-of-character most of the time, and at times you are required to play through a certain number of side scenes to continue the main story.Others have pointed out the lack of player choice. By itself I don't think that's a problem, but compared to Coteries of New York it makes this fall flat, especially since the story presented drags so often.

_childDocuments_.review: Much better than their first game "Coteries of New York".The main character is fleshed out and plays an important part in the story, unlike the 3 copy-paste cardboard main characters from the 1st game.A nice story and good writing. Background music was nice but MVP is the dark and moody intro menu track "Julia".Both games can be barely called "games", they are simple visual novels..I remember the superior Japanese visual novels that have multiple routes/paths, countless endings and enough story to last you 200-500 hours. That is how it is done!These "indie" Western attempts are pathetically MID in comparison. Small nuggets, one is $20 and the this one $10.No wonder I got both games for a measly $1 buck.I just have to ask, WTF is the company "White Wolf" doing?!?After the beloved 2004 "VtM Bloodlines" Troika game, the gaming department decided to commit harakiri????:2014: The highly anticipated MMORPG "World of Darkness Online" was cancelled.2019: Coteries and "Shadows of New York" released. The company finally decided to give games a chance again, after 15 years. MID games.. After 15 years, such a safe and cowardly choice...2021: The absolute pathetic failure of "Werewolf: The Apocalypse – Earthblood" being one of the worst games in history.2022: "Swansong" fell short with its horrible graphics and animations on top of comitting the crime of being Epic Games Store exclusive. The game promised to be all that which Coteries and Shadows of New York could not do, but failed.2022: "Bloodhunt" showed potential despite being YET another game in the Battle Royale genre. Shame the game died.2019: "Bloodlines 2" release was teased but since then it has been in a turbulent state. Cancelled at some point or not. No in-game trailers to show us the game and no information being available as if they are hiding something. They blame it on the pandemic, yet I blame the company restructuring. The official YT channel proves that they changed from "mildly woke" company culture to "radical woke-ism". Does not sound promising for the future...The World of Darkness setting is so rich and interesting!I even put it on the same level as Warhammer fantasy and Warhammer 40k in that regard.But what do they have to show for themselves?With the political route the company is taking, the franchise has no future.White Wolf needs good games to save itself.Coteries and Shadows of New York are simply not good enough to achieve such a task.MID

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really great visual novel experience! I see a lot of reviews for this game which seem to have confused this for something it's not. No, this isn't Vampire Bloodlines 2, you won't be designing a character or having a ton of input on the course of events. But why is that what you're expecting when it's clear that's not what this is meant to be?As I said previously, this is an awesome visual novel, and if you're familiar with some of the other literary works based in the World of Darkness, I would put this in the upper 25% of what's been published previously. There are basically only two endings, and you get one those based on five decisions that you make earlier in the plot. Both endings are very satisfying (perhaps the "Good" one a bit more), and I don't think that you'll feel like you wasted your time reading through the story, I know that I didn't.And that's all I'm going to tell you! If you want to know more, go ahead and play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played the previous game in the series, the Coteries of New York. I really enjoyed that game and also really enjoyed this game. Though both were for different reasons. In Coteries you have more freedom of choice in your own character while in this game you are locked to a single character. Both have their advantages and disadvantages. Should you pick up this Visual Novel? Well, that depends on if you like an interactive story. There are limited choices in this game that change how your character acts, the consequences of what you do and stuff like that. The main thing to keep in mind is that this is an INTERACTIVE story, not a Choose-your-own-adventure novel. I personally really enjoyed the character, the references to the previous game because I had played it a while ago and know generally what happens, and because I felt rewarded for picking the things I did. I love the Vampire: The Masquerade world and the lore and everything, so this was a welcome purchase when I found it. I think I would recommend playing Coteries first as that game does a lot more world building and it's a lot more free-form, but I think this one has a much better story.Be it as it may, what will you choose?

_childDocuments_.review: I grabbed Shadows of New York as soon as it came out. Personally, I enjoyed it better than Coteries as I believe it’s the stronger of the two. I can see how the development team tried to use some of the feedback on the first game to expand on this one.It feels like Julia has more of a personality besides choosing random dialogue options like Coteries, for starters. I really enjoyed playing as a member of clan Lasombra and I’m happy to see the other clans getting recognition besides the main 7. You’re an immigrant that’s just trying to figure out her life (or new un-life, that is), where she stands with her religion as well as her relationship while always feeling like an outsider.The choices you must make, while for some it still felt like they were still limited, I would have to agree with another review that it fits for clan Lasombra. They’re Julia’s inner struggles on being true to herself or her clan’s values. Furthermore, I was relieved to find out we had more than one ending to this game.Unlike Coteries where it felt rushed and ended as soon as it was getting underway, Shadows pacing felt more natural. I wished it could’ve lasted longer, but only because I wanted to see more into Julia and Dakota’s relationship as well other characters. Honestly though, it didn’t need to be longer and I felt like it tied up a few loose ends from the first game.I really admire the grungy art style that fits with the story as well as some animated scenes. I remember complaining that Coteries characters’ only had one illustration for each character, but here they actually have more than one. You see some scenes and characters from Coteries, but I felt as if it was another way to tie everything in together.All and all I definitely suggest picking up and playing this game, especially after playing Coteries. I hope for the possibility of seeing more VtM visual novels from this developer in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a followup/expansion to Coteries of New York. Someone has put some great effort into creating a stable of characters and atmospheric setting, but it feels like watching somebody else's TTRPG campaign. It shares many of the downsides I found with Coteries, so I'm just going to cut and paste my negatives here: "Although a visual novel in most respects, Coteries does not have the option to fast forward dialogue you've already seen, or if it does I couldn't find it. It also doesn't let you keep multiple saves. Both of those things are standard with VNs, and the lack of them drastically reduces replayability. I really want to get through all of the side storylines, but at the same time I don't want to have to sit through the same intro and tutorial screens every time. The other issue is that there don't seem to be any branches to the story paths. There's a ton of atmosphere, as you'd expect, but you'll always be taken in by the same character and brought to the same conclusion. There are a few spots where you can get killed, but they're few and far between, and no matter how you act toward major characters, the story and their reaction to you doesn't change."Shadows does add a second ending, at least, but your choices don't affect the story until the very end, at which point they determine which ending you get.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: I must be forever doomed to not like the games that I actually buy, because I bought this (as opposed to getting it for free, or getting them as gifts), fully expecting a full closure to all the unravelled ends in The Coterie of New York. And so if you are reading this with similar expectations as I had, then no, you will not get the closure that you so crave.The game itself is rather blah. Lasombra has recently joined the Camarilla, and the protagonist is basically the newest lackey in the ranks. Just the like the previous protagonist, she's clueless, generally ignored, and are commanded about. This is totally fine; you generally start your character in WoD as some (higher-up vampire's) lackey. But let us recall what happened at the end of Coterie, the characters, the players. You expect the characters to not disperse to the wind without piquing SOME interest in the rest of the Camarilla; a well-respected (if young) Tremere and the Childe of the Regent is out of the picture and nobody cares? Really? Including the Regent? I have a hard time imagining Maximillian Strauss (From Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines) being that blase about HIS childe's fate turning into that, so that was jarring. Hope turning into what she did was also... not very Malkavian. Malkavians are irredeemably insane, so her turning out to be like that was also jarring. Torque was jarring. And we never really learn WHY they all turned out that way, just that they did. It almost felt like seeing someone you haven't seen for a few months, and they'd gone full 180 on you but you never figure out why. And you also learn that the protagonist from The Coteries just disappeared, which I find VERY unlikely. Arturo is relatively young for a vampire, and despite what we learned about him in The Coteries, I doubt he has much clout in other sects. So where did the protagonist go? And more than that, nobody (including the companions, who, to me, appeared to have a little more understanding than just business associates) seems to wonder what happened to the protagonist? Or Sophie Langley, for that matter? If I were a Camarilla vampire, I'd want to know what happened, not because I like any of my fellow vampires but because it might be dirt I can use later on. Their lack of interest feels... un-vampire-ish. The protagonist also feels... a little less predatory, more Brujah-ish than Lasombra. Angry, yes. Manipulative, determined, ruthless and Machiavellian? Not really. Because the character already has a personality, it's difficult to play this with the mindset of an RPG, something that was a little more easily achieved in The Coteries. Everything about the characters seem... off. Ever so slightly off. And that is really distracting. If you're a fan of WoD, you'll buy this anyway, but don't expect the immersed feeling that you got playing VTMB or Coteries; you'll always be an outsider in Shadows of New York, a kine looking into the life of a vampire without really learning anything about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: Full Disclosure: I worked on VTM 2/3e, did a lot of review-work for 20AE, and also consider 5E V:TM to be worse than 4E D&D in terms of being utterly clueless about the source material, canon and why people liked the game in the first place.All that said, I liked this game a lot. The story, albeit it a "Murder on the Orient Express" for V:TM is well done. It's very much like what you would see in one of the early 1e or 2e published adventures. It is still odd to me to see NYC as a non-Sabbat city and Lasombra in the Cam, but the latter isn't unheard of. Heck, a Lasombra Anti was Prince of DC until dethroned by a Setite, who was another antitribu himself.Anyway, the story is well done, and you get a dramatically different ending based on the choices you make in this visual novel. This is quite the difference from Coteries of New York where the story ends the same regardless of what clan you take and the decisions you make. The endings in Shadow are based on how you play your character. Do you hold the tenants of the Clan, or to your Humanity. After all, the two are at odds with each other, and this plays out for the full length of the game. You also get to see all four of your potential allies from Coteries of New York here, which is nice. The end of your previous character is nebulous at best, but it makes sense as to why. My thought is that that character from the first game has met Final Death, but I'd be pleasantly surprised if that wasn't the case. The writing is top notch, the art is fantastic and once again Draw Distance does a better job of VTM than the actual 5e version of the RPG. Take that for what you will. Either way, I got my twelve bucks out of the game and I hope to see more from the company. V:TM is getting Choices games, visual novels and another Bloodlines, so the game is prospering in digital form even if the actual tabletop game is being bled dry. There's a good deal of irony in that.  Best of all, the game ties directly into the VTM game from Redemption. Blink and you'll miss the tie-in though.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: Coteries Of New York was railroading the story in a fun way by giving you the opportunity of choosing different dialogue options to create a sense that you shape your own character's personality. But dialogue options in Shadows Of New York is not so different than each other which is a huge problem if you consider that VTM is one of the most known RPGs of all time. On the other hand, setting is good. You can feel that characters that you are talking to have personality, but the protagonist kills the atmosphere by just not being fun to read. In my opinion, playing as D'Angelo would be more fun.I think the problem is in writing. If there will be any more to Vampire The Masquerade - New York franchise, surely it needs a better writing for the good of the future games.Note: I might have mistakes in my writing. Sorry for that.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a graphic novel with a few choices and very mixed writing.The game is not totally bad - just below average and is a step in the wrong direction from the first game.First of all an issue from the first game was carried over to this title: you can't select chapters. For instance, after the introduction you will face a choice that can lead to a game over. The only option, if you want to see the rest of the game is to click though the whole first section of the game again - skipping text for five minutes.This should be the best part of the game, right? Unfortunately it isn't. The writing constantly reminds the reader of the struggle of the writer to manufacture something coherent. There's a lot of idle uninteresting talk that doesn't set a mood or deepen a character, just filler stuff. Unlike in the first game you can read the protagonists' thoughts what is mostly not particularly well executed. Sometimes thoughts state the obvious or are trying hard to attune the reader to the mood of the protagonist - that is a person who changes her behaviour and thoughts from melancholic to badass to sexy to self-loathing to depressive to ironic from moment to moment. And that might be the biggest issue regarding the writing: the tone is so all over the place that it feels very inconsistent. The absurd amount of slang should be mentioned too. It's so much, that many dialogues read just not very convincing. Actually the games' best parts are the funny ones - but that's probably not a good benchmark for a vampire story that longs to set a dark tone.The story is okay at best, more on a better fan fiction level than of a good novel.There are lots of references to movies, music, novels and the like, in the fashion of "hey you know that book from 1977 where this and that happens?" with some more textboxes dwelling upon the books content. One can surely take inspiration from books and movies, but just referring to them in this manner is outright lazy and, what is worse, boastful - "look at all the highbrow stuff I know!".The background artworks are mostly serviceable but many have been reused from the first game - and that one used some licence free photos from the internet that were slightly overpainted digitally. For some reason there are multiple portraits for the protagonist that are supposed to express her current mood: Julia looking neutral, Julia smoking a cigarette, Julia holding the cross that's on a chain around her neck, Julia scowling - regarding these limited expressions I would have preferred to have just one portrait and to let my imagination do the rest.The music is probably the best part of the game. When there is actually a mood, then it's due to the music. Alone in scenes concerning the protagonists relationship with another woman the music is too much and overdoes it in sweet coziness quality time atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: So I will say that while this game focuses more on a singular person that you build in the process rather than being one made from scratch, it makes *phenominal* use of this. Almost every aspect of the game has been improved on from the Coteries, including the subtle sprinkles of kooky Kindred phenomenon such as the Abyss (and some other things I don't want to get too into). It feels like the tittle owners finally gave the developers the go-ahead to include more force behind their story and the writers really took that freedom to heart by placing the central mystery of this game so deeply tied to the TTRPG equivalent. Add onto that the beautifully haunting visuals, great dialogue and confidence to build on an admittedly rocky first game and this is well worth its $12.99 price tag. You also get to play in V5's meta-plot and, wow, it actually holds together if you ignore certain restrictions that were layered in deep into the original edifice.

_childDocuments_.review: In Coteries I distinctly remember that I never felt bored playing it and had a good time up until the ending. In this game, it was more of a frustrating experience for me than anything and I had to take pauses to get through it on multiple occasions. No small part of V5, but that's not my only reason for deciding to not recommend this one, whereas I did (with caveats) recommend the first. TL;DR though? I'd save my money and watch a playthrough if I really wanted to see what was in here.Gameplay: 4/10For the most part the gameplay is identical to the first game where you just click forwards and now and then you get a choice or two along the way. Alas, there are even fewer choices to go around this time than there were in the other one which made me feel even more railroaded and impotent than I did in Coteries. You have fewer opportunities to use Disciplines, there is no hunting or hunger mechanic left in the game, which I was hoping they'd improve upon since they're fairly important aspects for a Vampire game, and there isn't really a way to fail the game other than the false choice at your Embrace scene. The thing that saves it from a 3/10 for me is the fact that some choices actually do matter this time around. They can give you certain traits that shape how Julia will, at occasion, comment in certain scenes and what framework she works off of. In my experience there appear to be two options to each trait set which are a bit barebones in description, but nonetheless this is a good thing to see which adds replayability and impact to some of the choices made. These traits will also affect what sort of ending you end up with.Writing: 5/10In the previous game, you had a bit more of a blank-slate sort of character. They did have something of a name and face, but most details and their personality was up in the air. This time around they wanted us to play an established character they make up. I wasn't too keen on Julia as a character. I don't want to call her a bad character, just not my cup of tea character. I find her annoying, broody and kinda pretentious, so I can't say I had a good time with most of her monologuing.The characters around her didn't leave too much impact on me. Benoit was mostly just annoying, with a good moment towards the end I felt, and I kinda liked Samira even if she didn't show up much. I guess it was nice , but it's kinda eh by the fact that you're on some level gonna do that anyway. And if you were hoping to get to throw one Arturo's way, keep dreaming.Qadir was one of the more present characters and that's where I felt most of the effort went into. We get to see more of him, both when he works and a little bit on the side when off the public eye, and he's as charming as ever. The old coterie were basically cameos and didn't add anything new for the short moment they appeared, but they did each add something to the story which I will praise. At least in the good ending. Other characters like Torque almost feel like a 180, and Callihan raises more questions. And not just cuz the game revolves investigating his murder mystery, a plot that wasn't too interesting to me. And I also wasn't much of a fan of the romance with Dakota. I guess the point of it is that they are dysfunctional together, but it's nothing I personally enjoy watching.What I really wanted out of this game was the rare opportunity to get to play a Lasombra and experience their ruthless yet pragmatic approaches while also getting to play with shadows. Not to mention seeing how the Clan is handling their move from the Sabbat to the Camarilla. Admittedly not a V5 move I'm happy about, but if you're gonna do it and show off a Lasombra, that is an element you just have to touch upon. Which Shadows kind of don't really. Here's where V5 ♥♥♥♥♥ it up for me, which reflects on the writing; I can't fully blame Draw Distance for this since they work off the V5 material, of course, but I also can't say that this isn't one of the biggest reasons I was so frustrated playing this that I fell rather firmly on "don't recommend" in regards to this game. Things like these made me feel less like a Lasombra and more like a Malkavian going through this game. Part of this is because Obtenebration and Necromancy got merged in V5, but I don't think even they went as far into the trippy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I see in this game, and it does the Lasombra image no favors. And if you're hoping to actually invoke some of the Oblivion tricks I just described, you're gonna be disappointed for the majority of the game. I've seen two chances in the entire game to do so, the rest are gonna happen regardless cuz the plot demands it. It needs more of a Lasombra vibe and less of a Malkavian one.What I will give the game credit for though is that while there are only two endings, a good and a bad one, those two endings are properly written out and feel satisfying as a conclusion to me. They wrap up the plot and give you a window into what happens next for Julia without compromising what she's already been through with a cliffhanger or some unfinished business or whatever. By the time you end the game, you will have gone through the premise of the game from start to finish and anything that'd happen next would be a new installment rather than a continuation of what you should've wrapped up the first time around.Atmosphere: 8/10The strongest point by far in Draw Distance's two VtM games have been the atmosphere. Those animated backdrops are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorgeous, and the new ones are even better here as they have greater touches of animation to them. It makes me kinda regretful there isn't an option to hide the hud so I can just stare at them and listen to the ambience like I sometimes do in Coteries, and I suspect that I will in Shadows.What makes me give it the same score as the last time around despite the aforementioned praise is the music. I heard in Coteries they made music inspired by Bloodlines 1, and in my opinion that music was excellent. I liked every single score made from it. In Shadows, the composer did more of her own thing, and my take from that is that it's a downgrade from the first one. There even were a few from the soundtrack that I didn't like, that I felt where too noisy to be considered music, and left off from my VtM playlist. Most of the tracks where okay, one or two were great like the previous game's. A step forwards with backdrops, a step back with the music.Technical: 5/10In the previous game there were instances of ambience glitching to stick around even after you left an area, Disciplines you shouldn't have access to bleeding into characters that shouldn't be able to use them, and a barebones customizable option. This time around there were no issues with ambience glitching so I never had to restart the game for technical issues. Being only one character too, nothing ever bled in from another one, as one might expect, and no choice I made ever seemed to glitch or cause oddities with how people reacted to me. The options are still as barebones as ever I found, and I still miss a hide UI button. But at least there is a skip button! I don't  there was one of those in Coteries. At first anyway. All in all it doesn't do anything to impress you on a technical level, but it does work competently at what it does throughout, so to me it's a neutral rating there.

_childDocuments_.review: I won this game through SteamGifts.I was quite intrigued to start on this game after I had tackled Coteries of New Yorkand was pleasantly surprised by the story and seeing familiar faces from the first game.However I was quite disappointed by the lack of .. side story and extra things to dothat were in the previous game. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Shadows of New York is a bit more of a straight line narrative than it's predecessor, Coteries of New York, but I would still recommend it for Vampire the Masquerade fans that like to read.Like the first game, this is a visual novel. The writing is as good or better than the first, really hitting home runs for me in terms of touching on the dark nights of 2020. The music is strong, the art is very inspired by Tim Bradstreet's famous VtM style. You have but one character to play, a female Polish-American journalist embraced into Clan Lasombra; where in the prior game you had a female Venture corporate executive, male Brujah dead-end office worker or male Toreador indie artist to play. Also in the first game you had more freedom to go where you wished most nights, with a variety of allies and side adventures you could pursue, but here you are meeting the same people in the same order, as the same character, leaving there only two real play through to be had where I played through Coteries five times before feeling like I had exhausted all the branches the story had to offer. That said, each play through is a bit longer than Coteries, so you end up in the same ballpark of number of hours, at 10-15 depending on how quick you read the text and how long you take to make Julia respond. I liked that the game play shifted to a more personal and deep dive into this single character. How she navigates through the Court is an interesting follow-up to the ending of the last game. Enough assets were reused from the last game to make it feel like a stand alone expansion to Coteries more than a true sequel but the price reflects that well I think.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended because the story is good and the price is right. HOWEVER, the whole point of Roleplaying Storytelling Games is to be "a part of the story" - to know your decisions make a difference. I don't think there were more than a dozen decisions to be made by the player. The rest was a few hours of one way storytelling that is good if you're reading a book, but not as good if you're the main character in the story. I am a long time VTM player and fan, since the first edition books were released decades ago. I was disappointed when the trashed the World of Darkness they created, then tried to recreate something new in Requiem. The 5th edition brings some of that original magic back and I'm grateful. So, get this "game" for the story and to "live" again in the World of Darkness, but remember, you only get a few decisions while you are there.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: The writing of this game feels like a distinct improvement on the first one. The pessimistic, sardonic humour was thoroughly entertaining and satisfying throughout. Having a singular protagonist this time around allowed them to be much more fleshed out and interesting, with a distinctive voice. This led to somewhat of a reduction in player-choice, but the narrative being told was fun enough and the protagonists' personality entertaining enough that I didn't mind. I very much enjoyed the development of relationships of characters with the protagonist, notably Qadir and Dakota. The endings were also more satisfying than that of the first game.The low amount of choices does make this game less replayable than the first game, but I had more fun in my first playthrough of this game than in any playthrough of the first one. Ultimately, that is more valuable to me than replayability.

I will also admit that I was genuinely surprised with the way the ending turned out. I knew something was coming, but failed to predict what it was.

_childDocuments_.review: I was more invested in this game than the original, which is interesting as sequels are usually "worse". However, Shadows feels like it refines the tension, characterization, and choice of agency that Coteries was semi-successful in. Having one solid MC to play and mold the world with got me far more invested, and I was floored by the free will a short visual novel game gave me. Love this one. _childDocuments_.review: An excellent sequel. You really should play Coteries of New York first though since it references that game constantly. A more focused game than that one since you cannot choose from a variety of clans this time. But, its narrative explores Lasombra in a lot of depth. Very much enjoyed the plot and characters and it brought the duology to a satisfying conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: This story tends to wear a mask to the Masquerade, just like its characters do — it’s an overly pretentious, sarcastic, disorganised mess, and it benefits from being one. The writing voice though is strong and resonant, some lines will leave a mark on you even though you won’t actually remember or quote them. The music is top notch here. It will plunge you deep into the atmosphere of the story, it matches the art and writing really well.Very few choices that matter. Only two endings, a “good” and a “bad” one, ambiguous in their nature, inviting you to go for a reread immediately. A reread is a must, because it will add a new layer of depth and your personal understanding of the story’s essence. First read: 6/10. Second read: 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I am the type of person who generally buy something only if thinks that it will be integrated with an interesting and enjoyable story. _childDocuments_.review: If you like the first game or the general theme of Vampire the masquerade, there is a high chance you'll like this story.That's right, it is more of an interactive story with some dialogue choices than a real game, but the story is intriguing and the sound and graphics really help to create an unique atmosphere around it. _childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very linear visual novel with a handful of choices that'll give you two different endings. Can be 100%ed in under 5 hours. Check out the Choice of Games VTM games if you need more options and systems. This is also a sequel to Coteries of New York, and you won't get as much out of this without playing that first. With those caveats in mind, this is a very well executed and presented story. Stellar music and art, solid writing, interesting characters, and a pretty engaging story. Some people probably won't love the protag Julia, but I find her very compelling and way more interesting than Coteries' pretty milquetoast protags. Overall it just feels way more focused than Coteries, and that's to its benefit. Above all, it nails the unique mix of "personal and cosmopoliton horror" that makes VTM so unique. In fact, while Bloodlines is of course the best VTM *game* I honestly feel like SoNY is the best representation of the VTM tone and style in a video game so far. Or maybe I'm just a sucker for vampire lesbians. Probably that one. 8.5 overall for fans of VTM and/or visual novels. Likely not gonna do much for people not into either.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a VERY tentative recommendation. There is a lot to like about this game - the artstyle, the music, being set in the World of Darkness, the gothiness if that's your thing - but some... let's call them *quirks* of the writing seemed to deliberately try and sabotage the good things it had going on.The problems of the game's writing (and being a visual novel, it's 99% writing) can all be summed up in one single word: "Julia". See, most of the characters are pretty good as these things go. They're well written, varied, occasionally inflicted with wanky dialogue, but overall, solid performance. But our main girl Julia... Oooh boy. She starts out alright, as a reporter getting to the bottom of some twisted controversy archetype, but after she inevitably gets turned into a vampire, her few appealing qualities quickly get drowned out by a neverending cascade of endless, pseudo-philosophical inner monologues, insulting characters that are much less infuriating than herself for partially really flimsy reasons, and hogging a lot of playtime that could have been spent focusing on literally anyone else.I can respect wanting the story to be focused on your main character's perspective, and on principle, I think sticking to their internal perspective like that is a good approach, since it allows the player to get to know them better and become invested in their struggles. But all of that only works when your main character isn't such an infuriatingly obnoxious drama queen that you would rather stake her than empathize with her.I'm giving Julia flak because I genuinely think that I might have liked this game quite a lot if it had gone with a different kind of protagonist. As it stands, if you think that she's someone you can relate to or vibe with, then you most likely will appreciate her constant presence and will probably have a good time with the story. And I will say that despite my annoyances, the ending I got didn't completely leave me cold. It also did not leave me with much desire to go through the game again for the other ending option, but nevertheless, overall I mostly enjoyed the game in spite of my problems with it, and you might too, or ideally you might get a lot more out of it than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: video review here: written review:Vampire The Masquerade Shadows of New York is a second instalment in New York based World of Darkness Visual Novel series. First instalment was Vampire the Masquerade Coteries of New York. You can play this one without playing the previous one, but I would highly not recommend.Cons:- almost all quality of life issues present in Coteries of New York are still present in Shadows of New York. No "skip till dialogue" button, for example (though you can hold control for fast text skipping, but still, you need to hold it). No Gallery of unlocked backgrounds either. - No way to revert saves. There's only auto-saving. I understand that actions should have consequences, but there are not a lot of consequences to be had in a visual novel with only two endings. I have played through both, but Steam hickuped and didn't register one playthrough, so unless I want to sit here pressing control for a good hour in order to get to the ending again, I'm just not going to have all the achievements. - Main character is so much more whiny than anyone in her position would have been. The girl is an immortal being with super powers, yet spends her free time sulking in a fast food joint. - Biggest joy for me was seeing how characters from Coteries of New York were doing, meaning if you haven't played the previous one, you'll have far less enjoyment out of this one.- BenoitPros:- It took me 13 hours to play through the game once and the game is good for about two playthroughs. - The game portrays a stereotypical Lasombra and I absolutely loved it. - I did not find a single outcome of Coteries of New York characters to be uninteresting. I thoghroughly enjoyed all of their stories.- Writing has improved significantly since the last instalment. - I liked both the good and the bad ending. - Art, while some of it is taken directly from Coteries, is still incredibly  beautiful. Most backgrounds that I've seen are also animated in some way. - Music is great. As long as it is not trying to demonetise me on Youtube. Overall - Shadows of New York is a lot more linear than Coteries of New York, but I feel like this works a lot better for a game in this genre, the writing was much better and despite not liking the main character I had loads of fun. Would highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This following part is about 60-70% of the game: The main character is supposed to be this relatable emo girl who stands up for what she believes in while being quirky in a "ugh, I'm so lonely" way. I'm sure my 16 year old self would have found her a lot more fascinating, but as a young adult I keep thinking about how stupid or immature she is. That's not me being presumptuous either, the player has to read through her monologues almost more than the dialogue between characters or the events that occur. The times where I don't mind her type of character is when we don't have to read so many of her monologues and when she's just a normal character interacting with the theme. I by no means am asking for a better character here, I'm sure some people are into this type of character. She's a believable girl, more social than smart or insightful despite her introverted nature. At one point she gets letdown by people wearing "normcore" clothing because they're uninteresting and I think that perfectly describes what kind of character it is you're going to play as. I don't know how else to describe this but "If you want to get inside the head of a girl, buy this". It's not a bad game, just very ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nicheThis next part is for the other 40-30%:It's a riot. Story goes off the rails and you need to really lean into the madness to experience the fun. Just turn off your brain once it starts to happen and enjoy the power fantasy and the momentum. Ride it. They turn down Julia's stupid boring monologues and replace it with schizophrenic Lasombra shadow people and have really interesting character speeches from the past game delivered to Julia. The game shines through when it's not about Julia, but the other characters interacting with each other (very brief moments). Some of the new characters are interesting too but rarely get any screen time.ConclusionIf this game replaced 2 hours of tedium with the parts that make it good it'd be a contender for beating the first game. As it stands now I can't recommend it because that tedium is real. It's like, I just finished the game and the last hour or so was great but there's this almost instinct not to replay it because the beginning and middle is mostly awful.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a big fan of VtM in general and I really enjoyed Coteries of NY.  Unfortunately Shadows is less of a game than just a graphic novel where you are railroaded through the single plot line.  Compared to Coteries it limits your options in three major ways.  First, although introducing the Lasombra was interesting, it means you can't pick your character.  Then, for each night your choice of scene is more limited; but it doesn't matter because once the scene you pick is done you get shuffled right into the main plot (and the choices you make during the selected scene don't matter).  Lastly, even within the scenes you have fewer opportunities to make choices and with the exception of a handful of choices, none of them really matter to the flow of the story.  Lastly, while social commentary is key for VtM, it takes skill to avoid slipping over into getting preachy.  Shadows crosses this line several times (contrast with Deus Ex: Human Revolutions which does this flawlessly).  They had a winning formula with the first one; hopefully they can get back to it.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellently written (in a somewhat modernist tone, infused with introspection, flashbacks, and deep forays into the protagonist's psyche) visual novel that is equally a thriller and a drama based on political intrigue. The characters and the dialogue are fascinating, as is the setting. It is more potent as a thriller and drama than as a detective novel, which it partially tries to be.The vocabulary feature is also extremely useful for someone not accustomed to the lore of the universe (like myself), which is quite intricate.The only point that might disappoint you is that there are very few impactful choices. Like with Telltale games, most choices are purely formal and only lead to a few lines of dialogue being changed. I suggest that you play with this in mind and don't try to look too hard for a significant impact for your choices. Nonetheless, there are two different endings (and a secret one), so that is not to say that there are no meaningful choices at all.Therefore, please do yourself a service and try this out if you're looking for a well-written story (even if you're not necessarily into vampires or this specific universe).

I liked this approach: It wasn't so much memorizing facts and details, it was understanding how to be a vampire, and how those seemingly basic choices affected the investigation.Overall, very enjoyable, fully recommend.PS: Received free through Humble Bundle. _childDocuments_.review: I bought Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York because I enjoyed its predecessor, Vampire: The Masquerade - Coteries of New York. Unfortunately Shadows of New York is far less engaging and the narrative frequently bogs down in endless internal monologues. This visual novel wants to be smart and irreverent, it wants to have an excess of existential cool and make its readers identify with the protagonist as she wades through her unlife of angst. Alas the results are uneven at best and the central character mostly comes across as a whiny and self-absorbed bore. Some may enjoy it but, for my part, this visual novel was a masochistic read. I felt locked into an unlikable character whose journey became ever more irritating as she reluctantly made her way through the story.Vampire: The Masquerade does lend itself to tortured characters who far from dominating their supernatural world are actually hemmed in by its myriad rules and are dominated by ubiquitous ruling hierarchies within vampire society. In Coteries of New York the three possible player characters had enough of a blank slate aspect to them for the player/reader to define their personalities. In Shadows of New York there is a single protagonist and player choice is limited to determining which of two endings the game concludes on.If the narrative was better paced, the characterizations were more consistent, and the plot was more engaging, I would have given this visual novel a positive review regardless of how annoying I found the protagonist. As things stand, however, I found little redeeming value in this game beyond the artwork (much of which is recycled from Coteries of New York).

With most games that have more than one ending, there's always an ending I prefer. One that feels more satisfying and complete. For this game, I had an equally great time playing both endings. I would absolutely love to see more from this team one day.

_childDocuments_.review: Vampire The Masquerade visual novels seduced me, and I’m loving being in this world, unfortunately this one was much less enticing to me than , which was my first time. That and I can’t recommend Shadows without playing Coteries, because it not only occurs in the same environment, and maybe it’s my impression here, but I felt it assumed I knew some things beforehand, like Coteries’ events.I also felt that  decided to have trade offs instead of improving on the previous product. It introduced a couple of cool things, like personality traits and the dependence on them on determining the end of your story, but the trade off was playing a character with very predetermined characteristics, and even objectives, which will reflect on the limited or non consequential dialogue choices. You will have a lot of musings and interesting conversations, but not much agency. Technically you have much less dialogue and of that dialogue only something like five consequential choices that will play either for or against the two possible endings. One Coteries playthrough also took me about 5 hours, while 5 hours gets you two runs in Shadows if you feel like completing the story twice for ‘Good’ and ‘Bad’ ending.Other thing this one had in its favor is how it is related to current 2020 events. It mentions the polarization in America and New York, the effects of the pandemic, and explores the somber moods felt in this timeline in our real lives. Fortunately however it does not go too deep and does not deviate from the actual story and characters, after all, there’s an investigation to solve. Having an original character like Julia made these real world reflections better because you could relate to them but feel like it was a perspective not your own, otherwise it would be risky doing this like Coteries where you pick a more custom character. The Clan Julia belongs to is also very fitting, and there’s this constant fight between going against the system or taking part in it to play from the inside and make a difference. That’s how I understand it and the latter is how you do politics properly, and how vampires can make themselves heard in the Camarilla. That’s pretty much a running theme in both novels, though.Look folks, I love the environments, the way they’re drawn, the music (which is the same as Coteries), the characters and to be in the middle of all that rain, skyscrapers and nightlife. It does a great job at delivering something familiar yet an immersive culture. I prefer Coteries by a mile and once again I’m not compelled to make another play through (yet), because basically it’s just changing 5 answers, get maybe a different twist and that’s that, so I leave that for you to decide whether to replay or not. I got this from Humble Monthly and they can keep coming because I’m loving them.

_childDocuments_.review: When I finished reading the first product, Coteries of NY, I thought if the rich content that World of Darkness (WoD) provides were combined with a compelling narrative from a skilled writer, it could be an entertaining experience worth a couple of dollars, even if it were just a visual novel.After Coteries of NY, I made some constructive criticisms, suggesting that it should have been more dialogue-driven, our choices should have had a greater impact on the story, and there should have been more gameplay content beyond just a novel. Additionally, the visual and musical elements could have varied more. Nevertheless, the game entertained me, and I spent about 15 hours on it over 3-4 days.However, looking at Shadows of NY, I was simply disappointed. While I liked the first product overall despite its flaws, Shadows of NY felt lacking. The first product provided a 15-hour, 7/10 scenario, whereas Shadows of NY offers a 5-hour, 4/10 experience at best. The writing quality has dropped, the narrative is boring, and the visual and musical content lacks variety—many visuals are even copy-pasted from the first game. Rarely do the dialogue options affect the outcome.In short, Shadows of NY is a boring and short visual novel that fails to bring anything noteworthy to the table.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm leaving a negative as an information to the cretors. This is not the way. Go back to what you did in Coteries of NY and don't look back.I've enjoyed this "game" though. It's "game" as this is not a game at all. This is a poorly written fanfic. But first to good things.I've enjoyed Coteries and Shadows mostly for its mood and art style. It's exactly as I always saw Vampire (who knows, maybe this is a Polish thing). Music, arts, the way that it's presented and the narrative. Perfect.Music here is just a bit worse than in Coteries (so 9/10). Arts got a bit extended and there were some new formulas mixed in (multi-character vignettes). Over all - nice.But the formula of the "game" and how the story goes is terrible.This game has no choices in it. Thus it's not a game. It's what you got when someone wants to film a movie but have a game framework. There are literally 20 points in this game when you are allowed to click anything except the NEXT button and only 6 of those clicks are important (and one in an overzealous way - ). The game does not even try to hide this at some point and the narrator clearly says that both choices that you have at the moment are good and “it’s basically a coin flip”.Next place of no choices - in Cotteries most of your choosing power came from picking how you want to spend the night. Judging you encounters meticulously. Here you can pick only one thing every night. Those choices are vaguely described and ultimately non-related fillers.If it comes to the story it was weak. And here it was the most obvious that this was supposed to be a movie in writers head. It’s a noir detective movie with a typical series of twists at the end. And the problem is that such movies always leave tension release to the end, with the detective solving the story in front of all involved (including the viewer). And here it;s the same. My character, in a game, is solving a story without me… all “aha” moments, all “gotchas”, all analyzing was done by my character. I was just a viewer and nothing more. Was it tense? Yes. Was it fun? Yes. Was it what I’ve paid for? No.Also the story is full of deus ex machinas. All over the place. As if the writer just can’t write a good story. Every main discovery is done by some random chance (). Some things are also not logical at all (). Draw Distance - you can and should do better than this.The game is about developing a character and finding a place in a Kindred society. But it’s done with too much haste and too immaturely. It’s not compelling at all at the end. The character arc is just overblown.There are also some mild spoilers for Coteries so you have to play them first. This was totally avoidable as those spoilers are irrelevant to the “story” of this game.Overall I recommend this product. But I will not buy another one like this. Yellow card.

_childDocuments_.review: "At this point, I'm almost somnambulic, but nothing interesting has happened yet." - This quote from the game perfectly sums the game itself up. Draw Distance, a suggestion- this is NOT the meta commentary you should be embracing. Holy f*ck. I'm about 45 minutes in, granted about 8 mins has been spent jotting down thoughts on this mess, and NOTHING worthwhile has happened. The fact that the opening of the story fails to grab attention like "Coteries" at least managed to achieve is downright damning. The game opens with a wanna be Lovecraftian-vibe, incoherent, monologue about mysterious castles and the moon. Then we're suddenly in a not-Denny's generic late night restaurant at 3:31 am. There's a new inner monologue; an elitist rant bashing people who are up late as unproductive members of society. And the insufferable whining, pretentious, self-deprecating bullsh!t just continues to stretch on for several more passages.The story notes it's now 3:47; and yeah, maybe it didn't take 16 minutes to read all that, but it certainly FELT like 16mins of self-indulgent BS. "(Godd@mn). This is pure trash"- Once again, a quote from this game jumps out at me. It seems my response to "Coteries" time-traveled and found its way to this sequel, but the writers failed to learn anything from it. WTF. Still, I decide to continue on with this story, hoping that it will get better, or at least that I'll find some hidden gems of characters like "Coteries" managed to cough up despite how often that game was shooting itself in the face. I jokingly think to myself that I will go ahead and blame the Malk Madness Network for failing to pass the "this is trash" message along clearly, grit my teeth, and continue clicking through nonstop monologuing in hopes some interesting plot or choices finally arrive.Then we get to Lodestar magazine office. The music that kicks in when Brian Ng first shows up deserves positive mention as being atmospheric and notably awesome to break up the mind-numbing nihilistic prose that is still happening without relent. Three cheers to the sound designers for at least nailing their job. Brian is your average mid-level boss it seems; though from Julia's vindictive and self-absorbed monologuing you'd think he's the devil. He's trying to talk to her about her latest piece; while she's got her head up her own @ss, bent on idealism and self-destructing because she's got no better alternatives to offer Brian, but adamantly thinks he should blow up his life (and ability to provide for his family) and the company just for the sake of an article that's not going to make a difference in the grand scheme of the world anyway because the target is some random rich dude. "You still want to go through the motions, just to make me feel listened to." - And once again a quote from our protagonist's incessant inner monologue can be directed at the developer because there hasn't even been a single choice up until this point to even feign player interaction. I am now actively WISHING you people would throw the non-choices of "Coteries" at us for this supposed game to break things up some. How the heck are you making me miss playing "Coteries"?! Really?! "You're too in love with weaving a good story and establishing a seductive narrative to let facts get in the way." - So says Julia's boss as they're discussing why her latest piece is a problem. I'm once again having sarcastic thoughts rise up because this entire scene is boring as sh!t and I'm wondering how a story-centric game like V:tm has managed to end up with writers who don't give a d@mn about a good/seductive story OR a factually/logically sound one. Julia is fired, which is completely unsurprising and she all but brought it on herself. An entire paragraph of un-punctuated, jumbled up partial sentences strung together, internal monologue better fit for Tumblr tags ensues. Again- holy sh!t, is this hard to read. And then Julia suddenly starts mentally and verbally bashing a random movie reviewer, Nick, who works for the company; all while lighting up a cigarette in her now ex-office space and ratting him out to the boss for turning off the smoke alarms. Apparently she once wanted Nick's job, didn't get it, and Brian supposedly ruined her dreams by instead pushing her into investigative journalism; and then her being too good at IJ has now gotten her fired. Yet again, Julia obviously pushing this self-victimizing idea that Brian=Evil Boss Figure; Julia=Awesome idealistic artsy underdog. No gratitude for him giving her a different job at least, or the few years he's continued to try mentoring her and helping her improve her skills and make connections. He's just an evil symbol of all that is wrong with their field of work and "oppressing" her. Julia continues her ego-centric ranting, working herself up into an even bigger rage. Then she starts trashing the office she worked in, ultimately needing to be escorted out by security. She's a complete loose canon and liability. It's no wonder Brian and the higher management assumed she'd not take the news of her article being abandoned very well and would need to be fired. They had her completely pegged for being unhinged and uncompromising. Then Julia hops on a subway and continues to have her non-stop pity party monologues.And that's when I gave up on playing this particular game. I can't. Julia is one of the most unlikable, badly written, extreme stereotypes for a character I have ever encountered- and she STILL hasn't even crossed paths with vampires and been influenced by their culture or the Lasombra bloodline yet. I cannot bring myself to try spending an entire game having to deal with these asinine inner monologues of hers, especially whatever takes she'll have on whatever harebrained vampiric scheming plot she gets pulled into. So, congratulations Draw Distance- you managed to produce a sequel that lifts "Coteries" up enough by comparison to steal its spot of "worst story told in the V:tM franchise." Coteries of New York at least had the catchy start to bring you into being a vampire, even if it nosedived immediately after. You managed to create one of the very few games/storylines that was so abrasive and unappealing that I was unable to force myself to get through just one playthrough of it to give the full plot arc a fair shake. I've played hundreds of games over the years, read thousands upon thousands of books across so many genres- and THIS piece of media has the dubious honor of joining those I can count on one hand for being unfinished because it is just that miserable to sit through.I gave myself a few week break between Coteries and Shadows to make sure I'd be coming into the new installment with a fair attitude that wasn't carrying over resentment for how bad Coteries was. Shadows ruined itself. I'm going to set this franchise aside again for a few more weeks, and then I'll attempt to play the next game/story- Night Road. I want to say it can't be any worse than THIS game, but the developer seems to like proving me wrong. If nothing else, it'll be interesting to see if the next game can match this one in sheer volume of ironic quotes from the opening scenes that lampoon the writers and developers for churning out such dreck that can only be getting passable reviews because the V:tM label was slapped onto it and so many V:tM players and/or general vampire media fans are just starved for SOMETHING to play and will pant over whatever bones we get tossed from the corporate overlords. Buying it for like $1 on sale was only worthwhile because the musicians/sound designers deserve to get something for their work. Sorry you lads and lasses got stuck with such a sh!t project. You deserved better.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a sequel to Coteries of New York and picks up some considerable time after the head-scratching ending they leave you with, and the game seems to trust that players coming into this one are reasonably acquainted with either the previous title or at least VTM. This works to the game's advantage to some degree; it lets them cut the fat around regurgitating the "new 'nate who dis" stuff, but it also sacrifices the themes of quiet uncertainty, predator and prey. In fact, it's a more of a vampire noir story than anything resembling your usual VTM narratives.New protagonist is Julia, instead of offering an option among three, allowing for a more focused if streamlined experience. Julia is, for better and worse, a very defined character whose worldview is firmly cemented - you do get some binary options on what introspections she reaches, and these do contribute to determining which ending you receive, but they all stem from a foundation of someone who already knows who she is. This makes her the strongest written of the newly introduced cast and at other times, just downright insufferable. This is preferable to the literally-who that also is introduced in this game and shows up for the beginning and ending segments, and is lauded as being somehow important.Previous protag's Coterie that do make a return are sadly quite brief and somewhat muted in their reappearances. I assume because this is Julia's story and not the old Coterie's, but still, they were very likable while we had them. Julia is about on their level. As for the other two newcomers,  is not as much and  is definitely not.There are no mechanics in this one like Blood, and this means the side-activities have literally zero purpose other than to pass the time or roleplay. However, this also means that you can focus on the meat of visual novels: the dialogue and the choices you make in the heat of the moment. As novel as the Blood-tracking thing was, leaving it out this time was for the best I think.Soundtrack knocks it right out of the park in this one. It's more pronounced than in the previous games - which is not a knock against those, but rather an appreciative nod to the fact that it emphasizes the mounting pressure that the newly turned Lasombra punching bag is under.Overall, I enjoyed my time and would recommend it on a sale, but I wouldn't replay it.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Coteries of New York, and this is a thoroughly disappointing follow-up.
