_childDocuments_.review: I have the same misgiving about this "game" as many other players have on this one and its first opus ... that's it not really a game but, rather, a mix between a hardcover book and a comic.But what a beautiful one it is though! The lack of choice, real choice in the story is irking me a bit but on the other hand, the story itself and the hardwork ... WOW!Now that's something. The story itself is quite intriguing and a very good continuation of coterie of new york. The graphics are really beautiful and with animations that are both subtle, yet very appropriate for the game, not to mention it gives the whole an otherworldly feeling quite appropriate for the WoD setting.I did have more 'playing' Julia in this on than coterie of new york (though I suppose I should say "read" the story through her eyes). She's quite a handful, though, as far as I am concerned, she would have made much better Anarch or Brujah material. Contrarly to what I have heard in previous, while, sure, some graphic assets have been transposed in this game from the previous one, I never really did get the feeling it was done in a cheap way. They do have enough programming and artistic talents to do something good here or, even better, to pair up with the other dev team making world of darkness games.The former (here) are very good artistically and storytelling wise, but not on the "choose you own adventure". _childDocuments_.review: A short but ultimately compelling addition to the list of Vampire: the Masquerade video games, "Shadows of New York" lets you get in the head of its main character, the Polish-born investigative journalist Julia Sowinski. Unlike in "Coteries of New York", which offers three possible main characters, all of whom share the same story, this game eschews the use of a blank-slate protagonist for one who is full of emotion, motivation, and conflict.My one big gripe about the game is that it offers very little in replay value, as once you've played through the story there really isn't another story to tell. Though there are some divergent options to take, ultimately the narrative leads down the same path. The final outcome does depend on actions taken during the plot, but after exploring the game for the first time and achieving one ending, the second one feels a bit hollow. It's very much a "Now let's choose all of opposite options and see what happens!" situation, rather than encouraging exploration of different dialogue choices, or even different scenes.I would recommend giving the game a try if you're into stunning visuals and absolutely gorgeous music. For those and the excellent writing, I would say the game is worth every penny. If you're looking for anything other than a visual novel where you mildly influence the outcome, then I wouldn't recommend this game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: THE GOOD:- Finally you get to play a  in a NYC Camarilla's power play visual novel!- I got to the "Good Ending" on my first playthrough.THE BAD:- Compared to "Coteries of New York", even though the story is far more intriguing, it's much shorter and the "choices" you make are limited.- There are apparently only 2 endings, a "good" and a "bad" one.Overall I'd rate this 7/10 and I'd recommend picking both games up on discount if you're into visual novels and solid Vampire the Masquerade political scheming story narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: I played this after coming off of playing Werewolf: Heart of the Forest. This game is more linear and that may be a turn off for some. If you like World of Darkness you probably would like it regardless. Personally, I chose to play this game because of one word: Lasombra. These former Sabbat vampires are arguably one of the coolest clans in Vampire the Masquerade. The main character is cool and she doesn't even know it. The music is dark and unique and fits perfectly with a manipulator of shadows in the big city. The story keeps a steady rhythm and doesn't have you getting sent off endlessly to do chores to please the higher-ups.That being said, if you like open world games and lots of choices, this game is probably not for you. If you have patience for a good story, wait until it is on sale and snap it up right away. Personally I wish they would have done a little voice acting as it would make the game feel like a more complete package, but that is a minor gripe. Also, if you want to compare this to Coteries, which I am currently playing, I would say this is a superior game in almost every way. Shadows is standalone, so you don't need to play Coteries in order to get into it. So yeah, I would recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: I played Shadows before I played its predecessor, Coteries. Both games were worth my time, but I enjoyed Shadows slightly more. Shadows of New York gives the protagonist some teeth and some between-the-scenes familiarity with managing both her supernatural capabilities and with knowing Kindred society's rules. This is good because it allows the player to have the confidence to feel free to use violence OR diplomacy at many points in the story.  (I liked Coteries, but I often had the impression that if my character has only been a vampire for a week, the player was by definition THE weakest vampire in the city. With Shadows, I had the impression that I had more options.)Also, Shadows of New York does an impressive job at telling a story where the player can soak up the morally meaningful gray areas of being immortal in a game of personal horror; throughout the story it's difficult for the player to know whether they're winning or losing in terms of moving towards a Best Possible Ending achievement as opposed to a You Really Failed achievement. That's impressive writing! Shadows of New York is the sort of video game where you can get to one ending and honestly not be able to define it as the desirable winning ending or the undesirable losing ending. (Shadows felt like I was reading hard-to-grasp classical literature for a class rather than watching a directed-by-the-shareholders cash cow movie. Shadows doesn't insult the player's intelligence.)Shadows and Coteries does very well in the personalities of the many NPCs. Half the fun of the tabletop and LARP Vampire the Masquerade games was in meeting any new Kindred and trying to figure them out, both via first impressions and by repeated encounters later. This company did that very well in both games, and just like IRL, it was sometimes difficult to know if someone I just met would be a recurring rival or a disposable only-for-this-one-scene NPC.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I do recommend the game if you are a fan of the franchise, it's still a good and enjoyable story fitting the genre.Now, why the dislike... While it is arguably a better story than Coteries, it's a massive step down gameplay-wise. There are much fewer spots where you choose your reaction, even though I get that it's basically a trick and the dialogue goes back to the same railroad after mabye one or two chat windows, it feels more engaging. I also like that you could failed in various quests in Coteries, while I don't think there is ever a wrong option here (except for an early possible game over). All side quests are one-time events (unlike Coteries where they were often whole series of encounters). In the end, I enjoyed replaying Coteries because I could still find new stuff, while I just frantically clicked my way through Shadows to get the second ending - there is little replay potential (even though there are two endings, while Coteries had one which was a bit different depending on choices during the game).I have to say, I have some reserves about the story too. It somewhat drags and some parts seem to be included just to bring back characters from the first game or to make the game a bit longer. There are a few interesting new characters but they tend to disappear from the story for long periods or dont get much space. There is no bonding with other characters with one exception, but that relationship depends on the ending of the game, not dialogues you have with the person. All in all, I would rather recommend Coteries than Shadows.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: VTM: SoNY is a fascinating game. It basically screams at you to buy in with the PC, Julia, and the rest of the setting. And if you do you will want to know more after you finish the game. I highly recommend the game to any Vampire fans.The game has only a few branching paths, but has a cool system to change the mood of the PC and the story without you knowing what is reacitve and what isn't. I am not 100% sure but it seems like "winning" isn't the most important part, it's more about shaping Julia, telling her story that would fit.In a way this kinda disincentivises a replay, the first time through will be your "canon" and changing such a personal story feels wrong. If you have played Disco Elysium you may recognize that feeling.One problem for me than was: I bought in, I wanted to be Julia, but there were several missing scenes I think, like time-skips where I didn't know what she was doing (or where she has knowledge from somewhere I couldn't see). I know this was to build tension, but for example skipping the (usually) dramatic first few days after an embrace felt wrong. The whole game I expected to relive those days as a flashback/retelling. Also Julia's constant Masquerade breeches make sense in her personality, and should have been a huge conflict with her new reality as a Vampire.I realize now looking at the last paragraph that I just want more of everything heh.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked Shadows of New York, specially after it's predecessor - Coteries. To me this is a big improvement. I didn't love Coteries, in the end it felt like a sour experience which I had alot of gripes with, but it left me enough curiosity to try out it's "sequel", this game, Shadows of New York, because behind all the weird ways in which Coteries was engineered, I saw that this team could do alot better, and I'm glad it did. Ironically, it was the negative reviews on this entry claiming it was different from Coteries that piqued my interest.I'm happy to say that alot of the gripes I had with Coteries simply don't exist in this entry. The decision for having only one protagonist played much better in it's favour in my opinion. The story was just much more focused, the protagonist actually had a personality, somewhat dictated by you, and as a result it felt much more fleshed out. This was just overall a big improvement to me. I see that some people didn't like the protagonist, or more noteworthy, her pessimism or misery-like outlook on alot of things, fair, if you don't like the protagonist you are stuck with her, but the story benefits from alot more focus and development. Personaly I liked her alot, since I like more pessimistic outlooks anyway.Overall, I didn't love Coteries, but I actually kind of loved this one. I hope they stick with their single protagonist formula in the future, or vastly improve the design of multiple protagonist choices in the future.The ending was quite satisfying, even if brutal and ruthless, somewhat bittersweet, but perfectly fitting the clan and the protagonist.
_childDocuments_.name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Shadows of New York

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the Coteries earlier this month, I wanted to move onto this as I really liked that game. This is exactly the evolution that you would want out of the first. Instead of following a more generic character, you are now someone who has an already established role in the universe. The clan you are part of is in a really interesting place within the politics of the world. I can also compliment the fact that you define your characters reactions, but not have an A/B choice for the ending, it feels like a true result of what you've done. I would really love if they continue down this direction so we can keep getting more of the Vampire universe.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastically drawn "Whodunit" story. Taking place sometime after Coteries of New York. We take on the role of Julia, a young journalist and a soon-to-be Lasombra neonate who is thrown into the thick of a political powerplay between Camarilla and Anarchs. Will you embrace the legacy of The Night Clan and rise to the top or will you cherish last shreds of humanity and push the shadows away?As a GM I adore well-camouflaged linearity and have no qualms that this game is a pretty straightforward railroad only with two endings. Yes, you can make a couple "important" decisions and some flavor choices to spice up the game, you will still get a "good ending" and a "bad ending". The rest is a well-written script with marvelously drawn decorations and amazing soundtrack to boot.Thank you, Draw Distance. Hope you will keep on making these amazing WoD gems.

_childDocuments_.review: The stand alone expansion to Vampire: The Masquerade - Coteries of New York, Shadows of New York continues the story of the first game from the perspective of Julia Sowinski, a fledgling of the Lasombra clan, tasked with investigating the death of a prominent vampire.Shadows of New York builds on the foundation set by Coteries with even better art and music. Really, this game is a feast for the senses with its dark and moody character art and jaw dropping CGs. The story and the MC is a major improvement as well with Julia being an infinitely more interesting protagonist compared to the original three in Coteries. She's intelligent, inquisitive, resourceful but also deeply cynical, vulnerable and, occasionally, ruthless. The game isn't particularly long with my first playthrough taking just a bit over four hours but it compensates its length with a genuinely intriguing plot. It's also great to see the Lasombra clan represented in VTM media as they do a great job of shaking up the familiar formula of more vanilla clans like Brujah, Toreador etc. A few criticisms are that the game has no skip option and no manual saves, issues that were already present in Coteries with the skip option eventually being patched in before Shadows released. It makes me wonder why they couldn't have integrated the skip option into this game right from the start.All in all, Shadows of New York is a promising sign that the developers are really looking into deepening their video game experiences and I'm excited for potential sequels. I think it would be fantastic if they can expand upon the choices in the game with branching paths and more varied endings. A full VTM VN with 20+ hours of content requiring real thought concerning the choices you make would be amazing!

_childDocuments_.review: Simply put if you played the coteries of New York you will want to play this game. The game itself is inferior in every aspect. I am left feeling mostly unfulfilled and generally disappointed. I cannot go further into detail without spoilers as this really is a story driven experience. However, I can go further about the shortcomings of the game as a sequel. Balancing feeding and power use is gone. There are opportunities to do both, but they do not actually matter.  The choices are sadly given as much weight as the old bioware Jedi games. Meaning you are either Good to the point of martyrdom and stupidity. Or you are heartlessly evil selfish to the point of mustache twirling. It kinda sucks. Further, even though they were quite clear about there only being the lasombra clan as a choice I still feel is a detraction from the previous game. This game is inferior in all regards to the previous entry while also not even remotely working off of the cliffhanger the previous game left us upon making the previous entry feel almost pointless. I believe if you are a fan getting to visit this world again will be decent enough of an experience to warrant a purchase, but I wouldn't recommend this to anyone else. I will, however, apologize and grovel my rear off  if both of the games come together in bloodlines 2 or perhaps a third game.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of New York is an interesting but ultimately too-brief and too-shallow VN that serves as a sequel to Coteries of New York. As a DLC to Coteries it might have succeeded in providing a cut-price and alternate-perspective epilogue, but as its own game there is simply not enough. My listed play time is heavily extended by leaving the game open while my computer was on. In reality, there is less than an hour of story, and replaying the game shows very little new content between what amounts to two total endings. I 100%ed this game's content so quickly I could have returned it. I didn't because that's unethical and I believe in endorsing good storytelling in the format, but where Coteries at least made me feel like I wanted to explore different options and quirky plots, Shadows offered nothing. Decisions did not matter, blood-management felt irrelevant, and as interesting as the lore was, I don't think it alone could sustain the game, especially given the next-to-nonexistent replayability. Add on the fact that character development and interaction felt frustratingly shallow... there's just not enough here.For a stand-alone expansion, I don't think I would have enjoyed Shadows at all if I had not played Coteries, and having played Coteries and enjoyed it, Shadows only left me disappointed. Given that, I can't recommend this game to anyone; even die-hard fans will be left wanting, so at least pay as little as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: Following hot on the heels of last years “Coteries of New York”, “Shadows” starts roughly around the same time as its predecessor, but then leaps forward several months. Unlike the first game, which was told from a second person point of view, this game is told from a First person perspective. You also only have one character, Julia, a new addition to clan Lasombra. You will meet many characters from the first game, both loved and hated, as well as several new ones. The writing is good, maybe a little less engaging than the first one because it’s told through Julia’s eyes instead of yours, but characters are consistent and fleshed out. My favourite arc continued from the first game is Quadir, showing that the Camarilla assassin’s human side is still very much alive. Character models are not static this time around, so you do get more emotion from them. If I were to nit-pick, I would have liked to see more new art for returning characters. A very welcome change this time around is that your actions can lead to the story playing out differently, including the ending, easily justifying more than one play through. Small touches like referencing the free state of LA are also a nice touch for long-time fans of the world of Darkness.Not quite better, but definitely not worse than “Coteries”, "Shadows of New York" is a welcome addition to my “Vampire: The Masquerade” collection. I hope I can say the same of the upcoming “Swansong” and “Bloodlines 2”.

_childDocuments_.review: Short and mostly pretty sweet.Shadows of New York does a number of key things very well: it nails the tone of its universe, aided by the smart choice of having a fixed protagonist. Julia is not a blank slate and it does wonders for the narrative, you have some freedom to shape just where and who she ends up, but your options are limited, and every possible conclusion feels natural. The downside to this is that, your agency is extremely limited, no replayability here, which might doubly annoy you if you find the roughly 6 hour playtime a dealbreaker. This is a tight, focused narrative, with a clear focus on its protagonist (the vast majority of dialogue is internal monologue), so it goes without saying if you find yourself disliking Julia (as I initially did), you might hate this. That said, if you're in the market for a beautifully presented urban fantasy, with sharp, if a bit erratic, writing, give it a shot.Soundtrack is the best i've heard so far this year too.

_childDocuments_.review: I reviewed their first game, Coteries of New York, and gave it a negative review. In that review, I said that I was close to 50/50 on it but a handful of issues pushed me over towards the negative side for everyone but diehard V:tM fans like me. Similar deal now, except it's eking over the finish line. I'd recommend it for just about anyone who's into World of Darkness or visual novel games more generally.There remains some of the same criticisms I had from the first game. Spelling and grammatical issues are a big one, especially for a visual novel game. Although, credit where credit's due, the developers did a much better job of catching them this go around, and I only noticed two or three through the entire game. In Coteries I believe they issued a few patches to update and correct the mistakes made in that regard, so I would expect something similar for people playing this game a little later than I did. There is also the issue of the game feeling pretty railroad-y, as if your choices don't really matter. In Coteries this was especially problematic because there was only one ending no matter what you did, and a deeply unsatisfying one at that. In Shadows there are now two (not counting one where you die). In 8.5 hours I was able to play through the narrative twice to get both endings, and in my personal opinion both are much more satisfying (especially if you played Coteries, as one ending in particular feels a direct answer to the ending of the earlier game). If I had one criticism unique to Shadows compared to Coteries, it would be that despite multiple endings the narrative itself feels much shorter and rushed along than the first game. In Coteries you got to know many more characters, involve yourself in many more subplots (some of which didn't have much to do with the main plotline) and had a more "exploratory" feel to it, as you were a fledgling groping blindly around in the dark, utterly lost in a world wholly above your ability to navigate. In this you are singularly focused on tunneling through the main story. There is no "part 2" to any of the little side stories / feeding excursions you participate in. It always feels as though it were a distraction, and a pretty pointless one at that. Optional feeding / power use (and therefore the spending of blood) also seems to be something rendered completely pointless by comparison from the first game, as from what I could tell from my two playthroughs there are no real consequences to avoiding or indulging in either. All that aside, I do think this is an improvement over the first. It does a good job of capturing the mood of Vampire, which is perhaps most acutely embodied in the Lasombra themselves. Some subtle nods to games long ago (V:tM Redemption) also gave me some quality member berries. It's definitely worth a playthrough for V:tM fans, and I hope the development team continues to churn these out. If you guys are reading this: maybe we could get a Tzimisce one next? Pretty please? ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art, great soundtrack, satisfying plot line Side characters left undeveloped, lacking critical visual novel featuresLike the first game, Vampire the Masquerade - Shadows of New York is visually beautiful. It's exactly the kind of aesthetic you'd want for a gothic horror visual novel. Some of the assets are reused from the first game, but it didn't really bother me much - there was enough new content to keep me interested. The music is also great, very dark and creepy. It fits in well with the atmosphere.The gameplay is about the same as the first game - each night, you get a series of choices as to where to go, leading to a different subplot. In this instance, there's never any plot threads that carry over from night to night, except the main story. There's also no hunger mechanic in this game, as the main character, Julia, has a regular source of blood in her partner. Unfortunately, the same flaws are still available - there's no skip function, save slots are still useful and get erased after you finish the game, and there's no CG gallery.As far as the story, this is where Shadows of New York surpasses its predecessor. Unlike the previous game, this game wraps up nicely. There's no cliffhanger, and there's even two separate endings depending on what your choices were. You even get an idea of what happened to the last protagonist and their coterie. None of the choices really matter, but they do add up to different traits within Julia, changing the way the ending goes. By focusing on one character instead of the three different backstories, we also get a much better fleshed out main character and it feels much less like being railroaded. Overall, if you liked the first game and enjoy visual novels, I suggest checking this game out.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I've spent a reasonable amount of time trying to figure out how to properly review it, so we'll go backwards.Tl;dr: highly recommended with a few very serious caveats.Graphics are identical to what they did in Coteries of New York, so is the gameplay.  If those two things are selling points, then this isn't a departure.  The music is as good as the last game (though, personal opinion, I thought it was even better).  Game length is about 4 hours for a playthrough where you read every word and the associated entries in the glossary for flavor.  I was able to 100% the achievements in about 6 hours.So with all the technical stuff out of the way: the reality is that this game style hinges on the writing, and I felt like SoNY was a lot tighter and more interesting than CoNY.  CoNY let you pick your affiliation and in doing so, it kind of Mary Sue'd the story; you were supposed to be the new born, so they didn't have a whole lot of compelling characteristics.  SoNY, on the other hand, is all about Julia - a new born Lasombra who is very much her own woman.  But the issue with that is that it's her character...being put in the aftermath of CoNY.  The story makes sense without the back story, but it also doesn't - and a lot of the interactions make even less sense between Julia and the licks from the last game.At heart, this is definitely an expansion.  I really enjoyed it, but I wouldn't have gotten nearly as much out of it as if I hadn't played CoNY.  So, recommended...but you really need to play through CoNY to get the whole story.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows of New York is both a sequel and a self-contained story that takes place right after the events of Coteries of New York. It references those events, mostly indirectly, and you will meet a lot of the characters that populate Coteries.  Personally I am impressed by this sequel, mostly because it's writing seems to have improved a few notches. This is especially noticeable in the dialogue. They have gotten a Tarantino kind of quality; snarky, witty, lightning quick back and forths. In fact, if I had any complaint then it would be that it seldom settled down.  It does at a few moments for a short time, but those moments feel mostly as if they are  just a pause to gather the energy for another bout of sharp tongued conversations. A lull in the storm(s).  The main protagonist, Julia, bounces between the cynical and sarcastic. You might think that such a person doesn’t exist, but believe you me, I know such a person. In fact, the relationship between Julia and Dakota feels unsettlingly familiar, except that I didn’t single white female her. Personal experiences aside: I was moved. Which means I am probably not very objective.The game, like it’s predecessor, isn’t a game. It’s a story with options to change the flavor. I didn’t mind. My only observation is that they might have done more with the shadows. I really thought that was something fascinating that could have been explored(or used) more.Anyways.. There are some developments that are interesting, suchs as the traits. I hope that in future versions they will develop this more so that you as a player can shape the game more and feel it is your game.  There is maybe one closing remark for the developers. If you have Malkavians make them insane. Neither Hope nor that corporate felt truly insane. I know it takes a heck of a writer to pull off sane insanity, but to me, neither of them felt really like Malkavians.  I mean, Julia felt more insane than Hope did. I don’t think a Lasombra should out insane a Malkavian? Oh well.. I am nitpicking.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game today and finished it for the first time after 3.2 hours of play. Admittedly, I was clicking through it pretty quickly, but I can't imagine it lasting much longer for anyone who isn't a downright slow reader. You shouldn't be under any illusions: this isn't so much a game as a barely-interactive novel, and it's not going to last long.Having said that, however, I still enjoyed the experience and thought I got my money's worth. On a per-hour basis, it cost me a bit less than it would cost me to go to the average movie, and I was definitely engaged with the story for the entire thing. I'm glad to see some of the characters turn up from the  title as I enjoyed that one too. It was nice to have some follow-up after the events of that title.My best advice as a review is simple. If you like the world-of-darkness setting and enjoy tales without much in the way of actual game play, then this is probably right up your alley. If you're expecting a lot of dramatic plot twists and turns in light of your choices, or you demand a game last at least a handful of hours, then you're not going to be happy with this one. I'm looking forward to "playing" both of them again--experiencing them is probably the better word--even though I know the results won't vary all that much.

The decisions don't seem to change the dialog or direction of the game too much. There's no hunting, only one or two uses of your vampire skills, and without a choice of clan/character, there's little reason to play again, other than maybe chasing the other ending.That said...... the production is still absolutely gorgeous. The art is beyond beautiful and the music is so perfect. This really nails the feel of the White Wolf universe.I hope to see more installments in this series, and I *will* continue to buy them despite the stumble on this game. I think they have a hit concept and team here. Just need to get a little bit closer to what they created in Coteries and a little bit away from this very non-interactive approach.J.Ja

_childDocuments_.review:
You're a nobody. An outcast in your own vampiric sect. A political prisoner of no particular value. An immigrant who never found her roots in a city of immigrants. A chainsmoker whose favorite pastime is staring blankly at the streets through the windows of a fast food joint at 4AM. The sinking feeling in the pit of your stomach tells you that you're doomed, and distorted voices from the shadows seem to agree. The curse of your clan makes interacting with everyday technology difficult. Dissociation is your natural state.

But when New York's Anarch leader meets a gruesome end, out of all the bloodsuckers in the metropolis, you're the one picked to investigate. Make no mistake: this is obviously a trap, yet another move in the horrible game of Jyhad, the eternal struggle for power between warring vampire generations. But you're Lasombra, and if there's one thing you know, it's this: if the Ventrue Prince and her followers underestimate you, they're going to deeply regret it.

Vampire: The Masquerade Shadows of New York is a visual novel set in the rich universe of Vampire: The Masquerade. It acts as a stand-alone expansion and a companion piece to our previous title, Coteries of New York. While Coteries was a general introduction to the world depicted in the 5th Edition of the hit tabletop role-playing game, Shadows presents a more personal and unique tale.

_childDocuments_.review: Good beat 'em ups with a cooperative mode have been around since the legendary Double Dragon, but the number of really good ones on the PC is limited. Last year Streets of Rage 4 came out, which is really good and can even be played by up to four players. With Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues, another excellent new representative of the genre has now been released, completely unexpectedly for me, at the beginning of 2021.Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues is based on the Netflix series Cobra Kai (2018), which in turn continues the story of the Karate Kid feature films from the 80s. You may like the series or not, the game is damn good. As a rule, one should always be careful with games based on a film licence, but in this case the game is definitely not a licensed pickle. The story in the game is completely new, by the way.Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues is a classic left-to-right scrolling beat 'em up in isometric view. You walk a few steps, fight the enemies attacking you and walk a few steps again until you finally reach the boss. However, the variety during the fights is enormous - different punches, special abilities, rechargeable ultimate attacks and the many possibilities to include the environment in the fight do not let the ongoing brawls become monotonous. Usable objects such as chairs that can be kicked around or bottles and baseball bats can be used to maltreat the opponents. Of course, there are also edible things to find to replenish your life energy. The variety of enemies is considerable, and the different opponents also have completely different fighting techniques. During the fight, it is shown whether enemies are currently performing a non-blockable attack or are stunned and can be thrown around. There are also temporary power ups to be found in the levels, as well as hidden collectibles.In the game you can play two long campaigns - either on the side of Daniel LaRusso and the fighters of the Miyagi-Do Karate Club or on the side of Johnny Lawrence and the fighters of Cobra Kai. Only those who play through both campaigns will see the real (ultimate) ending sequence. In total there are eight playable characters (4 per side), each with their own punches, combos, ultimates and other abilities. Between fights, the money you find can be invested to either improve your fighters in an extensive upgrade tree with over 40 unique abilities, or you can invest in improvements to your dojo, which benefits all fighters - almost like a role-playing game.The game can be played alone, but it's really fun to be played together, like Double Dragon. All in all, a very comprehensive, modern beat 'em up.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't give a dime for this game upon watching previews or trailers, it's safe to say it didn't really give the best first impression, it just looked like some lame, uninspired mobile game. Is it perfect? Not really, but much to my surprise, actually...it's pretty darn fun!!! It's a budget game, very much so...but it looks ok and it's well done where it has to be, and what's even better, it's got a surprisingly robust combat system and some pretty NEAT mechanics in place!! While the controls are a bit stiff here and there, it's super easy to pick up and fight, and once you get some additional moves and start experimenting with graps, parries and environmental attacks, it actually becomes really, really fun! True, nobody expected a game about Karate Kid/Cobra Kai to be precisely cartoony, and that was a turnoff at first sight, but the game is very much tongue-in-cheek, and the tone grows on you after a while, especially as it gets the 80's vibe that permeates the show (and films) and turns it up to eleven, so it never feels entirely out of place either. Apart from the characters having elemental powers (fire for Cobra Kai, ice for Miyagi-do), and some video game-y nonsense (which is fully lampshaded), it's not THAT far off from the general absurdity of the show. Even then, it's all framed as a retelling of the show's events from the POV of The Hawk and Demitri, so it's all played out as both nerds exaggerating things as if they were this huge epic. Something else that is impressive is the game's size as well as the scope of its campaign. It's got a ton of levels (accesible via a map after the first stage), all lifted straight from the show (such as the arcade, the Larusso dealership, or the All Valley arena) with tons of minor references, and each dojo has its own storyline with its own particular levels and bosses (and with its own unique characters, each with different abilities and moves, that you can swap on the fly as they join your party, which adds a level of strategy into the mix). There is a true, final boss fight unlocked after playing both stories, so make sure you play them one after the other (while you can use two separate save files to play through each dojo's story, the game advices you to play both on the same save file). All in all, even more so for the super cheap price its at, this little feisty game is a pretty nice bargain, sure to entertain you for a few hours. It may not be quite up there with the likes of Streets of Rage or Final Fight, but it definitely stands on its own and then some (and, if we're comparing, this game feels in more than one way like Double Dragon Neon, so if that game was your cup of tea, then you'll feel right at home here). Again, is it the most "logical" use of the license? Maybe not, but it doesn't mean it disrespects the franchise either, because the attention to detail and reverence is there, and all main characters from the show are there as either playables or bosses, and you get a few VA's from the show (including, of course, William Zabka and Ralph Macchio). If you're done with the AWESOME 3rd season and are craving for some more Karate Kid madness, then give this sucker a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Too much BS for a thumbs up. I had originally given a lukewarm "ok but..." but after playing a bit more, I just have to revise that rating... Be warned that the game gets really cheap really fast. The game-play then boils down to spamming your 8 specials (4 which are character-specific, 4 shared between all your roster) in turn, then running around until things recharge. At some point, I've had no less than 8-9 enemies on screen at the same time, meaning you can hardly tell where the hell you are anymore. Bad guys will frequently turn red or yellow (armoured and invincible, respectively) and charge moves which essentially mean to need to dodge or parry (and the parry has an annoying recharge time, and ANY movement while pressing B -parry- will make your character roll instead). Now, in lesser numbers, this is fine and fun. The issue is that when you have 6+ annoying characters on screen which all basically turn yellow in turn, with one guy constantly sliding in your legs and over-riding your air attacks, while you have 2 roller blade girls hitting you with their spray-can attacks (which basically you can't 'wake-up' from when they hit you) that take about 1/4 of your life bar (each), with 2 idiots throwing ♥♥♥♥ at you from the edge of the screen, and the soccer mom that keeps spawning more and more kids (and these are normal enemies, not powered down summons), it just becomes stupid and not particularly fun. Oh yeah, and that f'ing mall cop on the Segway. It becomes impossible, and you might as well just stand there, die, and restart. The screen is really zoomed in close to the action, and generally there's really not a lot of room to manoeuvre on screen, which makes things even worse. There are very few health power-ups, but swinging weapons are really over-powered and plentiful (which is an odd direction for a karate game, a few weapons are fun, but here it's just too much). Anyway this all means that fights quickly lose the fun factor, you don't really feel powerful, and spawn mechanics/RNG will determine whether you progress or not. Just... restart at last checkpoint and try again... "Oh look, I've won now, but only because the game didn't spawn the same unbeatable mix of idiots in the same sequence as last time." Not really satisfying.Grinding back older levels to get tokens to power up doesn't seem viable, because there's a serious diminishing returns factor there. There's also zero freedom in terms of choosing which stage to do. As far as I've seen after close to 10 hours of play, there's really only one route through the map.I've found that the hit boxes for the environment specials and the grabs (which basically require you to move the analogue stick towards an enemy when they're stunned -it's so f'ing random, and doesn't work well at all, not sure why one of the top triggers couldn't have been used for that) or attacks of opportunities when someone is on the ground are iffy at best, and really require you to be at that exact spot or else it doesn't work. On top of overpowered enemies that keep having shorter and shorter "windows" in which you can attack them, the ridiculous ganging up on you, the game just has too much of a complex control scheme. I'm not sure why one trigger HAS to be to pick ♥♥♥♥ up, while the other trigger HAS to be for the ground attacks (which for some reason only work half the time, if that) It's the same trigger for environment attacks as picking stuff up, so you still run into that issue of having dude pick something up when you don't want to, and vice-versa. Making the character run is also really annoying. Going forward-forward on the mini-joystick on a controller works like ♥♥♥♥. You can switch movement to work on the d-pad, which makes that type of motion easier to do, but that's the ONLY button reconfigure you can do.  The combo system is not the best I've seen either, it's not particularly satisfying. You REALLY need to spam those left trigger/right trigger attacks to really do any damage, and given the nature of the moves, it's not really worth wasting the moves in just trying to combo. I don't know, sometimes it works, most of the time you're whiffing against enemies that turn yellow/red or that moved beyond the rather limited range of most of the attacks.Verdict: Maybe pick it up on sale, but don't expect the most finely-tuned beat'em up. Controls aren't particularly good/intuitive, and the game is way cheap, even for the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues is a Beat ‘em up, Martial Arts Fighter, which allows you a greater peek into the Karate Kid universe.Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues compliments the hit Netflix series, Cobra Kai. Not only does it serve as a backdrop, but the game also enables you to play as eight iconic characters from the series and four each from the two rival Dojo’s. The game doesn’t really add much more to the Universe of Cobra Kai than the movies and the Netflix series already have (except for a surprise ending), but it does give the fan base a unique perspective and lets them experience the world and the characters first hand. Plot: 34 years after the events of the 1984 All Valley Karate Tournament, the rivalry between Daniel LaRusso from Miyagi-Do and Johnny Lawrence from Cobra Kai is raging again after years of being dormant.And this time they are not alone; the students on both sides have become entangled in their rivalry and no one seems to be backing down. The only way of knowing who's winning and who's losing is to go along with their stories and keep fighting. Gameplay: At first glance, it seems and feels like Cobra Kai is another basic beat ‘em up fighter, with all the same glitter and gimmicks. But it turns out to be so much more than that. I would describe it as an experience through gameplay and progression, which doesn’t really involve the story of the game.  The rivalry between these two Dojos is icing on the cake; it adds a unique flavor to the game, and it’s a good one, at that! As soon as you get into the game, you will have to choose between Cobra Kai and Miyagi-Do Dojo. Both are unique in terms of their fighting abilities, skillsets, character, principles, and perspective. If you choose Cobra Kai at the beginning like me, you will be introduced to offensive abilities in terms of fighting skills, and Fire as an elemental. You will get to use and fight with four iconic characters from the Dojo - Johnny, Miguel, Hawk, and Tory. Each has his own unique sets of skills/abilities that he can obtain, which can be used in primary moves as a combo attack. And while using these combos, the Fire element of the Cobra Kai Dojo kicks in and adds extra damage to each attack. Then there are the Dojo-specific upgrades.All of these upgrades can be obtained and unlocked in game Tokens. Tokens are fairly easy to come by. You can earn tokens by beating opponents, finding collectibles, doing finishers, and using your environment to beat opponents. And the same deal goes if you choose Miyagi-Do Dojo.  You will be playing through almost the same environment and opponent types with minor changes at the very end, but you will be getting to use and fight with a totally different set of characters, abilities, skills, and will be introduced to defensive abilities in terms of fighting skills, and Ice as an elemental.As with Cobra Kai, you will get to use a unique and iconic set of characters: Daniel, Robby, Sam, and Demetri. And like before you will be getting unique skills, ability, and fighting style for all of them, including the unlockable extras from the Dojo and Dojo-specific upgrades. Now let’s get into the fighting itself.  For someone like me who doesn’t have much experience in Martial Arts beat ‘em ups, the gameplay and the key layout felt a bit weird.   The fact that I couldn’t change them bothered me a bit, but as I started playing it grew on me and turned out to be very enjoyable. The basic movement consists of WASD and J for jumping. There are two different sets of skills that you can use and you can mix and match them and turn them into combos as well. Personal Skills – U, I, O; each character in the game has his own unique personal skills and appropriate animations associated with them.  As you progress and earn tokens you can unlock more personal skills from the Dojo. Dojo-specific skills, unique to the Dojos and their students, can be unlocked from the Dojos.  You can use U, J, K, which perform their own unique actions and can be combined with personal skills to perform unique combos as you unlock them. Then there is the Unleash Ultimate, Q+L, with which you can perform character-specific ultimates, which are devastatingly powerful. You can also swap between characters from each Dojo on the fly as you unlock them, by hitting 1-4.  If one of your characters is injured or eliminated, he will remain that way until you get food to replenish his health or finish each respective level. Overall, it seems complicated at first but it’s actually a super fun layout! From an outsider's perspective, it takes some time to get used to. Visuals: A great representation of Los Angeles from the Cobra Kai universe, from the colors to the city features. You won’t get to experience much, due to the game's layout, but what you do get to witness looks great and is very well detailed in my opinion. Music and sound effects: An excellent selection of music goes very well with the Martial Arts combat. I kept it running at full volume throughout my playthrough and it didn’t once get repetitive for me. The same goes for the Sound effects, which are nicely detailed and well implemented. Narrations: Voiced and acted by the cast of Cobra kai, it gave the game an authentic flavor from the Netflix series. Considering all aspects of the game, it turned out to be a great immersive experience from the show, from its well-crafted gameplay to its great selection of music. Positives: + Decent Plot + Great Music Selection + Fun beat ‘em up gameplay + Great visuals + Voiced and acted by the cast of the show + Great number of skills and combos to try outNegatives: - Rather small playable area, which made things harder - Throwable items acted weirdly - Opponents landing/hitting from different lanes- No trading cards yetExperience the heat from the hit series, Cobra Kai, with both of its iconic Dojos and their respective characters, and witness a great Martial Arts Saga. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: The game follows the same style of gameplay as Streets of Rage, in fact the combat is very similar (it is far more forgiving than streets of rage though, and more manageable for single player)You will unlock 4 characters for each of the 2 teams, and you can freely switch between these characters as you see fit. You can use them to extend combos, too. They have an attack when you first summon them, and if you land this, you can carry on the combo (TBH the combo goes off a timer, so as long as you don't get hit, and hit something before the timer ends, you're good)The game does deduct points for using the same moves a lot though, so you must switch it up a lot to get high marks (I've only managed a B so far, but I don't have all the skills unlocked yet, and I don't have the last character yet neither, so plenty of room to extend further)There is also a Dojo mode where you can unlock more skills and upgrade your characters. This was actually surprisingly fleshed out, too. You choose a path (other skills become locked off) and tailor your skills to suit your playstyle/build. There are also nodes for statistical improvements (I love the extended critical hit window, which makes it more lenient, when it comes to pressing just after a hit lands) the ones that give you more HP back when they're switched out are awesome as well, they've been a life saver. Each character also has 4 unique specials, and each Dojo has 4 specials too (which all 4 of the characters have access to) These skills can be modified in 1 of 2 paths, so there is a lot of room for experimentation. (There is a reset option though, so if you feel you messed up, you can always reset things and start again)If you like Streets of Rage and Karate Kid, you will love this game. It follows the same basic template as Streets of Rage, but fleshes it out further. It also makes the game more accessible as it's not as difficult, and because you don't have to use health to use specials, you can pull off some really cool combos. It's not too difficult to pull off neither, it has you feeling like a badass for just knowing how to do the most rudimentary  combinations. (as long as you can do mix up's and delays, you are set)I would definitely recommend this game. PS: has some of the voice actors from Karate Kid/Cobra Kai as well.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has suprisingly very large moveset for a beat'em up: - Punch, kick / Combos, delayed combos- Grab punch/kick / Throw/reverse throw / 5 (!) ground hits: kick, punch, smash the face, swing by leg, elbow drop; almost like in Combatribes- Environment attacks (it's a pure joy to break stuff and luxury cars by slamming hippies and punks into)- Dodge/parry attacks- 4 Specials, 4 unique Specials for each character which can be different depending on upgrade choice / 1 Super Power Attack- Weapons / Power Up items / Juggling enemies. And you can run. And make elbow drop on the run!- 8 playable charactersEvery enemy fights differently and has armored attacks, so the enemy variety is great and sometimes is very challenging, so it is not for casual players.Minor complaints: I'd like to see more stage hazards, some challenges are tedious, the game is quite long to get the true final boss.Soundtrack is another instrumental rock/synth/metal masterpiece with tons of catchy tunes.One of the best beat'em ups for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a hell of a lot more fun than the NES Karate Kid game, that's for sure!Look, if you're expecting a AAA level game, just look at the pricetag and think again. This is clearly a budget title.  That being said, it's a reasonably fun beat-em-up that should put a few smiles on big Karate Kid/Cobra Kai geeks (like me!).  It's not overly complicated, nor is it too simple.  The 2.5d movement can be a bit clunky at times, and the countering time window seems a little off to me, but overall this was frankly more than I was expecting given your typical rushed cash-in games.  It won't win any GOTY awards, but if you temper your expectations you may be pleasantly surprised like I was.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great homage to the side scrolling, character-swap, and 2 player co-op beat em ups that started way back with the Double Dragon arcade machine. This isn't to say that CK isn't a fully modernised version of such games. You can buy permanent skill powerups for each of a myriad of characters from the Netflix tv series and customise each of them to play differently. I Tried the Cobra Kai path briefly first then switched to Myagi Do just to see how it was and preferred the skills and styles of the characters in the latter so stuck with that. The two story paths, and repeated plays of each section to find collectables, makes the game a long and fun ride. Combos and special moves can feel a little like mindless button mashing at first but the only way you are going to get high grades in each section is if you learn how to use them properly and accurately making the game a lot more tactical than anyone would expect.The voiceovers are done by the actual actors from the series, the cartoon style graphics actually fit the purpose given that, whilst accomplished, this is a breezy high octane game that doesn't take itself TOO seriously - much like the series itself. It's MEANT to give refs to an 80's hokey trope both in its storyline and in the fact that the game itself is a souped up throwback.Overall I am surprisingly impressed by what is a fun brawler that reflects perfectly on its retro revamp subject matter.

_childDocuments_.review: Straight off the bat, very enjoyable game. Now onto the reviewI find myself in a position where I have to make a gaming apology. Upon the initial reveal trailer for the game, i immediately trashed the graphics, assumed it would be a horrible shallow cash grab game and probably some other irrational statements After spending my first few hours with the game, I find the graphics have grown on me, the voice acting matches the TV series, the game play (beat em up double dragon style not normally my jam) is satisfying while being both rewarding and challenging at times, customisation of skills is good without being over the top, music is good and overall fun factor is 9/10So I encourage anyone who was on the fence to give it a try. And I will try and not judge a book by its cover as quickly in the futureSo I would like it to be known, that I was oh so wrong about this game

_childDocuments_.review: If you like any of the classic beat'em up games, such like Streets of Rage or something similar, then chances are you'll probably like this game too.In this game you have the choice option of playing Cobra Kai's story ark or Miyagi-Do's story ark (either way, after beating one or the other, you'll continue on to play as the opposing team to see their side of the story as well... which to note, you'll want to play both sides on the one same "Saved File" in order to see the final chapter of the story, the final final boss, etc.).What Characters you'll play as:If team Cobra Kai: Miguel, Johnny, Hawk & Tory.orIf team Miyagi-Do: Samantha, Denial, Demetri & Robby.Each team has their own "Dojo" Skills, whereas additionally each character also have their own "Personal" skills... in which you earn Tokens as you progress through the game, that you can use to buy and upgrade skills with the use of those Tokens.Overall I'd say it's a pretty good game for anyone that likes "beat'em up games."Also just to note, to any of the fans (aside from myself) of the TV series Cobra Kai, the story in the game isn't told the same exact way as in the TV series... in which case, you may want to buckle your seat belt and just enjoy the game for what it is (seriously, don't get to wrapped up in the "oh but that's not how it goes in the TV series!" ...it's just a game).

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect revivals. Despite what some people may think, they do happen. Now and then a long forgotten name appears with a great new story that involves both old and new cast. If you're into teen dramas, you probably remember , which revived  and 's legendary show.  and  returned with kids in .  is still fighting . And, of course, there's . A sensational revival of the original  trilogy that brings back  (),  () and pretty much all the rest of the original movies' main cast one way or another. Aside from  () for obvious reasons. The main story, of course, revolves around the new bunch of kids. Which are absolutely great and make perfect characters on their own. The show is done in a less serious tone than the originals, but still, it's a great show and is totally worth your time. Make sure to check it out if you like the original  movies. It looks like together with the old karate story, though,  also revived an old tradition. A tradition to have at least one video game for every major movie / TV show out there. Think 'bout that. How often do we get something like that nowadays? So... Let's take a look, shall we?The guys who were hired to do the job here are  from . And it's important for you to know because of their first game. A game called .  was a pretty unique fighting game, in which there were no health bars. To win against your opponents, you were supposed to rip their limbs off by using unlockabale special attacks. Don't expect anything like that here, in  game (it's much more family-friendly than that), but remember that  guys a) know their fighting games and b) can think outside the box. Now, what  we have in  game?Well, we've got ourselves a beat 'em up game. Pretty old school one too. At least, on the first glance. Naturally, it's based on  show and  takes place somewhere around second season. I mean, this game was released before season three, while 's rocking his  look, so...  don't think 'bout that much. Because instead of following canon, this game takes place in its own alternate reality, in which characters can use battle magic of sorts. The game comes with two story campaigns. One for  and one for  (you'll need to finish both, though, if you want true final boss and real ending).  specializes on damage and fire “magic” (), while  is all about the defense and ice (). Sounds crazy, but it's actually pretty smart and stylish decision. Even the fact that you need to beat the game twice to get real ending is actually pretty smart. I'm trying to avoid spoilers, though, so you'll need to take my word for it. It  make sense.You know what's even better, though? The fact that we've got the original cast. That's right. The game is actually voiced by real actors from  show. Not all of them are here, unfortunately. Major examples would be  replacing  as ,  playing  instead of ,  replacing  as  and so on.  both  and  are here and so are  and , who play  () and  in the show. Personally? I just loved that. I mean, we rarely get any games based on contemporary movies and TV shows nowadays, but with the original cast involved? YUM!The best thing about this game though, is, surprisingly, its gameplay. To be honest, I didn't expect that. What I did expect is yet another one of those ultra-cheap beat 'em ups. Maybe something akin to . I mean, it's hard to expect good from something with such a casual look  the first couple of levels here do feel really,  basic and casual. But. Right after the game introduces its skills mechanics? It begins to shine for real. See, it's one of those smart games that try to use our usual controllers in some pretty unusual ways. Remember what  did with the mouse? There's no way to compare these two games, but in a way  is trying to achieve something like that. With gamepad instead of a mouse. Four buttons on the right side ( if we're talking 'bout ) can be used in our usual beat 'em up way,  at the same exact time they also represent two groups of skills.The first group is personal skills. The ones that are unique for every character (each dojo gives you access to four characters – , ,  and  for  and , ,  and  for ). The second group is so-called dojo skills. Those are shared between all the characters from dojo you chose at the beginning of the game. Each group comes with four different moves for you to perform and level-up (you'll also be able to customize those a bit to fit your own personal preferences in battle, which is really,  good idea).  Four buttons. Eight skills. Plus four regular attacks. How is that possible? The answer is – by holding triggers. Holding the left trigger will bring up dojo skills, while holding the right trigger will bring personal ones. Also, pressing both triggers at once will activate one of those big-ass special attacks (naturally, it's  for -san). Sounds simple? Well, yeah. But that's the beauty of it. I mean, this game? It's surprisingly addictive. Two triggers and four buttons? There's a lot of fun in that. Even grinding for higher skill levels here is fun just because the core mechanics is satisfying. Congrats, , really nice job.Unfortunately, aside from better visuals, polish is something to be desired here. Can't say that this game feels especially cheap, but yeah, it's far from being perfect. Using environment attacks (there's quite a lot of those and they're quite funny) can be more problematic than needed at times, sometimes the reward currency lands in places you can't reach, some attacks have weird hit detection, it's hard to tell which objects can be broken for pickups and which cannot, it's hard to pick up the right item at times (when food lies near the weapon you may want not to risk it if you're aiming for better score and therefore avoid picking up food for healing), etc. The whole package of slightly cheap aftertaste.Does it feel bad, though? Heck, no! Personally, I had a lot of fun with this one. Like, . Way more than I expected. This game is addictive, those moves are simple (not even original if we won't count controls and customization), yet satisfying,  did make characters feel like themselves in battle, it's more challenging than it looks (at least during the early stages, since even one fully leveled character is, like, a one person army) and, well, it's fun. What else can you ask for? You like the show – I'd say go for it. $19.99 does sound like a fair price. Especially if we'll keep those actors in mind. And on sale? It's a bloody steal. By no means what we have here is a perfect or must-have title. But it's a very nice entertainment in the between of  seasons. Dixi.

_childDocuments_.review: To start with, I *LOVE* the Cobra Kai show. I recommend it to everyone I can. It is clearly a show made by people who love the franchise, the characters and it has so much heart and fun. I wanted to love this game. However, this game has some of the worst enemy design and AI I have ever encountered in a Beat 'em up. Just about every enemy has an invincible attack where they flash red and can not be knocked out of the attack. Ok, so that's to stop you from just spamming attacks recklessly. Except, the red flash doesn't properly reflect when they are invincible, as they will frequently start their invincible attack and flash red AFTER you've already started attacking them, and should have been stunning them.Next, the devs idea of challenge is just for the enemies to non-stop spam these attacks. It's pretty much all they do. On top of that, the enemies pretty much never walk anywhere, they just instantly run from where they are to you, then spam their invincible attacks. The chief concept of beat em ups is to beat down waves of enemies, often facing groups of enemies in different combinations. This means that not every single enemy has to be a difficult annoying obstacle. You sometimes need dumb mooks to work on your combos or practice parrying on. Instead, every battle is a CHORE, because you are constantly dodging or parrying because of all the invincibility of the enemies. Seriously, watch any let's play on youtube past the first level and just watch and see how often the enemies are flashing red. It's basically over half the time the enemies are on screen, and they are actually invincible for MORE than that time, due to the bs coding.The combos and attacks are actually pretty cool, and would be fun if the enemies weren't so damned unfun. The best part of playing co-op beat em ups is to play with people of various skill levels, like my kid nephew. This game started with promise then became rapidly unfun for both of us. I bought this game to support the Cobra Kai franchise, but I regret wasting my time and money on this.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice game and totally overlooked by many. I played all side scroll beat em ups since Double Dragon on my commodore 64 and even Streets of Rage pales in comparison to this game combat wise. Miyagi-Do is defence and has ice effects, Cobra Kai excels in offense ( the best form of defence) with fire effects.Each character has access to 4 dojo attacks but also 4 special individual attacks. They can all be rotated onto the battleground on the fly . I found a few combos, chaining special attacks and essentially air juggling groups but I am certain I missed many more. Very deep combat system and fun to boot.The campaign loosely follows the TV series Cobra Kai with both dojo's having different outcomes.Recommended for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: A fascinating case study in how to do a technically competent job of building a game while failing to make it fun.  The pacing is off (it took me over half an hour to finish the tutorial level), the fights are slow, the hit detection is too fiddly, the fanservice inaccurate, the experience as a whole is tedious.I suspect that I'd be less offended if I didn't like the IP as much as I do.  I just the strong feeling that the creators aren't fans of beat 'em up games, and they're not fans of the show.  Which is why it's so disconnected from what makes an enjoyable beat em up, and what I love about the show.

_childDocuments_.review: Streets of Rage 4 this game is not and that's why I like it. I mostly play rpgs, action games, beat 'em ups are not my cup of tea. I'm what you might call a button masher when it comes to fighting games. Or to put it another way I suck at these games and do not usually enjoy them. This on the other hand is very enjoyable for me and I'll explain why. For a beat 'em up game the movement and attack speeds of the game are incredibly slow. For me that lack of hyper speed game play allows me to do more than button mashing and not only learn all the combos but use them in combat. It's fun and I now understand the charm of these kind of games. I still don't think the genre is for me. If this is a kid's beat 'em up I am ok with that because it's just fun.Another aspect I quite like is the outdated cartoony graphics. Sure, it may look like a xbox 360 side scroller or a mobile game but it works. It reminds me of the old beat 'em up arcade games and less like the recent ones released to console and PC. It's very much like the old T.M.N.T. and Simpsons four player arcade beat 'em ups. A lot of the moves remind of the T.M.N.T. game but the speed and wonky hit detection etc. is more akin to the Simpsons game, which was fun because it was the Simpsons but compared to other arcade games of the time was slow, clunky etc. Which brings me to my final point, I liked that old Simpsons arcade game for what it was, as a Simpsons fan. I am also a Cobra Kai fan so the actual voice actors and nods to the series make it a very enjoyable lockdown time waster. If you're a Cobra Kai fan and even casually into beat 'em up games I would give this a 7/10If you're a Cobra Kai fan but totally hate beat 'em ups I'd pass on it.If you could care less about the series and just enjoy beat 'em ups, i'd say as a stand alone beat 'em up it's a 5/10.  Tl;dr - great time waster, beginner level difficulty but great fun to be had for fans of the show.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was meant to be played with a controller. With that said, I've been playing withmy keyboard and it takes some adjustment at first because you can't adjust keybinds in game. However, playing with a keyboard gives it a more arcade-ish feel. And after you get used to thedefault binds, the game is fun. You can get through levels with just your kick and punch, but it ishard because as you progress you will need to use your abilities (Dojo and Personal) to really take out some enemies. It is fun juggling and getting a lot of hits on your combinations. The graphics are interestingbecause they really looking like arcade machine graphics from 2002 or Sega Dreamcast, but that'swhat I like about it. The enemies also look interesting like "Sloth" the fat skeleton.This game is solid, but it needs more work. Overall, still a great buy at 16.99.

_childDocuments_.review: this is like something you find in the bargain bin and have a blast with. it's a good game with many flaws. it's your normal beat'm up but here outside your normal move set you have a 4 characters to tag in/out, a super move on a gauge, and 2 sets of 4 power moves (that do not take hp to use). each team will unlock and upgrade 4 moves based on the dojo, the cobra moves are based on fire/burning and the Miyagi ones are based on ice/slow and all 4 of your team can use them. each character also has their own 4 moves. you can use any of the 8 moves at any time they are not on cooldown (after use they can't be used again until a counter ticks down). once a move is unlocked you can upgrade it. if you unlock a moves skill tree to the end each one has a upgrade you need to do something for it but it's free when you do. some are do X damage with it, toss x enemies in the air with it, or kill X enemy Y times with it. this is a pain and very inconsistent as you first need to finish a tree before you can start on unlocking the last upgrade, then you need to have said character out with said move when x enemies are about and hope you can kill them with said move. all this as some move just unlock passively on their own.as for the story it's your normal beat,m up smack talk with a lose predictable story where you need to play through both sides on 1 save for the better ending. levels for both dojos are basically the same with the talking bits being different.the fighting is fine but as the game goes on most of the enemies will just tank your hit as they move in to slap you in the face. they explain it as some "armor" thing but they turn red and will not fall down when hit though some ground specials can knock them down if they are in the right range. i have not run into any glitches like other reviewers so i can't comment on that (yet).like i said it's a good bargain bin game so grab it on sale but if you're not into cheap (flawed) games you may want to give it a pass though i really don't see much better from other beat'm up games on steam so i feel it's a solid buy. if you do get this the first thing you should use points on is unlocking the 4 dojo moves then each characters 4 personal moves before upgrading anything. you'll want to spam these moves whenever they are up so you want all 8.

_childDocuments_.review: The trailers definitely didn't do the game justice. I thought the same about it as everyone else when I saw them; low budget cash-in, etc.Turns out the game is a lot of fun! It won't set the world on fire but if you have a craving for a side-scrolling beat 'em up, it gets the job done. The fighting is fun and the characters feel just different enough to make you want to try each one out. Upgrading each character in different ways is great, so you can focus on damage for one and defense for another. I got this game for free in a giveaway but it's worth the reduced price tag. I've paid more money for worse/shorter games. There are two campaigns in the game (Cobra Kai/Miyagi-Do) and I'm not even done with one of them yet.One downside is the lack of voice actors from the show. There are only about four or five of them. Most do a decent job but Miguel's voice actor sounds nothing like the character and I don't know what's going on with Brucks (one of Kyler's bully friends). The story itself is nothing special. It's like a comic book spin-off of the main show; aimed at a slightly less mature audience, so only light swearing, and some characters are almost like caricatures of the ones on the show (I got so sick of hearing "Tory with a Y" every time I switched to playing as her). Another downside is the game recommends using a controller and I hate having to scroll through menus using the analog stick, rather than the d-pad. My only real complaint about the graphics is that some characters look ugly during close-ups in cutscenes. In-game, it looks nice enough.If you're into Cobra Kai, I recommend it. If you're just into beat 'em ups in general, I also recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of the show, so this is more content for me to enjoy. The game is stylized more like a comic book which isn't off-putting to me as I've seen this art style already with newer Power Ranger games. Some characters are over-cartoonized and just look a bit too goofy too. The environments are plain but not overly so, there's some enemy variety but considering this is a beat'em-up you'll soon be fighting a lot of the same. Missions are basic, work your way through the map to story missions inter spaced by short "adventure" missions. The fighting is fun, you can chain together all sorts of skills and switch characters to keep the punishment going, if you don't switch it can be bland but if you take advantage of the mechanics it can be a blast curb stomping everything.My only complain about it, content-wise, is they actually have some of the real actors to do the voices but some of the key ones are missing. I felt this the most with Miguel, I really like the Cobra Kai side of the series with Johnny and Miguel and it's just really jarring to hear Johnny but not Miguel and the voice actor does NOT sound anything like Miguel.Other than that, I really liked it for what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues tries to piggy back from the popularity of a TV series but fails miserably. While the TV series focuses on passion to a very real sport, that traverses not only generations but also walls of a dojo, the game somehow managed to add fire and ice magic, physics breaking jump kicks, unblockable special moves and temporary invulnerability.If that wasn't enough, it went out of its way to show as many colourful flashes and flares as possible, creating visual clutter that more often than not renders any deliberate strategy useless. Why the flashes and visual cues? Well, because back in a day it wasn't possible to implement an actually decent fighting mechanics. But nowadays we have flow-driven combat gems like Assassin's Creed, Batman, Shadow of Mordor, Mad Max and countless others. Not here. Here you spam B when enemies flash red indicating an unblockable attack and button mash otherwise. That's about 90% of the gameplay.Officially the game tries to pay homage to the retro beat em ups but I still play some of those games and they not only feel responsive but, most importantly, are predictable - when you get hit, you know why, where and how you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. In Cobra Kai it's mostly random. Maybe the hit box glitched or the input didn't register - you won't know. It's just bad implementation. So bad that they had to make the game extremely easy by stretching the health bar to the point it's boring. I really tried to like it but I can't.NOT RECOMMENDED.

My first time playing I thought it was a glitch because one enemy kept spamming his uninterruptable attack without break. After a while I realized this was normal enemy behavior. Second, the boss fights. Who's the c*cksucking motherf*cking b*tch that designed these fights?
