_childDocuments_.review: $30 for a C-list horror movie with glaring flaws in every other scene.The best way to outline my review for this game is to separate the various elements that contribute to the overall experience. The premise is wonderful and I wish they did better; It has everything you could ask for in a horror movie / game. That being said, combining some of the things they did in execution is like wearing a hat on a hat.The gameplay itself grows tedious pretty quickly as you're exposed to the 4 or 5 different mechanics implemented for actual interaction with the world and characters. I understand there are massive limitations in a 'choose your own adventure' game, but that doesn't absolve the developers for relying on the same tired tropes we've all seen be used before in games of this ilk as vehicles for exposition or what have you. Click this shiny thing for a collectible / piece of the story, move your character past this barrier to be railroaded into the next section, choose between two dialogue options (Neither of which actually reflected how I felt most of the time), etc.Speaking of the dialogue-- It's unremarkable at best. A game that revolves primarily around the characters and the choices they make must have a strong sense of purpose revealed for each moment that allows conversation. These are the threads that tie together as the story unfolds to give each character real depth and maturity. It's not that this game lacked those moments entirely-- It's just that they were so sparse and so poorly placed that they didn't feel rewarding at all. Instead, I was left wondering why they would decide to have the development happen then as opposed to the other 100 more appropriate moments. For a frame of reference, some characters will experience truly traumatic events (As is common in horror) only to immediately turn around and discuss something wildly insignificant compared to the mortal danger they are perpetually thrown into. Also, I'm just going to come out and say it. The voice actors did the best they could, and they didn't detract from the experience with their performance. However, I feel as though there has to have been better choices for voice actors. A couple voice actors in particular irked me with their cadence and timbre, which lead to me having trouble connecting them with the character they were supposed to be portraying. Putting the voice acting aside, the script needs some serious work. If you decide to play through the game yourself, you'll understand where I'm coming from if you imagine this story being told through the media of film as opposed to a video game. Were an actual cinema director to have control over some of these lines, I expect they would've turned out far differently. Of course, that's assuming the director is at least marginally competent so I'm not exactly holding my breath for a film adaptation of the story.And then of course I feel the need to mention that this game suffers sometimes tragically from the Fallout 4 dialogue system nightmare of not knowing what the hell you're actually doing when you make a choice. Multiple times I made a choice that resulted in a consequence I had no idea was the linear result of the nipslip of dialogue I actually got to see. It can make for an immensely frustrating time when you choose something that is the complete opposite of what you wanted to. That being said, there were a couple times I made a choice, it turned out to be something completely different, but then the game ended up going in the same direction I wanted to anyways. Unfortunately I'm just not invested enough to actually dig through other people's playthroughs and see if the game has true choices and branching paths or if they all amount to roughly the same climax. You can call me unfit to review this game for choosing not to investigate that thoroughly enough if you want, I really don't care. It doesn't enthrall me in the way I wished it would.Another pretty monumental issue is that some of my inputs didn't seem to go through properly. Believe it or not, I have a couple brain cells rolling around up top, so I'm well aware that the issue is not my mouse / keyboard. There were several moments in the game where I consciously made an input correctly and watched the prompt blink red as if to mock me for even caring whether or not I tripped on a rock while running from the monster. So do with that information what you will, I suggest you use it to decide the narrative isn't worth the cash or the frustration involved with playing the story yourself.Finally and most critically, I want to discuss how aggravating it is to play a video game that embraces the absolute worst tropes of horror cinema. I'm just going to say it loud once and be done with it.If you want tension in your video game, establish a clear threat and don't pull punches. I don't want to be bombarded with six enemies in a cutscene only to interact with three that have to pull a bakery ticket and wait in line for their number to be called before attacking. Furthermore, I really don't want to see two of those enemies killed, and then randomly assume the other four magically disappeared because of the sheer luster of the character's plot armor.And you know what? I especially don't want to see trained U.S. marines make piss poor strategic decisions that in any other applicable setting would get them killed immediately. I'm not even talking about the monsters. I'm talking about a CIA field officer who has a clear shot from behind cover at an unsuspecting human enemy turning around and running away as opposed to, jeez, I don't know, instantly neutralizing one of the game's antagonists? The game is chock-full of painful moments like this. I mean, I'm not expecting a piece of media to get every detail correct when it comes to something as nuanced as CIA / Marine field protocol but for goodness sake make it believable.Maybe I'm the problem. If you are not easily bothered by obtuse oversights, lazy writing, and a lack of narrative control, then by all means, drop $30 on this game and enjoy the pretty atmosphere.Oh yeah, there's also some lighting errors, texture clipping, and poorly rendered objects with low resolution.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, in my opinion, not just the best offering from the  series, but the best of the genre from Supermassive. It establishes a whole new universe, literally. I think the setting is completely novel, the twists are unique, and it is the most rewarding of the games to unravel the story of. It also tackles some very poignant political issues, being set in The Gulf War, and the cast of characters are diverse and likable. Even the unlikable characters in this game have beautiful story arcs that I think redeems them by the end and shows realistic character development. Whereas with some of the other offerings from not just this series but Supermassive in general there are usually a few characters that fade into the background or you just don't care much about the fates of, I grew attached to all five of the protagonists. I think that is a rarely achieved feat in not only these games but gaming in general. The story is very serious but there are also breaks for relationship turmoil and the setting right from the start is full of drama, which I love. It sets the stage right away. This was my second time playing this game and my second platform that I've played it on, the first being Playstation. Overall, this was my fourth playthrough and I still loved it just as much as the first. I played it this time with a friend who hadn't played it before and we definitely enjoyed playing it together. This was also their favorite they've played so far, having played all the other Supermassive games so far ( except The Devil In Me and Until Dawn ). TL;DR: It's my favorite from Supermassive. It gets high marks all the way around and I think they've somewhat shot themselves in the foot by setting a standard this high. It will be a high bar to reach again, and I think they've already struggled to reach it again with The Devil In Me ( and obviously some of the games that preceded this one, like Little Hope ). 10/10, a major feat for Supermassive.

_childDocuments_.review: I only watched the first trailer when it first came out and had no other exposure to the game prior to release. This led me to have expectations that were not promised and may make or break the game for some. I thought this game would be about an ensemble cast, half compromised of American soldiers and the other half Iraqi soldiers, alternating through both groups throughout the game without learning too much about each to build up the "can they really be trusted?" sort of dynamic. That is absolutely not what we got, its pretty black or white in regards to who's good and who isn't, which I thought was something that could have really added to the tension of the game. The game hints at themes of trauma and discrimination, but doesn't build on it and only gets mentioned in passing.Storywise, I also expected it to focus heavily on the dynamic between two opposite sides having to risk their lives by trusting each other to make it out alive, both sides having equal stakes. Instead the story takes a generic turn towards the middle that I really thought took away too much of the mystery and horror behind the monsters, along with it being clear that one side always had an advantage over another. Mostly being an action packed game with little horror and emotional moments, you either like it or not.Despite that, if all you're expecting is an action game with soldiers fighting in and out of ruins, you won't be disappointed. Only technical issues I had on my first playthrough were a few framedrops in certain areas and one crash. Still a fun 5-7 hours and more engaging than the previous entries in the anthology.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I absolutely love Mesopotamian history, and I saw the blend of American/Iraqi forces circa 2003 have to come together to survive, and I thought, wow. What an interesting premise, this could be right up my alley.Unfortunately, I'm having a hard time recommending it.If you love choices matter type games, maybe you can overlook a lot of the other elements that I had issues with. Firstly, the story. It's... a stretch. It's not very coherent and takes a lot of liberties with events and mission set to force things into happening. For example, two men are vying over a woman, in an active life or death situation. Suspension of disbelief is gone. There are many more examples of this, but I digress.Secondly, and this one *really* bothers me. You can tell they did (some) research on the US military, and some on the Iraqi Forces. This might not sound like a big deal, but for me, it's like when a doctor or nurse watches a medical show, and it's just wildly inaccurate. Why is the Lt Col from the USAF (an O-5) not in uniform? Jeans and a shirt. Okay. No beard, but hair out of regs. Okay, special forces do get liberties in the field (there are issues here too but). Why does everyone treat him like he's the upstart LT (O-1) straight from college? At O-5 this man would have nearly 20 years of service, and outrank 99% of the entire US military. But no, he's not in uniform, just his Sunday chill clothes, and comes off like a weenie, and everyone is one step away from giving him a noogie and a jab on the chin, and calling him sport. Also Aviators? IS THIS GUY EVEN A PILOT?The lower enlisted marines show nearly ZERO customs and courtesies, and one of them renders a BRITISH salute (?). But wait, I'm getting to the best part. The DOD or DHS or CENTCOM or whomever you want to be the authority here let a man with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ PROSTHETIC LEG go to an ACTIVE WARZONE, and then GO OUTSIDE THE WIRE, and attached him to a special operations group. I mean for ♥♥♥♥♥ sake, in real life you have an allergy and don't take your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ red dog tags with you, you're in deep ♥♥♥♥, but this guy, doesn't even bring his real leg and that's no problem. Also. where are the rest of the CIA? Where is the Army? Just because the USAF controls satellites, doesn't mean they would drop a Lt Col down with his prosthetic leg just to supervise his pet project. I mean, the suspension of disbelief is totally gone in this regard. The Iraqi forces hardly even get touched on, other than Salim (who appears to be one of the best written characters), doesn't want to fight anymore, and his captain threatens to "Commissar" him right there on the spot. The beginning really pulled me in, too. Nice style, beautiful Sumerian clothing, masks, moon pools, and they even wielded the mighty khopesh. But then the king stares directly at an eclipse, the main characters find 75 year old gas that still works (?) and then find duct tape. I mean - it's all just a bit much. Then like I mentioned about the love triangle - the Lt Col, as mentioned, is competing with a Sgt in the squad of marines he leads, for the love of his CIA Operative wife, all the while they are in the movie the descent.Edited to add, because I got a little upset about all the wild inconsistencies, that the thing that is consistent is the writing. And it's consistently bad. This feels like a B movie, but not the fun kind.

_childDocuments_.review: So here we are, the long awaited third instalment in the Dark Pictures Anthology, House of Ashes.I wish there was a neutral review option, because I genuinely have mixed feelings around this one.The third-person/over-the-shoulder view is a welcome change to the fixed camera view, still feels a little buggy, but works.Also it seems that the desync / saving issue is fixed, so I'm happy about that.Sadly House of Ashes is nowhere near as brilliant or gripping as Man of Medan or Little Hope.It honestly feels more like an action game, there's no real horror element, no "oh wow" or "what the hell" moments, or even a hook that connects you to the story or any of the characters and there's no sense of completion when completing the game. (e.g Little Hope [co-op] + good ending = high five & hell yeah, followed by oh wow / House of Ashes = Ok, nice sound track at the end, Oooh new trailer!).Even though I enjoyed it, I was still disappointed. I'm only recommending it because I'm not seeing it as part of the Anthology, but a COMPLETELY stand-alone game and because it's not a horrible game. If you are a fan of the series, make a call for yourself if you want to play HOA, otherwise wait for the 4th instalment.For those curious/new to the series, try HOA if you want to get your feet wet, but play the first two games if you want to get a real feel of how the Dark Pictures Anthology story-telling & gameplay really is.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for October 2023, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before November 7th, 2023, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A gory horror game. House of Ashes is what Dark Pictures Anthology has become known for.  A horror-style game, with a strong story, interesting characters, and complicated relationships between them. Player choices affect how each character will act in the future, and players will also be able to explore the environments as part of the story.  The writing is good like much of the series, and the concept is interesting, especially with the main game being about soldiers trying to capture WMDs after the fall of Saddam Hussein 20 years ago in Baghdad.  Yeah, that’s 20 years ago, Damn.However, House of Ashes feels a little weak when it comes to some graphics and animations.  I think at least one character has an elongated neck I can’t stop noticing.  A few animations have characters looking off in a strange direction, that should have an establishing shot before it.   There’s a cinematic style to the first section of the game with the horror that seems forgotten in the next section, and I hope it’s just that part of the game. Pick this up if you like monster movies, horror, Supermassive Games, or Want a unique story-driven experience.  Yeah, this is also very similar to The Quarry as well, and all the previous Dark Pictures Anthology games such as Man of Medea and Little Hope.  If you haven’t played any of those, maybe it’s worth checking them out firstIf you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: The game for the most part offers a good experience, it has a descent story, characters are interesting though not as much as until dawn's but good enough and can be played in one-two seatings (it's a 6-9 hours game).My major complaint is the FOV that is not adjustable and looks like it's fixed at different rates in different scenarios in the game, I understand the concept of low FOV in terms of giving the game the claustrophobic feelings it has, but in scenarios where you are in an open space it just doesn't make sense there and makes exploring hard because of not having enough camera view.From a technical perspective, I didn't encounter any bugs but I found the RTX options to be completely useless since the performance hit was way too big and it felt like they were just flipping the rtx switch on UE4 rather than the team actually working in making rtx features in the game work better. In other words, you put rtx just to put rtx without it working properly or making much of difference since 90% of your lighting was hard baked and not utilizing ray tracing.Generally, it's a game I'd recommend if you are a fan of a choose your own adventure, horror, movie like game, great game to play with friends/family or even alone.Rating: 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: House of ashes easily has to be my most favourite of the Dark Pictures Anthology franchise. the visuals are absolutely amazing - from the enemies, to the flow of character movements, the dark, eerie, and claustrophobic vibe within the environments. i also personally felt that House of ashes had the most gore/creepiness within it and its environments more than the previous - specifically with Little hope and Man of Medan, i felt those two were VERY centred around the use of jump scares to invoke reactions within its players. - This is not a bad thing! however it did personally feel a little overused. whereas in House of ashes, i don't believe there were many implimented jump scares at all, and yet the gore, environment details/sounds, emotions of the characters, and the camera angles themselves brought on its own unique sense of dread.Gameplay - i felt personally that House of ashes really upped the intensity of action/button prompts required, which i very much enjoyed. i found myself sitting on the edge of my chair, clenching my controller just trying to prepare for the next sudden set of prompts to do, unlike the others - which don't get me wrong, are great! but a lot less intense i guess? in the previous games i personally felt there was more cutscenes to watch, but less prompt/interactions to make. Story: I personally really enjoyed House of ashes in its entirety -  the characters and how they interacted with one another/altered their relationships overtime, the historical backgrounds/roots, are something i found myself easily getting invested in. All in all easily my favourite of the series, deff recommend (you dont have to of played the others) and i hope to see more amazing gameplay and story creation/use such as this.

_childDocuments_.review: House of Ashes is another Supermassive Games horror title, sharing its mechanics and style of gameplay with SG's previous titles (Until Dawn, Man of Medan, etc). This time, you see yourself primarily taking on the role of five characters in Iraq in 2003 amidst the surely successful search for Iraqi WMD depots, and likewise to previous titles from Supermassive Games, relies heavily on player choice, quick-time-events, and interpersonal character relationships to drive its multiple outcomes, while an optional exploration and investigation of its world through documents and discoveries can lead to the uncovering of deeper secrets held within an ancient Akkadian temple which our heroes find themselves trapped.Taking me about 7 hours to beat, Ashes combines a warm mix of fairly campy horror character tropes alongside those of cursed temples àla Indiana Jones, alongside some nice interpersonal drama, and solid sound design and orchestration. Meanwhile, its quick time events continues in the SG tradition of injecting immediate tension into action scenes, making your characters' survival feel all the more intense and heroic with the knowledge that you could have easily messed it up. The game also has a hearty amount of accessibility options, ranging from dyslexia-friendly font, to giving players the option to changing the nature with which QTEs play out and are completed, it also is programmed to be played with an Xbox One controller, and can have its keys be rebound.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth the money. You already know that the story is quite deep and has a lot of secrets in it, and that the graphics are beautiful. So, let me talk about what's different in this game compared to the others. Here's a few things I've noticed.1. This time, every choice really does matter. Missing one quick-time event could end up with somebody dying.2. I was on the edge of my seat most of the time, which I liked. Most of the game was packed with action scenes rather than exploration scenes. Or sometimes even both at the same time.3. There's almost always something to worry about while playing. I myself got caught off guard a few times.4. It took me around 6 hours to finish the story on medium difficulty. You might think that the game's playtime is low, but believe me it's not. You can still go back and find the things you have missed or make other decisions, hunt achievements etc.To sum up, if you have played the other games in the series and liked them, just buy this one and play it as well. I don't think you'll regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: QTE with some slight walking around. Some dialog choices to make, most mundane and obvious but a couple difficult decisions. That’s all. Pretty good graphics, especially when close-up to characters. The animations can be a bit wonky, as well as the character model build for all male characters is pretty copy-pasted. Overall though, looks good. A true telling of how good a horror game is, and the tension just isn’t present here. Despite walking through dark corridors, I never once heard a sound that made me go “Uhh… I don’t want to continue down there….” I was even playing the entire game with my headset on. Definitely a missed opportunity. What is offered in the game is around a 6 hour story with various choices that determine the fate of the characters. Unfortunately many times these “choices” boil down to whether or not you passed a QTE. As for the story itself, I felt like the first 2-3 hours were pretty good, when the spookiness was still a mystery. The latter half of the game is just filled with eye rolling moments that can only be conjured up during a writers strike (note: there was none at the time, to my knowledge). Not to mention, all of the decisions the characters are prone to making can be covered in Horror 101: Stuff Not to Do. Everything from splitting up constantly to a dumb love triangle being more important than survival, to going in the OPPOSITE direction from home for some reason…I just can’t even. None apart from replaying for missed achievements or to see a different turn of events. Once you beat the game, the main gameplay loop has been experienced. I have only played two Dark Pictures games: this one and Man of Medan. I personally thought MoM was the better of the two. While it seems all of Supermassive horror titles tends to fall into exhaustive horror tropes, I felt MoM was less cringy.  at full price. Only if you are a diehard horror fan, or if you can find it for under $10. You can find my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: This one's actually decent. The characters, for once, aren't annoying teenagers (which is why I liked Man of Medan more than the others), the QTEs are not terribly easy on the medium difficulty, I just wish, as always, that there was a little more agency. Keeping everyone alive was pretty simple, to be honest, there's lots of times where you can ♥♥♥♥ up and that having no negative impact.The story itself was suitably spooky, there were actually "scary" bits in it, despite so many claiming this game didn't have horror in it, the enemy design was neat, the characters mostly fine if you like military dudes and dudettes. Some questionable "relationship" decisions, like, dude, you're about to die, priorities!Graphics on the other hand are just fine, especially faces and their animations are kinda atrocious here. Felt a lot better in Man of Medan and Little Hope (and the Quarry, of course, but that was higher budget). Not sure why... maybe the faces they used just look very odd. I don't want to "body shame" anyone, but they all seemed extremely uncanny and unrealistic, lacking features, lifeless eyes and animations, etc.Apart from that for a budget title you get just as much actual gameplay (actually more if you cut out the pointless talking without anything happening) than you did in The Quarry, which is twice as expensive. These DPA games are bite sized experiences, best shared with friends. 6 to 7 hours is fine, 8 to 9 is too much, to be honest. Just wish you could actually fast forward cut scenes and dialogue, that would make replaying certain sections actually worthwhile.

_childDocuments_.review: House of Ashes is another game in the "The Dark Pictures Anthology"-Series. My friend and I played through the entire game in one sitting because we had such a good time. While I thought this title was going to be somewhat scary and a horror game, it came to my surprise that it felt more like a thriller that quickly turned sci-fi. The game itself is about 5 hours long while taking time to check for collectibles etc., so it's quite short but that's what several playthroughs are for. You get to make decisions and those decisions do not only affect the person you're playing in the moment but also other characters.I have to admit that this one was way better than Man of Medan. I have yet to play Little Hope, so I can't base any judgement on that. The game felt smoother and the story was more interesting. It was less scary but it was still quite entertaining. It does have some little jumpscares here and there but nothing too wild.Even though it was a slight disappointment on the scare factor, it still gave us a lot of entertainment from just goofing around and finding our path through the story together. I absolutely recommend this game.Also, do yourself a favor and just get the Triple Pack with all three games instead of just this one because you'll get a much better deal and three decent games.

_childDocuments_.review: [SPOILERS]This is by FAR the best game in the Anthology. The whole vibe of the game, the story, the monsters, the war, the relationships are just so interesting and fun and I love it. First things first, Jason and Salim. I was a bit confused at first at how Salim was going to interact with these other characters being from another place and on a different side than he's on but I think they handled it perfectly. Jason starting as this whole 'Kill everyone of them' to becoming pretty much best friends with Salim is the best relationship throughout the whole anthology. The love triangle between Rachel, Eric and Nick was also super interesting to see play out because you are choosing which one Rachel goes for pretty much. I remember the first time I played this with my friend with online Co-op, we decided that Rachel should be with Nick. Eric later chose not to save Nick and got him killed. We were so upset but i still absolutely loved that the choices we made actually did something to the story. The monsters were definitely what made this game the best out of the 4 so far, mostly because it was the biggest threat id say. With man of medan, the monsters were hallucinations, so not a huge threat once you learn the secret. With Little hope, the monsters just arent real at all and with the devil in me, there is no monster, its just some guy hunting you down. I loved the Alien side and thank god that they were actually real and it wasn't just some gas or some bad dream because i think its exactly what the games needed. A real threat. One of my favourite parts that I think they did really well was the part where you play as rachel, walking through a massive lake of blood. I liked that she met Clarice and that your choices made with her impacted what she did later on. e.g. if you dont help her across you wont be able to kill her. If you cant kill her then she later kills other people, e.g eric in the massive fight sequence. I loved the throwback to the intro by making this other main stronger monster the last one to die at the prologue. However it was a bit confusing how they managed to turn into this monster and survive in the first place. I hope that what they do for 'Directive 8020' follows this route and is similar to the feel of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Supermassive games, once again, delivers a spectacular horror experience. House of Ashes is a massive improvement from Man of Medan and Little Hope, which are already great games in their own right. The Dark Pictures Anthology is setting itself up as an outstanding horror series with this entry. This one is totally worth a play, and in my opinion, worth every penny at full price.So, since this is a very early review, time will tell if my opinion is unpopular or not. I found House of Ashes to be a phenomenal game. The narrative and storytelling was masterfully done and is vastly better than other entries in the anthology. If Man of Medan or Little Hope left a sour taste, I strongly recommend that you give House of Ashes an opportunity to change your mind about the series. House of Ashes is WAY more intense than both of the previous games in the series and the story, acting, and writing is immensely better. That being said, the game isn't necessarily "scary" but there are many tense and thrilling moments. Mechanically, my only criticism is that with M+K, QTEs were very easy (Made it through with 4 characters alive on my first run). Players familiar with the franchise should expect a similar twist in the narrative, but it is far better executed in House of Ashes compared to Man of Medan and Little Hope. I would place House of Ashes more on par with Until Dawn in terms of the overall quality of the story. There are a few negligible bugs, sometimes facial animations didn't perfectly match up to what was being said. I only discovered one glitch that caused a crash but it didn't break the game. Supermassive games once again delivers a spectacular narrative/cinematic horror experience and I am absolutely dying with anticipation for the next game in the Dark Pictures Anthology.

_childDocuments_.review: A ton of highly professional work clearly went into this title, and presumably this is also true of other games in the series, which I haven't played and very well may not. I find this type of game too much like bingeing a show interrupted by sudden points at which you need to participate - a little like having to grab the remote to skip ads. Arbitrarily placed QTEs mean you can neither relax nor work yourself into the adrenaline-fueled mode you need to be in to stay on top of rapid action. So in order to experience the story I chose to play the whole game in accessibility mode, minimizing the impact of the QTEs, which predictably killed the tension and made it more like sitting through a way-too-long movie with a moderate number of choose-your-own-adventure moments. Also, the third person walking sim parts of the gameplay are fiddly and slow-paced, often with non-ideal camera angles.If you prefer shooters, or even actiony RPGs like I do, be prepared to fall asleep several times during this style of game (and probably get characters killed as a result). I only fell asleep once that I remember. This kind of game is famous for replayability but the last thing I want to do is watch so many hours of >90% of the same stuff to see the <10% differences. If I could have skipped through some of the endless cutscenes that would have brought it down to a more digestible length.The criticisms from Gulf War vets are 100% understandable. Though I lived through those times, I wasn't there and can barely claim even indirect involvement. As such, I have to view this as just another game with a fictional setting loosely based on real places, literal monsters alongside Jung/Nietzsche-style metaphorical ones, and stuffed with melodramatic character conflicts. Even so, I found the Iraqi Mary Sue character overdone. Sympathetic, even cool, as he is through most of the story - in fact, as a single father I found his character traits more thought-provoking than any other game character I can remember offhand - the moralistic one-sidedness with which he is portrayed later on becomes off-putting.Almost all the other characters are unlikable and annoying throughout, even when you make them do the right/heroic thing. At least three were a pleasure to watch getting chomped on by monsters. But that's probably intentional for this genre. There were loads of story issues, too. As one glaring example, there's this thing called night that's basically an hours-long eclipse that happens pretty often.OK, a lot of that sounds bad. But the setting is intriguing, a reminder that places we often dismiss as third world zones of perpetual instability are the legacies of ancient, inscrutably exotic civilizations. The monsters are reasonably fun, a couple of characters are cool until they aren't, the story action has many of the elements of being okay, the dialogue is mostly good minus the excessive f-bombs, the ending is entertaining if unoriginal, and the voice acting stands out as some of the best I've heard. Graphics are immersive except for one flaw I kept noticing: while almost all the characters' faces (with the curious exception of the googly-eyed female lead) are remarkably realistic, the body mechanics are what dip into the uncanny valley here.

_childDocuments_.review: The first act of this game won't allow you to save and it has ZERO chekpoints. This means that if you fail the QTE at the end of the first act, the only way to retry it is to repeat THE ENTIRE FIRST ACT again from the VERY BEGINNING... and you CANNOT skip the cutscenes either. This would be awful if it were simply bad game design but it's actually worse than that. The devs WANT you to fail the first act so that they can show of the gory fate of those characters later on while making you think it's your fault. However, they realized that someone might just replay that section so to prevent that, they didn't put in any checkpoints and disabled saving until after the first act is over... and they even disabled skipping cutscenes (which you can actually do with later cutscenes) just to make it extra tedious to replay that section of the game. This lacks integrity. If you are going to force a kill, at least have the decency to be honest about it. Designing the game with built-in "dark patterns" to punish the player if they decide to restart the first act rather than cooperating with your plan to make them feel guilty for missing a QTE is just disgusting. I usually applaud games for including coop but the coop in this game actually makes it WORSE since it doubles the chances that one of you is going to fail a QTE in which case the story will be ruined for both of you. What's more, that makes the deliberate wasting of your time even more punishing if you do decide to restart since that means that rather than just having your time wasted, you will be wasting someone else's time as well.As if the use of dark patterns to push you to feel guilty for being stuck on a plot railroad weren't bad enough, this game also tries to create the illusion of everything being your fault via choices that literally don't matter. Will you kill a prisoner? It doesn't matter because if you don't someone else will. Will you kill a guard? It doesn't matter because if you don't, the monsters will. Will you betray your companion? It doesn't matter because the entire first act of the game is built around ensuring that BOTH of you die horribly.This is NOT a game; it's a manipulative attempt to gaslight you into thinking that everything is your fault. I regret buying this game and I hope no one else makes the same mistakes. Games which are autosave-only but do NOT have many checkpoints shouldn't exist and neither should manipulative trash built around dark patterns. I would like to recommend this game because I like the concept and the message but the game design itself is vile.

_childDocuments_.review: So 3 down 1 to go (Devil in Me), I loved Man of Medan, I hated Little Hope because it was Man of Medan in a more cliche little town setting? (It's all in your head).Nobody I think is questioning the approach the Supermassive Games takes towards presenting The Dark Picture Anthology so all who play the series know what they signed up for.  (All games are a bit of a walking simulators / interactive movie)Now that out of the way lets talk about House of Ash, I'd rate it about equal to Man of Medan with it being better in some areas and worse in the others so they are about equal in how good they are in my eyes.Key benefit obviously was that this time "It's not all in your head attempt nr. 3".You get to see some action and some pretty decent writing, one 'unexpected' thing for me was that sometimes, in order to succeed you've to actually fail which goes counter-intuitive to the monkey-brain "ME DO GOOD ME GET BANANA".Also if you're smart you can actually fight back this time it's not just run and hide but don't expect run and gun, it's still the same QTEs but also consequences of how you treated other characters.Sometimes brain isn't the solution sometimes it's the heart which I believe is another deviation from the previous games yet it felt very natural.It's hard to write a review on this game without spoilers but I'll try to get give you a TL;DR pointer list.In House of Ash you GET:1. Action horror (Not pure horror there is action which is nice this time protagonists aren't puny civilians)2. The time periods presented 2231BC, 1945-1947 and 2003 (Game happens in 2231BC [prologue only] and 2003 with 1945-1947 being narrated slide-show.).3. Salim best boy.4. Jason best boy.5. Salim and Jason Bromance deserves a game of its own (I'll buy it).6. Plenty of exploration and very nicely crafted areas.7. Solid story but without too crazy twists it's more like they layer it like a cake for you.8. Did i tell you there is a Vickers machine gun and it's not just a decor piece?WARNING SPOILER BELOW:---------------------------------------------------------One bad thing I can say or maybe it was a low hanging fruit for devs, I feel like the Alien parasite and the Alien architecture was heavily inspired by well "THE ALIEN", those vampire corpses in their seats? Yep screamed space jockey to me. The Alien parasite (Last collectible) when I examined it, it really really felt like they just took the Alien Larvae / Chestbuster added more 'disease' to it and spliced it with some tentacles and bug eyes. Basically more disgusting version of chest buster spliced with some fetish material (for some fetish material I'm not judging I just know you guys exist.).---------------------------------------------------------END OF SPOILERSDISCLAIMER: It's late, I'm tired sorry if this review is messy but I hope it helps people in figuring out if the game is for them or not.

_childDocuments_.review: INTRO:Recently played through & finished House of Ashes from the Dark Anthology Pictures Anthology (Steam for PC).I don't think this one's going to re-write the book & formula on making and playing these cinematic-adventure games, as it's similar in style to the Telltale ones (Telltale's Batman games, Telltale's The Walking Dead games, etc). You will make decisions that shape the journey and its story, as you have different survivors that you'll be trying to have survive by the end of the game and hope that you can also get them a good ending, if possible - but regardless, this is still a good one worth playing & well-executed.Besides lots of decisions-making there are of course the usual assortment of finding things (like Lore) in the game-world & collectibles, QTE's, and sequences where you can do shooter-game type stuff, but there isn't much of the latter - and I wish there was at least a bit more, given this game's focus on the military.THIS CINEMATIC GAME.Though, it's still quite good. While I did play The Quarry first and this might've made a bigger impact b/c I did play that one (The Quarry) first and b/c of its 80's and 90's Summer Camp/Friday The 13th & Jason vibes. I enjoyed House of Ashes, despite noticing SuperMassive having a formula w/ there cinematic-adventure/horror games having a bunch of survivors, a narrator (the curator here, for this DPA game...and probably the rest of them), and whatnot - but, it didn't hit me like The Quarry did.The writing, voice-acting, and story was still good & is very 80's horror here, often feeling purposely hammy & campy with its direction & writing. It's feeling like it pays homage & also has their takes on films like The Predator, monster movies, and some of the war films over the years. In this cinematic-game, once you get past the openings Tutorial/Prologue which is interesting (don't want to give too much away there), you will guide a bunch of survivors who are with their respective militaries, both U.S. and Iraqi. You will make decisions on what to do w/ each other in situations, other situations at hand, backgrounds & info on their stories, relationships with each other, and whatnot - as the US Soldiers are looking for WMD's during the war in Iraq in the 2000's to early 2010's....and get a lot more than they bargained for, searching for WMD's over in a certain old location and finding actually something else. I don't want to spoil it, but...that "something else" - yeah, I enjoyed what the something else is and turned out to be.Regardless, after around the 10-15 hours so or more hours it took me, I enjoyed it. The graphics are fantastic and so is the lighting, if you throw Ray-Tracing on. It certainly performed a lot better than The Quarry did on my PC (R5 5600H, 16GB RAM, 1 TB SSD, 6gb RTX 3060m, Windows 11 x64) and the character models themselves looked really good - but, not as great as The Quarry. Regardless, if you played The Quarry - and likely any of the other SuperMassive's games - you'll probably at the very least like this. Whether you love it, that might depend on what was your first SuperMassive game, the setting (does it appeal to you?), and if their formula is running tiresome for you yet & might need a bit of tweaking.OUTRO:Regardless, if you like this "stuff" - you'll probably like it, at least. It's still worth playing for sure and quite good, if you're a fan of this kind of "stuff". What kind of "stuff" here do I mean? Well, this is what I mean for "stuff": SuperMassive's game, military movies (and its take on the military), Monster Movies, and/or cinematic games of this sort. If all of that sounds good to you, definitely check it out.And also with this one (House of Ashes) being in the October Humble Choice here for $12 along w/ The Quarry (and even other titles), can't really go wrong here; no better time than now, TBH here...especially in October, which is the month in which where Halloween falls in & on.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10This is easily the best game in The Dark Pictures Anthology, season 1. While not being quite as "horrific" as the other entries, this game provides a better focus on characters and mood rather than cheap jumpscares and a constant fear of death. Still, it does not quite live up to Until Dawn or The Quarry, which is a shame. It has the potential to be better, but the unoriginality of the story keeps it from being more than a solid game.The game is set in the early 2000s, right after the US assassinated Sadam Hussein. The player takes control of five characters, each military, in their quest to reach an underground facility which alegedly is used as a bomb-making site. However, an earthquake sends the characters plumeting deep underground, with no easy way up to the surface. They also discover that they are not alone underground.The gameplay consists of quicktime-events, free exploration of the underground caverns (one small area at a time) and choices that greatly alter the story. This entry often acts like a third-person shooter (without the shooting part), with the perspective often being an over the shoulder-view of a character. This works well in a horror.-setting such as this, with a lot of dark corners hiding dangers and spooks. It almost feels like Resident Evil at times, which certainly works in order to create atmosphere.Out of all the entries in The Dark Pictures Anthology, season 1, I feel as this game has the best pacing and length. We get to explore each character and their personalities and relationships. The horror is paced well and there is a good balance between action and slow and spooky creeping around dark corridors with danger lurking behind every corner. It is a shame that each character is a version of "soldier dude". I feel as if the characters are not quite unique enough for me to find anyone that sticks out. The same goes for the overarching story. There are no fantastic twists or turns, once you figure out what horror-trope the game has, that is basically it. It works, but does nothing revolutionary with the plot or the writing. In short, this game feels like you took the plot from Aliens and just set it in Iraq with a dash of The Mummy sprinkled in. The most original thing about the game is its focus on sumerian religion, which is fresh and cool. Sadly, it is nothing more than a "skin" for the game, which made me slightly disappointed. The acting is alright, with some actors being more outstanding than others. Nick Tarabay as Salim and Paul Zinno as Jason do a great job with their characters while Ashley Tisdale, Alex Gravenstein and Moe Jeudy-Lamour all feel like their characters could have been played by anyone. They do not make the characters their own, which is a shame. Finally, in ordet to find every collectible and get the whole experience, you need to play this game in multiplayer. This sucks, as I just want to play this interactive horror-film by myself without needing to involve other people. Having it as an option is alright but forcing me? No thanks!It is time to summarize:+ Good pacing and balance of horror+ Great visuals+ Nice lore and focus on sumerian culture and religion- Mediocre story and writing- Predictable ending- Forced multiplayer for 100% completionI think that this is an alright game, the best in the series even. Still, it is nothing spectacular and is only with the price if on a sale or if oyu are a diehard fan of Supermassive Games. If you have not already done so, play Until Dawn or The Quarry instead. If you still crave more, give this series a shot if you find it on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though I have a prejudice against horror-like games, this one is pretty decent. It's rather an action thriller with a few screamers and small splashes of suspense. It also raises the question of whether the enemy of my enemy is my friend, and partially allows the player to answer for himself.The motivation of most characters is clear from the beginning. However, some choices allow you to reveal them better.Some people complain about facial animation, but in my opinion it is at a sufficient level of quality.If there was a movie with such a script, it might seem mediocre. But the involvement in the direction of the story smoothes this feeling out.In general - 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Length 5hrs+The third ‘Dark Pictures’ game in the series and sadly the worst of them, while it feels like it corrects problems found in the first two games, it does it at the expense of not knowing what it wants to be. ‘House of Ashes’ wants to be both a movie and a game, so much of my time playing was simply cutscenes with rare QT events. When you actually controlled a character a lot of the time it was simply a few steps to the next cutscene, or was an exploration moment where I got to pick things up. While there were some moments of actual gameplay towards the end of the game.You can say I play a lot of Horror games, some say too many. I literally have a channel where I play everything I can. Out of every game I have played this is the first one where I don’t want to go back for the other endings. I was so bored by the lack of interaction, the banal horror moments and the endless cutscenes. It really drags, so much of the game like ‘Man of Medan’ was just pointless. I am not here for romance or emotional moments of relationships, I want Monsters and Horror, the slog ruins it.Literally the best description of the game is ‘The Mummy’ meets ‘Aliens’, with 85% cutscenes, 10% QTE and short walk between points. 5% Gameplay. At this point the Dark Picture games are not far off wanting to play itself. It does not help that the game was longer than the previous two games and really did just make a slog of a game, it reminded me of how bad the later ‘Transformer’ movies got and just wanting the movie to end.We finally got actual monsters, and they are not scary. It is like a wave swarm attacking soldiers, when you can take them down and don’t fear them, you lose the horror vibes and have an action film. The game's story did not create horror or fear, but of mystery to what the vampires are and how they exist. The problem is a lot of these moments are only when the correct characters survive, so it can be really easy to miss the story of House of Ashes. Then you literally have a game where you are watching action moments.I really found something jarring about the graphics of ‘Houses of Ashes’ and I can’t place my fingers on why I find it so plastic. Expressions feel flat and in comparison to the previous games the characters all look off. This is really noticeable at the beginning of the game, and feels like a step back from Little Hope.I could keep going on about how much I don’t like the game, but it’s pointless wasted time. _childDocuments_.review: It was shaping up to be my favorite of the three (four?) until it wasn't.  Like most of the other players, I started with Until Dawn. I enjoyed that game so much for the writing, the presentation, the interactive nature and how your choices really actually impacted not only the way the story played out, but also the ending.Then there was Man of Medan.  And honestly, that game just made me sad. I had looked forward to it so much that when it finally came out and I played it, I was just disappointed. It looked like it should have been better. Maybe if I wanted to deal with the problems others had with maintaining connection on multiplayer it would have felt less hollow. But hollow it was none the less. All the charm of Until Dawn somehow removed, most likely in the pursuit of creating a more enjoyable experience to play with others. For those of us who like to play solo, not so much. Little Hope had promise. The writing was a bit better and a little more entertaining. Definitely better than Man of Medan, but still not reclaiming the experience of Until Dawn. The pace was better, but still felt a bit disjointed in the telling. You're just sort of thrown into it and are expected to care about characters that frankly are only a little more likable than those in Man of Medan. The ending was better, I'll give the writers that. So when House of Ashes was announced, I was skeptical and more than a little hesitant. It sort of became obvious what the developers have been trying to figure out; how to balance story, action with consequences and yet still somehow make it an enjoyable multiplayer experience without forgetting about solo players.  I LOVE the environment in House of Ashes.  I LIKE the story. It does feel like the put a little too much into it and some aspects of the story were left a little thin. That might be just the way I played through it though. I'll have to see on my next play through.  The creepiness is definitely there in this one. Despite what other reviews have claimed about the pacing, I found the first half was excellent.  But then the second half happened and I realized all too well what the others were talking about.  I'm not sure why the developers didn't provide more opportunities to interact in the latter part of the game. It really did feel more like watching a movie. Not bad, but I did purchase a game and I'd like to take part in the drama. The performances were a little stiff. This might  be from the way the actors were shot and had to do multiple takes, etc. But it's bearable to watch/listen to. The writing only felt a wee dialed in for the Marines. It was almost like watching Aliens again with all the stereotyping they wrote in.  Again, not a criminal offense, but it took me out of it a little. I think some aspects of this game may trigger those who have been in combat. The first 1/4 of the game has some scenes that felt a bit too on the nose and if I had real life experience with that sort of thing, I might not like the memories it could bring up. So to combat veterans and refugees from wars, be prepared since it is graphic and intense. Overall, this was the first out of the 3 titles I actually want to replay. If I include Until Dawn, it's the second.  For my taste, the list from best to worst: 1) Until Dawn2) House of Ashes3) Little Hope4) Man of MedanThis was worth the $20 I paid for it. If you can get it for less, jump on it.  But twenty was a fair price. I hope the next title will have the improvements from the previous titles, since it's already looking pretty good!

I played for an hour, made specific choices, died immediately because I was still trying to get a feel for how the QTEs work and felt like I really screwed up dying so fast.  So I restarted did everything correctly only to find out every choice I made in that segment of the game literally doesn't matter and the same cutscenes will play the same characters will die. _childDocuments_.review: I'm assuming since we're on installment three most people buying this kinda understand that they're signing up for what is essentially a long interactive film; in which their decisions are less about hugely changing the narrative but allowing for immersion into the narrative. Of course looking at negative reviews I would be wrong so let me spell it out.  Look if any of this is a deal breaker that's fine just understand that instead of buying this thinking it's not an interactive film and getting mad cause you wanted something else. It does what it does well as I'll explain below for the none of you that read this.The previous installment of this Anthology "Little Hope" really did leave me with little hope for this series of games. As far as audience insulting twist endings go it had one that made me livid, I mean I was pissed. But still it delivered a good atmosphere and co-op narrative for what it was worth so there was no way I wasn't going to give this one a chance. And it doesn't disappoint. House of Ashes delivers The Dark Pictures Anthology's best setting, plot and characters so far.House of Ashes looks pretty, it's a definite upgrade in visuals and especially lighting from previous entries and this helps with the games overall atmosphere allowing the narrative to become more effective. To me personally this doesn't really matter what gets me is two things. One, I love exploring the setting that is Iraq post Operation: Iraqi Freedom and some of the feelings that come associated with that. It doesn't do as much as it could but does touch on some of the questionable morality and effectiveness of what was going on. Two, there a couple of characters that stand out in particular which are Salim and Jason. The plot effectively revolves around the idea of enemies becoming friends due to a third evil party and even though its a simple premise I found myself attached to the main group and genuinely sad when things turned out poorly for Nick and Salim when we failed some QTEs. Boils down to the fact that you never leave a man behind Oorah to ashes boys.I guess the next biggest point is that the threat is actually real this time not just hallucinogen gas or a weird PTSD Silent Hill dream sequence. I'm just really glad there wasn't a dumb twist ending it makes the struggles we went along the way more worth it in my mind. Other than that there's just a great amount of cool adrenaline pumping set pieces like manning a Maxim gun and stabbing several dudes with a big stick.It's a good time go find those WMDs Marine.

_childDocuments_.review: I think Supermassive Games forgot halfway through developing House of Ashes that they were making a "game". This game could have been so much more, but it was a total let down. For starters, I have six hours clocked on this game and I barely played any of that because this "game" is actually just a movie in disguise, except there's choices involved. A lot of the QTEs were ridiculous because they give you so little time to actually react, which in some circumstances affects the whole rest of the game. And because there's no differentiating what's a cut scene and what's not in this game, you could very easily screw up one of the QTEs; so you're only options are either to actually pay attention to what's happening on screen and immerse yourself, or stare at the screen until the next QTE pops up so you don't ruin the story accidentally.Talking about the choices aspect of the game, I feel like the devs wanted to troll players because you pick a choice that is very reasonable and appropriate for the situation, but then you get an annoying twist with, surprise, ruins the outcome of the story. It's either nothing happens when you pick the right choice, or a character dies when you pick the wrong option; there's no in between and no indication of what is right and what is wrong.There are a lot of other issues I have with this game, but I will say that the game looks absolutely beautiful. For a game that was as detailed as it was, it ran perfectly on my older PC. It was very pleasing on the eyes and it made immersion, when you could actually immerse yourself, much easier.FYI, I've played Until Dawn and actually liked that game. But now that they don't have that Sony much and there just pumping these games out quicker than they should, the quality takes a real hit.

_childDocuments_.review: House of Ashes is a gripping addition to The Dark Pictures Anthology, offering a chilling and immersive experience that will keep you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.Set against the backdrop of the Iraq War in 2003, House of Ashes follows a group of soldiers who, after an intense skirmish, find themselves trapped underground in a buried Sumerian temple. As they navigate the claustrophobic depths, they discover they are not alone. Ancient and malevolent creatures lurk in the shadows, and the soldiers must fight not only for their survival but also to uncover the mysteries hidden within the temple.The game excels in storytelling, with well-developed characters and an engaging plot that keeps you invested throughout. The tension is palpable, and the fear of the unknown is effectively conveyed, making every decision feel weighty and significant.Overall, House of Ashes is a thrilling and memorable gaming experience. Whether you're a fan of horror games or simply enjoy a well-crafted narrative, this game is a must-play. Supermassive Games has once again delivered an exceptional addition to The Dark Pictures Anthology, leaving players eagerly anticipating the next installment.

_childDocuments_.review: House of Ashes takes the series into new, thrilling territory with its story set during the Iraq War. A military unit stumbles upon an ancient, underground temple filled with monstrous creatures. The shift to an action-horror blend adds intensity, with the claustrophobic caves and lurking threats keeping you on edge.The game’s strongest aspect is its atmosphere and the moral dilemmas presented as you control soldiers and civilians forced to cooperate. Character development is better than previous entries, and your choices feel impactful, influencing relationships and survival.However, while the game raises the stakes, some horror elements can feel predictable, and the quick-time events may still break immersion. Despite this, House of Ashes offers a gripping, cinematic experience, making it one of the stronger entries in the anthology.

_childDocuments_.review: House of Ashes is what made me play the DPA for the first time. It's very rare in a game to have the military placed in an inescapable horror situation, but I think it couples well with House of Ashes finally presenting a very real and terrifying threat to the protagonists. The average college student of the previous 2 games is not going to have the mindset or discipline to have a chance to survive in this setting.The characters are amazingly designed and for some of them (Jason, Eric & Salim) you can decide what their character development is like based on your dialogue choices and decisions, especially Jason - you can break through his front and have him show his vulnerabilities or have him keep up his facade and close himself off from everyone.I think the one issue I have is how much the subplot of the love triangle between Eric, Nick & Rachel can overbear the main story. Jason & Salim are thoroughly motivated to escape the temple and see daylight again, but sometimes it feels like the other three are more preoccupied with their relationship troubles rather than trying to focus on the obvious threat they face in front of them and it can culminate to devastating effect near the end of the game. The game is very replayable - the bearings are able to create unique situations every playthrough and certain dialogue choices can open up more conversations further into the game, one example being . Overall, I'll say House of Ashes is a massive improvement despite not playing the previous 2 games.

Also, the little love triangle annoyed me too no ends, and by the end I only kept them alive for the achievement. My friend and me only really liked two of the characters by the end. _childDocuments_.review: After the ghost ship and the abandoned small town, the new and independent story takes us into a distant past in the first few minutes and after the prologue and a brief look at the "horror" it quickly takes us back to the 21st century.More precisely in With a new technology, the Americans have managed to discover a secret underground chemical weapons cache in the Iraqi mountains.Without further ado, a squad of soldiers is sent to investigate. Arriving on site, disillusionment spreads quickly because, as was somehow to be expected, no secret chemical weapons depot could be found.Instead, the soldiers are ambushed and involved in a firefight with Iraqi ground troops until a hole opens in the ground and the combatants are "swallowed".From then on, the squad is in a kind of underground temple complex and there seems to be no way to get back to the surface. Unfortunately, that's not her only problem. The squad find themselves in a strange place that has been claiming casualties for centuries...Right from the start you notice that House of Ashes is different.The third part of the Dark Pictures Anthology series stands out from the other parts right from the start and could make the game a very unique experience.The mysterious setting, which somehow reminded me of movies like "The Mummy", "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom" or "The Descent", is certainly creepy, isn't it?To put it this way:if the hairs on the back of your neck stand up at the sight of a monster, then definitely yes.Otherwise, the word horror in the genre description doesn't really apply to this game.Despite it. The result is a game in which friends of the two predecessors will feel "at home" and may tempt newcomers and whet their appetite for more.If you take a closer look at House of Ashes, you will notice that the game sticks to its traditional gameplay, but the characters are not, as usual, naive or weak.The squad consists of battle-hardened soldiers with willpower and tactical thinking. The equipment is also much more extensive this time with knives, flashlights, ropes or radios.Perhaps the biggest difference to the two previous parts is that the plot or the respective secret is not only gradually revealed, but the "evil" is presented in all its strength right at the beginning and already in the prologue.I have to admit, I wasn't really sure at first if I was going to have fun with the game. But that was probably because I expected something different simply because of the other two parts.Although the protagonists act or move like zombies at times and don't know where to look and the collision query is a bit tricky, the fixed and mostly rather annoying camera perspective has been replaced by a kind of third-person view with a rotating camera.It is also commendable that you can now make your gaming experience even more individual. You not only have the option of adjusting the level of difficulty, but also more accessibility for, for example, the reaction test, time limits or the timer, which you can even switch off completely if you wish.You can plan around 4-6 hours for a run through and the replay value, which is given by the branching and chaining, is still there.The decisions that can have a direct or later influence on the story are again indispensable. There are also scenes that later in the story can no longer be influenced, or should we say, because of this, and if so, then only to a very limited extent.The chances of survival still depend on the QTEs, which sometimes still feel like "Guitar Hero". However, the focus here is more on the action, which is particularly important when using firearms.Especially in the co-op mode, I had the feeling that sequences were suddenly mixed up or even missing.All of a sudden, the protagonists are separated from each other even though they just fought together. Characters yell at each other only to talk to each other normally again the next moment or give the impression that they have just met for the first time. I can't say whether the game just messes something up depending on the decision or what exactly the problem is. As a result, it is sometimes not easy to fully engage with the atmosphere when I have to ask myself where my colleague has gone.And unfortunately it now looks like it's time to say goodbye to the curator. Kind of a shame, I liked him...As I mentioned in my review of  I've never had the chance to play Until Dawn. I'm sure I'll catch up on that sooner or later, but I'm quite glad I haven't played it yet because I suspect I would have let myself be carried away by a direct comparison. And I still think that's not always fair to the games.The games from the Dark Pictures Anthology were the first of their kind for me and I have to say that I was pleasantly surprised. I wouldn't say that the games really knocked my socks off, it just lacked that little something extra. Still, it was an interesting experience and I definitely don't regret playing the anthology.After Little Hope I thought I'd found the part I liked the most, even though I hadn't played House of Ashes before. Now I'm not sure anymore.To me, these two parts are like comparing the apples and the pears. I liked them both, but since House of Ashes is something completely different and in no way comparable to me, I see the two games as equals.✅ cinematic staging✅ difficult decisions✅ Secrets and bonus content✅ Different storylines✅ atmospheric setting✅ good light and shadow effects✅ new camera from the third person view✅ Accessibility settings✅ Customizable Quick Time Events✅ Replay value through choices/endings✅ alternative death scenes✅ Hardly any horror, but more action❌ Cracky character and (face) animations❌ sometimes audio and texture bugs❌ simple and short trash story with no twist❌ Hardly anything interesting to discover❌ Hardly any horror, but more action

_childDocuments_.review: The Dark Pictures Anthology is a series (trilogy thus far) of video games that have the cinematic build your own adventure style of Tell Tale's the Walking Dead & Supermassive's Until Dawn. House of Ashes is the third, and presumably final, installment which follows a collection of military personnel investigating a dig site in Iraq.-Light Spoilers-It took 8 hours to finish my first play through. I didn't search for many collectables which may have contributed to a shorter overall finish time. Of the three, this game feels like the most polished but still has similar positives and negatives. There's moments where I'm still getting a little frustrated at one or two overly impactful quick time events but for the most part the choices you make are what drives the game.I would add that this game has an additional drawback\benefit of being able to adjust your camera angle to a greater degree. This was especially noticeable when going back and playing Man of Medan where you walk through a lot of forced camera angles. I saw benefit because it allows for a greater degree of exploration and I say drawback because it kind of made me kinda dizzy with how much have to turn it to see everything. At times it was like doing constant 360s in every room, down every hall. By contrast, if you look at man of Medan, there's some movement side to side but it mostly keeps you looking one direction. I would still highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily the best of the trilogy – exciting, engaging story and characters, less lazy jumpscares and genuine tense moments, you actually like the characters and care if they live. Loved the addition of the video logs for the historical sections. The ending is incredible. There is a staggering number of alternate versions of events and everything matters - what lore you know, what you've picked up, character relationships, conversation options shape your characters. This is really, really good.The only criticisms:- The dialogue can be clunky for some characters in the beginning but improves. Weirdly Salim is the best written of the characters, as if he was written by someone different from everyone else. The writing improves significantly after the beginning, it’s weirdly the initial setup that suffers from shaky writing.- There is no way to fast forward cutscenes - this makes it very frustrating when doing trophy hunting and you need a specific setup. Means many additional playthroughs of sections, or even the whole game, and having to watch cutscenes again and again.- Had to verify game files three times due to corrupt installation files.Loved this, it’s so good, they nailed this one! I am so relieved after the disappointment of Little Hope but there’s nothing to fear – this is incredibly good. They really listened to the complaints about the first two games and addressed them. I adored this one, well done Supermassive. Can’t recommend this enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Though this is the third installment of the anthology, I got (and played) it first, so it casts a pretty big shadow over the other games. (But don't worry, they are solid too.)I was pretty much biased because I enjoyed playing Clive Barker's Jericho in the Bronze Age (at least it feels it was that long ago). Nevertheless the devs made their magic the third time too. Same mechanics, totally different details.House of Ashes immediately makes you feel something different by introducing the protagonists (plus the prologue duo), they are not a band of friends or fellow students, no, they are professional soldiers.This intensifies in how they are dealing with danger.First... they got into the nasty part when they... deal with each other. One minute you try to shoot the other guy, the next... well... you got to reconsider, who is your true enemy. After that, yes, they run, but not fleeing in panic. They retreat, covering their brothers-in-arms, using tactics, explosives, ancient hardware, bullets and even a primeval metal bar.Their inside conflicts are also more intense than those of previous titles. You can pretty much make them murder each other if you make harsh decisions, and by that I don't mean accidental killings, but cold blooded executions.In case of physical suffering, this quintet gots more than the protagonists of the other games. (I wasn't a big fan of Rachel, but man, what she endures, she earns more than your respect. Queen Beetch, hoorah!) You bond with them, watch for them and if you lose them, you feel sadness and rage for revenge them. (Jason is the one from the five I liked the absolute most, play the game and you will know it why.)My story ended with two casualties but the three survivors were forged into a Titanic Trio.The Epilogue here is more elaborate, I just watched in awe and said to myself, Boy, you got to grab the next game of the series too.You know the drill, soldier! Get! Play! Enjoy! Repeat!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to make a response to "Buzz Killington's" negative review. He said, "1/5 for the gameplay. You do almost nothing. It is an interactive, animated movie." Anyone who is familiar with the series, or Until Dawn, isn't surprised by this. In fact, it's how it's advertised, even in the steam description, which he obviously skipped over. Much of the game is cinematic base with QTEs, and you make decisions for dialogue, and there's a lot of other in-combat actions/quick decisions. It's very similar to an interactive movie, but there's also normal 3P gameplay, just not an overwhelming amount, as the game is not marketed as such. This is the first game in this anthology series that wasn't crashing and buggy as hell for me, so I'd recommend. Still nowhere near as good as Until Dawn, and it starts to feel very heavy on the action-thriller, rather than survival-horror, but it's fun and worth more than one playthrough. The QTEs definitely seem more difficult in this title than in the past ones as well. It definitely move in the positive direction for a lot of aspects, but I do not like them moving away from horror elements. Hopefully, their next title will have less focus on action, and more on "survival horror." Still worth playing, though. If you don't want to spend the money, wait for a deep sale.

_childDocuments_.review: "House of Ashes," part of The Dark Pictures Anthology, expertly intertwines Egyptian mythology, military drama, and vampire horror into an engaging narrative. It's a game that demands attention, offering a rich, interactive story with decisions that lead to many outcomes. This ensures a fresh experience with every session, inviting players back to explore all possible paths.Rated 7 out of 10, the game shines with its unique genre blend and immersive gameplay, despite some areas needing polish. "House of Ashes" stands out for its compelling storytelling and the eerie atmosphere it crafts, making it a must-play for horror and narrative-driven game fans alike. Dive into this dark adventure for a horror experience filled with ancient secrets and moral dilemmas.

_childDocuments_.review: What I did like:-The characters felt like actual people that develop over the course of the game. -The game play, while like the other ones, feels better in this one. -Lots of scenes that make for pretty cool screenshots-This one has the most "your choices matter" -The endings are pretty decent and fitting to the story that was told. What I didn't like:-My buddy and I had one pretty major de-sync bug towards the endHaving played them all, this one is easily the best in the Anthology. It works, the characters, setting, and story are interesting, questions are answered without having to do a completionist playthrough, and it looks pretty good too. The whole "your choices matter" gimmick of these games really shines in this one, since choices made early really matter towards the end. I bring this up because my buddy and I technically saved everyone (i.e everyone was alive in the character recap section at the end of the game), however we did not get the achievement because of choices me made way earlier. I liked this a lot, but I know some people will be frustrated about it. Overall, check this one out if you are thinking about playing one of these games. The least scary, but the most functional and enjoyable.
