_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal sequel to one of my favorite games, Spongebob Squarepants: The Cosmic Shake does almost exactly what I wanted a sequel to be. Other than a lot of great things about this game, I want to make this review a bit shorter than usual since everything not mentioned is to absolute perfection. The combat is greatly improved, as well as the overall levels, especially when it comes to the sizes of the levels, as it can take even a couple of hours to do everything in a level or more. I also liked the overall progression within the hub world, which is another improvement, although I do wish that there was a balance between the progression of the hub world, along with also balancing out the increased amount of abilities Spongebob gets over time. I think in terms of what the previous title did better, the exploration was definitely better in the previous title, as this game does feel more linear overall, in addition to the collectibles being not as rewarding in this game, as the costumes and achievements are the only real incentive. In terms of the way that side quests work, you can't really start working on the side quests until after completing the main story, or at least this is what is optimal, which to me, makes for just, replaying the game again just for the sake of unlocking costumes or achievements instead of what the previous title did, which was having a more balanced option of just, doing whatever whenever. I also don't really like the way that some of the buttons or unlockables for additional abilities work, as the game is rather unclear in terms of what symbols mean what until after learning the abilities, and even then, certain buttons within previous worlds aren't very obvious in terms of what abilities are required, and neither are other unlockables in general. Still, this is a rather great game to play, and I highly recommend this game. This game is a 9/10 in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I could tell basically from the very beginning that this game is just a giant love letter to Spongebob fans of old who enjoyed the classic Battle for Bikini Bottom or its Rehydrated remaster (or even the Movie game, if you can find it in yourself to enjoy that one somehow). The gameplay was so smooth and controlling Spongebob in whatever way you could was SO so satisfying, it truly felt like they took everything people loved about the gameplay mechanics in Battle and improved so much on it.Story wise it was pretty good! With my personal taste I would have personally preferred it had been a little longer, but I'm not completely dissatisfied with how it turned out. It was very well paced and I enjoyed the linearity aspect. I know everybody would have preferred a slightly more open world feel to it, but we know what we can do with video games now, and stories aren't that hard to tell if you're good at it. I told family and friends that, in my opinion, this game felt like one stretched out episode of SpongeBob, and I mean that in all the best ways, because if you know me you know that I love and cherish the SpongeBob series so much (at least prior to the unfortunate passing of Stephen Hillenburg), so as far as the game's storytelling goes, like I said a bit too short, but ticked all the right boxes. (Also, the there were SO many callbacks to previous episodes, so if you like insider references this game is 110% for you lol)IN CONCLUSION, if you have ever enjoyed SpongeBob SquarePants on television, or for that matter enjoyed the fun collectathon experience of Battle for Bikini Bottom, I cannot stress it enough; just pick up a copy and play it, I guarantee you will have fun some way or another!

_childDocuments_.review: Spongebob Squarepants: Battle for Bikini Bottom is quite possibly my all-time favorite childhood game. In an era where we were flooded with subpar licensed games from kids TV shows and movies, Battle For Bikini Bottom stood above the crowd as one of the best platformers on the Gamecube, full stop. By present times, we’ve had much more luck with licensed games, with certifiable masterpieces like 2018 Spider-Man, the Arkham series, or Telltale’s The Walking Dead. In 2020, Purple Lamp game studios took up the mantle and released the remake, Battle For Bikini Bottom Rehydrated to great success. While I love the remake, it always struck me as unnecessary - I feel the original holds up great even today, so what I was really hoping for was a sequel. And by Neptune, here it is! The Cosmic Shake is very noticeably a sequel to Battle for Bikini Bottom, but it doesn’t take the high parts and evolve the way that I would have wanted it to. I’ve very much enjoyed the game, but the second half of it is for the most part where the best levels are, while the first few levels are stuck being tutorials with slow progression and overlong bloating. Still, some very imaginative environments, actually challenging platforming, and a few good jokes here and there keep the experience fresh. Spongebob and Patrick begin the game encountering Kassandra, a charlatan mystic who sells them what she believes is essentially snake oil as magic bubble formula. Spongebob soon finds it can grant wishes, and predictably goes off the rails trying to grant the wishes of everyone in Bikini Bottom. Eventually, the universe rips, and various characters and parts of the city are sent to other dimensions while Patrick is transformed into a cute little balloon version of himself. Balloon Patrick serves as Spongebob’s companion as he ventures forth to clear the cosmic monsters and dimensional jelly from bikini bottom and 7 other large linear worlds, rescuing a different character from the show in each one.The biggest downgrade from Battle for Bikini Bottom is certainly the level variety. While the first game had 12 semi-open levels, each one was short and sweet, the Cosmic Shake contains 8 much longer and more linear levels. Instead of specific quests inside the level to earn golden spatulas, the goal of The Cosmic Shake is to simply make it to the end of the level and beat the boss. The Cosmic Shake opts to make its levels completely linear, with one combat or platforming challenge after another, and leaves little room for exploration of any kind. The structure is the weakest part of the game, and the wonderful environments would have been better served as semi-open zones as well. While the first game back in 2004 was heavily, heavily reminiscent of the structure of Super Mario 64, The Cosmic Shake structurally feels more like Crash Bandicoot. Combat is solid, with this newest entry giving Spongebob a lot more in his kit. Although it removes his upwards helmet attack and the fan favorite cruise bubble, the new kit includes a karate kick that acts as a homing attack, a grappling hook, a bubble wand that traps enemies, a ground pound, and a few other small tricks. Unfortunately you cannot play as Patrick and Sandy in this game. Their abilities have been made part of Spongbob’s own kit, but it’s just not the same. There is a solid enemy variety once you get past the first two levels, which feel like very long tutorials. Most of them are similar to enemy types from battle for Bikini bottom, but certainly not just reskins. Combat sections are both broken off into waves in the same arena and sprinkled around the levels. I like having enemies in games like this just hanging out around the level, rather than concentrated into hordes, but overall there’s enough variety in Spongebob’s kit in the second half of the game that combat never gets tedious. The same kinds of small challenges that granted golden spatulas are still present, but they don’t give you any reward except to just keep moving through the level. I think the absence of a large collectible like that hurts The Cosmic Shake notably. Luckily there are rare collectibles that are golden doubloons in each level, used to unlock new costumes for spongebob, but they’re more the result of looking in hidden places than actually completing some kind of challenge. I’ve alluded a few times to the fact that the second half of the game is more fun, and it very much is. The first three levels specifically feel like a gigantic 2 hour tutorial, with Spongebob getting new abilities every so often, lots of tutorial pop ups, and honestly the least exciting levels. There is some genius environment artwork in The Cosmic Shake, but it’s all in the second half of the game. I encourage players not to get discouraged - while the first half of the game is fine, the second is extremely good, and I did still have fun with the first half. Halloween Rock Bottom and the Medieval Sulfur fields were definitely the two best levels, and Glove World was a great ode to the traditional haunted carnival theme. The boss fights were for the most part excellent, with each of them focusing much more on platforming than on direct combat. This is a small pet peeve of mine, when a boss fight in a platformer suddenly is all about fighting when the rest of the game has not been. A boss fight is a test of the abilities and skills you’ve acquired in that area, a summary of what you, the player,  have learned. The boss fights in the Cosmic Shake are a perfect test of the level’s mechanics as well as all mechanics in your kit, while keeping the focus on platforming rather than smashing a button to do damage. The sole exception to this is the final boss battle, which is predictably Kassandra, which was possibly the most anticlimactic final boss I can call to mind right now. It was so easy I only took damage once and it didn’t even have a second stage. Honestly, it soured the ending for me a good bit.Overall, if you’re looking for a solid 3D platformer with next gen graphics and great performance, you found it. The humor is similar to the humor found in the show in the last few years, which is to say not nearly as good as the first few seasons of the show, but there are some great jokes here and there. It’s always nice to see Spongebob and Patrick on another adventure, and I really had a blast with all that positive energy. While it didn’t recapture the magic of its predecessor, I think the $40 price tag is right, and if you’ve been looking forward to it I heartily recommend it! 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: The Cosmic Shake is something that I've been unreasonably excited for in a long time for reasons I didn't even know I had anticipated, and I'm glad to say it met my expectations. The game's presentation, while a little rough around the edges in some areas, is immensely faithful to the source material with abundant references and fourth-wall breaks, vibrant colors, animations, and stellar voice performances. Although nothing particularly ground-breaking stands out, I found it to be a relatively solid and worthy successor to Battle for Bikini Bottom that we've been anticipating after nearly 2 decades as well as a refreshing throwback to a type of game we simply don't see many of anymore.+ Actions flow into one another, resulting in fluid platforming and combat+ Levels, while linear, boast impressive scale+ Abundant and appropriate use of callbacks/references- Isolated side content makes completing the game particularly tedious- Quirky pacing: drawn-out beginning levels and underwhelming, abrupt endgame

_childDocuments_.review: Spongebob. This game is fantastic. The levels are fun, with the platforming and all. The movement options are super fun to use in combat. It still have the sliding and swinging mechanics from the first game, which I thought were the most fun ways to move in that game. The original music is great, but this game also implements the songs from the show in cutscenes and the like.  The game, however, can at times be buggy, although it hasn't taken away any from the experience for me, since the only glitches I can remember right now are tikis that aren't supposed to float floating, and the music cutting out after a couple of deaths. Also sometimes when things appear they just... appear, which also was a problem in BFBB Rehydrated. Also like Rehydrated, the lip-syncing in more primitive cutscenes where it's just textboxes and a couple of animations used in multiple of them is off. Other than those problems, though, the game was fun. I do wish the game was longer, however. Also, the story is fine. I don't think you would play a Spongebob game for the story, though. There are a lot of references in the game, too, though.
_childDocuments_.name: SpongeBob SquarePants: The Cosmic Shake

_childDocuments_.review: A modern spiritual successor to 2003's Battle for Bikini Bottom which was remade 2 years ago. The level design and gameplay philosophy is kept very similar to BFBB which makes it feel intentionally dated. While not as good as BFBB (which I had as a kid so nostalgia may color that view) it carries on its legacy and is a solid 3D platformer of the PS2 era. If you set your expectations appropriately, or maybe wait for a sale, you won't regret the purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: SpongeBob SquarePants: The Cosmic Shake

_childDocuments_.review: I've gotta say, this is a really good game when you look past the 6 hours of playtime to beat the storyline normally.Cons: - The game is extremely short compared to BFBB. It almost feels like a DLC, and not a completely separate game. It isn't worth 40$. Maybe 20$.- Gameplay serves a linear purpose, and you don't really get tasks to do for characters unless you're in the HUB world. - The final boss battle of the game is the easiest, with the boss battle in the middle of the game being the hardest.Pros: - It has a nice and simple story to tell with a unique premise set within the Spongebob universe.- It has much more combat methods and features for spongebob to use on enemies or to traverse the land.- You can ride a seahorse.All-in-all, I don't agree with the 40$ price of the game, and it was a little too short for my taste, but hell, it's worth playing if you want to experience a brand-new spongebob adventure.

_childDocuments_.name: SpongeBob SquarePants: The Cosmic Shake

_childDocuments_.review: This is an extremely fun game to play. I managed to 100% it in just over 16 hours. It's a very good game to follow up BFBB, the story was super fun. Getting to use different costumes, having Patrick float alongside you and the level designs were really nice. Honestly would be great to see what people can do when there's a Speed-Running community for this. BFBB speedruns are hella broken, so can only imagine how people will manage to find shortcuts for this. If you are a Trophy/Achievement Hunter some of them are quite difficult and others just take a bit of time. My only "gripe" really is that I feel it's a little pricey as the standard price for the game, it's about £10/$10 more than BFBB, and you only get about 2 more hours of game-play (less so if you don't fail a bunch at boss mechanics like I did).  I don't at all regret my purchase, but if you can grab this on sale, then 100% go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Watch Here What a ShowAfter This Fishy Mermaid gives SpongeBob cosmic reality warping bubbles, Spongebob sinks Bikini bottoms into multiversal  apocalypse opening tears in the space time continúem, after this realization you must travel to these new worlds to save your friends and return time and space back to normal lol I mean if everything get there own multiverse  then why not SpongeBob introducing the Jellyverse and the funny part is it all WorkGraphicThis is a Big improvement over BFBB running on unreal engine and it looks awesome the amount of details they where able to cram is impressive to put this way SpongeBob holes have holes ( what ) like it’s insane you ad to that 7 truly distinct locations like western manta fe or the movie set  there’s tons here to look and marvel at not to mention a gorgeous color pallet filled to the brim with all that saturation you could possible cram into a title . All the characters we love are back as well and they look great all be it modified versions of them selves like sheriff sandy or wanted Mr.Krabs with a clean mustache. But the best change is the fact that we aren’t retreading same old bikini bottom again these new portals bring life to what an old locations for long time fans like myself and they can only be unlocked with new costumes which is a cool way to do progression more on that later. Point is the game looks really good and brings use those classic areas and characters but with a twist.Audio: the gang is all here in my previous review for battle for bikini bottom I lamented that not everyone was here mainly mr. krabs the voice actor was a busy with jak 2 but now everyone is here and marvelous it also warms my heart to see that the Voice Actors still sound great as they gets up there in age They have been reprising these roles since "99", theses performances are up there with some of the best as each level really plays out like episodes which is awesome the dialogue is much better this time around it’s smarter wittier I didn’t laugh one time in bbfb but here I laughed and smiled a lot. The sound track is a testament to this as well the old school beach vibes each world with modern twist and brings some new song to the table this sonically might be one of the best Game based on a Show.Gameplay: if bfbb was a sponge bob movies then Cosmic shake feels like a SB season 7 locations that are very different from each other bring our old favorites characters and new challenges to the mix they also remix the classic locations with some dare I say variants and it’s not just the locations it is a full blown improvement through and through 10 fold. everything is better and in this they addresses almost all of my gripes from the first game. The platforming better focusing on SB multiple abilities, they added a progression system in the costumes and the new moves you get in every level. They added side objectives after levels are complete. The levels them selves are more like god of war or a metroidvania where to get a reward you need a certain power  basically addressing my back tracking issues. The boss battles are even better they are good And the side activities fun as hell. I mean we finally get to flip some grabby Pattie’s as SB. What a gameBad- It Did crash 30 minutes  in but I think that’s a false alarm. We do get some stuttering here and there when way too many explosions go off. The Background music went mute for a little in one level until I died but then it came back. All of those don’t really affect the experience and don’t bother me what does is the simple fact that SB does repeat lines while in there world now less this time around then last and now he does comment on his new outfits and areas but when gliding he will quote the crusty crab pizza over and over again and that just get annoying sometimes.Conclusion - Cosmic Shake is one hell of a Sequel and in my opinion one of the best games based on a show of all time. Final Score 9/10Fun - hell yea Worth - definitely worth the price of admission at $40For you- any one who loves sponge bob , old school action adventure games like Spyro or current gems like destroy all humans. Easily recommended for kids and adults of all ages

_childDocuments_.review: I have now played for 2.5 hours and the experience is rather mixed.- Bugs are annoying. Cutscenes just end in the middle of the sentence. I had the impression that I missed some parts of the story because of it. Also I had to restart the game twice because the game would not let me progress because of what was obviously a bug.- The game has some slight elements of an open world and it looks like you can do anything you want. But you can't, it's effectively a very linear design. That's not bad, but that mixture is a bit confusing. Map boundaries are mostly "here's water or an abyss so this is the limit", but weirdly there are also dotted lines to signal that boundary. When you cross it, you die.- I really like the graphics, the art style and the audio. But the some of the gameplay animations look rather unrefined.- For a platformer, the jumping feels off. Sometimes you can barely make a jump even though it should totally be possible. Same with the pizza box gliding. Also at some point spongebob just started to grab and climb up ledges all of a sudden.- Fights are incredibly easy. Unless you got that one enemy-spawning-boss-guy that stuns you even when you are further away from him. Combine that with the ranged enemy and you die very quickly. Weird balancing.I will update this as I progress. So far it's been a good experience but it suffers from not being polished/refined enough.

_childDocuments_.review: A no commentary video trailer, intro, and first mission of Spongebob Squarepants The Cosmic Shake!  This game turned out fantastic and is fully voiced and has tons of cinematic scenes as well as platformer gameplay. There is a huge amount of costumes to wear and even some in the preorder that I show off in the video. The music in the game is also great but sadly had to be disabled on launch day for uploads because they weren't able to get it cleared through youtube in time, but the game is so strong that it stands firmly without it. I am honestly impressed by how well this game turned out. There is tons of worlds that all have their own theme that spongebob enters to rescue his friends in order to save reality itself! The mise en scene of the spongebob universe is perfect and it feels like you're playing out your own individual mini series of the spongebob tv show. Patrick accompanies Spongebob with constant witty commentary and all the main characters make constant appearances like Sandy, Mr Krabs, Squidward, Plankton, Gary,  and even minor characters like Ms Puff! Many times throughout the game, the gameplay style transitions to different types to racing scenes, side scrolling, and 3d platformer style to keep the gameplay fresh. Overall, this game ended up being extremely polished and is definitely worth picking up if you platformers or spongebob are your thing.

_childDocuments_.review: A must have for any SpongeBob and/or Collectathon fan!Incredibly fun SpongeBob game that feels like a direct sequel to 'Battle for Bikini Bottom' despite being so many years apart. Meaning gameplay, humour, locations, music and overall effort put into it are a direct upgrade while staying true to the format to a T. You can tell how they used the remake as warm-up to this game and man is it good.The entire concept and added features & abilities of this game while keeping the feel of the original is fantastic and incredibly fun. I was hooked as soon as I started the game and the loving homages/fanservice to popular memes is just a showcase on how much they care. Cannot wait to see where they'll take this game series from here on out and hoping we will have a lot of fun games to come in the future. Had an enemy in the ground but was able to get it easily unstuck with a bubble.Little downside is having no graphics options whatsoever, but it runs rather smooth even on older hardware!10/10 absolutely recommendable game, I do not regret pre-ordering in the slightest, as someone who rarely buys games not on sale :D

_childDocuments_.review:
Wish-granting Mermaid's Tears in the hands of SpongeBob and Patrick... What could possibly go wrong? Sure, the very fabric holding the very universe very together could come very undone, opening up portals into Wishworlds full of knights, cowboys, pirates, and prehistoric snails. But that's nothing everyone's favorite sponge can't handle - with the right cosmic costume! Everybody do the Cosmic Shake!

Features

* Unlock classic and new platforming skills like the Fishhook Swing and Karate Kick
* Don more than 30 F.U.N.tastic costumes like SnailBob and SpongeGar
* Travel to 7 distinct Wishworlds like Wild West Jellyfish Fields and Halloween Rock Bottom
* Experience all the buddy movie banter with SpongeBob's permanent companion Balloon-Patrick
* Meet all your favorite Bikini Bottomites from the series, voiced by their original actors
* Enjoy the in-game soundtrack featuring 101 songs from the series, including Sweet Victory

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting take on the tactical RPG genre. I really enjoyed it, but bear in mind that combat (especially early) can be a bit of a struggle if you are new to the game (or genre). It is very much an X-com-style game, with you utilizing cover and elevation to reduce damage taken and increase damage done.Pros:Combat is fun. Setting up a round properly and watching Laughing Deer run through and completely devastate the enemy team is very satisfying. The card system is interesting and allows for some flexibility in how each character approaches battle. Weapons are less strict than other games about which is better, with all but the best weapons having tradeoffs. Often you'll choose a weapon because it has burning, bleeding, bullseye increase, or some other stat boost rather than because it has the most damage per shot.The combat is fairly brutal, if you make a mistake you will pay for it. This has the bonus effect of making it very satisfying when you play a round properly. It's very important to do this, as MANY areas are very long. You will often find that levels are 4+ fights and you do not want to start the last fight with low health (except maybe Old Bill).Cons:Not very many characters to choose from and some are very lackluster. There are a few characters that you will probably never use outside of the missions that require them.The loyalty system is extremely shallow, you will be able to max out loyalty one maybe 2 characters in a playthrough. You cannot lose loyalty and the perks gained from loyalty on some characters is practically useless.Not many weapons to choose from. There are roughly 5 different kinds of each type of weapon (shotguns, rifles, melee, pistols).The card system is interesting, but doesn't actually allow that much flexibility. You will almost always have clubs on Laughing Deer so he can move around the battlefield for less AP and hearts on Bill to use him as a damage sponge for his ability. If you are running Four of a Kind on your characters, one character is getting +4 of a stat while another is getting +24.The game is very linear. You have an open-world map, but you are still mostly locked into doing things in a certain order. Each chapter is a new map area with a fixed number of story elements to be done in a certain order. There is no leveling, your character gets stronger through gear and unlocking passive traits via the card system. Ultimately this is fine and doesn't detract much from the game, but it's an RPG element that I wished was present.Loading screens took longer the more I played, I had to quit and restart the game to get them back down. Annoying, but not a deal-breaker.Ultimately, I felt that this game was absolutely worth the price. The combat is fun, the animations are good, the story is interesting (though a little limited), and there are a lot of different ways to approach combat to achieve the best results. Overall I'd give it 8.5/10 and I'm hoping for some good DLC content for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard to review.I cursed it in equal measures as I loved it.The best: not just another iteration of number based squad combatThe worst: some of the things that others don't do by designThere are 6 characters in the game - which isn't much compared to other games like it. You don't even get to field all of them since for some arcane reason only 4 go into any fight. The other two just play with themselves, I guess.Who you pick for a fight doesn't matter much since they all use the same equipment anyways and the equivalent of leveling or promoting is done via cards - which you can assign and take back arbitrarily.You get the cards for meeting challenges in the missions which is one the best and worst features. A challenge of "kill x enemies in the first turn" can be fun or impossible depending which charcter hold which cards and weapon when you start the mission. And you start the mission without knowing who is going to start on which spot.That whole beat-challenges-to-get-cards should mean that you either have multiple chances to get a card or that you can replay a mission. Unless you count starting over, there is no way to go back.By that time it doesn't really matter anymore that you can't shake the feeling that the voicelines were written by a toddler and phoned in by the VA without context. No other way to explain the delivery or content of some of the lines.What I am really torn about is the length. About 18 missions, give or take a few? If it had been twice as many, would it have become just another chore? Or is it too short to get really into it?It is deeply flawed but also pretty enjoyable

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game with some lovely writing in a nicely realised setting.   The Wild West with a twist has been done before - but i think this is a very nice version and follows on from the story of the original and adds to the lore of the setting.Gameplay wise its a mix of a map to wander around to interact with locations to start dialogues, shops or combat missions.  The combat itself is a nice blend of XCom style gameplay with a couple of tweaks.  3 Actions points instead of 2 gives a quicker flow to the combat as pistols / shotguns only take 2 points to fire - only rifles need all 3.  The other major tweak is more akin to Gears Tactics.  A kill resets your action points - so its all about chaining kills allowing your to clear rooms in 1 turn. The 6 characters are nice and different and there unique ablilites can synergise well with certain combos.  4 characters at a time in combat, so missions require a certain character.The final thing carried over from the first game is the poker cards, these are used to give characters new perks and upgrade their ability by creating different poker hands as you find the cards.All in all I've thoroughly enjoyed my play through.

_childDocuments_.review: is one of those deeply niche experiences that I never thought would get a sequel, but I'm happy that it did.  Unusually, this time-conscious sequel isn't content to simply be "more ," but also doubles down on some design decisions from the first game and abandons others to create a thoroughly disparate game experience despite having the same art design and world, likely owing to the franchise being adapted by new developers, Ice Code Games.Unfortunately, this iteration is something of a "two steps forward, one step back" affair.   was already a very cleanly designed game, and  doubles down on "gamey" elements not entirely to its own success.The DNA that  shares with its predecessor is considerable.  Both games are Wild-West "Firaxis XCOM"-alikes, with the standard isometric tactical gameplay, move-and-shoot actions, and contextual, flankable high-and-low cover that have become  for all games of this pedigree.  The major innovation of the first game, for better or for worse, was the "Luck Pool," a kind of shield that could be depleted either by activating various magical abilities or by being shot at.  More likely-to-hit shots (like, say, a shotgun flank at extreme close range) would deplete more luck and allow a character to take damage and die, where less-likely shots (like pistols behind cover at extreme distance) would barely tickle the luck pool, leaving the character's health safe.In this way,  was a very nonrandom, "gameable" tactics game, with exact and telegraphed outcomes where the player need never fuss with randomized chance-to-hit.  I liked this, but it did render the strategy of the first game somewhat simplistic and very non-simulationist by tactics game standards, with the only "messy" part of the first game's design being its massive array of gimmicky firearms with different gameplay effects.Playing  as a veteran of the first one, some of the first changes I noticed were that the firearms array was considerably more streamlined, and the logic of Luck has been retooled entirely: now, XCOM's "chance to hit" is back, in 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% increments, but Luck is used  not just to use special character abilities, but also to 'rig' shots to guarantee that they'll always hit.  This is a stark departure from the first game where Luck was used  to prevent characters from getting shot, and makes the gameplay cadence of this game much more aggressive than its predecessor, something which is reinforced by several characters getting gameplay bonuses when they're out of cover and exposed.  It's a design philosophy which mimics the development of Firaxis' own  to : both sequels seem to have independently come to the conclusion that players will only attempt the strictly optimal strategy of inching up the board only taking shots from full cover if given the chance, and so took different mitigating strategies to force players to act aggressively.Where  opted for strict mission turn limits,  doubles down on its 'get out of cover and get more accurate shooting' gameyness by having a system called 'Bravado.'  'Bravado' allows a character to immediately regain their full activation upon killing an enemy, further reinforcing the intended aggressive playstyle.  However, the game is  balanced around players mastering this feature: enemy counts throughout the game are  compared to the first , with some missions pitting the player against an initial onslaught of up to 15 foes all of whom have similar damage profiles and health pools to the player's own characters.  Strategic use of Bravado to thin the herd is often the  thing that can prevent the player from getting completely dumpstered in the very first enemy turn, giving  a very prescriptive, very intentional, and very limited gameplay loop compared to the first game, one that often veers entirely out of the tactics genre and straight into doing geometry puzzles.  I found this extremely mechanical, 'playing the systems' game loop to be interesting enough to compel me through the game, but it's very different from the first title and I can see why more devoted fans of the tactics-strategy and tactics-RPG genres would feel that this is too much of a departure.The rest of the game is something of a wash compared to its predecessor.  The story and characters are better than the first game, but are still fairly bare-bones when compared to tactics-RPGs like the  franchise, although whether this is a necessary consequence of 's approachable length is a matter one could discuss.  The art style is more appealing than the first game's, in my opinion: it's mostly the same style in the same low-fi engine, but features more diverse environments and color choices with less 'let's just slather an old west boomtown in gore and pentagrams and call it a day' laziness.  Lastly, the soundtrack is unfortunately a huge step down, substituting in generic, unobtrusive "Wild Westy" motifs to replace Marcin Przybylowicz's powerful Mad-Max-meets-Ennio-Morricone bombast from the first game.At the end of the day, I'd say that like its predecessor,  is a game that you can probably safely skip unless you're a tactics game junkie or looking for material within the underserved horror-western genre niche.  It's more polished than the first , but some of the janky character of that game has rubbed off in the process, leaving a very polished game that's nevertheless more of a horse-drawn carriage than a freight train.  An "interesting 7/10" title that would be best purchased on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever find yourself standing in line at a bank or a grocery store, and having imaginary gunfights play out in your head? That lady reaching into her purse is clearly about to try to hold up the place, so you need to dive over the counter and grab the 9mm taped to the back of the register, but first you need to throw this can of peaches at the lookout... No? Just me? Well, if it's not just me; I think Hard West 2 may be the game for you. So here's my hot take: Hard West 2 isn't "Cowboy Xcom". Sure, there's some shared DNA with a grid based movement system, action points, and even some very similar mechanics (the game's signature 'bravado' system is basically what happens if you use serial/ reaper in XCom). However, besides the above I think it actually has far more in common with games like Desperado's 3, Shadow Tactics, or even cult favourite Into the Breach. Calling this 'Cowboy XCom' is selling this incredible title short and I would easily describe this as one of my favourite games of the year. So much of Hard West 2 is figuring out that combination of 'start with person X, open with ability X to hurt mob A, so that person Y can catch a bunch of people with a shotgun blast and 'bravado' into another set of actions...'. In this way, the game feels more like a gorgeous rube goldberg machine, waiting for you to see through it's various steps to chain together these perfect gunfights. While I'm sure you could just play this as a straightforward 'move into cover, take shots, receive shots, rinse and repeat' style of game, it's clear that so much of the game revolves on this idea of 'staged' set pieces and being aggressive to snap one combo into another. Something I absolutely love about Hard West 2 are the characters. I know some people were really down on games like Chimera squad for having set characters with personalities and stories as opposed to 'being able to make their own heroes out of random PCs', but I've never agreed with it. Making set characters, means making backgrounds, and getting voice actors, and maybe even writing a real coherent story that isn't just procedurally generated fight after procedurally generated fight. Between the set dressing, the voice acting (admittedly, some characters feel so much more grandiose than others), the story, and the character design; I think Hard West 2 did a really good job of giving you characters to fall in love with, and cheering them on as they get their revenge. The mechanical choices the game presents you with are also really interesting. Aside from bravado being the way in which you’ll chain one characters kills into a full set of action points, is ‘luck’. Famously, the XCom series is notorious for presenting players with a ‘75% chance of success’ which seems to fail about 100% of the time which can be really frustrating in a game where so much of your choices/ abilities hinge on setting up that chain of dominos that need to go one after the other. To offset this, Hard West 2 uses a luck mechanic where you can spend points of luck to make up the difference in your chance to hit. If you have a 25% chance to hit, but 75 luck points; you can swing that up to 100%. Inversely, shooting at someone with a 75% chance to hit (without spending luck) and missing grants you that amount of luck for future turns. It means that while missing someone you had a 75% chance to hit is a little frustrating, but knowing that it sets you up with 75 luck points for later use to maybe guarantee a hit makes it worthwhile. It even makes it worth trying for those long-shot 25% attacks, because you either get a little luck (always handy), or maybe you hit; which is a gamble we wouldn’t normally take in Xcom. Speaking of mechanics, I think Hard West 2 may also be the first tactics game I’ve played to incorporate the use of moving maps. I absolutely loved every mission involving a train, just because it was really novel to try navigating a racing landscape while bullets were traded. It’s just a really novel thing and it makes me wish for so much more from this series. Ricochets to get around cover is also a really novel addition, and again makes your characters just feel like absolute bad asses. The last amazing thing I wanted to mention was the levelling/ talent system. Giving you the opportunity to build poker hands to define character abilities is both thematic, and really interesting from a gameplay perspective. It is a design choice that encourages players to try different playstyles without penalty, as compared to choosing abilities that are locked in for characters; which in turn means that the challenges of each map don’t have to stick with ‘Hope you brought Flynn and gave her talent X, or you’re just not going to be able to do this level’. Instead the game throws open its missions and goes ‘I don’t know, you figure out how to solve this’. Alright, so that’s a lot of gushing. There are still some things about this which could be better/ might make this less of a ‘must buy’ for some. The first is that this definitely is more of a puzzle game than a tactics game. I think Xcom veterans may find themselves put out by the 4D chess nature of the game, where you have to plan turns several steps ahead in order to make it through the fights. If you’re someone who gets frustrated at not finding the ‘perfect’ solution to a fight, Hard West 2 is likely to be very frustrating to you. Personally, I enjoyed the back and forth of reloading fights to try to find that perfect sequence, but I can see that getting frustrating. My hat goes off to those of you who are ironman enthusiasts because I think this game may make that way too hard. To be fair to Hard West 2, I think the UI does a pretty good job of showing this when you’re considering which space to move to; but it doesn’t do such a great job when you’re going to use an ability (like Flynn’s shadow step). A fix for this could be an undo button that only trips on abilities (as opposed to shots where someone might want to see if they get a crit or not). Fights in Hard West 2 are pre-designed as opposed to being procedurally generated, which for me means that they generally all felt special and grand, but I can see how people who enjoyed the style of serial combat from XCom, Fire Emblem, or Wildermyth might find themselves put out by how staged Hard West 2 is. It means the replayability of Hard West 2 will suffer, but for a game that is priced around the $30 price point; that’s not a bad price for a game with a great story. (Put another way, you’d likely spend $30 watching the latest Thor with friends, and I think Hard West delivers a far more engaging story over its 30-40 hours of gameplay). All in all; Hard West 2 is easily one of my favourite games of 2022. The core gameplay is tense and rewarding, the story and characters have charm and personality, and I so want to see more of this world should a Hard West 3 (or even a DLC) be in the making. So round up your posse, check your irons, and get ready to yell ‘Hoka Hey Mother f***er!’.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West II isn't really a turn-based tactics game. It's more a puzzle game where the player manages movement, action points, and damage to clear screens of enemies. Teleport or move around enemies and it's fairly easy to get a 100% chance to hit, you do a fixed amount of damage per weapon, and as long as you can figure out how to kill one enemy you get all your action points back for that character. It's very predictable. Some people may think that is fun, but I prefer more realistic tactics that incorporate uncertainty and risk management. XCOM 2 does the best job of this of all turn-based tactics games I know, followed by Jagged Alliance 3. I'd recommend one of those other games instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 is a very unique and enjoyable turn based strategy game. There are a lot of alternatives in the genre, but a lot of them are so close to X-Com that you are usually better off just playing X-Com instead. HW2 does enough of it's own things to be a truly unique experience instead. Instead of base management there is light RPG exploration. Instead of cloned generic self-inserts there is a party of pre-built characters with their own personalities. Instead of leveling along some skill trees you build hands out of poker cards that unlock (significant, playstyle altering) perks. They can also be reshuffled for every mission so you can tailor your loadout to every mission. Instead of randomized generic maps every encounter is handcrafted. There are also significant changes to the "standard" TBS battle formular as well. You have 3 instead of 2 action points and weapons and skills that range from 1 to 3AP, so your default action every turn is not just move and shoot. It's usually worth thinking about every game turn instead of just moving from cover to cover shooting. That is emphasized by the mechanic that every kill completely refills your AP gauge. If setup correctly this can lead to dozens of dead enemies in a single turn. As if this all wasn't enough, there is also a unique mechanic for RNG. Everytime you miss or get hit you accrue "luck points" which you can later spend on making difficult hits of your own guaranteed. Oh and you can bounce off shots of the environment, to really bend your mind with possible options sometimes...Since the party is so powerful with all these mechanics, the game's difficulty was tuned to really force you to make use of all of these systems to the fullest too. The release version was tuned absolutely brutally, with seemingly little margin for error in some instances. A beta patch has since been released that downtuned a lot of the most critical aspects quite a bit. I played the last third of the game with the beta patch and it still wasn't a walk in the park however. I believe with the beta patch the game balance is quite well hit. If they tune it back up a tiny bit it'll be nailbiting while still very doable again. Overall I really enjoyed the game. I played X-Com, I don't need to play X-Com again with a different skin. HW2 is a tight, well crafted, not overly long experience (~25 hours). If you like TBS game but don't believe every game should be exactly like X-Com, buy the game. Just don't expect X-Com: Western Edition.

_childDocuments_.review: The first Hard West I thought was extremely fun.  Unfortunately, the previous developing company left that game a broken mess.  The enemies would get stuck clipping on the environment making them infinitely walk in place without completing their turn. This forced you to restart and lose your progress only for it to happen again and again.  The forums were littered with posts about this but it fell on deaf ears and I was never able to complete the game.  When Hard West 2 was announced I was reserved to say the least and thought they had some nerve releasing a 2nd title after how they left their customers in the dark from the first game.  I noticed the developing company was under a different name now.  I don't know if HW2 is  completely new people or just a name change, but seeing that and also hearing good reviews from people that actually played the game, I figured I would give it a shot.I'm having a blast, this game is fun.  It runs smoothly for me, solid 144fps at max settings, no hiccups.  Each character has special traits that you unlock through your relationships with them via dialogue choices throughout the adventure, as well as a pretty robust and interchangeable character "leveling" system through the use of playing cards.  This allows you to fine tune the parties traits and special abilities that also will complement the loadouts you gear them with.  This is not a puzzle game and it's really evident that well known review outlets, since some of them used that term, everyone else just keeps regurgitating it back up as if they're saying that it's not really a strategy game.  That's simply not true.  The poker hand system opens up decisions on who you take in the group and how their traits and abilities will play out.  You unlock cards as you progress and each character can hold five cards.  The better the hand you give them going by traditional poker rules, the more powerful their traits and abilities become.  This can be interchanged as many times as you like between battles to mold your selected party into how you want each character to play and synergize.The luck mechanic should be managed by toggling it off and on when necessary, using it for only the most risky shots, or to activate a powerful character trait in later turns.  This is how you get the most out of it and not to be left as some passive thing that you ignore.  The entire luck system is built around taking risky shots, getting shot at, missing your own shots, or banking your luck points until a certain threshold to activate powerful character trait.  This is not a *complete in one turn or you take damage and have to restart* type of game. This is why there are plenty of healing items, characters that are more powerful the lower their health is, or characters that transfuse blood to heal the group or become more powerful when another party member dies, etc.  Calling this a "puzzle" game as if to diminish it's worth in the genre of turn-based strategy is really a disservice to the game, the genre, the potential players that missed out because they listened to your lazy review, and your reputation as a review outlet.  To everyone else that's curious, the game is excellent.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, this game exceeded all my expectations. It captivated me with its uniqueness and immediately after the tutorial I was completely immersed in the world of Hardy West. I think that the first and foremost thing that deserves to be appreciated is the combat system. It's very enjoyable and intuitive, and each battle makes you want more. I really like using Bravado to make epic compos on enemies.  The last time I felt such satisfaction from a turn-based game was when I played Heroes 3, so after such a long time I thankfully lived to see a worthy successor. The world in which everything is set is a real masterpiece - the combination of the wild west with esotericism, magic and superpowers definitely got me. The dialogues, along with the plot, are very polished, and I'm constantly so curious that I want to go into every possible interaction to learn more details of the whole story. I also love the comic videos, which go very well with the atmosphere of the game. I feel like this game combines elements from some of the best iconic games and merges them to create something so unique and impressive that every video game fan should play it. I love it and can't wait to play more!

_childDocuments_.review: A nice sequel to the occult western original, with new mechanics and ideas. The bravado system (full action point refund on kills) and the lack of overwatch makes for an aggressive play, and turns many combat scenarios into a puzzle game, where one mistake can be fatal. Character traits unlocked by hands formed by the accumulated cards is another fun addition. Finally, you can save literally anywhere and anytime, plus the game provides several auto save and quick save slots. It's crazy that such a basic feature is to be praised these days.One of the mistakes I often run into with games like this is that I tend to strive for "no injury" play. Funny thing is the tutorial puts you in a position where this cannot be achieved. And you really shouldn't want to waste time for it, except in those combat scenarios, where the secondary goal is to finish it in 1 turn. The reason is you can heal the whole party for $20 after battles, and there's a ton of money in the game.I've finished the game on Nightmare+, which was a good, honest challenge. On Easy it's probably a walk in the park and a chilling experience, so I recommend it to anyone who likes turn-based tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutly recommend the game; it fixes common problems with the genre.Even tho the combat is turn based, the system that allows you to refresh your actions by killing an enemy makes combats feel action packed and very exciting.I also ususally dislike games where you have a certain chance to hit with attacks. However in this game it is very easy to get 100% chance to hit; either with the luck system, or ricochets and good positioning.My only complaints are that imo nightmare mode makes no sense without save-scumming (you have a round limit but everything has 90% chance to hit, meaning that if you mess up the chance once the round limit might be impossible to beat); and so far I only have 1 unique ability for every party member. _childDocuments_.review: A slightly unconventional squad level turn based strategy that depends upon a different set of constraints compared to others in the genre. That can either mean "A breath of fresh air" or "Bad because it's not what you're used to" depending on what you look for in a game.The main mechanic that changes play is that killing an enemy refunds your action points, essentially giving the killing unit an extra turn. This makes it possible for your small team to beat many times their number by chaining kills to scythe through much bigger forces, but also that you'll be wiped off the face of the map by enemies that outnumber you if you don't do a good job of setting up and executing chains.It's a little less random than some other games in the genre because it offers the ability to mitigate dice rolls. When you miss you gain "luck" equal to the chance to hit and when you attack you can spend it to raise your chance to hit up to 100% (at a 1:1 ratio) so a character who only takes 95% percent shots will only miss once per level because that miss will give them 95 luck and turning all future shots into 100% sure things costs 5 luck a time. Some players enjoy that thier strategy matters more than good dice, others find the game feels too puzzly because actions having deterministic results makes it feel like there's a single right answer (There isn't, there are videos of people playing the same level different ways, but emotionally it feels like there is).There's a fair effort to make the different characters feel unique. Their personalities are fairly generic but the weird west setting affords the chance to give abilities that set them apart in terms of how they're used. A witch teleporting friends and enemies. A zombie exploding bullets from his body doing damage based on how much damage he's taken. A priest swapping health totals and statuses with enemies. There are six in total though you can only use four in a mission and it's easy to gravitate to a favourite four with the others not being of much use.The battles themselves also have a fair bit of variety. You'll hit all of the trope staples: Ambushes, bank robberies, train heists and so on. Enemies are given schticks you need to play around that make them feel more varied than "Gun guy" "Gun guy with hat" "Gun guy with slightly bigger gun" which is a blessing and a curse. Some players find they hit a difficulty cliff when a new enemy with a massive difference in kind shows up, on the other hand it does make fights in later chapters feel legitimately different to earlier chapters rather than being the same thing with bigger numbers.The rest of the game is there to bolt the fight sequences together and it works well enough. None of the writing is going to blow you away and the side quests aren't incredible, but nothing is bad enough to be distracting and it's nice to have a breather between action sequences.It could use a bit of quality of life work. The loading times are longer than other games in the genre and there are annoyances like no "quit to desktop" button necessitating a loading screen to bring up the menu so you can tell it to quit. There are a few weird UI choices which make it possible to make accidental moves until you get used to them. It's all minor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥* and the sort of thing that'll hopefully be patched over the next few month.Overall, it's a good game if you like this sort of thing. Hope you have fun :)* Spelled enn eye gee gee ell ee ess, defined as "a trivial criticism, discomfort, or annoyance." and having no history of use as either a curse word or a slur. Chill out censorbot.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 is a tactics RPG set in a supernatural version of the Wild West, where a failed train robbery results in Gin Carter and his gang of outlaws chasing a devil to reclaim Gin’s stolen soul.•	Combat is turn based, and if you’ve played Xcom or other similar tactics games, you should be familiar with the basics of Hard West. Each map is divided into a square grid, and your party of four characters have action points to move, attack, activate special abilities, and use items such as medkits and dynamite.•	Enemies include living and undead bandits, demons, witches and wendigos. Most enemies will attack with either guns or melee weapons, while some have magical abilities to heal or summon minions.•	Companions can equip two weapons, including different varieties of pistols, shotguns, rifles, and melee weapons, which have different stats for damage and range.•	Walls and other environmental objects can provide half or full cover, which reduces the hit chance of an incoming attack. Missing a shot will give a character luck, which increases their chance to hit the next attack, preventing long miss streaks.•	Many ranged weapons can perform trick shots, where you deflect the bullet off a metal object like a barrel, lantern, or sign, to bend the shot around cover. Enemies can do this too, which caught me out several times.•	Each companion has a powerful special ability allowing them to fire through cover and hit multiple nearby enemies, run long distances and deal bonus damage for each tile moved, swap places with an enemy to get them out of cover, or heal by swapping their health bar with an enemy.•	In most missions you’ll be heavily outnumbered, but every time one of your party kills an enemy, their action points are fully restored, allowing them to move and attack again on the same turn. This means that each encounter becomes almost like a puzzle where you try to work out how to chain together as many kills as possible on your turn. For example, you could move one character to a position where a shotgun blast will hit multiple enemies, then have someone else finish them off one at a time with a pistol.•	The only thing that I didn’t like about combat is the absence of overwatch, which I tend to use a lot in other similar tactics games, however I suppose this did force me to use the other tricks and abilities more often.•	Completing quests and bonus objectives will reward you with playing cards numbered 9 to ace of each suit. Equipping companions with poker hands will increase their movement speed, damage, health, and luck, and level up their special abilities. You don’t draw these cards during combat like a deckbuilder, they’re just equipped like a ring or necklace in an RPG.•	In addition to the main quest, you’ll find side quests while exploring the world map. These might involve hunting outlaws to collect their bounties, or helping civilians with other problems. While main quest missions almost always lead to combat, side quests are mostly text based, and you might have to make a decision about how to complete the quest.•	I played on hard difficulty, which is the middle of 5 options. This was challenging but not frustrating. Some of my companions got knocked out during missions, but I was able to make consistent progress. The AI is quite good. Enemies never made any stupid moves and I often had to spend a few minutes on my turn trying to figure out where to move to hit them without leaving myself exposed.•	Story is simple but entertaining.•	I didn’t play the previous game so I don’t know if the story is related to those events, but I didn’t feel like I missed anything.•	Some quests feature dialogue choices, but they don’t seem to change the story at all. The only difference relates to which companions you agree with, which gives them loyalty points leading to some passive combat bonuses.•	Voice acting is good, but only some lines of dialogue are voiced, with the rest being text only.•	It took me 23 hours to complete the story and most side quests.•	I didn’t have any problems with crashes, bugs or framerate.Hard West 2 is a great game which fans of turn based tactics games should enjoy. There’s enough content to buy at full price or a small sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it!Hard West II is a game that lives and dies on it's comparison to the big boys in the genre. Like tatical RPGs, An x-com style shooter tactics game needs something to stand out, And boy does hard west II stand out. The bravado mechanic is one of my favorite additions to the genre I have ever played. A lot of shooter tactics require slow methodical play. A good plan and defense are often the best option for any x-com level, but in hard west, because you regain actions by killing units playing aggressively is not just as viable, but more viable than defensive play.Outside of that the game has just a general level of polish in visual and gameplay design. Outside of one specific level, there was no other levels in 30+ levels that I would say is bad gameplay wise, and there are no visually bad levels outside of few confusing moments about multistory buildings.The voice work and sound design is probably the weakest part of the entire package. The sounds and enemy quips are extremely repetitive, it's completely arbitrary what lines are and aren't voiced in the over-world. There is a lot of repeated voice actors across multiple characters, or a few of the voice actors sounded a like so I got confused during some of the voiced scenes.The story at it's core is serviceable, it's a good enough vessel for some fun character interactions, but some of the major beats in the story seem to come out of nowhere. Not in a bad twist kind of way, just in a no mention of it until it happens kind of way. Neither of these points make it a bad game, it's like store bought frosting on a gourmet cake. The cake is still good, the frosting isn't bad. It just could be better. I liked it.

_childDocuments_.review: So, just beat the game first time through on Hard, which is basically the normal setting. Feels like no matter what you choose, the next sequence of events is going to happen regardless. It's also true that much of the game play itself feels like a giant puzzle. Each battle is essentially a series of enemies that you have to figure out the most efficient way to defeat. There's not much tactics to it besides figuring out which of your team's abilities to use and in what order. But, if you like puzzle after puzzle, this game is good. And it does have that occult old west feel of the original game, which is a cool motif, even if it is a bit less well delivered this time around. Still, if you can get this game for like $10, $15 bucks, go for it. It's a decently fun way to spend around 40 hrs of play.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a massive fan of the original Hard West. Sure, its not the most polished or even the most balanced XCOM clone you can get on the market, but i found it very charming, a fun story and beat it twice. Hard West 2 takes several steps forward in the gameplay department and is a general improvement on its predecessor. It is the sugar rush of XCOM, promoting super aggressive plays to link turns together, and while its abit slow at the start, once you get your full posse and a few playing cards, things get really fast really quick. Many missions are fun, fast and rewarding, and the over-world elements and side-missions were fun to do, and had cool unlocks in them. The gameplay again is not the most balanced (stacking Crit on Laughing Deer was very OP) but as with the first game, I think the players themselves could balance the game if they wanted too. Now, there are a few things I miss: I understand the focus on a single posse and its story, but I would have loved them to keep the same style of storytelling they did last time, with several stories interlinking into each other and creating a grander narrative. The Music is not as good as the first game, but that is subjective. I also wish you could change or get new powers for your posse, since a few felt much stronger then others. Nitpicks aside, I really enjoyed this game, and I do recommend it. I also recommend the original Hard West, because that game is solid as well.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a HARD PASS for me. I can't recommend Hard West 2. Here is why:  The mechanics are really wonky, there is no over-watch, the gun damage is weak. They expect you to try to make trick shots all over the place, whereby you aim at a object so the bullet bounces off of it and hits an enemy behind cover. I could see this as a special ability, but it's annoying that you have to plan your whole movement strategy behind having to make this trick shots every round. Not realistic... and annoying. ALSO there really isn't multiple ways to win each map. It's more like you have to plan your route perfectly, and if you make one mistake, you get worn down by the end of the map and then you end up in a NO WIN situation. After all that hard work you are forced to just scratch the round and start over... 20-30 minutes wasted... it's annoying. PUNISHING: If you like starting over and over and like punishing games that require exact precision to your decisions with 0 room for error, then you might dig this game. But it's not for me. My time is valuable and I like to play games that have a little forgiveness and opportunity for recovery if you make a bad move. I mean I like a challenge, but one or two wrong moves and your party is done for.   THE CAMERA: The camera is very annoying, hard to zoom up and down and try to determine the best view. Not digging it. STORY: The story/plot is weird and honestly feels just super far fetched and uninteresting on top of that. I just couldn't get into this weird evil spirit theme in a western genre game. It's just not my cup of tea. It's a shame because I love Xcom 2, Pheonix Point, and King Arthur: Knight's Tale and overall games in this genre. I was really looking forward to this game too as I LOVE Red Dead Redemption. But after 5 hours i'm just finding the game to be frustrating and the story to be boring. Along with that I'm not digging the system. WHAT I DID LIKE: The graphics, art and characters are well designed and the idea of combining poker cards for bonuses is a great idea! The overall sound, music, and voice overs sounded great. Final verdict: 1 / 5 I wish they would have done a more traditional western story. I might have been able to get into that a little more. But then again they need to revamp the game play a lot to be more fun, realistic and less punishing.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played both HW & HW2, I have to say the second is a big upgrade and a welcome addition to my library. To start I would play this game on hard, I think after the first patch it is balanced in terms of difficulty. The game is split into 2 game styles; outdoor exploration with some decision making events, discovery, and story telling. The second part is the actual combat, many people downplay this part but it is actually quite fun. Yes it does drill down to a puzzle combat system. You rely on chaining kills to regain action points, this means organizing your team of 4's actions to best clear off the map and protect your team. It can be unforgiving at times but once you start to understand it adds a layer to combat vs. other traditional strategy games. Character customization is excellent you can equip a variety of weapons, consumables, trinkets to your team. Characters have unique skills however a few are more powerful than others right now (you can figure that out yourself). The game also uses a unique skill unlock system using a deck of cards to make hands, I found this part of the game well fleshed out. Overall the characters are all compelling and the story is above average. I would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to enjoy that game but I just feel that it provides more puzzle gameplay than turn-based tactics, and there is no real variability to make real fun of game mechanics. I've covered my points in a short video review and will provide main points below. I'll start with the good part - visuals and story. In general, I enjoyed both storytelling and visual style, with the exception for the world map which looks pretty mediocre. Also, I enjoyed that idea with card combinations for unlock of skills for characters. I cannot say that is really great system because till you are limited with cards some heroes just get PAIR combination so they are much less efficient but in general, I liked that idea. And also the Luck system (you get Luck if you miss, get damage, and in some other situation) - allows to slightly mitigate random which is pretty cool.Other things in slightly more details:1) Main feature, BRAVADO - ability to regain full action points upon getting a kill. From one point, in some situations, it is really impressive to get those 5+ kills in a row. From another point, when you have a solid amount of enemies (and in that game you have many of them all the time) - you just feel a lack of variability. Maps are small and in most scenarios, there are not many options to deal with each fight with enemies. If we add to this enemies that are not one-shot, there are a big amount of situations where you will put your heroes in strange positions just to try to get the BRAVADO streak. And if you fail to do it due to a mistake or miss by a shot - pretty likely that you will get a crazy amount of damage. Developers in the latest patch deleted time limits on 2 first difficulties so that shall not be an issue but even without time limit fights don't feel like positional tactical play, more like a puzzle where you try to guess the perfect combination.2) Loyalty system. When you make some choices in the game you will get loyalty points to one of the heroes who have a similar vision to you. But this system is directly linked with a few core passive perks for each hero. As a result, you make choice based on the character you want to upgrade and not your opinion on the situation. That totally breaks atmosphere.3) No overwatch and attack on an opportunity. Not every game needs this but without those features, I just feel that game loses its tactical potential. The game becomes strongly focused on Bravado spam and I wouldn't say that is really satisfying thing.4) Only one special ability for each hero. While they are unique and strong, strategies are just too obvious and after 5-10 hours I don't think that may be really interesting to use the same skills (while with progression they become stronger, I wouldn't say there is a game-breaking difference upon progression).As a result, the game may be interesting for those who finished all other recent tactical games and need some puzzle-style gameplay, for those people max difficulty is a good way to go. For those who have not really much time to play - I would recommend to try other recent titles like Expeditions: Rome, Chaos Gate, and latest Pathfinder - those games feel like a more engaging experience for me.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like turn-based strategy and enjoy spending time on EVERY SINGLE move, this is a good game.This game encourages a new concept called Bravado, which could regen all your Action Points when you kill an enemy! So, the more Bravado you can do, the lesser the enemies would hit you.  Also,  the chain of Bravado becomes very important since the hardest difficulty limited you to complete the mission within a number of turns.People do suggest Dev to implement an Undo for the last move which is pretty essential in my opinion. Since the combo of moves to achieve Bravado is the key to win this game, I did 'Save-load' pretty often to see every attempt did work. so, if you can manage the hard difficult with maximizing Bravado approach, you can manage the hardest difficult (nightmare) the same way.Since the enemies are almost the same throughout the game, people would find this game is very difficult at the early to mid-missions and you cannot not grind anything to help; however, this game would become easy on the later missions since you almost got all the perks in the game but dealing with the same kinds of enemies. _childDocuments_.review: Really wanted to enjoy this game and the demo was amazing.  Gameplay was so solid,  characters were great, atmosphere, soundtrack, all of it was awesome.  However, the game after that becomes such a chore to play that I just can't recommend it.  I'm playing the game on Hard which is really Normal and it is insanely difficult.  It's not hard because it makes you think too much, it's hard because the odds are just so stacked against you that it becomes not fun to play.  Missing RNG checks ruins your entire turn, at that point you might as well just save scum it because that one turn will likely kill your character or bring 2 down to one shot and then at that point you have lost the mission.  Everybody saying "Oh get good dude!" I don't want to have to be a genius, a lucky one at that, to enjoy a game.  I want to have fun after work not sit at the game and stress after playing for an hour and not actually winning anything, that isn't fun at all. _childDocuments_.review: Super on the fence about this one.  If you were a fan of the first one or you're a big fan of the genre, you'll probably like this one too.  If not, you won't be missing much by passing.Pros:- Great setting.  I'd love a TTRPG game set in this universe.- The luck mechanic and information about when you'll be moving into a square where you can get 100% accuracy on an enemy is good.  It's not like XCOM where you have to just give your best guess about whether you can even fire off a shot at the enemy.Cons:- Not a lot of depth to the combat.  It consists of just figuring out a broken combo or two and repeating that on every single map.  For me it was having Bill shoot everyone in his field of view for enough damage to get them below the threshold where they could be killed in one round, and send Laughing Deer running around the map in a giant bravado chain.  Worse, if you want to get the achievements for finishing missions in a certain number of rounds, you HAVE to do this.- Characters, quests, and story all also lack depth.  Especially compared to the first Hard West.- Very short.  Around 5 hours of my playtime was when I had to run off and take care of something and left the game running, so 15 hours from start to finish, and no real replay value.I'm still giving it a thumbs up because I enjoyed the game despite its flaws, but I realize I'm not really selling the game here.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice strategy game that falls into the Tactics genre.  It should in no way be advertised as a RPG any more than Fallout tactics was many years ago. It has some nice mechanics like cards that you deal out to characters, trinkets and character perks as well as bullet bouncing, several status effects and ultimate abilities. It's easy to see how casual players get bogged down in all this, but on the flipside it can be extremely easy when you create broken builds with bill deleting everything on the screen on a low/high max health and Deer able to move across the map in a turn mopping up any survivors. This inevitably makes missions fairly boring after a while even with it putting you on horses. The addition of trying to complete missions in as little as a single turn may add replayability for tactics fans, but it also sucks the fun out of just enjoying the game, especially when you realise you need to reload old saves just to swap things about because 3/4 characters are stuck on horses.For hard west 3 I think the developers should stick to adding in more fun, customisation, dark humour, character depth and less turn constrained chess style tactics or label it as Hard West tactics so it is clear to buyers.

_childDocuments_.review: Long story short; I like everything around the game, except for the actual gameplay. Tediousness =/= Difficulty**EDIT** Finally finished the game. No wonder these devs resorted to such underhanded "anti-player" methods, it's short as hell. My review below still stands, heck I think I hate it more after the grueling unfairness of the last few levels. I need a real tactics game to cleanse my palate now **EDIT OVER**I have to preface this by saying that I've played lots of Tactics game ever since my PS1 days. I've played good Tactics games and I've played bad ones. And honestly I feel like this one is part of the latter. It's a shame because this game has some pretty good stuff like lots of voice acting and stellar theme direction, but the balance of the gameplay is horrible imo.I get the feeling that these developers come from the school of "if a lot of players can ace a level, then you're doing something wrong". There's a lot of "anti-player" mechanics prevalent all over the place. They frequently force you to rush levels by enforcing strict timers, all the while funnelling you into tight sections where enemies spawn out of nowhere to ambush your chars on their turn. Another thing is they use what I call the "Fixed RNG" mechanic, where your characters are already "set" to either MISS or HIT a shot no matter how many times you save scum, not that you want to once you realise LOADING TIMES are ATROCIOUS. Regardless, save scumming should be a personal choice to make a game easier from players that want to use them, and taking that choice AWAY from players just adds to the school of mentality that I mentioned earlier. Other things that are "anti-player" also include stuff like mooks having boss-like abilities like healing to full health on their turn, or able to swap HP with your characters so that they heal while damaging you. It's fine if these enemies are few and far in between but this game has them for every level. There's scarcely a level where you just mow down regular mooks for fun. All this while you're doing piddly amounts of 4-9 damage to their sometimes 30+ HP.All of this just boils down to levels being tedious to finish, which is why people say its like a puzzle. If you don't follow the specific few sequence of moves and know where and what enemy you'll be up against, finishing a level leaves you poorer off because did I mention you keep your HP AFTER EVERY FIGHT? Yeah one more thing that's "anti-player". Would've been fine if you also didn't have to fight bosses in mooks clothing every level, or even at least have non-essential battles to farm money/hp in between so that you can prepare yourself. Not like you can overlevel the enemies anyway.Anyways enough rambling, SAVE YOUR MONEY. BUY OR REPLAY X-COM 2
