_childDocuments_.review: Ice Code Games takes up the mantle of Creative Forge's original to bring you Hard West 2. There were some things I enjoyed and other things I feel need to improve. So let's get to it.What I likedPolished: Beautiful Artwork, Voice Overs, and a clean presentation of its concept.Solid Tutorial: Clever way of explaining key factors of game play without putting you through hell (no pun intended)Isometric Hard on: A vast usage of isometric vantage points, with horse riding engagements and smart moving concepts. NiceCamera: Does the job, but could have been better in its implementation. Point and Click: Nice simple straight forward story telling that compliments its art style and story.Aesthetics: Sounds, Controls, Effects, and Music all done with professional execution.Gun-slinging: At its simplistic best. Visuals and Settings: Wonderful usage of visual effects to its story-line and solid difficult settings to challenge you. What I feel needs to improve:Clone: Same version of game one doesn't mean better. A compliment to Creative Forge's original, but not what you should be doing to create a true advanced sequel. 4 vs system: Old, stale, and again another game that brings nothing new to the genre, with newer games giving you warband gameplay, pvp, and expanding mutations of this old chess format. Distance: isometric is boring standard, it keeps you far away from the action. Another developer that did not pay attention to Mordheim or X-com's first and third party perspectives that keep you up close into the action. No point to manually zooming in if the action pushes you back. ShameMechanics: The same as game one with no new fun dynamics added. Duplicate card effects, upgrade system, or equipment doesn't mean you are bringing is something new.Party: Switching characters in a Final Fantasy 4 party mode is boring. You want to introduce playable characters. Then use them all. Expand on your vs enemies. Bigger is better. Blood: If you don't like blood then bring a mop. Final Thoughts: Hard West 2 is a nice comic book. This is not a vast innovative sequel of Hard West, but simply issue 2 of a comic book. Much more powerful Western games you can enjoy than this one dimensional game that must evolve if its going to continue to Hard West 3 one day. That being said, I credit the hard work of making any game to enjoy. Hard West 2 is a fine game of the old west vs the demonic realm, but up against games like Wild Guns and Red Dead Redemption you better up your game. A nice job by this Indy developer that I am sure will improve. Hard West 2 is a nice comic book western tale for turn base lovers. My Score: 3.1 out of 5

_childDocuments_.review: I've re-played and finished HW1 before playing this one just to refresh my memory. So far (3 big missions + 1 small encounter) I'm mostly positive about the game. It's definitely not a solid 10/10 like some people say, but it's MUCH better than first game in terms of gameplay. I'm playing on normal difficulty (which is called "Hard" in this game somehow) and so far I don't see every battle being a puzzle where you have to do everything perfectly or restart the game (unless you go for achievements in which case - yeah, it's almost a puzzle game).++ Better visuals. Obviously. Would be weird if this weren't the case. Textures, character models, interface, special effects - everything looks better and looks good in general. Visuals kind of remind me Wasteland 3.+ One complete story instead of several scenarios with different characters. Works better for me, personally, and, apparently, for most of people too, considering that developers usually also take this path instead of several stories and several protagonists.+ A LOT of QoL changes that make the game feel much better. FINALLY you can speed up the battle which is a necessity for games of this genre. After hours upon hours you probably will want to speed animations up because you already tired of watching them and now, finally, you can do this. You finally can duck behind cover increasing it's effectiveness. Now you can see what all those fancy poker words actually mean. I personally know only pair, two pairs and three/five of a kind, so, in previous game I had to google wth is Flush, Royal flush, Straght, etc. Now you have a button that shows you all possible combinations. And that's only a few examples.+ Game feels easier, in a good way. A lot of cheap things that made previous game difficult were disposed of / changed. For example, enemies don't have an area around them which made them shoot at you if you accidentally get too close anymore. Now you can finally see which enemies you will be able to hit from specific tile and with what percentage. Balance also has been remade making the game easier, faster and overall more pleasant to play.+ Saving during missions. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ finally.+ MUCH better optimisation. Previous game, despite beingmade in 2015, sometimes dropped FPS to 20 and had freezes every time I open inventory. Here everything works perfectly. Loading times obviously take longer, but on SSD game usually loads for around 10-15 seconds which is fine.+ Bravado sound is very good.+ Adequate regional price. I rarely buy games full price, but because of this decided to make an exception.-- Atmosphere completely ruined. HW1 had a dark, brutal, violent and almost depressive world (in first mission ). Here it feels more like a clicheed cartoon wild west story for teenagers. The visual design looks more vivid and colourful, characters behave and say things in a way that makes them look dumb. And that is sad, because from a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sequel of HW1 I was expecting same level of atmosphere which was the strongest point of previous game.- Story is boring. At least so far. In HW1 I quickly became interested in the story and finished the game only to see how it will end. Here? I don't feel even remotely same. Probably because of the previous point.- Voice acting mostly varies from "meh" to "makes me want to mute all voices in the game". In HW1 there was only one VA - Death and he was amazing, exactly what the game needed. Here? I'm mostly fine with Gin and Bill. Cla'lish and Lazarus are excellent. Flynn is a complete miscast. From her looks and abilities, I was expecting her to sound like... I don't know, Raven from Teen Titans? Something more slow, emotionless and quiet. Instead we have a loud "howdy, partner" teenage girl who constantly curses and shouts. Laughing Deer is absolutely horrible to listen to. It sounds like anything, but American Indian. Plus everything he says basically can be downed to "Me dumb, Me want to smash".- Game has serious balance issues.  And these bandages are one-time use and can ONLY be used to heal yourself, you can't use a bandage on one character to heal the other. - Covers still work like ♥♥♥♥, almost like first game.Maybe in future I'll change things, but so far that's how I feel. Funny, that HW1 had amazing atmosphere and story, but horrible, boring and repetitive gameplay. Here it's almost a complete 180, story and atmosphere are "fine" at best, but gameplay finally makes me want to play it instead of download cheat engine to run through it as fast as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't want to give it a downvote, but all-in-all found the game to be "meh".  It's nice enough to scratch the XCOM-itch, but found parts of the game to be far-fetched and/or not fleshed out enough.  Main headscratchers (for me) were:* backstories from squad get unlocked gradually, but don't impact the game at all.. what's the point then?* once you find your 'comfort'-attack squad, there's no incentive/reason to switch with the benched ones.  Only a handful of mission have a mandatory participant.  Maybe introduce fatigue/healing period?* bravado is too broken.  I get that this is the HW2 innovation, but battles just become a puzzle, rather than interactive fight.  Maybe have it only trigger once/twice?* power level of special moves is unbalanced.  Some are too good to bench that squadmember, while others don't really have added value.* don't get why the melee-figther has the same aim as the pistol-expert.  Rather than fixed hit-chances (25-50-75-100%), a bit more RNG and differentiation between characters could maybe help? (or is that X-com talking?) * card system is cute, but not fleshed out enough... not sure on how, but surely improvements should be implemented.   Didn't feel the need to switch-up much between card-combinations. Finished the game (hard) in under 30h and don't really have an urge for a next playthrough.Closing off with a compliment on the visual style though.  Nice work and rooting for a strong 3rd entry of the series!

_childDocuments_.review: Not an easy recommendation.On one hand the game has charm, love the universe but on the other hand it feels like for each strength, there is a weak element.The idea to play aggressively in a tactical is interesting, however it kind of morphs the combats into some sort of puzzle where you're trying (And are encouraged to) to find the perfect combination of actions in the perfect order to kill every enemy and not be hit once, in the minimum number of turns.They got rid of the "reload" action, yay, however I hope you like missing everytime you don't have 100% precision. I know it's a meme in XCOM but here it's so bad that they added an option to reroll the chances when you load your save.Game feels very... limited. The map isnt that big, you dont have that much customization options, it's very bare bones, stripped to the minimum you need for a tactical RPG. There are no leveling, which is good since you can only bring 4 out of 6 members of your posse in fights, the only way to increase your stats (again, very barebones, you have speed, % crit pretty much) is with one accessory slot or the card system.On the surface the card system seems like good stuff in terms of customization but you will realise that in the end, just put a Straight Royal flush on every char and win.I finished the game in 15hours, which felt very low for a TRPG however I was getting frustrated with the % chance to hit by the end and was happy I was done.Neutral option would have been good here I think but since it doesnt exist on Steam, I choose recommend, the game wasn't bad but... yeah

_childDocuments_.review: The game's three levels of difficulty are Easy, Hard, and Nightmare. I chose Hard, because it was the mid-range one and I'm not new to these types of game. I assume it's actually Medium, but is called Hard because of the game's title. I don't know.This game had a lot of potential, but its downsides have forced a negative review.First, it suffers from the same problem X-Com had: cover doesn't seem to mean a whole lot. Standing in the open? Half cover? Full cover? Doesn't matter...you're getting shot. Especially since there are often far too many enemies shooting at you. Another problem with the cover mechanic is ricochet. You can be in full cover, but once the enemies acquire the ricochet skill, it doesn't matter where you are. I don't see the point of even having the cover mechanic.Another downside is having to figure out the one "correct" way of accomplishing the mission. If this guy shoots this enemy, and then this guy shoots this one, then this guy can run out in the open and wipe out four enemies. And if you get the order or the targets wrong, you're going to get hit with more damage than you can recover from (two slots for healing items). It just gets infuriating. There aren't multiple ways forward.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is very visually appealing but that and the western theme was all I cared about it. Like other reviews have said, it's not a strategy game as much as a puzzle game, and that is the reason I couldn't really get into it. Having to play a fight perfectly or reset with a 2 minute loading screen back to your save before the fight started so you can swap your inventory around or take a different character for the fight just wasn't for me. The game starts to feel repetitive really fast afterward and, honestly, starts to feel a bit bad. You may feel like you're being rewarded for min-maxing your actions per turn only to find out that everything you just did doesn't matter at all because the one hp spongey mob you didn't take out just full healed and chipped away at your team enough that you will now definitely not be able to clear the rest of the fight. You were supposed to find the right inventory, team, and positioning before you came in, and you didn't, so now 2-3 min loading screen and replaying the same first half of the fight over again to see if you can manage this time. The game tells you this is intended design in the tooltips, but I suppose that type of game just isn't for me.I played for almost ten hours to give the game a chance, but, yeah. It's a puzzle game at heart, and while the atmosphere and world are really well designed the gameplay mechanics just weren't what I was expecting going into it, and the theme, graphics, and voice acting just can't carry that part of the game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why some people would like the game for this part or that, and I have no objections. There are things to respect and enjoy for sure, but hey, all the more the darned shame. The stage is surprisingly great, but the actual features... well.. ...severely trimmed-down X-Com-like with a sort of twist on combat that sometimes provides this glorious 'have at ya' moment, but more often than not leads to 'dammit, I miscalculated this 1HP point, so my whole four character round went poor' situations. Little to no sense of progression, no sensible damage upgrades, and less-then-bare-bones RPG features, despite the fact that a large part of the game is about presenting the development of your Posse throughout the journey. And what I don't understand the most is how such heartfelt presentation, atmosphere, lit voice-overs, and cool, gritty side-stories come with such cheezy and unispiring telling of the main story. Gallivanting on horses, doing the little 'quests' during the adventuring part felt the best in what was supposed to be a complex turn-based, tactical game. Man, I usually try hard not to judge games for what they could've been, but when I do, it's Hard West 2. It was good for spending some time with, but it didn't felt like a game to stay at :( If only it were two steps closer to the adventure, RPG, and TTC hybrid, it would have been a game I would have gladly remembered.

_childDocuments_.review: Fittingly, this game is a bit of a devil's bargain.It's Hard West II. It runs smoothly and mostly without bugs. It's a tactical hellfire western. These are all good things.Unfortunately, a *lot* of the charm of the original has been sandblasted off. The writing is much less interesting than the original, and the voice acting for most of the characters feels like it suffers as a result. The story is told not as a series of vignettes, but as a single narrative about a single posse---without really making them interesting enough to sustain it. The worldbuilding hits solid big-picture notes, and it's overall stronger in the first act, but pretty quickly the game falls back on bland backdrops and referential humor. Also the game handles its native american characters in a way that stops short of feeling malicious, but doesn't give off a "I am writing about human beings" sort of vibe. Even the main character is unlikeably bland, and I would've expected for at least SelfInsert McGunman to feel connected to the core conflict of the story. Instead I could describe his whole character with "I tried to do a train job and it didn't work so now I'm trying to do another train job" without really losing any fidelity.These are sort of nitpickier points, but I liked the map system and combat system from the first game. Riding around a janky RTS map looking for context nodes doesn't really do it for me, and resource management in HWII sort of evaporates by the end of the second chapter.Hard West II's combat is more dynamic and rewards chaining kills across maps over figuring out how to cheese the janky luck system, but cover bonuses and obstacles blocking shots seem to calculate weirdly sometimes. I've had 12% odds to clonk someone with a tomahawk while I was standing right behind them, and it scuttled a killstreak that was essential for keeping other characters alive.So, why is this a thumbs up? Well, if you really liked the first game and wanted more, this is good enough. It doesn't live up to the original, but it's a bit more accessible. The setting is still neat, and there's some cool narrative beats, but a good hellfire western depends on the audience caring about the characters, and outside of the first chapter HWII really doesn't manage that.On the balance, it's a bit better than it is bad, but I hope the bravado mechanic is the only thing that gets carried forward from this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game frustrated me to no end because some of the systems like the card system were fairly innovative. As far as balancing is concerned as well you're granted a cadre of what are supposed to be some of the best cow-folk in the hard west... well these aren't those people, be it missing every shot, or not being able to see enemies unless you're five inches away from them the number of times you realize that you have to follow the exact line that the designers made (with zero randomness) the more you feel like you're playing a choose your own adventure story where the outcomes have already been decided and you will lose %90 of the time if you try something creative.Skip this please, even on sale right now.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of turn based strategy then I would highly recommend giving Hard West a try, both 1 and 2. I enjoyed the supernatural western theme, instead of a traditional level up system relying on acquiring equipment and cards to build a poker hand to power up posse members was a nice touch that I haven't seen before and makes for a nice way to experiment with different strategies without committing skill points to a character that you later regret.I found the story and characters to be entertaining enough, it's a simple, but coherent plot, you can pretty much get the gist of the entire story from the trailer. Having played the first Hard West I enjoyed the references back to the plot of the first game, however they're slight enough that if you haven't played it you won't be missing anything with the plot of this game.As with any turn based tactical game, there will be times when it becomes infuriating, whether you're missing multiple shots in a turn with 75% chance to hit, accidentally making a move you didn't want to or enemies pulling off a suspicious amount of trick shots. That's just a part of the genre.Outside of combat I enjoyed the exploration and side missions, they definitely help flesh out the world and the rewards make it feel like it's worth exploring every inch of the map and not like you're just doing pointless, repetitive busy work that only amounts to unlocking achievements at best.All in all, I really enjoyed the game and would love to see the series continue with DLC and/or more sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start off by saying that I believe I played a better game than a lot of the "initial" reviews that complained about the game.  There appear to have been many fixes prior to my play through.  (another reason I'm not big on early adoption)  I very much enjoyed the combat scenarios and found each of them appropriately challenging for the level matched up in the game.  The strip mine / 3 witches might be the only one I felt super over matched on for awhile.The story itself was "ok" - happy to quickly go through the dialogue to get to the next combat scenario.  The steam punk demon was pretty silly.  But none of that really mattered to me.  I came for the combat and I really enjoyed it.  The melee function was super helpful in my party.  My friend and I compared notes and we played the game completely different so the reviews that say they felt forced to play a certain way to win were either early on when the game needed fixes or they just didn't work hard enough to figure out alternatives along the way.I'm a big Xcom fan and it was nice to find another turn based strategy game with an interesting setting of the wild west.  I haven't played a turn based game in a long time and really enjoyed this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say yes but with some consideration. First and foremost the game is quite short, and you can beat the game and do all the sidemissions in probably 8 to 10 hrs. Second at higher difficulties hard west 2 is really quite punishing and the game plays more like a puzzle game instead of a typical trpg. The use of the bravado mechanic is really important and you always need to take advantage of it considering the huge amount of enemies are in a mission. The game doesn't really reward you for experimenting, instead you're forced into these game mechanics or else you get easily wiped out or punished severely for playing your own way. Overall the game is still really fun and the story is good. The bravado mechanic although a double edge sword gameplaywise, I would still say was a unique gameplay decision for the game. I would say the length isn't worth the full price but the game is a yes if you can get it on a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 gets a resounding "eh" from me.I gave the original Hard West a positive review with a lot of caveats, but I'm giving Hard West 2 a thumbs down primarily because they don't seem to have learned a thing in between making the first and the second.Story-wise, they've got the same rushed pacing issues of the first, in that it feels like the story ends when it's just about to start, and that you're supposed to care about an antagonist and a... deuteragonist, I suppose, that show up like... two times, ever, entirely on the basis of some pretty decent voice-acting and drawn art. They never really manage to cause enough trouble or emotional connection to really hit home, so once again the game feels like an outline that never got properly filled in.Mechanically, the game feels somewhat less deterministic than the original, which I dislike. In the original, once you got a hang of the mechanics you could more or less obliterate every encounter without any sort of random chance ever entering the equation as long as you were smart enough and abused the game mechanics enough. I ended up enjoying that more than the more dice-rolly Hard West 2 where I regularly felt like enemies were nailing hits that, from my end, would've been 25% chance hits and where it felt like maneuver was less important because of just how many enemies could not be one-shotted(I recall from HW1 that if you just had the right positioning, you could blow practically everyone away in one go before they could act).Money and supply mechanics are super vestigial, outside of the very earliest game I never really had to consider my money, and I only never used provisions to heal once, because I was curious, and just ended up stockpiling them. You never really need to make any choices, either. Supporting character favor is... kind of vestigial(I'm saying that a lot, aren't I?) since what you gain from it is mostly minor, and what you really want from it isn't anything you could actually predict(maxing one character's affection by a certain point lets you get one of the game's two Jokers, but you'd never be able to know that, so it kind of sucks, and none of the others really have an equal benefit). Nor do you ever really have to pick and choose. It's get +1 with one guy or +1 with another, but you can't ever LOSE affection or otherwise take any risks.The way that characters' active skills are tied to collecting your deck of cards also makes it feel like it takes a while for them to become mechanically "complete" and fun to play with. You can also bring a max of four out of six characters on any given mission, which results in a bit of "bring your favourite four, forget the other two exist." Except when a mission demands them and you have to waste a minute swapping all the gear and cards from one favourite character to them(For me, Cla'lish and Lazarus were permanently benched, their special skills just couldn't really compare).The voice acting is also nice, but damn if I wasn't getting tired of the constant repeated voice barks by the end. Just a bit too verbose AND repetitive. I also wasn't a huge fan of Flynn's voice actor, she just didn't really feel... period appropriate, somehow? I'm sure if it was her inflection or just the writing for her that made her often feel a bit out of place.Another weird choice is that Gin Carter, the protagonist, has the LEAST dramatic background of the entire cast. So with Cla'lish, Flynn, Deer and Bill all having deep drama in their past(I kind of ignored Lazarus, maybe he has some, too?) none of it ever really felt satisfactorily concluded, including Deer having a major antagonist in his background that never really got directly involved, Flynn's background getting resolved in a small side mission, etc.Bill was the only one I felt really got sort-of concluded and got to bump into a bunch of his past to an appropriate degree.Near the end of the game there's also some SUPER lazy mission development where enemies just pop into existence out of nowhere when you advance, so if you move a last character a bit too far and activate them, your enemies get an entire free turn while your goons are out of cover which can absolutely shred the gang. I don't like it, it sucked in the Firaxis X-COM games and it sucks here.On the level of minor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the interface feels a bit "sticky" sometimes and if it's completing something(a camera pan, some last character jiggly hoodery as they complete an action), it won't respond to your clicks and action selections until it's good and well done(not even buffering them, just ignoring you completely) which often felt a bit awkward. Animations are also often just a bit TOO leisurely in general and I found myself speeding through even the most dramatic ones(hold down space to double-speed any animation, thank God for that) just to get on with it. Oh and the tutorial, the start-of-game tutorial almost made me refund the game because it's one of those INSANELY tedious "press this exact button, and move to this exact space, and do this exact action"-tutorials that effectively teach you nothing and just make my blood boil for unclear reasons except that they suck and we should all have learned better by now. We've advanced as a civilization! Except for the Hard West team, apparently.So long story short it wasn't objectively bad, it just felt kind of underwhelming.Even the soundtrack was just kind of *there* without being particularly memorable. Shame.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid tactics game set in a supernatural wild west known as the Hard West. The story follows a gang of outlaws as they try to retrieve their souls from a swindlin demon who commands the feared Ghost Train. Lots of cowboy movie standards in the story missions like bank robberies, train heists, blowing up bridges with dynamite, etc. all in the name of retrieving the aforementioned souls. The world of Hard West 2 is also full of distractions outside the main story such as bounties or treasure hunts that can help you build up supplies to prepare for the final confrontation. Its not all violence and money though! Outside of combat you can get to know your companions and build your relationship with them which will unlock perks when IN combat...so actually it is all violence and money pretty much. Game hits all the points for me, good story, good gameplay, good tunes, and I love the setting and the lore. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Good, Bad, (not) Ugly. The game is thrown quite a lot from side to side, so the great ideas of the creators very often coexist with strange decisions. Before the release of the first patch, it was almost impossible to play due to continuous memory leaks, which led to crashes from the game every 2-3 minutes. With the new patch, everything has more or less improved in the technical part, so now you can directly evaluate the game part. Here it feels very fresh, diverse and offers interesting new solutions. Exploring a hellish variation of the Wild West, we will have to face many enemies, participate in strange rituals, rob trains and help each other out. The company of characters is very diverse and wild, with their own individual characteristics, and since only four can be taken on any mission, you will have to carefully select your team composition.The game is extremely aggressive in the proposed game style. Everything here is aimed at the attack: the skills of the heroes, the design of locations, the ricochet system, the ability of enemies to get you in almost any shelter. And the main factor forcing you to act super-tough is the Bravada system. When you destroy an opponent, it instantly restores all your action points, often granting bonuses to damage and accuracy (with appropriate character skill upgrades), giving you the ability to create long chains of eliminated opponents. It's a very cool mechanic that brings a lot of fun to the action. Equally praiseworthy is the skill system of the heroes, implemented using a deck of cards. Skills are obtained by making various poker combinations from the cards found, but the beauty is that the deck is limited by the cards you have and you can constantly move cards between characters, constantly experimenting with builds, strengthening at a given moment in time exactly those characters on which want to focus on the mission. A very flexible, very modern skill development system could have an impact on the genre as a whole. The arsenal is also very impressive, for most of the weapons there will surely be some kind of fan.Speaking of weird things in the gameplay, it is immediately worth noting the lack of the ability to place your characters at the beginning of the mission (which is sometimes VERY annoying), some strange handling of the fog of war, when the enemies move in it, and you have no idea what they are there is. And in practice, it turns out that you calmly cross the cleared location, finish your turn in perfect calmness, and then 7-8 enemies fall out of nowhere on you, crushing your health during this very move. Some of the enemies are just ultra-difficult, proving to be even much more difficult than the final boss, requiring careful individual approach. Someone may not like the high complexity of the game, but I personally had no problems with this, I'm always glad for a good challenge. It goes without saying that something needs to be done about finding the two most important cards of the game - the Jokers, because if finding the Red Joker still looks more or less reasonable now, then the unreasonable stealth and condition for obtaining the Black Joker is simply not good.After fixing the technical part, Hard West 2 finally becomes the game that I want to recommend. Interesting characters, a huge number of tasty ideas, a hurricane of action, this game will challenge the skill of any player.

Unlike Hard West 1 where there are branching storyline split into multiple playthrough, Hard West 2 keeps the story lenght acceptable. Not too long, nor short. Just perfect with engaging dialogue and branching choices. For hardcore fan and strategists like, the gameplay would be frowned as the devs took away the complexity of gunfight from the first series. The notable scorns are pointed at the Trickshot Skill where it can be abused. But don't let the negative reviews of that mechanic dissuade you, newcomers who are interested in this franchise. This game is still worth my 25 hours of writing this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. If you love turn-based and tile-based strategy game, you may like this game. What I like or is interesting:1. The system of Bravo really makes this a different strategy game than others of the same genre. This system favors offense over defense. Instead of positioning and taking covers, players would focus more on counting damages, calculating odds and chaining kills. Very different experiences than playing other games in the same genre.2. The poker card system. This carries over from the first game. By changing hands of poker for each character, one can change their stats, skills and ultimately change how each character is played. 3. Good voice acting. Not all conversations have voice acting, but they have done fairly good job casting some conversations into voice acting. 4. One can ricochet bullets to reach enemies behind covers. what is meh:1. Story is quite bland. I would say definitely not as good as the story in hard west 1. 2. Pretty easy and not long. I played through one time on "hard" difficulty (because I'm veteran of such genres) and tried to get all the achievements of "finish xxx within N turns". If you play on "normal" difficulty and do not care achievements, I think you may look at 15-20 hours play time. Not too short but also not quite long. One of the reasons game being easy is the existence of dynamites. 3. Lack of variety of weapons. There are melee, handgun, shotgun and rifles. As the story progresses, they just do a bit more damage. It feels quite bland. If the variety and specs of weapons are richer, or maybe a weapon modifications system,  weapons would be much more interesting4. Royalty points matter little. Each character has a royalty point value, but it affects only some side quests. It feels quite irrelevant.5. Choices do not influence the endingWhat may make this a better game:1. Different story endings depending on taken actions, for example, a good ending, a normal ending, a bad ending, and a secret ending when all conditions met. Basically choices matter kinda of game. This will give much more replay values.2. Royalty points affect available decisions, and then affect what endings one can get.3. A more variety of weapons, gears and/or modifications to weapons, and gearsOverall I enjoyed it. But I see this already good game has the potential to be a great game. Maybe hard west 3, devs?

_childDocuments_.review: A must play for fans of turn based tactics game. I played the first one but it felt somewhat forgettable however the sequel not just improves in every way but also comes with some excellent new additions to the genre. Chief among these is the Bravado mechanic which encourages more aggressive playstyles and also had me planning in advance way more than I ever did in similar titles (such as X-COM) as you can chain move after move after move in a single turn. Another welcomed addition is the card system which forced me out of my comfort zone to try different party members and loadouts based on the cards I had. Overall the game is solid on all fronts and I enjoyed the art-style and graphics, the music and voice acting, the story progression and party-based management, the party members, the skills, mechanics (such as luck or train missions) the weapons and so on. On the technical side the performance was good and I had no crashes although I wish the loading times were shorter (they seem to become longer the more you play).Here's hoping the game is a success and it gets an expansion.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone that loves Hard West, I went into this game completely blind, avoiding the beta and all the dev posts, now after 44 hours I've hit the credits, so lets get down to business... No story spoilersThe Good Melee. Thank you god for adding melee, it was quite refreshing and highly enjoyable. It encourages the player to be reckless while still using their brain, because like everything else in this game if you don't do it smart, it hurts. The new bravado mechanic is lovely, on some level it changes the entire tactical landscape of the game, and make no mistake, it is not optional, the system seeks to instill a bloodthirsty nature in the player that we rarely see in turn based games, as racking up that kill streak is not a matter of style but survival. The music works and the sound effects are fun.The BadIf I never see another horse again for as long as I live it will be too soon, trains too for that matter, you can keep'em. I won't be playing the game on nightmare mode, while the idea of more complex combat is intriguing, timers kill the fun for me in turn based games. Real life has enough timers, and putting a turn limit on combat in a game that feels like it doesn't have enough combat hits me as anti-fun. and last but not least by a long shot. I WANT MY OLD DECK BACK. More on this in the next section.The Ugly... TruthWhile I really enjoyed Hard West 2 it is a very different hard west and I hope the developers take a hard look at where they want to go in the future. The west is different... long gone are the perilous rivers wells and mine shafts waiting to inflict grievous injury to the posse, traveling is just a boring ride from one location to the next. There are few things to discover, some encounters will allow you to side with one party member or the other, but the impact of these choices are almost meaningless. They serve to unlock backstory bits for characters, but these are small bits, you'll have to play the game again to unlock them all if you think it's worth it. The powers of the cards are gone, leaving you with only small stat bonuses. Each character has only one special power and a few passive perks that you have to unlock by giving them a better hand. This radically changes the tactical dynamic from the first game as you're now reliant on the elements of your posse. The player is forced into the role of squad chef, as they mix and match the elements of the characters and weapons, and certain characters deal more damage with certain weapons, this might not be so restricting in other games, but in a chain kill murder fest with razor thin damage margins, playing sub-optimal is too close to playing wrong. The game would actually have to try to move farther away from the unrestricted tactical freedom of the first game. You get a six man posse, but can only use four at a time, further limiting your choices. exploration is so low stakes and low energy, I found myself praying for random encounters, and that's when it hit me... With all the big design changes the developer should have just turned the game into a full blown RPG. Don't nerf the DECK, which is the beating heart of the game and put all the tactical weight on a bunch of thinly written characters that we barely get to know. How great would it have been to use the old powers from the first game, with these new unique character, the evil card combing with their personal gifts in unique ways, Hopefully we'll find out in Hard West 3

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR Hard West 1 is betterWHAT IS GOODI got to say at first the game looks great, graphic, atmosphere, audioPROBLEMS?The game design choices. The devs are different form the first game and I suspect that lead to many changes in design choicesLUCKLet's start with luck, my personal choice of biggest change. Luck is a mechanism that I really like back in Hard West. It is what you use to activate your ability, allows you to dodge bullets(Or from another perspective, punish you if you let your character expose)The way of obtaining it is very similar, get hit, miss or use itemsInstead of activating more utility powers/abilities of characters, now luck is simply used to increase hit chance. To me it takes away the fun in combat, makes it feel like puzzle or chess. Together with Bravado, turn limit and the map design, the game now forces you to think of a best tactic of going in and kill enemies in sight as fast as you can and calculate action points carefully so you can get the most out of action refund. It greatly rewards well executed plans while take away much randomness in play which I can say I HATE SO MUCH. THE HUGE SNOWBALLThe reward for well planned maneuvers are so big with so much snowball potential. Combined with the linear level design with limited alternatives it forces you to play every encounter in certain way. This is not a gun blazing game in the wild west, more like a plan your next 10 steps or die horribly kind of game. I know there are people who are into brain teasers and puzzles but that is not why I used to enjoy Hard West one. Hell if those gunslingers are the type which plans carefully in their life they probably won't end up in this hard west. It makes me want to reload every move for a perfected game. Reason is that one failed attempt can be soooo punishing that it denies you multiple actions and the snowball in the encounter. You don't make that one shot, you lose extra action and kill potential and multiple enemies could survive because of that. Not to mention your snowball is not stopping because you need to reload. Which then leads to you getting shot more frequently and since now luck no longer protects you, taking a risky shot can mean death of your character in the coming round. After a while it quickly becomes boring and too demanding.LIMITATION OF CHOICES IN GAMEI want a game with crazy abilities that award different styles of gameplay instead of telling you to go in, use everything and kill everyone as fast as you can. I want a game that both side looks upon lady luck but a risky attempt can in turn gives you new situation and options instead of success or reload. What I mean is in previous game, if you miss you get luck and it protects you from shot so you are not too punished for a risky move. Since you get more luck it may allows you to use more abilities which means more meaningful choices. As Cid once said, game is a series of meaningful choices. I myself definitely don't want a one solution linear encounter but more interesting choices I can explore. ABILITIESSo I didn't play that much, for now we got AOE, movement, distraction summon. There may be more later into the game.They all serve one purpose: enhance your capability of going in and shoot people in the shortest time. They just feel not fun to use. While some of them has no cost other than a CD, combined with turn limit the number of usage actually becomes way more limited. TURN LIMITNow the problem of CD and Bravado is actually enhanced by having a turn limit. The less time you have, the bigger the snowball by Bravado as you essentially get more things done. It also limits the use of cover. Instead of choosing a well defended position to force enemy doing unfavorable resources exchange(action/hp/shots/luck), you have to charge in because you don't have the time. It is actually the one thing I hate in XCOM2 and now Hard West 2 have it. However the fun of different choices in XCOM2 is way better and covers the problem while in this game? NahMISCMore hp feels like design choices to encourage people having their characters shot at for luck, also reduce the need of healing. UI can be better and have more details on what action you are choosing. The new map can be more clear in showing what can be interacted with, aka larger icons. However these are all minor and I wouldn't say they affect the game that much.CONCLUSIONThe design choices place the game in a position that I don't like at all. Maybe there is demand for that, I do not know. If I want to torture my brain after a day, I will go play GO/Chess. If I want to have some fun, I rather open Hard West. I haven't rage in the game yet, more like bored and decided I had enough of it. Some people may still like it, not for me and those I know who enjoy the first game. Before someone say I am bad at this genre or not the target audience, I spent dozens of hours in the first game, hundreds or even thousands in other games like XCOM, RTS and games in 4x genre. If I am mistaken and a player like me is not who the devs are after, then so be it. To me, it reminds me having enjoyed Dawn of war 1 and 2 then saw the gameplay of 3. Or warhammer totalwar, Or Xcom with Chimera squadI dont think this will change with upcoming patches. I do see some other problems that other commentators addressed which I think will be solved eventually. Bugs can be fixed, contents can be added but it is unlikely to revamp how the game is played.Edit: after careful consideration, I don't think I am going to play it again unless there is huge change say get rid of Bravado and turn limit. Refunded

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid game, simple as that. It's got a lot of general improvements over the original, in that it has more complex combat and character mechanics, visually it's been spruced up and leans much more into the 'weird west' genre style. I also really like the direction they took it. Where the first one is a mission by mission campaign, 2 is much more of a traditional RPG. You have access to an open world map with optional quests and character interactions, all of which have varying rewards dependent on choices made. As a criticism, none of these decisions, are very deep or reflected in the game world, but not every game needs to be a Baldur's Gate or Fallout. Overall it's just pretty bloody good, it jumps between a 7 and 8 for me, dependant on the exact mission I'm in or mechanic I'm interacting with.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a lot of fun with this game.  It's much more aggressive and user-friendly than the first game.  Not the longest game for the genre (20-40 hours) but great for the price.It was hard at points, but that's in the name. It's not randomly generated like XCom so level and enemy placement is set up to do some crazy combos.  Decent vertical gameplay and the ricochet combos are fun when you can set up the right angle. It's all about thinking ahead and figuring how to get your characters to max out their Bravado combos.  Very satisfying when taking out groups of enemies in one turn.  There are 6 different characters to choose from, each with unique abilities. 4 per-mission so while there are different ways to play, I tended to gravitate towards a couple characters...  The overworld map and side "quests" were decent but that isn't the focus.  It's the gameplay that stands out.  Highly recommended if you like turn-based tactical games and want something a little different.

_childDocuments_.review: I chose the option to recommend this game, but beware, it lacks staying power. It's good fun if you enjoy turn-based, team-based combat tactics, but only for a while. Very quickly the battles become a grind, as the bravado game mechanic that resets a player's action points is the only way to get through large groups of strong enemies alive, and the whole process turns into mostly setting up the correct sequence for your closer of choice to go on an epic killing spree. For me, it turned most of the characters into generic supporting roles so my real damage dealer could finish everyone off. Others have voiced that the battles came off feeling more like puzzles than a fluid, strategic battle of wits, and I have to agree.With the combat growing stale over the course of the campaign and a forgettable story full of characters that aren't particularly well written, there's not a lot of replay value here. There's plenty of fun to be had advancing through the game's three acts, but don't expect to find yourself coming back to it again and again. Playing with stock characters means you'll never meet anyone new, and options for customization are scarce. You can try out a small variety of different weapons, you can build loyalty points with your posse in a shallow mechanic of siding with one person over the other in decisions that have very little impact, and you can choose which characters should be the first ones to have their unique abilities unlocked with the strongest poker hands once you've collected enough cards in the world, but for the most part you'll be playing the same missions with the same options to beat them. Without a truly top-notch combat experience, that's not a game with much replay value.Harsh as that all may sound, it's only meant to serve as a caveat. This is a fun game, and while not much of it stands out, none of it is poorly executed either. If you want an enjoyable turn-based adventure with a Wild West theme, there's plenty here for you. I just prefer games that run a little deeper and give me an excuse to devote 400 hours of my life to them instead of a mere 40. But I suppose it's possible I have a second run in me somewhere down the road.

_childDocuments_.review: I had to do a quick review bc I see alot of people rate it as "too hard". I wouldn't even call it particularly hard. As a comparison I find, at the current moment, King Arthur on "very hard" & Expeditions on "hard" both equally hard or harder than this game on "hard". There is some missing signposting in maps, so you will want to prepare to load save states. You do have Quicksave & 10 Autosave slots tho, which saves per turn, so you never lose too much progress. The game has uncommon mechanics, which I appreciate, as it gives new problems to solve. But with that it's not always obvious how to prepare for a mission (add to that the missing sign posting). I think on hard, the game expects you to use gear with consumeables, team comps and card to your advantage. Your abilities are quite overpowered, so I don't really expect it to spike. I'm in the middle of the second map atm.The good parts: refund points on kill (bravado), horse combat, interesting character abilities with different play styles (your melee guy is especially fun). Overworld, writing, voice acting is okay but nothing to write home about. The sound design works well with the mechanics tho and gives it a cool vibe. Quick save is quick and always possible besides in dialogue.The bad parts: missing signposting before missions (e.g. tell me what to expect before hand so I dont have to do a trial run, if I didnt prepare properly). Some smaller interface gripes. No undo move button (seriously if you ever missclick you can basically reload). Dependant on playing with save/load.

_childDocuments_.review: ===AFTER NIGHTMARE WEST COMPLETION===Overall 6/10, would recommend for lovers of turn-based tactical puzzle games and the wild west. I may have recency-bias due to reading Blood Meridian this year (10/10).This is more of a puzzle game at higher difficulties, as many have said. The RNG system seems out of whack as well, if you reload some saves and perform an additional step, the RNG changes. Not sure how it is taken into account/calculated, but it isn't random for each attempt.Some stones were left unturned in my playthrough -- I never found out how to make 5 of a kind despite accomplishing each side mission, talking to every NPC, and achieving all of the optional/side objectives during missions.The skills were nice but minimal, and customization was lacking, despite the card and trinket/weapon systems. I would have liked to see more options to explore.The ricochet system was a nice touch, some pathing for it was wonky.The AI was overall pretty dumb, and seemed to target the person with the least cover (pretty straightforward).My final composition was (without spoilers):BCGD===INITIAL THOUGHTS===Hard West II introduces some fresh, new mechanics in turn-based games, both combat and outside. Exciting setting and a neat story, I can't wait to play more.

_childDocuments_.review: WHAT I LIKED:- Both HW 1 and 2 were pretty good games, I really enjoy western fantasy and turn-based games like xcom, this was a must play for me. - The intro cinematic was very well put together and gave the player a straightforward main objective.- World design and graphics were improved from the previous game and the graphical optimization definitely felt like an improvement. The game also had the posse ride horses and explore the world instead of just and icon on the map like in HW 1.- Characters design was alright, but who ever wrote Old Man Bill needs a raise, his introduction was memorable, the way he talked and his story was engaging and very interesting, the banter was also stellar.- The bravado mechanic was very enjoyable and fast passed, rewarding players for creative kills and resource management. The bullseye mechanic(critical hits) was also a nice addition to the game.-Sound design was pretty good, the sound of the guns, abilities, bullet ricochets and voice acting was of good quality.THIGS I DIDN'T LIKEI've played the game on HARD difficulty and wile I enjoyed the game and had fun, the game didn't feel like a sequel to me, for all intents and purposes this felt like a prequel.-No mentions or easter eggs to Warren, Florence or Father from HW1, No item referencing the Masked Man. The only character that makes an appearance in HW2 was Solomon.- Mechanics from HW 1 were scrapped. No reload and ammo mechanic, No gun fanning, no subdue mechanic. - Cards no longer give special passive and active abilities instead, card combinations give character predetermined abilities and stat bonuses, a downgrade from the previous system. -Luck no longer affects a characters dodge chance and cover was nerfed.-Guns and gun mechanics were reworked and lots of the more interesting guns are not present in HW2.-The Final Boss was a bit disappointing, However, the end cinematic was good and it set the game up for either an expansion or a new game.All in all I enjoyed playing the game and had fun. On its own I'd give the game a solid 8/10. As a sequel, it would be a 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to give this a thumbs up because I do think there's plenty of rootin'-tootin sixgun shootin' tactics to enjoy here at a discount price, but I have to put a big ol' asterisk on here: An interview with The Sixth Axis says the Polish development team did consult with a professor of Native American descent for sensitivity issues, but the end result still feels a little... questionable at parts. It's well-intentioned, sure, but even though the characters are more than their tropes (except the villains), the tropes are still there and kinda uncomfortable. (Also, wendigo appear outside of the Great Lakes/Plains regions.) I'm not a native so I'm really not in a position to judge, but just broadly know that this is definitely an albatross around the game's neck.The turn-based cover-based tactics here have a couple of thematic additions to spice them up. The Bravado mechanic that refunds your character's whole turn every kill means you can play aggressively and win, to almost ludicrous extents. It's balanced by the enemies being numerous and hitting like trucks, which occasionally makes the game feel like a turn either goes game-breakingly well, or ends in near disaster when the enemies connect. The trickshot mechanic was super interesting, but I felt like I could rarely take advantage of it due to the level design and range limitations on most trickshot weapons. Meanwhile, once enemies that can trickshot appear, it often gets frustrating as there's almost nowhere you can hide because they can almost always find a shot to bounce around your cover, due to the layout of objects. It's really calling out for a little more depth to make it less situational (or at least give some more options around when you can use it and deny it to your enemies)Balance is the game's achilles heel, though. Of your party members, two are so good that they are broken once properly built, while others are hard to really appreciate. Once you start getting enemies that can swap their HP with yours and ones that regen almost all their health each turn, the game becomes frustrating as you have fewer options: Either you put these enemies down in one turn or you pay for it in your next. You have the tools to alpha strike insanely hard with bravado, but after a while it gets tedious when that has to be your answer to everything.Outside of the core of the game: Poker-themed character upgrade system is thematically cool, but doesn't have a ton of depth. Story is a little formulaic, but fun enough to follow. Choose-your-own-adventure roleplaying sections are a neat little side diversion, at least. Couple minor technical issues as of time of this writing, but the upcoming beta branch fixes the worst of them.

_childDocuments_.review: A massive improvement over the first game. Hard West was an ok game mostly held together by its atmopshere and the setting. Many skills were pretty much useless since you would often lose the required ressource during enemy turns.Hard West 2's design is much more robust. The different skills and weapons are actually useful and collecting playing cards to strengthen your characters feels very rewarding this time around. The missions are well made and while every map is unique, I would have loved to revisit some of them with different enemy layouts during optional quests. Quests outside of the main story are mostly text based events on the map and I think reusing maps would have been a nice way to introduce additional challenges to the game.HW2 felt very polished and I did not encounter any noticable bugs. Some commenters mentioned that Hard West 2's missions feel like puzzles and while I do agree somewhat, it's not as restricting as it sounds. I always felt like different approaches were viable during my playthrough on the default hard difficulty. If I had to make a comparison, I'd say HW2's mission design is akin to something like Valkyria Chronicles where missions have an optimal solution if you want to solve them with the least amount of turns. Though there is no punishment in HW2 for taking it slow (outside of the the highest difficulty).

_childDocuments_.review: Such a great turn based tactics game! I know everyone will compare it to Xcom but it's moment to moment game play is very different. Like in all strategy games you're given a small amount of moves, but have to exploit to create more moves. I didn't fully understand how it all worked in this game, but once I started using the shotgun (you can hit multiple enemies in one shot) and your posse's powers, this game became so fun. I'd swap places with an enemy using Flynn's teleport, aim my shotgun across 3 or 4 enemies hitting them but killing one, get all my action points back, and keep walking around the map mowing down guys repeatedly. And Bill, you can pretty much make that guy The Terminator. Once you realize, losing health can be a benefit, it's not even fair. Same with Lazarus: get hurt a lot, then use his ability to swap HP with a healthy enemy. So not only did you get the enemy to shoot at him (gain Luck and other characters didn't get hurt) he kills an enemy and heals after. You can also make Lazarus a healer in effect by swapping your HP with your party's.This game is nuts. Once you learn the abilities, you can really tackle any level your way and dominate fairly easily. I really hope they release DLC or a sequel. Definitely my favorite strategy game in years.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 is my favourite turn-based/tactics game since Mutant Year Zero, which was the game I felt was the second best game of that year. The Bravado and card mechanics add a couple of really interesting layers to a well-constructed western-themed tactics game that a lot more people should play. The map exploration between missions, where you can also resolve some conflicts through non-combat means, is really satisfying and enjoyable too. I'm not a big fan of the 'complete X mission/objective in Y number of turns', because some of the real joy of this game is patiently setting up Bravado chains, and these objectives seem to have very specific character builds/requirements to pull off. Also, obviously any chance-based combat system will have this issue, but the trial-and-error-y nature of some of the missions (especially when you accidentally stumble into a situation you're not remotely equipped  for) can be frustrating. But, with a strong sense of graphically/aural/presentational style, and such a strong underlying gameplay foundation, Hard West 2 is one of my favourite games of this year.Hard West 2 was one of the games spoken about on the podcast I'm on, and there's a video versions of that podcast here: I also Checked Out Hard West 2 here: , if people are curious.

_childDocuments_.review: After beating the game on medium ("hard west" mode), I'm satisfied with my purchase. The game is challenging but not overly so, and the core gameplay loop is very satisfying. If you're familiar with the first game, this game is actually very different in feel. The game is much more like XCOM 2 and relies on the same momentum mechanic from kills that is used in XCOM 2's expansion with the zombie-like "lost" enemies. This is called "bravado" which can trigger special character statuses and buffs in addition to getting another turn.The result is a very satisfying tactical experience that feels like a puzzle, but it's also not the same vibe as the first game where you're managing luck and looking for big plays. You build up a posse of characters, and each character has unique abilities which can really change the battlefield and find synergies in interesting ways. Melee combat is very viable this time around and probably one of the more satisfying forms of puzzle to solve, establishing a kill streak that crosses the battlefield before working your way back into cover.One of the weaker elements of the first game was the half-hearted stealth missions. Those missions are thankfully gone, though now there are new horseback missions which center around trains. Your characters can transfer back and forth between train and horse, enabling big moves due to the enhanced mobility of horses. Overall this gimmick is actually fun and can create interesting tactical situations as you try to figure out how best to use posse members on horseback, on the top of traincars, and working their way through traincars hopping from cover to cover.The music is pretty good, the graphics are good but not great, and the writing is fairly good for the genre. The design overall works well and the game has a solid core loop. So if you enjoy the genre or the first game, I think you'll generally enjoy this game and get some good mileage out of it.The weaknesses in this game are fairly minor. There are some performance issues from time to time and I've hit a crash or two during my playthrough (thankfully autosaves are frequent so I never lost progress). Voice acting is good at certain times for certain characters, but for others or in certain moments it can come across very poorly. There is not much enemy variety so once you master the core loop and get into your rhythm, the difficulty drops off sharply until the last 2 missions of chapter 3 where there's a bit of a difficulty spike,There's a lot of learning from doing involved in missions which would be more fair on a replay. There are a number of times where you complete the last visible core objective, then the game triggers a cutscene, adds a new objective and spawns in some enemies. It doesn't trigger a new turn or give you your action back, so if you used your last action you're going to take a full round of enemy maneuvering and incoming fire. In a game built on kill streaks and momentum, that can be pretty lethal. The result is that before you finish any objective you're always going to want to waste turns as you gather everybody together and enter into the victory zone cautiously to trigger the enemy spawns. This is a huge pet peeve of mine in SRPGs, tactical RPGs, or TBS games. I end up impatient and want to skip ahead to the next objective or end the mission. I'm rewarded for playing paranoid but it's not necessarily fun.I'd also say the campaign is much more of a directed experience following the story of a small group rather than the set of multiple stories that converge in the finale like the first game. There are no unique overworld mechanics per-campaign like in the first game, and you won't explore many different perspectives like the first game + expansion. The more focused narrative is perhaps more satisfying, so it's a mixed bag and I think reasonable people will disagree over whether this change is positive or negative.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Game is interesting until about 2 hours in when several hidden mechanics pop up, making the game a frustrating slog conveniently right after you can't get your money back.I try to stick to positive reviews, I believe this is my first negative one, but this really rubbed be the wrong way. I'm sure there are tons of people that enjoy it, and more power to them, I'm glad. I personally did not enjoy the game, there were a lot of things hidden about the game behind a very long intro (for me the title screen didn't even scroll until almost two hours in). After this two hours they finally reveal some core things, like what types of enemies you can expect to face, how many they will send at you at a time, and who you can even play as (one of the advertised party members in all the trailers isn't actually playable). Seeing as they, as far as I know, only released the game on steam, it's pretty suspicious that core mechanics like enemy types, enemy skills, and encounter balancing are hidden behind a roughly 2 hour long intro weighed down with a lot of text, dialogue, and scripted fights with enemies you won't see again.Beyond this, the main issue, and why the game is inherently unbalanced, is the core mechanic, Bravado. They made it so powerful that if you can pull it off consistently it makes the game a cakewalk, so to combat this they just made it incredibly frustrating to pull it off, and throw a ridiculous amount of enemies at you. Throw in that there are round limits (I specifically set it to the difficulty setting that said "no round timers" to avoid this, but key progression missions have them anyway) and you have to throw yourselves into fights (as enemies won't seek you out until you're in their proximity) and let them wail on you first before you can hit back, hopefully triggering some bravado that's necessary to even the odds, if you can. They built the whole game around a single mechanic that was badly designed, so they just punish you for using it by forcing your people out of cover to set them up for others, or forcing you to take low percentage shots, gambling on you hitting that 25% because it's your only option and if you don't you're dead. It's not just frustrating, or unsatisfying, it's actively sucking any satisfaction out of playing. Because the developer manipulated the start up time and hid a bunch of gameplay features behind the steam 2 hour arbitrary point, and steam doesn't have a support team other than bots auto responding to tickets, I can't get a refund on it. Maybe I'll get bored one day and give this another shot, but I feel lied to and cheated. If you're interested, I'd do my homework on it and watch a lot of gameplay vidoes because you won't be getting time to evaluate the true game until after your window has passed.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West was so good, they made a Hard West 2.Hard West II is  very good, so I expect that eventually there will be a Hard West II 2.It's the story of a posse of hardened desperados who rob the wrong train and end up on a quest to wrest their souls back from the devil.  devil, anyway.A tactical old west rpg with eldritch themes, it features a diverse cast of characters, each with unique abilities and motivations. Combat is standard shoot-and-cover tactics with some fun additions like ricochets and supernatural abilities. Additionally, there's the bravado mechanic: a character who defeats an enemy gets "bravado", and their action points for the turn get refilled. This almost feels like cheating, but it's  satisfying to tear through an entire enemy posse in a single, well-orchestrated turn. Hard West II is definitely more mature and polished than the original, but I feel like the first game pushed more thoroughly into weird territory. Hard West II is great! If you liked the original or enjoy tactical rpgs or weird west, give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: A significant improvement from the first game. It's as if the developers had read my mind because so much of what I wished for in "Hard West" was implemented in the first game. First and foremost the (semi) open world. There's a number of different maps that you can explore, visiting a number of interesting locations where certain interactions might occur. Loot, combat, a hidden side quest or just simply a dialogue option between members of your posse. This brings me to the second thing that was done right in this game. It has a continuous, coherent story, and a cast of diverse and memorable characters that your protagonist can assemble to assist him in unraveling the plot of this game. Sticking with the members of your posse, there's tiers in relationships with each of your companions, which does unlock one more part of their backstory, that they can share at the campfire. Each decision in favor of a certain character (if Gin Carter, the leader of this group, follows his or her advice) improves their loyalty. It's not possible to lose these points, so no-one will ever really get mad at you, even if you constantly ignore their opinions. Other than that, however, it doesn't really serve a purpose. To improve the attributes of your characters, a familiar mechanic from the first part returns: The magical deck of cards. Throughout the game, you will collect playing cards. Each with its own attribute. Hearts will get you more health and so on. Each character has five slots for these cards, and also each character has a special ability. Switching places with an enemy for example. Or summoning a demon-kinda thing that acts as a decoy. These abilities are unlocked by posessing certain combinations of cards. Like a twin. To unlock the next improvement of this ability you need to posess a more "complicated" combination. A flush, a full house or a straight. Then, to stay with the example of the summoned demon, it will not only stand around and attract enemy fire, but will attack them itself, thus becoming an additional force on the battlefield. Other than that, each character has two weapon slots and two times one equipment that it can carry. Dynamite and a healing item for example. Plus one slot for a non-consumable artifact that, for example, adds maximum hp or improves accuracy. That's all there is in terms of customization. Not really an improvement upon the first game there, I'd say. Where the game really shines, though, is the combat. On the first glance it is the same tried and tested formula of xcom-like turn based combat, where all members of your squad (up to four can participate in combat at all times, except for the final mission) take their actions before the enemy moves against you. But Hard West 2 profits from several unique mechanics. The two most important ones being Bravado and the Trick Shot. Bravado basically means that you get ALL (three) of your action points back every time you manage to kill an enemy. A fun mechanic that rewards aggressive gameplay, even if it's dampened by the fact that most weapons consume at least two of your action points. While bravado is innate to all members of your posse, the Trick Shot is a feature of certain weapons. It allows you to shoot certain objects where the bullet continues its path from a different angle, hitting enemies hidden behind cover (thus ignoring it) or outside your field of vision. Now if you think that you can use these two abilities to become an unstoppable berserker that cleans the map in one turn there's one thing that stand in your way. Your luck. This is the (as far as I've noticed) only constraint on the probability of you hitting your target. Which can be a bit of a disappointment when you've gotten rid of two or three enemies with a guaranteed chance to hit them (meaning 100%) and suddenly you only have a 25% chance to inflict any kind of damage. Shots can be "infused" with luck, draining it, or they can be attempted without it. Each time you miss, you get a certain amount of luck "back" as does each time the enemy misses. I'm not sure about what happens when the enemy hits you. Luck was present in the first game already, but not that prominently, if I remember correctly. This is something I would've wished for this game as well. I mean, making shots only dependent on luck is kinda...one-sided. I didn't thoroughly test it, but I'm pretty sure distance and health of a character make no difference when it comes to the accuracy or percentage to hit. A mechanic that's missing in this game is Overwatch. You don't have any means to trigger a reaction shot when an enemy moves through a certain area. The only thing that comes close is a weapon feature called "duelist", allowing you to counter (as in "shoot back") the first enemy attack. Overwatch, in my opinion, would've allowed for much more tactical depth. However I understand that this mechanic would run contrary to the intended aggressive gameplay style, that the two unique, new mechanics imply. To sum it up this is a solid tactical turn based game with a unique spin. Not only through it's unique blend of the supernatural and the wild west, but also through the unique mechanics that add fresh elements to a tried and tested combat system.Oh and the soundtrack is not nearly as epic and memorable as the one in the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's amazing, I love it. While it dropped a few of my favorite things from Hard West 1 (such as the numeric luck system = no RNG in to hit, or the oppressive atmosphere and Death as the narrator), it is vastly improved in almost all other aspects and then there's new cool mechanics introduced to make it stand out more. I really like their resolve not to just follow blindly in the footsteps of XCOM. Bravado (kill an enemy = > your turn refreshes) might not be my favorite mechanic ever but I'm glad it was in this game. It felt pretty fresh.I like how it went for a single continuous campaign with a static cast of unique characters. I wasn't sure about some of them at first but eventually I ended up liking them all. The story was also pretty alright, while the plot itself didn't really stand out the writing was great with plenty of humor and badassery. Graphics are pretty, music is awesome, levels are quite varied, difficulty seems to be just about right (not a fan of timed missions though). As for negatives the achievements are a little bit uninspired, I hate how jokers are not only missable but outright made into secrets you have to stumble upon with no clues. Unity is a dumpster fire of an engine but luckily I've had no issues other than raging GPU/CPU usage and somewhat long loading times. All in all an excellent game. I sincerely hope there's gonna be Hard West 3 or something in that vein.Took me 19.5 h to finish on normal (called "Hard" ingame). There's some replayability potential as I'm tempted to go play hard ("Nightmare"), hunt for the missing achievements and use Cla'lish and Bill more than in my first playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't quite understand the negative comments. 1) Difficulty:- If the game is too hard for you: play it on easy. That's what I'm doing to have an enjoyable casual first play-through.- there is actually a save and load function in the game. You can retry the mission and reload single engagements. Somthing I really like. If you complain about difficulty, try playing 'Into The Breach' - no save points, and ITB is brutally unforgiving. One mistake will ruin your entire run. This on the over hand is fun. You can do a mistake, figure out a better solution, reload and learn.2) Combat Mechanics:- Bravado: I find the 'bravado' style combat really refreshing. You feel incredibly powerful killing 5 enemies in a row with just one character.- Luck: I always disliked the chance based hit probability in X-COM. No matter how well you set up, in the end RNG always f***ed you over. To me that sucks all the fun out of a game. 'Luck' in this game acts like a battery you can fill up and use up to boost your hit probability. It greatly reduces the frustrations I had with X-COM and makes combat predictable and actually allows for actions to chain and to depend on each other. In X-COM every action can mess up your game plan due to RNG.3) Combat flow:You can't go into this game with an X-COM mentality. This is a new take on the same genre. There is no 'overwatch' here (tbh I found the overwatch system not that fun in the first place) and the pacing of combat is very different.Example of how I approach combat in this game:- I scout out the enemies (go in and out with a fast unit)- I get my characters into position- I wait for the enemies to move in- Finally: I release a chain of ('bravado') actions onto the enemyIt's less of trench warfare, where each party trades blows over several turns until there is a winner (as in X-COM). It's more about assessing the situation, making a plan, setting up the engagement and then crushing the enemies in one move. It feels really good.4) Upgrades and Progression:There are weapons, a loyalty system and cards. These are all ways to enhance your characters and customize their skill set to your liking.5) Story mechanics:I also find the way you engage with story line quite fun. You have a map you can explore, pick objectives, talk to NPCs, trade, etc. It feel more exploratory and less like you're just jumping from combat into combat. It's a nice break in between.I'm only 8 hours in so my opinion might change. But so far I'm enjoying myself.
