_childDocuments_.review: Originally I didn't recommend this game, but after playing it a bit longer and finally mastering the mechanics, I find that I am having a far easier and fun time. Yes, it is indeed possible to play defensively as well as offensively. The bravado and playing card systems take some getting use to, but once you get it, you get it. For the people curious/frustrated about the game, I'll share some hot tips that helped me:- Always focus attacks on explosive and spell throwers, their debuffs far outweigh the damage done by gunslingers- Buy the chain gun as soon as possible, it's a rifle with less AP cost so you can both move and shoot when fighting offensively and stay down when fighting defensively, all with more long range and damaging fire.-Throwables may seem attractive at first, but rarely will you find more than two enemies standing next to each other, and ultimately it's better to prioritize first aid.- When you need to play defensively, set up your men behind cover overlooking an open area, and send a speed buffed party member (probably Laughing Deer) to agro the enemies ahead and kite them to your kill zone- When you need to play offensively, use weapons that only use 1-2/3 AP and use your remaining AP point to move up and flank enemies inorder to negate their cover bonus- Do as many side objectives as possible, these will give you plenty of cash, as well as weapons, buff items, and most importantly playing cards- Each suite of cards buffs a certain attribute: luck(accuracy), crit chance, health, and movement speed- This is relevant, because you'll want to make sure to specialize your characters by giving them both the items and the cards of one suite once you've built up your deck to buff the stat relevant to their skill setFurthermore here's an example of my typical load out when I'm not required to take a certain member-  I always have Laughing Deer (melee specialist) in my party, at his base he can decimate enemy numbers once the rest of the squad has softened them up, buff his speed with the right cards and he turns into a cruise missile since his special attack is affected by how far he moves; assassinating high value targets (nade spammers, bosses) sitting at the back of enemy lines before murdering everyone else. Give him items that restores his health after every kill and he's almost immortal.- I buff Cla'Lish's (Ranged specialist) luck, so she's more effective as my designated marksman- I always keep Flynn on the party because her shadow swap skill is useful for exposing particularly annoying enemies to the rest of the party-Bill has the highest base health, so of course I give him the cards and items that buff his health to turn him into a Juggernaut, which also makes his special ability more useful since the damage it does is based upon how much damage Bill has taken.       Some complaints I have:Note to developers, don't balance your game around the quick save key, especially when it takes your game 3 minutes to load.Yeah the game started off easy enough with the first few gun fights against normal bandits feeling sufficiently challenging and fun, and best of all fair. That last one's important because the other more magical focused enemy types you encounter are absolutely miserable to fight, the Shadow Dancers especially. You slam head first into them like a brick wall in the first chapter, and their shaman unit is completely annoying, if you don't kill those bastards in the first turn (difficult because they're tanky as hell) they'll (1. Instantly restore their all health with a spell that nearly insta-kills your guy (and induces bleed) (2. throw an AoE spell that lowers accuracy, and (3.run for cover ALL IN ONE TURN and with no chance for it to miss in a game where you only have 3 AP, though these refresh whenever you kill something.Speaking of mechanics, I really don't care for how slim your characters' utility is compared to something like Jagged Alliance. Why THE HELL can I only bring in two items per character? On that note, why THE HELL can't I share these items between characters during a fight (Especially when I have one character on the brink of death with no items and another with full health and both of his)? There's zombies in this game that heal like 90% of their health for free every single turn, but GOD forbid you throw a brother a can of beans. And why THE HELL can't I use these health items inbetween fights? Do bandaids stop working when you're not being shot at or something?The difficulty curb is steep, but it's not impossible to climb. However, this game leaks memory like crazy and grinds loading times to a halt, so the learning process can be quite annoying the longer you play. Though my opinion on the game has improved with time, I would only recommend if  you're patient enough to learn the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Turn based weird west strategy game with overworld story and choice segments, mechanically plays closer to a puzzle game than most in the style, that sometimes works quite well. Bravado system of regaining a character's action point when they get a kill leads to a lot of chain action and trying to position your characters to attack in the most advantageous order. Looks good. Entertaining moments in the overworld sections, though the main story is fairly lacking and is over quickly. Allows you to set gameplay speed to .5, 1, 2, or 4 which is nice to speed up travel or character movements in battles. Weapons give a decent variety of options with different passive abilities, status applying effects, ranges, possible cooldowns, damage and action point values, etc. A recent patched toned down the annoying regeneration powers of some of the undead enemies which was good to see.Some interesting and fun ideas but most aren't used enough or to get the most enjoyment out of them. You unlock cards that you equip to characters ideally to create poker hands with the stronger hands unlocking more of a character's abilities as well as giving small to large benefits based on the card itself. It's a cool system but some character abilities aren't that useful, fun, or practical with the way levels or times missions/achievements/side missions are set up, might just not fit the playstyle in how you are using the character, or they overlap with other characters having some of the same skills. There are missions that have you and enemies riding on horseback which they did in a good visual way as the stage scrolls along as you play with you either assaulting trains or chasing after other mounted riders. Where the enjoyment is lessened a bit is the limit stage types where mounts are used and that horses just disable abilities instead of giving new ones. You can use objects in the environment to bounce your bullets off of but this tends to be a bit limited in use, becoming the most useful if you make use of certain weapons that give bonuses for it but these weapons tend to start showing up when the game's maps seem to start having less objects that allow you to use them in that way.Can be too much uncertainty from map advancement as movement through fog of war/enemy spawns as you might just suddenly stumble into an area where it will just throw ten enemies at you at the end of your turn with some throwing grenades, causing massively debilitating effects, or teleporting your characters elsewhere. Some poor or annoying side objectives that can give pointless limitations, or might barely even be completable if you took certain party members before they were even revealed. Hit and crit chances don't really work well with a game that focuses entirely on its bravado system, and like many games with critical hits you will be frequently wanting not to crit targets as it won't factor into sensible strategies and hitting that 5% chance can mess up your strategy or prevent side objectives from getting completed. Conversation choices that depend on loyalty often just asking people to do basic things not at all out of line with what the character can or would probably do most of the time. Deer with a melee weapon and grenades are so much more powerful than anything else that anyone not taking advantage of them will likely find the game significantly more difficult (likely why I saw so many complaining about difficulty before a recent patch when I wasn't having issues on hard). Lacking basic movement options like choosing where you want to be standing when using certain abilities and problems like being able to flip over a table to create cover but the table takes up two tiles and it only allows you to interact with one side of the table to flip it. It also never allows you to position characters at the start of a mission which can range from being a minor annoyance to a massive inconvenience on some of the mounted levels where characters are prevented from getting to certain spots based on the obstacles around their deployment point (you think, I'll bring my more melee focused character, but when the mission starts the game says sorry they aren't ever allowed to get on the train with the characters that can).Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: As an adult man with a job playing rpgs has gotten a lot harder. Completionism is part of the fun to me so starting a 70 hour rpg that threatens to spiral into a 200 hour experience is a much rawer deal than it used to be. It only takes one or two dialogue options or one rough encounter for me to become disinterested in the new epic sagas, but finding games like Hard West 2 has kept my spirit alive. Straightforward but always with something to unearth in the corners, variable so to scratch my tactical itch, clever in its mechanical design and with an emphasis on plot and character dynamics; this game is everything you want in a short rpg. Pick it up, the bravado system will definitely make it a unique tactics game if nothing else.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West2 is a new take for Turn base tactics. When playing X-com, I had the feeling this genre has a lot of missing potential. And frankly, I have the same feeling now when playing Hard West2. It's still fun though.Pros:* Fun basic gameplay* Game feels more fluid than X-com, with more reasonable options per turn.* Some cool mechanics, like ricocheting bullets.* Assigning cards to playable characters to unlock abilities through poker combination is a neat idea.* Looks good.* The luck system as a way to balance RNG.* Optional missions in fights to get larger reward can make some fights more interesting.Cons:* The game relies on the bravados system, where killing an enemy gives you a turn. This was fun at first but now this is starting to feel to arcady.* The biggest problem with the bravados system is that the game reliance on long "combos" works terribly with the RNG element. You missed a 75% melee strike so your plan to kill 6 enemies ends with instead ends up with you standing in the open surounded by still alive enemies. Not looking forward for playing ironman mode with this one.* The game is linear and I rely heavily on saving/loading. To can't lost fights in this one. But saving-loading is also very slow and wastes a lot of time. I don't think this is justified- The game shoudln't have to reload the map when I take it half a turn back. There should at least be a way to undo movement actions, it's very frustrating to wait a minute for it to load because you misclicked.* Ok I admit I didn't actually understand the luck system.* I could do without the heavy supernatural theme. I thought the wild west is interesting enough and the magic doesn't add much to the story. That could be why I am also not very invested in the story.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Hard West 2. It does feel like an improvement over its predecessor especially with the more immersive over-world. The new Bravado system makes it fun to string together multiple kills, and it really made me think about what my next move would be. The game took me 56 hours to complete and that includes all of the sides missions, so it's a little on the light side in terms of content. I do have some minor complaints. Having character select and move both mapped to left click is poor design choice that inevitably leads to misclicks and mission reloads; everyone knows left-click is select and right-click is move. Given the inevitable misclicks an Undo button would also be nice. However I never lost much progress because the game frequently auto-saves. Hard West 2 solves the Player frustration problem of X-Com games when you miss a shot with 99% hit chance at point blank range, this doesn't happen in Hard West 2, if the target is out of cover and reasonably close you will usually have 100% hit chance.I would recommend this game for any strategy game or tactical shooter fans out there.

_childDocuments_.review: So, the first thing you're gonna want to do with this game is go into Settings and lower the voice volume. Right, there we go... All the way down to zero, yep. Now with that out of the way, this is a seriously enjoyable turn-based tactical game that brings a number of unique mechanics to the XCOM formula -- Luck (odds of hitting the next target increase when you're injured or miss a shot), Bravado (refill your action points with each kill), and the awesome and thematically appropriate Cards system that lets you build Hands from collectible cards to power up your posse in a huge range of different ways. Hard West II improves on the first game in almost every way, including the world map and sidequest system. Just don't expect any awards for the voice acting.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is quite good and I'm enjoying it a lot. I played the first Hard West game, and while also enjoyable with some interesting ideas, it was a bit rough around the edges. This game takes a lot of those original ideas and fleshes them out, while keeping the same "Supernatural Wild West" theme.I'm not sure what all the moaning about the game not having true tactical combat is about, or that's it's "puzzle combat" and forces you to play a certain way. That's idiotic and also completely false. The game is very tactical, and will punish stupid decisions while rewarding good ones. This is not like X-COM where you can just rush in guns blazing. You need to plan out your moves in advance for optimal efficacy, pay attention to each character's unique abilities, and use cover and obstacles to your advantage. As far as battles having puzzles, each battle has at least one optional objective that you can fulfil for bonus rewards. Sometimes meeting the conditions can be tricky and require careful planning or trial and error, but that just means you have to actually use your brain. And if you don't feel like it and think that's too hard, at the end of the day those bonus objectives are OPTIONAL.Moving on, two really interesting mechanics are Bravado and Trick Shot. Bravado gives a character a full AP reset when they land a killing blow. With careful planning and party management, you can abuse this mechanic to chain kill several enemy units before they can even act. Trick Shot allows you to use things like metal barrels to ricochet bullets to hit otherwise untargetable enemies, even allowing you to chain ricochet shots in some cases, although each "bounce" lowers the chance of hitting your end target. A third mechanic, Luck, plays a more passive but powerful role. Luck increases your chance to hit, and any time you miss you get a nice chunk added to your Luck meter for future use. When your luck meter is full, you can essentially cheese your hit chance by burning your Luck to guarantee a hit. This can come in very handy when used in conjunction with Trick Shot.Recommended for people who enjoy turn-based tactical battles, and like having to use their brain. If you enjoy this game, I also recommend checking out Weird West. If you have Xbox Game Pass for PC, you can play the game without buying it.Edit: I will say, the one issue I do have is the long loading times anytime you enter a battle. It's more of an annoyance than anything else, but it seems excessively long considering how smooth everything else is.

But this game pulls it off in a very fun and almost "Arcade-like" way while still requiring planning and strategy. It isn't so in depth that you need spreadsheets and websites dedicated to maximizing your play and it doesn't take itself too seriously, but it isn't too easy and devoid of depth either. I think this game strikes a great balance.

_childDocuments_.review: A mid-way comment:The central if not the only mechanic is "bravo", but this mechanic is way too powerful while not very easy to utilize it well. Therefore, the player either find it very satisfying or very frustrating, depending on how good they can use this "bravo".  As a game, this curve is very unreasonable.BTW, this mechanic can be found in other similar games. For example, a recent game "King Arthur A Knight's Tale" has the mechanic that you gain some action points whenever you kill an enemy. While in Hard West you only get limited approaches (cards) to empower your character, in that game you can empower a hero much much more. So player find abusing this mechanic by stacking stats on a single hero and get that "one turn kill all" relatively easy but boring, and this mechanic is later nerfed. What I am trying to say that, this "bravo" mechanic has been tested a lot, and it is generally considered a very tricky one with a very steep feedback curve.Some more comments upon finishing on hard. Well, due to the bravo mechanic, it does feel like the balancing between weapons is at least slightly broken. Shotgun is way too powerful especially when many mobs are around...

_childDocuments_.review: Plays more similarly to the Wasteland games. No overwatch - which is a welcome change. The cards as a way to improve stats is clever, and the characters have a nice variety of abilities. It's definitely more shallow than XCOM, but a significant leap forward in polish and style from the original Hard West.Update: after about 7 hours in, the game is starting to feel more like a puzzler than a strategy game. If you make one wrong move, you basically enter a precarious situation and thus lose the mission. Pretty annoying, I wish the game was more forgiving without reducing the difficulty. It's not a matter of git gud, it's a matter of does your 75% shot miss or not (and save scumming doesn't change the outcome).

_childDocuments_.review: Please take in mind that this review is based on my expectations and not necessarily a measure of whether or not the game is worth buying.  First and foremost, I don't play these games because I enjoy edge-of-the-seat, nail-biting suspense the entire time.  I play games for entertainment.  As such, I usually play on the easiest level.  And that is the biggest reason why I would not recommend this game.  If you are a casual player like me, looking for a game set in the Wild West, running around with your gang and shooting things up, then give this one a pass.I honestly wish developers would get a damn dictionary and read what "EASY" means.  I don't consider a game that puts you up against 20 revenants with your 4 guys an easy game.  Especially when you can only shoot once per turn, unless you score a kill.  Well, hard to score a kill when all your targets have 10+ health and the best you can do is 8 points with a rifle.And I don't understand why developers insist that their product be challenging even on easy mode.  Easy mode should be just that.  EASY.  Let the thrill seekers play on Hard (normal) or Nightmare.  My brother loves a challenge, he might enjoy this game.  But then again, maybe not.Don't buy it.  Stop rewarding developers for putting games out that are not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, I don't normally write reviews, but I have to write something here. I enjoyed playing the first part but this one is much worse. The balancing is really bad. The game throws wave after wave at equal opponents counter. You can't switch between characters within turns, and you usually have an action point left over that you can't do anything with. Then there are relatively early opponents who can usually be brought to 1 life point but can heal themselves completely in the next move. Unfortunately, the balancing only completely tipped after a few hours, so that you've been playing for too long to be able to return the game. I can't understand how this game got such good reviews in magazines.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this because I thought the first game was incredibly good.  Music, ambiance, the story was a take I had never considered for the Western genre.  So a sequel was a natural purchase.  I installed it and I've gotten sequentially more and more bored and disappointed.  The graphics are better, yes.  The music however is a complete letdown.  The combat music in the first was...badass!  Like if Morricone had gone into metal.  Here, its just random generic, gritty music 101.   The combat is...there.  Not a lot of innovation and a lot of the "sameyness".  This one has the bravado mechanic which basically turns every encounter into a puzzle of deal x-y damage and use character z to finish the enemy off.  Any deviation of this mechanic results in the player eating bullets for breakfast.  No healer characters.  No jumping.  No knocking down characters.  The ricochets are a nice gimmick...when they work.  The player always has to advance so they have to constantly be in a vulnerable position.  The enemy is always a Sun Tsu, ultra-instinct bastard that almost never ends turns in ricochet angles.  The vision cones are abysmal, no using your teammates to scout and let your riflemen snipe from afar.  The character abilities are meh and some are blocked behind cards so many characters have NO special abilities in the first arc of the game, making a distinction a moot point.  Except some characters are inherently ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ than others.  I don't know who they developed this game for but its evidently not me.  Its not Xcom, its not Jagged Alliance 2 1.13, its not even Fallout Tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. A refreshing change from turn-based strategies like XCOM that's focused around being aggressive rather than defensive (no overwatch ability)! As you get better, it almost turns into a puzzle game where you find ways to line up enemies and knock entire groups down like dominoes with the bravado mechanic. Healing is cheap, and characters can't die for good so you're free to advanced without worry of permadeath. Great production value, the characters are interesting, it feels like a slightly campy western, and the graphics are pretty. Rather than levels and skill trees, your characters are governed by a deck of cards, and they get better/stronger abilities depending on the hand you create - for example, a royal flush is one of the strongest hands so most of their abilities get unlocked/boosted - which I found quite interesting. I do have a few complaints:- The game strongly encourages being aggressive and quick but there are so many times where you will run face first into an area and arbitrarily trigger a cutscene which spawns a pod of enemies that you had no way of knowing would happen. After the cutscene it goes back to your turn like nothing happened - only now there's 10 new enemies in front of you and your action points aren't refreshed. This only happens during main story missions - side missions don't really have this problem because the new enemies you find in new areas will naturally filter as they're already there to begin with, rather than spawning in a cutscene.- No incentives to using other characters once you find the 4-man group you like. There's no leveling or fatigue system or anything to dissuade you from using the same team every mission. For pretty much my entire playthrough, Cla'lish and Bill sat on the bench unless a mission required them because you have no reason to switch up your posse.- Levels are incredibly linear. This becomes more apparent the longer you play, and you realise that at its core it is a puzzle game with only one or two solutions per level (depending on your team comp). There are no alternate or side routes on the map to get to your goal, just a single line to follow. Would've appreciated side doors or new paths I could blow open with dynamite or something, especially since early on the game stresses how important it is to have dynamite on you.That said, I would recommend this game if you like turn-based games. It is more of a puzzle game, but it is still worth playing because the aggressive style of gameplay is quite fresh and can lead to some awesome moments.

_childDocuments_.review: Another missed opportunity for a good Weird West game <sad face>It is a long time since I felt such a strong regret for buying a game. Here, even though it was on discount - I am angry at myself for wasting every penny spent on it. It is not because the game is outright nonfunctional, bugged into oblivion or has some scummy monetization - like plenty of "modern gaming" AAA titles do (that's why I don't buy'em...). It is because it achieved a rare mix of being bland AND tedious. Which, for a turned-based "Wild West X-com clone" is just a double tap: one bullet into the head, second into the heart.Why bland? The setting completely did not catch me. While a decent premise is... there, both the characters and the surrounding world juggle between generic and pathetically edgy. And I don't blame the writers that much - it is hard to sell a compelling story about devils, bandits, crazed murderers and bloodthirsty Indians with their magic, using mainly static screens and forcing the player to bounce left and right across the world map.Which brings us to tedious. The devs somehow decided, that forcing one's hand is the most consumer-friendly thing they can do. On one hand, the Bravado system: on paper, a neat idea, that allows one to enjoy combos and fancy themselves great strategists, because they managed to wipe the board in 2 turns. In reality - and on higher difficulties, but then I am not here to play on Easy - because of limited supplies / healing options, it forces the player to take certain paths and optimize the strategy beyond fun. It no longer is a turn-based tactics game - it is a puzzle to decipher what the level designers had in their hands.On the second hand, the progression system; and I think this is what I hate the most. Partially constraining the progression by means of creating a common pool of level-up points (read: poker cards). Again, it is cool in theory: allows quick "respecs", gives freedom to tinker with the builds. In practice: every time you find a new card, you have to "refurbish" your whole team's abilities, because "oh, now I can reach this skill with Flynn, but for that I also need to take that card from Lazarus, but I need his skill, so now I need to bust Gin a notch". This turns probably the biggest source of endorphins in skill-based games, i.e. unlocking a new skill, into a chore. And this is a true mortal sin, for which this game cannot repent and won't reclaim its soul. I rarely leave the games unfinished - but here, I really don't see a reason to waste any more of my time. If Mammon would come to me today and offer me a game of poker, where i can win all the wealth of the world, but if I loose, I would have to play Hard West 2 until my final days - I would fold.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary:So this game is like x-com, but not as good or as deep.  I've been playing on hard difficulty, which I think is the way the game is meant to be played.  At its core, this game is a puzzle game, its not actually a tactical game.  The puzzle is to figure out how to kill all visible enemies without ending your turn, so enemies don't get any chance to act, and this is doable almost always if you equip the right cards and equipment on your characters and use the bravado system.  But it does take some time studying the map to figure out, solving these puzzles, for me, is generally fun.The bad:The game slows down as enemies get far more numerous and also have more hp, it just takes the puzzle work longer. I don't like that the pacing goes like this, it starts to get tedious.  I would appreciate the ability to position my characters before the fight starts and to have an idea of what enemies there are.  I feel like the rifles are not nearly as useful as the other weapons, and that's a shame because snipping is fun. Conclusion: It's worth $15 or so right about now, and I'm enjoying it.

_childDocuments_.review: A Linear story with Xcom combat without the roguelike elements, I think they did a really good job on this game, with some very hard side missions that will be having you start the mission over to figure out how you could have done something differently, you don't have to do the side missions, but you want to!I think the Story was good and the characters likable, the weapons were just plentiful enough for the game length to be about 25-30 hours on Hard, and the removal of overwatch replaced by luck and bravado allowing you to be hyper-aggressive is a nice change.The only issue I encountered is after many hours of play and saves being loaded the loading times get very rediculous, up to 4 minutes as I encountered, just restart the game every now and then to avoid this.The things that are missing either to a game direction choice or lack of resources is a hub for upgrades like Xcom, you never get to increase your party size from 4-6, and the health speed crit and luck increases are all done threw the card system (Cool system btw I really like it) but I feel like there was one angle of progression missing, maybe in Hard west 3, we can take control of the ghost train as a new hub, closing Deamon rifts in the west, being able to add new train carts for upgrades and weapon customisation.Lastly, I think the abilities and upgrades given are just enough for the game length, but I would have liked to see more, Maybe some augments to existing abilities or a skill tree with new ones.They get a solid 6/10 from me and I can't wait to see what the studio has in store for us next.Oh, and I'm deducting points for no environmental damage with explosives that's just not on in a game like this in 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: As a tactics game, this one includes so many new mechanics and tweaks that you don't know you want but will inevitably love. Bouncing bullets off of barrels makes you feel slick as hell. Bullseye is the traditional crit system, but you can push it up so high that you're landing crit after crit. Bravado lets you mow down baddie after baddie like the biggest badass in the West. And when your killing streak inevitably comes to an end from a bad shot, the Luck mechanic ensures you'll be able to bounce back next turn.My personal favorite ability is an explosive burst fired in all directions from a character, which is more powerful the more hits he's taken. I load him up on HP-boosting items and let him drop to just above death, so he can bring out that crazy mass-explosion of an ability, and the game becomes a tantalizing game of keeping him safe from any harm while close enough to turn the tide on the enemy.It's no triple A game, but this is Grade A tactics fun with a spooky, Wild West theme. Try your hand! It might just be your next gaming binge...

_childDocuments_.review: The skeleton of a great game is here, but it's too linear and devoid of variety for a turn-based tactical shooter.  Below I will detail all of the areas that it falls short, in my opinion.-Missions are linear, leaving little room for creativity or approaching fights from different angles.-Only 6 total playable characters in the regular game (keep in mind the party size is 4), each of which only has 1 unique skill.-Weapon/item variety is minimal-World Map exploration is very shallow and unengaging. -World encounter decisions will spell out your reward for each available option - leaving nothing up to surprise.I will say that the Bravado system is a breath of fresh air and the whole game is balanced around this mechanic so it is crucial that the player takes advantage of it. The ricochet system is fun but in the late-game, the enemy gains the ability to do it as well. The number of ricochet objects ultimately became excessive, rendering the cover system practically useless in a few fights.Hard West 2 did offer some enjoyable moments and it did provide a pretty respectable challenge on "Hard" (difficulty 3 of 5). I don't relish the "Thumbs Down" rating but the game was just way too simple in its design. It could have been so much more if they added more equipment/skill variety and opened up the maps.

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid game, getting a lot of Wasteland 3 vibes which I love. Tactically it brings some interesting new stuff to the table that I've not seen in the genre before, making it better than 'just another XCom' clone. Haven't encountered a single bug or issue, runs fantastic. A few people saying its 'too hard' - its not. Trust me. There's a few tricky missions so far but it's nothing you haven't experienced before and load times on an NVME drive take all of 3 seconds so get after it. My only gripe so far is there isn't a 'confirm move' button. I can't tell you the number of times I've clicked what I thought was cover and my dude runs on the opposite side for no reason and is now wide open. That's frustrating. Otherwise this was a really nice breathe of fresh air. Snag it.UPDATED August 12th, 2022: Ok, after progressing into Act 3 I am going to leave this a thumbs up as the game IS good, solid, enjoyable, and interesting but just note that there is a LOT of frustrating content ahead of you.- A select group of enemies are massively overtuned. There are Mad Dog's that will throw 8 damage + bleed AOE grenades every single round. That's 11 instant damage, with another unavoidable 3 for 14 total. Most characters have around 22. This is just one example.- The undead type revenants can fully heal, every turn, for 0 cost. Early on, they require being focused but it takes 3/4 of your team to do this generally. - No overwatch means rifles are worthless as the enemy will never allow you to use it. Rifles require 3 AP and 99% of the time, the enemy is starting in cover and any attempt to move to reposition takes an AP and now you can't shoot. Enjoy that game of musical chairs. This is further made laughable by the best rifle in the game being restricted to one shot a round. So much for that whole Bravado mechanic. Meanwhile you can eat a Tatanka Liver and have Deer chain-kill enemies for upwards of 40 or 50 damage a turn if you do it right...- The Witches in Acts 2 and 3 are possibly the worst designed enemy in the game. Every single turn they spawn 2 undead. Good luck trying to bull rush them to focus them down or ignoring the adds. By turn 3 theyll have an entire army. Oh and even IF you do kill one, her summons don't die or despawn. AND the devs decided to 'hide' witches in these tiny little buildings so you'll never get LOS and they'll sit in there perch just filling it with summons. AND THERES EVEN A MISSION THE DEVS DISABLED FLYNN'S ABILITY TO SWAP WITH THAT PARTICULAR WITCH SO YOU **HAVE** TO RUN AT HER LIKE AN IDIOT. (They actually do this several times for a few bosses in hard to reach or impossible positions...like, cool, thanks for disabling my entire characters tactical ability...)- Enjoy the 'Mystery Train' maps..."Objective: Board the train".... you'll likely spend about 30 minutes and multiple reloads just trying to figure out how to board the !@#ing train. It appears completely random based on proximity to specific boarding points? I think? The f do I know...- You'll often be thrown against an insurmountable number of mobs. Im talking, for every one of you, there are 4 or 5 of them. - There's a particular enemy in the game that, when (and only when) they become damaged, theyll hit you with a MASSIVE lifesteal and suck it all back. So for example, you spend a turn focusing one, you do 16 out of 18 health. He survives. Next turn, he picks a target and nukes them for 16 damage and heals for 16 health back to full. You can almost think of this as a 48 point move that he can do, for one AP, every turn. 16 for the initial damage, 16 damage negated, 16 damage given to you. This requires some really dumb and cheesy tactics like flat out ignoring them even if they're completely exposed UNLESS you can for sure kill them that round. - I can't for the life of me figure out why you spend 35 coins on Provisions to heal your party, when the Surgeons all do it for 20?- The lack of any kind of action confirmation is the most triggering thing of the game. Hell, I'd recommend not even using the mouse. Just use your keyboard, tab, and the number keys. Otherwise youll be like me and mis-click the 'use table' icon and instead just run over right next to it and stand there with my ♥♥♥♥ out instead. Or you'll be clicking a target to get a % check, and instead you'll just start shooting because you were already in 'aim' mode and you didnt know. Or you'll still have your secondary weapon equipped from the previous round and you go to attack thinking its the primary and oop...sorry, reload.- And finally, reloads.... for some reason when the game first boots, loads and reloads are fast as hell. Over time, they gradually start to slow down to like, 30 to 40 seconds on an NVME SSD. I don't understand why but given you'll be doing a LOT of save scumming here, it's a problem.

_childDocuments_.review: Sort of an interesting game but again as many have said, it's unbalanced; specifically, the difficulty. Easy is too hard. I wonder if the reason it's made so hard it to extend the game since you have to replay certain missions due to the difficulty. I personally would prefer more content. The enemies that heal after one hit are ridiculous. If there are two of them, it it pretty irritating. I understand that games have to have hard fights but they're all extremely challenging. It gets draining.  This one certainly focuses on making you use the Bravado and to play aggressive. If you don't use it, it would be very difficult to progress. Granted it's a core mechanic so I don't have a problem with this. The one issue with this is that is the best approach is always to be aggressive. There are no other real options. You can't have one character sneak because the AI knows where you are at all times even though they can hide from you which is kinda silly. I would like the option to have one character who could sneak up to the enemies and expose their position. It would make the battles more varied rather than just running in guns blazing all the time. Am I having fun, I'm not sure. I keep playing it so I suppose I'm having some fun. I also just hate leaving a game unfinished after I start. I do use WeMod if a level gets too hard so at least I feel confident that I'll be able to finish the game if the difficulty continues to be an issue. This has handcrafted fights that play out like puzzles and their outcomes carries over to other fights: health damage persists unless you heal it someway, if you can't accomplish side goals, you get less money to buy things that would make future fights easier etc. Nothing wrong with any of that, but without any optional side missions or "random encounters" or something like that, after a couple of missed side goals it starts to get hard to get even. _childDocuments_.review: I am melancholy about this game. I played through Hard West One a few times, it's a short game after all - despite having several campaigns that are from different perspectives of one story, and several one-off stories that have interconnecting parts. The first game felt larger by comparison with it's multiple side campaigns, despite its shorter "main" campaign. The first game lacked characters speaking (except for Scars of Freedom DLC, where the main and side characters both speak for themselves, which most likely is the interconnecting step between the first and second game's ways of story telling) and had only the narrator, well, narrate the story. The first game had interesting characters but lacked effective character development due to us being told everything in a third-person perspective via the narrator. The second game improved upon this by having all characters be voiced (in all cutscenes and most textboxes). The characters in Hard West 2 are all charming and your posse members are given detailed backstories you can learn by having your posse trust you more, even with a returning character from the first who references the first game's plot in some dialogue. Hard West 2's gameplay is much like the first, being split into map events and shootout events. You can go around the map, choose what option you'd like to pick in a map event and move on - choosing one reward over another or selecting shootout events. Hard West 2 improves map events by actually letting you leave the events for later after you've discovered what quest items or what level of friendship you have with your posse members that is required for getting said bonuses in map events. The level of trust, or friendship, is improved by choosing various choices in map events. An issue that has followed since the first game however, is that you must have some sort of previous knowledge of what choices to make (for item usage only in the first game, posse trust wasn't in the first) to get the best trust with everyone, or just by choosing the better option by luck (some events you have to choose between posse members, getting better trust with one member but staying at the same level with another, or some events that may benefit the trust in more than one member but require a level of trust with a third member). This leaves me wanting more than enough events to get everyone's trust maxxed out, but for the time being, you must have prior knowledge of what choices to make. The level of trust also allows for bonuses during shootout events, making trust a valuable thing not only in map events.The posse is also bigger since the first game, with a maximum of 6 posse members on the map events, but only 4 posse members in shootout events. Being able to swap out characters in your posse prior to shootout events is easily understandable and effectively introduced, yet I often found myself using a select 4 characters, leaving the last two just sitting in my roster - except for the shootout events that forced me to use them due to plot reasons or due to plot reasons when you'd have two shootout events in a row and the characters I preferred had become hurt. The combat in shootout events has improved since the first game, each posse member now feels as though they fit a certain role with specific weapon proficiency, rather than just loading all posse members up with the best guns and moving into shootout events. Guns have distinct sounds (for the most part) and your posse, as well as enemies will quip in the middle of battle - although the small number of quips can be grating when a character may repeat the same quip twice or even thrice in a row. Bravado is extremely rewarding and the game often relies on it to beat levels in higher difficulties, which can be frustrating when you have to repeat the level numerous times to beat the shootout event with all side objectives. For instance, in Calla Calla, I had to repeat the stage approximately 30 times to beat the level on Hard difficulty. Laugh all you want but the difficulty in the game is exponentially harder depending on what you choose. Easy, you can pretty much go in winging it on each mission. Hard, you have to plan 3 steps ahead and rely on the luck aspect of the game. Impossible, you have to plan 5 steps ahead and rely heavily on bravado and luck. The difficulty feels like you have to rely more on save-scumming rather than actual planning/skill - very similar to the first game but made more clearly by difficulty choice. The difficulty does not feel balanced between the options. Oh, and there is no stealth gameplay in the second Hard West compared to the first, which is probably for the best.Side objectives during shootout events have returned and are of greater importance. They offer more weapons, cash, provisions, or cards (only the jokers and a few other cards - most cards are available just by completing shootout events that progress the story in some major way) than the first game had done. It is sometimes satisfying to retry missions to try and get all the objectives, but like I said earlier, in Calla Calla and later shootout events it can take a few hours to complete just one shootout event (with or without all side objectives) and can prove tedious rather than rewarding. Oh, and now you must heal between shootouts in the map via camping and using provisions or by going to a doctor in some towns. (doctors will always be $15 dollars cheaper than buying provisions in stores, so its only useful to use provisions if you acquired them via side objectives in shootout events).The art style is more alive than the first game. There is more, higher quality audio during cutscenes as well as faux-motion during cutscenes. Like the advertisements you see above, its cutscenes are of images that are moving slightly or have the camera pan during them. In the first game it was only still images of mainly tan or brown colors being panned over sometimes. There is however, animations before or after shooutout events that are in-game rendering of characters moving around, albeit their mouths do not move and they move stiffly. These animations during shootouts could technically be considered cutscenes but I do not consider their action figure movements to be substantial enough to personally consider them cutscenes.The plot is excellent in everything except the ending. Just like the first game, the ending is abrupt and the payoff for all your effort  is lacking. The buildup is there and it keeps chugging along past important story beats and by the end of the game you are super hyped but it ends in about 5 minutes or less of cutscenes - without a proper conclusion!I must say that when I played the beta for Hard West 2, I was excited. It let you play the prologue chapter in its entirety and knowing how many different campaigns with their gimmicks that existed in the first game, I was excited! I figured the beta was merely a small taste of what was to come. I was wrong. The prologue chapter is one of four chapters in the game - the longest ones being the first 3 (including the prologue that is playable in the beta) and the 4th chapter being noticeably smaller, mainly just to wrap up the story.Overall,  I cant recommend it in its current state for $30 dollars. Being a Hard West fan myself, I was excited to see all the gameplay, artistic, and storytelling improvements - however, it all fell short with a bad ending and with what little content that there was (compared to the first). If this game is on sale, for 33% off, I could recommend it as it would be the same price of what Hard West One is now. If you can deal with being spoken to only by a narrator (except for the DLC) with a more stiff artistic style and slightly more rigid game play, I would recommend the first Hard West over the second as at least the side stories in that game end more satisfying then it's own main campaign ending - as well as the second game's only campaign ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game with interesting mechanics that create far more engaging combat situations than your regular X-Com style game.  Ignore the clueless feebs who post negative reviews on here because quite honestly, they either don't know what they're talking about (or lack experience in this genre, as is clearly the case with many of the reviews) OR they're playing the game in a unique way (like the hardest possible setting and then whining about how hard it is, SMH) and as such are facing weird scenarios that the average player won't ever have to deal with.There's a reason that the STEAM review system badly needs an overhaul. _childDocuments_.review: Exceptionally good improvement over Hard West (1). HW wasn't really well-baked in way too many areas to mention, but Hard West 2 does all the things it want to do quite well.That's to say it doesn't turn the game into RPG or a tactical combat simulator, or anything else too grand (a lot of people are expecting that for some reason). It still remains in the same shape as HW - a tactical combat game with some slight variability and minor RPG elements. They threw away "strategic" layer puzzles as they were in HW, but that's only an improvement as in HW those were extremely primivite and not really worth their time.Tactical battles is the main dish now, and with all the balancing and tuning they turned out quite enjoyable (on the hardest difficulty). Since the number of combat encounters is very finite and all the circumstances of such battles are fixed, it's naturally not a full-fledged tactical game, more like a set of challenges you need to figure out. HW was the same, but balance wasn't there, aside from the very first mission the entirety of HW was braindead-easy. Well, that's not the case any more with HW2 - missions are not so easy for you to blindly push through without thinking out good approaches, and you also have quite a few options to shuffle around (equipment, skill-boosting, etc) so that you can try something different.Visually, it's also much more impressive than the first game, being much better in graphics, animations, sounds, etc.All things considered it's a pretty good game - just don't go searching for a RPG here, or an XCOM game. Hard West is of a much smaller scope.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a lot of reviews with misinformation so I thought I would do an FAQ style review.  tl;dr I like the game and recommend it but it does have some flaws.  Several of which will most likely get fixed and could be attributed to it being freshly launched.1) Does the combat in this game work like a puzzle?NoI've personally put 30 hours in this game on Nightmare difficulty at the time of this review and I've tried numerous combinations of the characters and never had any issues clearing any stage.  Additionally the characters have wildly different abilities, they play very differently from each other.  There is a healer character and they're extremely powerful and effective.  You can definitely play defensively and succeed.  Most combats I clear with 3+ rounds left which proves to me that I could've done a lot of things differently and that there wasn't a specific order I had to eliminate enemies.   There is definitely not "1 right way" to clear every combat.  I will say that there are a couple of reasons why people would say this that I can acknowledge.a) There is 1 character that is noticeably stronger than the others.  Though all the characters can be extremely strong in the right situations, there's 1 that is universally strong.  So I could see why people feel like strategies revolving around this character are more dominant.  I personally have gone without playing that character for several maps and it works just fine. Never once have I had to abandon a squad load out for a stage because I couldn't beat it.   b) There are a handful of stages that could probably use a bit of optimization.  Having a really tight number of rounds does push you towards more aggressive strategies in those stages specifically.  I think that this is 1 of the things that could easily be corrected by patching the round count for a handful of stages and the vast majority of stages can be played either aggressively or defensively.  2) Is there a lack of RNG?Sort ofIf you like RNG and don't want to play on Nightmare difficulty then I would not recommend the game for you.This is a fairly legitimate concern IF you're the type of player that likes RNG in their games.  The only mode that has RNG is Nightmare mode and I can see why someone who likes RNG wouldn't want to be railroaded into playing the game on the highest difficulty.  If you either don't like RNG, don't care about RNG, or don't mind playing on high difficulty then you shouldn't have an issue.  Again this is easily fixable by adding an option to enable the Nightmare difficulty targeting system without the other features of Nightmare.3) Does the game have long loading times?YesThe game suffers from a common launch issue of memory leakage.  This means that the longer you play it the more temporary memory it takes up on your machine and once it hits a certain point the load times get multiplied.  This is a pretty common issue that a lot of games have at launch for some reason.  You'd think that eventually game designers would learn to correct this ahead of time.  There's about a 99% chance that this will get fixed in a future update just like it does for most games.  For the time being you can quit out of the game to reset the memory or worst case scenario restart your computer.  That will get your load times back down to normal.4)  Are there too many enemies?For me the answer is "No" but this is highly subjective.  I will say that your party members get 2-4X the HP of enemies so there should definitely, unquestionably, be more enemies than party members.  Whether they put too many in, again, that's subjective.  My in game experience tells me the number of enemies isn't the problem so much as the round limit on a handful of stages.5)  Are enemies too powerful?Definitely notIf anything I found the majority of enemies to be too easy.  I could see why, if you had a very 1 dimensional character build, that certain enemies would hard counter it.  Like if you had a character that could only do melee and no ranged or something.  There are ways to remove all the status debuffs, the healer character specializes in that specifically.  You can also just build your party so that are flexible enough to adapt to status debuffs and no healer required.  There are also lots of cheap consumables that remove status debuffs.  The most crippling status debuffs last for 1 round.  The longer ones are more straightforward like damage per turn.  Also, I would add that the game is built around the assumption that your party members will get defeated in combat.  A lot of abilities in the game are triggered by 1 or 2 party members being eliminated and the game is very forgiving about restoring party members.  There's no permanent death or ongoing penalties if a party member gets defeated.  I suspect that some people are imposing their own iron man rules and are frustrated because this game was not really designed with that in mind.  It was clearly intended for your party members to get knocked out, you can see it just by opening up any characters abilities and reading them.  If they got knocked out really early in a stage that would be challenging but it's probably assumed that at least 1 character is going to be knocked out somewhere past the half way point of each stage.I think those are the main complaints I've seen so far, but if anyone else has questions feel free to ask me.

_childDocuments_.review: So this is definitely not a standard X-com clone of a tactics game. It has quite a few unique and different mechanics that make it stand alone in flavor and function, all of which lean heavily into the Hollywood Wild West feel of the game; leveling up is done via a poker deck, ammo doesnt exist, and a 'meta map' a la Wasteland to explore and go from fight to fight. That being said its not really even a tactics game at all. The combat has almost 0 RNG in it, and what little there is is completely negated by a stackable 'luck' mechanic that you cash in every time you miss/get hurt/something doesnt go your way. Leaning heavily into that is the function of the games objectives and enemies punishing you for un-optimal moves and builds even harder than X-Com 2. The game does actively reward and push you into reloading turns and even restarting entire combat sequences until you get that perfect optimal run though. All this combines into the game being a very good and engaging puzzle shooter, but if you're being drawn in by its advertisements as a new age turn based tactics game look elsewhere, because it cant be played as such.

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun with it. It is a good game and ill surely play it again at some point. There are ups and downs as in every game so don't expect it to be perfect. The game has no overwatch as most tactical games but instead has Bravado that rewards more agressive play. Basically Bravado restores all your action points after you kill an enemy. There is no leveling system, i wish there was one but sadly there is no such thing. Instead you have a card system as in the first Hard West game, you collect cards, get bonuses from those cards and so on. All missions have bonus objectives that award you items or weapons when completed, with that said i find those weapons a bit lackluster. One of the main issues i have with the game are timers. I hate timers, in my opinion they just ruin the experience as a whole. In the case of Hard West 2, here is where the game turns from tactical game to puzzle game where you have to find the right puzzle piece else it just wont work. Few examples - You are chasing a train and get a 2 turn timer to kill all enemies in the last 2 vagons. You have to spend 1 turn moving because you are too far behind and are left with 1 turn to kill everything else the objective fails. For me this is a bad design. Also putting a timer on your LAST mission? I find it really hard to enjoy the game with those timers.As for bugs, i haven't found any game breaking bugs except one major memory leak. The longer the game runs the longer loading times get. I have it installed on SSD the first time i load a mission it takes about 10 secs and later on it gets longer and longer to a point it is faster to restart the game than wait a loading screen. Overall it is a good game. A bit too short but still good. If you can get it at a discount it's even better.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has nice graphics, atmosphere and a great majority of game mechanics - progress of relations between the team, rpg elements, graphics, music, stylish presentation of the wild west and most of the missions. But the very basis - tactical turn-based combat - is unfortunately very unbalanced, and after the initial missions it is often a matter of frustration. For example, it is not possible for the heroes to heal each other, the enemies are overlevelled (some types are able to take away the character's entire life with a spell, or they are as strong as the heroes themselves, from the beginning they are, for example, in covers, etc.) and in the mission there are 4 of them against heroes usually have several dozen (even 30+). Although I enjoyed the game, unfortunately I don't have the time to get killed over and over and over in one mission and go through it for hours trying to figure out the only correct course of action. And I play on normal, or easier level. I hope that maybe over time the levels will be made easier or even easier difficulty will be added.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the first game many years ago for the really cool setting with cowboys and demons, and the personal story of the dad and son. This one continues to have the dripping atmosphere of the first, though the main character is a lot more generic - Solomon, the undertaker etc, were so much cooler. But the combat is so much fun that this is barely noticed. A new twist of no overwatch, and a killing blow refunding all action points makes each level a nice dance of trying to chain kills by being hyper aggressive and creative. Speccing characters with the right equipment and cards (which you arrange into poker hands to unlock new skills) to reach new damage breakpoints is very rewarding. My posse was so strong by the end and so used to the rhythm that I beat the final level in half the number of turns required. Will definitely play again on the hardest difficulty, and recommend any tactics fans to check this out.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just finished the game as I'm writing this. And I gotta give this game like a solid 3 out of 5. It's a really fun game and has managed to captivate my time more then most games I've been playing lately. However, here are the pros and the cons.Pros: this game stands alone by introducing new, fresh and engaging mechanics to the turn based tactics genre. It allows you to bounce bullets off surfaces to both increase hit chance, and subvert cover. Each PC has their own unique set of mechanics and build paths that are up to the player to discover and build into. This game also offers a card based stat increasing level system which allows you to augment core stats for PC's. Enemies come in an interesting variety and factions with differing mechanics that must be kept in mind when engaging or else you will be punished. The game greatly rewards a high risk, high reward combat system. Wanna have your glass cannon kill an entire wave of enemies, then you're gonna have to put them in the position to, which might mean putting them in the middle of that wave. Use up all their Ap before putting them somewhere safe and they might get killed by any enemy they didn't manage to kill. Kills when you build a character correctly can be very very satisfying, which makes the bravado system even more fun. Allowing you to chain kill, after kill, after kill. This game is very fun and has a very interesting world to play in.Cons: The ending doesn't feel like an end. It's very obviously set up for more content but there isn't any and it makes the end very unsatisfying despite being good. While the card system is fun, it forces you to pick and choose stats that may be good for multiple PC's for just 1 instead or have your PC's not reach their full potential, and therefore under perform. While build paths are cool, you have very very little control over them, which while it does make the characters feel more like individuals, with their own specializations, preferences, and strengths, it also severely hurts your ability to play how you want the character to play. I really wanted Flynn to play basically like nightcrawler (x man) with a rifle but as I got farther in the game I realized she's actually better at putting the rest of the party in a position destroy enemies and occasionally hit multiple enemies with a shotgun to either soften them for someone else, or potentially kill them so she could bounce around some more. Not being able to change characters while they move is annoying but the game does allow you to speed up the action by up to 6x speed up. Friendship system is good for building lore on characters but only 1 of these actually genuinely matters, Lazarus's friendship gates a ace card which is the only way for a character to reach their highest build path, which is really upsetting to know if you get to it, didn't know and miss it because you didn't side with him enough over your other party members. Which makes it feel like siding with other people over him is completely pointless, outside of learning their background and each character getting one new passive locked behind how much they like you, which defeats the purpose of the friendship system.All in all, the game is fun but some more player agency would be nice, some quality of life updates, and some expansion on a few story lines that feel underdeveloped through out the story and tying up the loose ends at the end would make this game significantly better.

_childDocuments_.review: Sigh.I wanted to love this game. Hard West is probably my second favorite turn-based tactics game after Jagged Alliance 2, and it was one of the only games that really nailed the vibe of that one. There are still some good parts here. The world is still wonderful and mysterious, the writing is solid, the art direction is wonderful, but every time combat starts I get reminded that everything I loved about combat in the first game got thrown out the window.Deadly gunplay with no RNG mechanics? Gone. Characters and enemies are spongier than ever, and the damage scaling for cover and range has been replaced with a standard-issue percentile hit chance a-la XCOM. I mean, I don't hate XCOM, but the main reason I loved combat in the last game was that it played nothing like XCOM...Tactically leveraging Luck as an offensive and defensive resource? Gone. Luck is now only used offensively, and the only thing it does is increase hit chance and occasionally trigger passives at certain thresholds. I loved the Luck mechanic from the first game and the rest of the game feels empty without it.Using cards to grant environment-warping magical powers to your party? Gone. The cards grant small stat boosts, with poker hands giving additional passives with effects that rarely capture any interest. Each character has a single active skill, and few of them are as dynamic as the skills from the first game. Additionally, all of them are locked to cooldowns rather than Luck, making the ebb and floe of combat feel more formulaic by consequence.Perks, Injuries, and Overworld Mechanics? Gone. While the writing for the quests is top-notch, each quest basically boils down to hitting spots on the map, maybe having a quest item, maybe doing a combat encounter, and then collecting your reward. While the Injury mechanic from HW1 wasn't implemented very well, it gave you a sense of progression when it worked properly and it made overworld choices meaningful. In this game your choices basically boil down to which party member you want to like you more, one of the tropiest mechanics in modern gaming.Hard West 2 isn't a bad game, but it doesn't feel like the sequel to the first one. Maybe if it was a completely different game I could forgive this, but it just rubs me the wrong way that this is what we ended up with.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 is an interesting take on the genre, on one hand you could say this is purely a turn based strategy game but on the other hand you could argue that it also leans on almost puzzle like thought process where you "solve" a way to take out an entire gauntlet of enemies. In many ways I think both of those assessments have their merits: There are multiple viable approaches, you can choose to take risks, you need to adapt when things go wrong or when you get lucky and there are various other elements you'd expect from a tactical game but ultimately the gameplay loop is built around aggressive play where you take down overwhelming enemy numbers by planning and executing large kill chains with the goal of trying to wipe out most if not every enemy in a group during a single turn.This is achieved through the "bravado" mechanic where a character regains their action points upon killing an enemy (and potentially even other bonuses depending on if you have unlocked them), when you combine this with various deterministic factors (fixed damage values, ability to guarantee hits with positioning and luck bonuses, extremely powerful special abilities etc.) it gives you an incredible amount of control over the outcome of the turn and makes for a very drastic difference between a well planned turn and a poor one giving it that "puzzle" style feeling.While many reviews compare this directly to recent XCOM games, I think it is a bad comparison and can even set up some false expectations. Recent XCOM games at their core are all about managing risks, resources and adapting when your soldier somehow manages to miss a barn sized alien from a point blank distance - they feature much more open level layouts (and procedurally generated maps in XCOM2), in addition to large amount of troop, ability, gear and enemy variety. In comparison Hard West 2 is a compact experience that is considerably smaller in scope, it features a set of handcrafted level layouts that are linear and contain several static pre-placed and/or scripted enemy gauntlets you fight through.So what about the other aspects of the game then?- There are a decent amount of entertaining narrative elements but unfortunately it never really expands beyond a surface level window dressing, story mainly exists to drive you forward with a singular purpose, characters have their own little background stories and personalities in addition to some minor world building. I liked what was there, but it's a shame there wasn't more to it.- Majority of the voice acting was excellent but I wasn't a huge fan of the partially voiced conversations approach where some lines in the same conversation were voiced and some weren't. I can only assume this came down to budget constraints as good quality voice acting isn't exactly cheap.- Mission balancing for the most part is alright, even if there are 3 or 4 missions that in my opinion could use some additional polish as they felt somewhat poorly balanced due to a combination of level layouts and enemy types.- Some enemy types lean a bit too much on the "not fun" side of the spectrum, particularly enemies that tend to do the same behavior repeatedly (spam explosives with status effects from distance, loop summon or always end their turn in counter stance).- Replay value of the game suffers significantly due to the linear level design, low enemy type/behavior variety and the general "fixed" feeling of the combat.It took me roughly ~23 hours to beat the game with all side quests and majority of the side objectives done, I started the game with Nightmare difficulty but switched to Hard difficulty towards the end of chapter 1 as I disliked having a relatively tight round limit for every mission.That being said I enjoyed my time with the game despite it being somewhat different than what I expected and would recommend it to fans of the genre, as long as you don't go in expecting it to be XCOM with a weird west theme.

_childDocuments_.review: The technical issues I had seem to have been resolved in the recent patch, so I got some space to explain where I was going with this review. After seeing so many people struggle with the new mechanics, I mostly talk about everything that constitutes the backbone of the sequel's gameplay. It's useful to understand how and why Hard West 2 shines if you don't skim on learning its inner workings.Hard West is exactly what I wanted from a game in this setting. With all the well-paced cutscenes, set pieces, badass characters, weapon designs, and impeccable style, it's evident that the budget was put to good use. The art is positively metal, one-liners land perfectly, the music and ambience are just right, creating a rich, distinctive Western atmosphere. Notice how they didn't add any subtitle. No Hard West 2: Mammon's Curse or Hard West: Ghost Train. Some devs seem to feel naked when they don't put at least anything after a colon. Here, Hard West is the name of the game, its setting, and the difficulty I self-inflicted. It speaks for itself.Namely, with its concise writing, which always manages to give a vivid characterisation to a person or a place at hand, and delivers the plot in a compelling manner. The setting begs to go batsh*t insane with it, but things were kept clear-cut. Your party needs to kill a devil, Mammon, who cheated them out of their souls in a game of poker and, what's worse, looks like a hipster. They'll do it with the help of freshly acquired demonic abilities and larger-than-life characters met along the way. To flesh out its lineup of desperados, the game resorts to amusing vignettes where you get to make various choices as a part of a simple reputational mechanic. Studying your posse is a reward in itself, but it's nice to have.Scandalously, the sequel has shed its roguelite elements. You still roam the plains, doing your missions, shopping your heart out, taking sides, and enjoying the results of your choices. The major difference is the switch from bite-sized scenarios with everchanging characters and barely any continuity to linear storytelling and big chapters, facilitating fairly expansive maps. Your posse goes through them while keeping their loot intact. I liked the gimmicky approach of the original, it added replayability, but permanence is a better investment. Oh, there's plenty to invest in! Like pistols, rifles, shotguns, melee weapons, trinkets, several types of explosives, and a wide array of consumables.The sheer amount of items with contrasting properties can be confusing. A word of advice: always carry a fistful of dynamite into battle and some coagulant on the ones who still have blood in them. It would also help to pay attention to the involved card system. Solitary cards don't give abilities anymore, only stats. You get to assign your poker hands depending on what skills from a character's personal list you need to unlock. The only way to get the cards is by completing as many secondary objectives on the missions as you can. I usually went for all of them since they were fun and intense. Like picking up optional loot or killing enemies in a certain way. The objectives added variety to an already diverse tactical feast.There are a few heists with similar premises, but no mission feels the same. The game even jokingly teases it once when it pretends to make you rob a bank twice in a row. Thankfully, things went awry, as always, giving me something fresh and exciting to wade through by the skin of my teeth. Savescum is allowed, but I still ended half of my missions on the last possible turn with most of my party dead, including its already dead members. And I didn't mind, given the stellar encounter design. Not all missions are equally hard, some are about having fun rather than overcoming the overwhelming odds. The game loosens its reigns periodically, giving you a chance to enjoy yourself, to then pull the rug, sending your smug ass face-first into the manure. I call it good pacing.See, Hard West went to great lengths to unchain itself from XCOM, but only this instalment was equipped to outpace it. Let's unravel the peculiarities step by step. There are no dedicated move or attack actions, everyone gets 3 indiscriminate Action Points per turn. Like weapons, abilities don't use luck and instead cost AP. Gone is the apparent Heat system, this game's aggro is hidden but still exists. While permadeath got buried completely. Fallen people get up after a fight and healing is cheap. These features allowed for, say, Old Man Bill, who seems to inherently attract more bullets, to be extremely effective with his AoE ability, which scales with lost health and acts as a perfect initiator. Place him in the right spot, endure, then cash in the damage and say: this turn, everybody dies. Worked for me!Said damage is set in stone, so it's like solving a complex determinate puzzle. Getting lucky crits comes as a bonus, not a crutch. I never took a single <75% shot, there's always a way. Although, sometimes it can be helpful to miss or get hurt since suffering provides Luck Points, which now can be used to raise the hit chance by 25% and trigger certain passive abilities. Normally, the hit chance is counted in 25% increments, and it's always 100% if you flank an enemy yourself or with a well-ricochet bullet. Now, ricochets are a property of guns, not cards. As before, you can bounce bullets off the highlighted objects, nullifying your target's cover bonus. It's also available to some enemies... and isn't it a pain in the ass.It is! And the bastards are swarming. But you have the upper hand this time. The biggest distinctive feature of this game's combat is the Bravado! kill streaks. After killing an enemy, a party member enters the mode, fully recovers their AP and, depending on who's the perpetrator and what skills they have unlocked, also achieve bonuses to crit and damage. For this to work, the ammo limit and reloads had to go. Don't mourn them, for Bravado! is the prized crux of Hard West 2. Setting up the grim fandango is your immediate goal on every turn. To boot, moving doesn't break combos, so it's Blitzkrieg all the way - kill, advance, kill. This creates powerful combinations, allowing to cut through the levels like a knife through butter.Don't fret, no hurried rampaging is typically required. Being crap at math and prone to embarrassing mistakes, I mixed my strategies, playing it safe and going all out interchangeably. Yet, even if you're a mathematician, don't expect an easy ride. Mere basic riflemen and shotgunners have something nasty up their sleeves. Wendigos can tear your guys like paper, but what can they do when their legs are broken? Duelists and their cursed counter-attacks make you remember the ricochet. Ghastly grenadiers make you mind your distance and fear the status effects. Revenants and Witch Doctors fully heal if left alive. At your expense, too! They are but your DPS check. If you can't melt one in a turn, you need to go back to your squad screen.People complain. And it's okay, but remember - every predicament can be outsmarted or outscummed. With all the tools and a telling UI at your disposal, you can accurately anticipate the results of your actions. To me, the game is a pure tactical delight, untainted by everything we begrudgingly consider the norm in this genre. Ice Code have made the boldest of changes and they paid off. Hard West 2 looks and plays fantastically, driving a great bargain by being cheap as dirt. I liked it a lot. But especially Old Man Bill. He could've been a character in The Dark Tower books.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I am really enjoying the game. I feel like most of the negative reviews are from people expecting a western clone of XCOM. but it's not... Grid style movement does not equal XCOM. The combat is fun, and somewhat challenging, its like a puzzle figuring out who to take out first. there is a decent amount of strategy involved. The luck system is useful {mostly for purposely missing shots}. each character has their own special skill, which can be upgraded and unlocked within the card system. Trick shots are useful and very satisfying. one of my favorite mechanics is the Bravado system, which isn't traditional for most TRPG's. it feels nice and fluent, which sets the game apart from most games of the same genre. Overall I'm having a lot of fun with the game , and I plan on beating it on hard and nightmare difficulties.That being said, there are obviously a few cons... the guns are pretty cool, but they get stale, there isn't enough of a difference between most weapons {besides damage} to make them interesting enough. trying to complete optional objectives on a harder difficulty with time limits is tedious. The AI sometimes acts really dumbfounded, and my last minor gripe is that I really wish environments or some obstacles were destructible with explosives or other means.Overall Hard West 2 is a really solid and fun Turn-based game, It's worth the price tag, and if you're expecting a western XCOM clone, then this game isn't it.
