_childDocuments_.review: A unique and addicting indie game that combines the best qualities of roguelites with a smooth and slick aesthetic while not falling into the generic tropes that turn me off most other roguelites.  Its art direction is a wonderful mix of that Sega Genesis 16 bit style and color palette with DOS map character sprites.  Character art is sharp and striking.  The Lich's cosmic aesthetic or the piercing eyes of the Hunter are striking and just a pleasure to look at.Perhaps most notable is its impeccable sound design.  The game makes every attack, every resource, every tile placement, every upgrade and level up sound so satisfying that you have to go around for just another loop and keep getting that aural feedback to enjoy the satisfaction of improving even further.Classes are varied and each one is as viable as the next, as well as satisfying to explore the proper card and item/trait combinations to find the best way of building them out.  There's a flavor for everyone to enjoy.  I myself love the necromancer.  Camp building is a great method of keeping you invested in whether to push forward or retreat and find a new method of making your future loops that little bit less difficult to survive.One stumbling block is the game's writing and translation.  For one, this is a Russian game.  And from the country that brought us some of the greatest works of dynamic and transgressive media ever made, I would've been surprised if this weren't somewhat of a game-wide synecdoche.  The dialogue and interaction between characters seems like you're walking some Möbius strip of ideas with no clear distinction of thought.  Some of this, I'm sure, comes from that Russian mindset, and others from a failure in translation.  Some of the humor I feel doesn't hit quite as well as it could because of this, and most importantly the game suffers from confusing and conflicting distinctions in its core mechanics because of it.  Certain traits are given certain descriptions that do not make it clear what they do, and while some of this is clearly by design, other areas are definitely a simple case of bad translation.  These issues can be fixed, however.  What is most important is that the core gameplay is engaging, and in that Loop Hero succeeds in leaps and bounds.By all accounts, this game should be everything I hate about an addictive mobile-like game that keeps you hooked.  And yet its systems are complex and arcane, while the game itself is a cryptic puzzle to figure out.  Some may find the complete lack of direction and explanation frustrating and a major negative, but I would say that is a part of the game and a core reason it has been such a smash hit.  If you enjoy a mindbending and novel toybox that doesn't so much demand your attention as it does entice it, then play Loop Hero.  You may lose hours of your life to it, but at least you'll be playing a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loved how authentic the retro elements of this game felt. It's a very addictive game which builds on top of tower defense style games. There's a rich variety of possibilities between the village building and the variety of cards. There's a story that progresses each time a level is completed or a new building is placed. It feels very minimal though. I wish there were more points where you engage in the story though. It would make it seem like you're progressing more in the game because it started to feel very stagnant after a while.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a Rube Goldberg machine of various game mechanics, with each mechanic flowing into another in a seamless loop, gradually opening up the breadth of options the player has to customise the game to their liking on every level as they continue to explore everything it has to offer. Loop Hero has a lot going on mechanically as a result, but it never feels overwhelming. Players are given complete control over what, when and how they learn the various game systems and everything's kept in its place.Visuals and music work splendidly together to create a tone and mood befitting of a lone hero building their world anew, and the obstacles that lie in the way. The artists have done a fantastic job in this regard. The writing, where present, creates a clear impression of the characters, world, and story.The only real flaws I could point to are that the game's default speed settings are a little slow once you get settled in (though that's soon to be fixed by all accounts) and that a few of the in-battle sound effects can grate over time, though naturally you can adjust the volume on those as you like.9/10 it's like a TTRPG where you're both the Player Character and the DM, nestled inside a deck-building game, that came with a soundtrack CD to play to and a textbook of lore you can read if you like.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I thought this game would be a boring waste of time; on paper it is a waste of time.  Somehow the dev's have added all the ingredients to keep the players coming back.This game is a genre of it's own.  It's the funnest boring game you'll ever play.  It seems basic and simple, yet there's depth.  It  has an interesting story (usually I don't care) and tons of unlocks.   There's puzzles, strategy, even a little gambling (as in can I make another loop without dying to get resources to upgrade and make it easier).    I highly recommend Loop Hero.  If you have doubts, try the demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a game about playing your heros memories, not the hero.It therefor acts as a strategy game with light RPG mechanics.You use cards that give you a tile to place on the map. Every tile has effects like spawning monsters or increasing health.Combining tiles can form new unique tiles that cause new effects, like palcing 9 rocks in a square formation forming a mountain that spawns harpies.You are equally playing against and for your hero, as your sole task is to balance out the threat on the map caused by monsters and the support from other beneficial tiles to increase your heros strength.In short, you are defining the framework around your heros expedition but you arent playing the expedition yourself.Loop Hero is basically the Dungeon Master Role of a Pen and Paper RPG, while the hero is played by an automated system.When you return to camp, you can expand it to increase your options for new tiles and other supportive items.Visually it provides a really nice pixelated look that feels superb.You have the option to tweak the menu fonts and you get a CCTV filter to turn on or off.Thats basically it regarding visual options/graphical settings.What stands out is probably the music. Its insanely good chiptune. In this industry you have games with good music and games with ok music but once in a while there is a game that has this one epic soundtrack that just has you instantly getting goosebumps.Loop Hero is that game.Rarely i recommend to buy a soundtrack but here i do.Content:You are unlocking new classes at the camp that come with their own boni and advantages.There are i think three chapters with bossfights and i have seen at least 2 dozen cards to use.So i would say there is content for easily 10 hours but i have seen people playing the limited demo for much much longer.For the price asked its an insanely good title and absolute recommendation.The quality regarding gamedesign, presentation and accompaniment of music make this a no brainer.There are games coming once in a while that end up being highly regarded top tier class games that make their name in the industry for being instant classics.Shovelknight was one such game, or Celeste.Loop Hero is another.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is an acceptable but imperfect game.It requires too much attention to serve as a true clicker or idle game, it's not much of a deck-building game, it's content is randomized but not substantial or demanding enough to really require much thought.It's nice in a hypnotic way but it's not really great at anything it does.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is probably the biggest love/hate relationship I have ever had with a game...I usually don't like doing this, but this is a case where I feel I should give this game the thumbs down, despite the fact I do play and... sort of enjoy this game - mostly to balance out the fact it's already currently very positively received.To try to put my very conflicted feelings towards this game in as few words as possible, my issue with this game is that it is an amazing and unique idea in theory - but when you actually sit down and play the game it's very dull, repetitive, and slow paced. You'll still find some enjoyment from the pure satisfaction of growing a little bit stronger with each run every time, but honestly, I think the flaw I cannot get past with this game is the absurdly grindy nature of it.---| GRINDING---The most fun part of this game is just the satisfaction you get from making progress, but the progression is slower than most microtransaction-ridden mobile games, which is especially confusing for a game that doesn't even have microtransactions. It would often take about 8-10 full runs each lasting around half an hour just to get ONE more damn building, and ultimately after all that effort, the benefits would often be as trivial as "oh, now your health potions heal 7% of your health instead of 6%". I can only guess the developers were worried the game isn't long enough? It technically does only have 4 "levels" (unless there's some secret post-game content I'm not aware of), but I honestly feel this would have been much better off as a short and replayable experience, than the absolute slog it is right now to inflate the playtime required to beat it.---| RESOURCES---Beyond the grinding being ridiculously tedious, every resource in the game required to make any permanent progress has its own special conditions for acquiring them. This is a fine idea, and most resources are obtained through reasonable enough methods - defeat these kinds of enemies to get this, walk through these kinds of tiles to get that - that sort of thing. One very important material needed for most buildings and upgrades in the game though, are orbs of expansion, and the game never tells you how to get them. I checked the encyclopedia and found that no enemies or tiles in the game would give you them, and when looking at the material itself it told me all I had to do was fight multiple enemies at once to obtain it. I then proceeded to do about 5 runs spamming as many enemies as possible into single fights, and at the end of all of them I had gotten 0 orbs of expansion. That's because the limit to the amount of enemies on a tile is 4, and to get orbs of expansion you need to fight groups of 5 enemies (game says 4 works, but I never got one orb from 4-enemy fights, and even with 5 you only have a % chance of getting ONE orb). So how the hell does that work? You have to get a tile with 4 enemies, and then have a nearby building which has some sort of gimmick to add enemies onto an already existing fight to get the fifth enemy. I had to look up guides to figure this out, and even once I started using the best strategy the community had found for grinding these orbs, it still took hours just to get enough for the tiniest of incremental upgrades. This is both extremely unintuitive to figure out, and extremely unfun to do - but you need those incremental upgrades to have a chance at the later boss fights, so get grinding.---| GAMEPLAY---I like the idea that because you are building the world, you control the enemies that spawn, the resources you'll earn, and to some extent the equipment you'll get throughout a run - however, other than that, the game plays itself entirely. No targetting options for attacks, no movesets for your character, and not even any activated abilities - I can understand maybe wanting the battles to go mostly automatically, but I'm honestly kind of baffled that as far as I've played, this game just doesn't have any way to interact with a battle as it is happening at all.Of course, the equipment you choose over the course of a run, and the cards you build your Deck with are going to have an effect on the outcome of your battles, but if say you realise "oh I'm a little low on health, and before the next loop I have one more big fight coming up" you genuinely can't do anything most of the time but just watch your character walk blindly into their death. Health potions? You're not allowed to use them manually, the game decides when to use them automatically. Activate some kind of ability to help you? As I said, you don't get any, the only effects you get in this game are passives or one-time use abilities that trigger automatically when the game decides. Play a Card in your Hand? What are you going to play? The vast majority of cards have little to no impact on their own, and also often take a long period of time to give their benefits. The only Card in the entire game that can really save you there I have seen is Oblivion, the one that just deletes everything including enemies on a tile - but you can only get so many of those.It feels like most runs of this game are just rolling the dice, seeing if the game randomly decides to give you the equipment you need to win this game, and if not - tough luck, go again for the 783rd attempt of doing the exact same thing. It feels to me that for the point in the game I'm at, the only viable strategies are:1. Attack speed spam with Rogue until you kill so fast nothing gets a chance to hit you (I went infinite twice with this strategy, but you gotta get lucky with equipment for it to work, unfortunately)2. Attack speed spam with Necromancer to summon a ludicrous amount of skeletons (more consistent, but less likely to scale well into late-game in my experience)And while these strategies were fun at first, it feels like they're the only strategies in the game that really work even over 50 hours into it. Every time I've thought of trying out a different Deck, the new Deck has been vastly inferior to those 2 Decks, so every game ends up being the same. If I was at least progressing at a reasonable rate, I may have been able to stomach that, but that's just it - I'm not progressing at reasonable rate. I'm spending hours and hours just to get 1% bonuses to certain stats and it just feels like... Why am I playing this game anymore?---| CONCLUSION---I realised that I spent more of my time playing this game feeling bored or frustrated with all the grinding than actually enjoying it, but that I kept pushing through that for a long time because the initial idea had captivated me so much that I felt like I couldn't write this game off until I'd completed it. I kept thinking this will get better soon, I kept thinking I'll probably like it by the end - and maybe I still will, I still plan to at least finish this game at some point, but I'm no longer in a rush to do it. Taking a moment to step back and realise that I have now spent over 50 hours on this game, and that I only really enjoyed the first 5 or so hours of that, and spent the rest of those hours pushing through because "surely it gets better, right?" has really put in perspective for me why I think I have to give this game the thumbs down despite how much I love the concept - and despite how much I want this to be good.All that being said, I did say I don't think this is an outright bad game, and believe it or not, I do still stand by that - I just think if you want to play this game to completion, you have to go into it with a certain mindset to enjoy it. Since every run drags on for so long while you have very little control over the outcome of it, this game is much more enjoyable as a sort of "background game" to play while listening to something else or just trying to unwind while doing something to keep you a little busy.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The art, soundtrack, and vibes are amazing and second to none. When you get into the zone it really gets its hooks into you. The strategy aspect of being the one who gets to build out the world you’re fighting in makes it never feel unfair, you always feel like you could have placed better for a successful run. And the “just one more loop” mindset really scratches my monkey brain.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: There's very few indie games that have ever made themselves distinguished from the rest. Games like Binding of Isaac, or Super Meat Boy. Games that not execute a concept well, but re-envision the concept and build it into their game from the ground up. Truly owning the concept through their execution.Loop Hero has done that, and although not as loudly or brazenly as Super Meat Boy or the Binding of Isaac, still just as well. Loop Hero used multiple concepts as building blocks, but didn't just implement a concept you've seen before and leave it there. It's not just about getting broken cards, it's not just about running a certain setup, the game is honestly difficult and built around a probable chance at failure.It's honestly unlike anything you've booted up in the past year or two, I'd almost promise you that. There's so much fine tuning and balance to do within your runs, saving cards in case of emergencies, or trying to build that perfect path. There's so much to hope for, and everything to lose. It's refreshing that I can be invested and care about a run but not be edge of my seat button-mashing for the next 15 min as I play a run. It's a slow burn. Am I doing well? What equipment am I hoping for? I need to hold out for XYZ...Just be aware it's a slow game. It's not nail-biting action for the next 15 min as soon as you start a run. There's time to invest and work on your character. Long as you keep your adrenaline expectations in check, I don't think this game will fail to deliver a solid time for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I can totally recommend this game.Alot of people think, it´s only a idle game and it will run by itself.But that´s not true at all.Alot of people who try to describe the game. They say, it´s like a tower defense game, but reversed.And i can say agree in some way.You build your own battleground and try to get enough or let´s say.The best possible gear to beat the boss.So not only the deckbuilding part is important, also the gear you switch out, with different stats are important.I totally recommend the game and i´m hoping, the devs add alot more new cards, enemys and more classes.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Could be improved upon, but very solid already and certainly worth the money. About 10 hours of my time was afk in the menu and I pretty much saw all of the content already (didn't beat the last boss yet and it seems kinda tough, but I think there's about 30 hours of gameplay in this until you're done, unless you watch guides and stuff, then it's probably way less)
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite of this year so far! Its combining so much genres that I love with aesthetics from the old SNES days :) Its a mix between Deckbuilder, Auto-Battler, RPG, Roguelite and even has some strategy/building aspects to it. You create your own world and dive loop for loop deeper into it while your character but also the monsters get stronger. Its a simple concept, but its very deep with lots of synergies and theory behind it, everyone should give it a try :) An amazing experience, Devolver released a Masterpiece with this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Love the art style and setting but it didn't feel like a deckbuilding or roguelike game to me.You don't build the deck as you go - instead you unlock cards and design a deck in a menu like a collectable card game. Okay for people that want a game like that but I'm more a fan of Slay the Spire and board games like TFM. Grinding to unlock things and then experimenting like a sandbox game wasn't for me. You could argue that the deck building is really the environment, as you do chose how to build that, but the synergies you get are all decided before the game begins in the deck building menu.The loop of the game is strange - whilst other games like Slay the Spire have a clear goal (to reach the top and defeat the boss), this game makes you constantly question if you are doing the right thing. Do I actually want to place structures and get to the boss? Do I retreat before fighting the boss? After a while I discovered that placing 9 rocks can create a mountain which spawns a new enemy - is that a good thing? I don't know. You might kill some of the new enemy for a while, and then be overwhelmed later. Figuring out the cause of your problems is tricky. Whereas if you pick up a card like Normality in Slay The Spire, you will quickly discover if it was worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A unique twist on a rogue-like rpg. Each run you slowly build up your hero who fights automatically with the creatures that spawn in the loop that you are creating. Do you make the loop difficult to maximize your hero's experience and loot, or do you play it safe and make sure they survive to go around again? A deceptively simple looking game with charming graphics and a surprising amount of depth an replayability.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A friend purchased this for me. What a banger of a game. Addictive and I am most certainly caught in a loop... The depth was unexpected and the concept is refreshing. EDIT:  I forgot to mention the soundtrack.  Personally it is the best soundtrack for a game I have heard in over a decade.  It is unique and absolutely fantastic and the only game's soundtrack I have ever felt the desire to purchase.  Amazeballs!!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! New fresh ideas where this might make a whole new game genre! While I personally have not encountered any bugs after 32 hours from release, the devs have been working hard and putting out new patches several times to fix any bugs that might show up. The only thing I feel this game needs are some small quality of life things, such as getting more information when hovering over certain terms which you might not know what it exactly means. An example of this would be "Gives hero +4% Strenght", here I would like to just hover my mouse over the word 'Strenght' and see a small window pop out to tell me what this exactly means in terms of stats(So far I have not seen this stat anywhere and because of that "Strenght" would be. Is it damage or health, or even both?)Other than small QoL things like I mentioned, I think this game is fantastic as it just is right now and easily worth a buy!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is one of those games you play for short periods of time. You chip away it in your library and you enjoy your time with the game. The downside is that means it can often fall off the radar.I think games that fit that category are ordinarily on the grindy side and Loop hero is definitely no exception. The challenge is considerable, the mechanics are solid, but it just got very repetitive so I couldn't make myself finish it. Still, I don't regret playing so I've got to give it a hesitant thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

I have run it about ten times now. it seems to keep screwing me on new weapons. I get to loop 4 or 5 and still have level 1 weapon, and armor. then it drops a level 2 weapon with great stats, only to immediately drop a level 7 weapon with no stats. a little annoying, but not game breaking I guess.I do enjoy the cycle and will power through.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I love this style: the intricate pixel art, the sound design, the storytelling -- It all works together to create a beautiful atmosphere. The game play itself is a clean and simple loop (ha) that really feels rewarding every run and maintains a constant feeling of progress. Additionally there are several secrets to discover in the game that help make the player feel excited. My only complaint with this game is that once you get powerful enough it gets stale very fast and loses a lot of its replayability.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Great, simple gameplay, a fantastic soundtrack and beautiful visuals yes.But my favorite part is the lore this game has. Kept me coming back after defeat to learn what exactly is happening and who is who in the story. You can spend a lot of time just reading up the descriptions/lore for the various cards and characters you encounter. It's good. Well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A very short rogue-lite where you don't control the hero but instead build up the world around him. As you build more, the hero faces more challenges and on top of that each loop monsters grow stronger. You will want to balance the risk of getting overwhelmed with the need for good loot which comes from the more challenging monster fights. Totally up my alley, I was hooked from the start.The game is short and there are some hints (such as disabled equipment slots) that suggest that the developers had more in mind for this title. Maybe we'll see it in a sequal?
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game and figured I would leave a review.  I played this right at launch and rushed to finish every achievement as I like the core gameplay loop.  It is absolutely worth the buy if you like the look of the gameplay.Upsides:  Fun ideas, interesting tile interactions, and a fun story are all great.  The equipment system is generally pretty good, and the rate of advancement feels nice and steady.  There are good attempts made to make different characters feel generally near one another in power while each having a distinct thing they are better or worse at.Issues:  The game felt as if there was planned content that never quite made it in, especially with the available heroes/equipment slots, which was slightly offputing but not really an issue.  The strength of different tiles varies wildy, and there is generally very much a "best" combination of tiles for what you want done.  Its really hard to justify not running river and forest, for example.  I would have loved to see meadows and mountains be better options later on in the game.The townbuilding aspect is a bit rough.  The best way I can describe it is that it feels like someone had a plan, started to set it up, and then the idea was handed off to someone else who was told to "finish it up".  It isn't bad, and still adds good depth to the game, but minor things like when you get certain buildings, why lumberjacks are so late game and not actually worth getting, what you are actually supposed to do with alchemy once you have it since you are likely done with the game, etc. all stand out a bit.It might just be me, but the necromancer feels good right when you get him, but later on it really feels like he was probably considered too strong at some point in testing and was slightly overnerfed as a result.  Thing are just a bit longer and more tedious with him, and he is more reliant on level up abilities.Other comments:I would love to see workshop support, but am not really expecting it.  Seeing community made tiles/heroes would make this game far more interesting, especially for others like me who didn't feel like there was much reason to keep going after finishing the final boss, getting the achievements, and hitting the secret bosses.I wish the secret bosses would show up in the catalog after being seen.I have heard other say they had issues figuring out where to get resources, or that they were stuck repeating the loops over and over with no control over what happened, and really can't agree much with that.  The actual part of getting to the end and beating the boss was pretty steady, with very few defeats after the couple early on as I built up buildings and such.  I can't even say it was particularly slow, as of my playtime I would be surprised if it took me over 20-something hours to complete the 4th stage the first time.  Most of my time was some combination of trying for achievements, leaving the game on overnight on accident, or trying to find some card combinations to finish the catalog.I look forward to any future content updates, assuming any are coming.

_childDocuments_.review: Immaculate design, tight balance and gorgeous art, sound, and music make Loop Hero a no-brainer for the price. Rogue-lite gameplay cycles between building your town and auto-battling on a closed loop road that you play cards onto, to add buildings and such, which increases the complexity and brings more enemies into the fold at your own pace and to your own taste. I won't say anything about the story since it's fun to discover, but it's solid and plays out at a pleasant pace, with an ethereal fantasy theme. There is tension, close calls, strong comebacks and power fantasy all in perfect balance. If you like games, you will like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a weird sort of mix of Reverse tower defense + ogre battle's style of non direct combat +  a few borrowed features from rogue-lites such as meta upgrades to improve your chances of successful runs.For the price they are asking which is around 15 USD the game delivers, the graphics the sound effects and the fun factor is all there with enough feeling of challenge to keep you running more and more loops trying out different things. However it needs to be said that this game is not without its flaws , and these are major flaws. *The game goes becomes an excessive grind fest starting on the second level. You immediately hit a brick wall where you are suddenly very weak again and need to grind out new buildings and upgrades.  *Once you learn the combinations of tiles in  your "deck" and itemization you have essentially solved the game for the most part aside from figuring how to get around the nuances that the game throws at you at each new level. * There really isn't all that much unlock-able content and in fact it feels like the levels stretch further than any meaningful or interesting new content the game hasn't already given you by around the time you hit the third level. Everything else is just upgrades to existing buildings that will require insane grind to get. * Some enemies seem very poorly balanced and once you figure out that you should just nuke those tiles off the loop or not bring certain tiles with your deck. They essentially no longer have much purpose except to occasionally put you into a scenario where your character might get killed due to an abnormally strong enemy.*Loot rarity is not always consistent, numerous times i have found items of the same rarity , same types of stats and differing levels where the lower level item had BETTER stats than the higher level one. Quite strange and only a minor flaw but it causes you to waste more time looking through lower level items to double check stats when that shouldn't be the case.Those all being said, the game is still fun and i would recommend it if only because its asking price is not that high. Not only that but a lot of these things can be balanced in the near future and content can always be added thus I don't think it is exactly a bad investment if you will.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game that mixes several elements together: roguelite procedural/RNG gameplay with permanent unlocks, deckbuilding, tower defense, base building/upgrading, class/card/tile synergies, and light crafting/augmenting. It has very nice pixel art and music, but IMO it's held back from greatness by a few things: I think there is far too much grinding required to unlock essential resources and tools. I didn't have to do too much of this through the first three chapters, but I hit a wall on the fourth one, and now I find myself having to look online on how to best get the resources I need, and even then, it's taking more time than I think it's worth. Second, the slow game speed is an issue. There is only 1x and 2x speed choices, and once you are used to the game loop/structure, you will thirst for 4x, 8x, and perhaps even faster speeds, especially on those resource grinding runs. Third, there is no way to currently save in the middle of a run, and since they typically last 45-60 minutes or longer, it's extremely inconvenient not being able to save and come back to it.  I'm going to stop playing for now, and perhaps after some potential QoL updates and balancing patches, I'll give it another shot. I would still recommend the game for fans of roguelites.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a refreshing and addictive roguelike game that brilliantly combines elements of strategy, deck-building, and RPG mechanics. The game introduces a captivating mechanic where players place cards to build the world around a looping hero. This innovative approach keeps the gameplay dynamic and engaging, as players strategize to create the best environments for their hero to navigate. The retro-inspired pixel art is visually appealing, creating a nostalgic yet modern aesthetic that enhances the overall experience. Each card placement influences the hero’s journey, offering countless possibilities and encouraging players to experiment with different strategies. The balancing of resources adds an extra layer of depth to the gameplay. The game features an intriguing progression system where players unlock new cards and abilities, keeping the gameplay fresh and motivating players to explore more. Overall, Loop Hero is a delightful blend of creativity and strategy that offers a unique gaming experience. Its innovative mechanics and charming presentation make it a must-try for fans of the genre!

There's no one way to win a level - it's all solveable once you learn how to loop.I spent the time to earn every single achievement because I like Loop Hero THAT much. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Looks like they finally fixed perks, so changing this to a soft recommend. Great premise, doesn't quite achieve the potential I'd like to see. Serious design flaw in the way traits work. The system is poorly explained to players and is implemented in way that baits you into taking traits as a "reward", only for you to discover afterwards that this is a pure detriment. (Particularly for the necromancer, who lives and dies by rolling certain traits). This is also irreversible, for some stupid reason. Sours what is an otherwise novel and intriguing, albeit bite-sized, experience. This is by no means an indie "must-have" in my book, though it could be with a little system patching and better pacing/more robust content. I thoroughly enjoyed it for a while, but cleared it far quicker than I expected. I lost all enthusiasm for playing the game once I realized I screwed myself on the traits (I've cleared the final loop several times, but was considering maxing out the town, bestiary, etc). Starting over from scratch in a game like this is totally unappealing to me. Music/Art direction is top notch, on par with shovel knight/etc, but like the games' content - I wish there was a bit more.Someone should take this game format and run with it, especially if the Loop Hero devs aren't able to see it through. They definitely honed in on something promising. I think this could explode into its own sub-genre. If you're the kind of person that likes to give interesting indie games a shot, go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: A great example of a bad good game. This game has great presentation and a neat concept and isn't buggy. It's very well made, but fundamentally fails at what makes a rogue-lite great, and offers very little repeatability. Simply put, the game is to consistent. Enemy drops are random but so abundant that you're always going to get your strategies gear eventually, and the deck building aspect, while interesting can actually restrict you, because the game is designed to be challenging enough to warrant a certain level of optimisation in your deck builds. The only actual random element is level up rewards, which are mostly insignificant with a coherent plan.Once you have a winning strategy, you're only incentive to change it is sheer boredom.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: What seems to be a simple card deck roguelite quickly evolves into a unique blend of many other genres and an incredible amount of hidden depth. It feels like a game which could have been made 30 years ago and not in a negative way. The developers found a mixture of mechanics and styles which work so seamlessly hand in hand you're gonna ask yourself "Why has no one thought of this earlier? All the ingredients where there."Despite it being an autobattle game, there are very few dull moments during each expedition. You will constantly be strategizing about tile placement, calculating the ideal loadout and sweating about every single evade those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ goblins perform. And what happens if I arrange these mountains like this ... OH!The soundtrack is an absolute treat, with special shoutouts going to the boss fight music. Each one gets you pumped for action and elevates the (on repeat playthroughs monotonous) bossfights.The aesthetic is beautiful, ranging from the most simplistic arrangement of pixel to represent a bare minimum silhouette to works of pixel art perfection both in design and animation.It may not be the roguelite I will play the most but it definitely is one of if not my favourite in the entire genre. I hope DLC's will add more boss variety and movesets as that's really the only thing lacking in the game currently. And of course more tiles/interactions.Highly recommend to give it a try. It's a unique experience you won't find anywhere else.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a game that grabs you with its core conceit, building maps that you attempt to survive, but will slowly whittle away what charm is can garner, revealing an arduous, unrewarding system underneath.Much of the games enjoyment comes from exploring the ways different cards can change or combine, pushing your luck in a given run, and finding interesting ways to build a hero for success:- Finding new card combos can result in new, interesting tools you can use to either get new resources (more on that later) or provide new ways to tackle a given run. Most of these discoveries, however, reveal tiles that are situationally helpful at best and downright useless at worst. This results in you quickly gravitating towards a small pool of tiles that you'll use every game, disincentivizing you to try new ways of playing.- Pushing your luck is a tried and true mechanic, but requires stakes for it to matter. Here, you'll be gambling getting more resources to use to upgrade your home base, and your hero by proxy. Die during a loop and you'll only drag back 30% of your loot. This works early on and makes the game tense when you're trying to get just a few more things before heading home, but as you reach the end-game, fewer and fewer resources are valuable, and you'll reach a point where you almost don't care whether you die or not, just so long as you have a chance at tackling that chapter's boss.- Building your character in numerous ways can allow you to tackle the same challenges again and again and have them feel fresh, and as you unlock new features and abilities, you can certainly feel that gradual opening of your core abilities. However, once certain features are open, specific stats or tools will become, in my experience, overwhelmingly better than anything else, resulting in you specializing in a specific facet in a way that negates all other strategies. And ultimately, I found that there was one way to easily win any loop... that is, until the final chapter, where RNG reigns supreme.At the end of the day, this game has a neat idea that I enjoyed for the first 15 hours or so, but shows just how boring everything else is surrounding it. The enemies are pretty cookie-cutter and forgettable, and the bosses boring in design and mechanically feel very similar to any other minion you fight. The setting is generic fantasy and the story was interesting at first but felt meaningless by the end. Nothing about this game stands out as memorable, and the final chapter becoming such a chore to play as damned this game in my eyes to be a poorly packaged idea that could have shone brightly under other circumstances.

I find it a simple enough game to knock out a few runs during breaks and/or when you have some time to kill, however it is difficult enough because of the future planning you have to do when placing terrain and the knowledge of the cards you can get, picking gear and seeing which stats might benefit you in the future, and (might be one of the important things) choosing if to end your current loop and collecting all the resources you have gathered or trying one more loop for some more resources or risk loosing almost all of them (you keep like 30% when you die).

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool concept and very well executed. The UI is clean, every mechanic works smoothly and feeds into the others, failure never feels cheap, the music is good background stuff... There is quite a lot of depth to the gameplay as you strive to discover card combos that fit your strategy. This game is challenging, rewarding and fun in that "one more run" sort of way.Your character moves around the loop and fights automatically, the only thing that you can do is place down tiles and swap equipment pieces. The tiles that you place around the circuit will spawn combat encounters that reward exp or will provide some form of bonus to your character. Some tiles seem completely negative at a glance but combined with certain others turn out to be a huge boon. The trick to winning is finding the right balance of difficulty to allow your character to grow strong enough to kill the boss without creating a deadly circuit.There is also a meta-progression element with base development. As you play, you collect resources that allow you to construct and upgrade buildings. Those building provide stat increases, new equipment, new cards, new classes... All sorts of things.

_childDocuments_.review: I almost can't believe I'm giving this a negative review, because I think the concept is really interesting, and there are some parts of the game that I enjoy a lot. I think what kept me playing for 30 hours was the game's theme, I just wanted to uncover more layers of the world, and I respect this game despite not recommending it so I'll write some words about why.The core gameplay loop, most of the time, is not very fun for me. Even when everything is going well, it isn't very fascinating or enjoyable to watch your character go round and round while you sit there and do nothing except occasionally swap out this or that piece of equipment. It takes a very long time to farm the more advanced resources, so if you want 3 more of some particular orb you have to spend 30 minutes to get them, while accomplishing nothing else. You can't leave the game unattended while it farms away for you, however, because enemies are constantly scaling, so you have to keep an attentive eye on the nothing that's happening. I felt bored in my 5th run, and I felt bored in my 50th run.Part of why I think this game is boring is that the meta progression doesn't feel very impactful. Broadly speaking, I have very little idea why I'm expanding the village or what I'm working towards in that regard, even after 30 hours. I know the effects of each building and what they do, but I don't feel a cohesive goal to any of it. I have almost every structure built, and it doesn't seem as though I'll be unlocking more, so shouldn't I feel some kind of accomplishment, or feel like I did something good and worthwhile by making all these buildings? I don't really feel any purpose about any of it, and the development is kind of incidental to me. I don't feel as though I've built anything significant. I think this is both because expanding the village didn't help me in any very significant way or change my runs in any very significant way, with exception of the buildings that unlock new classes. I think it's also partly because I was given very little information about what I was working towards, or how each new structure or upgrade fit into the bigger picture.The way they present information hasn't really worked for me. There's an encyclopedia with most of the information you'll need about the things that you've discovered, but within a run you're given very little info about how enemies and effects interact with one another or how to get a resource, and it feels disconnected. My instinct is always to just do things and see what happens, so it was only bit by bit that uncovered information like which enemies drop what, and what their abilities are, and so on. Uncovering that information ended up feeling tedious, and yet was also one of the only things that gave me any sense of purpose, since I felt I had something to discover. I think if I had relied on the encyclopedia, I would have just stopped playing immediately.Part of why uncovering that information was boring and unsatisfying was because the meta loop, village progression, felt mostly pointless. Once or twice I got a new resource and felt excited because I could finally build a new thing in the village that I'd been waiting to build. And then I built it, and nothing much changed, and I wondered why I had bothered.Another part of why it was unsatisfying is that, at least for me, the feedback you're given about why a run is succeeding or failing is not very useful or reliable. One morning, I did a few runs, and they were all very successful. I scaled very well and reached some nice stat breakpoints, and it was quite a satisfying result if not terribly exciting along the way. My long toil paid off when I took down a couple bosses and claimed some large bounties. Later in the day, without changing anything, I started losing horribly and couldn't scale to save my life. I couldn't tell you why there was a difference between them or what the difference even really was.I don't think the game gives you a good sense of what is working and what isn't, and it sometimes blindsides you, like when you run into the bandit's hidden 5% chance to destroy your equipment, which will almost certainly get you killed on the spot. (Try going from 75% dodge to 0% dodge because your boots disappeared without notice and you died before you realized, it's not an interesting way to lose a run. Keep in mind you'll always be playing at 4x speed because nothing happens for long periods of time, so tragedy can strike in the blink of an eye.)Anyway, if I keep writing more I'll probably just be complaining about random things, and I think covered the broad strokes. I will probably keep playing this game a bit more, and hopefully it gets better and I change my mind about it, but right now this game feels like it should be in early access and is missing a lot of polishing. I wish I had liked it more.Edit: After around 40 hours, I had unlocked and fully upgraded almost everything, and finally noticed real changes in gameplay. At this point the game finally became fun. Not super fun, just standard fun. If it takes that long for a game to get anywhere, I am never going to recommend other people play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a shallow experience hidden behind a decent idea and a solidly nostalgic presentation. While its core is entertaining, within less than a hour you'll have experienced nearly all Loop Hero has to offer, and subsequent runs offer little more. It is, essentially, an idle RPG disguised as a roguelike deck builder. The general idea behind Loop Hero is that you are the nameless protagonist caught in a time loop and destined to eternally battle a mysterious Lich. Doing so requires you to walk a looping path. The general shape of the path is different for each run, but the loop format is constant. As you walk, you'll battle slimes, which you can defeat to earn tiles that you can place around your loop. Bear in mind that all the combat in Loop Hero is simulated: your hero and the enemies will auto-battle as you sit and watch, with victory decided by the quality and stats of your gear. Placing tiles alters the loop somewhat. Some tiles spawn more dangerous enemies that you can fight for better chances at stronger equipment. Other tiles create resting points or augment existing tiles. The premise is solid: you are using your tiles to create a challenging journey for your protagonist. The strategy comes in sufficiently navigating the level of challenge you take on. Playing it too safe means you'll not earn much in the way of resources, tiles, or equipment, while being aggressive and placing too many tiles can quickly get you in deep water and lead to you being overrun by large groups of monsters. The primary issue is that once you've completed a few runs, you've already seen most of what Loop Hero has to offer. There is very little in the way of additional layers of strategy, and not much in the way of extra modifications to the loop. There are a small handful of "secret" tile arrangements, particularly for terrain tiles, but most folks will be able to grasp the more "advanced" concepts of tile placement in short order. Indeed, an hour or two practicing the initial loop will be all you'll need to defeat the Lich and move on to other loops. Once you reach that point, however, Loop Hero shows its biggest flaws.There is little in the way of skill-based play in Loop Hero, and nearly all of its progression is a matter of dull grinding and time sinks. Since you have no control over the titular hero in their skirmishes, growing powerful enough to defeat subsequent challenges is simply a matter of mindless farming to gather the resources necessary to unlock the small handful of extra tiles you'll need to win. Each successful run through the loop will award you a certain number of resources, and you can use those resources to construct new buildings in your village headquarters, gaining access to further resource-earning cards and some new monster generators. Defeating more challenging loops is simply a matter of spending the time necessary to collect the resources for the new tiles, with no engagement beyond placing the tiles themselves along the loop. You'll spend hours doing this, with little variation in using those tiles - each tile has an optimal placement, and once that's been discovered, you'll use them mostly the same each run, further reinforcing the dull, hands-off adventuring. With more variety in equipment, more characters to choose from, a larger and more diverse selection of tiles, and actual weight to decisions such as placement of buildings in your village, there could be something on offer with Loop Hero. However, those tiles you do unlock feel as if they barely matter in the long scheme of things, and some are nearly useless, and earning them requires an investment of hours spent watching a game play itself. As it stands, Loop Hero is a decent idea with little content to offer hidden behind tedious grinding. You'll be enthusiastic at first, but very quickly that enthusiasm becomes tempered by a remaining sentiment: is that all there is, here?

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: Haven't beaten the game yet, on the last chapter but feel I can take a break to post my full thoughts on the game.Loop Hero is the latest from indie darling Devolver Digital from the studio Four Quarters. The only other game I know of from this team is "Please, Don't Touch Anything", which is a cute game revolving around (not) pushing a singular button. It's a idle deck building city building world building roguelike RPG.I repeat. "idle deck building city building world building roglelike RPG". I understand that sounds like madness.The gist is that the world has been suddenly wiped from existence and no one remembers how it was. As one of the few survivors only you have the power to rebuild what was destroyed.The gameplay loop (hah) is you acquire upgrades in your base camp. Build new structures to unlock various cards, classes and abilities to use in your expeditions in the now-destroyed world. Cards are used to place objects in the world. These range from mountains and forests to vampire manors and spider nests. Each affect the map in a different way and some even interact with each other to provide unique new effects.You may wonder why on earth would you play cards that create enemies that harm you. Well your character needs loot and experience to deal with the mounting threat: Every time you 'loop' the map the enemies grow in power and you need to be sure to keep up with them. Loot is randomized each run and each class (out of three) has their unique gear properties. A Warrior can put on a shield by default for example, whereas a Rogue can dual wield to dispatch enemies quickly.Your best companion will be your campfire: Not only do you heal every time you pass it, it's also your only escape route if things go south. While you can retreat at any time you'll lose some upgrading supplies. Dying makes you drop the majority of supplies.Combat is automatic. You have no impact on the fight: Your hero and any allies they have will smack targets at random (Unless one has a 'first target' modifier). While part of the RNG of the game it can be a bit frustrating to see your characters smack a chest over enemies actively attacking you.Your overall goal is to build up the world enough to attract the boss of the chapter and defeat them. After this, you can continue looping your created world or move on to the next world with your spoils. There's four chapters total and certainly a lot of replayability with the deck building aspect and the multiple classes.Despite the automatic nature of the game there's a lot of strategy to keep in mind: Timing events so that you can hit them before or after a loop, having your preferred strategies against certain enemies with certain classes. Runs are fast and it's easy to lose track of time playing this, especially with the top notch soundtrack. The pixel art is also very great and the dialogue is equal parts fun and interesting.Few complaints though:-Class balance: You may be giving this a sideways glance as I bring up balance in a single player game but it is an issue. The last unlockable class, the Necromancer, is worlds stronger than the Warrior and especially the Rogue. Despite him appearing as a physically weak caster, he can summon skeletons to fight for him. He can make high DPS skellies or tank skellies that soak damage for him. He has access to amulets which provides a free magic shield before his HP gets damaged every conflict. He has health regeneration items. With a certain card he can equip a shield to further enhance his durability.Compare this to the Rogue who's only survival tools are a % dodge chance and a 5% lifesteal. Warrior has plenty of survival tools but his damage is heavily gear dependent. Both are much more difficult to be successful with as opposed to the Necromancer.Personal experience but I was stuck on Chapter 2 for the longest time playing as the Warrior and Rogue until I played Necromancer. I beat Chapter 2 my very next attempt and then one shot Chapter 3 with the class. A bit of rebalancing probably wouldn't hurt because I know I was getting pretty frustrated playing as the melee boys.-Game Speed: As the game is almost automatic a decent chunk of gameplay is waiting for things to happen. The game only goes up to double speed which still feels too slow at times, especially when grinding upgrade materials (which you'll have to do).I feel like it wouldn't be a bad thing to have a x3 speed, especially after beating a boss where you're doing extra loops for extra materials. While it's part idle game it feels weird alt tabbing while free farming mobs and focusing on something else.-The RNG Nature: Some runs you're just not gonna win. Sometimes you get multiple cards of the same thing that you can't play on it's own. Sometimes you won't have a good item slot and no gear drops. Sometimes mobs may proc multiple passives and do something like break all your gear.All roguelikes are affected by luck but other roguelikes you can kinda carry yourself with individual skill (Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon or SYNTHETIK), but even with good deck building with a ton of synergies you can just get unlucky and unfortunately that gets a bit frustrating.It stinks to have to bail on a run early (if you can escape) but sometimes that's how the cards fold. There isn't any way to 'tutor' (find ways to get specific cards in your deck) your deck: You're 100% at the mercy of RNG.Despite these complaints, I've been playing this almost nonstop since I got it: Got it last Friday and already have 15 hours in. It's absolutely charming and I love just about everything about it. I'm just hoping for more, especially mod support. It is a fantastic game and one of my favorite games 2021 thus far.Can you build something out of nothing? Can you be the Loop Hero?Absolutely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is an incredible RPG that removes the slow turn based grind but keeps all the feeling of leveling and growing stronger. The only thing is that once you've progressed beyond the first few episodes, there is no reason to go back to them. Right now I can consistently beat Episode 3 with all of the camp upgrades and the deck variety I bring I don't mess with much since I need those synergies.Improvement? Perhaps to increase the synergy strength of other card combos and also a better explanation as to what the upgrades do. _childDocuments_.review: Firstly i was impressed by the game but there are a few thinks putting me off the initial euphoria.Rings and boots and amulets are considerably better in common compared to uncommon and rares since they have fewer abilitys but have a higher value leading to watering down your character with higher rarity. Thats fine initially but with a more specialized character they become useless and its putting a dump on your personal risk reward equation (Stronger enemys and more complex gathering reward you more rare items). This wouldnt be too bad since it mostly affects the Single runs in no major way but there are other mechanics bothering me like the pause system sometimes unpause for no apperend reason or The City progression feeling a bit forced on you. Overall the game should be more in a 2-5$ range in my opinion this overcharge is too much for me and i wont recommend it.

ANYHOW, please do keep in mind, you only get 1 of the 3 skills randomly chosen. if i were to of made 1 change to this whole rng process, it would be so that, the quicker you rush levels, the more likely you will get the best skills for the class, or the higher level, the more likely you are to get the best skill for class. however thats just my preference and my 2 sense. i still very much enjoy the game as it is and it does have hope for expansions or so in the future, like more classes and such.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine a game where you're the dungeon master, but on the player's side. That is, you don't control the player character, you control the environment around them.You place objects on the map that will help the player character get the resources, items and EXP to become stronger for the boss that they'll inevitably face, but at the same time there's the risk of adding too many things that might get them to an early grave. Knowing how to balance risk and reward is key to surviving enough loops and beating the boss.Each tile you place does something on the map. Meadows give you hp regen, the village recovers some of your hp and gives you quests, the Vampire Mansion spawns vampires, and so on. Knowing the combinations of these tiles and putting them carefully on the map will help the player character get stronger and stay alive.Speaking of combinations, they're the heart of the game. Mixing tiles gives us different effects, like a river surrounded by desert dunes turning into an oasis, or a village with a nearby Vampire Mansion turning into a dangerous spot. They're creative enough that you could try builds with different tile combinations and classes and have wildly different runs from each other. The problem is that they're trial and error - the game won't tell you which combinations exist and what they do until you accidentally stumble upon them, which is something I disliked.Every resource you collect is taken to a fixed base where you construct buildings that add new classes, tiles and boosts to your runs. The game has beatable loops without these bonuses, but they significantly help change the game.Playing dungeon master for the sake of strengthening the player character is fun through tiles that pose both a risk and a reward is a fun and addictive idea. The problem is that these tiles and strategies become very static very soon - there will be that one reliable strategy that deals with most of the challenge, most of the game's progression is very predictable  -there are no events, differently from games like Slay the Spire, and you know exactly what each thing does, so it's all about getting varied equips and the right cards in your hand. TL;DR The game is fun but it's very static due to having only a few, repetitive builds that gets you reliably through very similar, event-less runs, where the only variance is in the quality of the equips you get and the cards you get to your hand.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an autobattler. It doesn't work like a roguelite, because there isn't anything to differentiate one run from the next. Your character built from a flood of samey random-stat items (with only a couple of generic RPG stats to choose from), and your map is built from card draws from a pool of a dozen. It all just averages out to the same repetitive slog.It also penalizes you quite heavily for experimenting (and dying) instead of conservatively, preemptively retreating, by taking away 2/3 of the farmed materials that are the only source of progression from run to run. This is strictly a grinding/farming game, where you grind the same way again and again to unlock the next ill-defined base structure. Can't be called a game of the roguelite tradition.But unlike the typical autobattle RPG, it adds just enough micromanagement to stop you from AFKing - but that's bad, because neither the itemization or map-building give you enough real decision-making to make your at-keyboard time engaging.Map cards really have minimal interaction / emergent behavior, and clear optimal usages (if there even is one) for each. Character growth/itemization is just a jumble of tiny +stats and unimpressive traits you can't really build around.On top of that, there's the painfully slow ramp-up for every outing, and obtuse and limited progression between outings in the form of base-building with heavily obfuscated requirements, rewards and placement limitations.It's bad as a roguelite and bad as an autobattler.The slow slog early game easily sucks up the 2-hour return window. Don't even bother.

_childDocuments_.review: I am ♥♥♥ addicted to it, but right now playing is more a frustration rather than fun because of many aspects of this game that are not explained properly and you have to play guessing game or be surprised that some mechanics work in other way than expected.SPOILERS AHEAD: Don't read if you don't want any spoilers regarding mechanics or story, chapters etc.Good example of poorly explained mechanic is "Spikes" mechanic wooden warriors and flesh golems receive at later chapters. Description says: "Anyone directly attacking this creature will receive 4x loop hp of damage back". While this statement is true, it does not specify that this goes before "magic hp". Therefore, I lost 2h run because I killed myself as necro on wooden warrior when I invested too much in attack speed, exceeded my max skeleton numbers and started attacking enemy with fist. I didn't even know what was going on. Next example would be descriptions directly in encyclopedia in game if you would like to learn more. Swarm of bats has "swarm" attribute. This is not explained anywhere in the tab what does it actually mean. Then when you check vampire it says in his skill "pack form" that he "gets the "Swarm attribute during its attack". What the f* does it mean?!Vague and unprecise descriptions are unfortunately very common in this game, which for me is unacceptable for a roguelike game where every decision matters. Especially, when you invest a looot of time to complete some chapters just to die in a very stupid, unpredicted way. Of course, dying is and should be a normal thing in a roguelike game - but here is SUPER frustrating, especially in later chapters. In same genre games, e.g. Hades or Binding of Isaac dying is handled significantly better than here.Also game is very grindy and while first 3 chapters went pretty smooth, it is obvious that for 4th one (and further?) they rather want you to grind materials for your buildings and update them like in some kind of mobile game, which can be appealing for someone, but for me it is a cumbersome task that I would rather omit doing.Next unappealing factor is tons of rng. Starting from cards you receive and finishing at perks monsters receive at next chapters. I really dont like when difficutly increases and it is mostly connected with stupid rng factors like e.g. repellant squeak ability from mosquito - "everyone who doesn't have this ability gets the "ringing in the ears" effect which has a 10% chance of interrupting attacks. basically a disarm that resets your attack - very, very frustrating mechanic that can ruin your whole run when it triggers twice in a row in a beginning of late game fight.END OF SPOILERSI will try to finish this game because I already invested time and attention to it, but I wouldn't buy it right now having the knowledge regarding grindiness, rngness and poorly executed mechanics descriptions this game has.

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure why so many people love this. It has some fun moments, but it feels like a repetitive grindy chore after a while. I enjoyed the demo and put like 5 hours into it, but it just continues like the demo with more and more progression. The difficulty comes from requiring you to farm up good bonuses and other permanent stat buffs. So much of the game is RNG based, and while I enjoy some of the "push your luck" aspects of the game, it ultimately just bogs down in a slog of "do a run, get resources to upgrade town unless you get super lucky on drops and then hope your luck continues to defeat the boss." Rinse and repeat over and over.There are some things you can do to mitigate the luck and increase player agency, but it definitely isn't much. The game often feels like it is just on auto-pilot. Like an idler game that you can't actually idle...Try the demo. If you like the demo and want more of the same then go for it. I enjoyed the demo but thought it would reduce the RNG and reduce the progression requirements to advance, not just add more and more. Oh well.4/10EDIT: Looks like they took down the demo. You can find it here: Click "Install" through that and it should install the demo in your Steam client.

_childDocuments_.review: This grinding-the videogame.Not a bad game but keep in mind that grinding is very much the core gameplay here. It's autocombat and movement, the thing the player has influence on is the map which you can edit.It also does not play like a standard deckbuilder at all-even though the steam tag says so. I went into this thinking its a card game, it is not. The game presents you a choice of which cards you want to be able to draw during your run. Enemies drop these cards and you use them to place tiles on the map. Tiles are either monster spawns or pieces of envrioment that have some sort of effect on your hero or the surroundings. Your goal is to balance the map so your hero is able to level up, gather resources but not be in risk of dying. Eventually you'll fight a boss. -Grinding might be the core idea of the game but I disliked basic features like exp and level up systems being hidden behind a resource barrier. No reason not to have these things from the get go. Overall the game is a nice timesink but it's just not what I expected. It gets pretty repetitive after a while so it's not really my thing. I still recommend it because I think it can def be enjoyable if you feel like laid back grinding.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: It's good to see a roguelite that knows what roguelite actually means and how to implement it. Loop Hero is exactly as described, and makes a great podcast game. There is plenty of depth and progression while keeping the difficulty on the easy side, so it would be perfect for an introduction game to the genre. Nails the sense of discovery which is spread perfectly throughout the game, though the grind can take a long time if you're not paying attention to what exactly you should be going for to progress.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't ever judge a book by it's cover, I saw Loop Hero for the first time in screenshots, didn't look like a game for me, started hearing good things about it, then I saw one of my fav streamers playing it, fell in love, the OST was a banger, fell in love twice, liked the game's mechanics, fell in love thrice. So I decided to give it a try, and it was just as good as I hoped it to be. This game is a classic.Now, to the technical details, this is a game that it's definitely not for everyone:Do you like Sandbox games? If so, you might like how vast and open to everything this game is, it makes you try new things each time you fail or win.Do you like Roguelikes? Well this is a roguelite, You won't lose progress in the story and the things you've accomplished, but you'll have to start from scratch every time, but don't worry, every expedition will be different.Do you like Idle games? Here you're idle, and not idle at the same time, you can let your hero run for hours while you eat or anything, but you'll have to build him yourself and prevent him from dying.Do you like hard and punishing games? A single mistake can lead you to your failure, but losing isn't all that bad, you learn from it and you overcome with your knowledge. If anything of the above isn't good for you, then look for another game.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting take on roguelike games, fairly fun and plenty of replayability to it.The game has an amazing soundtrack that I'd love to see expanded which only gets more awesome when you spawn in a boss.The gameplay can be a little tedious but that's the style of game it is, to me it's a semi-idle rogue-like game.It's more about managing your characters equipment than anything else.Overall, I do think this game is amazing in its own way, but it could do with a mix of things, those being1. More stages and enemies.2. More music.3. More characters.4. More to do with the players base.5. Faster speed settings (It gets a little tedious just waiting half the time, even with the speed boosts you can get in-game)All in all, I'd give this a solid 7 out of 10 for gameplay, a 9 out of 10 for music and a 8 out of 10 overall.Without a doubt I'd recommend this to other players.P.S. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Love all of the visual and audio design. Story is surprisingly interesting. Gameplay starts strong, turns into a slog around the 4 hour mark. Personally, I'd recommend this at 50% off.My feelings are mixed. I absolutely adore the visuals, sound design, and music. The pixel art is excellent, the sound effects are delightfully bit-crushed, and the music never gets old. But, I can't say the same of the gameplay.For the first two hours, its extremely engaging as you learn the intricacies and unlock new tiles. Around 4 hours I started to feel like it was getting repetitive. By the time I got to the Act IV, the game was an absolute slog. I honestly wished there was an "easy mode" so I could just skip the grind and see the end. That's only reason I finished the game, to see the conclusion to the story, which I found surprisingly interesting. It's simple, but the story decently makes sense of the incredibly abstract game mechanics of incrementally building a world in the empty void, as well as your battle against cosmic, god-like beings.Overall, I enjoyed my time, but I wish there was more content (specifically, more tile interactions), and wish the grind was shorter or less necessary for advancement. I think I'd be more comfortable buying this at a 50% discount.P.S. A bit of a rant here about specific mechanics. I really disliked the stamina system that's meant to counteract stacking attack speed. Basically, if you attack too quickly, your stamina is depleted. Then, you lose half your evasion and attack incredibly slowly until you recover. It's ridiculously unsatisfying for this to happen, not to mention needlessly punishing when you rely on evasion. Why would you ever choose this system to compensate for the strength of attack speed? Just lower how much attack speed I can stack instead of punishing me for playing the game and trying to make a powerful character.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: After 13 hours of gameplay, I can say that Loop Hero is pretty amazing when it comes to roguelite. It is much more than that, though. The gameplay is great for someone who's a bit busier because of the looping mechanic so I can finish the loop I am on and come back later to do some more. The reverse tower defense aspect is a great idea and I always find it fun to mix different tiles and find out what happens to make different combinations. Lots of different options for different playstyles, which I am definitely a huge fan of. There's also a sense of mystery when it comes to going further in the game in different dialogues with NPC's and enemies. It reminds me of games I used to play when I was younger, so it's nice to have a bit of nostalgia added in.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of spinning your wheels, going around in circles, or being thrown for a loop - or several thousand - then this game is for you. And you won't even get dizzy doing it!In all seriousness, the game is a simple but effective one. It fits well for those that really like pixel-type graphics, so there's a sense of nostalgia in that regard without being heavily redundant. While I haven't played for long, I do think that the game is a bit grindy, which is fine, and if you're okay with what will likely take a lot longer to complete certain achievements because of it then this game is definitely worth your while.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is weird. By the name it's pretty obvious it's going to be repetitive, but the first two acts of the game (of which there are four) don't feel too repetitive - you unlock new tiles to place pretty fast, usually a new character to play as, still seeing a fair amount of new dialogue, etc. It felt a little cut and dry, but it was relaxing and I didn't feel like I was wasting my time (more than I would playing any other game, anyway). But I'm on Act 3 now, and I've hit what could be best referred to as a difficulty *wall* rather than a spike, and the repetitiveness is starting to set in. There's a few reasons for this:- There is a specific resource you start needing to upgrade camp structures and build new ones that can only be acquired by fighting 4 or more enemies in one fight. The "more" is pretty tricky since the number of enemies you can fight (directly) is capped at 4 anyway, and the chance for the resource to drop scales with how many enemies you are fighting, so it's tough to get. I've spent a few hours trying to farm it across multiple runs and even with fighting as many as 8 enemies on a tile, and it just doesn't drop enough to justify how necessary it is to progress.- by now, I have unlocked like 80% of all the lore and dialogue, and the rest is hidden behind making arbitrary combinations of tiles to synergize new ones and then farming *another* resource to unlock the encyclopedia entry (which isn't all that special anyway in many cases - stuff like the lore on a generic rock could really be left unwritten).- the difficulty of a given fight scales with both what loop you are on (enemies get a certain percent stronger per loop) and what act you are on (which changes that percentage and gives enemies new abilities). The thing is, you pretty much start from 0 strength-wise every run - you have more healing but your DPS is pretty much entirely controlled by what equipment you get. You don't get better weapon or armor draws, and you can only increase your strength with a specific camp building and by a small amount (unless you want to farm the resource from the first point and not use it on other things).- one of the game's best points is trying to optimize the geometry of where you place different tiles to enable synergies and maximize the value you get - but I've stopped unlocking tiles (at least, tiles that are any good), so it's basically just repeating the same geometric patterns every run.- there is a cap on how many resources you can farm of *any* type (both the useful ones and the ones you get a lot of anyway) for each act, so you can't even farm infinitely on one run if you wanted to.So I'm at the point where, in order to add variety and progression back into the game, the easiest thing to do is to just farm up a bunch of resources and upgrade/unlock everything - which involves doing like an hour of boring map setup with patterns I already know, then just sitting and staring at the screen, only pausing to change equipment as it comes in. The game has a lot of strong points to balance out the inherent repetitiveness but I can't recommend a game that turns into full-on Cookie Clicker halfway through.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool concept. first couple runs are great, first time beating the Lich is awesome! Beat the lich again, and he has new dialogue, thats super cool!Card combos are cool when you discover them, but are bare bones to say the least. Lighting temple + Forest? yeah, the forest is now on fire, and gives you a different buff, cool. Later,  I unlocked the river tile, and was super excited to see what happens when i extinguish the forest fire with said river. Nothing happens. All of the other card combinations are like this too, very little depth. For what the game play is, placing tiles and comparing item stats)  having incredible tile combos to plan ahead for in the space available would have been incredible. Speaking of item stats, why is there not any way to auto equip items, or at least sort them in the inventory based on level? Just check a box for which stats you are trying to max in your build and auto equip those items? Oh right, because reading Item stats (and placing tiles) is the only game play this game has. Music is incredible Though.
