_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this game, it really rewards planning forward even though it relies a lot on RNG, the art is spectacular, the interactions are varied enough to keep yo entertained when you find new stuff. What did it for me was the lack of hand holding, you figure out yourself what's going on and what you are supposed to do to progress, beating the first boss was the first and almost only hard thing, every following boss I could beat first try and actually made me feel proud. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Simple game with a simple concept and it does it well, and the story and NPCs dialogue on the loop and within the village is fairly interesting.The soundtrack, the sounds, and the art style are great, and the old NES games came to my mind the moment I loaded it for the first time. Also, the game is tiny when it comes to space (138 MBs!).The hero which you have no effect on other than itemizing is walking in a loop and you have to place monster spawners and other tile sets to create an interactable "board". The inventory is not special, but the way to dispose of items is unique: You have a certain amount of space, you get a new item, the other items move until there is no room and the items begin to salvage into materials which you will need to upgrade the village. You can move them around incase you are waiting for items to work with ones you already have. Overall, fairly cool idea.Some tiles would create new tiles when placed in certain order or next to others, and overall you can control what events/tiles you can get by arranging your "Deck" that you get to unlock new cards as you play.If you die or retreat, the loop will start over again and the hero will have no gear, so rinse and repeat.Cons:The game is extremely grinding heavy. You will have to go again and again through the same enemies, get some materials, go back to the village and upgrade/build stuff to unlock new features. It is enjoyable for a few hours until you understand that that is all there is to it. It turns into mindless grinding with countless of harsh setbacks pretty quick.It is very slow, takes time, but you can figure out good startegy with your gear on how to plan a board that will work for you - every loop the board is getting tougher though, and some runs you get horrid gear because of RNG.You also have no control over your hero's actions. Sometimes they will fight an enenmy that is clearly not the right one strategically, and all you can do is sit and watch how the enemy chips your health away without being able to do anything other than holding your head and do the Darth Vader "NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO!!!"The other thing is when you die you lose 70% of the materials you got. And if you choose to retreat because the board is getting to hard, then you lose 40%, which is not that bad, but you can't choose what to keep or what to give up on, which makes it very RNG heavy - you can have tons of good materials, but the game will be like "Nope! You can only keep the low level materials and you spent 30 minutes on basically crap."I understand planning and thinking and strategy, but maybe give the player some choice? Maybe not all of it, but perhaps 2-3 items that he could exchange? Because it is a slog.Also, the unlockable classes are worst than the one you start with. Speciffically the Rogue.So my verdict is:I think the direction of somewhat rogue-management-idle is cool and all.But unless you really have lots of time on your hands, doing the same thing over and over and over again, and you enjoy to see your hero getting crushed by a boss that does half your health in one hit because you suppose to grind for hours and upgrade your town first that requires numerous brain numbing loops, then this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Giving a thumbs up because I did beat all the chapters, but it was frustrating at times and very repetitive.In order to upgrade your base you need items so be prepared to do the same levels over and over again. Furthermore, once you find a good strategy you like there's no reason to try any different ones because you risk losing, and losing means you only get 30% of the items you collected, so you end up just doing the same stuff over and over again.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I'm greatly enjoying this game.  In its simplicity there's a lot of fun to be had with it.   It's a bit of a grind at times to gather resources with each loop, but when you do get enough resources to purchase something you feel like you actually accomplished something in the game.  I like how certain combination of tile placements also create different outcomes for enemies and other events.  I have barely scratched the surface of this game and I'm still on the first chapter, but it's definitely a game that sucks you in to see just how far you can make it and see what you can unlock next.  Of course the RNG Gods can also be VERY cruel in this game for some runs.   If you don't like games that have a heavy reliance on RNG for item drops, I'd recommend giving the DEMO a run first to see if it's your type of game.  I personally loving the RNG aspects of some games and trying to overcome those odds.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: It hails back to a very nostalgic time in gaming. What I dislike about intense gameplay in other Rogue likes changes here in a stop and go strategy game where all your choices matter. Play it safe or go the distance are choices you make rather than stressful game play you have to commit to. For the price you're getting a lot of content, your brain is moving more than your hands on a controller. I prefer this style of engagement when playing a PC game of this calibre.

_childDocuments_.review: + interesting idea+ various combinations of cards and mechanics+ 3 different characters- simple graphics- minimum gameplay- brought grind and coincidences affecting the resultLittle game from Devolver brings a simple attack in the roguelite gameplay similar to deckbuilding games but also significantly different. The player is in the form of one of the three heroes thrown on a path that begins at the end of the base camp. Using a deck of cards from different places, he builds a map with enemies and bonuses for his hero, which revolves on an endless path of loops and gradually gains equipment and experience until a number of cards unlock the duel with one of the bosses. The only element of gameplay is the strategy of building a path, where the player has to balance the difficulty of obstacles, the choice of equipment and traits and their synergies. Each loop is harder. Nothing else can be affected and the game will fill up automatically.Each expedition ends either with the defeat of the boss, the defeat of the hero or the retreat to the village, which the player improves with the help of fortified raw materials and which, of course, helps him in the next loops. The problem is that the amount of grind is really large and some runes are better to retreat and not meet the boss at all, because at death the player loses in most cases 70% of resources and all special items.And fights are like everything in the game with a large file of coincidences.The positive of the game is a number of different hidden combinations of cards and their location, just a pity that most of them are used mainly in farming, some of the materials needed for upgrades and not so much in gameplay.Despite all the negatives, you can return to the game with the fact that a person can relax in a completely relaxing period, while having coffee or cooking dinner and at the same time try one of the other mechanics or different setup cards.I strongly don't recommend the game to anyone who doesn't like grind and is looking for wide gameplay ... there's nothing there either. The rest, which likes deckbuilding roguelite games, can try it for a lower price.6/10
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Bought on a recommendation from the Besties podcast, A great game to play both actively or passively, You can just have the game running on slow in a separate window and check in every once in a while, or run on fast and pause frequently to place your cards. This game is a great way to mix up the core game loop (pun intended) of a rogue-lite style game. The closest analog i can think of is Soda Dungeon which has a similar RPG setup with automated fighting. This game isn't for everyone, but it's great for people who can get into it. Give it an hour to see if you like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously a rogue-lite, and it's a great one.I got bored of Slay the Spire after like 20 hours, and I'm already at like 60 hours now (was playing offline a while). Comparisons can probably be made, but everything about this is better than that snooze fest. It's styled like an old school RPG, except you don't have to think about each boring fight (it plays itself out based on your preparations), you just think about your next piece of armor or weapon to equip, and the loop is the map, which you build as you go. There are strategies on the map/cards you play, many hidden secrets and combinations to uncover, and a TON of things "back at camp" to upgrade, which keeps you involved and actually progresses/unlocks a fairly interesting and entertaining STORYLINE, which I think is what most rogue-lites lack. It's not a huge amount of dialogue, but enough to really make this game feel like more than other rogue-lites do, know what I mean?I have 25/50 achievements at about 60 hours so far (was playing offline). So it's probably at least 100 hours worth. THE MUSIC IS FRICKIN GREAT! AND THEY ARE ADDING MORE STUFF TOO??! So buy it, but maybe you should wait a minute before you start playing it to have, I'm not sure I'll return for updates once I finish this build. I think 100-150 hours is about right for this and then I'll probably be bored of it. At a certain point you can just let the loop play itself each time, at least for the Rogue character, so there can be some waiting, once you have the good equipment you like. You can still affect the game a little, and need to be mindful about the difficulty as it increases each loop.

_childDocuments_.review: Purchased on a rainy afternoon and dug in. Despite the look of the game, it is very accessible. In minutes, you'll be looping. In half an hour, you'll be confident with most mechanics, and experience the sense of the game opening up before you. Yes, it's a deckbuilder/autoplayer/roguelike, and yet you won't be bowled over by anything too fiddly here.I'm looking forward to looping for hours more, but came to recommend. That said, I'd gladly drop a few more bucks for a dlc if one came my way.

_childDocuments_.review: Deceptively simple, drenched in pixel-art and sound design delicacy, Loop Hero is a game of pure ~stonks go up~ you can play while listening to longform podcasts, though to be honest, when those podcasts ended, I often found myself too involved in aggressive % micromanagement to bother to put on another one. _childDocuments_.review: Nice roguelite game with a quite unique gameplay:Your hero walks on a loop, and all you do is place terrain tiles that can spawn monsters or give bonuses, as well as selecting gears / traits for your hero. Fights are done automatically a bit like in some idle games.Pros:* Quite fun to discover the interactions between tiles and monsters* Interesting gameplay loop* No particular issue / bug encounteredCons:* Even though game is relatively short, it already feels a bit grindy. * A bit annoying that some camp buildings need to be placed next to specific other ones and you don't know about it beforehand so you have to destroy buildings and place them again sometimes* Unlocking tiles does not feel very useful. You don't need many tiles that you don't start with to beat the game* Not much replayability once you beat the game as your camp bonus makes you overpowered for the 4 expeditions available. It would have been nice to have some maps with a fixed strength / set of cards, a bit like the "In Time For Lunch" achievement

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game that doesnt hold you by the hands to tell you what to do, it is simple yet complex in the ways you position the buildings and landmarks you place down and surprising interactions with certain ones as well. A joy to play through and through. The negatives come down to the river being a tad bit too strong which can make the game kinda trivial using it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting take on the RPG/Rogue-lite genre. Eschews combat choice completely (fights are all automatic) in favour of emphasising resource management and equipment optimisation. This does put it dangerously close to idle game territory, but the fast pace of each expedition keeps the player active and entertained.The main drawback is that after while, the game begins to feel like a grind. Earning some of the rarer materials required to expand your camp (a fairly linear task taking place between each expedition) can take quite a long time. Certain rare orbs may only drop once in a 20 minute round, and when 10 or more are required to build a new structure or upgrade an existing structure, the game begins to feel rather tedious.There are three distinct classes which keep things varied, but all three are unlocked fairly quickly, and once you have identified optimal builds for each class not much changes from run to run. Rogue-lites are all about repetition, and this is where Loop Hero starts to fall down. By removing combat from the equation, each new run ends up a scavenger hunt, waiting and hoping that the ideal loot will drop.That said, it took me a good 25 hours to get to the point where things started to feel tedious. I enjoyed the game, and although I doubt I will ever finish it I reckon it's fun enough to be worth a play.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I'd call this game my surprise indie hit of the year! For a good while I was totally hooked by optimising my build and unlocking things. Got nearly all the achievements and wrote a guide too!P.S. An obscure reference but in some small way this game reminded me of the NES dungeon crawler Swords & Serpents, which I loved even though I was too young to fully appreciate what was going on. I didn't speak too much English back then.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Fun at first, but the difficulty ramps up so fast that unless you make a perfect optimized build you're just wasting time on your current run. And since achieving an optimized build depends on RNG, you are going to waste a lot of time.Just buy the soundtrack instead, that's the best part of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Super Grindy, but an awesome grind! If you like to grind in games, this is the one for you. It requires a good amount of strategy and learning your enemies as well as the world cards you play. It takes quite a while to finish the story and then there is also post-game content to dabble in if you are a completionist. I picked up this game as I was looking for something I could idle while I was working during the day. This game is not that. You can idle this game and have your hero repeat loops to grind out low level materials, but all of the higher level mats require strategy and planning. Repeating the loops over and over again while grinding out materials to upgrade your village is extremely satisfying. By the time I reached the final boss (160 hours in because I spent a LOT of time grinding), I was having just as much fun as I did when I initially started. If you like to grind in games and also like a decent amount of strategy, this game is perfect for that. It eats away a lot of time, but that time is enjoyable!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: So, you're curious about Loop Hero, huh?The tl;dr of my opinion is that it's a good game with a few quirks.As of writing, there are some quality of life fixes/changes in the pipe that I hope make the management of your equipment and card reel a bit less frustrating if you make mistakes. They also don't explain to your face that you can only pick a handful of boss perks per SAVE FILE. Aside from these few things, the game is fun. The dialogue is quirky (some weirdness goes on as a result of russian to english translation).
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: First few hours are awesome and fun to play but late game is pure grind and preying to RNG. Dont get me wrong the game is catchy and has big potential but there are also blatant problems. Progression system with everything locked behind one specific resource (Orb of Expansion). Deck building with no real deck just card drops. And dont want me to tell you about RNG - no information about drop probabilities and so many times was my run killed because I didnt get specific card from deck or dropped items were 1-2 levels lower than normally. So, what started as 'wow this is good' ended like 'why it is so grindy and frustrating'.

_childDocuments_.review: So I usually HATE card based games, autobattlers and tower defense games (two of them get way too repetitive and one is entirely based on luck), but this game puts them all together like a perfectly fitting puzzle, having the good of the 3 genres and none of the bad. It is so much fun and weirdly addictive, the art in the game is AMAZING, the story is really interesting (I LOVE timey wimey stuff) and above all it genuinely surprised me. If you are not sure about the game, they have a demo which nets you enough gameplay to know all the basics of the game (up to the first boss, which can still take a couple of HOURS)

_childDocuments_.review: Unique But Not My PaceI'm no stranger to grindy games and jumped into Loop Hero with anticipation. While I respect its innovative mechanics and see why many adore it, the slow progression felt restricting. The looping concept, though fresh, added to the repetitiveness for me. I appreciate the game's unique blend of roguelike, deck-building, and strategy, but its pace just wasn't for me. It might be the perfect loop for others, but I found myself wanting more progression. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really cool game with a really weird difficulty curve. It starts off simple and easy to understand but it very quickly grows into something complicated and confusing. This is a game which mostly "plays itself" and you just make decisions on what tiles to put down in the world and how to upgrade your hero. There is also meta progression in between games where you improve your town which gives you various bonuses and changes in game which can have so many different combinations depending on firstly which class you choose to play as and secondly which cards (the tiles you put in the world) you bring with you. Highly recommend getting the intel centre built in town as quickly as possible. This gives you an encyclopedia which will help a lot in explaining where things come from and how to get them.Overall I think this is a really fun and interesting game which won't be for everyone. It is a really cool mixture of a number of genres and if you are interested in any of them it might be worth checking out. Also the music is pretty great.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is addictive in the best way possible. It's clever, engaging and challenging in a way that never feels frustrating. _childDocuments_.review: I struggled to understand what the game was going to be like from just the trailer/description. After seeing so many good reviews and that the game launched on a small sale, I decided to give it a try. It is a really addicting game! Basically, it's an idle strategy roguelike rpg. You start each "Loop Run" (Let's call this a "Dungeon Run" instead for this review as that's a bit easier to understand without playing the game yourself) on a randomly generated circle road. On this track, slime monsters randomly spawn. You kill the slimes using an auto-battle system (The only input you can change during this time is what equipment you are wearing. So if the fight is going badly, you can try to change your gear to something else more defensive or vice versa), they drop armor/weapons you can equip as well as "cards". These cards range from forests you can place on the track so you can fight wolves to get better xp/loot/cards to mountains you can place outside the track. For each mountain you have next to another mountain, you gain bonus HP! The system is really neat and fun. It is RNG dependent so keep in mind when playing that luck is a part of success. The goal is to stay on the track long enough that the boss spawns. You try to kill it and if you do, then you can try a new dungeon run on a harder but more rewarding difficulty. All the while you're playing the game, you gather building materials. After you die or willingly return to your home base, you can build it up with the materials you've gathered to unlock new classes, new cards, new everything! All of my complaints have already been addressed by the creator and will be implemented in a future patch(s)!1. Can't save during a "dungeon run", only when you're back in your home base. This makes it tough to play when you know you only have 15-20 minutes before you need to do something else as a full boss attempt run can take 30-45 mins. If you close prematurely, the game treats it as if you "retreated" which case you keep only 60% of your gathered items (30% if you die!). So if you want a full 'last as long as you can' run, make sure you have time! In the near future, the developer will add a better autosave feature.2. The game has a double speed feature which is great, but honestly having an even faster speed would be great. Again, the developer is working on adding more speeds. 3. This is a personal complaint that may apply to only a small number of others, but the game at launch already has options that cancel this! The games visual features are really neat and does an amazing job of giving you 80's vibes with it's old school rpg text font and "CRT Shader" which gives the game this bubble effect like you're playing on an ancient monitor with a curved out screen but unfortunately I can't stand to play with these settings for more than a few seconds due to nausea. I get motion sick very easily and having the bubble effect on my flat monitor triggers me real quick haha. I also have a tough time reading the font but you can turn these settings off to a normal flat screen look as well as two other options for text that make it much easier to read! Love these options! Just wish I could play with them normally haha.Love this game so much! Great bargain for $15 for the amount of time you can sink in. Still working my way to beating the 2nd Boss. It's pretty tough! Can't wait to see what future updates come out (More Classes, cards, monsters, etc.)!

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful, clever and new take on the roguelike genre w elements of other genres that would seem contrary, yet it works perfectly as a whole. Graphics are good for the style they're trying to emulate and there's a definite minimalist aesthetic to the game that adds much to the overall story and themes of the game itself. Honestly, after all the time I've spent, I really just want more of everything and hope there's an expansion or, at least, DLC coming. I'd take a sequel too, as long as it maintains the core of the first one. This is, of course, best for people who actively already love the genres this straddles, have an open mind and love experimental games, or, at least, are not slaves to the graphical arms race of the triple A field.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazingly simplistic, frustratingly addictive. Loop hero is a unique rogue-lite management game that requires just enough attention to pause and make decisions every minute but not so much that you can have another eye on netflix. A charmingly stripped down entry whose goal is to send your little warrior around the screen killing enemies and equipping him with the loot they drop to fight increasingly tougher enemies. The combat is automatic and it continues infinitely until you call it quits and bring back your hard earned resources for upgrades. Place perk and monster tiles to influence the progress the way you like and hit that sweet spot of pressure to rise above it all and dominate. Once you have that and all the upgrades it really is all about praying to RNGeezus and as some runs take upwards to nearly an hour to fight the boss, it can be frustrating if you are waltzing in with a poor build only to need to start again from the beginning. Such is the way of most rogue-likes of its ilk. Worth a spin but it is a slippery slope if that strokes your cortex into a groove.

_childDocuments_.review: (To provide context for my review, my system specs are Windows 10/RTX 2080/i9 10980HK)- Very well-done pixel graphics- Music is serviceable, but not really all that memorable- I won't get spoilery, but I will say that I like how the plot gets dropped little by little as you progress through and level up your village. The pacing of the story is one of the highlights of this game and adds to the intrigue- Beyond that, the game feels a little thin in terms of plot- Your gameplay experience mostly consists of placing tiles and waiting to see what happens. If your character runs into a monster, you'll watch the automatic battle. If you run over tiles that heal you, you get healed.  Other tiles grant passive bonuses. That's basically it- Beyond that, the game is more or less a grindfest. You'll gather resources, level up your village, and change up your deck until you're able to beat a boss. After that, you'll change characters and do it again- It's good that the game largely plays itself, because you'll want to have a show or movie to watch in the background- There's a lot of forced replayability. You can't advance without it- The gear system is interesting since it does give you an opportunity to switch up builds early on if what you're doing isn't working well on your current map- This is the first deckbuilder I've played in this style, and I'm confident in saying it's not for me. I can tell by the number of positive reviews that I'm the one who's off-base here, so it's likely that you'll probably enjoy it- . Some nice and novel features get buried beneath a grindy snoozefest

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero Review - 4/5AbstractLoop Hero is an incredibly well executed roguelike game that picks and chooses the best features from adjacent genres to create addictive gameplay that is only held back by execution on a few features, mainly its visuals that are well stylized but often fail in their ability to effectively convey information to the player. GameplayThe core gameplay loop of Loop Hero is pretty simple. Your hero walks around in a loop and has different things happen to them (fight enemies, regain health, etc.) based on the board state. Enemies drop various cards you select before starting your expedition that you can play as the game goes on to manipulate the board in your favor.It’s part roguelike, deck builder, tower defense, autobattler and probably a few others that I’m missing but the way the stew comes together from all these inspirations is very addicting. It taps right into that “one more turn” dopamine dip at just the right dosage. Learning how cards interact with each other, slowly tweaking a strategy that fits your playstyle and seeing just how far you can greed with keeps each run exciting. And the game never really gets to a point where you can fully auto pilot and keeps you engaged in a way that feels fun. Like on the runs where the board was pretty much full and I was discarding extra cards every round, you still need to be wary of better equipment coming into your inventory, having your active equipment being stolen by enemies or high rolling an oblivion card to make the board a little less hostile.The only issue with the gameplay for me takes place outside of the core gameplay loop in the camp building / prepping for expeditions. Picking your loadout for each expedition is very passably executed and can serve to have some quality of life improvements (say being able to copy builds from one act to another) but not too major to complain about here. The camp building feature of the game, where you upgrade your camp using various resources you pickup during your runs, is the only real standout flaw for me with Loop Hero. I don’t think the idea of it is bad for a game like this! What makes this part of the game a pain is mostly the visuals. Because of the art style, I have no clue what half of the resources I need to craft improvements are by just looking at them. And when you go to try to craft and you need more of that resource, hovering it doesn’t tell you what it is. You have to go into the encyclopedia and then from there find out what the item is and what kind of enemies drop it. Ideally you’d be able to tell what the item is from just looking at it and then have the option of making an educated guess on what kind of tiles/enemies might drop it (Wooden Warrior drops wood, makes sense) or check the in-game encyclopedia for more info.And this isn’t something you can ignore. Some of the options later up the build tree and upgrades to parts of the camp are damn near necessary to make deep runs into Act 2 and for surviving act 3 and beyond. Gamers are for sure spoiled with how good menus/UIs have gotten in the modern era but this heighted expected level of quality makes these flaws much more noticeable. Additionally, the visuals also start to feel lack luster as the game progresses to later acts where you’ve got close to a full board and it can be hard to know exactly what the hell is going on. Like can you spot the goblin camp I want to oblivion on this board? And how long did it take you to find the hero who has a damn arrow over their head to help make them stand out. They do a great job at executing on the bitart/old school style for the game’s characters and world but some implementations of this design makes the game not great on the eyes or incredibly inefficient at conveying information. The visuals don’t make the game unplayable or impede gameplay in a way that gets frustrating but these are the kind of issues that would surely sour the experience for last seasoned gamers.Music/SoundThe tracks that play during the core gameplay are great at keeping you locked in and getting you hyped up for the boss fights. The only issue is that for the core game, there’s two or three tracks that it cycles between. So by about 5-6 hours into this 20-30 hour game, you’ve already heard these tracks far too often which could easily have been alleviated by adding a few more tracks to the game. I will say though (most likely through some type of stockholm syndrome), I circled back to enjoying those same three songs more during the tail end of my playthrough but still the point stands.The sound design for the most part plays its role well of directing your eyes to the corner of the screen that needs your attention to keep your quest marching on. There were a few sound queues that I still wasn’t quite sure what they were supposed to be signifying by the end of the game but with how hectic game boards can get in the later acts, I’d chalk this up more as a nitpick against the sound and more a flaw more aptly levied against the game’s visuals. StoryI think the story is about time or killing god or memories or something? Because the gameplay doesn’t really compel you to pay attention or care about the story in any way, it really just feels like an afterthought. From the oodles of extra info that you can unlock about everything in the game via the encyclopedia, it does seem like there was effort put lore behind the pieces that make up the game but the game does not inspire any desire to learn more. While I don’t think a compelling story is needed for a game to be good, for a game to be perfect for me–it needs to have me invested in the story to some extent which Loop Hero undoubtedly fails at. I do love the black hole pups though. 10/10 character. ConclusionIf you are fan of roguelikes or strategy games in general, Loop Hero is no question a must play game for you. If there is anything that peaks your interest about this game, it is absolutely worth giving a shot especially if it’s on sale because you’ll know for sure if you’ll love it or not well before you hit the refund timer on steam.

_childDocuments_.review: While its a good game, for what it is, IDK if i would really suggest it; so this isnt really a solid No on recomending.The premise is to loop around an area and kill things while making the area more difficult with tiles that you place on the road, and at first it's a cool concept; but come the 20th run and nothing really changes, or you've died to the boss every time you encounter him because he hits you for 100+ hp per hit and your health is never really over 1.5k, it gets kind of tiring. You can get upgrades in the village which acts as sort of a hub that you upgrade to unlock classes and features. Another note, you start as a warrior class, and you can unlock the rogue pretty easily, but good luck surviving anywhere near as long as the warrior. As the warrior you have access to vampirism, so every hit gives you an amount of life, but the rogue has no access what soever to any form of life gain outside of the limited amount of potions you have (3), and they run out very fast. _childDocuments_.review: It's an excellent game which has your hero do battles automatically and you gain loot from defeated foes. Loot dropped can be equipment for your equipment slots or a variety of cards to place down on different tiles during your many expeditions to gather resources for your camp with each structure granting you access to different rewards, mechanics or even a new character. If you are looking for an auto-battler with a deck based world building system with a variety of cards to place on tiles with a few having interactions with each other, I recommend you pick up this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll recommend because it's a classic 'great-jewel-of-an-idea' game that's worth playing around with for a while (especially true at this price point), but sometimes your library gets stuffed with these $5 cool ideas and you start to find out which ones really have legs, and which ones you might not stick with. My limit with Loop Hero seems to be the second of 3(?) major bosses. I've found that I'll be enjoying a run, accruing power through the fun roguelite synergy mechanics, and then not standing a chance against the boss. This is, of course, a skill issue, but I've gone looking for tips and found that my struggle is largely based on neglecting the meta-progression (you build up a little village between runs). "Ok, cool, a roguelite where it's actually necessary to consider your meta progression, that could be fun," I thought to myself. Unfortunately, in this case, I simply find those mechanics dense (again, skill issue), and more importantly: time consuming. Basically, it seems to me that you're supposed to be bailing on runs to bring home 100% of your supplies. You don't actually try the boss every time, and instead you build out this town, and gather boons for future runs. To me, that's a huge flaw vs other roguelites, in which the whole fun is scraping your way towards an unlikely victory, run after run. Maybe I'm dead wrong, and the skill issue is worse than I thought, but that premise really hurts the game for me, and I'm not sure I'll find myself returning to grind out the W. Had fun, won't finish. The $5 cool idea graveyard (not to be dramatic).

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR 9.5/10 Worth 15 bux for sure-QUICK TIPS FOR NEW PLAYERS-Mostly just some quick pointers to help you figure out resources as it can be confusing to start. -Build your Intel Center ASAP, this lets you know how to get various seemingly rare materials and what each enemy can drop as well as their abilities. -You will get high end materials more often when you run a higher level. Most notably Shapeless Mass, Living Fabric, and Craft Fragments needed for mid tier buildings. IDK if grinding these out using the first Level will even work. I seemed to get very few. For example, fighting 5 or more creatures can yield an Orb of Expansion. While running level 1 I seemed to get them about 25% of the time where as on level 2 I got them early every time I fought a 5 stack or more. How do you get a 5 stack when 4 is the normal max? Vampires Mansions. Any fight that happens next to a Vampire Mansion will have a Vampire added to it regardless of the cap. -Use the first level to grind some boss tokens (Skulls), you'll need them. You use them to keep your loot when you die. Now for the long winded part. Pixel Art 9/10  Enough frames of animation to make it look good but not SotN level. Rogue Like gimmick 10/10Normally, you die, lose your stuff and get some points to spend. Loop Hero has a few takes on the "fail"-Retreat anytime (keep 60% of loot) Use this when you know your gonna die in the next few fights-Retreat at camp (keep all loot). Use this when you got a bunch of materials you where looking for and don't want to lose them to a boss fight. Or just to end the run early cuz you got the mats you needed. -You die (keep 30% of loot)This is obviously never ideal, but bound to be part of a rogue like. Letting you keep some materials is nice. -Pay with boss tokens (keep all loot)At anytime you suffer loot loss due to death or emergency retreat, you can pay with boss tokens (you get them for downing bosses) to keep all the loot. Music 7/10Can get old at times,  but it's already gotten to me... that "new expedition" music or when you summon the boss. Like booting up your Ps1... here we GO!Controls, 9.5/10It's an auto battler (sadness) where most of your control is simply placing tiles or pausing the game. I could stand for maybe a 3x speed mode especially early on but other than that no issues. Deck Building gimmick 9/10Your deck consists of buildings and landscapes that you place across the map to buff yourself, spawn certain enemies (place 9 rock or mountain tiles in a 3x3 square to get a large mountain that spawns harpies for instance). There are a fair number of surprise combinations (place a Vampire next to a village XD). You unlock more card options by building your home base with the materials you bring back from runs. Base Building Gimmick 8/10It's pretty simple so far, few buildings have requirements (place the smelter next to the smith sort of thing). It could use a little more "life" to it. Get to know the people you're rescuing and the town your building and such. Combat... ?/10I mean... it's auto fight so there's not much to contribute as a player aside from what you equip your hero with. I'd sure like to see some abilities or something and maybe a 3 man party sort of deal. Gameplay Loop 10/10, I mean it better be good Loop is in the title right? lolI've died a bit and never really felt like it was a total waste of time or loss. Always down for another loop. Once you get some boss tokens built up you can experiment with more deadly setups that way in case you get wupped by them you can still trade tokens to keep your hard earned materials.

_childDocuments_.review: Entertaining but a bit grindy after a while. _childDocuments_.review: When I went to buy this game I thought it would be a tower defense style game but it actually turned out to be something much more unique! This game is a lot of fun and I tend to play it in short 1 hour bursts once or twice a day, playing a loop at a time. You can keep up a loop longer and longer as you progress through the game, but the ability to retreat whenever you want allows me to sneak in a game even if I don't want to play for long. The game is also GORGEOUS, the pixel art is lovely and full of style and personality. I especially think the main character is adorable. The music is also great, it has that crunchy 8-bit aesthetic along with the atmospheric tones that immerse you in the world. I sometimes get the song you hear when you first start a loop stuck in my head and I'm not at all complaining.I have really only one serious complaint about the game and that's the incredibly slow progression. I have played for around 13 hours at the time of writing this review and I don't feel like I've made much progress in the story at all. I have definitely made some progress, but if you are looking for a game to complete all in one sitting this is definitely not the one for you. Because progression is so slow often times loops can feel near identical to each other because there is no change, unless you want to switch up your class and cards just for fun, which is why I don't usually play more than one loop at a time. Progression IS really cool and it's so fun to discover the new things the game has in store, but it will take some grinding away at the loops and experimenting with tiles to find them. This really doesn't ruin the game and I still really love it, but it is something that I and others have noticed. As long as you're okay with chipping away at the game one loop at a time then it is an awesome game with amazing atmosphere, art, character, and gameplay!

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say, this game is amazing.  Don't let my playtime fool you, I've got about 12 hours in after one day. The core gameplay loop is very clever and the ways you can play as you unlock classes increases exponentially. Really, exponentially. _childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is basically greatest Super Famicom game that never existed. Until now. Playing it kind of makes me feel like I'm playing an obscure fan translated ROM of a game that I should have known about 20 years ago. Anyone remember Phantasy Star III? Where your characters were determined by who you married? This game reminds me of that. The game's grandparents are Rogue and Carcassonne, who's bizarre offspring married an idle battler. Their kid then hooked up with Diablo style gear slot machine game, and some obscure japanes anime style indie crafting game no one ever played but was really good, these two never knew they were half siblings and fell in love to insestually produce:Loop Hero. I expect I, and many others, will log many many hours happily grinding away at this thing. I also find myself very excited about the prospect of expansion on the game. Much like Slay the Spire this appears to be an absolutely perfect platform for just adding more, without unbalancing things.An excellently crafted game, well worth paying the makers just for their fine work.

_childDocuments_.review: I might come back to it on a later date and change my mind, but, after 15h+, I didn't enjoy it that much.One thing I really enjoyed is the terraforming of the environment and making things interact with each other the way you please. But the gameplay isn't fun enough to grab my attention full time, but, meanwhile, the game can't be played on idle.The worst part for me was how the equipment works. You'll get lots of garbage, but you'll have to read the description of each one of them before discarding them to make sure they are in fact garbage. By default, when you hover over the description of equipment, the game pauses, which makes things way more monotonous. But I'm not sure if disabling that is ideal, especially if you're on the 4x speed, because you can become overwhelmed by the addition of new equipment to choose from, and equip the best equipment as soon as they are available might be crucial for a good run. A solution for that would be to reduce the game speed, but then it becomes more boring than it should be.I'll try again this game in a couple of months because I really liked the concept. But, for now, it's a thumbs down, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not bad it's just not rewarding in the way games like this should be.Fantastic game but just too punishing and that guts it. Progression takes too long, if you kept 50% or more of the loot after a fail instead of 30% maybe it would keep the momentum better so that I'd really want to keep coming back to it. As it is it is addictive and has all the right elements in there but there's this unnecessary mobile gameish wall with bosses. You have to grind to be OP. Otherwise you throw most of your progress away and then have to go through the same boring setup for each run, which means you grind a lot of safe boring runs. I understand that it's a roguelike/-lite but the core loop in this genre should be interesting enough vs the difficulty, and this in this it isn't. _childDocuments_.review: presents itself as an interesting and quirky idea for a rogue-like, but that's all it really remains. The novelty runs dry quickly due to a heavy grind throughout, as well as a vast lack of variety, pacing and balancing of difficulty that make each run feel more like a chore than it needs to be.• Manipulating the map to control what enemies spawn is a fresh and interesting mechanic, even though it never gets developed much further• Three diverse character classes, though the Necromancer feels like the superior class by far, offering a very different playstyle compared to the rest• The general concept gets run into the ground and becomes monotonous quickly• Lack of variety between runs severely damages any sort of replayability• Lack of player engagement• Lack of depth to mechanics makes the game feel extremely dull• Slow-paced and extremely grindy• Poor difficulty balancing between chapters forcing players to do resource-grinding runs• Hard to stay invested for long play sessionsIn , you'll be running around in a randomly generated loop with barely anything on it besides a few slimes. Each run you'll be able to manipulate the surrounding area with cards that you collect from killing enemies as well as gear that you can equip to survive the loop. These card effects range from spawning enemies, granting additional HP, restricting the number of enemies that can be on a single tile etc. You’ll receive specific resources when you walk over cards that you place on the path rather than the surrounding area. These are used to build new structures inside your camp.Each chapter tasks you to defeat the boss in order to progress, in order to spawn the boss in the first place you’ll need to fill up a bar. Everytime you use a card the bar will slowly fill up, once it’s full, the boss will spawn and you’ll have a choice of fighting or retreating back to camp with all the resources you’ve gathered. If you are unsuccessful in this attempt then you’ll only receive 30% of the resources you’ve gathered.Upon experiencing your first few runs, you'll probably get into the swing of how things work. The main problem that persists for  is that the player engagement and mechanics never evolve or have much depth. One half of the game is deciding on what gear to equip and where to place your cards, the other half is brainlessly watching the character run around and slay enemies. It would be an insult to call  an 'idle game,' but I couldn't help but think this when I was only half paying attention to what was happening. Simply watching battles play out, with your only influence being the stats on your equipment, doesn't call for much engagement.Unlike other roguelites,  seemingly pads out the playtime by making the bosses you fight extremely difficult. This not only forces players to grind for resources in order to build structures in their camp, but also causes a lot of frustration. The first boss was fine, took a few tries, but after that it gets viciously difficult, which begs the question of whether there is skill to this game. They've stripped away battle mechanics so what influence do you actually have? You decide which stats to prioritize (evading, regen, defense, counter-attack, etc.), how many enemies to spawn and which terrain cards will benefit you the most. When the entire game boils down to these decisions, it's hard to feel like you're having much of an influence on the game at all.Manipulating the loop with cards is probably the most interesting mechanic that this game has to offer. You'll discover, through experimentation, that putting together specific cards on the map will cause new things to happen. A basic example of this would be if you place nine rock or mountain cards in a 3x3 grid, then would turn into a Mountain Peak that gives you +48% max HP but spawns a Harpy every two days. All of the terrain cards act in a similar way, spawning enemy encampments on your path. Even if some of the other beneficial structures can also spawn new enemies that you'll have to deal with.It's safe to say that the variety is severely lacking in this game which is a major issue for a title that focuses on repetition. Unlike other roguelites, this one doesn't add enough random elements to the table to make each run feel different and to warrant playing it over and over again. Yet, the game encourages you to do exactly that, grinding over and over again to gather enough resources for building new structures in the camp to make the next loop more bearable. The only way of making a run feel different is by changing the cards that you bring to each loop, however, this contradicts with how brutally difficult the bosses are. If you have a good set of cards that you know work well together, then why would you bother changing up your entire deck for the sake of making it more 'varied' in exchange for making the game even more difficult?The only variety the game has to offer is found in the character classes that all play slightly differently from one another. The Warrior, the Rogue and the Necromancer with the latter being my personal favorite. These characters can only equip specific items making you focus on different stats depending on your class, but if you boil these down you're literally just focusing on different stats and haven't got much influence on the battle— aside from the Necromancer where you can manipulate how many skeletons you can spawn at what level and the quality of the summon.The resources that you collect during your runs, via placing terrain and traversing through road cards, are used to build new structures of the camp that will aid you in future runs. These can range from giving you healing potions, friendly archers fighting alongside you, to reviving your character once per loop etc. These structures make each chapter more bearable to tackle, however some of these structures are just too pricey. You might grind for a few runs, build the new facility and then stop because of how tremendously dull it is to collect those resources.That being said, I still appreciate the few unique structures you can build and upgrade inside the camp. It's a shame that the build tree is so linear and doesn't branch off into different directions for more diversity with structures. provides an interesting concept for a game, but drags it through the mud and then runs it over multiple times before you can even get halfway through. The need for constant grinding is laughable at times, the balancing for bosses seems purposely over the top to pad out playtime, the lack of variety makes every run feel monotonous and almost exactly the same.  is simply a good idea, executed poorly over and over again with each progressive chapter feeling too repetitive. Rather fitting, given the name.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is definitely a gem of a game that i would put in the same category of games like Papers please because it's very fun and addicting but i don't know why. While papers please has you doing actual 9-5 work, Loop hero has more traditional game mechanics and takes from many different game genres. Its a deck builder but not really, Its a rougelike but not really, its a city builder but not really, its an auto battler but not really. So what exactly is it? erm i don't know, but it is fun.You walk around a set path in a big circle and you fight monsters as you go (combat is done automatically). Defeating monsters give you armour and weapons that upgrade pretty vanilla RPG stats. there's also a change for monsters to drop cards that allow you place things (on the loop) these can be mountains dearests that increase attack speed and health, or Cemetery's and spider dens that spawn enemies and give you resources to upgrade and build new stuff at the home base. This is the main gameplay loop, the interesting part for me was the different combinations of cards that have different effects if you place certain cards next to each other. For example a 3X3 of rock and mountain tiles significantly increase health or putting a river next to a dearest tiles to turn it into an oasis. There are many different ones that have some pretty game changing effects so experiment. When you place enough stuff down you will fight a boss, there are 4 in total and there all very unique, although there's not really much you can do except equip the best armour you can and get lucky.Apart from thinking about where to put the cards you get the other main decision you will be making is when to GTFO. If you want to play it safe you can leave at anytime and keep 60% of you resources. The best way is if you complete a full circle you get to leave with 100% of your stuff but it can only be done on one square so you have to way the risk and reward. Do you want to risk losing 70% of your stuff or go around again and get more stuff for you home base, it's up to you. Also quick side note even through its a rougelike you don't actually die permanently and get kicked back to the beginning of the game, you just get teleported back to your home but you lose most of your gathered recourse's. So you will always be making progress towards your next upgrade it's just how long it takes.          I don't usually care much about these 2 things however there both really good. First the character designs are all really good especially the bosses one dude is a lich with the body of a universe another is a hunter with a gun and 2 black whole dogs. Okay and lastly the music, you will be spending a lot of time just watching stuff happen, luckily the game has a great soundtrack to make sure you don't fall asleep (not to say the game's boring but you can get into a trance just placing stuff and watching combat if your playing for a while.  For a game about going in circles over and over its pretty fun and is a pretty relaxing game, maybe just to end the day with. although going around and around in circles all day can get pretty draining so i could only play for a few hours at a time without my brain turning to mush. Still for like $15 it totally worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a true trap. Loop Hero is one of those games that is great initially and seems like it's going to really blossom as you start to progress. Unfortunately, it does the opposite. I've put 13 hours into the game and I'm on Chapter 3. I only have a couple of buildings left to build and I kind of just don't care. The game has already become tedious. I think the thing that kills the fun the most for me is having to constantly stop and think about the new equipment I've gotten and if it is ever so slightly better than what I currently have. It really breaks up the flow of the game and makes me want to end my current loop sooner rather than later.Ultimately, there just isn't enough content in this game to keep it enjoyable for more than a handful of hours and the the tedium of some of the major mechanics just destroys what fun there is to have.

_childDocuments_.review: The first couple hours of this game were fantastic and I was very excited, but any semblance of depth falls away after you beat the first boss and the initial mystique wears off. There is very little to this game. I enjoyed my first 5 or 6 hours but after building about 2/3rds of the buildings and trying out all three classes, I realized that the gameplay was extremely binary and honestly, balance did not feel very good. I found myself going Lifesteal Warrior over and over again because it was the only thing that seemed even remotely successful for me.  (I have not replayed but they did add in speed sliders after I made this review which probably fix this), which only adds to the tedium, even when you aren't going Lifesteal. The card variety is pretty scarce as well, with something in the ballpark of 30 available excluding the combos, of which there are about ten. Many of them were very uninteresting, however, and many had drawbacks that didn't really seem necessary, such as buffing enemies with the same buff you get, or applying the same debuffs to you as enemies. Because of the drawbacks all the "good" things have, nothing is/feels rare because you can always have everything. Initially, it appeared there were 11 gear slots (which was exciting because I only had access to four initially), but I found out through researching the wiki that I can only get a fifth slot per character, and getting that slot applies a penalty to all of my other pieces of gear? This actually disincentivized me from building the structure you unlock this from, as I didn't want to gimp my base gear for a helmet slot that always had retaliation damage (for the warrior). Why show them all for each character, then? Not sure if it was a deliberate misrepresentation of depth or what? Maybe I'm just dumb and someone will comment and correct me, if this is also important to you. Overall, I did enjoy my time with this, but I don't think it's worth $15. I don't usually buy things not on sale, but got sucked into the hype on this one. Rookie mistake. Should additional (probably free because honestly I feel like I already over-invested) content come that fleshes out the core loop of the game or introduces new variables or things to pursue that are interesting, I'll gladly swing back in, check them out, and update this review. If not, I'd say wait until you can get this guy at least 50% off before you pick it up, Otherwise, I'd say play NGU Idle if you want to play an Idle game, or Slay the Spire/OverDungeon if you want a card based  RPG, as I enjoyed both of them more than this overall. For any 20+ hours conquerors of this game who are prowling reviews for some reason, if anything I said is incorrect please let me and others know as I don't have any intentions to mislead. EDIT: Wasn't allowing comments initially. Whoops. EDIT 2: I tried the  and it didn't blow my socks off.

_childDocuments_.review: This is MUCH grindier, slower, and more unexciting than I think it could be while still fulfilling what the audience wants from it. The mechanics are very dry, the runs are incredibly repetitive, and it involves waaay too much interaction to even play like the idle game that it probably should be for how shallow the mechanics are.I gave it 20+ runs while playing as an attention-keeper while playing D&D online (easily distracted from the game otherwise), and it was a decent way to keep my hands mindlessly occupied, but it really wasn't anything more than that. Honestly, I'm astounded to see I played it for 12 hours, I feel like I made no "progress" at all in that time.The "town as skill tree" system is incredibly incremental, there are no meaningful power spikes or rewarding moments, everything you get just feels like a tiny drop in the bucket of an endless grind. There is also *very little* you can do to control a run or opt into any specific build. You basically just HAVE to equip the best items you find, you almost NEVER have choices in which ones to equip because the levels/rarities are so inconsistent, and there's no clear way to control the variability there or what you get. Even for what it's trying to do, it's failing to do it well.Gameplay Design: 4/10User Experience: 7/10Aesthetic: 7/10Narrative Design: 2/10Story/Writing: 0/10

_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The idea is great and execution is interesting but this game has a MASSIVE issue : Victory is obtained by farming.You can place your cards the best way possible, be lucky with your loot and gear and you will absolutely fail that level because you were supposed to unlock a building in your town that give you access to some new cards that give you what you need to win.Building are obtained by spending ressources. You gain some in levels and you ONLY retain 30% of these if you fail the level. So you just start levels, farm ressources, leave before you get killed, upgrade your base when you can, rinse and repeat until you obtain the building that will unlock that one card to help you. You realize that far after the refund timer.As a result, the game is padded massively with boring grind. For the comparison's sake, imagine Slay the Spire: but you need to lose 30 runs on purpose to obtain the basic cards you need to win your first run with.It's like the devs realized the game was only 5 hours long, so instead of having some interesting 5 hours, they padded it with a 40 hours long grindfest.It's quite a shame, the idea of the game is great and quite addictive, but I can't recommend it due to that.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: There's no denying that this game is ffffiiiiiine? It's fine, it's well-priced, but you'll pay with your time rather than your wallet, and be left feeling like you wasted most of it. I've no idea why it took off as hard as it did: it's got lovely visuals and a great moody soundtrack, but its entire premise is barely built upon, and instead stretched out into monotony.So you have a lil guy who walks around a pre-built path in a loop and you place objects around in each others' proximity to create enemies and loot and whatnot for them to pick up. It's a good idea for an almost-idle game, but chapter 1 is the same as chapter 4, and the bonuses you get from placing anything other than monster spawners is just negligible.It sounds lovely, the idea of building a landscape in a void out of a hand of cards, improvising as you go, but none of it really does anything, other than increase your health by 1 point, taking you from 2098 to 2099, or giving you 23 health per day instead of 22. The persistent town building is exactly the same, meaning what is meant to be the big reward for your grinding away is instead just kind of mandatory to progress, but wishy washy and minor. So the aesthetic board building aspect is gone, so is the pay-off with the city building, fine, I guess that's not what they were going for. But what about monsters? Gameplay? Well, there aren't very many types, and their numbers just go up the longer you play. Well... loot? Nope, maybe 5 or 6 sets that don't really work well with one another, so you sit there waiting for a full vampirism set or riposte or whatever, basically just playing snap with the game.As I said, chapter 1 = chapter 4: you place things as you get them, concentrate it all on the bendiest section of the loop, and watch it unfold. You can't quite switch off though, or you'll die, so you have to keep swapping out equipment, arbitrarily switching out builds depending on what drops. It's not really satisfying; there's very little strategy, which would work as a minimalistic idle game, but this falls somewhere in between where it just ended up feeling like a lacklustre chore with great ambience. By the end I was running the game in 10x speed and wanting it over just because I'd already sunk a bit of time into it.It's fine, I'm just not sure what it was meant to be, nor why it's been spoken about so much: I finished it and wouldn't recommend it to anyone, because it's not quite easy or simple enough to be a fun throwaway afternoon mobile game, but nor is it any more engaging than your average skinner box.

_childDocuments_.review: I can personally recommend Loop Hero to anyone who likes rogue-like or rogue-lite games (paired with card elements). The pixel art style is kept quite minimalistic and gives off a pleasant retro vibe. The controls are very simple (passive), so anyone interested in the game will have to think about whether they might like it. The game manages to make you want to keep going with each new round to find out what other card combinations might trigger.Definitely a buy recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: In loop hero a litch causes a cataclysm that destroys the world and it is up to you to rebuild the world and grow more powerful by defeating monsters and gearing up to take on bosses who want to destroy the world all over again.The Good: Loop hero has a very good feel to it of slowly building up a character and making the map full of little buildings, forests and monsters. This leads into the deck building where you create the world based off what you choose and makes for some interesting choices before runs start. I personally like the visuals, especially the character portraits but I can see how some people can be put off by the pixel graphics. The stats are also very easily readable and make it clear what you can do and how your character is built up. There is also a good variety between the 3 classes mechanics.The Bad: There is a massive lack of content in loop hero, only 5 bosses (4 main ones and a final secret boss), 3 classes, and a small amount of item effects. Bosses have no major way to interact uniquely with the player since the game is an auto battler it's easiest to just make your character a massive stat stick who cannot die rather than thinking about their mechanics just hoping that you get lucky and hit the right target first. This problem extends to the classes because their mechanics don't matter and you just want sustain. The root of all this is that there is not an interesting loot game you get multiple rarities but they do not matter because all you want is evasion on thief and necromancer, and you want vamperism on warrior, all other stats just don't matter as much because bosses hit too hard and normal enemies have major number advantages in the later stages. I wish we had more skill based options because the current skill ceiling is just based off your deck building and land placement. The last major negative is the meta progression. Normally in a rogue lite you can slowly gain power for future runs so even if you die you gain some small advantage, in loop hero you are punished for dying by losing 70% of all resources you picked up. Usually a dev will expect a player to die and not punish them this harshly, the idea of losing future resources you could have made being enough, this forces you to retreat back to camp and throw away the current run to build up your camp. For a normal player they will crawl through the meta progression unless they throw away runs and skilled players just won't bother with camp because they can just beat the game and fight the secret boss in 7 runs. This makes the deck progression slow as well since getting most new cards is tied to making new camp tiles so the most interesting choices in the game are locked behind a slow grind or are just never used. There is also passive items you can bring to runs but they do so little besides the really strong one that it's obvious which to choose from a glance. Overall this game just needs more, more heroes, more item effects, more ways to progress and more choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Great idea, poor execution. I love what this game is trying to do, but it just gets very boring after a while. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not quite sure how to feel about Loop Hero. I enjoyed the art style of it very much and think it's the most beautiful aspect of the game, but the same cannot be said about much else. Before I even got acclimated to the gameplay, the first thing I noticed, and as the more I played, was that the writing and dialogues were just not very good; Characters talk as if they're in a Marvel movie, and the writers were clearly out of their depth when choosing existentialism as one of the underlying themes of their story. The writing is lukewarm, to put it mildly, and since Four Quarters is a studio based in Russia, I'm unsure whether it was the fault of the weak translation or if the writing itself is just that forgettable. Thankfully, the gameplay is somewhat redeemable. I said "somewhat" because, frankly, it can also be boring at times due to its minimalistic approach to combat. In short, there's none. The act of walking and killing monsters is automated and done entirely by the computer, and your responsibility as the player mainly focuses on resource management. Unfortunately, I didn't find this aspect of the gameplay all that fun or engaging either, and I often wished I could do more than stare at my screen while the computer did most of the work for me. Moreover, the game is a lot more grindy than I expected. Trust me, the gameplay won't be that interesting by the time you get to your 100 runs, but that's precisely how much you can expect to do if not more if you want to unlock and upgrade everything. And by the end, much of it feels like a chore, and the game could've benefited greatly had the developer not made it so grindy as if you're playing a mobile game. Overall, I would say Loop Hero is just an average game. One that manages to introduce a novel gameplay structure but overstayed its welcome by the ten-hour mark, whose playtime got padded out by grind, and with a story that left me mostly unimpressed. I have mixed opinions, and it's moments such as these where I wish Steam would provide reviewers with more options than just a binary choice between a simple yes or no. It's for this reason that I'm forced to give Loop Hero a thumbs down, but if bought on sale, I think the purchase can be somewhat justified as a worthwhile experience for casual players. But, personally, it's not my cup of tea, and I feel like I could've gone without playing it and not missed out much.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting game that completely embodies the idea of risk vs reward. Killing enemies gives you gear which is always nice, but it also gives you cards you can use to add extra hazards to the map. Placing extra enemy spawners makes things harder but all those extra enemies mean more chances for upgraded gear. It's a tough thing to balance as greed can quickly outpace preparedness and leave you overrun. Will also run on a potato and feels super nostalgic.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very solid for a dozen hours while you are still learning new things and discovering new interactions. Unfortunately, you will likely run out of things to learn a good ways before beating the game, and then it begins to feel repetitive. Perhaps DD had this monotony in mind considering the themes of the story, but I digress. The game has taken great care towards being polished and well-rounded. The soundtrack is wonderful, the spriting is elegant, and the foundation of the game is so firm as to be unshakable. It really is an excellent experience while it lasts, it's just that it doesn't quite last as long as one would like. In spite of these problems, I still recommend Loop Hero if only because it plays so well initially.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good roguelike with typical progression system after death. Death penalty is big (70% is lost), but can be strategically reduced (to just 40% lost) or even completely avoided by strategically stopping the loop earlier.The loops works like a magic: fight a bit, leave when it gets harder, upgrade/unlock, try new strategy until the very last boss is dead. Kind of hard to stop playing even with that little control the game require.It can be played as idler at some point after starting the loop, this is from where my hours mostly comes.+ working game loop: build/fight, then upgrade base, repeat to progress;+ interesting mix of game mechanics: strategically build your loop and gear your fighter while game is basically auto-playing itself;+ good enough balance, reaching last difficulty and killing last boss doesn't require too much farming or too many upgrades;+ good variability: 3 classes, choice of cards and boss perks for next run, its interesting to experiment;- RNG and difficulty spikes, usually after a wrong choice, it could be a smooth run and then sudden death with all potions and ressurections used in just one fight, kind of hard to predict or avoid, this is where one may get frustrated and give up;This game is hard to compare to anything. But it's surely the one of the most addictive game loops I've experienced. I can only imagine how many hours I'd spend with more content. Crossing fingers for Loop Hero 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a highly addicting game. After getting it on release, i found myself drawn to this game over and over again, just wanting to do another round to upgrade my camp afterwards and unlock stuff.The game is a rougelite game, with a card mechanic that lets you place cards on tiles of the map. Some go on the road, some next to the road and some away from the road of your randomly generated loop. The most interesting part is, how those cards influence enemy spawns, your hero´s stats, other effects and even each other. Its a lot of fun to find working setups for clearing the chapter or going for an endless round. Placing/erasing cards, changing equipment and choosing traits on level ups is how the player mostly interacts during a run, while the rest unfolds automatically.The game has also a camp building/upgrading mechanic between rounds which gives you access to new cards, classes (3 at release), small passive boni and other stuff. The classes are pretty distinct from each other and fun to play around with. I personally also like the game sprites with its dark aesthetic.The price is pretty low and i can definitely recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The game consists of two elements. Expedition, which is a mix of auto-battling, looting/gear sorting, and card placing.And there is a base building/upgrading part.The expeditions are the core part of the gameplay. Your character start going in a loop and you obtain cards and gear from monsters slain. The player character fights them in an auto-battler element.Most cards are to be placed on the field. Some of them will become monster spawners, some will benefit the player. The former mechanic works really well, because the more spawners you make, the more loot you get, so you must determine how much your character fights.There are also special tiles that you can make by placing specific tiles beside each other.The camp is fun in early-game and useful in late-game.Here you can place tiles that unlock new cards/features and benefit your runs passively.It is extremely broken late-game, but that is not a problem, since the runs can go infinitely.The only annoying part is that you must place some building next to other specific ones.There are four bosses in the game.He is my personal favourite. His design is really good and  a great mechanic.There are three classes in the game.The default class, you can beat the entire game with just him. The other classes are just for flavour/variety.The story of the game is not anything special in my opinion, but it aligns really well with the gameplay.

And something you can put up and put down in a matter of minutes or an hour here of there - no heavy investment if you aren't keen on learning all the controls of some major RPG.I played it to the end and whilst there is still more coming from the crew who developed the game I think it really deserves a go if you want a new type of game in your repertoire.Instead of the cut and copy styles of the past titles this game offers a new type of play-style which I will look interested in seeing more of as this style develops.

_childDocuments_.review: is a very weird game. It’s a cross between a management game, a God game, an RPG and a rogue-lite. Yet it forms a coherent mix which is an excellent game. I had a lot of fun playing it.The major contributors to the fun were: the music, the amazing pixel art and the very interesting lore. All the tracks in the soundtrack are simply amazing, but the boss music tracks specifically are a joy to listen to (and there are two unique themes !!).I expect people to be surprised at my praise of the graphics for a pixel-art game. Most of the time a dev uses pixel art because it’s just the easiest way to create a coherent art style that holds up the entirety of the game. For example, I think Celeste (even if it is an excellent platformer) looks like crap. But clearly the developers of  have put a lot of attention in the graphics. For one, unlike most pixel art games, the sprites are always on the pixel grid.  Second, there is no blur, glow or any effect beyond the simple CRT filter (that you can disable) which I personally think highlights the quality of the pixel art.  Finally, the devs stick to the same 16 colors color palette from the beginning to the end, creating a coherent feel. There is also a lot of great details in the animation of bosses (especially final one) and this is not exhaustive.The gameplay is, as I said, a mix of a lot of genre. Each complement each other surprisingly well. All said, I’m actually shocked: I wasn’t expecting anything from such a mishmash. The main gameplay loop is an “expedition”, which starts you on an empty top down tile map with only a gray looping road. Your character then auto-walks in the loop, auto-fighting monsters when encountering them.  The combat is simply a RPG-style combat screen with no player interaction, you don’t even choose which enemy to attack. Each loop through the road increases the level of the enemies (and the rewards you get from them.)As you kill enemies (only slimes at the beginning,) you obtain cards and gear to improve your hero. Cards let you place tiles on the tile map, which slowly fills the screen with scenery. The cards you place can be landscape: Disconnected from the road, which can improve your stats; Or road augmentations, which usually spawn monsters more interesting and difficult than slime. Better monsters are more dangerous to your character, but they are more rewarding, and sometimes can balance off other monsters. There is a lot of secret interactions between tiles, which can be advantageous or sometimes a sure-fire way to kill yourself.  You’ll have to learn those interactions and chose wisely how you layout the tile map to your best advantage. It is very rewarding to see the empty space fill up with stuff you placed yourself and see your hero getting out-of-control strong and steamrolling everything on his way.There is also a meta-game. When you complete an expedition, you get resources you can use to improve your base, which let you unlock new classes, new cards, lore, or improve your characters in the expeditions. Each class are very unique in feel and strategy.Overall: 100% yes. This is a seriously amazing and innovative game that more than deserves the hype surrounding it and its coverage. Props to the devs for pouring their heart into such a jewel of indie game.EDIT:  THANK YOU SO MUCH I LOVE YOU.

_childDocuments_.review: Version 2.0Loop Hero is another game that I want to like due to its novel concept, but in the final analysis it can't make up for its flaws. The core concept of the game as a 'reverse' tower defense is the highlight.
