_childDocuments_.review: This game, in it's core, is 2D action adventure game, with some serious quality of life issues in almost all of it's aspects.First, exploration.Tails of Iron uses what I would consider very outdated save system. You reach a bench or something, game saves, and if you die before resting at same or different bench, game has no idea what you did. That may seem like a minor detail, but ♥♥♥♥ me, it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful to have your rat kneel next to a hat, or some insect eggs every time you pass by it because game has no idea you did that few minutes ago before you died. Oh, and one more little detail. Respawning does not replenish your health, potion, arrows, poison or anything. But almost always has some means to replenish those things close by. Why...?Now game doesn't have a whole lot to explore (thank god), becouse it really isn't made to be carefully explored and experimented with. Your rat takes fall damage, has no way to travel faster (except few fast travel points), and traveling across the map is pretty slow. But hey, even if you do get a desire to explore on your own, you will be punished for it pretty soon. Because if you do side quests (kill x at location y), and early on game let's you know you must do sidequests, you will have to simply retrace your steps to one of the areas you've just been to. And since only thing your rat can do is run and jump in terms of exploration, that really becomes tiresome after a while. So yeah, don't explore, game will take you to every location on the map anyway. Oh, and few secrets it has, could hardly be called that.Second, combat.In Tails of Iron, combat is nothing fancy. You have your Fast attack, Strong attack, Bow attack, 2H attack, dodge, block and parry. Simple, except no. You see, enemies might attack you with one of 3 types of attack. Red attack, which can't be blocked, but can be dodged. Yellow attack, which you can parry, but can't dodge, and red flashy attack, which has to be dodged, and can't be blocked. What's the difference between first and second red attack.. No ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea. Second has bigger range I guess. Oh but wait a moment. I forgot 2 other types of attacks. But it's fine, game forgot them too during tutorial fight. There is also white attack, which can't be dodged but can be blocked, and no warning attack, which does nothing special. And I might be ok with that if game had one handy little thing that would make combat much more fluid and enjoyable. And that brings me to...No i frames. Now some may say "But hey, game was made to be played that way". And yeah, I can understand that. But when you're fighting enemies who are shooting arrows at you (white attack), it really would be nice if you could.. oh I don't know.. dodge the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ arrows. But nope, unless you have your shield up, you get hit. So you might be wondering, "So how do you dodge at all if there are no i frames". Well it's simple, you get out of the way. Most times, you simply press dodge, which makes your rat go a bit faster, so he can get behind the enemy before enemy does it's thing. That way, enemy swings weapon into nothing. You can also simply run away from an attack, same result. Now that might get you some fresh ideas about dealing with arrows, but nope, forget about it, because if enemy is shooting a bow, it will ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ turn around and still hit you. Why game, just why...?There is more I could talk about, characters are bland, equipment system is very simple, story is fine I guess, but I already spent way too much time typing this ♥♥♥♥. And while there is potential, and game has some very strong positive points like graphics and storytelling (seems like Geralt of Rivia is the narrator), it just has a bit too much of stuff I can't deal with. Maybe second game makes some much needed changes and makes gameplay more enjoyable, but I just can't force myself to finish this game, or recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: , revolving around brave rats, immediately caught my interest due to its beautiful hand-drawn visuals that reminded me of some of the childhood’s books I used to read years ago, so I naturally wanted to try it out. Even though audiovisuals are not usually on my priority list when playing games, the incredible amount of details that please your senses from start to finish made me adore this title.Because of that,  managed to hook me from the beginning. Yet, that was not the only surprise! A familiar voice greeted me— one, whom you might know as  from  trilogy.  lovely voice is the only one that will bless your ears, as he narrates the whole story while all of the animals only make incomprehensible noises. Then, the catchy soundtrack only underlines the audiovisual qualities, forming a charming, atmospheric experience.However, is that enough? Or is this just another eye-candy game without much else to offer?Let us start with the premise; your peaceful rat kingdom flourished until it got invaded by villainous frogs who left their scummy pond to plunder your homeland. Unfortunately, they succeeded and left it in ruins. Yet, there is a last light of hope, as our protagonist, prince Redgi, intends to claim the crown, restore the glory of his lands and seek that sweet vengeance.That is about it, as it is the classic tale of a hero gathering their strength and, along with friends, standing up to the greater evil. Sure, that is not a unique nor complex narrative, but I would say that it is just enough in this case. While there are few interesting twists here and there, I rather enjoyed the story because some of its parts were pretty wholesome, and  delivers them amazingly.How does it play, though? I would describe it as a simplistic take on the  subgenre, as you have to travel through several diverse maps, search for various items and then backtrack to use them to get rid of the obstacle that forbade you from progressing further. I said “simplistic” because the world of  is not exactly interconnected, as there is fast travel between the main areas. I am okay with that; however, the issue is that the game forces you to revisit the previous regions often and participate in fetch quests required for finishing the storyline. As  only lasts about ten hours, such an approach is a bit disappointing, as I would prefer a new additional area for those quests. At the very least, the visual representation of those locations change as you progress through the narrative, so there was at least an attempt to make it a tad bit better.On this journey of yours, you will get ambushed by numerous types of animals, whether it would be those barbaric frogs, aggressive insects or other wicked beings. The combat system is simple; you only have light and heavy attacks, plus parrying, dodging and rolling. Despite the abovementioned fairy-tale vibes, the animations are brutal yet delightful to watch, as Redgi performs various finishers on those vicious frogs or dissects the corpses of bugs for their fluid to fill up his health flask.Thus, participating in encounters is enjoyable, especially when you fight with numerous enemy types at once, as it feels fairly challenging and satisfying to play. However, the combat system becomes problematic with some of the later boss fights, as the hitboxes related to their attacks are wonky; once you roll through them safely, while the other time you get hit. Moreover, some bosses tend to spam one type of attack, which can stunlock you, resulting in your immediate death. Even though I overall had a good time with it, these instances were annoying enough and might prove even more challenging for the newcomers to this subgenre.You can influence the combat a bit by choosing from multiple weapons, like swords, hammers and spears; each has its own attack pattern that can prove useful in different situations. My favourite one would be the spear, as it is fast enough to deliver continuous hits before the enemy reacts properly. Additionally, ranged weapons allow you to deal with the annoying flying insect, or you can put a bit of poison on your blades. While both have their use, they are not really a competent part of the weaponry, which is a bit of shame.Apart from that, you can choose from a variety of armours and helmets: light, medium and heavy ones. Each can provide additional defence bonuses against certain enemy types, so it is worth changing them often. They also add to your weight bar, but I honestly never noticed much of a difference nor felt any disadvantage for wearing heavier armour, so I ignored it completely and used whatever I wanted. This whole system is not necessarily bad—it is just way too simple.I guess that would be all, as there is not much else to say.  nails it with its amazing audiovisual presentation and a simple yet wholesome story, but the gameplay drags it down, as it could have been much better. However, I cannot say I was bored at any time, so I do not mind recommending this title for what it is; perhaps it would be better to wait for a sale, though.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: I really hate to do this because I was greatly looking forward to this game.  I'm a huge fan of side scrollers, metroidvanias and soulslikes including the very best of the games that combine these genres like Salt and Santuary, Vigil, Hollow Knight and others.  There's a reason those two games are the gold standard in this genre, they each do a few things exceptionally well beyond just art design.  Let's start with this, Tails Of Iron (TOI) is a beautiful game, character design is great, the art style is wonderful the levels look spectacular but the love and care that was put into everything associated with the games visuals is sorely lacking when it comes to how this game feels to play.  Hollow Knight is so good it's almost unfair to compare it to other games but TOI isn't a $5 game, this is selling for $40 on console and $25 on Steam.  In a 2D game movement has to feel good and here it feels downright bad.  Everything is too slow.  Walking is slow, climbing ladders is slow, jumping is almost horrendous.  Every single action, from dodging, to swinging to jumping feels bad.  If you boot up S&S or Hollow Knight right after playing this game you'll be stunned at how terrible it feels in comparison.  Moving about the levels needs to be fun in a side scroller and it feels bad here.Then there's the combat.  Tails of Iron is CLEARLY trying to be a soulslike game despite ditching the stamina meter.  That's great!  There can never be enough souls influenced combat systems.  The issue here is TOI doesn't seem to understand what makes a souls like combat system feel good.  Hollow Knight isn't all that similar to soulslikes aside from the most crucial aspect.  Enemy attack patterns.  TOI thinks I like souls games because the enemies do a ton of damage on each hit but that's not what makes souls great.  What makes it great is enemy attacks are consistent, readable and fair.  TOI has none of those things going on. Attacks literally change the timing up all the time.  This cannot be in a game like this.  When an enemy lifts it's club it has to bring that club down at the same time, every time.  Here timings feel almost random. Hit boxes are ATROCIOUS.  The Sekiro, dodge, parry or block system utterly fails because the timings aren't consistent.  This leads to damage that feels like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You'll get hit even though you dodged behind an attack becasue the game says you need to parry.  This is stunningly terrible and something that Sekiro doesn't do.  If you dodge away from parry attack as long as you don't get hit you're fine.  TOI ignores the hitbox, it ignores that you are literally 3 feet away behind the enemy facing away from his sword and hits you anyway.  Slam attacks are spammed and impossible to dodge if it gets thrown out when you're close.  The combat here is a total failure.  Complete and total failure. Its just poorly designed and feels more like a list of From Soft mechanics was compiled and then implemented with no regard to THIS games movement system, enemy patterns, or 2D perspective.Build variety doesn't exist. Armor ratings don't make sense, weapons are all the same, you choose one of 3 weapons and then it's basicallly just skins and damage ratings.I could go on but there's almost nothing about this game, outside of the gorgeous visuals, that makes it worth considering over just replaying the vastly, vastly superior Salt and Sanctuary.  Or the monumentally superior Hollow Knight.I find it stunning anyone thinks this is anything other than a total failure mechanically. From it's annoying back tracking, to it's miserably slow movement, to it's terrible jumping, awful controls, miserably bad combat and broken enemies this game isn't worth your time much less your money.It is beautiful to look at though and it's an indie game so I guess that's all that matters these days on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is like a table with one short leg. The art is amazing and it is the best aspect of the game by far. The narrative is simple, but a tale the player feels invested in immediately. The music and sound design fits the setting and does its job well. The gameplay, however, leaves much to be desired. While I was not dissatisfied with my experience, I cannot recommend the game. If the combat, quest system, and travel had some improvements, this game would be a very solid indie experience, and I would gladly change this to a recommended title.The combat is not "punishingly brutal" in terms of gameplay, it is actually quite easy if you play very safe and defensively. However, if you drop your controller, mess up too many times in a row, or try to play aggressively, you die really fast. Combat looks and sounds brutal and weighty, but is essentially a game of "rock, paper, scissors" with some occasional mix-ups. To break it down, enemies have attacks that are telegraphed (practically shouted at you) with different colors, symbols and sounds, which the player then responds by taking the appropriate counter action. Red line attacks mean an enemy is performing an attack you can only dodge. Red circle attacks mean the enemy is doing an area attack, and you must double dodge (or so the tutorial tells you, you can also elect to just walk away from where the attack will land). Yellow line attacks can be blocked, parried, and dodged, but it is taught in the tutorial to parry these attacks for a window to deal damage. White line attacks are ranged attacks, which must be blocked. The only other attack an enemy may throw out is an attack telegraphed by animation only (I'll call them light attacks), which can be blocked or parried. Attacks are telegraphed way too hard. The enemy winds up, shakes, then attacks. Enemies are practically geriatric when it comes to speed, giving you massive windows to read the next attack.  I have many complaints about the combat system. For one, the attacks are often very slow and easy to counter. Enemies will often charge, stop in front of Redgi, then attack (enemies stopping before attacking makes it far too easy to dodge. Simply see the red attack, run at the enemy and press dodge). Someone who plays Souls-like games defensively will find no trouble with this game. Tails of Iron seems to be designed to the defensive playstyle (it is established that Redgi is small and not particularly at an advantage in the prologue), as aggression is heavily punished in this game by most enemies. Spamming light attack should not be rewarded, but you should be able to exploit more openings than yellow attack parries and red attack dodges (very few light attacks, like the spear frog's downward slash, can be parried for a large attack window). Fights will often drag out when not necessary, with enemies having only one attack out of many to actually punish. Some bosses are rather annoying to fight. Shield bosses come to mind, as the AI plays defensively and you can't be aggressive, you have to wait or trigger the AI into making a mistake. For instance, Moleberg, the mole arena boss with the shield, can practically be exploited by repeatedly running to the edge of the arena to bait the attack with the biggest opening. Other enemies with shields have light attacks, which you can parry with a timed block. Parrying those attacks give you one free hit at best, and the enemy often counters the attack by throwing out a shield bash that is very difficult to dodge. It simply takes too long to kill enemies at times, and it makes encounters take longer than necessary. Some other things that take longer than necessary is progression and travel time. The quest system is a stonewall to plot progression. The game has "side quests" which are not optional. Sometimes you need gold to continue the story, and gold is only gained from side quests. I would prefer if I could either gather gold naturally along the main story or if the main story didn't require Redgi to go on fetch quests in a linear game. Tails of Iron has a Metroid-like layout, with rooms on the map all being connected via a square grid and freely allowing travel between them. However, the game is not seamless in its level transitions, and loading every single room is frustrating at times. It takes ages to leave the sewer or make a pit stop at The Crimson Keep. For example, The Crimson Keep could certainly benefit from being composed of larger rooms. As an example, It would flow better if the cook's room didn't require four loading screens to get to, with no fast travel back out to the courtyard. The problem in general is travel time, with no shortcuts, and some obstructions respawning (such as the vines in the sewer or the frog barricade). People accuse the game of padding, I hope it is just amateur design.Some good things I'd like to note: I love all the rodent characters and their little Don't Starve instrument voices. I really don't like rodents, but the art team made me care for Redgi, his family, and his friends. The little details in the narrative are nice, such as Lans Alat (Lancelot), the frog boss with a lance. Or the Moleshevik Republic, komrat, and auto-mole-bile. Minor but interesting details. I could gush for ages over the art, their team did very good work. The narration (done by Doug Cockle, voice of Geralt of Rivia) really elevates the story. TL;DR Art, writing, and sound design are very well done in this game. Get it if you want to support the amazing work they did. Do not get this game for the Souls-like experience or combat, you will be disappointed.

Fighting in this game feels like you're trying to swing a lead pipe underwater at piranha, as they keep gleefully biting chunks of meat out of you. _childDocuments_.review: Time to 100% - 7hrs 33 minsQuick review:  This is a really good game.  Here's the negatives first:  The combat is infuriating until you get into the swing of it (took me about an hour and a half to get a decent grip on it but you might take to it better than I did).  Many of the items are filler, you can balance things out somewhat choosing one over another but it doesn't make sense for the game to have this many pointless variants.  They do look really cool though.  A couple of the bosses are a tad too unfair, but for the most part they are all good.  Sometimes you get spammed in between enemies both using different things you can't counter at the same time.  A couple of bugs, nothing major.  No replayability.Positives:  It looks fantastic.  Seriously, you guys absolutely nailed it graphically.  From the designs to the rendering, and the animation style to the brutal / cute nature of it.  Audio was mainly nailed, but some issues were there.  I don't think the audio dampening effect works as well as it could.  It sounds like the speakers are getting quiet every now and again.  If you added in some kind of drone that was subtly drowning out the sound it would be more effective.  Also, the Clangers noises were infuriating.The gameplay is solid.  There's a good variety of enemies, and they all seem to build from one another in a way which I think helps guide you to get better as you go.  The fairy tale squeaks with narrator is a thing I've seen done horribly this year with Biomutant (it was so bad it ruined the game for me completely).  In Tails of Iron though, it works a lot better.  I think it is because of the storybook aesthetic, accompanied by the wonderful vocals of the guy that played Geralt in the Witcher games, that it succeeds.  I do think the Clanger noises are a detriment though, as they are horrible.  Horrible.It is a shame that you still lose out on feeling for the characters due to the presentation style, but I don't think it matters in this case as it further makes it play out like a proper fairy tale.  I'm really glad to have seen this handled so well after Biomutant failed so badly.  I strongly recommend Tails of Iron.PS - Hint for new players below (No Spoilers):It doesn't matter if you are using a shield or the 2 handed weapon, blocking still fully blocks.  Doesn't matter what way you are facing either.  Parry works with both, and I think has different timings depending on shield / weapon used.  I think you need to be facing the right way to parry.Get past the first jumpy stompy boss and the game gets a lot better.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully artistic game with narration on top. The combat is simplistic yet challenging, and feels like it's almost perfectly balanced. I enjoyed every minute of this game due to its amazing world, interesting characters, and fun little story. The game isn't very long (not a con for me), but it sure is crafted with lots of heart.

_childDocuments_.review: After getting all achievements for this game and finishing it in the hardest difficulty, I have to say: what a ride.Let's begin by saying that using the VA of Geralt for the narrator was a super clever choice. I can picture Geralt telling Redgi's "tail" to Ciri in the Witcher universe.First, I'll point out the negative aspects of the game. The backtracking can get a little bit tedious when doing sidequests or exploring, I wish there were more fast travel options (even if they unlocked after completing some milestones) and benches (the save points) with healing were more frequent.I think that the way you unlock new gear with the blacksmith is okay-ish, you just bring a blueprint to him and that's it. I wish you had to collect some materials or something similar.The main part of the game is the boss fights. I love them, however, sometimes their attacks can be a bit unfair, especially when you get hit once and unavoidably get hit two more times, killing you.Now, the qualities.The artwork is superb. It's charming, the colors are well-chosen, and every tiny aspect of the scenario and the background are detailed and thought out. Especially the , it looks incredible and it's my favorite region of the game. Even the weapons and the armor sets look amazing. I still can't believe that all the art is hand-drawn.The OST is good and is really cool to see that the drums sometimes are little creatures in the background.I enjoy the combat a lot. There are indicators of enemies' attacks and at first, this can be seen as something that would make the game too easy or simple but having played the game on Bloody Whiskers difficulty, I think it would be impossible to play the game if not for those since it's designed to work that way.The core of the story is not original: is a dethroned princess trying to reclaim his title. That said, the characters are unique are have interesting personalities, even without VA, which is a feat in my opinion. The  is my favorite by far. You care about them and what happens to them during your playthrough.Even if the boss battles can be a little unfair, I loved them. They are really hard and require your quickest reflexes, after battling a boss for almost an hour, it felt extremely rewarding when I finally defeated them.I hope the studio can learn from these little mistakes that can be easily fixed and improve upon everything that made this game great and unique.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat was just not interesting enough to justify the repetitive nature of the quests. You progress though the game smoothly enough, and I, thinking I was smart, did every 'side' quest I came across as I played as I had read they were mandatory. However, after reaching a certain point the game then demanded the currency earned from those quests. Although I had done every available one, I didn't have enough. A new side quest had unlocked in the same area as before so I went and completed it. But this was not the end of it as immediately after this, I hit another wall demanding more currency. Even more side quests appeared with the same repetitive tasks as before. I started doing them, but upon dying and having to redo one, I decided it just wasn't worth it as the game was just not fun enough to justify it.If you liked this review, check out my

_childDocuments_.review: Would only recommend if you're interested in the gameplay. Watch some gameplay videos and see if its something you may like. Gameplay is really fun though at times it feels like your character is a bit slow and sluggish to respond to your button presses, could be due to the weapon/armor you have equipped but its like that even with minimum things equipped. The dodges at times feel like it hinders you more than help, especially when the enemy can hit you through it. The game can be a challenge at times but fair, especially during boss fights though I can't speak for the new harder difficulty that was added recently. Story wise, its really good at keeping you interested and having Geralt of Rivia’s narrate throughout the game is a great plus.If you want to get all achievements, play the game on the hardest difficulty, Bloody Whiskers, for the one achievement or you'll have to replay the whole game from the beginning if you want to get it later as there's no new game+. Unfortunately the game has no replayability once you play through and experience it the first time, unless you want to self impose restrictions in replaying the game again.There's also no indication indicating if you have gotten all weapon/armor in a particular section of the map. Be sure to search through an area carefully and thoroughly the first time you're there or you'll be circling the whole map later on looking for that one equipment you're missing. Of course, that's only if you want the achievement and not required to beat the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible. 10/10. It's tough as nails, but I never once felt like I died for a "that's not what I told it to do" reason: I knew the mistake I had made and did better next time. The save points are a fair frequency, and thoughtfully/mercifully placed right before bosses.I went through on KB + mouse, but my xbox controller worked fine. I'd normally go with a controller on a side-scroller like this but it just felt off in this case strangely enough. Not being able to remap controller buttons didn't help (you CAN now remap kb + mouse controls).I went through with light armor + spears and enjoyed that a lot. Heavier armor (with higher defense stat) reduces damage in a big way, but I preferred being nimbler. I can't put my finger on exactly what carrying higher weight actually does, but there's definitely a difference that made me prefer going the lighter route. I read a dev comment that higher weight slows down your dodgeroll but I'd have never pinned that down from gameplay, the effect is very subtle in my experience. Subjectively, weight really seems to slow down attack animations but I can't be sure.I think the story did a GREAT job of driving forward the action, and you even get a chance to keep playing after completing the main story which was a nice touch if you forgot something.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: Similar to Dark Souls as tag?I would give it Metroidvania instead. I mean, it is way much more this than the other tag, seriously.Aside from that mini rant, let's go to the game itself, shall we!?Tails of Iron is quite small for the length of it. But I was expected about it: Got me a bit longer than 8 hours to finish it and I didn't found everythings I need to fully found stuff around, including gears and sidequests items. The game is quite a small Corridor, Metroidvania type. I would consider it as similar as Monster Boy, Wonder Boy 3 in that matter. Yet, the combat system is heavily focused on a Rock-Paper-Scissors melee mechanic: Some attacks can dodge, while others can parry and the last ones can be blocked. Miss one of those and you can receive some sever punishments. As for the story, it is really narrative. With a dark theme of a fantasy world, rebuilding a ravaged kingdom over the course are what I wanted to pinpoint our attentions. Probably that's the reason why the game is more corridor oriented, rather than a labyrinth style like we know from Metroid games, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night or even Axiom Verge (here on Steam). But by doing so, the game offers more a panoramic view with a background being alive and very well represented.A funny thing that I love from that game is about the implantation of the musics against bosses or for some areas. I mean, possibly like in a Dark Souls game, there is no music, except a very few places and against bosses. In this game, to make it interesting, you have the musicians playing in the background to make the music against the bosses and so forth. Heck, you even meet a friendly npc with high tech gears that it has a pocket radio, playing some kind of 8-bit techno, helping you to fight against a boss. Basicly its radio song is the boss song. Quite funny to see these little details going.For a downside and I would agree with some reviewers here, the sidequests in the game can be quite redundant to do while gathering money to progress in the story. I aim more the hunter lodge sidequests where you do need to go in the sewers in almost at the same area, over and over, just to kill beetles. There was no variations at this point and it frustrated me. But after that, I enjoyed the rest.Tails of Iron is a good, short game. I haven't touched the expansion yet, but I will figure it out, soon enough. For about 8h to complete the story at normal difficulty, it worthed my time and my enjoyment to see the path of a little rat, started with nothing, becoming the king of his kingdom. A very well made game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing, there are several things that added together made this game one of my favorites and the first game I have 100%'ed (technically as of writing this there are three hidden achievements but they will not be achievable until the next update which I am waiting eagerly for.) Firstly there is the combat, the combat is solid and as to be expected for this type of game it has the basics of dodge, roll, and parry all of them seem to connect well with the enemy models and there has only been a rare occasion where an enemies (or my own) attack would connect when it shouldn't, which for an indie developer team like this is really great to see. Then there is the art direction, the medieval feel is captured beautifully and they are really able to capture these dark tones and moments that completely suck you into the setting along with the background actually feeling alive and not just some static shot. After that is the story, its solid for what it is a simple story of a newly crowned king trying to fix his kingdom and defeat his enemies that caused this. All of this wrapped up into one game forms something that I have honestly not seen from many Triple A developers in a while, but I mean hey if the game is completed then its already further along then most triple A companies now, and all of them make up for a game worth its price, but the last thing that just added the perfect bow onto this already incredible present is the music and sound design. Both of these not only supplied the feeling of impact from each swing that connected from both the enemies and my own swings but also added perfectly to the setting with the choices of music, where while your inside your kingdom  you'll hear a bard (or Thee Bard) playing a song or when you are facing off against the Toads you'll hear more percussion or tribal sounding music and you'll even have a small character in the background at times justifying the music by being either the bard with the strings or the little drummer boy for the bosses.TL:DR Great game a ton of things were done right and the game is well worth the price it is sold for, I am very excited to see what comes next from this team.

That and the actions are sluggish, like you wont roll or attack for a good half second after hitting the keys so you literally have to anticipate wanting to do anything. Graphics, visuals, story, etc is all good from what I've played so far but holy hell with the controls and response times.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright updating my review since i've now beat the game and almost all of its optional content. Still got two optional quests I gotta clean up but other than that, i've done everything. A quick rundown is, this is a soulslike metroidvania game, but the combat honestly reminds me more of the Batman Arkham games than it does Souls. Now its not a flashy beatemup, but the main gameplay loop comes from dodging 4 different types of attacks, and an icon will flash when an enemy is going to roll out a specific attack... kinda like Batman. In the training it teaches you how deal with each attack, but thats pretty much what you'll be doing is reading the enemy, dealing with that specific attack and dealing out punishment in return. So keep that in mind while you're reading this, most of my gripes come from the games' combat.I want to end on a high note here so i'll start by talking about what I don't like about the game. I actually addressed this in a discussion thread, but healing is far too sluggish for how much damage enemies deal. Now enemies in this game hit hard, usually knocking out most of your HP in 1 or 2 quick hits. Yes most damage is avoidable, but a fight can get chaotic fast especially in the later areas. It takes forever to drink the potion, it takes so long I honestly would recommend against using it unless there is a legitimate break in the fight such as a boss revealing its next phase where its invulnerable anyways. The shockwave attack. Now in training you'll learn about the 4 different attacks the enemies use. A ranged attack, a parry, an unblockable, and a shockwave. Now how its supposed to work, is that the shockwave attack can only be avoided by double-tapping out of the way. You would think that only a set amount of enemies would use these kinds of attacks, but really most of the cast just spams the ever living ♥♥♥♥ out of them, including every boss in the game. Now my problem with it, is simply that usually you can't get enough clearance to clear the hitbox before it crashes down on you. I've done some perfectly executed rolls and still got hit simply because I couldn't get far enough away from the sprite before it came crashing down. As you progress different types of shockwaves emerge, and sometimes you'll get a small notification of where its going to land in the form of leaves falling.. but not always, sometimes enemies will have two types, one being a jump in place and the other a jump forward both with the exact same windup making it impossible to tell which its going to use, and i've rolled into a forward one so many times.. Weapons and armor have a very little difference. Even wearing heavy plate, the damage mitigation it does is very little. There is a weight system like Dark Souls however unlike Dark Souls it doesn't seem to effect your dodges just your walk speed. Weapons just have a damage value and thats it. You just kind of stick to the weapon type that you like the moveset for, all two handers handle exactly the same so just pick the most damaging one.. I would've liked more variation there such as different speeds, maybe some crit, but it works. This is a minor gripe. I've encountered a few audio glitches, sometimes the enemies will completely mute themselves, the narrator will cut out, or it'll get so bad you have to restart the game. Its minor but thought i'd mention it.Another minor thing is that the optional bosses don't have boss music. You're just fighting it to complete ambiance which is a weird weird feeling. Would be nice to have some tunes to pump while fighting those, had to turn on my own.Okay, now we'll move on to the positives. The art style is gorgeous, its got a very storybook aesthetic and it all looks really good, the characters look super cute, and to contrast your character will be covered in the blood of your enemies most of the time like Bloodborne its great. Overall the combat is very responsive, and other than the shockwave gripe I had everything worked well, and I had a pretty enjoyable experience. Its not a spammy game, you have to think about your openings and I really like that about it. The story is pretty good, I really liked some of the later areas it was pretty creative. I don't want to spoil anything, of course having everything narrated by Geralt is awesome. There was quite a bit of side content, a lot of stuff to explore, and worth exploring. You could run into treasure bolstering your armory or even a whole secret boss, its pretty awesome. You have bounty boards listed with content you can do as many times as you want, and a lot of it are totally optional bosses that are pretty fun to take down. In conclusion, this is a short but sweet soulslike title that has pretty tight gameplay, a nice aesthetic and good story. Its got a few things that drag it down, but for the price point you get a game you'll enjoy a lot if you like these games. Tails Of Iron gets a solid 8/10 from me.

_childDocuments_.review: An Excellent game. Visuals are amazing, same as the sound(I love it whenever a bossfight has a character in the background, playing the fighttheme) and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, thats some good naration! The entire presentation just has so much love, care and detail put into it, that you can literally see the world change over time in a lot of areas.Then there is combat: It has been a while, where I had this much fun in a game, fighting basic enemys. the combat feels challanging but fair. You can totally dominate your enemys, if you watch out for the visual cues and act accordingly, but if you get greedy or careless, even a small grub can punish you harhsly, which is great to keep you on your toes! And there is a bunch of variety, both for basic enemys and bosses! It also feels very rewarding to find new loot. between damage, enemyspecific resistances, general toughness and weight, finding a single piece of great gear, can get you to change your entire loadout(also, you can see it visually on your little rat!)I am a little more than 6 hours into the game and it feels like there is still a big chunk left(I would assume 25-50% of the game, looking at the worldmap), which is just really great value for your money as well!There is pretty much nothing bad I could say baout the game, it's just that good. all of the elements are really polished and help to enhance another. the ONE bad thing I could say about it, is that you have a very small interactionrange to pickup items, or mine ore, stuff like that, which can sometimes make it a little awkward, wobbeling back and forth to pick something up. thats the one thing, the only thing I can think of thats not great about this game, so you can imagine how good the rest of it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, as long as you enjoy it's core mechanic - rat-to-foe(s) melee fights.Redgi is a rat. And he is king of the rat kingdom, which has unfortunately been overrun by the brutal army of the frogs. So your task as Redgi is to reclaim your kingdom, killing frogs and their allies on the way. You do this in deadly 2D fights - and when I say deadly, I mean deadly. This is no hack and slash game where you run button mashing though hordes of enemies. Every fight is a lovingly orchestrated deathmatch that can be your end if you are not concentrated.You have no stamina bar, so it is possible to attack, block or dodge quite fast, but button-mashing won't get you far. You have to avoid getting hit, and you have to make sure your attacks count, especially if you are outnumbered. This game requires learning the attack patterns of your enemies, countering their attacks with the correct response - dodging, dodge rolling, using your shield, parrying, jumping, counter-attacking with fast or heavy blows, changing your position, drinking healing juice, or using long range weapons. If you enjoy that, you will love the game. If not, you will die a lot and soon hate the game. It is a soulslike, after all, and there are no difficulty settings.The game consists of 6 worlds with different enemies, from mosquitos to moles or wasps. Apart from that, there are over 200 pieces of equipment to wear, which have an impact on your attack strength, damage resistance and movement speed. Certain weapons are better against certain enemies, so it helps a lot to use the correct weapons or armor. Changing equipment is only possible at special places. When you die, you can restart from your last savepoint without any punishment. Savepoints are frequent, but you have to activate them.Great 2D combat-heavy soulslike action RPG focusing mainly on the battles, in which good timing and observation are required.

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the whole game in one session and it becomes very noticeable the rock paper scissors game play. The game is fun but i can not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks beautiful, plays like a junker with a flat on ice: sure, you can learn to steer it, and it doesn't matter if you get into a few crashes (and you absolutely will crash into some stuff), but is it what you really want to be driving?Less metaphorically: the combat in this game is just not good enough. It's a very functional system in a lot of fights, but it absolutely falls apart when things start getting more interesting. The "double dodge" mechanic just doesn't seem to work and I can't believe that it's been left in the game in the state it's in. The dodge itself has wildly inconsistent rules about what you can and can't dodge through--even attacks that are signposted as dodgeable (red attacks) have a significant failure rate of actually respecting your dodge rolls. Further, even stacking up armor will have bosses dealing 2/3 your health in a hit, requiring you to find the space to heal to avoid dying to their 2nd hit. The 2H weapons seem silly to use in combat--if the foe has a shield up it usually seems better to dodge or block them to create an opening. In fact, the only parts of combat that felt cohesive were the 1h/shield fighting, which feels quite good actually, I just wish the rest of combat felt as polished.None of the mechanics (what is defense? what is resistance?) are actually explained to the player, so it's unclear how to focus your equipment to succeed in combat. I'm not sure if perhaps the weight system betrayed me at some point and perhaps using anything higher than light weight is a mistake? I'd love it if there were any in-game tutorials to explain literally anything about this stuff.I found the world itself to be amazing. I love the story. I like the crafting system and how straightforward it is (but a big downside is that the inventory system needs quite a lot more love). The game also has a ton of saves at convenient points, which feels less like a gift and more like an apology for the fact that combat will randomly murder you sometimes.The quest design is tedious and tested my goodwill towards the world. After rescuing a rat from a tower, you need to go back to your fort to speak with him, only to immediately be sent back to the tower where you just were to continue the main story. This happens several times! It's hard to respect the incredible world that's been constructed and feel like you're in it when the quests feel so gamey and annoying like this--I understand that if I don't travel back and forth I won't see the progression of the backgrounds, which is amazing, but it feels like beautiful wallpaper over a hole.Overall it's a beautiful game that I really want to love, but the combat makes it not worth it for me. Maybe I'll replay the game in their easy mode where the fact that combat is terrible won't matter, but I'll probably just not pick it up again.

_childDocuments_.review: Great little soulslike game. I loved the art style and music - they fit the game really well. And our favorite narrator Geralt of Rivia is here to tell Redgi's tail for us. My only complaint is that this game would have been a great odyssey if it were longer. It's a classic story, nothing new, but it's well done. Tails of Iron definitely had the potential to be a 20+ hour game, but a lot of the content is a little shallow and is quickly ran through. I was able to get every achievement (except beating it on the hardest difficulty) in only 9.5 hours. I think certain regions could've been fleshed out a little more and given more room for additional quests and content. I guess the devs were counting on replayability, but I'll be honest, I'm not that interested in running through this again on the hardest difficulty. Don't get me wrong though, what is there is really good, and is worth experiencing. If you're on the fence about copping, get it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me cry over rats.Otherwise, it's just so-so and I definitely wouldn't pay full price for it (beat the game on a second save in about 10 hours). Living in a world where games like Hollow Knight exist at a lower price point (on which I have over 40 hours), go buy HK. Everything Tails does, HK does better--unless you're a Redwall fanatic (which I'm not)--with the exception of the art style, in which case comparing the two is like apples and oranges EXCEPT for the fact that as far as I can tell, Tails' art style actually impedes its ability to have the crisp, clean game play that makes HK so darn satisfying. The only other thing Tails has that HK doesn't is the narration and--sorry Geralt--Bastion and Hades do THAT better with the crisper gameplay, more hours to burn, and comparable cost to boot like HK.Combat is really where this game suffers (as another review mentioned, it feels a bit like rock, paper, scissors against the enemies at times) and the only element of what I'm accustom to having in something calling itself an "RPG" that I found was a series of side missions that allow you to boost your max HP, otherwise your stats remain the same throughout outside of equipping different armor/weapons to manage a damage/defense/weight bar. Resource gathering seems a bit moot when the shops only sell ammo and the occasional quest item or blueprint for armor and weapons and imo there's absolutely no replay value, so I don't plan on getting that one achievement where you have to beat the final boss on the harder difficulty.EDIT: I did mean to say, however, that I appreciated the game giving an opportunity after the main storyline was through to have a bit of after-story cleanup where you could run around and continue to collect things, and finish up any loose ends you had.

_childDocuments_.review: Seriously, I do not get all these positive reviews. For me, this game is mediocre at best. Good things first: The graphics are nice and the narrator does a pretty good job. The not-so-good things: everything else. The story is near to non-existant, sometimes hints at deeper secrets (like in the crypt) but never gets to them. With the kind of tasks you are meant to do this game should be called "errand boy". I mean, they have a whole kingdom destroyed by frogs and you have to rebuild it and avenge your fathers death. What kind of an epic story arc could that provide! And what do the devs do? They send you on all kinds of mediocre and uninteresting side-quests that do not advance the story a bit and if left out, nobody would notice it. Combat is more like a chain of quick-time events: in other games (e.g. Hollow Knight, Grime, Salt and Sanctuary) you study your opponent and act according to his telegraphed attacks. Here, since they could not be bothered to make the attackes to be clearly distinguishable, and icon above above the enemy, and there is one reaction to every of the 3 attack types that you should do to counter it. That's nothing more then QTE, and badly executed. I do not look for the enemies movement, just for the icons. Maybe that could even be funny, but movement feels so unresponsive and squishy, that it is really no fun to either move through the levels nor to fight. Also, the companions that you have some times do, well, it is pretty close to nothing. I played until the last boss to see whether it would get better - spoiler alert - it does not. Could not be bothered to play the DLC. From what I saw it is just reskinned enemies of the maingame with some of their attacks combined. Sorry for the devs, the graphics look really nice, maybe you had the best of intentions, but Hollow Knight and Salt & Sanctuary are a complete different league.

_childDocuments_.review: If this game were 10$, I'd have given it a thumbs up despite it's flaws.As far as pros go, the game oozes charm.  The art style, the character design, and the sound design come together to make a very charming little game.  I enjoyed walking through the fort, town, and ranger station through various stages of the game as it did a very good job of showing a kingdom in despair turning itself around and prospering.  Add in narration from Doug Cockle (voice of Geralt from the Witcher series) and there's little to complain about on that front.Unfortunately, as easy as the combat was to get into, it did have it's problems.  Dodging was a bit wonky at times (even with a light build) and hitboxes were outright busted on some enemies.  The game telegraphs where an AoE attack is about to happen, and there will be times when you will be hit despite not being within that boundary.My biggest gripe is ultimately the length of the game itself.  I'm not a speedrunner by any stretch of the word, and I still reached the end boss in less than 9 hours.  If the game were 10 or 15 bucks that wouldn't be a bad deal at all, but 25$ for something so short that doesn't really have any replay value?  Eh...Buy it on sale.

I personally was frustrated from having to unlearn Souls controls, but honestly not a complaint, just a mention.Execution of the story is well done as well. _childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is a good 2D soulslike with a charming artstyle, cute characters (apart from Frog scum) and decent combat. Story is nice but nothing groundbreaking. If you play through casually, you will probably have a good time. But be warned that this is not an easy game, and combat heavily prefers being defensive than offensive.My gripes with the game are the "optional" content (side quests that you MUST do to get money for the main story, you need to do pretty much all of them), very clunky combat, nonsensical hitboxes at some points, narrator being a little cheesy (heh) at points, and especially BLOODY WHISKERS DIFFICULTY - enemies and bosses deal insane damage and are much faster than on normal difficulty, over half of my total playtime was just on this mode.Overall, if you like soulslikes, you should give this game a go. It has its issues, but can still be a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Like many others, I read the Redwall books when I was a kid, so when I first saw the store page that was immediately what I thought, and I couldn't believe it. I started to play and the influence of the books is present, which is awesome, yet it does a great job of standing on its own.The game itself is extremely well done IMO. Beautiful settings, great audio, characters that are aptly named and fit right in to the world, an archetypal story, and combat that plays very well. One can only hope Tails of Iron ends up as prolific as the material that influenced it! Big thanks to the developers for giving us this. A true prince of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is a very good game that ended up being much better than I thought at first. Just enough of metroidvania and Souls-like mixed in a pot with emphasis on combat and dramatic story of young prince Redgi reclaiming his kingdom from perfidious frogs. With no way to grind for power you must rely on equipment alone to succeed as your journey takes you from rebuilding the castle to underground as you find new allies. Fast and brutal combat where learning how to parry makes a difference, anyone familiar with Souls games will be right at home. Bosses escalating in difficulty will certainly challenge you and I almost wish I played on high difficulty from the get-go. Not because the game was easy otherwise, but because now I'm just one achievement short of 100%-ing a game that deserves it.Sometimes you play a game that checks just enough boxes from multiple genres or schools of design that the end result is familiar, but still more than enjoyable. Taking cues from metroidvanias and Souls-like titles, Tails of Iron achieves precisely that. Does it hold up on its own merits, though?Following a long reign, King Rattus' legacy of having scoured the realm of dirty Pondscum is suddenly cut short when aforementioned frogs besiege his castle, do away with his life and leave only couple of accidental survivors. Young prince Redgi among them as he swears revenge. So begins his quest to not only get his father's vassals to accept him as the rightful heir, since he's so small in stature and many favor his brother, but also to eradicate the frogs everyone thought were gone for many years. There are also other challenges in store taking him beyond and below what any common folk would think possible.Even though characters, rats or otherwise, don't use words but rather pictograms to communicate, Tails of Iron got a chuckle out of me multiple times as Redgi is self-aware enough to acknowledge he's doing everyone's busywork that normally his retainers should be all over instead. If only he had some. Pulling a lot of the weight is Doug Cockle serving as game's narrator and he doesn't fail to deliver a snide or cynical remark while carrying this Game of Thrones meets folk tale atmosphere. Characterization overall is pretty lacking, though. If you ask me I'd point fingers to narrative department as a whole taking the backseat since storytelling isn't the primary focus here so don't the RPG treatment or such. As the story advances and reaches post-game you have a marriage of things become really dire the closer to finale you get... and then various puns on wrestlers, musicians, etc. Who can forgetting squaring up against Molehammad Moli in the arena?It may be an easily overlooked aspect of the game as you're rushing from sidequests to the main quest, but I absolutely loved how the world kept fixing itself. Gradually, a ruined town gets repaired and royal guards are now securing the castle, for example. This is all fluff since the game isn't reactive in a meaningful way, but it's still nice to see even sidequests have visual feedback. Later on you get to spend some gold on castle ornaments bringing it even further to life. This also means you sometimes don't want to fast travel between sign posts, but take a stroll and see the changes.This is, however, an action game so let's get down to some nitty-gritty details and how the entire things works. I was surprised by how much emphasis there is on combat in comparison to very basic platforming or even customary “re-visit areas to progress with new powers” metroidvania design. Being a Souls-like is much close to Tails of Iron's ethos.Despite lacking a dimension compared to Souls titles which took gaming by storm, here we have a game that very much subscribes to many of those tenants while eschewing others. Perhaps to accommodate scaled back format? Providing you go with the recommended gamepad control scheme shoulder buttons will be your light, heavy and block functions, with the last one dedicated to healing. You get one jug of Grub Juice which you use for that purpose, but in a twist it doesn't recharge when you rest on a bench to save progress. Instead, you have to find juice dispensers or butcher grubs for smaller refills. It's good news those, as well as other goodies, are spread out decently across almost ten locations. Travel only becomes a chore when you have a specific sidequest and it's at the very end of a locations where there's no fast travel signpost nearby. Areas re-populate with enemies, but Tails of Iron doesn't subscribe to “every enemy can easily kill you” so it's just more of a hindrance. Such escapades become an easy way to loot for resources you'll rarely use.There's also no concept of experience to speak of as your character progression comes entirely from equipment. What can Regni use then? As far as armor goes you have slots for helmet, armor and shield, but alongside those your have murderous implements with sword & board, two-handed and ranged weapon slots. In my opinion there's too much equipment and it really becomes apparent towards the end when game starts throwing complete sets at you. Maybe there's a purpose to those if you haven't killed couple of side bosses who net you some of the best stuff in the game, but I do appreciate this extensive variety means you can play dress up and go with whatever Regni looks best in. Want a kingly crown? Plenty of those under light helmets. Want a riot shield? It's there. Want to cosplay as a samurai? Well, you get some look-alike armor AND a katana. Keep in mind you want to rotate and replace equipment as you're constantly finding better pieces, need some armor for resistances against frogs or alike, and you need to manage weight.Which pulls me back to combat since that's the bulk of what you'll be doing when you're not completing chores for the townsfolk as, by Thor, someone needs to clear the cellar of monsters. I survived by simple mantra: PARRY IS KING. Dodging also ranks highly for those unavoidable flashing red attacks or AoEs, but dodging is dependent on how heavy Regni is based on your gear whereas that perfect block will do so much more for you. Especially if you get it right for yellow-telegraphed attacks which are made to be parried. Game will also keep surprising you with enemy variety as you can exploit them as well rather than reserving “special moves” just for bosses. My one regret is devs should've pushed the player harder to master parry earlier. Already mentioned Molehammad Moli is one of those optional, post-game arena bosses... yes, there's both an arena and post-game stuff, who will punish you with his bee stings, but that lesson arrives way too late. Since I brought up bosses there is a steady escalation of threats and player performance expectations. Looking at my time played I've probably spent an hour or so repeating boss fights. It's a learning curve and not a learning cliff, is what I'm trying to say here.Presentation I left for last because game looks just plain gorgeous. If you ever wanted a 2D Redwall game this is it and that aesthetic carries the day. Some animations, particularly brutal executions Regni gets to perform, are sometimes wonky because there's a bit too much pushing and pulling to get the actors into correct positions, but that's negligible in the grand scheme of things. Soundtrack is all over the place, but just give me more strings. Frogs sure love their bongos, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is an excellent game and perfectly sized at around 10-15 hours in length! Full-price is a little steep if you're considering dollar spent vs. hours played but there is a high level of production value here that can justify the full-price if you can't wait for a sale. My favorite element of this game is the dynamic artwork. As you progress through the story, you'll see certain areas develop or change over time which is neat because it makes you feel like your efforts in-game have weight to them. All of the locations are visually interesting and map traversal is a mostly quick and painless affair (a saving grace because there is a fair bit of backtracking in this game). There is so much visual detail packed into a game that could have gotten away with far less so kudos to the dev team for going above and beyond.On a different note, the combat was fun for the most part but could definitely get annoying at times. While I appreciate the 'rock-paper-scissors' aspect to how enemies telegraph attacks vs. how the player should react, the players movement often felt clunky. Dodge-rolling and blocking feels inconsistent/imprecise and enemies can stun-lock you because of how long it takes to recover after hits and how slow your movement is. Despite its minor shortcomings, the combat was never too frustrating or difficult that I couldn't overcome challenging fights after a few tries. Other reviewers seem to blow their load over the in-game narrator being the guy who voices Geralt in Witcher 3. Honestly? Who cares....In my opinion, the narration was one of the weaker elements of the game. There are a few instances of inflection and quality narration but, for the most part, it's just some gravelly sounding man blandly reading lines. That's right - I said it. FIGHT ME, NERDS!:Pros:- Fantastic art- Solid sound design / music- Straightforward story with appropriate amount of side-quests- Character customization- Challenging combat:Cons:- Lots of backtracking- Player movement/attack speed- Lack of variety in finishing moves- Game starts to drag on a bit by the end

_childDocuments_.review: **Why You Shouldn’t Play Tails of Iron, or at Least the Bloody Whiskers Mode:Tails of Iron has a pretty fun story, but the combat is way too punishing, especially in the Bloody Whiskers mode. On the base difficulty, it’s not as noticeable, but the game’s progression has some issues. For example, there are mandatory side quests and non-linear gear improvements that can be frustrating.I like to try and 100% the games I enjoy, but I hit a wall when I saw that beating the game on bw was required. Bloody Whiskers is ridiculously unbalanced. I get that the difficulty is intentional, but the combat feels poorly designed. Every random encounter is insanely tough requiring sometimes the mindset you have for bosses. The game has two types of heavy attacks, whose developers themselves dont respect: many red attacks are too fast to react to (you can’t cancel your attacks and there`s almost no iframes), and the hitboxes are just terrible across the board. Also some red attacks can be countered with a 2h swing and some can’t, even though they look the same.Other frustrations include unskippable narrator introductions for some bosses and attack patterns with multiple moves that make it impossible to escape once you’re hit. Overall, these issues make the game more frustrating than fun.

_childDocuments_.review: What a conundrum. It's very pretty, there's a lot of attention to detail, combat feels good, and the story is simple but engaging. And yet the latter half is a horrible drag and the difficulty and combat design cause frustration rather than fun. I did beat it in the end, and I'm happy I did; the game really makes you care about little Redgi and his rat people. And now I'm fully equipped to help you figure out if this is something you'd like to play.Let's start with the obvious. It's so pretty. Feels like an old-timey fairy tale picture book. But that's not all - the environments constantly change as you turn the tide against the Frog invaders. Towns get repaired, NPCs come and do stuff, junk gets cleared, new structures show up. It's great, running through a town over and over seeing it look different every time.The story is grim. It might be a game about cute animals, but their plight is not cute at all. I actually respect the devs for the courage to make things as grim as they did, considering the subject matter. But don't worry - it's not TOO grim; it's a story about hardships and perseverance above all else.And finally, you can equip Redgi with so many pieces of gear. Sadly, it mostly feels like just dress-up with some numbers; fighting feels mostly the same no matter the weapon, and armour never really feels like it protects you. As in, you're still going to get your face bashed in by some attacks. I believe I mentioned the combat feels good. Yes, it does, against regular enemies. But as soon as bosses show up... it stops being fun. This one is a little hard to explain, but let me try:All enemies, including bosses, do a little colour-coded telegraph of what they're going to do next. Mainly it shows whether this attack is blockable or not. But most attacks are unblockable, and dodging doesn't really work the way you'd think. And since this IS a soulslike, you'll get hit -hard-. So what are you supposed to do? Can't block, can't dodge?The answer is: constantly watch the distance and simply predict what the boss will do. Sounds fun? Didn't think so. It makes combat frustrating and not enjoyable at all; and if you try to get greedy and get some hits where you're 'not allowed to' you get punished hard, and often have to redo. It's possible to heal, but it's much slower than in, say, Dark Souls, so healing is often just asking for more trouble.And there are a LOT of bosses. So many. At some point you can't continue the story because you need a certain item, and to get the item you need gold, and to get gold you need to fight more bosses. They don't even feel that different, even though they clearly are. This is a huge strike against the game, and since in the latter half the bosses get REALLY hard, you'll be just bashing your little rat head against the same fight, until you learn to predict what the boss does and patiently execute the proper 'dance'.So even though the fighting sucked, exploring the world was interesting enough to keep me hooked. But let's be honest: the main reason why I saw this through is because I understand how the dev felt on a very personal level.You see, this game is a memorial to their passed friends, the rats. In the options menu there is a cute hand-drawn picture of all the 'real' rats that the characters in the game are incarnations of. If you ever bonded with an animal friend, you'll immediately understand how emotionally important this is. Paying my respects to the love between living beings depicted here was the least I could do - that's why I followed Redgi to the very end.That's all I have to say. I didn't cover everything the game has to offer, but I think you should now have a good idea whether you'd like to play this or not. I recommend it in the end, because while the game is deeply flawed, the first half is a -blast-. If you ignored the side quests and just went straight on, chances are the momentum of that blast would carry you all the way to the end. I did the side quests; I don't recommend it. I do recommend the game, though. Enjoy!

I played on medium difficulty, had a hard time with Clubba because get it: THERE ARE NO INVINCIBILITY FRAMES IN THIS GAME WHEN YOU DODGE/ROLL. That's a big flaw or overlook from the devs, it makes the game unplayable because most attacks are AOE and you're not fast enough to get away from them even with the lightest armor or you are stuck in an attack animation so you get damaged when you can't even control it. So after Clubba, I get only a Save point and I'm low health, mind you Save points don't refill your health, nor your flask. So I have about 1 hp having to fight through 3 enemies without getting hit a single time, not impossible, but very unlikely because they attack all at once and don't take turns. Another problem is that this game is 2D so you can only dodge in 2 directions, which makes it even harder to come out alive from a 1v3 if you are attacked from 2 directions at once, where to dodge without invincibility frames? Very disappointed in this game, I liked the art style and looked forward to play it. I'm starting another playthrough on Fairy mode, where I'm a gentle noob who even if I finished all those other hard games, I'm soft in this game because the devs made it difficult on purpose and took away the most defining mechanics of this genre, dodge and i frames. _childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is a great game. Although the characters are rats, frogs, moles, and different kinds of bugs this game has a gritty and violent edge to it that really got me hooked on this game. The combat is very simple meaning that there are only a few keys that you use, but the actual fighting is not as easy. Each enemy has their own types of attacks, which could vary between a range attack (attacks players can block), unstoppable attack, area attack, and parry attack (attacks that the player can counter) which means that attention is key, because you can end up in a fight with 3-5 enemies using different attacks. The bosses in this game are all uniquely different, some easier than others. It has always taken me a few times to figure out all their moves, but when you finally beat a boss it is probably the greatest feeling ever. Tails of Iron has a really short story, but a very good one. The game is definitely a medieval fantasy, which is one of the main reasons I bought this game. Would definitely recommend this game if you've played Hollow Knight or it just sparks your interest like it did me.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this game and love that the extra content is free. Still have some of that to go. The combat feels deliberate and when I die, it's because I made mistakes (or my wireless controller decided to d/c...happens sometime for me). Looking forward to the sequel which is why I finally dove in (been in my library for half a year now). Not going to do the same for the sequel, I'm playing that right on release!Cute style, unique and simplistic presentation and some customization in your gear are all welcomed and unexpected when I first dove in. I'd recommend buying it up especially if it's on sale. The only drawbacks I had were:1. with the UI and it not being quite clear what some gear is doing when I swap to the different weapon types regarding weight. In the gear chest menu, weight decreasing is shown as a green change in the bar while increased defense or damage is also shown in green while the opposite is shown in red. It's not a big deal, just something I had to figure out. 2. In certain environments and when health gets low, the lighting can affect how enemy telegraphs show.  Red unblockables/AoEs are pretty easy to differentiate but the Yellow counterable and white projectile telegraphs look similar and the lighting makes it tougher to register with sight/peripheral vision alone.It's a solid game. Haven't played any games like it so felt quite refreshing to beat.

_childDocuments_.review: Set in a grim land plagued by war, Tails of Iron is a hand-drawn RPG Adventure with punishingly brutal combat. As Redgi, heir to the Rat Throne, you must restore your broken Kingdom by banishing the merciless Frog Clan and their ferocious leader, Greenwart. As you explore the deceivingly charming world, you'll encounter a cast of unique companions, ready to aid you in your adventure. And you'll need all the help you can get, whether that's new meal recipes, blueprints to forge deadly weapons and armour, or even a land-chugging, armour-plated mole mobile! Overcome your fears. Rescue your brothers. Restore Your Kingdom. Your tail has begun. Master Brutal Combat: From frog zombies to gargantuan grubs - and everything in-between - the Kingdom is awash with danger. To overcome each perilous encounter, you'll need to study your opponent's attacks and react accordingly! Thankfully, there's a range of deadly abilities at your disposal, including parry bashes and fatal executions, not to mention ranged attacks with your nifty bow and arrow. Explore a Treacherous Kingdom: Fully accompanied by the deep, raspy narrations of Doug Cockle (voice of Geralt of Rivia from The Witcher), prepare to embark on an epic adventure across the mediaeval-fantasy Rat Kingdom. Complete side quests and faction hunts for some additional gold-on-the-side, or join forces with a sharp-eyed companion to help even the playing field. Customise your Attack: Adapt Redgi's combat style to the task at hand. Heavy armour may provide better protection but can you really afford to slow down your dodge-roll? And then there's the question of weapon; axes pack a punch, while spears are quick and nimble. Perhaps you'd prefer the all-round performance of a trusty broadsword?

name: Chariots of War
detailed_description: Chariots of War is an operational real-time game where you can play one of 58 different nations on a huge historically accurate and beautiful map covering the entire Middle East! Build up your cities and keep their inhabitants happy by crating temples, entertainment and other building or deal with angry revolters. Control the Cradle of Civilization! 4000 years ago in the Cradle of Civilization, mighty Empires fought for water, resources and the arable land in the Fertile Crescent. Play as the Egyptians, the Babylonians, screaming Nubian warriors, or the Assyrians. Develop your county by producing commodities and selling them to you neighbors. Raise glorious armies and wage wars of conquest. Roll over the plains and seek victory in Chariots of War! Immerse yourself in Chariots of War. Build hundreds of buildings and city improvements, and collect 9 different resources such as Myrrh, Gems and Horses. Put your General in command of your army fighting real-time battles under the fog of war. Protect the inhabitans from roving barbarian tribes bent on attacking anything in their path. The Happiness and welfare of the inhabitants of your cities will depend on overpopulation, recruitment levels, garrisons and food, and by developing temples, entertainment and other buildings you keep revolution at bay. Recruit units from nearly thirty different troop types for you invincible armies. Barbarian tribes will roam the land, attacking anything they encounter. Trade allows you to buy and sell the 9 resources. Different areas of the map have access to different resources so trade is key. Diplomats can be sent out to gather information. You can eject enemy diplomats in a number of gory ways. Build your armies and wage a campaign to control the Cradle of Civilization!

name: The Planet Crafter
detailed_description: Embark on a chill experience alone or with up to 10+ friends in online co-op. Your mission is to survive on a hostile planet and turn a barren land into a lush paradize. Terraforming is the only way! You are sent on a hostile planet with one mission: Make it habitable for Humans. You'll have to survive, collect resources, build your base, produce machines to heat the planet, create an oxygen-rich atmosphere and eventually geo-engineer an entire planet! Gather minerals and resources to survive. Craft all the tools you need to fulfill your mission. Explore old shipwrecks and ruins and discover a planet full of mysteries! You'll need a base and all sorts of machines to make yourself at home, and be able to bring life to this planet! Progress through building tiers to upgrade and expand your base and explore the planet further. See life forms appear on the planet as you terraform it by increasing heat, oxygen and pressure. Witness the first signs of life with moss and insects and unleash the planet's full potential with thick forests and animals. From chill to hardcore, choose the difficulty level that suits you. Play with starting presets to create new games and experience endless possibilities. Multiplayer: survive by yourself or with friends (1-10+ online co-op) Survival: Thirst, Oxygen, Temperature and Health mechanics Base Building: shelter from a hostile environment and expand your exploration Crafting: equipment, tools and food to help you survive Terraformation: turn an entire hostile planet to a habitable paradise! Build machines to create atmospheric pressure and heat the planet Create a biosphere with breathable oxygen See your environment change as your terraformation progresses Creatures: create life by decrypting and mixing DNA extracts and make your own animals Procedurally generated shipwrecks: explore and find infinite rare loot Chill experience with no violence: the only enemy you'll have to fight is the hostile environment Adjustable difficulty to fit your level Adjustable presets for renewed experiences through time Creative mode

_childDocuments_.review: Its currently a short game, but i still have loved every moment of it and will be a repeat player.  I cant wait for future updates. The concept is awesome. The spacing is brilliant. I will note that i do have a pretty decent PC and had no trouble at the start but after putting down a lot of trees my frame rate would drop a lot in certain areas so just be cautious of this. The story i wasnt too fussed with. I cant wait for future building options and if you love storage and resource gathering, this game is a wet dream for you haha the second i got the drones my mind was blown.
