_childDocuments_.review: An enchanting game about surviving on a hostile planet, and progressively terraforming it.Terraforming effects are clearly visible, in multiple successive stages (sky, water, plants etc.), and modify existing environments, sometimes only for visual/immersive effect, but sometimes also with gameplay changes or item collection possibilities.In this early access stage, updates are frequent with new content, providing new environments, new terraformign stages, and so on. Chill music provides a very satisfactory exploration experience.The game is not completely without fault. The surprisingly most frequent but also less problematic issues are clipping issues: fairly frequent, but also fairly painless as they do not cause you to "fall through the world" as in most games - players can simply walk out of the rocks they got stuck in. More annoying in early game exploration, I noticed some inconsitencies in ice melting conditions, but that is a stage that players get beyond sooner rather than later anyways.The only persistently annoying issue I take with the game is base building. You have these foundation grids that are not the same size as the living compartments that should be built on top of them, they do not center properly, and their heights do not level properly: more often than not, they will be floating ten centimeters above the platform, or be embedded inside it. Exterior buildings that must be built on surfaces, such as reactors, will always have their support legs a good 20-30cm below platform level - which shows, as the platforms are transparent.As mentioned earlier, the game receives frequent updates at this point, so I can envision this issue being resolved at some point later before the final release. In any case, while it takes a bit of satisfaction away from a beautiful base layout, the game is still very enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Slow-burn game focused heavily on exploration and crafting. Played on a Steam Deck and it was a very smooth experience. IMO, worth the price, even at full cost.I personally got to late game, then things started to feel slow and I felt I'd mostly finished the exploration parts of the game and just had tedious gathering and crafting left. Probably would have finished the game in another ~10hr or so, but lost interest.Room for improvement:(1) Inventory management gets annoying mid- to late-game. Just too many clicks and it feels like a chore. Ideas for the dev(s) include:- a "transfer all items of this type" (as opposed to the existing "transfer all items"), - scrolling once left to get to the other container instead of needing to repeatedly go right- a later-game storage system that links storage directly in with crafting systems, getting you out of minutiae of digging around different storage containers and working through the whole crafting tree. Improving your storage system (i.e. one container per item) helps, but just feels like you're trading it for another kind of monotony.Admittedly, I know one or two things later game exist to improve this that I didn't unlock (I think drones are a thing?), but I feel like they become available way later than the problem they actually solve surfaces.(2) Items aren't always self-documenting and I needed to resort to the wiki a few timesThe role or importance of an item often isn't clear until you actually put the effort in to craft it. I realize discovery and exploration is important, but an in-game "manual" or something with more in-depth explanations of items (likely tied to the unlock system) would be nice. Of note:- The biomass system (which becomes more involved late game) felt like it was missing a "why" for me to look into it- Getting through things that requires explosions is confusing, because you unlock the powder *way* sooner than an actual means to use it in that way, and it's unclear that you can't just use the powder(3) Building could use some quality of life tweaksYou often need to entire tear down things before you can replace them. You should really be able to do things like switch four single rooms for a larger room without having to remove everything from it, especially with containers.The ability to simply move something instead of having to deconstruct then reconstruct it would also be nice. This is particularly annoying with storage containers.(4) Vehicles don't really feel worth itI unlocked the Jetpack and kinda just used it the rest of the game. I realize some upgrades exist for the vehicle, and the oxygen one in particular seemed worthwhile, but I don't think I would have ended up using the vehicle unless it started flying or something. Just felt - too slow- too limited with respects to water and being able to climb up mountains (like you can do to an extent with the jetpack)

_childDocuments_.review: Got bored with No Man's Sky, gave this a shot. Can. Not. Stop. Playing. At first it seems like it's gonna be 'meh', but it gets so much more fun as you go. Always something to do.47 hours in, and there's still a LONG way to go. And I'm not playing slow either, I'm trying to get it done as fast as I can.Few tips, the first thing you need to do is find all the food you can, until you can craft a food grower. Also, build the water collector as soon as you unlock it, because those little ice chunks used for making water bottles will all melt eventually. Other than that, it's not a hard game to figure out. Everyone says you can go at your own pace, which is true AFTER you build a food grower. Until then, you gotta manage your time pretty wisely, because your health will constantly drain as you work, but it should only be a few hours of gameplay until you can grow food and don't have to worry about it.It does have some bugginess to it, sometimes you're exploring around a mountain, looking for caves, and the mountain will just disappear, and if you're not careful, you can get kinda trapped inside if it reappears. The menus aren't entirely seamless, but they're not too bad to work with. And it seems to run my pc harder than it should, even on next to the lowest setting (lowest setting caps at 60 fps, anything higher lets it run whatever rate your pc/monitor allows). That being said, once this game is a little more polished, it has amazing potential!I foresee losing a massive chunk of my life to this game, but I don't even care. Totally worth it. Just buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so many technical issues it's hard to even keep count. Terrain collision is broken throughout the whole map, LODs seem to be missing certain LOD levels and pop in is atrocious, asset quality is generally quite poor outside of base pieces, you'll find resources you cant interact with, meteors have very unforgiving collision and can block you from entering and exiting your base, interaction hitboxes on some things are genuinely impossible to use, character movement feels like it was made by following half of a youtube tutorial series. You get the point.This game, on a technical level, is an absolute dumpster fire. That said it's a great game and I definitely recommend it for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, honestly rivals Subnautica however I think it would've been cool to have a rover/vehicle thing to get around and to require bases to be powered, that way it's slightly harder to just build a simple block base with a door to replenish oxygen while exploring. And having hostile mobs would have definitely added a slightly more dangerous feel to exploring and going into unknown territories. However, with all that being said, I still really enjoy the game for many reasons. The music is great and the way the game feels is incredible, it gives you an "at home" feel in your base while forcing you to explore further into the world to get materials. And the way the planet slowly shapes into a habitable world is such a cool feature and really made it feel like your choices had an impact. All in All, solid 9/10 game, definitely pick it up while it's still on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Planet Crafter is an interesting game. On the one hand, it's definitely engaging and enjoyable, on the other hand there's things about its progression system currently that make no sense. Performance is also a significant issue as you get into the later stages of the game, so be prepared.First off, the good:And then the bad:Overall verdict? Despite its issues, I still recommend the game, especially if you can get it on sale. It's good for about 40 hours of content at the time of this review, and most of it is enjoyable, if occasionally a bit tedious. I really hope they revamp the progression system a bit as the game evolves, because in its current state it has some obvious issues. But beyond that, it was a fun 40 hours and I don't regret spending it on this game.

_childDocuments_.review: For an early access the game works well. If you like games like Subnautica then this might be the game for you. Currently the only thing you have to worry about is fall damage, food, water, and O2. Other than that there doesn't seem like a lot of danger, which I'm fine with since there is enough to keep me doing stuff on easy mode.Will there be enemies, part of me wants it, but then that would kind of kill the whole idea that I'm bringing a planet back to life. Also, there is a story. Not much yet as well, it's not fleshed out but it should be interesting.Let's be real, is this game replayable? Right now that is a bit of a no or an almost yes. Once you've made the planet, there is only to do it again. Now if there is some randomness in how the worlds are created I could see some replayablity.It's early access so I'm hoping the graphics get a little more polish. Clipping is a thing so careful of edges of the world....the world changes so areas will break apart.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much fun!! After a few hours playing I start to get nauseous (not the games fault, I feel the same way after hours of Minecraft too, and even with the waves turned off on Raft I STILL get seasick) and I still CAN’T stop playing because it’s too much fun. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly?  It's not bad.  It's just not... good.  It still feels like an Early Access game, there's still all kinds of jank that I wouldn't associate with a full release. _childDocuments_.review: 7/10, would recommend. Game is great, but needs work and features added.This game is right on the cusp of becoming something very special. It needs automation, and excess materials disposal... Which is also just basically automation. I haven't gone all the way to the endgame and finished, but I'm pretty deep into the game. Many of the routine tasks should be automatable by now. The ore drills, resource compactification and processing should also be automatable by the late mid and early end game. The only other thing I'd suggest is putting in a digital storage system for the end game. Boxes for storage in the late game don't make any sense, and this can be greatly improved on with a little effort. Excess materials can be converted into or voided through a digital (quantum) storage system.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine someone just learned (on YouTube) how to make the basics of a survival/craft game, downloaded Unity or some other engine, copy-pasted a bunch of code he found online into it, and managed to get a "testing environment" going on. Then they started selling it on Steam.That's what this game feels like.As you open it, the main menu is as bland as it can possibly be. Then, there is no intro, no cutscene, no story, no explanation to how you got where you are or why you should bother doing anything; you are simply thrown in the middle of a shallow, sandy crater on Mars (is it Mars? I don't really know).The loading time is pretty fast, indicating the world is  procedurally generated (so your experience is going to be exactly the same as mine). No voice-overs tell you anything, no message shows up when you spawn. But hey, at least there is a tutorialesque to-do list on the top left corner of your screen. So, you go along with that.You find yourself inside a tiny square room with a chest and a console in it, which I presume is your landing vessel. Its door is permanently open but, for some reason, there's a stable atmosphere in it and you regain oxygen while inside. Cross the empty threshold, and you immediately begin to suffocate.As you step outside, you'll see  of minerals scattered all around you. You don't need to mine anything, it's all just standing there, in the middle of nowhere. Iron, silicon, titanium, ice, manganese, everything. And some chests too, inside which you'll easily find some advanced crafting materials, right away.In a few minutes you'll be building your base's first structure -- the living quarter. It's a square. Really, just a square, nothing else. You'll have some trouble setting it down where you want it to be, and probably end up leaving it partially floating in the air. You can build some leveled platforms first but, if you didn't, it's too late -- apparently, there's no way to demolish anything you have already built (I couldn't find it anywhere in the game, at least).Before laying The Square down, you'll craft your first Oxygen Tank and... a suit? I don't remember. But that's all the gear you'll apparently ever get to wear in the game. You start with a "Level 1" of each, and I assume it improves to level 2, 3 and so on later on, each one increasing how much oxygen your tank holds and whatever else the other thing does. , right?To give you an idea of how complex the game is: you mine with a left click. You access consoles with a left click. You open chests with a left click. You do not have an action bar. Did you get that? It's so simple that all you do in the game is to move around and left-click.I hate to say this, because I know how much work goes (or is supposed to) into making a game, but this one is just . Calling this a half-as*ed product would be a compliment. It does not get that far. There is no inspiration or true work whatsoever in here, it's just a bunch of extremely basic and generic crafting/survival mechanics roughly glued together and thrown on a bland, deserted scene. No thought was put into this, no one cared if there was  good in it.I refunded this thing after 11 minutes because, by then, any hope of it turning out to be a minimally decent game was gone. In fact, calling it a "game" is already quite a stretch."Overwhemingly Positive" is my S. The Planet Crafter easily deserves an overwhelmingly  score.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a a very good game. It remembers No Man's Sky, but instead of focusing in space exploration, it's planet exploration, and a great thing is that as you progress in terraforming the planet, you see the world changing around you, which is a unique aspect that I don't see in other games and it makes you want to continue the progress, instead of just doing and seeing "more of the same". It also has some cool automation aspects, not so focused in micromanagement like satisfactory or factorio, but this is not the focus of the game anyway, and this simplicity can be seem as a positive aspect in the context of this game. This is a relaxing game, and except for some resources you have to make sure to get at the beginning of the game to not die, like oxygen, water, and mainly food (because you just start producing food later, so you have to get it from crates and wrecks in the beginning), the game itself is not difficult, it has basically no real penalty if you die, and as you progress you should not need to worry about life resources anymore.This is one of the few games that I played that I got all achievements. If you want a challenge, this game may not be for you, but if you want a relaxing exploration game, with base building and automation, and seeing the world change as you progress, then it's a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: As early access games go, this is a fairly well-done game.Pros:+Less stressful game due to lack of enemies to combat. It's just you versus the planet.+Devs seem quite engaged. I'm on their email list, and they send out regular email updates, and there are regular software updates. They also do follow our message boards and respond to users.+Nice visual style in my view. I like the delineation of different zones using color.+It's not a hard science game that's totally unforgiving. Make no mistake, if you are unwary, the game will kill you, though it does make an effort to help you avoid it, but at least you'll respawn back at your base.+Great new updates to the game as it continues to develop.Cons: (I understand it's still early access, but I still need to mention a couple of these things.)-It still needs optimization of some kind. As the game goes on, even my PC with a 3900X, 32GB DDR4-3600, a 2TB PCIe 4.0 SSD and RX 6900XT will drop down to the 25FPS range during rain or meteor storms or if there is a lot of vegetation. I'm at @ 1Tti in my latest playthrough, and the best frame rates I get now are when I'm in my base, in the low 50s.-There are still a number of places where you can glitch through objects, such as the cliffs over the freighter and by the sand falls.-There are still a few places where materials are visible but cannot be mined, such as a Cobalt near the entrance to the Iridium cave.-Once there are lakes and ponds and you have a water filter, you can't mine some materials if they are by the surface. It seems you have to be under water completely submerged next to them, but of course you can't get fully submerged by the shore line.-The game can feel grindy. Mine materials, build stuff, build power plants, rinse and repeat. In fairness though, it is a terraforming game. If you were a terraformer, there would be a lot of grinding in terraforming a planet over a long time frame.-In Early Access v04.008, there are still a number of things still to be implemented. This is only really a minus if the devs were to take the money and run as other devs have. I think in this case, it's just a FYI that things like more items to decode with microchips, insects, fish and such are still not yet in the game.I enjoy playing this game quite a lot and recommend it, if for no other reason than the rewarding feeling of watching your base grow and your biome come alive with vegetation due to your efforts. This game shows a lot of promise, and I look forward to seeing what the devs are going to throw at us in the future!UPDATE 11/24/2022: The game is still being updated, and it has improved quite a bit. You will still experience FPS slowdowns as your planet becomes more alive, but the team is still developing the game at this time. They are improving and optimizing the game, and they are adding new content. At this time, there are several new biomes and more of a story of the planet you're on. Definitely worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: From the moment I caught the 'Let's Game it Out' video, I knew I wanted to play this. Now that I have, I am seriously impressed! First time writing a review, figure a small developer can use all the good word of mouth as possible.So... let's do a Top 2 of the Good and the Bad with a Neutral in-between.+ SIMPLEThere's a bare minimum of tutorials, because frankly you don't need them. If you have any critical thinking skills whatsoever, you should be able to pick this up and feel like you've got the hang of the gist of it within the first hour.+ UNIQUEI was hooked on TerraGenesis for iOS and always wondered how a game about terraforming could work from the first-person. The concept lands extremely well--as long as it's the sort of thing you're looking for.+/- MICROMANAGEMENTIf you like setting up a working production chain, optimizing every step of the process to eke out that extra umpteenth-percent boost, this is for you. Especially late game. If that sort of thing doesn't interest you... well. Don't play.- PERFORMANCEThis is a small developer, and I am very impressed at how well it all works together. Still, there are the occasional glitches that can range in severity from minor to severe.- PACEConnected to the micromanaging, it can be difficult to distinguish if you're not making progress because you have missed some key element or simply because the amount of grinding to achieve an even moderately speedier result just doesn't feel worth the effort. There were multiple times I found myself leaving the game up and running while watching a movie just so I could make the time pass.Know-What-You're-Looking-For-Score: 9/10 - Do it. Do it now.Blindly-Jumping-In: 7/10 - Could be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Pro's - - First the eerie feeling of exploring the planet and finding bits and pieces of the storyline.- Then the sereen feeling while exploring after you get to know the planet.- Seeing the progress of the landscape  changing while you make the planet habitable.- The progress of seeing flora and fauna making their appearances.- The storyline about the planets history is very interesting and I kept wanting for more. (still do)- The possibility to shape your own base and create an automated system to help create items while you can explore.- The added feature of going through wreckages and getting rare items. Nice.Con's:- Not a lot of story is out there. I would have liked a more in depth storyline. But not sure if that is a work in progress. I will start over in a new game to see if I missed new stories, but for now it does not seem so.- I do like certain things to be leveled and straight, so not being able to put frog and butterfly spaces on foundation grids is a big thing for me. Now I have to accept that everything looks 'bad'. :')- This is me being a whiney child, but: why does it take so much effort to raise my biomass. It's so slow :') I understand that other animals will be introduced, but I can't wait to see them make an appearance.- What is up with the huge amount of seeds and flower pods? They are everywhere. And why do I want to hoard them? Is this even a con? What?Overall: I like the game. Sadly, my laptop is older than the average age of a tiktok-user, so it can;t really handle the game. I once indulged myself by putting the graphics on the highest quality and the game looks stunning. Sadly, lowest settings is the best my laptop can handle and still sounds like an rocket trying to take off.If you don't have patience, then this game is not for you. If you liked Subnautica, this game is similar to that and you might enjoy this aswell.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this a nice chilled relaxing game or a hectic rush to get things done? Well after 30+ hours I think it depends on the player, you can craft a few machines and sit back and watch things happen nice and slowly or run around like your rear is on fire to speed things up. Both ways lead to the same result, I find myself playing both ways and I love it because it's always at my pace. Only I'm not sure it would be quite the same on harder modes. About the modes you can play perma-death known as 'hardcore' down to relaxed including a creative and custom mode.  It`s so brilliant watching the changes slowly happen across the map as time passes, marvelling at it then panicking as the planet starts to warm and the waters start to rise around your base camp.Anyway I have to get a lot more hours in.P.S. Pretty sure there's a demo to try the game but I don't think it gives the game justice as the the first 30 minutes you feel pushed to survive. I wasn't sure after trying it but the game was on offer at the time and I made the right move.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, any game that can pull me away from my 4000+ hr addiction to Factorio has to have great potential...and the Planet Crafter did just that.This game is amazing. But give this game its chance and you will not be disappointed.Get this game! The aesthetics are off-the-chart awesome for a Unity-powered game. _childDocuments_.review: Numbers going up should not be this relaxing.Its a game all about going through the stages of ecological succession to turn a desert planet into a thriving biological paradise.  Yes, there's also a breadcrumbs story about survivors and aliens trying to get away from humans and a big meteor and all that, but that's not what the game is ABOUT.  Its about watching the sky turn blue and lakes form from rain.  Its about worms crawling out of the muck to greet a new breathable atmosphere.  Its about building a huge base just the way you want it with lots of scenic vistas nearby.  Its about exploring and finding weird treasures in every nook and cranny.But mostly, its about numbers going up.  And those numbers lead to something special.

I tend to break a game with how I play and boy oh boy did this one crumble XD. This game had me on for days. Crafting grinding, searching, finding more stuff and then digging further. It turned me into a lootbug. I had gone crawling in places I didnt think 'd dare to crawl, in many cases I ended up outside the playable map as well, sneaking through cracks in the world. I came across areas blocked off until you'd reacha  certain goal and know what, I wont be bound by the world, I found a way through. Not with cheats or hacks, but by consistently flinging myself with my jetpack at a wall or a blockade till I became a mush puddle of a creature to slurp though. I became a slime that vored all items infront of. The metoers hailing down? So what, Slam it against my face. That copious amount of resources infront of me, I became a vacume. And I still never had enough XD. _childDocuments_.review: At the planet-survival, exploration, and building level, the game is much like No Man's Sky. That includes the mechanics, building structures, etc. However, from there the two games diverge. Planet Crafter is all about terraforming a single planet whereas NMS is about galactic exploration.In the first stage of Planet Crafter you must focus on survival until you get 2-3 food growers working. After that you can start serious work on terraforming. That said, the way you unlock various technologies, like the food growing is by achieving specific milestones in two specific terraforming categories. By building heaters and raising the planet temperature, and building O2 generators and raising the oxygen level, you eventually unlock the food grower. Drills, O2 generators, and heaters are key to achieving the food replicator unlock. If you squander your exploration food packs that you find along the way you will starve. This is especially true at any game level above relaxed mode.As a beginner I found Standard mode frustrating as I was always running from base to base trying not to suffocate. The survival aspect in this game is very strong in Standard or harder modes. Be prepared to constantly watch your food, water, and 02 suit levels until you manage to unlock tier 3-4 O2 tanks, boots, and backpack.

_childDocuments_.review: I am normally wary of paying for early access games, but as this one offered a free demo version, I gave it a go.  Right away there is a Minecraft/Space Engineers feel to it, and while there is a little bit of a learning curve in how to survive the first few minutes, long enough to start building anything of use, it was picked up quickly and mostly intuitive in how the game works.  The survival elements are there enough to remind you that you are on an inhospitable alien planet, but are not so prohibitive that a little time and resource management wouldn't let you keep going, which I feel gives it an enjoyable immersive quality.  The building habitat pieces and equipment, and unlocking of technology as you progress in terraforming, is also fairly straight forward and reasonable.  Most things will cost between 2-6 resources, and the progression of technology is well balanced in terms of what you need to continue.  There are other things that I liked, such as being able to enter and salvage resources from various space wrecks, finding certain areas with rare resources, the different filters for various biomes, meteor showers that strike nearby, often with additional minerals, and of course, watching the planet gradually change as you terraform it and giving you a sense of a reachable but not too quick achievement.All that being said, the game is definitely not finished, as it is an early access and still in the process of being created.  Clipping and there's some disconnect between rocky formations creating some "floating" rocks after meteors land.  Progression technically continues up to a certain point, but the effects stop well short of that.  The way buildings link together, or don't, needs some fine-tuning and the habitat build options are somewhat limited so far.  There's elements of a story that can be discovered (no spoilers about that, but they are there), and I'd love to see more of that.  Most, if not all, of these issues are directly attributed to the fact that the game is still being made, and are indicated to be resolved as updates from the developer are uploaded.If you're just looking for a quick, relaxing building game, the demo will probably be enough to fill that niche.  For myself, I liked what I saw enough to pay for the game in the hopes that it will continue to build on what is already a solid foundation.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't going to give this a negative review, but after writing it, I realized that there's almost nothing positive I can say about it. It's not just about ultra low budget production, but the quality of release, amount of bugs, artificially stretched grind and plain negligence.A lot of the meshes clash and go into each other. There are gaps in the world EVERYWHERE. Insane amount of textures aren't solid, and you can go through them. Even rockets do not have any sort of physics to them, and can literally fall down, clip onto each other and fly around the base if you push them. None of the wrecks on the map appear... wrecked, it's just stock parts kitbashed together without much care. I was also almost sure that it was made by a non-English speaking persons, because of the really weird almost childish-like texts inside the game, but twitter of the dev implies otherwise. Comparing this to Subnautica would be extremely unfair to both games. Subnautica is a polished experience, complete with some characters, voices, proper graphics, actual semi-realistic biomes, lighting (it's atrocious here, it just pops in and out). This game can almost be considered a sophisticated asset flip, with just how badly things are strewn together. Sudden environment changes, cartoonish asteroid barrages, janky tile borders which you can clearly distinguish, poor meshes and overall generic "vibe" - I am extremely confused at all the positive reviews and comparisons it got to Subnautica.The worst part is the grind. For me, this game is unplayable without mods. Inventory at the start of the game is restrictive beyond any reason, you can't stack anything, and you would spend hundreds of hours just lugging resources. Progress is way too slow. Moving back and forth around the map would've probably made me bash the monitor if I didn't speed things up. Unless you really want to torture yourself - just go on nexus and install akarnokd mod bundle, which fixes literally every single neglected issue, oversight and some bugs. You'll be able to stack items (shocking, I know), automate depositing resources, highlight nodes, get minimap (my god, the in-game is the worst I have ever seen, you can't even control or zoom in and out with mouse), quicksave, craft from containers, see a lot of useful information and get automation early.The only reason I would've given this a positive review is that I like the idea of terraforming, you can manage some nice screenshots occasionally, and I don't want to punish indie developers too much, but there are certainly much better games for a similar price out there. For god’s sake - they left the "unstuck" button which allows you to literally fly around and noclip through anything, that's how bad the release is, and how uncertain they are in their creation. Also note, that in 30 hours with mods, you can accomplish (I got all achievements and finished it) what people are doing in 400 hours without mods, simply because of inventory and stacking restrictions, and very late game automation, this is just a bad game design, and very clear attempt at stretching what amounts to few dozen hours of gameplay otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting start to something with great potential.If you've played Subnautica, then imagine a very stripped-down, early prototype of the game. There are a lot of similarities between the two: you're alone on a barren planet and can build structures from the raw materials lying around. However, much of the elements that make Subnautica so memorable are completely absent here. There is nothing on the planet surface but rocks and dirt. No animals, no plants, no thermal vents, no alien artifacts, no aliens, no biomes, no character.In Subnautica, basic resources are plentiful at the beginning, but you soon realize that the more advanced items require materials that are only found in more dangerous areas. This game  has none of that. Resources are strewn about the surface like someone dropped a bag of marbles around your drop pod. There's no rhyme or reason to their placement. Just run about and gather up the highly visible objects on the ground.Crafting is very weak. There are no components to build; you go from raw materials directly to finished product in one go. Some items, like a wind turbine require a single chunk of iron to build. You could have a field of wind turbines within minutes if you wanted. Scarcity is non-existent.The concept of the game is to terraform the planet. There are a handful of variables that go into that, such as pressure and temperature. Within the game mechanics, you raise each of those levels, you get a terraformed planet. These variables correspond to a device; a surface drill raises the pressure. A 'heater' raises the temperature. A water cooler with a plant in it raises the oxygen levels. The thing is, that a single instance of these tiny devices are enough to slowly transform the planet. The more you build of each one, and the more advanced versions you build will get you there faster, but you could set up one of each, and just sit and wait. You would need food and water, but that's it. You could beat the game just finding ice and food packets strewn about the surface. That's not only immersion breaking game mechanics, but it's just poor game design.This has a ton of potential. Maybe they'll retool the mechanics to make some resources harder to find. Maybe they'll redo the terraforming elements to be more believable and more interesting to perform.Maybe they'll figure out a way to work in some kind of story element. Maybe they'll add biomes and realistic placement of resources.That's a lot of maybes standing between this and a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished all 3 endings after 68 hours (same save, just reloaded and chose different ending options).At first, I thought the game was too simple, then I thought it was too grindy, then I learned to appreciate it more despite some shortcomings.The hand-crafted world looks pretty nice, but the world is similar to ARK and Subnautica, in that I constantly clipped through terrain and fell under the game world a couple of times.By the time I reached the Animals stage there wasn't much to do with them except pet them a couple of times to get a few extra genes.In order for me to purchase a Planet Crafter 2 or a potential DLC, I would expect it to have a random world generator.I would be happy with something procedurally generated (similar to No Man's Sky) with the special locations (wrecks, waterfalls, POIs) coming in the form of a 'terrain stamp' somewhat like 7Days2Die's city building so that they have a random feel while also containing the necessary parts to further the plotline of terraforming a planet.After completing the game I do not have any desire to play the same world again, but I enjoy the system enough that I would play a random world... especially if the Animals had more uses (like the honey from bees).Lastly, all three endings were lame, uninspired nihilism that even a Goth would roll their eyes at.So Devs, if there is a Planet Crafter 2... or DLC... just give us a random world and let us leave the planet when it is terraformed, because in your own terms, there is no point in writing more story than you already have.

_childDocuments_.review: 1.0 Release Update: It's incredibly easy to lose an entire day in this game and not feel like you've wasted a minute... I love it. I haven't tried the co-op version but I don't feel like I'm missing anything; single player is a complete game unto itself, and is deeply satisfying. Building has definitely gotten better since early access, although it can still be a little frustrating at times. I still think it would be nice to have a LITTLE bit more in the way of (for example) a tutorial screen that gives you a quick rundown of controls etc at the beginning of a new game, but the game isn't that complicated so it's not make or break.(OLD VERSION) Early Access:First of all, it's Early Access so I'm not factoring any bugs/glitches/things that just happen with EA games. EDIT: I have more time in the game now, and I have to say that it feels extremely polished and stable, and what issues I've had have been minor or negligible! In an age where AAA titles are released half-finished and with game-breaking bugs, it's incredibly refreshing.Second of all, it's a delight. It reminds me of the parts of No Man's Sky that I like best, which are the terraforming and base-building, but with metrics, unlocks, and environmental changes that reflect your terraforming and make it feel like you're having an impact on your little planet. There are no weapons or combat, and never will be! It's just a chill, (mostly) quiet game of gathering, building, terraforming, and dying because you forgot to bring extra oxygen canisters AGAIN. I like it for that, although your mileage may vary. About the lack of combat, I mean. The oxygen thing is just a fact.There's IS a story, although I haven't experienced much of it yet so I don't really have any opinions on that front yet.Things to note: tutorials are pretty scanty, but it's not a difficult game to figure out. Building can be a little funky because it's hard to line things up with each other and with the ground and there's no function for standing still and adjusting where you're placing things, but some items do "lock" to each other which helps. Clipping is surprisingly good for an early-access game! Things largely interact/overlap in sensible ways so far. It feels a little silly that you can build heaters that warm up an entire planet's environment inside your 1x2 cube home, but like... it's a game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game about surviving, exploring and ultimately terraforming an alien world.  It has the expected survival elements (food, water, O2), which I found to be well balanced - a serious threat, but not too tedious to manage.  There's no combat in this game, which I personally found to be a welcome relief.In the beginning, you won't be able to venture very far from your home base without running out of supplies.  But as you progress, you'll be able to craft 'modules' to upgrade your suit, allowing you to explore further out and for longer.  And there is a LOT to explore.  You're rewarded for exploring with rare resources, additional module blueprints, and even some lore/secrets.The terraforming aspect of the game is thoughtfully done.  Terraforming the planet involves building structures to increase the levels of heat, pressure, and oxygen for the planet.  The combined scores form the 'terraformation index' for the planet.  Making progress on terraforming also unlocks new structures and modules at certain milestones, which you'll need to build to accelerate your terraforming progress, as the later terraforming stages require more work than the earlier ones.As the terraformation index increases, the planet will transform through linear stages - turning the sky blue, creating lakes, etc.  What's fun about these transformations is that they aren't immediate, but gradual; for example, during the lakes stage, it starts with small puddles which get bigger and eventually grow to form full size lakes.  This is much more satisfying than if say the lakes just magically appeared out of thin air upon completion of the stage.  It's also fun to go and revisit areas you haven't been to in a while and see how they look different since the last time you were there.The game does have some rough edges...for example, I found it very easy to clip out of bounds and through various landscape barriers.  But I didn't encounter any major issues, and the core gameplay is quite solid.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a lot of fun with Planet Crafter; it's a very zen game that really helped me relax. Watching your planet evolve over time is very satisfying, and the transformation from the beginning to the end of the game is remarkable. There are also many little secrets to discover through exploration. The game is stable, though I encountered a few minor graphical bugs—nothing major. In Planet Crafter, you have to build everything yourself. Initially, you don’t have a map or a compass, so you must rely on your sense of direction for part of the game. If you prefer having quest markers, this game may not be for you. There is very little guidance in the game. Your main objective is to terraform the planet and make it habitable, but there is much more to do in Planet Crafter (I won’t spoil anything further). The soundtrack is subtle and fits the game perfectly, enhancing the zen-like atmosphere. The graphics are good—not spectacular—but they are more than sufficient for a game like Planet Crafter.: The story is minimal, but what matters is the story of the planet itself. I won’t say more to avoid spoilers.Planet Crafter can be compared to No Man's Sky, but the two games are quite different. No Man's Sky uses procedural generation and its story unfolds on a universal scale, whereas Planet Crafter focuses on terraforming a single planet. The environments and various secrets in Planet Crafter are handcrafted, unlike in No Man's Sky.

_childDocuments_.review: 290 hours into this game and I will still load it regularly, despite having "finished" everything that progression has to offer for now, because for some reason I just find it very therapeutic to wander around this world that I nurtured back to life. I am interested to try it in multiplayer once I coax some friends into getting it, but this game has been just the right level of addictive progression seeking without having to worry about being jump scared by space monstrosities. I am gearing myself up for another play-through now that it's been fully released so that I can see if implementing things in the intended sequence changes the experience at all but I really have no hesitation in recommending this to people who want a game they can peacefully immerse themselves in.Update: I have now replayed the game from start up as far as "Fish" and was honestly surprised by how engaging it was to redo the whole process. I did find progression this time around a little weird in terms of the order of when things were unlocked and I am pretty sure my prior knowledge of the game lead me to mess up the sequence of things a bit so that didn't help, but it was nice to see the things that had been implemented along the way evolve at their intended pace. I do agree with some other reviews, however, that the game itself is not always transparent about what has to happen to progress, and given the extreme importance of gearing yourself for exploration and salvaging from wrecked ships in order to get resources in the early game, not to mention the necessity of going BACK into those wreckages once you advance enough to unlock better salvage options, I do think some sort of more elaborate tutorial at the very least is almost mandatory. Knowing how to advance and unlock things is also vital and, at this point, now that the game is fully released, I do think the game leaves far too much ambiguity for new players. Still a great game though, still thoroughly recommend it and look forward to convincing some friends to come multiplayer with me.

_childDocuments_.review: v1.0 Review:The Planet Crafter is unfortunately a shallow experience. The early game is interesting as you establish yourself, however it quickly becomes apparent that you will be doing the same thing throughout the game.Continuing the comparison to Subnautica, where each biome presented its own challenges and threats, the biomes in Planet Crafter are all effectively the same with little other than visuals to distinguish them.By the time you have reached breathable atmosphere there is nothing left to see beyond spamming generators to grind your way to complete terraformation. Automation and animals do not fundamentally change the underlying issue with immersion.There is some story, however this consists entirely of walking to co-ordinates which you have been given and reading logs, complete unchallenged. Platforming, puzzles, or any form of obstacle would have been welcome to spice it up.Immersion truly is the key issue here. Resources are neatly scattered around the world, constant meteor strikes do nothing to hamper your efforts, generators such as the heaters and drills do not interact (such as making the area around them damaged or hard to grow plants on), and ultimately devolves to making the numbers go up as quickly as you can.It's not a bad game by any means, made tolerable by co-op, just hard to recommend in a world where Subnautica exists.Original Review:There is a lot of potential here, which I appreciate is the point of early access, however there is also a long way to go before this is on the same level as Subnautica.Immersion is the game's key issue at this point, which will likely be resolved when development goes from core mechanics to dressing.As a side note, I feel that mining for resources with smaller low-tech drills would be more thematically appropriate than picking up random scattered nodes everywhere.

_childDocuments_.review: "Do something simple, do it well."This was the goal stated by the game devs in a news update back when I first reviewed this game in version 0.4.008. Back then, I said the game lived up to it, but needed some polishing. Now, coming back to the full release version, I can safely say that it's received all that polish and then some.I love the concept of terraforming games in general, and I especially love when they're done well. This game is all about the terraforming, and it doesn't waste time getting bogged down in combat, economics, or other distractions. And it's BRILLIANT.What we have here is a planetary terraforming game that starts as a base building survival game that requires you to explore and gather food and water to stay alive, while maintaining your oxygen levels while away from your base. Eventually, you gain the ability to produce your own food and water, at which point it transitions from survival to the most perfectly chill game I have ever seen.Once you've reached the chill stage, it's basically a giant sandbox where you just gather, build, grow, and explore... and then explore again, once your terraforming level goes up and the environment changes. While you can technically make the game "harder" by altering game settings, all that tends to do is lengthen the timeline of a given save file. It doesn't really make the game more difficult, especially after you've gotten familiar with the gameplay loop, but honestly, that doesn't matter. This isn't the sort of game you play for a challenge. It's the kind of game you play to just relax and build your bases as you watch craters turn into lakes, barren fields into grasslands, and valleys into jungles.If you don't like that concept, this one probably isn't for you. If you do, this is gaming perfection.10/10. Legitimately one of my favorite games ever.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game! Absolutely recommended :)The gameplay resembles "Subnautica on land" because you need to explore the game world with its different biomes, you'll gather and grow ressources, craft and build (equipment, bases and different types of machinery). Later on you can even dive into large lakes, (albeit currently without underwater plants), plus just like Subnautica, the game is not providing you with actual quests other than the tutorial tasks (no rewards for those) and is not really telling any story to follow (so far), instead you'll find messages that others (NPCs) have left here and there with a bit of a background story.Your task of terraforming a planet is really unique though, and that's why I'm in love with Planet Crafter :) It's awesome to behold how the look of the barren desert game-world changes into a beautiful green scenery with blue sky, all caused by the work of your own hands. It's really cool to watch how the lakes fill up, how the ice melts, the water level rises (and rises, rises, and then rises even more!), how the yellow-orange sand slowly turns into green "moss", how grass tufts start to sprout, how algaes start to form around your growers on the water, grass and beautiful flowers grow anywhere you want them to, then even unique looking types of trees... And I totally love the (new) different kinds of meteor showers!Another unique task of this game is building "base camps" along your way to provide yourself with oxygen and water at first, also storage, later on with food etc. This is something that I always loved to do (like in GRAV for example), but no other game than Planet Crafter actually requires. Plus: plundering the wrecked space-ships and underground hideaways is a real fun activity too :DThe game is very well made, I didn't find any game-breaking bugs found so far even though the game is still in EA :) Just beware of saving and reloading inside of wrecks ;) FYI: I've currently only just reached "insect stage" and a "fish stage" will be up next. It's a nice thought that we can bring the initially "dead" planet to life this way :)Can't believe these amazing graphics were made by only two people! Love the large space-ship-wrecks so much ^_^ Their different shapes look really cool. And the bunks even come with small toilets - so cute :D Actually, everything else is awesomely designed too: the many things we can craft and build, the lovely sky, the meteors that come crashing down, the falling sand from the cliffs - it all looks very beautiful and makes your stay on this planet enjoyable :)Story-wise there's still work to do though I guess... Well, it's EA after all, so let's see how this will evolve :)Also in terms of game balance, I'm not 100% happy (yet) - while being aware that everyone has their own ideas and taste of course.Here's some additional thoughts:1. We're a convict with the task of terraforming a cold desert planet and bringing it to (green) life. Someone (presumely the "Sentinel Corps" that left the message on the screen in our capsule) must have invested a lot of money: we were brought to this planet, were dropped down in a sturdy capsule, we got a fine space suit and a sophisticated multitool.On the other hand we aren't provided with much food in order to survive, and we brought no seeds to grow?! Even worse: our food grower blueprint is not available from the start? This significantly reduces our chance to survive and by that our chance to fulfill our task. If we fail, all the investments for this project will have been for naught... This does not make much sense to me.* Possible solution: just let the food grower blueprint unlock very early in the game or even be unlocked from the start, and provide us with at least one pack of seeds. We'll need to find aluminium in order to craft the food grower anyways and then we will also have to wait for the food to grow.** I'd like it if the different game modes could come with different starting options - relaxed game mode with more and better seeds for example, while hardcore mode could come with accidentally spoiled seeds so that we'll have to find seed packs first.2. (Randomly) filled chests are lying around all over the place. Also: you'll find better and rarer stuff depending on your terraforming progress. Why? Who dropped those in the middle of nowhere - and why would chests in your starting area contain much rarer stuff if you only open them later in the game?* Possible solution: wouldn't it make more sense if we found backpacks next to spacefarer's remains (empty spacesuits or something) instead of chests?** Wouldn't it be better to have fixed findings in all those storage containers - but differently depending on the chosen difficulty mode? The current randomness will just make players save the most chests for later, and also will lead them to saving their game progress just before opening any storage container, then reloading until the randomly generated content will satisfy them...3. So we can deconstruct chests, a few solar panels, heaters and specific iron girders, but nothing else in those really large wrecks? I would love it if we could gain cloth by deconstructing bunk beds in spaceships rather than randomly collecting cloth from chests. Actually: the more we could deconstruct and re-use/recycle or even fix in order to make it work again, the better in my opinion ;)4. How believable is it to build a whole building module that also procudes oxygen (!) out of nothing but iron and titanium? And we don't even have to craft semi-manufactured products beforehand for such large multifunctional objects? Not even to speak of Biodomes T2 with several tree types inside even though we don't use any tree seeds for their construction...* Possible solution: how about adding oxygen-producing algae or slime or so to the buildings? Basically an organic substance that our capsule should have integrated somewhere, since it too produces oxygen? We could take part of this substance from the capsule and when erecting a building, this substance would be put either in tanks next to the door in order to produce oxygen, or maybe even into a whole layer of the building. After it multiplies with the help of sunlight, we could then again gather a part of it in order to erect more buidings that will produce oxygen as well ... and so on.5. I'm also a bit irritated by message screens left by former crash-survivors, while our crafted "signs" are much smaller and we cannot write and leave behind message screens ourselves. * Possible solution: it would be nice to read different messages - those that were sent to the now-wrecked ships or abandoned bases (so that they could provide bits of the game world's background-story) rather than "last words" left by the castaways themselves...** Alternatively, I'd actually also be happy enough if we could "write" our own message screens ourselves too just like the shipwrecked ones did ;)

_childDocuments_.review: From the list of survival and crafting games I've played, this is by far the one which I found to be the most relaxing. It is also important to mention that it was also the one with the simplest and most straight forward game mechanics out of them all - collect building materials, build, survive and progress.You will need to balance your survival stats and at the same time improve your ability to advance the terraformation process (denoted by a terraformation index - TI) of the planet you have been assigned to, by progressively being able to build structures and machines which will help you achieve this progression at a faster rate. I found the environment to be pretty diverse and interesting, so when I just wanted to take a quick break from crafting, and carry out some exploration, this was not just only possible, but easier to do so as you craft better equipment and progress from one stage to the next. The accompanying soundtrack helped to keep the overall mood of the game peaceful as well. A great pairing in my opinion.There might be a few minor clipping bugs here and there, but in my opinion, these are overshadowed by the overall great quality of the game on all other fronts. Story-wise, there are a few tit-bits of lore strewn here and there, but it certainly is not the main focus of the game itself. Still, bonus points for adding them, since it adds to the scope and satisfaction of making these discoveries through the time invested in exploration.This game would be a great addition to your library if you are up for some casual survival-type kind of scenario. It also supports up to 10 simultaneous co-op players, so that might be something in common to share with friends or family when you are not feeling up to doing some solo gaming.To the game studio and the developers ... thank you for this game and keep up the great work!

_childDocuments_.review: Note: Early Access Review.It's like a cross between a survival crafting game and an idle game. The survival crafting part should be familiar: you explore the environment, gather resources, keep an eye on hunger and thirst meters, build a base and crafting stations. The idle game comes in as your research tech tree. You build machines to slowly terraform the planet, each contributing a rate over time to both a certain category and to the overall progress. There are milestones along each category and for the overall progress that unlock new technologies. The new techs then contribute to speeding up the terraforming process, or allowing you to do more. So the gameplay loop largely goes that you'll build some set of machines to speed up progress, then wander off to go explore, or build your base, or mine resources. While you're off doing that, the progress hits some milestone, unlocks new technologies, giving you new toys to play with and goals to achieve. It's also pretty satisfying seeing the world change around you due to your efforts. Overall I found this game nicely addictive, scratching that "having a world to myself to build and explore in" itch.It's still in early access, and there's still some rough edges to it. Things like the collision on the mountains can be wonky. However, in the entire time I played it I never had a crash or freeze. The demo's save game carries over into the full version, so that makes it a good way to see if you'll like the game without losing time.

This game, resources are just kind of spread across the ground randomly and you just run around picking up the randomly place stuff. I mean come on, do something more creative than that devs. Crafting was meh, construction also meh. Just not that interesting of a game.

After around 10 hours into the game (one play session, NOT ASHAMED TO SAY THAT) I saw how wrong I was to request a refund the first time I bought it. _childDocuments_.review: The game is still very obviously early access. About 24 hrs of in-game time so far and I'm already at or near 80% completion. I've explored pretty much every POI except for maybe one or two of the end game points which I will not spoil by mentioning them.It just doesn't have a lot of features, what features it does have lack a certain level of depth. Game play basically boils down to gather these to make this, which unlocks something else you have to gather for... lather, rinse, repeat. Not wholly original and frankly some other titles did it better.What this game does have that I've not seen before is the way your progress affects the environment. An interesting gimmick to be sure but it feels slightly lacking. Perhaps more is planned that has yet to be added and at which point I will continue/start over and develop a new opinion of.For some reason it just felt like less about being a game and more about the environment... maybe that's just me. I did enjoy some of the exploration once I got to a point where I could actually explore for a decent length of time. Resource gathering was a pain, storage management even more so. Base design/building was a little clunky and sometimes frustrating but it was easy to figure out and work around it's quirks. I've certainly played more frustrating building mechanics (looking at you ARK).
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: This game is two things I love: survival-crafting, and a world that changes according to the player's progress. As you terraform the planet, some places will open that weren't accessible before, new resources will appear, and of course everything will  a lot different. It feels great.Add to that a world that is beautiful before and after you change it, lots of places (and secrets) to explore, some pretty fun tech, and lots of room for future development, and you get something you definitely should try, at least if those things are to your taste.When I originally posted this review, I wrote:  That is of course now obsolete. 2 years and a bit later, the game is now past 1.0, pretty mature, and expanded a lot since that original review. Of course, it remains a strong recommendation from me. I beta-tested this game, and got a free key on account of that. But I was planning to buy it anyway, and of course I wouldn't have volunteered to beta-test if I didn't think the game was worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game to be addicting and fun.  It moves as fast as you want it to and just when you start to feel overwhelmed by one of the mechanics (e.g. gathering, harvesting from your machines, etc.), they add a feature to make that thing easier and optionally take that load off of your hands.  Load times are amazingly quick.  Every time I thought I was getting close to the end of the game, a whole new set of features unlocked and I had a new target.Also, inventory management was great - another one of those things where the progression of item box sizes was well done (and you can label your boxes) then just when it got to be too much, you unlock a better feature to manage it and it was golden.I also appreciated the fact that the game didn't feel punishing.  If you place something in the wrong spot, just destroy it and you get your items back.  You're out in the middle of nowhere and running out of air? Build yourself a mini-base to breathe again.  It just made it feel that much more fun rather than artificially punishing.It took just under 50 hours to complete the game (all achievements) while playing co-op and it was worth every minute.  Definitely worth the price I paid.If you can tolerate minor issues, then definitely play this game.  (By minor I mean clipping issues in some areas, the rare bug of an item icon being wrong, and at very end game (with thousands of nearby objects) my co-op friend couldn't see me after playing for a bit.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I've yet to finish the game, but with 23 hours on record, as of writing I can recommend this game, but it's not for everyone.Firstly, I highly suggest playing this game co-cooperatively. There can be times when the game could get tedious, or perhaps even quite isolating. Having someone to chat to whilst collecting resources, or juggling multiple tasks really makes this more enjoyable.The gameplay loop is solid and the progression of O2/speed/ storage capacities is well balanced so that just as you start to get frustrated with the pacing of your resource runs, you suddenly get a boost to productivity and scope to explore.I praise the game for its willingness to accept that later in the game, some mechanics are no longer necesssary. Breahtable atmosphere and drone automation (along with drills) essentially allow you to create a post-scarcity scenario allowing you to focus on building, exploring and the task of biomass restoration.The biggest + in my books - is seeing the impact on the world. Never have I been so excited at seeing a mossy decal, or a shift in the sky from red to blue.  Never has a tree been so amazing to me. A green vista means so much more when you realise its your work thet turned it from a barren wasteland to that verdant space.Theres a story and some fun stuff to explore, but it's not expertly written (it's not got a scratch on Outer Wilds)A couple of gripes: the pacing for some of teh biomatter stuff didn't feel right. I'd jsut put down my first tree spreader, but it ended up not feeling great, because I jsut saw the canyons natural trees which looked much better, likewise I was seeing butterflies before my first butterfly farm. Progression would feel more rewarding if the environment heldback on stuff until you had established it more first.My final hope is that when all is done, a map maker is available. I'm not sure how much this game will stand up to multiple playthroughs or random starts.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long-time player and fan of survival games. I love Subnautica, The Long Dark, The Forest, Green Hell, Valheim, you name it and I'll play it.Now with that out of the way, this game is not at all worth your money. It's barely a game. Yeah sure it's in early access, but the fundamentals are awful and won't be improved.What this "game" is, is a Unity asset store-driven Subnautica wannabe knockoff. They literally bought most assets straight from the Unity store - you can find the minerals they used here for cobalt, "super alloy" and so on:There are clipping issues all over the place. Rocks float above the ground. My character has no legs and is a floating mass. The environment / ground is barren. The environment looks like Mechwarrior 2 from the 1990s and that's not a compliment.Bottom line: the developers slapped some Unity store assets together to make a quick buck with a very half-baked "game" and it appears that's working for them. I cannot recommend spending money on it.If you crave this kind of game, grab Subnautica or No Man's Sky. Miles and miles better and more polished for similar prices.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very addictive open world survival game where it is mostly you versus the environment. If you ever felt Subnautica didn't let you build enough and upgrade more and you got tired of all the creatures in the way ... well, this is your game. It's an addictive loop of terraforming a planet so that you can eventually leave. That sounds so simple, but there will be tons of collecting, near death experiences from food/water/air loss, wreck explorations, hidden cave and mine reveals, and lots of building and upgrading as you unlock more crafting recipes and gear. The game has solid play, based in the Unity engine. Graphics and effects are quite good for this title based on its sale price. Sounds are decent, with a very light smattering of eerie and atmospheric music along with tool and machine sounds as you build. But this game has, "just one more thing," pull in spades.  You'll be returning to it quite a bit to go through the entire story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely beautiful game. Mind you, the graphics are nothing special but as you progress through the stages of terraforming, the environment changes and as barren wastelands turn into lush landscapes you will sense a(n admittedly irrational) feeling of accomplishment you likely won't get from any other game.On a more technical side, the pacing is well done, the world feels big without being tediously so. Even towards the end, it never truly felt like a grind which is a miracle with these kinds of games.The endings are a bit lackluster and the non-standard endings require some work. As it's not really a story driven game, I don't mind the endings because the journey there is what mattered.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game! _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A fun game with some high highs and very low lows, suitable for fans of base-building, exploration and a small degree of automation.So, The Planet Crafter took me and 2 other friends a few days to finish, we saw one of the 3 possible endings (the other two would require a level of grinding that we could not be interested in doing).We came into this game with the expectation of a mix of Satisfactory (one of our favorite games) and Valheim, given the survival elements. The game delivered partially on some of the promises, but not all.First, this is  a game about automation, until you're really close to finishing it, when it suddenly is. This transition is quite jarring, and it's a bummer that the process of automating things with drones makes the game a lot more interesting and dynamic, and yet the game thinks it's a good idea to gate it into the later parts of progression.For the majority of the game, however, this is a game about exploration, with a very light dose of base building (particularly early, where trying to establish a "home base" might hinder your progress way more than simply wandering around the map crafting small rooms to get some oxygen and then go back exploring). The shtick is: you need to terraform the planet, and that happens when you increase 4 factors: Pressure, Heat, Oxygen and Biomass. The first three are available from the start, and you get them by exploring, finding resources to turn into buildings that increase those numbers. As you progress, you unlock blueprints for different, better machines to increase those numbers, and some quality of life for the survival aspect of the game. Biomass comes in the second half of the game, when the planet is stable enough to start gaining plant life, and it's a little different, with you needing to do things like build animal feeders, aquariums and cultivating life forms for the planet. The game features a survival aspect that involves Hunger, Thirst and Oxygen. Hunger depletes the slowest of them all, but it's also one of the only ones that you will never 100% be able to ignore, since oxygen eventually becomes obsolete (the planet will have a breathable atmosphere, and all internal areas give oxygen, so as long as you carry enough materials to build a room and a door, you will never ever lose oxygen), and thirst, while still being something you need to deal with, is so trivially easy after a while that you will never die to it after the very start of the game. As for hunger, you will grow your own seeds and eat a lot of eggplant, but on the very start, there is a very real need to explore to keep finding food.There is no combat element, no enemies and no NPCs to interact with, save for written messages that you get once in a while. It makes exploring easy, with the challenge coming from the game's inventory system and the choices they made regarding it, which are as follows:1)You have a very limited inventory space, which has six levels of upgrading available, all of them adding more slots.2)No item in the game stacks, so EVERY SINGLE UNIT occupies a slot. If you want to carry 5 water bottles, 3 oxygen capsules and 3 pieces of food, that's a total of 11 slots of your backpack occupied only with survival. Need to bring Aluminum back? Every single unit of aluminum occupies a slot.While OF COURSE that is deliberate and intentional, it doesn't make it any less annoying, given a lot of the game's playtime is basically inflated via the fact you have to make several trips and build impromptu lockers in many spots to hold all the loot you need to carry back, which makes this game ideal to play with friends, since more people can carry more stuff around. The same logic also applies to any machines and storage units you make, every single item occupies a slot.Now I'll give a basic panorama of the base building and automation aspects of the game.As said before, there is, in the beginning, a very big incentive to building many small bases all around the map, because every base gives oxygen (so you get lots of places to stop and catch some air without dying), and because resources are all spaced out around the map. The base building is simple and functional, you build rooms one "compartment" at a time, and that compartment automatically links to adjacent ones, including vertically with the use of indoor stairs, so you will not have a lot of issues while building. It's important to note that part of the terraforming process entails the coming of lakes, waterfalls and rivers to the planet, so depending on the altitude you build, one or more of your bases might end up submerged in water (you lose no items, but all production for machines underwater ceases working), so it's smart to check the altitude coordinate and build planning for floods.After a while, you start building ore extractors, the first half of the  part of the game. Basically, Extractors come in 3 tiers, with each tier increasing your control over which ore you get. With tier 1, you can only place the extractor and get an assortment of all the available metals (plus a special metal if you place it in the correct spot), and you have to manually empty the machine (remember the 1-item-per-slot inventory? Yeah, that's an issue here) and do with the ore what you will. Given that all the important special materials are in specific spots in the map, that means for a while, you will have to build extractors spread around the map, and have people constantly walking around, bouncing from one to the next to keep the machines empty and running and depositing the products on a growing assortment of storage lockers (by the end of my save, I'm pretty sure I had over two-hundred lockers). You will then use these ores to progress by building more machines and etc.The next stage of automation the game allows, which I will call stage 1.5, is the ability to unlock Teleporters, that work beautifully and are well-done. Build a teleporter on every extractor you have, build the energy necessary to support it, and now instead of walking everywhere, you're teleporting everywhere. It doesn't really  anything, but not needing to walk makes the process a lot less painful, especially since by that point you still need to walk to find things other than ores, like all the many biomass parts.The final, and true stage of automation, the part that baffles me in how late it comes into the game are the drones. Drones simply change the game completely and turn it into an automation game through and through. You can get your drones to do the item pickups, deliver them to any item processors or storages, and do all sorts of automated crafting and refining of materials. By the end, you'll be creating automatic Fertilizers, growing and collecting food, making animal food, extracting all sorts of materials AND you'll have all the incentive to build a big central base to store and process all those things. By this point, the game in my opinion becomes really fun, but if you're not into automation games, this part can be really jarring, because if you don't make the best of it, you'll increase your playtime ten times solely based on relying on exploration to get all the important parts for the endgame grind.So, to wrap up my points, who do I recommend this game to?1)People with large friend groups. This game can be a grind sometimes, but it's also a lovely multiplayer experience for you to simply chat with your buddies while dividing tasks, and the game supports up to 10 people on a server at once.2)People who like peaceful exploration. There is no combat, and exploration is SUPER important in the game.3)People who enjoy automation games. There is not a lot of it in the early game, but it becomes important in the end.For me and my friends, it's a 5/10 on its low points (Inventory, some decisions) and a 7.5/10 on the highs (exploration moments, visuals and automation.)If it's for you, get it.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel I was slightly mis-sold on this one due to the glowing reviews. The core of the game seems to be right up my street, however, in 51 minutes playtime I died about 10 times simply for daring to wander a two minute walk from the starting area. By this time I'd had enough of it, low power, low oxygen, low water, when you respawn it seems to take very little time to get these warnings again.I'll try it again if this gets addressed, but for the moment it's too annoying to want to persist with it.EDIT for 1.0 release: So I've given it another chance, starting from scratch, it seems to be exactly the same. This has to be the dumbest survival game I've ever played, it is literally in your interest to just let yourself die. If you wander more than 2 minutes from your base expect to do relay runs to bring back the slightly more exotic resources you find. You can make oxygen and water quite easily but it takes up valuable inventory space that you are highly restricted on, at least in the early game that I have played so far. Having played 2.5 hours I am yet to unlock the ability to make food; solar and wind farms, heaters, no problem. I have a seed for food provided in the initial start point for making food, I just can't use it yet. It really is comically bad.I guess I should just be thankful it doesn't punish you too badly for dying. In fact, I did find as it doesn't remove all your inventory when you die and you teleport back to your base, this actually reduces the relay runs as you can let yourself die, drop off what you grabbed and still have in your inventory. Then go back with empty pockets to pick up what you dropped plus a bit more! Again, it is literally in your interests to die lolI just got to unlocking some agility boots that state a 15% improvement in movement speed, I barely noticed any difference, and because the early game is too tight to allow me more space for utility items, those boots got dumped into storage almost immediately.I want to like this game, I really do, and I will likely persist in the hope it gets better, but it really is just so stupid.The ambient music is kinda nice, it runs pretty well and is not too demanding on my system. I am still perplexed why this isn't closer to a 'mixed' score than the glowing reviews it has. This is a 5-6/10 for me when it could have been a 9/10 with some thought gone into. For reference, I am playing on completely vanilla settings.Edit after DLC: Okay, clearly I have now had my money's worth, do I recommend this game, yes. However, I am still leaving a thumbs down as I wish the balancing of progression was much tighter, and much less annoying in the early game. I bought the DLC and played right through it, with my experience of the base game it was much more pleasant, but still frustrating the way you get some unlocks. I believe this game was made by a team of 6, and if true, it is mighty what they have achieved, but ever the demanding gamer, I wanted it just that little bit better. I'm okay with a bit of clunkiness, I fell through the map once, my vehicle disappeared through the map a couple of times, but dying and a reload fixed these problems. In summary, if you think you would like this type of game, get it, you will find hours and hours of brain soothing, just be ready for frustrations in the early game.
