_childDocuments_.review: English isn't my first language, so please excuse errors.Cannot recommend, as it gets boring really fast. I played a single session for about 10 hours now on "Intense" and don't intend to continue playing it. When reading this feedback please bear in mind that this game is tagged as a survival game and that's what I bought it for.In contrast to what people post here this is, however, NOT a survival game, at least not if you have any meaningful amount of experience with other survival games. Here's why:- Global energy. Very stupid idea, because it allows you to spread your base across the whole map, defeating danger. If you want to avoid micromanagement of cables, at least restrict the energy to an area around the generators.- Living compartments can generate oxygen out of thin air (pun intended). Combined with the global energy this means you can just place single living compartments everywhere on the map and you won't have to worry about oxygen anymore. And it's illogical, considering that you otherwise have to create oxygen manually.- Generally NO upkeep necessary. Nothing decays, so whatever you build is there forever. Energy, water, food, living compartments ... everything. You build it, you keep it.- Similarly, neither your suit nor your flashlight or the JetPack consume energy/fuel. Again: You build it, you keep it.- Reagents required for survival are scattered everywhere. Food, water, etc. can always be found in the DOZENS of crates.- Food. Seeds are 100% guaranteed to return, so you only need three or four food generators and you'll be fine.- No danger. Ok, you can probably die from falling if you're stupid, but beyond that you only need to make sure that you have enough resources with you (of which there are always plenty) and you won't die. I realize the "no fighting" thing is intentional and I really like that, but you need to offset that through something else.- The meteorites don't cause damage. This may be intentional but just adds to the "not dangerous at ll" feeling- There are occasional dust storms, but they don't seem to cause any harm either.- Health bar seems underutilisedAll of the aspects above make this game VERY boring after an hour or two. Planet Crafter gives me zero incentive to keep playing, because I know "playing" in this case means waiting hours and hours for more "green" without any meaningful gameplay in between.And yes, I've already found three golden crates, found multiple underground bases, melted various pathways (shortcuts) and found the base of the previous planet crafter. It's still boring.On the positive side, I've had no crashes or any other game breaking bugs.To summarize: If you just want to terraform a planet somewhat similar to Minecraft creative mode, Planet Crafter might be your thing. Otherwise play a real survival game.Edit: Typo and fix "meteors" (they're meteorites, not meteors)

_childDocuments_.review: A great terraforming single player survival/base-building game.=== Original Review during Early Access: ===+ Difficulty selection -- from "Relaxing" (Death is inconsequential -- you merely respawn in your base with everything you were carrying) all the way to "Hardcore" (Death is a game over).+ Tutorial portion called "First steps" guides you with objectives in the upper left corner and simple gameplay.+ Once you finish the tutorial, the game opens up and it is up to you to figure out how to accelerate the different elements of the terraforming process. Thanks to the tutorial, you should have no trouble figuring this out, and the challenge here is basically finding the sources of the different resources you will need. At this point, there is no more a "List of objectives", because there are different paths towards the goal, and it's up to you how to achieve it. As an example: Will you cover your lake with Algae to produce a lot of "base" Biomass -- or will you have fewer Algae producers, but instead use space rockets to get a massive "times X" bonus for them? The latter requires you to construct rocket engines and collect tree bark, while the former requires growing eggplants and collecting algae. Similarly, you can go for the raw pressure boost of Drills, or you can use the weaker Ore extractors, which however yield useful ores as a byproduct.+ Simple survival metrics: All you have to watch is your Oxygen level (replenishes upon entering any of your bases), Hydration level (initially, you get water from melted ice, but quickly gain access to Atmospheric water catchers, and eventually, you'll gain a filtration system for safely drinking from lakes), and Food (this one depletes the slowest, and also doubles as your "Health", so if you fall from a deadly height, you don't actually die -- you just enter a "Critical hunger" condition, and if you quickly eat anything, you will be healed). You can carry portable oxygen and water tanks with you to quickly replenish O2 and hydration, and food is also transportable, although I eventually stopped carrying it.+ Anti-frustration measures:> > If you misplace ANY structure, you can demolish it and you will get ALL the resources back, so you can experiment with placement as much as you want.> >  Base elements can be placed in the air, they won't fall, and external staircases will attach to airlock doors to create nice access ramps.> > Base extensions can be added either from inside or from outside, and a helpful color-coded outline shows you whether the placement is valid.> > You don't have a minimap that would be accessible at all times; instead, you can place Beacons (I typically place them at major bases and at "ruins"), each given a color of your choice (16 million options), and these beacons that broadcast a useful symbol into your hud at all times, making navigation simple. It's also possible to carry the components needed for a Map Screen, and plop it down during your exploration to get a satellite view of your area - and then dismantle that screen to get resources back.> > Jetpack! This amazing transportation mode makes traversal easy and allows you to jump off high cliffs with no problem. The controls take a while to get used to, but then you'll love it.=== Addendum for full release: ===> Developers have added multiplayer, which I am unlikely to utilize, but it's still a plus.> So many new things have been added, new biomes, Endgame content, off-planet trading, automation... Very cool!

_childDocuments_.review: The reason I don't recommend this game is because it feels far too early in development to be available for money. Its not early access, its feels like a pre-alpha, and it most definitely isn't worth £20 in its current form. It should have really released as a free closed alpha test to get feedback instead of charging money.That being said, I think it has a ton of potential. It feels like its trying to be a Subnautica type game, so if they can pull that off then I will certainly change this review. Until then, I wouldn't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: For an early access, the game is very nice. After 5 hours and 30 minutes of playing, I have only reached stage 3 of the 10 terraforming levels in the game. Exploration is nice, even though you can cheat by regularly placing bases to refuel O2 without using bottles, and I have encountered no bugs.But the game still has big negatives at the moment:-   the basic construction is really not user-friendly and there are far too few crafts to make a base for a solitary terraformer-   The fact that each terraforming action only has bonuses eventually leads to ridiculous situations: currently, I am growing plants on the surface because I have reached the right concentration of O2, even though the atmospheric pressure and temperature are worthy of Pluto. Adding negative interactions between elements like "TerraGenesis" does on Android would prevent this kind of absurdity.The demo gives a very good overview of the game and should be a must-visit before buying the game at the moment. I can't wait to see the evolution of the game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: If Satisfactory and Surviving Mars had a baby, The Planet Crafter would be that child. For me, I got some wonderful endorphin rushes after reaching the progression phases: The first rain, seeing lakes form, launching rockets to rain meteoric destruction onto the planet. I've yet to see the first natural vegetation, but I am looking forward to it. Great game!

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica on Land. In space. Love it. Could become better than Subnautica with time and care.Is it early access? Yeah it is. A little janky at times, some spelling/typo errors here and there. There are some kind of blatantly exploitable gameplay mechanics involving dropping single-door-rooms all over the map to give yourself an infinite air supply. (I've seen devs using the same techniques on livestream) so that's a bit disappointing, but for now, it seems to be a "when in rome, do as romans do" situation. I hope that is a placeholder mechanic that will get nerfed as other features get filled in and developed.But it's generally well designed and surprisingly well paced. Some of the hidden things have legitimately surprised me. Nothing feels terribly grindy, although there are certainly a few really rough parts that still need to get beaten down with a balancing sledgehammer, I assume that will come with time.It's abundantly playable and enjoyable as-is and I believe it will continue to improve.

_childDocuments_.review: I love a creative game, especially if I don't have to worry about "running and gunning" and stupid zombies.  I mean seriously, zombies are so 1960's; let them go Dev's.  *ahem*  Yes, well, at any rate while this game may not have the breadth and depth of Minecraft, the graphics are sure better!  Yes, it's fairly linear in that you always land at the same spot, the planet is always the same map, and there are always the same discoveries of wrecks and resources to discover.  Once you've played a game through to (currently) late-game, any subsequent games are a breeze to find and gather what you need.On a more positive note, this does NOT hinder your creativity in any way.  You can build shelters from very basic to extremely complex.  I've enjoyed playing the game through a few times while creating entirely different bases and remote shelters each time.And, as a side note, updates may affect your shelters/bases.  After the last major update I went to my shelter in the huge crater only to find the bottom level (the one with the doors) was buried underground, and I can only look in through the windows up the upper level.  At first I was frustrated, but then I thought it was kinda cool that the environment is changing in a realistic manner for a developing, growing planet.  Lastly, I can VERY MUCH appreciate the fact that I can save my game at any point in any location as my job has me traveling daily with varying schedules (I'm a truck driver).  So I can play for 30 minutes or 12 hours and stop at any point and log right back in to where I had to stop.  I hope that feature remains with future updates.Yes, I would recommend this to anybody that's into creative games and tired of FPS and stupid zombies.

The gameplay is a lot of fun, the game received many updates between my two times through and I'm not really to the endgame even now, though it's close.  Well worth it IMHO.

_childDocuments_.review: obsessed with this. It's a pretty straight forward game: Get resources, build things, get more oxygen/backpack, build your base. Very addictive to play but there are a few issues (some of them might just be me) Pros: Really fun, very easy to pick up and play Not a lot of hand holding. They give you a series of starting goals to help you get started but there are no tutorials There are no enemies that are going to destroy your stuff which is niceGraphics are pretty decent but also not super heavy on a computerIt's really clear what resource is what. You don't have to be like "oh is that iron or titanium?" You can spot them from a reasonable distance and pick them up Terraforming the planet is really fun I like the concept of you being a prisoner who is doing this as an alternative to prisonThere's not a lot of plot so it's easy to play while watching something or listening to somethingCons: The map is the same so there's no randomness to the game. Every new game has the exact same layout I wish it was more clear that you shouldn't build right next to your landing pod. When you start making lakes, your pod WILL go underwater and you will lose power on anything that gets submerged. It does tell you to make your base on "higher ground" but it feels counter intuitive to go SO far from the pod (you have to go reasonably far). I ended up starting over when I realized moving everything would be harder than starting fresh with a better understanding of the game (I do like restarting this kind of game once you get the hang of it so it wasn't a huge deal to me) There are no enemies to destroy your stuff or hurt you. Not a con for me because I just like to build and collect things but it might be a dealbreaker for other people Sometimes you go through the environment and end up "inside" of a mountain or something. HOWEVER, I've never had an issue getting back. It seems like they've made it hard to get in (you have to get in at a weird corner) but it's very easy to just walk out of them and the ground continues beneath the rest of the terrain so you don't fall out of the world. The game is fun and I really enjoy it. I haven't played multiplayer so I can't give any info on that but I really like how simple it is in concept and still very fun. Very much the kind of game you can just kind of zone out and play

_childDocuments_.review: I was pleasantly surprised by this. As there are already so many "survival crafting" asset flips out there, I sort of had assumed this was more of a "simulator" experience, but the deeper you get, the more sense you get that a lot of genuine love and care went into the production and it really sets itself apart with some novel ideas. Having finished the entire thing, I'm rather impressed that this came from a two-person team. I'm a sucker for factory-style games (this has some of those elements in the late game, even if it's not really the main focus) and I always lament how in most of them you're clearly making the world a worse place as you play it. It's nice to have an experience where you're actually making the world more interesting, welcoming, and vibrant place. The steady transformation of the world is definitely the most rewarding aspect of this game.There is a little bit of jank - the game is not overly concerned with you placing things sensibly, things not colliding with each other, etc. For those whom this bothers, it could be immersion-breaking, but in my whole experience, I never found such things to be a negative. If anything it added a bit of whimsy for me, launching two rockets simultaneously and watching them wrestle all over the landscape. It feels a bit as though the devs grew more confident in their craft over time and things grow more and more fleshed out as you get further in.If they ever considered a sequel or someone decided to iterate on the concept, it would be nice to have a more robust terraforming system. Something a bit more interesting than just adding a bunch of relatively independent numbers only related by the technologies they unlock (though ice melting at temperature thresholds, water appearing over time, and O2 levels affecting player survivability are all neat mechanics). For example, perhaps higher atmospheric pressure reduces temperature swings caused by the day/night cycle or imposes a greenhouse effect. Liquid water is only possible under a specific range of temperature and pressure. Plant biomass directly produces oxygen, but plants can't be produced outdoors without the right temperature and water. Herbivores consume plant biomass and reduce O2 levels. That sort of thing. Rather than a strictly linear progression, managing those interlocking systems and keeping things stable becomes the new focus. This could easily spin out of control with systems that are very difficult to balance, but it would be really cool to see someone pull it off. I envision spending the early game mostly in your gradually expanding base as you slowly turn the outside world into something you can actually venture out into, maybe not spending as much time managing inventory or thirst/hunger bars and more ensuring that your base has water, power, and food as you gear up to finally venture out onto the planet and start making it livable (one nitpick I have for many of these games is that having to drink water every 5 minutes is more irritating than engaging - having to make sure you have *access* to water is a more interesting challenge). Fun fact - the temperature of open space is ~2.7 kelvin, which is the coldest naturally occurring temperature we know to be possible. This is due to the cosmic microwave background. I believe it's cooling at around a factor of 8 every 8 billion years so it would likely have to be an unfathomably long time in the future before a planetary surface could conceivably have a temperature in the micro or nanokelvins. To the best of our knowledge, any occurrence of a colder temperature in all the universe was by us or some other technologically advanced species. This isn't a criticism of the game, but it is neat.

_childDocuments_.review: Planet Crafter is an absolute gem in the world of gaming! From the moment I started playing, I was immersed in a universe of endless possibilities and creative exploration. The game's intuitive design makes it easy for both beginners and seasoned gamers to jump right in and start crafting their own planets.One of the things I love most about Planet Crafter is the sheer depth of customization available. Whether it's tweaking the terrain, adding unique features, or even designing ecosystems, the level of control you have over your creations is truly astounding. It's incredibly satisfying to see your imagination come to life as you sculpt each planet to perfection.The graphics in Planet Crafter are stunning, with vibrant colors and beautiful landscapes that make each planet feel alive. The attention to detail is remarkable, and it's clear that the developers put a lot of love and care into crafting every aspect of the game.But what really sets Planet Crafter apart is its sense of community. Whether you're collaborating with friends to build epic worlds together or sharing your creations with the wider community, there's always something new and exciting to discover. The creativity of the player base is truly inspiring, and I love seeing the incredible things that people come up with.Overall, I can't recommend Planet Crafter highly enough. It's a game that encourages creativity, exploration, and collaboration, and it's sure to provide endless hours of entertainment for anyone who dives into its world. If you're looking for a game that lets you unleash your imagination and create something truly unique, look no further than Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: It's something new... I would have probably went for Neutral but as I get closer to end game, the game is just too shallow for any replay value and under the surface, the mechanics are rather simple. Not going to lie, it was pretty neat at first creating the first few machines, turning the sky blue and seeing water levels rise then it quickly wore off. Once you realize the mechanics, it becomes a cycle of gather ore, literally toss the junk ore, build equipment, launch rockets for the multiplier and chase around the comet impacts for uranium and iridium if you need the extra, rinse and repeat. Oh and drink water.. all the time... that cycle is pretty rough and long at one point, sure you can frolic around and make your base pretty and let the process just slowly roll out... What really bugged me was the machines, primarily the ones with area of effects such as grass, flower and trees... the growth or area of effect had no real impact, the plants did not expand from the area of effect nor did the growth have any value, just a visual effect. It felt like a wasted opportunity to drive some mechanics in the game where growth would crawl from the machine points and boost production such as O2 or help at least visually impact the world, this could have driven the player to create multiple bases spreading machines out. The world, you drive heat, pressure and O2 levels up, and the world terraforms on its own, there is no direct impact of your machines or said placement of your machines in simple terms and rockets launches just amplify those effectsSo, with the price tag and at the moment, no replayability... I'd recommend a sale before purchasing.

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical when I downloaded the demo for this since I knew literally nothing about it. This game however has been a thrill! You show up on a planet as a criminal abandoned on the surface. Its just as barren and red as Mars with many moons? and planets? in orbit of it. There are wind storms, blazing sun, and no air to breathe. it looks so hopeless at first ... especially when your first swarm of meteors slams into the planet hard enough to shake everything and explode rock formations with their impact. This makes it easy to save air once you reach a wreck you want to explore so you don't use all your bottles up right away.Also this map is pretty huge. _childDocuments_.review: Positives: Overall the game is pretty fun. If you're into these niche survival/building type games, this is definitely a nice casually paced addition to the genre. There are no real threats in the game other than standard food, oxygen, and water, which is a bit disappointing, but is still engaging enough to overlook for me. There's a sprinkle of story mixed in with the collectable memos and readable notes, which is always an appreciated touch.Negatives: There are a few minor inconveniences worth noting.1. Asteroid impacts leaving rubble for far too long with no way to remove it other than waiting a couple minutes. This rubble can actually glitch inside of bases, blocking off portions of your base until it de-spawns.2. I expected there to be a faster form of travel between jet-packs and the later tech, such as a bike or rover type vehicle, but sadly there isn't. Without spoiling anything, having to run longer distances to get places in the early/middle and even later parts of progression got old really fast. 3. Further into the games progression things dial back to what feels like a full stop, with a lack of impact from the remaining unlocks in later technology and terraforming.Potential fixes:1: Remove excess rubble from asteroid impacts soon after they land, leaving only the glowing rock from the main asteroid.2. Add in some vehicle tech, or more substantial movement based tech before the obvious tech that is unlocked later on.3. Add more things to do for the later game. Specific requirements in areas of the map, like planting certain trees in one area, spreading grass in another, cover this lake in algae spawners, spawn this type of insect/animal at this location, etc. This would give goals and purpose to some of the later game that winds down immensely while you simply wait for the index to hit the final goal. 4. Potentially add more planets? Maybe instead of ending the game once your current planet is finished, require a solar system terraformation. Could introduce this in the way of Sentinel Corp punishing us for communicating when we're not supposed to or something. Could add new challenges by having to travel between planets and the like.

_childDocuments_.review: I am aware that this game is REALLY early access, so this review will likely become outdated at some point, and that the things I am going to discuss likely aren't permanent.I can see this game has some in common with Subnautica and No Man's Sky (though I will not directly compare), namely the little resource nodes and toolgun. Both of those games have things that personally annoy me, but in particular, the resource collection is the main annoyance. I spent most of my playtime on that save collecting resources, I would hazard to estimate about three-quarters of my time was spent doing this, both to progress or because I overloaded my power grid and needed to spam solar panels. The main issue is that each little resource node gives only 1 of that resource, so if you run a large area out of iron (resources don't respawn, as far as I've seen, ever), you are forced to relocate to find more. It would be better and make more sense to take the Factorio or Astroneer approach and make ores or materials spawn in large chunks in their own areas granting several per mining trip, and maybe make them respawn on a long timer or something.Another issue I had with the game was the way progression was handled. You unlock new tech by reaching milestones in each respective terraforming aspect, which is great, but why am I unlocking heat buildings from the oxygen tree? Also, once you complete the "Blue Skies" objective, the game stops guiding you with that quest notification whatsoever. I honestly found it extremely helpful to have some guidance. This even ties back to the resource problem, because I spammed a ton of drills to rush to the ore extractor so I could do a little more automation and a lot less running only to find out that the ore extractor requires a resource I've never even seen.My final major issue with the game in its current state is the gameplay itself. It feels like an idle game. There isn't much challenge besides gaining more terraforming progress faster. Theoretically, you could place 1 of each structure (heat, oxygen, pressure) then just wait. It would take you forever to reach a goal, but you will inevitably reach it. There isn't an incentive to build more asides making the numbers go up faster, again, like an idle game. There is also no real penalty for dying (I assume a harder difficulty fixes this). You will always respawn inside the last one of your structures you stood in. Dying causes you to drop some stuff, but it drops in a box at your death point, so there's no reason to use the survival mechanics. You can just go find one of your buildings, stand in it for a moment, die, walk out and get your stuff back. There's a bit of lore in the game about your circumstances (no spoilers), but I don't see any time limits or anything else relating to it beyond knowing it exists.There are some more minor issues like spelling, but I won't go into those.This game is pretty cool, I'd like to see more done with it, I'd like to see it progress, but if you're looking for very engaging gameplay, I wouldn't get it right now. It does make a pretty cool idle game though (in its current state).

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game in September as an Early Access game. It feels like a completed game already. I haven't hit too many story elements yet, but I also haven't started building communication arrays yet.Two things I really love about this game:1) You can see gradual changes to the planet as you terraform (like the sky gradually changing color, and a lake rising slowly).2) The way it rewards you for exploring. I frequently find storage chests full of great resources in out-of-the-way areas, some of which I need to be clever to get to.So far the game has been scaling well. Before I got too bored of picking resources off the ground, I unlocked the mining machine. There are areas that unlock in response to terraforming, which helps keep me excited about the changes to the planet.If you're not interested in exploring, this might be a frustrating game. A lot of the higher-level resources are a fair distance away from the starting point, and some of the cave entrances aren't easily visible unless you're looking for them.

Too many developers have missed the mark badly, in this delicate dance. But this game sikes the BULLSEYE on the pacing, which makes you almost completely oblivious to the shortcomings of this title.I have my eyes still GLUED to the screen, at ~20 hrs in. Taking my first bites into the games' juicy late mid-game mechanics, and still maintain extremely high engagement level for such a "small" indie title. I CANNOT WAIT for MORE! And I know I will be so sad, when I finally transform this ball of hell, into an Oasis of life, yet I see...Just half a year into the project the devs are coming with MORE ludicrous terraforming goals, now.I can only wonder... _childDocuments_.review: "The Planet Crafter" is a delightful game with lots of depth and player customization. You're alone on a hostile planet and your job is to make the planet habitable. Exactly how you do that is entirely up to you. You're by no means the first one to explore this planet. This planet holds many secrets. Visit crash sites and derelict settlements to collect valuable resources and information. Doing so may be at times perilous, but always worthwhile. There is no combat with hostile beings -only against your hunger, thirst, and air supply. Otherwise, the rest is about resource management. As more and more automation becomes available, you're free to build and decorate your own off-world palace just as you see fit. Cooperative gameplay is recently  available, but unnecessary.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Started with the demo, not 2 hours in I had to buy it. I like that there is no combat, no stress, no turret defense or some other silly mechanic.    This is a chill, sit back, and INVEST game as some things take time.   You never feel like you are grinding, nor racing, as there is always "one more thing" to do.  The game is well balanced in "unlocks" so that you feel like you're always making progress(albeit a couple of places that are already being worked out in the beta branch). FUN with friends!  Tried it the other night since I got him addicted and it was a nice co-op adventure, with a new challenge as you're both fighting for food at first...so coordinate/collaborate and get'er done!

_childDocuments_.review:
You are sent on an hostile planet with one mission: Make it habitable for Humans. You'll have to survive, collect resources, build your base and machines in order to heat the planet, create an atmosphere with enough oxygen and eventually geo-engineer an entire planet!

Gather minerals and resources to survive. Craft all the tools you'll need in order to fulfill your mission. Explore old crashed ships and ruins and discover a planet full of mystery.

name: Guild Wars 2
detailed_description: Guild Wars 2's open world is all about discovery and exploration. Check your content guide for suggestions when you set out on your adventures, consult your compass to find interesting landmarks…or just pick your favorite direction to travel in and let adventure find you. Tyria is full of characters with their own stories and goals, and you'll be rewarded for helping them out—or thwarting their plans—by completing renown hearts and dynamic events. Read our new player guide for more tips! When you meet other players in the open world, you don't need to join their party to lend a helping hand, investigate a secret jumping puzzle, or team up against a deadly world boss. Don't grind; play the way you want to play! Whether you're reviving defeated players, rescuing soldiers from a Risen onslaught, or gathering herbs, you'll earn experience points. Arm your character with an arsenal of new weapons as you play. Every profession wields them differently, and each type has its own playstyle, which you can refine and customize by unlocking and equipping hundreds of skills and traits. If you want to jump straight into structured PvP, go for it—every player competes at the same level, with access to the max-level gear and build options you need to make your mark. If you love fashion, express yourself with the perfect character design! When you equip new weapons and armor, you'll unlock their skins in your wardrobe. Make them truly yours with thousands of possible combinations and a massive selection of collectible dyes. Upgrade your free account with a Guild Wars 2 expansion and get access to log-in rewards, additional character and bag slots, expanded chat features, and more. Visit the Black Lion Trading Company in the game and use your Steam Wallet to upgrade. Expansions and Living World seasons feature unique rewards and new Masteries to expand your character's abilities. Unlock and upgrade your glider in Guild Wars 2: Heart of Thorns, befriend a stable of mounts with powerful movement skills in Guild Wars 2: Path of Fire, and learn to fish and pilot a skiff in Guild Wars 2: End of Dragons. Each expansion grants access to nine elite specializations that unlock new weapon choices, skills, and abilities for your profession. You'll also be able to select the revenant profession at character creation and channel legendary heroes and villains from Tyria's history. Living World seasons continue the Guild Wars 2 story between expansions and must be purchased separately through your Story Journal or in Gem Store bundles. Play Living World episodes to unlock new explorable zones, rewards, and Masteries. *Living World episodes become playable at level 80. Players may need to relaunch the game for the upgrade to take effect. **Please note that existing Guild Wars 2 player accounts cannot be accessed via Steam

_childDocuments_.review: Its fun at first .. the mount variety is what attracted me. After playing it though you have to pay for the DLC's that unlock the mounts. Then you have to progress through certain chapters to make them available and only in a particular order. Also there is only like idk 6 mount varieties but they all have a lot of skin options. You get skins through purchasing scrolls with RL money. Also each mount has different skill sets so its not like you use your favorite all the time so your switching through them a lot when your traveling. The skyscale which is the flying mount and the most useful you have to have the DLC and complete a bunch of chapters and pay a bunch of gold to get plus I think its like the last mount you unlock. There are chapters in their "item mall" that you can buy to progress through the story. It feels kind of money hungry and I've lost interest because of it plus the mount system is eh. The archer is the only class that can have battle pets and a few are better than others so its not like you can really have a favorite to run all the time. There are mini pets in the game that are all cosmetic but its a lot of repeats not a lot of variety and a lot are mini NPS which I think is dumb. You can however dye your clothes armor and mount which is a plus. But overall I've played better.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a certain type of magic that keeps on drawing me back to this game. Personally, this game does end game content way better than World of Warcraft. The mounts in Guild Wars 2 are better than in any other mmo. It's a shame that Anet gave up on dungeons and raids, but I definitely like the strikes that are supposed to function similarly, at least in terms of boss fights.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the Guild Wars franchise since the original was released in 2005. Far from the way the original game played, this games still manages to capture the setting but with incredibly fun new mechanics. It does suffer from "meta-itis" but with this game you don't have to do that to progress. You can slap anything on your character and still play through the story and do the large scale events. (Better gear does help a lot though lol) It's fun and rewards for both casual and hardcore play with AMAZING end game content AND a development team that is releasing regular free content as well as large paid DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: Guild Wars 2

_childDocuments_.review: There's tons of content that you can do solo, and a lot of more complex content that you can do with a group. No gear treadmill, you can put the game down and come back a year later and still be best-in-class with no additional grind. The community is very friendly, and the monetization is fair. Guild Wars 2 has stood the test of time and is still an excellent game to pick up and explore by yourself or with friends you find in game.Played it a bunch now, I still think it's great.
_childDocuments_.name: Guild Wars 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best MMORPG I have played in years. There is so much content it makes the other "Top" MMO's seem like cash grabs. The fully voiced main story lines are truly immersive. The combat is fluid and full of action. I have played several professions and they all bring something to the table. They are working on graphic improvements, but the current system is still beautiful. They seem to have a great take on eliminating "pay to win" and just about everything you can spend money on is available to purchase with just grinding, you can use gems or gold to purchase anything, and if you need one or the other there is an official currency exchange, rates are constantly in flux so you can always wait for the better exchange rate. The amount of group content is better than any other MMO out there at the moment, and believe me I have played just about all of them. If you download the free to play version, you are limited to certain account limitations, but you only need purchase one of the expansions to unlock full access and remove restrictions. I found this a little frustrating at first but I think it is to keep gold farmers from using mock accounts to farm. I would rather have a slight inconvenience than an auction house that is manipulated by gold farmers. If you haven't played GW2 you owe it to yourself to give it a try, and make sure you play more than one profession, what you think you would like to play may be different than you expect, check out all the professions early on, you will see what I mean.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun! plain and simple! It's the sort of game, everyone should put at least an evening into, just for the hell of it.It has its ups and downs, some expansions are better than others and some mechanics are kinda goofy. But on the core map, doing exploration and meta events, is when GW2 is at it's best. It's essentially a bunch of mini games that trick you into playing them over and over again because they're genuinely pretty fun. It's like being in an arcade from the 80's, you can play whatever you want, however you want, though sometimes there's a queue. I strongly recommend doing a bit of homework on the in-game store though, there is 100% some bait and garbage tier items that are not worth purchasing, however as a whole I am happy with the model. As it's largely cosmetics or pay for convenience items, which when you get hooked, it's fine to pay that because you will get enough fun out of it in return.I will say GW2 is not for everyone though, if you're here to have the biggest stats and the biggest sword, because that makes you feel good about your life, you'll probably burnout. If you're here to be toxic and troll people, you're going to get outgunned by probably one of the friendliest MMORPG communities around. If you're a furry, well you're probably going to have a good time, seriously there's a bunch of LGBTKPQ+ peeps on here and it's a little odd sometimes...

_childDocuments_.review: I am a 54-year old father, probably one of the oldest people playing Guild Wars.I am a single father to my son, who is now 14. My son recently started playing Fishing Guild Wars.In less than a week, he had already played for over 20 hours.This was terrible for me because it was already hard enough for me to spend time with my sonbecause he was always out with his friends or watching YouTube. So I decided to make a Steamaccount to play with my son. I started playing, but this was my first time playing a video gamesince the 90's, so I was quite lost. I asked my son for help, and together we spent some hours playing Guild Wars.I loved it as it was the best time I had spent with my son since my wife had died. Playing video gamesreminded me that there's fun to be had in everything, and it has broughtme and my son closer again, and now we actually spend time together outside the house as well.

You can after 5 min tutorial you can jump into PVP with all skill unlock. Have a very good dungeon boss mechanic. Structured open world boss like can be done every hours. _childDocuments_.review: I've been playing MMORPGs since almost two decades now and the two games I always come back to are WoW and GW2. WoW, to play versions of the game that don't exist since a decade and just to feel some nostalgia and then disappointment and GW2 just because it is a wholesome and fun experience.The best part about GW2 for me is that you can take a break for months or years even and you do not have any catching up to do, are outdated or disoriented. GW2 is a comfort MMO that respects your time like no other MMO. I played this game over 400 hours and there still is so much to do, I haven't even finished the story or done all the raids and fractals or strikes. There is always activity on old maps, unlike in WoW where you usually don't see people in anything else than the current patches' map. The cash shop only offers cosmetics or QoL improvements, not player power. I think this is the best cash shop in an MMO I have seen, though even this is not perfect. Some items like bag slot extensions are overpriced and should be account wide instead of character wide. The mounts in GW2 are the best in any MMO, so much so that others are copying from it and thus providing a better experience for their own players. It is very easy to play completely different play styles with a single class because of elite specializations and traits, which can be changed for free at any time.

_childDocuments_.review: Tried this game before, and now gave it a tiny try on Steam. It's just not user friendly at all. The tutorial is lackluster. Some skills have weird multi-tiered tooltips that explain nothing. No clue indicator of how states work, because they don't use the tried and true stat system found across almost every other mmo. There's no explanation, of what stats affect. Experienced users unwilling to even point new players in a general direction, they just hang out in the newbie area to show off their glowing armor.Poor community toward new playersPoor stat system that I guess you figure out  someday?Poor tutorial, it runs your through the obvious stuff but does not elaborate on more complicated systemsMassive pay walls. Want all the content? $100, want other content? Microtransactions. Want a mount? $30 for atleast one expansion.Graphics : cute and artsy in some cases, but dated, low poly style, and lacking in detail. I'd say as good as wow in 2004, but never updated.Gameplay and combat is wonky. I was unable to locate a sprint button, characters run slow, and if you're trialing the game, they give you a mount at level 10, but snatch it back after like 8 hours to entice you to buy an expansion before really getting to explore much.I'm not going to say it is without positives:The human city is pretty epic, though you cannot enter most buildings.The dreamy pantier style art does look good in some landscapesThe combat would actually be fun if they did a better job explaining it and simplified early abilities.I'm sure there's a lot more good that I just didn't get to see. But turning off a person who has played many mmos since 1996 and enjoyed most of them, it's hard to imagine this game ever seeing positive growth. They just don't care about the people trying the game out, and that's a bad thing.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR? Yes I highly recommend trying this game if it aligns with your preferred genre.Guild Wars 2 - A World of Endless Adventure and Engaging Game playBefore diving into my detailed review of Guild Wars 2, it's important to note that it is a massive multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) cherished by millions of dedicated players worldwide. This review is based on my personal experience with the game, supplemented by the overwhelmingly positive reviews expressed by the Guild Wars 2 community on the store page.1. Dynamic and Beautiful World:GW2 offers one of the most captivating and visually stunning game worlds in the MMORPG genre. From lush forests to desolate wastelands, each area is crafted with meticulous detail, breathing life into the game world. The developers' commitment to continuously adding new regions and expanding the lore ensures that there is always something exciting to explore.2. Engaging Story line and Quests:The game boasts an immersive and evolving story line, masterfully woven with intricate plot twists and memorable characters. Players will be drawn into a narrative that adapts based on their decisions, emphasizing the significance of their choices. Coupled with hundreds of quests that are far from repetitive, GW2 ensures that players always have a purpose and a sense of adventure.3. Class and Race Diversity:GW2's character creation offers an impressive level of customization. With nine diverse playable races and a wide range of classes, players can create a character that aligns with their preferred play-style seamlessly. This diversity encourages multiple playthroughs, adding replayability and extending the game's longevity.4. Dynamic Events and World vs. World:Dynamic events breathe life into the world of Tyria, ensuring that even mundane tasks are transformed into thrilling adventures. These events frequently occur in various corners of the map, creating a dynamic and immersive experience. Additionally, the World vs. World mode allows players to compete in large-scale battles, conquering fortresses and fighting alongside their comrades for global dominance.5. Strong and Supportive Community:GW2 stands out for fostering a uniquely inclusive and supportive community. Players are always willing to lend a helping hand, guide newcomers, and participate in cooperative game play. Whether through guilds, organized events, or the game's built-in social features, players can easily find a sense of belonging within the passionate GW2 community.6. No Subscription and Fair Micro-transactions:GW2 has a "Buy to Play" payment model, meaning no monthly subscription is required. The developers' commitment to players is further demonstrated through micro-transactions that concentrate primarily on cosmetic items, convenience, and quality-of-life improvements. This approach ensures a fair playing field for all players, regardless of their payment choices.7. Constant Updates and Expansions:GW2 is consistently refreshed with abundant free updates and expansions, keeping the game exciting and providing players with new content to explore. The developers' dedication to consistently improving the game based on player feedback underscores their commitment to delivering an exceptional gaming experience.In conclusion, GW2 is an exceptional MMORPG that captivates players with its breathtaking world, engaging storytelling, diverse character options, and dynamic game-play. The overwhelmingly positive reviews on the Steam store page reflect the game's enduring popularity and the immense enjoyment it brings to its dedicated community. Whether you're a veteran MMO player or new to the genre, Guild Wars 2 is an adventure you won't want to miss!

_childDocuments_.review: Art style, graphics are really good looking. UI is pretty functional. Character and Item progression is deep and rewarding. Story is probably if not the best story in a MMO its top 3 without a doubt.  Crafting is great and the fact they never increase power creep means you can gear characters and two expansions later they are still geared! Amazing.  Sometimes skill lag in WVWThoughts; I have played this game actually since Beta, it's always been something I could come back to and play because they have literally a ton of things to do. For example you want to do nothing but PVE? Thats fine they have scaling dungeons with fractals or you want to raid? They have numerous raids. You want to just do the world bosses? No problem! They have LFG commanders constantly spamming for boss trains, they also run hero point trains, karma trains and anything else you can possible think to organize in the open world to run. Not to mention each race has its own main story that flows through each of the zones, on top of that they have dynamic events that occur in the zones and you can do static quests called hearts in the zones. You like to just experience the story? Thats good because they have a ton of stories to play through and each one is really well done with voice acting, this is for every expansion and the living story which are apart from the main racial story line. You want to do PVP? Cool, heres SPVP where you can literally just click what gear stats you want and jump right in! Don't need to grind anything or level anything at all! Small scale PVP isn't what you meant? Thats fine they have World VS World where you and your guild can take on other guilds as you capture structures in one of four instanced battlegrounds. None of that seems appealing? You like to just concentrate on economics? That's fine they have that also, you can buy items cheap sell them for more and make a profit, then take that currency which is gold and turn it into gems which you can use to buy things that normally would cost real world money. Still don't have you hooked huh? You say you like to be a crafter/gatherer? Perfect! crafted gear is the strongest gear in the game and since gear power creep isn't a thing in GW2 you can constantly make money off crafting the cool down materials. Oh whats that none of that is appealing to you? WELL they do have mount collecting and achievement hunting that is rewarding, they give you titles, materials and all kinds of neat rewards for just playing the game. I gotta say ive probably spent tens of thousands of hours in this game and im no where near having everything and have done everything. I log in and always and I mean always have something to do or work on. Also the core game is free, why not give it a try? ITS FREE.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: 1000+ hours in and not slowing down. Get off your crappy MMO and come play with usRecently wanted an MMO and it came down to Turtle WoW Classic or GW2. GW really does fix many problems typical of MMO worlds so it won my time. So here are my 200 hour thoughts-Dying in Wow is punished by making you run back from far away. GW has enough waypoints to shave this almost completely away in comparison.-Better graphics in GW means the world is actually worth more stop-and-admire moments.-Chat in GW is generally pleasant and helpful. In WoW the chat window must be hidden for fear my IQ will drop.-Questing in WoW consist of walking from: Quest Giver, Area of Quest, Walk Back, Get another quest for the exact same area. In GW the Quest are just areas on a map, go to the area and do the quest, you dont even need to talk to the NPC. Most quest in GW can be solved with killing but most of activities involve some faster way to complete it like reviving NPC, feeding farm animals. splashing drunks with buckets of water, etc. If that sounds boring, well compare it to a 5min walk back before you can even do anything at all.-Have i mentioned walking yet in WoW because everything is so big and far away from each other it just doesn't work for me and the world feels empty considering its size. Who can physically open these 20 story tall doors? Who needs a door that tall?-GW max level isn't hard to achieve, only about 40% of base map completion gets you there so just do the story and the complete the maps it brings you to. I think it took me 4 days, I played a lot but elementalist lives up to being "complex" to play/learn when compared to easier classes-Level scaling here is better than in something like Elder Scroll Online(Level 5 characters killing daedra....). Some people dont like this but consider the fact of your gear never becoming outdated. It might mean you'll have to write a story and add mechanics to keep players involved instead of tricking them into needing bigger level numbers. Remember, Quality>Quantity -I got more Final Fantasy vibes from this than FF14-You can create new characters, complete the 2-5min tutorial, then immediately jump into Structured PvP. Here you are boosted to max level and unlocks all your class skills. Experimenting here on NPC/dummies/Players might help you decide on a main class. Equipment here doesnt matter meaning you dont need to grind gear. You could only play this game for PvP is you wanted(although without DLC Elite Classes your competitive ceiling is limited to a couple "core" classes, Paladin and Necromancer do fine from what I've read).-WvW isn't "fair" like sPvP because your level and gear carry over to this game mode. The good news though is the 2nd best gear in the game (exotic) isn't expensive (1/10 the cost) and the stat lost compared to the best gear is 5-12%. I've read this small difference makes little difference in WvW/PvP and counts more for raids, dungeon, etc. -Crafting Gear you can change the stats of on-the-fly is an endgame goal is you want. Considering the Astral Coin to gold exchange rate, you get a "free" 90 Gold per season. 3 Gold gets you basically endgame cooking skill of 400. Gear is far more expensive so do that later, its like 35g just to hit 400/500 in a craft. Crafting is a decent way to level up another alt-Recommend the expansion bundle with Heart of Thorns and Path of Fire after beating the story. You get mounts, gliders, 18 of 27 Elite classes including 1 new base class, and maybe most important is a Level 80 Token. So now you have 2 Level 80 characters just in case elementalist turned out too complicated for you like it has me (so far). Plus when you read about builds you might want a secondary character to cover a role your main cannot. My alt is Thief so now I have a WvW Roamer/Duelist too. Each of the other 2 (atm) Expansions contain a token too, so if you enjoy the game you won't worry about leveling new character which is another time sink you can avoid.I guess I could go on but my hand is tired and I'm out of spit.

_childDocuments_.review: I have about 3,000 hours in GW2 prior to the steam launch. The greatest thing about GW2 is how it respects my time. I can take breaks for 5 days, or 5 months, and pick up exactly where I left off due to the horizontal progression.Once you're geared to play all the content in the game, you are geared to play that content today, tomorrow, and years from you. That said, there are still some serious stretch goals with gear that you can seek out in the form of Legendary gear. It has the same stats as the easily accessible ascended gear, but with the added QoL to change the stats freely.Give it a chance. And take a break. And then give it another chance. You'll never be left in the dust. I have a set of armor that I made 7 years ago that I still use on some builds to this day.Additionally, if you're playing, you're progressing. Any content you do will get you materials that have relevance at almost any time. This goes back to respecting the players' time.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are an MMORPG fan, you definitely played this game before. If you didn't, give this game a try.Weirdly, Guild Wars 2 is not a regular MMORPG as expected.  (Requires Heart of Thorns)Every class are allowed to use more than one weapon depending on personal preference.Every class has three other elite specilizations which changes the class gameplay and adds one new usable weapon type. (Requires expansion packs)The character progression starts with expected MMORPG progression type. Level up, equip higher level equipment and such. But after reaching the max level, you will try to get the best quality for an item, (excluding legendaries) ascended.The Guild Wars 2's unique progression starts here. No matter how many years has passed, ascended gear always has the best stats. Crafted full berserker ascended set back in 2013? Good, it's still the best set for PowerDPS (I will be explaining these) in 2022.Guild Wars 2's entire builds revolve around prefixes. Prefixes are fixed, but there are a lot of them so you can always find what you wish to build.For example Berserker's prefix gives Power, Precision, Ferocity. Cleric's prefix gives Healing power, Power, Toughness. Increases outgoing strike damage. Increases critical chance. Increases Armor and aggro rate. Increases Health. Increases boon duration. Increases the damage done by inflicting conditions. Increases condition duration. Increases critical damage. Increases all outgoing healing your character does, including self heals.Guild Wars 2 has no official "holy trinity" There is no dedicated tank, healer or anything like that. Instead, there are healing builds, equipped with healer gear and such.There are a few types of PvE content in this game, and I will be giving brief descriptions. Fractals, Raids and Strikes have Challange mode which gives handicap to players or make the battle more complicated for more rewards. Basic (mostly) singleplayer storyline. Simple, easy, and gives enough satisfaction for people who is interested in lore. Very old content, not really relevant anymore. Every dungeon has a story mode and a exploration mode. Exploration mode is the actual dungeon with three different paths to take. 5-player content. Special dungeons which requires a stat called Agony Resistance (AR). If you can't meet the AR requirements, you will start taking huge damage during the dungeons and will not survive. At later levels, every level will have instabilities (1, 2 or 3 depending on Fractal tier) which adds unique challenges such as movement getting slower as you lose health or enemies getting random boons when hit. 5-player content. Still a bit relevant, harder content. They are like regular MMORPG raids, requiring cooperation, mechanic knowledge and class knowledge. 10-player content. Newer than other content, still very relevant. Think it as quicker raids. 10-player content. Open world random events, world bosses and meta events are always populated, fun and a shining example to all MMORPGs about how to design the open world content.There are two types of PvP in Guild Wars 2. Structured PvP (sPvP) and World vs World. (WvW) In sPvP, equipment stats and quality does not matter. You have to equip special PvP runes and accessories which the game will provide. In WvW, the equipment stats will slightly buff you, and your infusions, runes and sigils will work. Team versus team. I am not really experienced in this gamemode. So please refer to another review for more detailed sPvP review. One of the best PvP modes I have ever played. Three worlds (WvW servers) fights against each other in four maps. Blob/Zerg (Organized big groups) battles, roamer (single/small group battles/ganking) clashes, sieges, tactics etc. all exists in WvW. If you want chaos in your PvP experience, this is the one you should try. Basically, you and your server fights for more areas, towns and castles. Depending on how much things you hold, your server gets points every two hours. War lasts one week and when it ends, depending on your place, you either go one tier down, stay, or go one tier up.Thankfully, this game follows common sense and all equipment appearance unlocks are account bound. (YEAH FFXIV, TAKE NOTES) If you want to change your equipment's appearance, you need transmutation charge which can be found in several ways or bought from the gemstore. If you don't want to design something yourself, you can buy full outfits which are one-piece outfits that will change your entire armor's appearance and can be easily unequipped.You can turn , which is , to , which is , and vice versa. This should count as P2W, right?Like I said, this game has a very unique progression system. It's very easy to access ascended without paying for anything. After getting ascended, you will reach the highest stats you can get and you'll upgrade those with sigils, runes and infusions which are all easy to get.Lots of gold is only really needed for special infusions, fashion and lastly, legendary items, which has the same stats as ascended items, but can change stat prefixes anytime. Ascended items' prefixes can be changed, but requires some items to do so.Other Gem items are mostly for either appearance, or QoL upgrades.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible MMORPG in which you feel INCLUDED in activities, having fun with others from the very beginning. This is what MMORPGs are about.Fair warning - think whether having to play skillfully instead of stomping people with farmed gear, is your cup of tea. GW2 requires you to gain knowledge and work on your gaming skills, you can't just equip +100 smasher of n00bs and run around one-shotting everyone and everything. You have to actually learn the game.On top of that - vast and lively world, great storytelling, AMAZING voice acting I never saw in any other MMO. Lot's of events, activities, PvE wise, PvP wise, minigames, jumping puzzles, absolute ton of collectibles... It's just a gigantic box of fun :)The "killer feature" - GW2 progression is mostly horizontal. It's not about grinding months to be relevant in multiplayer activities. It's about finishing the tutorial (getting lvl 80 :D), buying some gear, and then being relevant in various activities you can join. This is the polar opposite of games like Black Desert Online (for example), where you progress mostly vertically and it can take months to be able to participate on even ground. I personally find that very much to my liking and I feel like we have been taught by the gaming industry it's all about vertical progression and gear grinding and nothing else make sense. Well, vertical progression is not going to give you much fulfillment over time, because when the numbers become big, you lose sense of improvement as you can no longer distinguish when your damage becomes even higher :). The second biggest downside of that approach is the ever growing and shaking balance between skills and classes. Of course it's not perfect if you stop increasing max level cap and gear rarity, but it's much better. All in all, I think this is what makes GW2 unique and lovely.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing a long time, well-before it launched on Steam. Steam says I've played about 120 hrs but it's more like 500-600 hrs.Overall I think it is fun, but there are some major issues. Before I get into those, I want to say that this game can be incredibly entertaining if you play with IRL friends - which is exactly what I do and the main reason I play.1. Gem store cosmetics do not specify the number of dyable slots. I bought a glider I thought looked silly with its default colors, and thought "No worries, I bet it'd look way better with [these] colors!" Only to find out it couldn't be dyed at all. Support did NOT help me get a refund. I even asked them to remove it from my cosmetics - I didn't expect to keep it for free. But nope... So definitely be careful with what you purchase - do some research first. 2. Out-of-game research is required for many things, the game's interface and information provided is not intuitive. For example... Refer to my point #1 - research gem store items before purchasing them!... Example 2:  Bounties in Path of Fire AUTOMATICALLY trigger FOR EVERYONE ON THE MAP when you get within a certain radius of the NPC, and these Bounties are time-sensitive. So if you accidentally trigger a Bounty when loads of other people on the map aren't ready, congrats, loads of people are missing-out on their Bounty because you triggered it just by walking by. This is no longer an issue for me, but when I was much newer, this stood out to me as a GIANT game design issue... There are MANY other small examples of missing information or unintuitive design spinkled throughout the game, some large, some very small.3. Performance!!! This game is heavily CPU-bound and the horsepower required to play at a smooth 60FPS grows exponentially with the number of players on-screen. You CAN limit the number of players on-screen via settings, however, pretty much all other MMOs can display at least DOUBLE what GW2 can without any major performance dips.... I have heard rumors that the Graphics pipeline coded into the game places a lot of unnecessary tasks on the CPU, when those tasks could've been coded to run on the (much for efficient) GPU and eliminate performance issues related to crowd density.  For reference, I have an AMD Ryan 9 5980HX and AMD Radeon RX 6800M (hardware from 2021-ish)4. Good luck seeing wtf is happening in group content. Even when you tone-down particle effects and skill effects, the sheer number of craziness that occurs on-screen in large groups makes it nearly impossible to see NPC telegraphs and ground effects. Even when nothing much is happening, the sheer number of shiny/glimmering outfits players wear is like everyone is vomiting rainbows and star bursts. 5. Some class specs are just objectively inferior to others. I think the devs are fine with the whole "There's a time and place for this spec" approach, but for me and especially newer players, it really sucks that a spec you thoroughly enjoy and find engaging is grossly lagging behind other classes/specs in the same game mode. In cases like this, you are sacrificing FUN for EFFICIENCY and that just feels bad. I'm not talking about, say, a 5% DPS difference, I'm talking about the difference between even being able to survive through an encounter AT ALL. Some of the differences are disgusting, and idk how the devs don't notice these things. I am the type of player who really enjoys themes/aesthetics, and it just really sucks when I find something that looks/feels cool is objectively awful. One example is Open World Chronomancer Mesmer versus Spellbreaker Warrior. On the Spellbreaker I can solo champs and bounties with very low APM, but on the Chronomancer I just... die... and the APM is much higher - so the effort put in is much higher, only to die anyways. Overall, I ended up having fun playing GW2 but it came with a LOT of compromises and mental gymnastics, thinking to myself things like "This thing sucks, but that's ok because 'X' is alright." or "I hate this spec, but it's OK cause I'm playing with an IRL friend and that's the important thing."Honestly if it was not for having an IRL friend to play with a lot of the time, I'd probably have quit a long time ago. So take my "I'm having fun" with a grain of salt. I can absolutely see why new players would get turn off from GW2... There are a lot of "little" things that just add-up and go against what most new players expect. I have a lot for memories of "That's total bull****" than I do memories of amazement  and joy. Do I enjoy GW2? Honestly probably not, but my IRL friends are what MAKE it fun... and so, I play.

_childDocuments_.review: It used to be the only MMO I could recommend to anybody, because it was (maybe still is) one of those rare MMOs where the journey to min-maxing was a huge focus for devs and it was a lot of fun. Endgame was there to some extent, but it felt like an afterthought to me. I didn't care about endgame until I hit about 2k hours doing other stuff in game.  Let me tell you about the negatives. I'll point out positives too, but it's mostly to avoid bashing adjacent stuff that is not bad.Core world is an adventure and a joy to explore. This world makes this game one of few MMOs  where the journey was so fun I didn't care about the destination.It is interesting mechanically, thematically and in most cases there's some lore to find too (including the scenery). As far as MMOs go I don't think there are competitors. WoW used to be a candidate, but GW2 still took #1 spot due to QoL features. Despite worlds being similarly fun to explore, GW2 game design that had you focusing on exploring and skipping all the boring stuff, like looking for quests, turning them in and farming experience.Core world certainly had a structure, but very little of it felt formulaic. All living story maps released in past 4 or 5 years feel mass-produced. Community cried about lack of content and devs built a framework to pump out the content faster. Over time new content lost the magic that made GW2 world amazing, as the maps were just containers to hold really bland time-sink grind in. Content of any living world map:DLC maps are always better quality than the free Living Story maps. They have a few goodies sprinkled in, but they follow same formula and take 3-6 times longer to complete.They used to be the same each year, but had a new set of achievements, unique rewards (always a surprise) and sometimes a new activity got added. Even after taking long breaks from the game I always came back for holiday events. Around the time I quit they converted those into generic grind. You can see more rewards than you can get in upcommin 6 years. All of those rewards are generic (like a skin set). The joy of surprise is gone and .Classes are only brought down by weird balance, but I'll get to that. GW2 gameplay offers some mechanics that most MMOs don't have which makes each class feel distinct. For instance: classes like mesmer or engineer are not a typical class in terms of playstyle if you compare them to other MMOs. Then if you compare classes among themsleves difference start with simple things like mobility and go all the way to things like playstyle complexity, synergies, utility options and such. I'll say mechanical side of combat is still pretty amazing and unique. Every class can do everything (some are better than others at specific roles), but how each class gains access to that "everything" is vastly different. Even if you play a specific role in different classes the playstyle might be different. For instance: warriors can heal you by shouting at you, while revenant pushes a stone tablet that heals anybody it touches.I am not a huge master PvPer, but I always felt like all classes are useful. Despite what some casual players might say no class rules over all. Some classes are easier to play as a newb, but anybody who knows a class and knows how and when to engange/retreat will consistently beat the cheese classes. The reason I put 9/10 and not 10/10 the fact there's always a cheese class/build to play. I don't think it can be completely phased out. In PvE classes are balanced exclusively around raids (by the way, good luck getting into those) and the only thing that goes into consideration is max DPS they can pull off. If any class goes over that raid DPS target (something devs have internally), they nerf it. The problem with that is, not all classes are equal in other areas.For example: You can compare elementalist to other classes in open world, and you'll quickly see the skill floor for elementalist is much higher, while it kills at a similar pace as others.I think Damage, survivability and utility should all be taken account when balancing a class, not just max DPS it can do.I bought the latest DLC and logged in, hoping I'd be excited to try it again.... well I was excited, and then after about 15 minutes of gameplay I wasn't. If you're already playing it, you won't notice anything wrong.If you jump in as a new/returning palyer, it feels ancient. Especially so, if you've been playing newer action games, that have proper attack feedback. GW2 fell behind.I would still recommend this for the (free) core game for exploration(read about F2P limitations). PvP content is great, but only with DLCs. Endgame (including most new content) is just a bucket list of grind and are nothing like the core game. If you choose to do everything you can expect to throw away about ~8 hours a week + 1 hour / day (this only stuff that has infinite grind value). It might go a bit faster if you get into experienced teams, but if you're new you'll probably not even get into average ones.For context: I was no stranger to grind. I was around 20k hours (2.28 years of playtime, when the game was like 5 years old), almost all achievements done (baring a few VERY long WvW grinds and a couple of PvP ones), and 14 (I think) characters fully built (+multiple builds) and world explored on all of them. GW2Efficiency (website that tracks what can't be easily tracked in game) put my account value (in gold) in top 0.1% and most other metrics were in top 1%. I am not saying that to brag, I am saying to emphacise my point. I played and achieved a lot more than most people and . It only got worse since I quit.

_childDocuments_.review: The community in this game is amazing. The combat is ok. The activities are varied. Sometimes I want to sit in one spot and whack things but this isn't the game for that. This is a game that rewards constant movement and exploration. Its an adventure game above all else, meaning its combat is secondary which can be a pro or con depending on the player.  The BEST thing about GW2 is that its a game with horizontal progression rather than vertical at the end-game making it rather unique in that regard. Personally I think horizontal progression is the best end game content possible.The cons is that this game has too many quality of life micro transactions. After paying for all the expansions you will feel pressured to spend even more on quality of life items, like re-usable salvage kits, storage expansion, gathering tools, etc. Another con is how clunky it can be uploading/buying expansions. They dont accept paypal unless there is a credit card/bank account linked to it, unlike most other games on steam. Furthermore, your steam purchases will not appear on your account if your account was originally made via battlenet. Out-of-game experiences are very important to me. This prompted me to stop playing after collecting a refund. Ultimately I would only recommend this game to a niche group of players that dont mind outdated graphics, prefer running around on mounts more than combat, and dont mind buying the full game/expansions and feeling pressured to spend even more on micro transactions.

_childDocuments_.review: i've played this back when it launched quite a bit, somehow fell off it and also lost my access, because i changed email and ... oh well.. glad to start over, let's leave it at that.i played the f2p version first, to see if i wanted to get back into it, and really the f2p version is literally just the complete basegame, minus the auction house. now missing the AH is a bit of a bummer, but you get taken out of f2p status with any purchase, if i'm not mistaken, so getting access to that isn't a big investment.i bought the addons then, but after 180 hours of play i haven't even finished the main content yet, so i can't speak to the dlc much.only that you get access to the raptor mount right away if you own the addon mounts came with, and that's super convenient.enough about f2p vs not, let's talk about the game.there is no petty competition over ressources because nodes and loot are instanced for everyone. events that plop up dynamically in the world are shared by players aswell. you see someone doing a thing? join in! the event will get slightly harder to accomodate for the extra person and you both get credit. it really encorages players to naturally help each other and cooperate.the community is super friendly and helpful, so the steep learning curve of all the content being thrown at you feels less overwhelming.the music is great, the graphics really hold up, fighting is fun...i'm not a big fan of the voice acting often times, i literally hated my female human character in their story missions because of how goody-two-shoes and righteous they come across... but that's easy enough to overlook.the character design is also way too make-upped for my taste, but with a "no middle sliders" approach in character creation you can still get some regular and interesting looking characters.it's just a really fun game, okay?especially if you enjoy 100%ing stuff, the map completion alone really appeals to me personally.
