_childDocuments_.review: I kinda have a like/dislike relationship with this game and somehow come back to it every once in a while after playing it for over 1000 hours since last year. It respects your time and the gear you unlocked or grinded for a few years ago still matters now. Resources and loot cannot be stolen by other players. There is no monthly subscription and the first two DLCs are worth their money (I have not played End of Dragons). The cash shop is a mix of cosmetics and quality of life items like unbreakable gathering tools.The mounts feel great and “heavy” and gliding helped me more than once so that I did not fall to my death.The free core game has a few restrictions when it comes to chat options, the trading post and how many characters you can have, but includes what you need to get to level 80, which is technically the max level. After that comes the so-called horizontal progression in the DLCs. New accounts get the first mount at level 10, for free accounts it is a time-limited trial, if you bought any DLC you can keep it. The core Tyria maps have enough waypoints though to get around by foot.There are 8 classes in this game (9 if you own Heart of Thorns) and each has their core spec and a total of 3 elite specializations each – 1 for every DLC. These elite specializations do not make the class necessarily better, but they get different playstyles that way. There is no holy trinity in this game and some classes play differently than you might expect them to do in other games. Every class has a slot for a healing skill and every player can revive another player. There is even an achievement with a title for doing so. None of the classes are race or gender-locked and the only differences for the races are the first few story steps, their starting area, the cultural armor sets they can get and a few skills which rarely get used though. Pretty much everything in this game gives you XP. You like to play the story? Every 10 levels you unlock the next story step and gain XP that way. You like gathering resources? You can get XP for doing that. You like to explore the maps? There are vistas, points of interest and jumping puzzles everywhere and if you explore all the core game maps you get an item you need for crafting high-tier weapons. Instead of fetch quests that require you to run around from point A to point B, just to run all the way back there are “renown hearts”. Just be in the general area of the heart symbol on the mini map and it tells you what kind of different things you can do there to fill that heart up to complete it. Then you can just move on to your next activity without having to run to some NPC to turn stuff in.You don’t like PvE that much and would rather play PvP? You can do that as soon as you finished the tutorial. In structured PvP matches every character gets put on the same level with every skill of their core profession unlocked and, if you own any of the DLCs, their elite specializations also are unlocked. The PvP lobby is also a good place to try out a character to see if you like the skills of your chosen class. PvP players can be quite toxic here and there, but it feels less than in other competitive games. There is also WvW, in which three servers compete against each other, though changes will be made about that so it will be teams instead of world playing against each other in the future. This mode is a mix of PvE and PvP, for which you bring in your own gear and flip camps, towers or keeps for your world either as a lone roamer or in a big zerg with other players.The open world PvE community is one of the friendliest I came across in any game, here and there even a bit too friendly. More often than not the mechanics of the bigger world bosses get explained before they appear and if you need any help, just post it in chat and chances are high you get a helpful answer or people coming to help you out fighting a bounty boss.So, welcome to Tyria! We have dragons! And pocket raptors …

_childDocuments_.review: I never write reviews, but I think it's time that I finally did for this occasion. For those that never played this game, I have played Guild wars 2 for about 6 years, and through those years I always came back to it and always enjoyed it. Out of all the MMOs I played from WOW to ESO, this one really takes the cake. Just imagine leaving the starting area thinking " welp.. time to find quests I guess" only to just be running into event after event back to back all the while you're just STACKING on the XP. Suddenly you run into a band wagon of players grouped up and you find yourself in a big ass fight that always rewards you no matter how much you contributed. Your attacks feel hard and heavy as you watch the poor ass bandit's chin shooting straight up to the sky as he screams in pain.  You can DODGE away from impending doom and not have homing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ following you no matter how far away you are from the enemy.  Something I think WOW should take notes of honestly.. Every single weapon has their own set of skills which makes finding a new weapon for the first time like opening present. _childDocuments_.review: Tough game, especially the "Living World" story line portions, but it has a little of everything.  AreaNet is always adding more places to it, more features. Most of the players are in the expansion packs.  The base game gives you a chance to get started.  To live long at all you need to watch the enemy, the ground around your character's feet (for area of effect or attack warnings), and you health - a lot to look at in a battle.  Like all MMORPG's you can simply teleport to a waypoint nearby if you die, though.  Crafting is enormous in game.  There are many types of crafting.  Personally, now that I'm on my second character in this, I recommend crafting jewelry as a starter.  I crafted jewelry better than the game was giving me in many cases, and it reaches it's peak at 400 (others go to 500).  You can do 2 kinds of crafting at once, so if you choose to do so I would say do whatever will give you more character storage.  Armor crafting can expand your characters carrying by providing larger (more slot) boxes to carry goods in, but it's only useful if your character uses heavy armor.  Find what does you the most good.  I strongly recommend getting the first two expansion packs at least, but play through the base first.  You can sometimes get through to the new areas (Heart of Thorns, Path of Fire) without playing all the way through the Living World episodes.  Play enough of them to get there, and then use the waypoints & exploration.  Do the Living World when you get better at it.  Those are my recommendations to get a newby started. _childDocuments_.review: GW2 is an excellent MMO overall, still. :)It does all the things an MMO should do, and it does them well. The lore is deep, the content delivers, and the game is built really well. Also, it's F2P and you can get away with not spending a cent if you don't want to while still enjoying tons of the game.#LoreNot much to say other than it's deep and well-thought out. Parts aren't great, and parts are. It's pretty typical in that regard, but they do well with it, I think.#Skill/Builds/ProfessionsDone well. 5 skills are tied to your type of weapon equipped (great sword attacks, pistol skills, staff attacks, etc), 5 are tied to your character (3x "utility" skills, 1x heal skill, and 1x elite skill), plus another 1-7 tied to your profession (such as Elementalist changing the element of their other skills, etc). You can change your "build" as well, enabling specializations which modify your skills and stats certain ways, which obviously grant many ways to play a character.This game tries to keep away from "Warrior is always tank, Elementalist is always DPS, Mesmer is always crowd control, cleric is always healer" tropes. There is no specific healer, but every class seems capable of healing/support if you build them that way. There's also flexibility in building your classes. Do you want your Mesmer to be a DPS/glass cannon, or do you want them to be a tank/damage sponge/aggro-puller? You can choose.Skills feel correctly intricate and complex while also simple and straightforward. I think anyone can pick up this game and jump in on a good build for their playstyle without too much effort, but tons of guides exist out there too to hone in on what works best for you.Oh, you can save builds as templates, however, you do have a limited number of builds you can save at a time in both character and account storage. This should be fine, but if you get into the game you may find yourself wanting more, which just means you need to spend gems (real-world equivalent currency).#Gameplay--Questing!Quests are made simple and feel great. You don't "pick up" or "turn in" quests... you just get them as you level up or pass through an area. Side quests are awarded and completed by just playing the game in a given area, and main quests are earned as you level up your character and complete the previous chapter. Progression is simple and feels intentional.--InventoryLike most games, it takes a minute to understand how to manage your inventory, but from what I can tell it feels good here. You will struggle with how small your space is at first, but just be patient. Eventually you'll work your way up to 18-24 slot bags in each bag slot and you might not even need half of it for a while.+ Carry salvage kit and break down unwanted armor/weapons whenever to create materials, then drop all materials into your bank no matter where you are.+ Sell any good armor/weapons on player market for gold, no matter where you are, by sending it to the trading post. (You'll need to find a TP NPC to collect any purchased items, coins earned, or cancelled sales, though, which makes sense.)+ Carry the rest back to your bank or keep it on your character. :)+ Some enemies drop junk trophies... you can sell them to a merchant ("sell junk" button).--EconomyMost of the currencies are shared account-wide, including gold, and are stored in a "wallet" separate from your inventory. Nice!There's a variety of currencies but most revolve around gold, karma (earned from questing), and then all the end-game stuff. There's also a gem store, which is your real-world currency, HOWEVER, it's possible to accrue enough gold from playing the game to buy gems with in-game gold rather than spend real money... but you'll have to play a while. Current exchange rate is high, and it will probably stay that way.Note about gems: it's a flat rate. Each tier of gem purchase is exactly the same dollar-per-gem; you're not getting any discount. So, if you choose to buy gems, don't sweat about saving up for the "best deal"... just buy however much you want because it's all the same. In USD, 1 gem = $0.0125. So, something that costs 400 gems is $5 real money.#ActivitiesI haven't done a lot yet beyond just leveling my characters (trying to get a few to max level which is 80, and get through the main story, before I branch off much), but there's tons to do and I'm excited to explore more soon. Here's what I know though:--PVERoam world, dungeons, story quests... End-game boss runs and raids and "fractals" and strikes and stuff... racing...--PVPJust warp to PvP land and now you're temporarily max level (80)) = get to fight people in matches, whoo!There's also WvW or "World vs World" which pits server populations against each other in larger-scale PvP matches with objectives such as "capture this base from the opposing team". I have yet to play it myself, but people gush over how well it's done here.# CommunityGenerally people are very helpful. In many starter areas, there's often high-level players who purchased a badge that allows them to advertise themselves as mentors, and even beyond that, there's usually someone knowledgeable and helpful in chat somewhere. You should get yourself into one of the many guilds people are recruiting for too... people are a great resource.That said, sometimes (like with every video game), chat can get toxic and weird... just ignore when it happens. No need to let political conversations get you down. And, for every weird conversation, there's also other people in chat thinking to themselves "ugh can we talk about something less provocative please"... so you're in good company even when weirdos set out. :)# CostFree To Play (F2P) - If you like the game, you'll find yourself wanting the paid upgrade, but content-wise there are no pay walls on the entire original story. F2P cannot access the paid expansions (obviously) which include a new class, mounts, new elite specializations, etc... cannot access the "living world" seasons which are basically seasonal story DLC (which I think are free to paid accounts)... and F2P cannot access map chat (only "say" chat, which is more local). Other restrictions include not being able to go to Lions Arch (LA), the central player city, until like, level 40 or whatever... but a paid account can go as low as level 5. All in all, though, F2P gets quite a lot of freedom, but paid accounts feel worth it, too.# SuggestionsThe default controls are great but I prefer ESDF as opposed to WASD. Fortunately it's easy enough to re-map things, and exporting your controls are easy too, allowing you to experiment with different styles if necessary.No native controller support, but there's templates available in the community-made section. I am planning on making my own that matches my ESDF keybind layout... with the eventual goal of being able to play Keyb/Mouse, Mouse-only, Gamepad, Gamepad/Mouse. It's great having options, and when I get that control scheme figured out I'll share it on the Steam Community.

_childDocuments_.review: Downloaded the whole thing on Steam just so I could put in a review to support the game. Having logged over two thousand hours in playtime on the original client this is definitively the most impressive and enjoyable MMO I've ever played. It's simply more advanced than the older games of this genre, while being far more intricate than the newer games of this genre.The game almost immediately sets itself apart from many other MMOs by the way its world is structured. The environments are fully traversable, players being able to run and jump around all manner of dynamic settings like caves, hills, ruins and mountains. Numerous platforming challenges are hidden throughout the world for players to find and struggle with for rewards and achievements. While the absolutely pristine mount system gives players even greater options when travelling the world through the ability to zoom at high speeds across a map in seconds, jump to massive heights that can scale mountains and colossal ruins, or fly openly across the map and just avoid everything.Each map is filled with many random events that will periodically trigger on their own. This adding an extra layer of depth to the exploration and levelling process as players will constantly encounter random scenarios that they can join in on. There are also many absolutely astonishing large scale bosses that appear across the world at set intervals, which players are encouraged to continue fighting for rewards long after they surpass the level of that area. The game actively downscales the player to any lower level area they enter, allowing players to experience lower level content at any time without being completely overpowered.Even more distinct is the way this game handles fetch quests. Numerous MMOs force players to do a variety of arbitrary chores that string them across the world as they have to repetitiously talk with forgettable characters to acquire and finish tasks. In this game you automatically gain tasks by simply entering the area where they are active, while being given a variety of options on how to make progress towards that task. When you complete it, the task is automatically cashed in. Players have full control over where they travel and which tasks they perform, the only linear progression in this regard comes from the story missions. Which are also completely optional. The story of this game is decent for an MMO but not extremely compelling, however there are a select few powerful moments. In general most of the writing that really stands out comes from the overall world design and random character interactions, many of which tend to be fun and wholesome.The game features nine classes each with: four or more default weapon movesets, around two dozen selectable abilities, dozens of passive traits and three specializations that further expand the class. Although players cannot change their character's class, all other facets of their class can be customized on a whim; allowing players to set up and swap between multiple different builds when desired. The combat is quite unique in that its complexity largely depends on how much effort players want to put into being optimal. Many combat encounters can be survived by doing the bare minimum, but there is also a lot room for reactivity and memorization. Outside of more difficult encounters, players can choose how much effort they want to put into the combat based on their current mood. Many of the more difficult combat sequences in the game however do largely revolve around memorization of the mechanics and patterns. Which does make the latter end of the difficulty scale very inaccessible as players have no hope of survival until they memorize the encounter. This only applies to very specific portions of endgame content though, which can be completely ignored. The vast majority of content in this game can be beaten with decent reactions and a casual remembrance of the mechanics at play.There is a massive amount of endgame content between map bosses, dungeons, fractals, strike missions, raids, achievement hunting, mastery unlocks, crafting and holiday events. The game has an extremely expansive achievement system that hides all manner of special rewards, along with a multitude of daily tasks. Unfortunately the reward system in this game is not very structured, so discovering all the things you can actually unlock may be awkward as they aren't openly advertised to the player.The game does feature a large scale and small scale competitive mode. However both are extremely abrasive to new players as they require extensive knowledge of the classes, mechanics and most optimal builds in the game for survival to be very plausible. There are a multitude of balancing issues with the classes in competitive, and in general really, but that's not exactly unique for a game with this much variety. Outside of competitive the balancing issues are largely unnoticeable except in very specific types of content, or when using very specific builds. Neither competitive mode is being aggressively updated at the moment though. But it is all fleshed out content that players can dive into if they choose.The game is free to play by default but has multiple expansions and story sequences which can be bought. All of which add a multitude of new endgame content such as maps, story missions, mechanics and rewards. Each of the three aforementioned class specializations is unlocked via having the corresponding expansion. There is a cash shop but it's pretty much just full of cosmetics and niche convenience items sold to sustain the game between expansion releases. Players can convert their ingame currency into the cash shop currency so it is completely possible to buy things from the cash shop without actually paying with cash, as I have done multiple times. Unfortunately the game does have a lootbox system but fortunately it's extremely inconsequential. Somewhere around ninety five percent of the monetized cosmetics in the game are bought upfront from the cash shop, only a very small amount are lootbox exclusive; so the lootboxes are quite forgettable.From the exploration, to the class design, the combat, the general mechanics and the endgame there is a massive amount of variety and depth to this experience. Although some grinding is required for very specific achievements or rewards, much of the game revolves around highly varied activities that players can pick and choose as they please. The game offers a huge amount of content entirely for free, and a massive amount of expanded endgame content can be bought after the initial free campaign is finished. This is definitively the best MMO I've ever played, and I honestly do not expect any other MMO will ever supersede it.If you're interested in finding more games that I positively recommend they can be found on my curator page .

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be honest if you haven't tried GW2 in 2022 then you don't know what you're missing. Even most people who played it back in the day will be surprised how ArenaNet have done a complete 360 in terms of engine support, updates, WvW improvements, communication and yes actual good marketing!Played hours are not reflected on my Steam obviously but I have about 6k hours played since 2015 and still going strong. GW2 is the true MMO experience running in an open world alongside thousands of other players and feeling that you are apart of something bigger. The latest instant content, Strike Missions (like FFXIV raid encounters), are absolutely the best content in GW2 right now. Overall all of the different game modes, my guild, exploration, story, achievements and more is what keeps me logging in daily. And to be clear this game is NOT pay to win. Yes, there are quality of life items and a cosmetic cash shop but in my 8 years of playing I've only had to spend money buying the expansions. All QoL items I acquired over time was via in-game means. So yeah, there is nothing holding you back the entire base game and first Living World Season 1 Story is free up until the expansions. Believe me you'll be kept busy for quite some time before even thinking of the expansions, also now that it's on steam there might be special deals in the future.GW2 is truly my game of choice and not having sub fees or being forced to make purchases is fantastic. I would however highly encourage people to at least get the first 2 expansions (they are bundled as one price now) as they do support the developers for making game improvements and future updates.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played many MMOs in my life time from big theme park-style MMOs like World of Warcraft, The Elder Scrolls Online and Final Fantasy 14, to obscure niche sandbox-style MMOs like Runescape, Project Gorgon, Albion Online and Black Desert Online. All of the previously named MMOs did not respect your time. Guild Wars 2 is the first time in an MMO that I do not feel pressured to play. I likened this feeling to the similarity of that feeling you get when you know you have to go to the gym to run on the treadmill for X amount of time. I can play at my leisure. I feel accomplished with what I do in game. I WANT to play. I WANT to socialize with players to achieve content goals.The game has MOUNTAINS of content. All of the content is still relevant from the game's release in 2012.I HIGHLY recommend this to any fan of MMOs. Yes, like any other MMO, it has issues, but they are few and far between. _childDocuments_.review: Hold onto your helmets, adventurers, because Guild Wars 2 is not just a game – it's a laughter-filled carnival ride through the wacky wonders of Tyria! If you're tired of the usual serious-faced fantasy worlds, prepare to have your funny bone tickled and your expectations hilariously shattered.First things first, the graphics – it's like the game was designed by a team of hyperactive artists on a sugar rush. Tyria is a vibrant, mesmerizing kaleidoscope of colors that'll make you wonder if you accidentally stepped into a Salvador Dali painting. Seriously, who needs realistic landscapes when you can have landscapes that look like they were crafted by the gods of Crayola?Now, let's talk about the characters. Instead of the brooding heroes with a tragic past, Guild Wars 2 gives you a cast of characters that seem to have attended the School of Comedy Arts. From the charismatic norn who thinks he's a stand-up comedian to the asura genius who accidentally turned her lab assistant into a quaggan – you'll be laughing so hard you might miss the next quest marker!The combat system is a comedy show of its own. It's like the developers said, "Why settle for serious strategy when you can have the chaotic charm of a food fight?" Smash those buttons like you're playing a game of whack-a-mole and watch the magic happen. Spoiler alert: It involves a lot of explosions.And the storyline – oh, the storyline. It's a rollercoaster of epic proportions, filled with unexpected twists, hilarious dialogue, and moments that'll make you say, "Did that just happen?" Forget about predicting what comes next – just buckle up and enjoy the comedic chaos.But it's not just the game that's a riot; it's the community too. Guild Wars 2 is home to the friendliest bunch of players this side of the digital realm. From spontaneous dance parties in Lion's Arch to impromptu roleplaying sessions in the most random places, you'll find yourself surrounded by the kind of folks who can turn any situation into a comedy sketch.In conclusion, Guild Wars 2 is the laughter-infused vacation your character deserves. It's a game that doesn't take itself too seriously and invites you to join the party. So, grab your sword, put on your silliest hat, and get ready to LOL your way through Tyria – where dragons are just the coolest neighbors!

_childDocuments_.review: You have nothing to lose and everything to gain by trying GW2, especially if you're first time through Steam. The integration is seamless and doesn't even require an account creation as it all happens through Steam.The free to play restrictions allow you to experience the entire core game and give you a 10 hour preview of mounts (from Path of Fire). Don't like the base game? You lose nothing.Want your mount permanently? $100 for ALL the story content or just $25 to keep the first two expansions (and your mount).Don't worry about not playing GW1, this game happens 250 years after the first Guild Wars.If you chose to stay, welcome to your Dopamine Drip!It's a great game all around, but be careful if you're a former MMO addict like myself since it can eat a good chunk of your life away before you know it.Playing via Steam to track my hours but I've had an account since 2015 at least. You can use "-provider Portal" in Launch Options to use your old account while tracking hours via Steam.Finally getting back into it again and this will definitely keep me busy for the foreseeable future. Gameplay is still solid, they upgraded to DX11, and playing alongside friends is still a great time. Now maybe I can make it to level 80 this time so I can try the expansions I bought forever ago. EDIT: I hit level 80 on 4/8/2023 so this is true now. Time for horizontal progression! So much to do and NO pressure to do it. I play because I want to.Note: Don't use a VPN, Arena Net tends to temp ban you for using them and will even shut your account off if someone suspicious tries to login to your account.

_childDocuments_.review: Made a new account after I lost my original that I had in 2015. As far as MMOs go, Guild Wars 2 provides extreme, bordering on ludicrous value. There is a TON to do in Guild Wars 2, from jumping puzzles, crafting, world events, dungeons, explorations, world quests (which might I add isn't just fetch quests, you have a lot of variety there to spice things up,) and more; mind you, I'm only talking about the base game here, I haven't even touched the expansions yet. As far as character creation goes, you have nine different classes with specializations you can take which unlock new weapons for that class to use and new abilities, so there's even more to do there. What kinda sucks is you don't have enough character slots starting out to have one of each class, you have to buy more, but I'll be honest I've barely touched my alts so that isn't as big a concern to me right now. In terms of skills and abilities they are all unique to your class, and you can even switch around your weapon skills by dual wielding, or you have a second weapon slot that allows you to swap from melee to ranged on the fly, which is pretty cool, and gives a ton of customization to your build. As far as character customization goes? It's pretty alright for the most part, you have some options that are locked behind the premium currency store which also sucks, but thankfully it's a small amount of stuff. Speaking of the premium currency store from what I can tell it doesn't really sell power as much as it does style and convenience, which take that as you will. Now of course depending on how much you like the game itself you can either outright buy the currency, or convert gold into it, which fluctuates based on the in game economy as far as I can tell which is neat. The in game auction store sells about everything you can think of, from weapons, armor, skins, sigils, dyes, you name it, you can buy it there, and make a decent amount if you level high enough into certain crafting skills. Lastly, the story for the main game was pretty good, nothing special but definitely serviceable and set up the game for it's expansions well. You have the living world stories which help give contexts to the expansions, but the older ones are for sale, and you can buy them individually if you want to experience the older ones. All in all if you like MMOs and especially ones that don't charge a monthly fee (looking at you, WoW) this is right up your alley and I definitely think you should give it a shot. Coming back I like it just as much now as I did almost 10 years ago in 2015.

This means, that even if you take a 1-3 year break and come back, you'll still have the best gear (Where in other MMO's your grind has to restart). But be careful, it's not like other MMO's where you get full of the best gear in 1-3 weeks... No no no... It will take you months, but REWARDING months.The game has some of the most fun endgames: Dungeons, Fractals, Raids, Strike, PvP, WvW, and more... So if you are looking for a fun MMO, with different races, classes, endgame... Then this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a well-made MMO, it's not a bad game. However, coming from someone who grew up with WoW, it didn't scratch the itch. Guild Wars 2 does a lot of things right; the gameplay is polished and engaging. However, I couldn't continue playing this game for a particular reason: the controls and interface. You get one tiny hotbar that changes depending on what kind of weapon you have equipped, but the skills remain similar. For instance, whether you have a gun or a bow equipped, you're still gonna get a main attack, an AoE attack, some sort of slow/poison/bleed attack, etc. This was a neat mechanic but it felt annoying somehow.The keybindings are lacking in this game. With one tiny hotbar that tries to change on you, you just don't get that sense of control. It's almost too dynamic to make your character feel definitive. Some may like that, but it didn't click with me. You have to open your bags to use items instead of being able to put them on a bar or hotkey them. It just feels like an MMO that you could play with a controller and I didn't like that. My mouse has like 14 buttons, let me use them.Overall this isn't a bad game, but if you're coming from WoW and are used to that level of control when it comes to your interface, you may be disappointed with this game like I was.

Pros:+ Massive world with endless activities and content+ Emphasis on account progression over traditional character progression+ Huge class system: 9 Core classes with 27 Subclasses+ Diverse gameplay: Raids, Strikes, Dungeons, META events, PvP, World vs World, and more+ Engaging META events that scale with player participation+ Flexible character development without losing progress+ Structured PvP provides equal footing with customizable builds+ World vs World PvP: Huge battles where servers compete for control by conquering keeps+ Story-Rich: Deep lore and extensive storylines to immerse yourself in+ Crafting & Gathering: Easily one of the best crafting systems in any MMO+ Events & Festivals: Frequent in-game events and festivals that offer fun rewards and activities+ Jumping Puzzles: Challenging and fun, these are one of my favorite things to do+ Fishing: A relaxing side activity that makes tons of gold as well as being fun+ Extremely helpful community+ No subscription fee ever+ Purchase premium currency with gold earned through gameplayCons:- Endgame content like Raids and Strikes can feel inactive outside of guilds- Lack of a queue system for public versions of raids/strikes- Can feel overwhelming due to the vast amount of contentI suggest going through their website to install and then launching via steam if you want to have your hours logged or simply for quick access. Often they offer things through their website that aren't available on steam i.e. bundles for xpacs.

_childDocuments_.review: I have over 3000 hours through non-steam client.  While you can't link your existing Guild Wars 2 account to steam it is not a big deal.  It's annoying to see people giving bad reviews based on that. You don't have to start over on steam and spend more money.  Just play the way you always have.This game is by far one of the best MMO experiences out there.  It's not perfect but no game is.  Yes it has micro transactions but there is absolutely 0 pay to win in the game.  It is all cosmetic or convenience items that gives no one an advantage over others.  Yes you can buy gems and convert to gold and back to gems if you want.  However the highest quality gear in the game, ascended, is account bound therefore you can't buy it with in game gold.  This game has no sub fee.  The micro transactions help the studio keep making more content.Combat: It's a hybrid tab target action combat with an option to go full action.  Honestly the most fluid combat in any MMO. PVE:The world is massive, mostly voice acted and despite aging graphics, still beautiful.  There is no traditional questing, instead you complete renown hearts which usually have multiple completion paths,  Events will spawn around the map which you can complete.  Some of these are one off events and some are chains that can end in massive boss battles.  There are raids as well as dungeons, fractals (mini dungeons that can scale in difficulty), and strike missions (like raids but focused on boss battles).PVP: This is separate from PVE.  There is structured PVP and WvWvW.  Structured PVP is 5 man content focused on teamwork and taking control points or killing other players.  Everyone can do structured PVP starting at lvl 2.  You are made max level for PVP and given access to all the same stats as other players.  World vs World is Guild Wars 2's version of open world PVP.  Basically large scale skirmishes where teams try to take territory and can siege enemy castles. I could go on and on about more features but then this review would be a mile long.  If you are looking for a unique MMO then this game is for you. If you want a WoW clone then go elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Guild Wars 2 is one of those games that just surprised me. At first, it seemed way too complex, but I was pleasantly wrong. The game does a great job of easing you into its features so you don't feel overwhelmed. It's like learning to swim - you start in the shallow end and gradually make your way to the deep waters, all the while building your confidence.The game world in Guild Wars 2 is an absolute stunner. Imagine a vast, beautifully designed realm teeming with lore and places to explore. With each new expansion, it's like opening a new chapter in a beautifully illustrated book. The graphics are top-notch, making the whole world feel like a work of art, and you'll often find yourself stopping just to appreciate the breathtaking landscapes.But the beauty isn't just skin deep. The game's combat system is another gem. It's like having a versatile toolbox at your disposal. Your character's class can take on multiple roles, which adds layers of strategy and excitement. It's a bit like choosing your favorite superhero, with each class having its unique set of powers.Now, let's talk about the endgame. It's a blast. You're not stuck in a never-ending grind-fest. Instead, you have exciting events, challenges, and achievements that keep you coming back for more. It's like a thrilling adventure where every step is rewarded, and there's always something new to discover.Another cool thing is the social aspect. You can be a part of up to five different guilds. Think of it like joining five different clubs with their unique interests and activities. It's a great way to make friends and find like-minded adventurers to roam the world with.But there are some rough spots, especially if you get the game through Steam. It doesn't always play nice with external purchases, which can be frustrating. Imagine you're buying a new car, but you can only get the cool accessories from the official dealership, not from the dealer down the road. It's a bit like that.Inventory space can be a pain too. Early on, you might feel like your pockets are too small, and you're constantly juggling items. It's like going on a shopping spree and finding out that your bags are way too small for all your loot. It's a minor annoyance that could be fixed, but you'll adapt and find ways around it.Now, here's the thing - despite these hiccups, Guild Wars 2 has won my heart. It encourages you to explore, much like going on a grand treasure hunt with a compelling story-line. You pick your character's race, which determines your starting point in the world. It's like choosing the path of your adventure, and the story adapts to your choices.For free players, there are some restrictions, but it's all about quality over quantity. You can't do every quest, but that's okay because the ones you can do are fantastic. It's like having a gourmet meal with perfectly portioned servings. And as you delve deeper into the game, you'll find it's a balanced experience, well worth your time.In the end, Guild Wars 2 is an impressive MMORPG that balances accessibility and depth beautifully. The world is a masterpiece, the game-play is engaging, and there's an abundance of content. It's free to play, and you can opt for additional content if you choose. Despite a few minor issues, I wholeheartedly recommend Guild Wars 2 to anyone looking for an immersive MMO adventure. Whether you're a newcomer or a seasoned player, it's a game that offers a rich and enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best MMORPG I've ever played and I've played a lot. From the (mostly) friendly community, all of the events there are to do within the world, the level of customization for armor and mounts including dyes, different armor skins and mount skins to the massive world itself with more regions still being added, fishing, mount races and time trials, no games come close to Guild Wars 2. After upgrading from free-to-play with one of the expansions, the game really picks up on the level of fun and depth so my advice is if you are coming to play Guild Wars 2, test drive it a bit and make sure you like the mechanics of the game and the overall feel of the it then consider upgrading to an expansion to make your experience many times better. I'll admit early on I didn't just pick up the game and get immediately satisfied by it, I played for a few hours, got bored of it and deleted it just to come back about an hour or two after doing a little more research on the game then redownloading it to give it that extra chance and after playing for a bit longer and actually getting myself immersed I thoroughly enjoyed it. 1,500 hours later ... Wow I can't believe I've played it this much -- there's still so much content I'm able to do and so much of that content is still new to me. I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for an MMORPG to get into, but again -- just give it a couple chances and sink a bit of time into before making your final verdict because its always a little unsettling and overwhelming dipping your feet into unknown water.

_childDocuments_.review: ❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️An MMORPG that respects both your time and wallet. It's incredible for casual play. The design is so forgiving that you never have to worry that you’ve messed up. Just play and have fun. You don’t have to min-max your character or chase the flavor of the week “meta” build. You don’t have to use the “right” weapon for whatever class you’re playing, just pick whatever feels nice to play. The open world content is designed to be cooperative – there’s no kill stealing, no ninja looting and no ganking. Frequent events bring players together to take down bigger foes, or just adventure together for a bit. Your character level also scales down when in lower-level zones, meaning you never out-level areas. Exploring lower-level zones (or adventuring with lower-level friends) is still fun at higher levels especially since your rewards are simultaneously upscaled to your character’s level. The game does this without making you feel too weak; it’s quite impressive how well they’ve handled it. Your character will feel stronger doing low level content, but not so powerful that it makes it annoying for other players, or to completely take away the challenge. When you’re creating your character, the game is very clear about what classes are easy to play and which ones are going to be harder, which I appreciate. Starting at level 10, each playable race also has a unique storyline to follow until around level 40, based on the background you pick for your character during character creation. The story then continues all the way to max level and far beyond, with choices to make along the way. The cutscenes are both abundant and voice acted, and friends can join you in story instances. I really appreciate how easy it is to make low intensity (few buttons to push, few actions per minute and/or mostly passive) builds and just have fun. Switching skills and trying something new can also be done at the click of a button, at no cost. The maximum character level has also remained the same since the game launched, which is great for returning players or players taking long breaks from the game only looking to come back when there’s a new expansion. You can easily get back into the game without having to spend weeks catching up. In fact, end game gear is purchasable directly from other players through the auction house, and it’s all very cheap. Once you’ve geared your character, it’s a lot of fun to mess around with the transmogrification system and hunt for more fashion options to make your character look just how you want. Instead of chasing higher “gear score” or “item level” or whatever. The game is lovingly referred to as , for good reason. It’s just great. If you do end up playing, don’t be a stranger!

_childDocuments_.review: I guess it's my turn now to give GW2 a review. It's a love and hate relationship for all of the years. - You buy the expansions to unlock more content. At least core content is free so new players can give the game a try. No subscription payment. Just hop in and enjoy the ride. Everything is obtainable without spending a single money.- Horizontal progression. The highest tier for gear is ascended and has been for many years. And max level is 80. Once you are at that stage, you're pretty much done in terms of gear and levels.- Vertical progression is based on YOU. You decide if you want to improve, learn other classes, achievement hunt, etc.- Can easily play with friends since levels don't matter. A high level will downscale you to the area.- Combat is great and fluids pretty nicely (although there are times that things don't align properly...)- Visuals are awesome.- True endgame: Fashion Wars- Tons of content that you can do from core, HoT, PoF, EoD, raids, strikes, metas, etc.- World vs World (server vs server). a PvPvE environment where you just go smack people as a blob- Best mount system- Balance team is just questionable at times. - Blue class is strong and Anet's favorite child- Anet hates purple class- sPvP is like <1% playerbase and can be super toxic- Bugs can be left in the game for years and becomes the norm. Anet will be like "yeah thats a bug" 10 years later- Leaving old content into the dusts. RIP Dungeons. No new raid wing for a long time since they went down with the Strikes route. The latest strikes for Challenge Mote is very difficult if PUGging. - Light blobs- Too much blob on ground- Absolutely a puke of a mess if you do not have Effect LOD checked but still a messShort answer is... yes. Give it a try if it's your type of MMO. If you do enjoy it, find an awesome community guild preferably small guilds as you can make yourself known there. Big guilds can be very intimidating for new players and may forget who you truly are. But really, it's a matter whether you put yourself forward and make yourself known to others.

_childDocuments_.review: BEFORE THE REVIEW: Please note this IS NOT truly Free to play. The BASE version of the game is free, which is the Core 2012 package us GW2 veterans have been playing back in the days (10 years ago). If you absolutely want the best experience ever, not only in the MMO scenario but in the online gaming, you should consider buying the full packages (all Expansion packs and Living World episodes).The game itself is FREE FROM ANY MONTHLY FEE, but it has to be said that playing the f2p version will gut you out from tons of content and functions.THAT BEING SAID:I have over 8000 hours of playtime on the Arenanet game version betwen more than 10 fully optimized characters and i've been on and off between years since 2012 and have been playing since the very first day.Let me tell you, this is something UNIQUE. A true gem like Guild Wars 2 is rarely found, especially in the MMO genre, as it caters to both casual players and to hardcore ones and i truly mean it.You could focus on the long term goals between each and every game mode and decide your very own pace. Do you wish to grind the game nonstop to reach your goal? Why not! Go ahead!On the opposite, do you find frustrating to grind and want to savour what the game offers when you want it, how you want it? Please do!You could "freeze" (MMO term which means taking a break from a game) for months, even years, and your account still remains relevant with the newest content released.Yes, the endgame content is horizontally shaped which means as soon as you've hit level 80 and are geared with the right equip for the job, you're good to go; and there is no amount of time that will invalidate that.There are several type of content to be done, an ocean of experiences to have and a plethora of side activities that will get you hooked in no time:- You can play it mostly solo, as some kind of online role playing game, while leaving the most demanding content for organized play;- Content is shared and doesn't require groups for the most part except for high end instanced content. You can gather from the same resource node and get kill participation on the same mob that somebody else is fighting!- No traditional quests, instead there's dynamic events which shapes the life of the world;- Instanced story missions with iconic characters and cool plots that will overarch in intense dramas and twists;- Thousands of skins to choose from for your equipment which you can also dye a huge spectrum of unlockable colors;- Everything gives you experience points so you can choose your preferred way of reaching the endgame: traditional world exploring, story missions, crafting, pvp or by other means;- Traditional dungeons, Fractals of the Mists (scaling infinite dungeons), Raids, Strikes (shortened, easier raids), Structured Arena PvP and a dedicated Pvp war zone with 3 servers fighting each other called "World vs World vs World";- Legendary quests to obtain legendary gear, crafting skills, collections, jumping puzzles, Guild missions, Achievements, side activities such as minigames, mount races, fishing and exploring secret zones;- Gorgeous open world pve maps with huge epic bosses, lenghty meta-events with hundreds of players that must collaborate to clear;- The item shop provides with loads of quality of life items and skins which can both be bought with real money and with earned ingame cash that can be converted.There is so much to do in this game that i'm sure i'm forgetting something. The thing that hooks me up and motivates me to play is that no matter how long i take a pause from it, i just come back whenever i choose so and i can jump back from where i've left it, with no power creep mechanics outplayingme or forcing me to catch up. I can be as performing for a raid group as i was if i'd take a 1 year break, no sweat and no tiers of gear to recuperate between me and my friends!All of the classes, called "professions", are fun to play and have their own unique flavor and class theme. There are many subclasses, or "Elite specializations" for each single profession which focus on different playstylesand are favoured through specific game modes. For example, a Warrior could specialize in the Berserker Elite spec to deal loads of damage in PVE or could pick the Spellbreaker Elite spec to bring utility and boons in the pvp battlefield.Fights are intense, action packed, full of reaction mechanics and encourages you to dodge and move around a lot to survive. Bosses all have their own mechanics to be beaten and the more progress you do in the game, the more unforgiving they are,culminating in the Raid scenario where organized of highly skilled players have to diligently follow mechanics and role, or perish. However, also WvWvW bosses are hard to deal with and they won't nudge if a powerful army of pvp players won't engage them.After you're done with high intensity activities for the day or you just want to take some relax time, i advise you go around the beautiful world of Tyria, uncover its misteries and unlockable secret achievements and collections. There are literally hundredsof tiny little secrets and collectibles for each and every zone in the game, being from the Core 2012 experience to the latest high end expansion zone. No region feels dead as many players are always looking for scaled, down levelled content in those regions as they still remain valid and provide a challenge.Or maybe you're a bit bored out of the look of your character and want to search for another style of your gear; i'm sure you will find plenty, even overwhelming choices for your look. And if you're bored of your character...why not try to level up and play another one? The game doesn't punish you for starting over again and have multiple toons to have fun with. It's absolutely not mandatory but it can be rewarding, such as having more crafting disciplines available, more characters for different game content and so on.Some times during the year there's timed events that bring all players together such as Dragonbash (the celebration of the death of the first Elder Dragon) or the Festival of the Four Winds, and each has their own achievements and meta rewards. They cycle all year long so no worries if you've missed some, they will always come back.The trading post and the open world are both shared features on all servers, so don't stress too much about which server to pick when creating your first characters. However, the only exception would be for the WvWvW PVP: if you want to conquer castles and fight with your friends you must create a character within the same realm.All the rest of the content of the game is shared between each and every player.As a last tip i'd suggest you a couple websites that will help you grasp and master this exceptional game: GW2wiki, Snowcrows, Lucky Noobs, GW2 Skills, GW2Spidy, Gw2 Efficency, Metabattle (they are all websites that provide help for building your characters and manage your resources in the game)Last but not least, i hope you will enjoy the wholesome community of this game, which always encourages and welcomes new players as the game itself doesn't care for how long you have played: it treates everyone on the same page!Guild Wars 2 shaped the modern way we play MMOs and it's still not popular enough for what i think it provided to the genre.Play it and have fun! :)Thank you for reading,Heretiko

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you're a casual player looking to spend 300 hours in a game it's an enjoyable experience. If you're looking to invest more than that you can very easily run out of enjoyable content that isn't a grind.The latest expansion added a player housing system. This is a decent implementation, but suffers from costing a lot of money for certain decorations and a relatively low decoration cap. Also, only 4 total friends can visit at once, making it bad for social gatherings.The game features a tab-targeting 3rd person combat system with a standardized buff/debuff system that is by far the best combat experience in an MMO. It scales very well from 1v1 to 80v80v80 and is an enjoyable experience to play at all times. Over time it's been hampered by poor developer balance and obnoxious visual effects that the developers seem to be incapable of toning down (or even allowing a setting to disable), but in spite of these flaws the combat system is still the shining example of how MMO combat should be done.The GW2 mount system is a very unique implementation. Unlike other MMOs where all mounts are effectively movement speed buffs, perhaps with the ability to fly, GW2's mounts are distinct and different. The Raptor, Springer, Skimmer, Jackal, Griffon, Beetle and Skyscale & Warclaw are very diverse and each offers a different style of movement through the terrain.Skyscale, a flying mount akin to a dragon that is maybe the most desirable QoL upgrade to the game. With the 4th expansion, Secrets of the Obscure (SotO) an additional less grindy way to unlock the Skyscale was added to the game. Along with this SotO's story is separate from the first 3 expansions - making this the best starting point for a new player. There are 5 expansions, HoT, PoF, EoD, SotO & JW; and much like WoW/FF14 there are post-expansion patches called "Living Story" by GW2 which also are paid (not included with the expansions). I strongly suggest buying the complete edition with all this content if you're thinking of buying to get a full story experience. Most players play through the story once, which takes around 35-45 hours and the bulk of it is forgettable with the quality dropping with time.Once you hit level max level the game opens up the mastery system, a way of earning account wide unlocks for use in the game. This is a one-time grind that is not that enjoyable and gates Gliding (HoT), Mounts (PoF) and Boats/Fishing (EoD); and takes about a week of active play. SotO/JW have little unique unlockable content compared to the other expansions.Once you're past the time/gold sink that was the mastery system the game's content dries up rapidly. Unless you're motivated by skins, titles or PvP combat the rest of the game is unrewarding. Unlike other MMOs, (WoW, Lost Ark, Black Desert etc) there isn't an expectation to increase item level as the game progresses. While this sounds like a benefit at first due to the very incremental non-disruptive method of balancing used by the development team once you have geared a character once you never have to gear them again. What this essentially means is you need to pick your own goals for the game as there is never an overarching goal to work towards after you have completed the mastery system.If your goal is skin/cosmetic driven unfortunately all the best skins are cash shop exclusive - there are hardly any available from actually playing content; something even more true with mounts where there is basically 0 in-game unlockable skins. While you can play the game to grind gold and swap the gold for the cash shop currency this is a slow method of getting skins and the developers are rotating the cash shop skins to try and bait FOMO purchases. If your motivation is titles and other achievements even more bad news. You're 10 years behind other players and literally can never catch up, as some of the larger/prestige achievements/titles are unobtainable now.If your motivation is PvP combat, sadly more disappointment. Of the 2 PvP modes one (sPvP) has had no updates for over 5 expansions except to remove content. The other PvP gamemode (WvW) has been neglected for so long there are multiple exploits that have been in the game for years that haven't been resolved and suffers from a declining population.If you wish to play the game like WoW and grind gear then there is legendary equipment as a long term reward. While identical to non-legendary equipment in stats this allows the user the ability to reallocate stats at will - meaning you do only need 1 set of armor/weapons/accessories forever. The problem with this is two fold. First, as aforementioned the balancing is so incremental that you very infrequently need to swap gear at all, and secondly the cost/grind associated with getting a full set heavily encourages you to engage in "micro"transactions. A full set of legendary weapons currently costs 43,200 gold or $2500, and there are 3 total sets and some weapons can be dual-wielded meaning you will want to unlock them multiple times. On top of this you have armor and accessories and overall the whole process heavily incentivizes spending money.Christmas, Halloween, Super Adventure Box & Dragonbash - seasonal content. Unfortunately none of it is updated or maintained. Every year the same content is repeated with a single new skin added along with cash-shop skins designed to get you to spend. There is a lot of potential here, but as it is never updated or iterated upon it's wasted.The game has a barely functioning guild system that is never used in any part of the game. The entire experience of the game can be played solo without a group unless you're doing instanced content (in which there is a poorly implemented LFG system). There is no "Guild Wars" system. In the first expansion the guild system was overhauled adding "Guild Halls" - a map owned by your guild that you can decorate. This hasn't been updated since, missing crafting/bank access and overall isn't finished - with the final EoD guild hall missing key features (like being able to easily visit/discover other guild's halls). It has instancing issues and no purpose, making it unused.Outside of guilds the bulk of the end game content is split into open world events and instanced content. Instanced content has a 5 or 10 man cap depending on the content, and open world content can range from 30 people to 60 people depending on the developer specified cap on the server. In the open world content there is at no point any reason to chat or interact with other players, and in group content unless doing raids there is little incentive to talk or interact either. Overall this makes the game feel lifeless and dead with only trashtalking remaining.There are multiple examples of features being announced years before they are added, or they are not added at all - with no announcement development has been paused or stopped. Poor developer communication around balance patches has lead to some awful times in the games history where 1 class has become extremely dominant. The developers have proven time and time again they have no desire to listen to player feedback until it's so overwhelmingly negative it starts to leak into their sales.The game is very enjoyable for the first ~300 hours, after which you're left to pick your own path through the game. In comparison to launch a lot of the long term goals are now unobtainable or in the case of skins are predominantly on the cash shop. If you're looking to casually play a RPG for 300 hours I would recommend picking it up, especially trying it on the generous free-to-play model, but if you're looking for a MMO to play seriously long-term this is not the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I'm a GW2-Veteran and have played several thousand hours since release and I will continue to play the game, as it is really good.I'm mainly downvoting because the devs have practically abandoned all competitive game modes years ago. They are still kinda alive but the community is a shadow of its former self, especially in sPvP (5v5 battlegrounds).I really appreciate ArenaNet transitioning from Living Story updates - which I disliked the idea of before the first story chapter even came out - to a more sustainable expansion-style with lots of upcoming PvE content additions.However, since I'm a more competitive player I will only upvote if sPvP is getting some long needed attention again. Which is, realistically speaking, never as they don't have devs who are interesting in PvP anymore.Some things about the game which may turn you on or off from the get go:The movement and combat systems are really good and pretty deep, especially with the combo system (creating combo fields and using combo finishers). A lot of new people don't even know this but there is a ton of stuff you can combo together (even with other people's effects) and tenfold your damage or sustain as a party.I would even argue that it's the single best combat system out there, as I think it is a perfect mix between tab-targetting and active combat, with silky smooth animations and intuitive movement. There's also a ton of content and something to do for basically any type of player. There are a some catches tho.If you like casual PvE, open world/exploration, .. stuff like that, then definitely try it out.However, if you love grinding dungeons and raids for better items and constantly getting stronger then don't even bother if that's your only motivation to log-in. You'll max out quickly and progress horizontally. This is one of gw2's main selling points and has a lot of advantages, as no content ever gets obsolete for example and you can just hop back in after a long pause and don't need to grind for weeks just to be on-par with your friends (or enemies in WvW).. but if you don't like it then the game simply isn't for you.The content is also not reeeaally difficult, especially if you run in an organized group. Raids and even the new strikes are really nothing to brag about (comparatively speaking, people without a plan or willingness to learn the mechanics/prepare properly will still fail miserably). There is a speedrunning community for raids tho, if this is what you are aiming for.Another main selling point, which is definitely not everyone's cup of tea, is that there is no well defined holy-trinity. There are certainly classes (specializations) which better fit a specific role than others but broadly speaking you aren't just standing around and pocket-heal your tank like in traditional mmos. I personally like how this is done in GW2's because you can still fill all the traditional roles (and more) but everything feels a bit more active and it's not as clear cut, which I prefer to say FF14 tho.If you like siege battles and PvP: They exist, they are alive but don't expect too much. Both game modes (WvW and sPvP) have basically been abandoned for the last 5 years+. Yes there's the Alliance update coming to WvW but there's absolutely 0 difference in gameplay, no new content, no nothing. Everything that changes is who you are teamed up with for the coming weeks.However, I do still enjoy running around in WvW and just duelling people or run around with a squad. There's no official GvG game mode but plenty of guilds set up their own GvG matches in an abandoned WvW map, so this is also an option.The competitive community is comparatively already super small and shrinking every day, however they are not tiny. You'll still encounter plenty of players in WvW at basically any time of the day and searching for a pvp match usually takes less than 5 minutes (unless you are queuing up for ranked in the middle of the night).While not nearly as bad as in most other MMOs, balancing issues are still a thing and the devs don't really care or just don't know what to do, which is really unfortunate. Nobody in charge has any deeper knowledge about the game (as they don't play it that much) so a lot of the time they just do what a few of their content creation partners tell them. Which is not the worst thing to do but is far from good.There are also not really that many modes for pvp, actually only 1 ranked (conquest) and 1 additional one (which can only be played in unranked), which is actually imo way more fun. You can't team up with more than 1 buddy in ranked, which I think is also pretty stupid. You can, however, make up a full team for unranked and tournaments (which are always 5v5 Conquest). One extremely important note on PvP: Your stats are normalized and your character is immediately maxed out on skills/traits as long as you are in PvP. So you don't have to grind for pvp gear or anything, it's all about skill and game sense - (team) builds do actually counter each other so you have to know your favourable match ups too!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like MMORPGs, give GW2 a try. Important points:* No quota. You only pay for the software.* Easy game to not get outdated easyly. Level cap it's the same as the beginning (80) and the same armor that you could get at the beginning is still valid, being the top stats Ascended/Legendary tier. What they usually do is add different combination of stats or change in how those work instead of increasing the level cap of character and armor.* Buy HoT and PoF Expansions together and the new EoD separately.* Buying the expansions DON'T give you access to the old Living Story Seasons. They were given for free when they went live, but as soon as a new episode launches, the old one can only be accessed via Gem Store Purchase (you can invest real money or in-game gold).* Is it recomended to have the LSs? Yes. I would recommend to start with LS4 to get the Skyscale mount (you need PoF expansion for that), and after that LS3 as in it's the best way to get Ascended trinkets.* With the free game you can access  Core Tyria Maps, Dungeons (really outdated nowadays) and Fractals (good way of making money and high end dungeons).* To access Raids, you need the expansions. To access Wings 1 to 4 Heart of Thorns is needed and for Wings 5 to 7 Path Of  Fire is needed.* To access Strikes, you need Living Season: IceBrood Saga (IBS) for its strikes and End Of Dragons expansion for its Strikes.* Dungeons and fractals are 5 players team instances, while raids and strikes are 10-player squads, being Strikes 'easier' than raids because they were introduced as a 'introduction' to raid content so more people try to get into raids.* From level 80, the progression it's horizontal, with a Mastery System that will allow the player to get different skills normally oriented to map exploration (like gliding and mounts). This system requires two things: Mastery Points (scattered accros the maps and also rewarded with achievements completion) and you need to get experience before to spents those points for each Mastery Track. Once the experience bar is full, one can spent some mastery points to unlock that reward and unlock the next level of the mastery.* Regarding the gameplay, unlike WoW this game is Action oriented. The dogde is an active skill instead of being passive and positioning is really important.* Each expansion increases the Elite Specialization accesible for each class (1 per class and expansion).* The game has Three main game modes. PvE (Open PVE and instances like dungeons, fractals, raids and strikes), PvP (3v3 or 5v5 matches) and WvW (Three servers (or alliances in the future) battling each other through 4 big maps. Each team can have 90+ players in the map with 50 player squads organized by a commander.* Most of the microtransactions are aesthetic or utilities (like increase bank space, material space, shared inventory spaces, infinite recicle tools, etc.) No Pay To Win in this game.* No mission system, outside history missions. The "sidequests" are hearts around the maps that need to be completed.For me, as a "casual" player that don't want to invest too much time playing, it's the easiest MMORPG to keep playing, as I can stop playing for a while, go back and don't have to worry too much to update my character, because normally my build will still be good.

_childDocuments_.review: If you buy the expansions to keep trying the game like I did, then you can't buy the living world separately, if you click it the link doesn't go anywhere. Why can't you take away the price of what you've already bought in the bundle and let people buy it if the expansions are required? I don't know, but they've purposely made their store this way.In the game they also sell everything. You can buy gold with gems, their premium currency, so you can buy everything in game with real money. Aside from inventory space and skins sold for real money, they also sell things that unlock hero challenge points on the map, so you don't even need to play the game if you spend more money. And of course they sell max level characters, experience boosts, permanent harvesting gear that doesn't break, permanent salvaging items that you don't have to constantly repurchase. They make all this stuff in the game as annoying as they possibly can, to manage your inventory and to keep harvesting things and everything, filling up your inventory with junk, just to sell you things to make this all less annoying.The story is the worst part of the game, and after the beginning of the main game, you can't skip the dialogue. You have to slowly walk with characters while they talk, or stand there while they talk until you can continue the story quests, which you need to do to unlock the maps and all the stuff in the expansions. It was so boring that I stopped playing for about a year after I bought the first two expansions.The rest of the quests are going to events, orange circles on the map that repeat after so much time, and either killing a mini boss, or defending an area for a certain amount of time. The others are escort missions, where a character slowly walks and you have to slowly walk next to them until they get to where they need to go, and you occasionally have to fight something. The other is walking around in an area, pressing f to pick something up and bringing it somewhere, either one thing at a time or several. You bring things until the bar fills up. This is they way events, this game's quest system works, the base game and expansions.You have to grind these events to keep filling up the experience bar after level eighty, then using the experience and mastery points to unlock something, then doing it again until you've unlocked everything in the base game and expansions.PVP isn't pay to win. You're maxed out, and only certain equipment you select for pvp matters, the only thing you'd need is the expansions to unlock the advanced classes. After that though, you could just keep playing pvp, you don't need to keep getting better gear or anything.There is WvW which uses your gear and everything else, so technically that could be considered pay to win, but after you've got all your gear, there's no way to keep paying for advantages, you could only skip the grind to reach that point, or get there a bit faster.There are eight dungeons in the game, it wasn't good, but they mostly seem to have people grinding fractals, which are pretty much dungeons. The difference being they scale, there are higher tiers, which require resistances for higher tiers to make it more difficult, but you're doing the same couple of dungeons.These dungeons, the fractals are the worst part of the game actually, worse than the story, at least the part of the story I actually played so far.There are platforming sequences in a lot of the dungeons, and if you fall you either go back to a checkpoint and run back, or you just lay there. Usually you're just meant to run past the mobs on the way to the two bosses, they don't really follow you for too long, they're not really a threat, people just run past them. _childDocuments_.review: I played Guild Wars 2 before it was on steam. So far, I have played for nearly 8 years.  The first thing to know it: This IS NOT a strength gaining game. You will meet your max strength relatively quickly. This IS a completionist's game. In the end, the point is to find and collect skins for weapons, different clothing items, and tons of other collectibles. HOWEVER! The skins and events alone are worth it.There are 5 races. Each race moves very differently. Job classes are available to all and pretty expansive with an interesting skill tree to give some variety. Job class also decides which weapons your character can use. Certain classes have higher tiered classes that have access to some of those usually unavailable weapons. The attacks themselves are the same regardless of race since they're based on the weapon/job class of the character. Job class also determines your dodge skill which I've personally enjoyed a lot.The story is HUGE. There are a lot of layers and information to read! I promise you will enjoy at least 1 of the race's historical or current events. My personal favs are the Sylvari. Who doesn't love a tree person? Constant updates will keep you deep in the story-play for hours. Each story chapter has hidden challenges some of which are somewhat difficult to solve. Keeping the replay of chapters interesting instead of tedious. Open world play is what you'd expect. Lots of maps with points of interest and events. Some events happen on a timer and some are dependent on certain requirements on the map to be met. Running around is highly recommenced and encouraged! Being aimless may actually help you find random hidden areas. They added mounts recently making map progression a breeze. Jumping puzzles are a large part of the game. Some puzzles are simple and quick while others can take literal hours to finish. You are allowed to use skill utilities in these and certain classes have ways to teleport or move in ways to assist in the puzzles!  Festivals(holiday events) are the BEST! There are 6 major festivals based on some real-world holidays. Most have a jumping puzzle part, a timed events part, map racing, and TONS of exclusive holiday items. Mad Kings Festival is awesome and a community favorite. The community is one of the nicest and accepting I've ever been a part of. Joining guilds is very easy and can help you speed along character growth and harder events like raids. if you don't want to join a guild, the chat is a newbies best friend. Don't understand the event? Ask in the chat. Don't know how to get to the next part if the jumping puzzle? Ask for directions. Don't know how to find that item you really want? Find a mentor on the map or in the chat. Someone will always be happy to help!  SKINS! Soooo many skins. They recently added mounts to the mix... I will be playing this game for the rest of my life. A majority can be bought but cost more than they're honestly worth. Finding/making the skin yourself would be about the same amount of effort it would take to earn the necessary gold. The cash shop is big and is constantly updated with new skins. I prefer to find/make the ones out in the world.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even know where to start my review with Guild Wars 2. My first experience with the world of Guild Wars was with Guild Wars 1. I bought Guild Wars Prophecies, and fell in love with the world. I played nonstop up to Eye of the North. Every hour spent in Guild Wars 1 I loved. When Guild Wars 2 got announced I got so hyped to the point where I was buying every gaming magazine with articles on the development of Guild Wars 2. It was my passion, and when Guild Wars 2 finally launched it was all I had hopes for. I started as an Asura, and seeing hundreds of us running around enjoying the launch finally will forever be an emotional memory in my heart that I hold close as one of the best experiences of my gaming career. Guild Wars 2 really started as a new beacon of hope for the MMO genre as a whole. It turned the genre upside down, and was a breath of fresh air. This lasted for several years. I would log on daily for dungeons, WvW, PvP, and Fractals. When they added the first raid, I was ecstatic to see their vision of what a raid would mean to them. It was an amazing experience. I still love the content Guild Wars 2 has to offer, but it just changed...Guild Wars 2 had an early peak, and has just been deteriorating since the first expansion. With the constant layoffs to the constant storytelling ♥♥♥♥♥, the game just feels different. The constant abandoning of content, and abysmal balance patches have pushed people away. There have been no new raids or fractals for years. There was never a new dungeon outside of the base release dungeons. PvP maps never evolved, and are the same boring base cap contest. World Vs World has been ignored for 5+ years, and the devs have promised big changes, and keep pushing things back. The story has gotten so bad to the point where you just have to play through it, and awkwardly laugh it off, or you'll get annoyed thinking about the writer's absurd decisions. Characters also get erased, and never show up again.I still log in time from time, but it just doesn't feel the same. I've spent around 30k hours between Guild Wars 1, and Guild Wars 2. I will always love this franchise, and hope it succeeds, but I can't in good faith recommend this game to anyone. Aside from the content drought, and other problems, the gem store is a whole other mess that prowls on people with spending addictions. I really hope the steam release does well, but I fear it will just make the game look worse than it currently is. I hope anyone that tries then enjoys the game, but again, I just can't recommend this game as a good way to spend your time.
