_childDocuments_.review: Exoprimal: Unexpectedly Fun Mechs Vs Dinosaurs ActionScore: 9.5/10Unexpected, Uproarious, and Unforgettable: That's ExoprimalWhen you first hear about Exoprimal's premise – mech suits against dinosaurs in a futuristic setting – you might be tempted to write it off as another far-fetched idea. However, this online, team-based action game is surprisingly engrossing, enjoyable, and well worth your time.Set in 2040, the game's storyline revolves around a dystopian future where dinosaur outbreaks are threatening humanity's very existence. However, the powerful corporation Aibius has developed exosuits, technologically advanced battle suits, and a predictive AI named Leviathan, presenting a glimmer of hope. As an Exofighter, you, alongside other players, will utilize these exosuits to stave off these unexpected prehistoric threats.One of Exoprimal's standout features is the exosuits, categorized into assault, tank, and support roles. Each suit comes with its unique abilities, catering to different combat strategies and offering an array of gameplay styles to suit any player's preference. Furthermore, the ability to switch exosuits mid-battle offers a dynamic, adaptable approach that keeps gameplay exciting and unpredictable.The addition of Rigs, equippable enhancements for your exosuits, adds another layer of tactical depth. Players are encouraged to experiment with different combinations of rigs and exosuits, promoting creativity and personal expression in combat.Exoprimal's innovative game mode, Dino Survival, is the epitome of excitement and teamwork. Squads compete against each other in accomplishing objectives, while also potentially battling massive foes together. With objectives and surroundings changing based on the players' progression, each match remains unique, creating a refreshing and ever-evolving gameplay experience.And of course, the dinosaurs. These aren't your typical beasts from a bygone era – they are 'Neosaurs', supercharged with vortex energy, taking the challenge to an entirely new level of intensity. The creativity poured into designing these unusual creatures deserves a shoutout.Exoprimal's graphics and environmental design are impressive, too, with an engaging futuristic aesthetic that manages to incorporate elements of the natural prehistoric world. This fusion creates an atmospheric backdrop for the fierce exosuit-versus-dinosaur combat, further enhancing the immersive quality of the game.What really surprised me about Exoprimal is its underlying strategic layer. Yes, it's an action game at heart, but winning requires more than just firepower. You'll need to cooperate with your team, tactically utilize your exosuits and rigs, and adapt to ever-changing game dynamics.Exoprimal brings an offbeat idea to life with polish and gusto. This game delivers unexpected thrills, strategic gameplay, and cooperative fun. While the concept might sound quirky, Exoprimal is a genuine surprise, a testament to the joys of unfettered creativity in game development. It's a reminder that in the world of gaming, even the most outlandish concepts can result in a gem when executed with passion and precision. I would highly recommend giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.review:
Exoprimal is an online, team-based action game that pits humanity's cutting-edge exosuit technology against history's most ferocious beasts - dinosaurs.  Exosuits are grouped into different roles, and players will pilot these exosuits to hold firm against overwhelming dinosaur swarms in online-only, team-based action game modes. Dino Survival, the main game mode, sees two teams of five players compete in a variety of PvE and PvP missions. Players will be transported to the scene of the latest dinosaur outbreak and follow Leviathan's guidance to complete objectives. The team that completes the mission first will emerge victorious.

Whether players are engaging the other team directly, or fighting alongside them against a common enemy, the aim is to accomplish objectives as quickly as possible. Missions vary depending on player skill and other factors, meaning no two matches will unfold the same way.

name: BPM: BULLETS PER MINUTE
detailed_description: WARNING: BPM contains flashing images. If you experience epileptic seizures or blackouts when exposed to certain light patterns or flashing lights, immediately stop playing BPM and consult your doctor before resuming. Fight as a mighty Valkyrie to repel the forces of the underworld from invading the world of Asgard. Gameplay In BPM, all of your actions and the actions of your enemies are tied to the beat of the music. Your enemies perform a dance-like sequence of attacks to an epic rock opera. BPM is inspired by retro shooters of the 90’s. It is fast, frenetic and rhythmical. You can double jump, dash, rocket jump and bunny hop to evade your opponents. Your goal is to reach the end of randomly generated dungeons, collecting different weapons, abilities and items each time you play. These weapons and abilities can radically alter the way you play, making each playthrough unique. You must defeat 7 bosses to reach the final boss. Each boss moves and attacks in a unique way that you must learn to exploit if you want to succeed. Some attacks require you to jump over fields of lava, some to dodge fast projectiles, some to hold fast for a beat. Features: Shoot, jump and dodge to the beat while battling hordes of enemies. Fight powerful bosses in challenging boss battles that will push you to the edge. Explore randomly generated dungeons. Choose from 10 different characters with unique strengths and weaknesses. Wield a powerful arsenal of weapons, all with different behaviour for firing and reloading to the beat of the soundtrack. Battle a diverse array of enemies, each with unique rhythmic behaviours. Get overpowered and fire shotgun rockets while flying through the air. Utilize abilities that radically alter the way you play the game, from teleport to freezing bolts. Equip over 60 items that buff your character in unique and interesting ways. Experience an epic rock opera soundtrack. Challenge modes for extra gameplay. Add Custom Music into BPM and shoot, dash and dodge to the beat of your own soundtrack.

short_description: BPM is a rhythm-action FPS rogue-like where you must shoot, jump and dodge to the beat of an epic rock soundtrack. Delve into a randomly generated dungeon where one missed note can lead to your death. Gain game-changing abilities and loot powerful weaponry to defeat your ancient enemy: Nidhogg.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, fellow warriors, gather 'round as I recount the epic tale of "BPM: Bullets Per Minute," a game that thrusts you into the heart of a perilous dungeon, much like our own ancestors faced in their heroic quests.In this audacious blend of first-person shooter, rogue-lite, and rhythm game, you, brave adventurers, shall delve into the abyss with the valor of a Viking warrior preparing for glorious battle. The relentless beat of the game, like the pounding of war drums, guides your every step. It's a rhythmic symphony of chaos and strategy, akin to the tumultuous battles of yore.As you venture deeper into the labyrinthine dungeon, you face an unending tide of monstrous foes and cunning traps, reminiscent of the treacherous perils that await in the dark recesses of our Norse sagas. The rogue-lite elements ensure that no two excursions are alike, much like the ever-shifting challenges of our epic quests.Your arsenal, my fellow adventurers, is a testament to the diversity of our Viking armory. Guns, relics, and artifacts await discovery, each with its own rhythm and power. The strategic choice of equipment, much like selecting the right weapon for a dungeon delve, adds layers of depth to the gameplay.But what truly sets "BPM" apart is its fusion of music and combat. The soundtrack, like the ancient chants of our skalds, drives your actions with a relentless beat. It's a harmonious blend of rhythm and destruction, much like the battle cries of our forebears in the heat of combat.In conclusion, "BPM: Bullets Per Minute" is a symphony of violence and rhythm, a game that beckons you to embrace the spirit of a Viking adventurer. It's a glorious battle cry, a saga of courage and skill, and a reminder that in the heart of the dungeon, the rhythm of victory beats ever true. Valhalla awaits, my brave companions!

_childDocuments_.review: Initially it's a lot of fun purely because it's a rougelike since you're always going around like "oh new shiny thing, what do you do??" but it overall has been quite enjoyable.This is more of a challenge game than a content game, seeing as how there are only a few designs and styles of maps alongside music. I personally think it could use a little extra design in some rooms beside flat floor or flat floor plus stairs, and slightly more music variation or alterations to allow more versions.The game however does quite great at creating challenges, allowing you to go quite fast not only with speed/item upgrades but also using bunny hopping and momentum. You can choose how on beat you need to be for each action. Not every gun is as strong as each other but every gun can win you the game. And mostly recently they have added more characters that give a nice change and challenge.I would keep playing for completion of challenges or getting a new high score.I would slow down on playing because everything has a similar kind of look which is generally the map color you're on and grey for the guns and items.7/10 for being an above average fps rhythm rougelike. Interesting style but needs more color. Great music but needs more variation/versions.

_childDocuments_.review: Expect a number of reviews to be from Humble Bundle subscribers (like myself) and while I technically only paid a few dollars for this game, I am reflecting on it as it would be a stand alone, ~$22 purchase, and even for that amount this game is half baked. It has an excellent concept of mashing 1st person shooter, rouge-like, and rhyme game but this game feels like its still in alpha testing. Yes, the aesthetic looks neat, at first. But it gets old and makes it plain difficult to see what's going on (make shrines more visible, every forum on this game has a few threads asking for this. The items and guns are not well planned out. Many have extremely cryptic descriptions or even misleading. Look at the two headwear items, Midgard Bracelet and Loki's Bargain. They are described in-game as "Pure Goodness" and "Sacrifice slot for stats". The two items actually do nearly the exact same thing (Bracelet will sometimes give an extra 25HP but is sometimes bugged/inconsistent for an unknown reason) by giving +1 stats up while worn, plus an additional +1 permanently for each floor cleared. The idea of putting in duplicate items, that occupy the same inventory slot, and never giving any explanation to learn how they operate seems like lazy dev work. Worst is the room to room gameplay. Shooting on beat is very fun actually, which makes the rest of the game even more frustrating. There is a main currency of gold coins that are picked up from enemy and chest drops. There are also keys (to use on unlocking more valuable chests and rooms) that are randomly dropped. As far as I can tell, there is no boundaries or ranges of how many coins, keys, or shops appear. This might be anecdotally but in all of my play throughs I was either swimming in a surplus of keys and opening every chest, or I was starved for keys and had to miss 70% of drops off pure RNG. I was able to complete 2 runs and each time it really only felt because I happened to stumble across one of the game-breaking items/guns and its momentum carried me to maxing out all stats and high tier gear. Anytime I got passed that hurdle it was easy mode but the challenge was getting to a spot where I could get a viable build. I never felt I was playing well, it was just that I was blessed with good loot and RNG. If you can manage to score this game for under $3 like a lot of us, then of course expectations would be much different. But for its current state and full price its a no from me, dawg.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing this for a few hours. Great soundtrack, fresh game mashup, and you want to keep coming back. However after a FEW hours the cracks really start to show.The concept delivers but there are not enough mechanics to keep it very interesting for long. Shooting and reloading are the only real rhythm mechanics in the game. So once you get a hang of that all that's left to learn is how to dodge projectiles really. It's unfortunate that it feels like there's so much potential to improve here. After beating the game a couple times you mainly just click on the beat and play a pretty mediocre shooter.There are also some major balance issues. After beating the first 2- 4 levels you may become completely overpowered because of an item or gun you find. After that you walk all over the game, its bosses, and even its end boss. This feels really cheesy, and robs you of any conception that the way to beat this game is to get good at it.This game is a great proof of concept. This genre definitely works and I hope either the devs or another company expand on the concept. I think the next iteration of this type of game will be much better. Still, I'd recommend playing it for the great soundtrack and interesting concept. Just don't expect to be hooked on it if you're looking for something with a bit more substance.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review for those of you with no rhythm.I LOVE the music and appreciate the gameplay, style, and all the elements of it, I see how they should mesh together. I also see that there are some issues that are common in procedurally generated rogue-a-likes, If you are ok with those elsewhere, you won't mind them here. I am not unfamiliar with rhythm games (Guitar Hero, Rock Band, and Crypt of the Necrodancer as examples) but my apparent lack of rhythm makes me suck at this game because it is brutal even on easy, I find myself in a loop of missing beats, failing to load or fire, and then dead by weak enemy. I am frustrated because /I want to be good/ at it to get past the first level and get more content of the game. Practice difficulty helps, but I wish there was a training mode or some UI tweaks to help with the timing of everything.Final Say:I am RECOMMENDING this game even though I lack rhythm because it is FUN, and the music and concept are great. But perhaps SKIP IT if you are REALLY BAD at rhythm games as there is minimal hand holding in the game and it is brutal.Bonus: Having said all of that I HIGHLY recommend getting  the soundtrack, I've been humming the games music and playing it separately.

_childDocuments_.review: if i had to choose a phrase to describe this game, it would be "jack of all trades, master of none".first of all, two things: 1-i've played games and loved games in all the genres that this game wants to cover.2- i've played only 39 minutes of this games, under which i manage to complete the first two levels and unlock my first character.this games does a lot of things, but almost all of them are in direct contradiction of one another. take the shooting for example, on its own is serviceable enough but add the roguelike elements and now you have to be on the enemies faces so they take damage, because bullet range is absurdly low on its own , and you will have to upgrade it over time making the beginning levels feel like a slug. and add on top of that the rhythm elements, now you can only shoot and reload at specific intervals of the song, Which is something that i would normally not complain about since it's the point of the game. BUT there is another problem with the music, all the songs (or at least the 3 first songs) have the same tempo, which makes it extremely easy get the hang of the rhythm, which makes it feel more like a gimmick more thank anything else. The point of a rhythm games is to learn and master songs, once you have mastered the rhythm aspect of this game (which is not hard, heck it took me 30 minutes) it just makes all the other aspects of the games that rely on its feel more tedious, like the shooting. and that's not mentioning the song quality. ( yes the songs themselves are good, but they are very basic in nature and since they all have the same tempo they get repetitive really fast. and of course due to the roguelike elements you are gonna hear them over and over, god i could not stand 30 minutes of the first song).if you take out the rogue like and the shooting out of this game and make another, it would be a decent product, as it stands the rhythm aspect of the game only hinders the game overall. If you plan on keeping it, for the love of god, and more dynamic songs.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has constant frame drops and stuttering which make it near impossible to keep rhythm. If you miss a beat you mess up firing your gun, reloading, and you lose your multiplier. Given it's the whole point of the game, the fact that this issue has nearly no fix I can find is frustrating. My system is more than capable of running the game, so I can't see what else could be causing it other than poor optimization or something.Outside of that, the game's roguelike mechanics seem basic and a little poor. It feels like a case of a neat game idea and concept that they shoved into the roguelike format just so it would sell better or something. The room layouts are boring, there's little item variety or synergy. The enemies on the first couple floors feel like absolute fodder, so easy to deal with, just a chore and slog to go through so you can get to the more interesting floors of the game.And the new guns that you get can just feel way too unwieldy to even bother with. Why should I mess around with an RPG that's tricky as hell to fire and reload, when I could just take the burst assault rifle which arguably does more damage and is easier to manage? It should also be noted that you can only hold ONE GUN at a time. Unless there's an upgrade that lets you hold two? It seems like a huge missed opportunity for gun chaining to be a synergy option the player could consider.The game almost feels trapped by the roguelike element. This would've been far better if it progressed more like DOOM or something similar. If it allowed you to keep an arsenal of weapons that you could switch between, maybe chain together to the beat? That way progression would make more sense, as you progress further and improve you gain a more complex set of weapons that you can freely switch between and use. The game wouldn't have to have stuffy and samey roguelike rooms, it could have rooms specially catered for what the game truly is: a rhythm based FPS game.It's so disappointing honestly, since the game (when it's not stuttering and dropping frames) feels fantastic to  play. I loved firing and reloading to the beat, dashing to the beat, jumping to the beat. But there's just too many things clashing, plus the stuttering issue, that I can't currently recommend it.

The more you know about the enemies, the easier it will be to survive their onslaught and the less restricting the beat will feel. For example, circling the room is a very strong strategy for a lot of enemies, but some enemies will lead their shots, so you have to keep an eye out for those enemy's attacks.The music and visual effects match the environment quite well. Though sometimes the lighting effects can get a little strong with the color filter. I personally used the options to turn down the color filters by about half or so. Made the light reflections a lot more bearable but kept all of the levels' unique color tone.Overall, the game is quite fun. With the newest update, a lot of cool stuff was added. _childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying, I really don't like leaving negative reviews on games, especially when I don't have the playtime to back it up, but I will explain my reason down below.BPM is a really good game, don't get me wrong. I enjoyed my time spent with the game, and it has been a while since I got as excited about a game as I did with this one, which is why I'm so sad about leaving this review. From what I experienced, the game currently has about 10 to 15 hours of playtime if you are looking to 100% it. That's not necessarily bad, but for a rogue-like, it's a little low.The main complaint you will likely see about this game is its insane red saturation and store-bought assets. I don't fault the developers for purchasing assets as I believe it is a small team of two people, and the main explanation I have seen for the saturation has to do with trying to blend the store-bought assets in order for the game to look a bit more normal. I'd recommend turning the saturation down to around 50% so that it will be much more bearable while still keeping everything from looking the complete same.I personally could deal with the reused assets and absolute absurd saturation, but the real reason I returned the game comes from its game play loop. The rhythm shooting in this game is really fun, and I'm surprised nobody has really tried it before. The items and upgrades are all really cool, and you can really feel the difference with each upgrade and the power increase with each new piece of gear. There's enough different items and abilities in the game that you can spec for a lot of different builds that can make different runs interesting, but it feels like there is a right and a wrong choice when deciding between items.When you get to choose between an ability that heals you and one that allows you to mark an enemy for death every so often, you are 99 times out of 100 going to choose the health regen ability. It makes you pretty much invincible and gives no incentive to pick up anything else. It is possible to get builds that make you completely overpowered and pretty much impossible to kill. When you get onto one of these omega god runs, the game becomes really boring, and you just start to wish that the game would end, so you don't have to keep redoing what feels like the same thing for the next 40 minutes.The variety of guns in this game is really cool and you can feel the difference between each and every gun, however it also feels like there are some guns that are a lot better than others regardless of their price (this may just be something I ran into regarding how comfortable I was using each different gun.). Due to the nature of the combo mechanic in the game, it leaves some games completely useless when pursuing a high streak/score. Guns like the mini-gun are incredibly overpowered, but pretty much completely disallow you to get over a 1x combo.Depending on who you are, this game may or may not be for you, however I do not feel that in its current state it has enough content that doesn't feel repetitive to justify buying it at full price. I will definitely be keeping my eye on this game and if the devs continue to provide new content for it, I will change my review and likely buy it again in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing my first successful playthru, I feel qualified to say this game has a great unique gameplay style and gamefeel, but is missing certain layers of polish that are by now expected or necessary in the roguelike/roguelite genre. The act of moving and shooting to the rhythm felt, by itself, very intuitive, expressive, and addictive all at once. While there don't seem to be many options for more musical forms of expression (further note subdivisions, syncopated rhythms, melodic interactions, etc.), the base model that's there provides enough of a flow state that it doesn't need to be modified much, at least in my opinion.Gunplay in the game balances heavily between shooting and reloading, which, while a bit excessive for certain weapon types, felt necessary to counteract the 'on' moments in the flow. As a point of a example, there is an item in the game that gives you unlimited ammo for whichever weapon you're currently wielding; glomming onto this in the few playthrus I found it always yielded grotesque and promising results, and it's probably thanks to this item that I was able to finally finish the game on easy in the first place. The bosses in the game are designed in a 'Dark Souls' fashion, which, while possibly cliche at this point, certainly provides the most promise in terms of player interactivity. Other FPS games have had success with integrating this model--that being the 'boss with several or many different attacks it can do at random, each with its own choreographed response to allow the player to continue without taking damage'. Sometimes you'll have to dodge from side to side to avoid pillars of light. Sometimes you'll just circle-strafe. You might have to jump off the ground to avoid an earthquake... things like that.Now, with all that good stuff said, here is our list of grievances:- Room teleportation. It should be standard in any genre of game that wants you to move between randomly generated areas, *especially* in a first-person game. Gungeon had this figured out forever ago, every sensible roguelike involving a map has done it, this game should do it too. The only *slight* value I could see to backtracking was encouraging players to look through rooms additional times to help them find shrines and/or platforming secrets... but the secrets are always in the same configuration based on the room type, and the shrines shimmer when you get close... why not just have them light up from afar, while you're at it?- Allow players to do something with 'garbage' loot. Nothing feels worse than spending your hard-earned keys or coins on a reward and finding out it's utterly unusable. Some people will say this is 'part of the fun/inherent randomness' of the genre... but again, this has been solved. Dead Cells lets you recyle things you don't want into currency... just do that. - You can't see pick-ups on the map. This could again be argued to be 'part of encouraging players to explore'... but if there are coins in a room, I'd really appreciate you telling me there are coins in a room. Same for keys. Same for health potions. Nothing is more miserable than backtracking through a series of maze-like rooms repeatedly because you can't remember where you think the health potion you didn't need a few seconds ago was. Oh god.- There's no reason not to make information like weapon names available to the player. Even after enough playthroughs that we got to use almost every weapon, I still can barely tell what most of them are from appearance, and that's the only way to identify them in-game.- It isn't directly communicated to the player what the bonuses for 'okay/good/flawless' clears are, if any.- This is most definitely a personally oriented complaint, but flat damage values in an FPS feel wrong to me at this degree. Getting bit by a worm will *always* deal a quarter of your health on easy, which to my mind is a ridiculous portion, A, and B, should have some variable calculated based on where or how the thing bites you. Instead, it's a flat number that gets deducted from your health pool, which, instead of saying '100', could say '4' instead. Even Nuclear Throne is slightly more generous than that, and it's balls-hard.- The platforming felt clunky beyond belief. No momentum or angle adjustment during a jump. No climbing onto or grabbing ledges. Trying to get up a few mushrooms took us upwards of five minutes before we just gave up. Doom & Ultrakill both fixed this to different extents. It felt gross to us, here.- Looking at the game's later unlocks and achievements, I saw at least two "you die in one hit lol" characters, which to my mind is  a gross and lazy type of achievement. It's such an unpleasantly perfectionist experience... and then again, I can see having *one* character or achievement based on this. But two? Going down the Crypt of the Necrodancer route, perhaps...- You can't see from the main menu what a character's ability's do, or what a challenge's requirements. The first time I unlocked the 'Retro Challenge', I clicked on it hoping to be brought to something describing what it was about, not to be loaded into attempting it immediately with no information on what it consisted of. - The level feelings and boss modifiers, while interesting at an outset, are almost entirely negative, and some of them make the stages/boss-fights borderline unplayable. None of them really feel well thought out or fun.- Load times are long. Even on an SSD, later levels can take upwards of a minute to generate.Probably there are more small specific things, but these are the ones that stood out to us during our playthrus. I would say if none of the things that bother us would bother you, this game is still definitely worth checking out just for the flow and gamefeel... but if anything on that list sounds like it would bother you, maybe wait and see if the devs get around to fixing them.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at bottomJust beat it for the first time, and I have full intentions to beat it again. This game definitely has issues but it is just marvelous to play.Rhythm games are pretty popular but I don’t think I have ever seen or heard of anything like this. BPM is a rhythm based FPS roguelike with some of the most satisfying gameplay I've experienced. The idea is that you have rock music playing and you have to fire, reload and dodge to the beat. Killing enemies with this type of shooting is so so so fun.Certain guns have different firing and reloading types, like pistols can fire and reload on half beats, you have to prime shotguns after every shot, etc. I really like the different fire and reload types. One thing that makes the reloading so fun though, is that there are steps to it. Like I said, it depends on what gun you are using but you have to continuously press “R” to the beat to reload to the beat. And it just ends up sounding like, “Bang bang bang tick tock bam boom chik chak bang bang” It’s just so fun. But the gameplay goes hand in hand with the music, because if the music is all over the place then so is your timing and tempo.I can definitely say that's not the case here. The music is consistent in timing and for the most part slaps as well. I've seen people say it's on par with Mick Gordon, It is DEFINITELY not but it's great to shoot to. The only song I really dislike is the one from level one, which you'll end up hearing quite a bit. It's just an annoying song, but the others slap and have a real vibe(purely subjective).Going from audio to visuals, I'm not the biggest fan of how it looks. I don't really know what they were thinking when designing how it would look, but I know what they did. The grabbed the saturation bar, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pulled it so far up that they're PC caught on fire. Thankfully there is a saturation bar in the settings that you can pull down to your preference. Otherwise you'll burn out your retinas with the pure eye rape they force onto you. As for the actual character and gun designs, It's hard to tell from the redness but they never looked so bad to the point where I got distracted, so take what you will from that.Coming back to the gameplay, I have more to say. Shooting to the rhythm and beat is super fun but that's not all. There's also mechanics. You'll have to rummage around the dungeons you crawl, and find little bowls that you put your coins from chests and enemies into. These will upgrade your valkyrie, and with time and hopefully not ♥♥♥♥ RNG, you'll be up to the same power level as the gods you came to kill. To aid you in your battle you also have armor you can get from chests and shops that will buff you. It can seriously vary, you could either get such a massive buff it's almost a free victory or you could get an empty bottle of water, once again, up to the RNG but that's just how roguelikes are I guess. With all that, you also have shops and blacksmiths to get yourself some healables or new guns, and upgrades for such items. Some guns are ass and some are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ OP. Like if you find the grenade launcher there is basically no reason to ever switch off of it. It's just sort of unbalanced is what I'm saying.For my next topic, the enemies. The basic dungeon enemies are fine, some more annoying than others, COUGH flies COUGH, but all are beatable. You have spiders, fLiEs, worms and big demon men I dunno, most of the time you are just killing big insects which may sound weird but I was never really thinking about it while shooting them. The flies are seriously the most annoying, tiny fast projectile spammers that take like 3 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ shots, they have been the reason of my death so many times. Then u got the mini boss fights and real boss fights. The mini boss fights are just dudes you'll come across randomly and they are a real foe to fight so don’t underestimate them, but they are all pretty fun to battle. Then the big bosses. Unlike the mini bosses, you'll know it when walking into their room. At first they are pretty overwhelming, mostly because you don't have good equipment yet, but as time goes on I only found them to get progressively more underwhelming, as I got more powerful. Despite that, I would say they are the most fun fights in the game. Once you kill them they start floating and you just shoot the ♥♥♥♥ out of em while the music follows your bullets, and you get a real satisfying ending to the fights. Just truly epic.TL;DR / VERDICTI really like this game. A blast to play and a blast to listen to. A good amount of replayability comes along with it when you consider the amount of weaponry, abilities, characters and difficulties. Some enemies and weapons are unbalanced but overall it is only fun. Graphically not the best and mechanically it doesn't shine, but the gameplay far more than makes up for it. But this game really just proves that it’s all about the gameplay. If it weren't for the musical aspect I don't know if I would be giving it as positive of a review as I am, but it really is just that good.GameplayIsKing8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a "meh" recommendation button, because it's what I'd give BPM Squared. It's not bad enough to say I wanna give it a bona fide thumbs-down, but it's behind most games that get my unreserved thumbs-up.BBP:PMM was my first experience of games that are technically rhythm games but don't involve much in the way of the arrows or other big body movement to the beat (I don't count Crypt of the Necrodancer, as that is literally played principally with the four cardinal directions, after all). Whether or not it was "the" first, it definitely took some liberties in cramming a metronome (and metal) into a roguelike, only some of which worked out well in the end.For starters, roguelikes, rhythmic or otherwise, are as a genre prone to rollercoaster-grade difficulty curves, based upon the procedural generation of each run. Bullets Per Bullets Minute Per: Minute suffers from this more than even most roguelikes I've played: get low-grade items generated, or not enough coins, and prepare yourself for a short and sad run that only Hobbes could be proud of. Alternatively, get unusually lucky, and cruise through the game largely unimpeded, splattering mythological creatures on the pasted-texture walls right and left, all the while unsure of how you've gotten so far so quickly. What was that level just now? Were you supposed to learn something? Oh well, best make hay while the sun shines!Bippem to the second power also has its characteristic sort of washed-out graphical "aesthetic," which is certainly a bold design choice, but frankly, I hate it. In a game about precision dodging (and even more precision aiming, depending on your weapon), being able to clearly read what enemies are doing and distinguish them from the background is key, so this strange and arbitrary infusion of grainy murk adds needless difficulty without any feeling of payoff (who feels rewarded for successfully squinting?). Certain random level modifiers make it even worse (I'm looking at you, "retro"). I would've been alright with the washout being one such modifier, such that it could only be that  something else, and even then only rarely, but having it as the continual baseline and then subjecting it to worse is just not fun.And while roguelikes are frequently skinny on the storyline (unless they're Hades or Children of Morta, apparently), B2P2M2 has, quite literally, none at all. Why are the Valkyries going on a metal rampage through the realms of Norse mythology? Beats me. I guess the end boss  is a big problem for somebody. Too bad he keeps coming back to life every run. I ultimately have zero investment in which Valkyrie I play, as they say nothing and have no introduction; each simply presents a different set of starting advantages and constraints, a la Binding of Isaac but with no particular flavor (or at least, none which I could tease out; perhaps if I'd read more of the Heroic Eddas I might have a different opinion of them). What's more, with how often you die, you will be hearing the first level theme , and it gets old quite quickly (my stream audience was complaining rather vociferously about this one). I usually turn the music off on roguelikes after a number of runs, due to this very kind of effect, but that is quite literally imprudent (if even possible in a game where  While there is apparently now a custom music mode, which I haven't tried, I wouldn't be able to get much use out of it, streaming as I do, due to copyright issues--unless I wanted to go to the trouble of porting generic, license-free music into the game, I guess. Ultimately, BPM: Bowels Pretty Moving was cast into the spotlight more for being new and different than for being pretty good... or even just being pretty. It's not utterly terrible--there's still plenty to learn and engage and feel dimly accomplished for figuring out--but if you hardly ever get to try out neat combinations if they're not the ones which magically give you a Get Out of Helheim Free card, any such sense tends to be fleeting at best. With the only form of cross-run upgrades being stocking up on banked coins and occasionally being able to afford upgrades to the (surprisingly delightful?) shops, along with unlocking the small number of Valkyries not initially available, you have even less reason to feel like you're getting anywhere with all those deaths.Good thing you're a Valkyrie, I guess. If you live in Valhalla, can you ever really stay dead?

_childDocuments_.review: First I want to say, this game and Crypt of the Necrodancer are two very different things. They are similar at the core but when it boils down to it they play totally differently. Necrodancer is far more strategy orientated, making you think down to your next move while this game is a lot more of "no think just shoot to the beat".I would 100% recommend this game to anyone who like Necrodancer, and would recommend giving it a try. Guns are great and they feel fun to use. If anyone is curious as to how the game works, heres your answer.You have a visual que as to when the beat will hit, you can preform most actions like moving, jumping, and looting off the beat. Dashing (I think), Shooting, and Reloading must all be done on the beat or on a offbeat. It is challenging and you will die A LOT. As you progress you get stronger guns, equipment, and stats. You can also unlock new characters as you progress and reach milestones.TLDR; If you liked Crypt of the Necrodancer and are a fan of shooters buy this game. Be warned it is very difficult.

_childDocuments_.review: All to be honest, this game is pretty exciting in it's own original concept of it.It's a first person shooter mix of Binding of Isaac, Crypt of the NecroDancer and Serious Sam where you must shoot to the rhythm and all your opponents have patterns at which they do their attacks to the rhythm too.There's different characters with different challenges on their own with progression as you defeat the game you unlock new powers.It packs up to 8 bosses, 10 different tracks of up beat to more metal and sinister metal music (it varies through levels), has a fairly to say a nice variety of weapons you can choose from either pistols, shotguns, to SMG's to explosives and a minigun with a skilltree you have you can upgrade with the coins you collect, giving them to a bit hard to notice shrines in the rooms you're at.There's of course the good and the bads, but this game really is that good. It's maybe taste dependent in a way, there's a thing or two you can nitpick - but it doesn't lower the quality of the game unless a crash or two, which happens super rarely to me with a Fatal Error in the middle of the runs to, or a couple of texture glitches (also the bank chest room's wall just bursts flying through me when it opens it's secret room I found it kinda shocking and funny).The game needs balancing cause I feel like it's bosses just die waaay too fast, but that's only when you've either got lucky on the run to get a powerful weapon that it'd obliterate anything in it's path, same with the item combos you can get and do. Even the final boss can apparently be obliterated within 10 seconds, or waay longer.Tbh this game plays on luck and how well you manage your coins, either you can buy bigger health extension or you can buy upgrades, there's also items you can buy which really affects your gameplay of the game, but it's a matter of choice how you want to play this game overall.The good part is that this game is quite challenging on it's own, as you progress there's more sorts of enemies you're gonna be dealing with them, more health and new attacks to deal with, but most deadliest things in this game are - bats and flies. Literally. Not nitpicking this one, I find it slightly funny cause that's very accurate if it's a NecroDancer reference (cause, heck- bats are the worst.)Overall, even when looking past few issues, consider if the game looks good for you in visual standpoint. For me personally I love the aesthetic and hellish feeling and you can toggle the graphics of the game to be maybe more suiting to you.I think this game is worth giving a chance, even if the dev team is very new we can always hope there's gonna be more, cause the concept this game is going for might be very worthwhile to invest time in as popularity grows.Though a note to the devs - you need better customer support, or a discord group to be communicating with your players directly to hear out their thoughts. Also if you attempt at making more content for this game - try making beta testing branches going out first. As you add more content, try getting yourselves out-there with marketing and the hype. Not saying you should, but I'd love to see what you could come up more for this game as it releases to other platforms.

_childDocuments_.review: BPM is one of those games that is personified by a Boss with a glowing target weakspot on his body. The fight is fun, you're enjoying it as much as you can, but you can't help but wonder how better the fight would be if the common convention of the Achilles heel wasn't being used. That's BPM in a nutshell: only the weakness is so big, that some will struggle to enjoy the game even with the other games strengths.The game's unique take on FPS gameplay may just seem like a FPS stacked with a rhythm gimmick on the surface, but there's level of detail underneath. Each gun and how you face enemies changes based on your reloads, your abilities, so much so that you do have to unlearn somme of the basics of 90s FPSes to really take advantage of all the game has to bring you. It's a hard learn curve: you will die several times in the early going, sometimes to what seems like complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but over time you will get better if you have the frustration tolerance high enough to deal with it in the early goings.If you're looking for a balanced experience however, you may not want to look here. There's definitely problems with balance as the game can literally give you everything but what other parts of the game are giving you (like never giving you a single key except for in specific mini-boss fights), and the game's procedural generation will screw you at times. With that said, when you're ridculously overpowered with infinite ammo and a gun that can 3 shot bosses.....you sorta don't care about those other ones.Back to the Achilles heel: which in this game, is the visual presentation. Make no mistake, you can change all you want about the graphical settings here, mess around with the saturation levels per the options menu: nothing will make you happy. While this seems to have come from a limited budget, the problem is that it constantly gets in the way of gameplay. Whether it's enemies blending into the background or being blinded by large flashes of lights, you'll find yourself squinting even in the midst of battle, and wondering if you're missing something. The UI beat in the middle of the screen may be the worst offender, as specific actions to do can become Herculean tasks in the middle of the chaos of battle as you literally can't see what it's trying to tell you. You would think that you would eventually adjust, but even after 15 hours I've had problems and I never got used to it. This is especially troubling for those who have red-green colorblindness, as with the nature of several of the levels, you basically won't be able to play.Sure, the game has other weaknesses, but that one stands out as the one that will stop several people in their tracks.

_childDocuments_.review: I salute every new and fresh idea in video game making and the soundtrack in this game is an absolute blast. But the whole "shoot to the beat" mechanic doesn't work for me at all. It just feels so limiting and cumbersome. And with all the stuff going on around you and the truly insane difficulty - even on "easy" - makes it very hard to get "in the flow". The graphics are very stylized and while the game looks badass in places, it can be very hard to make things out, predict enemy movement or even realize where the upgrade stations are.It doesn't help that this is another overly punishing rogue-like where you lose all your progress as soon as you die. There is almost no meta progression. You can unlock new characters, upgrade the number of items the shops offer or spend money in the bank so that the saved up coins are available for your next run, but that doesn't help with bringing down the difficult enough. It's not motivating.So yeah, not even an hour into this I gave up frustrated. Only try if you have tolerance for high difficulty and like the concept behind punishing rogue-likes. I'd wish we could get over the point where so many neat concepts are bound to some overly hard rogue-like/lite game nowadays, just to stretch the playtime. In my opinion, BPM could have worked much better with actual level- and encounter design in it.

_childDocuments_.review: I clicked "recommended" for this game, but it was with severe reservations.The concept is excellent. I had a good feeling I would enjoy this game just from the description, since I happen to like shooters like Doom 2016 and rhythm games.The first thing I noticed was that there is no tutorial. Things like shooting and reloading on the beats and half beats were fairly easy to grasp, but that's as far as my intuition took me. The various buffs, items, map icons, etc. were left completely up to me to figure out, which made the beginning a bit slow. Not a huge problem, I got it figured out after a while.More importantly, I feel that the devs really missed an opportunity to expand upon the idea of a rhythm shooter to its full potential. As it stands, it seems the only things you can do are click on the beat or half beats. That's it. It would have been cool if you could tap out triplets or something to activate different abilities or attacks. It feels more like a tap tempo function on a metronome than a rhythm game.The biggest issue I had - one that significantly took away from the experience - was the randomized nature of the game. Almost everything relies heavily on randomization. The dungeon's structure changes every time you start over. Different rooms have different combinations of enemies, which, if executed correctly, would be a cool mechanic. However, I sometimes get tossed into rooms chock full of every different enemy, while at other times there's two worms. Two. Seriously? Also, merchants appear at random in each level, which makes it feel as though the merchant I need is never there. The rewards for getting kills are all over the place too, with some runs yielding enough coins to get ridiculously OP guns and full armor, and others only coughing up two coins. Last but not least, there's the level modifiers. Oh boy, those are annoying. At random, each level can have a modifier such as slippery floors, low gravity, exploding enemies, double damage, etc. Make that an option or a consistent feature, not a random requirement. This game really has me perpetually praying to the RNG gods. When I ♥♥♥♥ up in a game, I want to feel as though I did something wrong that I can correct later. The overuse of random mechanics just makes me feel like the game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ me.Otherwise though, the FPS elements are superb. Smooth aiming, satisfying guns, crisp movement.This game is quite enjoyable barring its many flaws. I really, really wanted it to be better.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game, obviously, as I've refunded it.If you go into this expecting something like a Necrodancer + Doom hybrid, you'll be very disappointed.First off: Enemies are so, so, so very bland and uninspired. Besides the bosses (which as far as I've seen are recycled Paragon models btw) the height of normal gameplay is having some sort of insect either shoot or jump at you. It's not very fun and super obvious that these are just bought or open source assets. These assets don't even fit together very well, hence the insufferable amount of native filters that bleed everything together (you can lower those).Secondly and most importantly: It's not really a rhythm game at all. I'd call this "a rhythm game for people who want to feel like they are playing a rhythm game without actually playing one".Let me explain: In Crypt of the Necrodancer the fun and hard part is learning to do everything on-beat. In the beginning you'll have a hard time with that and will often be off-beat, ruining your streak. It won't ruin the game because if you panic and spam some buttons to get out of a pinch, the game lets you do that.Now comes this game: You literally, yes literally, can not be off-beat. If you hit a button with the wrong timing, nothing will happen. You just won't shoot that shot or reload your weapon.This is what makes this game very boring, in my opinion. There's no real learning curve and the rhythm feature feels more like a forced limitation and not something to figure out and get good at on your own.Lastly: Item RNG is completely messed up in this game. Worse than in any rogue-like I've ever played. 80% of the time you'll either get no items at all, making the game super tedious, or you'll find a broken item in every corner, making the game way too easy. A run where progression feels well paced and balanced really is a rarity in this game.I'd really wait before getting this game. Or play < 2 hours and get a refund if you don't like it. Tl:dr This game is a messy combination of bland, bought or open source assets that are bled together using weird shaders and filters.The rythm feature feels like an annoying constraint as it forces you to do everything on beat and just ignores every other input. There's really nothing to get good at and the gameplay flow suffers noticeably.Item RNG is messed up beyond belief. If you want a real rhythm game, get something else.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to go ahead and say that I had a good amount of fun playing this game. I like rhythm and I like shooters, but this is far from the rhythm shooter experience I'd imagined. Game's got some interesting mechanics like shooting to the beat and such, but it's a somewhat surface-level mechanic that isn't very well expanded upon. I find that audio queues would be a necessary addition to the game, as well as a revision to the way the combat should feel (). Granted, I haven't played a tremendous amount of the game so you could argue that I haven't gotten into the groove of things yet, but I find that rhythm games, at their core, should capitalize heavily on the way games , and I haven't gotten much feeling out of the game.BPM has an interesting approach for its visual style. Very Doom-esque architecture, though I'm told much of the game's assets are simple general-use Unreal readymades. The color saturation is an interesting approach which looks nice on trailers but makes everything blend into an incoherent mess at times when actually playing. Certain aspects of the game make me feel like I'm playing two college kids' final project as opposed to the product of true game developer.Overall, the game shows fair promise but definitely needs continued developer involvement for me to call it even a half-realized game. I might be more lenient on the game if it was marketed as Early Access (which I would still urge the developers to do, if possible), but as it stands, I'd recommend to others like me who seek a good rhythm shooter to simply keep looking.

_childDocuments_.review: BPM is an odd combination of fps, rhythm game and rogue like that works incredibly well and gives a fun and fast paced experience for a good price. Once you are able to get into the rhythm the game sets it gives an incredible rush when you're able to bob and weave between enemy fire while taking down all the enemies that you face, all while listening to a great soundtrack that you help enhance with the sound coming from the combat. While the game is great fun it isn't without its flaws. The biggest are the visuals, and somewhat the content available. The look of the game is brought down heavily by the amount of saturation that hangs heavy on every facet of the game from the environments to the enemies. It leads to issues of being able to determine where enemies are located sometimes during the chaos of combat, which can lead to some cheap and annoying deaths. The other issue, the content is not where near as egregious as the visuals, however there is not as much content as I would like. While every weapon and item is fun to discover and mess with there aren't a huge number of them which leads to runs feeling somewhat similar after playing for a while. Along with that the items don't really lend themselves to creating builds but rather getting items to simply make yourself more powerful, which leads back to the issue of runs feeling similar after playing a few. This is alleviated somewhat by the different playable characters but that can only do so much. Overall, while all of the game's content can be seen pretty quickly, it is still and incredibly fun experience that I feel is worth the price

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of this game is interesting. An FPS where you have to fire, reload, and dodge to the beat of the music. The gameplay is solid and the devs have executed the idea extremely well. This game has a pretty cool art-style as well, but the monochromatic color scheme completely ruins the entire experience for me. Due to the fast paced nature of this game, you'll be spending a lot of time zipping around as you attempt to dodge incoming projectiles and jumping enemies. Unfortunately, the moving mechanics along with the color scheme causes EVERYTHING to become a coagulated, uniform mess. Enemies, incoming projectiles, useful items, platforms, and even the UI gets lost. It's impossible to read. You can change the color scheme, but that honestly doesn't help at all. It's an interesting and fun concept that is ruined by an aesthetic choice that does nothing to enhance the experience in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not tone-deaf by any means and I've played other rhythm games, but after struggling for +60 minutes, I find it difficult to discern what the game considers the beat of any given track. _childDocuments_.review: I only played enough to beat 1 whole run on easy (default) difficulty. Don't treat this as a full review as I haven't played enough of it yet.It's a gimmick-game, but it works. Frankly problems I have with it are unrelated to the rhythm mechanic.It's an easy recommendation, because even if you end up hating it - you'll figure it out quick. That way you can always try and refund if it doesn't play to your tune.BPM is best described as a Crypt of The Necrodancer, but first person shooter.Attacking, reloading and using abilities are all done to the beat of the song. You fight and explore randomly generated sets of rooms. Each level ends with a boss, each room usually rewards you in some way with keys or coins. Those can be used to upgrade your character through various ways, like stat increasing shrines or shops with weapons and items.You have 1 weapon, which you can replace if you find a new one. Weapons reload in a different manner. A pistol requires 2 reload button presses - one to eject and the other to insert a new magazine - all done to the beat. A revolver requires 1 reload press to open it, then each successive reload will put a round in the chamber until it's full. Some weapons need to be reloaded after each shot. There's decent variety to the guns and abilities, but the game doesn;t seem to be loaded with content.It's a tried and tested roguelike-like formula popularized by games like Binding of Isaac. There aren't many interactions between items, BPM is mostly dependant on your skill, not items.Flawless-clearing (never missing a beat and not getting hit) a difficult room feels good. You can understand how the game works and dunk on bosses or enemies that gave you trouble early on.Not a fan of this monochrome stylized graphics.I may be wrong, but during my first 2h I've seen same items and weapons appear multiple times. I didn't play enough to be sure about this, but this doesn't seem to be a very big game. My first finished run timed at 1h, and I needed 2h total to get a run good enough to do it. There are characters and starting abilities that you can unlock by finishing runs or completing other objectives, so I may change my mind on this later.You may have noticed that I didn't say anything about the soundtrack in pros/cons, but that's beacause the music is... ok. It's not great, not bad. It works for the game, but isn't something I would listen to outside of it, even though I like the genre.I like BPM, but it's something you need to try for yourself. I don't feel comfortable recommending it blindly.I won't give it a score yet, because this isn't a full review. I will update once I play a bunch more of it. I still wanted to get this review out since it's a sales season.

_childDocuments_.review: IT'S EXTREMELY GOODThat's it, that's the reviewwhat else do you want from meAlright, alright, fine, I'll talk about itLet me start by saying this: This game has a few quirks. Lemme list it off:Enemies: They always feel like they were simply scattered into the room with no thought put into placement or "enemy combinations" (you know, which enemies to appear alongside which enemies in which positions). Most of the ai is very simple. Some of them use the rhytmn mechanics of the game and those are REALLY COOL, but most of them don't.Mechanics: A LITTLE HARD TO GRASP AT FIRST GRANTED, but once you get the hang of it? There is nothing in the world more satisfying than reloading, dodging and jumping to avoid specific attacks to the beat. Each attack that uses the rhytmn mechanics is always marked on your "rhytmn counter" thing. If you need to dodge a specific way for the rhytmn, a special note will come from the side, if you need to jump to the rhytmn, an upwards note will come. It's very simple once you get a grasp of it! Although it is hard to understand since the game REALLY DOESN'T EXPLAIN A LOT. You basically need to figure things out about it on your own.Levels: THEY FEEL BLAND HONESTLY. Some of them can be cool! But after a while the rooms really start to feel repetitive and "samey". Some of them have a few platforming challenges and interesting tidbits, but most of them are really just "big open space with enemies"Graphics: THE STYLE FEELS COOL HONESTLY. After some time in I started becoming not a huge fan of the graphics and started wishing they were better or more stylistic than just "bright color" but it's not a huge deal for me. The overall vibe almost feels like an early PS2 game honestly!Boss fights: BY FAR THE EASIEST PART OF THIS GAME. Most of them are really easy and quick to get through honestly, it's just getting there that's an issue. There are some things that are odd, certain boss attacks that are really weird and hard to grasp since again, the game doesn't tell you much about itself or it's mechanics and you just need to throw yourself at that wall in different ways until it cracks, but that's really my only gripe with them.Music: YES. WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ DO YOU WANT ME TO SAY, JUST LISTEN TO IT, IT'S SO GOOD. I just wish there was a system like in crypt of the necrodancer where you can import your own songs into the game since after a while they start to become repetitive as, well, there's only 12 tracks in the entire game.Roguelike elements: This is... hard to explain, but by far the worst point of this game. If this game wasn't a roguelike it would be perfect. But it chooses to be a roguelike and that... that's not a thing it succeds in very well. The items are very basic, most of them not being exactly creative. The weapons feel satisfying, yes, but they're all generic, you know? There's nothing creative like "a rocket launcher that fires sharks" or "a bow that fires laser arrows", no, they're all just generic guns. They feel satisfying! more satisfying than in any shooter game I've ever played! But it's nothing to write home about by roguelike standards. And the items that buff you and the overall systems of the game... Even for a roguelike they're luck dependant. What I will give to it is that, this is a game that you can very much get through even with bad luck if you're symply good enough at it's mechanics since that's the main focus of it, but the roguelike elements themselves are very... "scattered", if that makes sense. Dungeon design is simplistic, most items don't really do anything creative, you can carry very little at a time, increasing your stats is entirely dependant on luck, there's things in it that just feel straight up not worth it since the game barely gives you most resources, especially if you're not lucky... There's this one thing in the game where you can throw either your coins or keys into it dependant on which version of it you get, but all it does is give you a stat up. For multiple coins/keys. To put this into perspective, there's another thing in the game that does the exact same thing, for simply 1(one) coin. And these are both just found scattered randomly across rooms and usually hard to spot thanks to the graphics.This is a reeeeaalllly good game, but god, if it wasn't a roguelike it would be so much better. And I like roguelike games! I've played Hades, Binding of Isaac, Wizard of Legend, Risk of rain 1 and 2, Scourgebringer, Gungeon, Necrodancer, Gunfire Reborn, Dead cells, Loop Hero, Dicey Dungeons, you get the gist of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a short explanation and exercise to help you decide if you're going to enjoy this game.  Try it out.The Music:  Look up the song "The Rhythm King" off BPM's soundtrack and give it a listen.  You will hear the rhythm of the beat for the first ten seconds and then the beat and off-beat afterward.  Depending on your weapon, you'll want to focus on one or the other.Weapon Mechanics:  The shotgun pistol is an early weapon that holds four shots and has a three-step reload.  It can be fired and reloaded on the offbeat.  What this means is that you fire the weapon four times then press reload three times on both the beat and off-beat of the song.  There is no delay between reloading and firing beyond losing the rhythm.The Exercise:  Now listen to the song and tap your mouse and keyboard to the beat and off-beat: M1, M1, M1, M1, R, R, R.  Repeat without missing a beat and that's basically the gunplay in this game.  Do this for the first minute of the song and that's basically the gunplay in this game.  Now, when the song picks up, imagine 12 flies zipping around a room shooting fireballs at you and that you'll die if you stop moving for a single beat.  Congratulations, you're probably already stressed out and that's basically the game itself.Tips:  1. Don't rush to unlock the extra characters - somehow powerful skills but they tend to just make the game even harder.  Hildr is my current unlocked favorite, she starts with the shotty pistol and a key but has lower HP.  2. The boss and mini-boss always drop a key unless a level modifier prevents it, so you always get two keys per stage.  3. A 'secret' stage exit can spawn only on the first stage of the game, it'll be a set of stairs.  ALWAYS take it if you want to be OP.  4. If you're having trouble finding the rhythm, pause the game and just listen to the song.  It's much easier to do when stuff isn't trying to kill you.  5. Save your money and check the shops before you spend, missing out on infinite ammo because you spent your coins on subjectively bad weapon upgrade really sucks.Verdict:  I've played 23.5 hours and beaten the game 6 times.  I've died  ~20 times between each win.  On easy.  I love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: BPM: Bullets Per Minute is a rhythm-shooter game. _childDocuments_.review: BPM borrows heavily from Binding of Isaac. So much so that BPM isn't just inspired by it, but directly copies many of its mechanical elements including weapons, modifiers, rooms, and enemy types. It does feel like the devs initially thought "hey, what if Isaac had a rhythm mechanic," as a starting point. If you're like me, that combination seems fantastic on paper. But BPM has it's share of issues. The main problem I had is with it's art direction affecting gameplay. Everything shares the same limited color palette in BPM; the walls, the floor, the enemies, projectiles, etc. This creates an effect where all the elements in a dungeon blend together, making it difficult to see enemies telegraphing their attacks, or projectiles coming at you. The projectiles issue might not matter if the game had a top-down perspective, but this is an FPS. Often times you'll get hit by attacks that seem to come out of nowhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not entirely sure where comparisons to doom come from when it comes to this game. Maybe the vaguely similar music, or slightly hellish environments but in the end I think it has more in common with games like Paranautical Activity and Tower of Guns than with Doom. You go in to a boxy room, you shoot some enemies. you get a small amount of loot repeat. Simple formula, and it's not...terribly? Executed? It's just a bit stale, lukewarm, middling. As it stands the mechanics that allow you to grow more powerful in a run feel incredibly halfbaked, sure there's your usual 'get more health' 'more damage' 'move faster' 'more ammo' but thats also all your options. It's not other roguelites where you might get a crazy combination of items and effect that synergize perfectly and cleanse entire continents of their living and unliving populations. It's mostly a shooter where eventually you can shoot more and your bullets hit a bit harder.The gimmick itself, shooting on time with the rhythm, is well executed, feels good to do, and is mostly well feedbacked. Some weapons have some dodgy sound design here and there, the lever action rifles reload, the railgun things reload. Where it's hard to tell by sound if you're in time but most of the weapons work quite well. The main limiter I find is just how basic the implementation of the mechanic is, once you have the rhythm down you've solved the whole game. It doesn't change level to level, you're always firing to the same beat, just different music. I think it's a missed opportunity to have interesting or unique beats that might allow you to fire in quick short bursts with longer lulls between them. Or other extensions of the system, rewards for perfect timing, a less obtrusive reticle, etc.There's also of course, the Paragon assets. It's been said plenty of times but it's worth repeating. The theming of this game is just really really basic. A supposedly norse theme with enemies that look more like aliens really clashes. Bugs, bats, scorpions? Obviously creating assets is difficult, but stronger theming and presentation would go a long way. Stages are mostly just basic boxy rooms with pillars strewn about, save for helheim itself with is more like a dark cave. More varied environments would be great honestly. I dunno what else to really say about it. It's a great gimmick wrapped up in bland presentation, ill fitting assets, half-baked upgrade mechanics, mostly okay music and weapon sound design and little else of substance. No enemy sound effects really, no voice quips or vocalisations, no narration. It's just empty quiet gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, awesome music. Once you pick up the rhythm, playing to the beat isn't difficult. Really feels good having playing an arena shooter type game with a badass soundtrack to go along. Further enhanced when every shot, dash, and reload further bangs, clicks, and dings along with the beat.Downsides to the game. For a rougelike it's not difficult. Enemies 90% of enemies don't shoot at where you're going, but where you are currently. So strafing basically avoids everything. The boss fights aren't too hard either and if you can get a better gun and some upgrades, most enemies die in a 1 - 2 shots.Overall fun game would recommend for music and feeling epic when run n' gunnin, it's good for a few hours. If you're looking for a challenging rougelike, You'll get over the challenge in about 2 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: BPM: BULLETS PER MINUTE

_childDocuments_.review: This game might not have tons of depth, and I guess that later bosses could be more inspired, but..Oh, it's so much fun. So much fun. The core loop of the game is executed perfectly, and that alone makes the game insanely satisfying and addicting. And the soundtrack? Maybe it's not Mick Gordon, but it's still brilliant. I don't mind turning game on just to "check settings" purely cause of how great the menu music is - and that goes for all of the game, really, but the menu music (also present in level 5 and in official trailer) is definitely my favourite.I just HAVE to recommend.Update post Metal Hellsinger release: so, Metal Hellsinger is a fine game, and has really amazing soundtrack, but... BPM is just a better rhythm shooter. Audiovisual feedback is just much greater, and rhythm mechanics actually dictate more than just shooting.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun concept with some good music dragged down by bad enemy design, inconsistent rewards, and some frustrating mechanics.The rewards for a "Flawless Room" vs "Okay Room" vs "Room Clear" did not feel consistent. Sometimes I got a single coin for a flawless clear, sometimes I got a key, other times I got a bag of coins - it just didn't make much sense. Also, a flawless clear with a room of 4 1-shot enemies feels like the same level of reward for a flawless clear on a room with 10 enemies and that's just bad. Landing 4 shots perfectly on beat is pretty easy, landing enough shots to kill 10 varied enemies is much harder and should be rewarded as such.The first boss had an attack you're supposed to dodge that just never felt consistent. It felt like it came out too fast and that the timing of the dodge just wasn't clear or telegraphed particularly well. I ended up stacking health and shields to get past him.In the end, I uninstalled after running into two different types of enemies that explode into tiny little flies that you have to shoot individually. I was OK dealing with one of those but the flies take more than one hit to kill with the default pistol and they're tiny little things that are just a pain. I was generally enjoying my time until that point but playing any more just doesn't feel worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely wonderful game in my opinion. Came out of nowhere and I just love everything about it. BPM : Bullets Per Minute is an FPS Rhythm game. Basically what that means is there is a beat in the background and you can only shoot, reload, jump in sync with the beat. If you are out of sync the gun won't fire. Without this the game would not feel this special at all. I only play this game on the hardest difficulty as that is where the true fun and point of the game is.Pros+ Great music.+ Lots of variety in your Valkyries, Guns and levels.+ Levels are procedural so every run in different and fun.+ On hard difficulty it is suitably challenging making it very rewarding to play.+ Good movement of your character - jumping, double jumping, dashing , bunny hopping etc.Cons- Over-saturated  visuals (This was a deliberate choice as game is made by a small team and they used assets from various sources so using this look blends things nicely. You can also tweak the settings a bit).- Easier difficulties are a bit too easy (I know weird complaint but if you were to play the game on easy you would miss the entire point of the game. This is meant to be played on hard).As stated previously I am a huge fan of this game. Every now and then I get an urge to play this game. I play for a few hours and then move on and come back again some time later. There are plenty of guns available in your runs, different Valkyries with different play-styles, random dungeons that change every-time sometimes resulting in truly funny and bizarre ones.This is a small indie game that is on decent sales frequently. They have even added the option to add your own custom music. Haven't tried it but I can imagine it adding more enjoyment even though I think the original music is fantastic.Sample Gameplay :

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend it in it's current state. It's a load of fun if you're in the right mindset, but the reward balance is terrible. Sometimes you clear a room of a dozen enemies and get 1 or 2 coins, sometimes you kill 3 dudes and get 3 coins. Little things like this. The RNG is just outrageously out of control, and this is coming from a Roguelike vet. The saturation effect that everyone is complaining about isn't terrible visually if you turn it down, but it makes boss attacks extremely difficult to read when they are the same seizure-inducing shade of neon. Overall, it's a great idea but in it's current state it's like they ran out of steam or money before they crossed the finish line.
_childDocuments_.name: BPM: BULLETS PER MINUTE

_childDocuments_.review: A solid example of a fresh twist on a classic genre. BPM: Bullets Per Minute is a great FPS rhythmic shooter packed within a  roguelike framework. While the roguelike aspect of the game isn't as robust as it could be, its satisfying core rhythm mechanic, catchy rock-opera soundtrack, and percussive sound design helps make up for it. Overall, 9/10. It's a great experience that trailers alone can't fully convey. If you have the cash to spend and want to try it out, go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: BPM: BULLETS PER MINUTE

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the take on two very different game genres made into one game. The shooter part of the game was pretty solid and actually got much easier the longer i played due to having more variety at the shops and getting used to the mechanics of the game. The rhythm part of the game was quite fun and wasn't too hard to keep the rhythm of the songs. Just don't panic or you'll start hitting off beat a lot and may ruin some combos you've got going. I do like that there is the option to play without the rhythm portion and just play it as a shooter.The only issues i had with the game were when playing with the last character Odr, i would get caught up on the ground as though there was a wall in the way. Never really ran into the issue with any of the other characters, though if i did ever have that issue it usually didn't result in an instant game over due to being able to take more than 1 hit.I thought the art style would make things kinda hard to see, and at the start it did, but I got used to it. The designs for the enemies and bosses were really nice. They were easy enough to tell what kind of enemy they were and their attacks were pretty easy to read, but much harder to avoid when you've got 10 monsters in a small room. I also really liked the shop NPCs. The NPCs at the bank, not so much.Great shooter with a nice little music game gimmick.
