_childDocuments_.review: After finishing my first play through of Disciples: Liberation, I'm rewriting my review with a complete view of the game (outside of Liberation mode which I'm still working on completing). As with my previous review, this comes from a fan who originally played Disciples: Sacred Lands, and every installment in some capacity since. To begin, the reason why I'm not recommending this game is because of how it handles the lore of the previous games and just completely retcons roughly 85% - 90% of the original pre-established lore. Whenever it does reference certain characters from the lore - Bernard of Cahuzak (the first boss of Disciples: Sacred Lands), for example, is no longer a renegade noble trying to break free from the empire. He's one of the Kings of the Hale. Hubert De Layle is no longer a power-hungry despot seeking to sell his soul to the Legions of the Damned for power to consume the Empire, but rather an altruistic man who wished greatness for his people. As a turn-based strategy game, I believe the combat is geared more towards a modern audience - and to that effect, with how certain units synergize, I'd recommend this game to people with no knowledge of Disciples lore, or general fans of TBS style games. From a writing standpoint, I believe this game is lacking and as a semi-professional writer myself I believe the writers tackled so much during development that they wanted to bring across, that everything fell apart. Certain character actions aren't logical, and in most cases don't make sense given their perceived loyalties or motives. I feel as if this game was given more time for development, and certain portions were packaged into DLC content for further storyboarding, that this game would've been significantly more immersive and enjoyable. However, the game we got is what I generally regard as a bit of a hot mess - the aforementioned writing feeling rushed and sloppy, each character feeling like a way to progress Avyanna's story, instead of being standalone characters with their own personalities past a certain point. What good writing and plot points there are simply fall apart due to the over-saturation of romantic/sexual themes which at certain points may leave the player going, "Really, is this actually an appropriate time for this?" I understand that the game was marketed as, "Mature, Dark Fantasy" however, it's better to let the game speak for itself instead of trying to lump several tags to appeal to as wide of an audience as possible. As I mentioned above though, the game play is typically where this game shines, but it took the parts of Disciples III, which the audience generally hated, and improved on the combat instead of taking a step back to previous Disciples titles that used more of a stationary grid style of combat. The combat though, from a thematic sense in regards to previous titles, may irritate fans of the series, as the game's general plot involves attempting to unify all factions under a single banner - that of the protagonist Avyanna. Why this doesn't work is because of how historically each of the five (now four due to them writing the Mountain Clans and Wotan as canonically extinct and dead) races have been at war on a theological level. The Humans, and Elves - prior to Disciples 2, being historic allies, and the Undead Hordes and the Legions of the Damned being dubious allies once motives aligned (Not to mention how the Greenskins and Merfolk are now suddenly extinct too...). Better yet though, to unite the races - during the game's events - Avyanna slays the physical manifestation of Mortis, the god of death, herself - as well as destroying Gallean's Beast avatar due to her "incredible" power of being a nephilim, an Angel/Demon hybrid race. I believe this game would've been better served as an ode to the classic series; that being several self-contained stories that intersect at certain points of the various factions as they fight for their place upon Nevendaar. However, what fans of a long-awaited sequel got was a Mary Sue, powered by the sexual lust of a Tumblr erotica writer, with limitless godslaying capability taking control various points of limitless power to subjugate the world under a single banner with the tool to even subjugate gods should those that survived managed to get out of line. As a disclaimer, I did enjoy the game - I think the gameplay is great, but it would've been better served to have taken a different name and lore to become something that can stand on its own, instead of crawling into the corpse of a dead franchise and bastardize everything that it previously had going for it story wise. If anything, what this game does with story, is take a little of everything that happened previously in the story, and mash them all up with each taking on aspects of an alternative universe that just don't make sense with the previous storylines. TL;DR: The game play is pretty fluid. The story is lackluster, and is more like a sex-fueled alternative universe with how most everything contradicts previous story arcs and elements. I'd recommend it if you're not familiar with the previous Disciples games, but would recommend others stay away if you were previously invested in the other installments as this will not be the game you're looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, since I see so many friends are interested in this game, I better write down a serious review about what's the problem I have with this one, and why I do not recommend this game.BriefThe sole reason why this game received a 'not recommended' is the bug commonly we called it 'conversation loop' which hasn't been fixed yet, it triggers very often when you have a chat with an NPC or campaign story itself in the game, when it happens, NPC just repeats its last line and the game won't progress. I've forced to click many times to get pass them, later, some serious game breaking bugs triggered after, resulting me being locked to a story stage and never be able to progress. I've submitted a ticket to the developers in the past, but never have a reply whether they fix the bug or not, I couldn't waited that long so I replayed the entire chapter to dodge this particular game-breaking bug that later I found the solution is: every time the conversation loop bugs trigger, I have to quit the game immediately and restart it, the bug won't be there again. By doing so, there isn't any after effects that would seriously break the game for worse, I was able to play up to this point by using this alternative method. The problem is: this bug is too frequently to be seen, there are about 13 maps for the campaign, each map I've bumped into this bug at least 4 times, sometimes a lot more. Its unforgiving and utterly affects the overall game experience in a very low way. AND IT HASN'T BEEN FIX YET since 6 month and more time of its release.The Reputation of FactionsLet me put this issue aside, and literally talk about the game itself. Disciples Liberation is unlike any other disciple games. In my opinion, its more like an RPG rather its traditional turn based on strategy game, because outside combats, there is no turns limits, you are free to explore the map as you like. Also, not like the previous games, you are not playing one faction alone in a campaign any more. Instead, you can build an army with variety of creatures from different factions based on your relations and reputations with them. You build reputations by making different choices through the story and side missions, and taking sides with your favourite faction to improve your relationship with it. When it’s improved into a certain level, you gain access of hiring higher elite creatures of each faction.I like the new system, but there are also problems. The one I want to point out is, the choices sometimes can not be so obvious, developers should have put a symbol to indicate which choices led to which faction's favor, like Star Wars Old Republic has done. Because lots of talks trigger after an combat immediately, there is no option to save or auto saved, so, taking an example, I want to gain reputation with the Legions of the Damned, but after some confusing choices, I ended up get it reduced. Then I would have no choice but to replay the entire battle again, get the game to trigger these choices again and figure out the right one, which I wanted was to improve the relationship with the Legions of  the Damned. Annoying, isn't it? Personally, I also don't like the choices sometimes can be contradictory. They've got moral problems with me. For example, I'd really like to taking sides with Undead Horde, then I found some quests they're killing innocent people, I couldn't allow myself to do that in order to side with necromancers, it would make me feel really bad, trust me, even in a game, no way I'll do that. So, in the end, I had to give up my original plan allying with the dead. I ended up steeled my relationship with the Empire. However, you can see the contradiction I meant here, can't you?Battle and the DifficultiesThere are also problems with the combat balance I'd like to specifically mention here. I will split them into 2 parts, The hero. And her companions, army creatures. Since its more like a RPG game, our protagonist Avyanna has different skill trees and classes. Different classes will have different access to some certain skills. The problem is: in the later game, when all skills are fully opening, you are free to build any class as you wish, the magic class are way too OP than melee classes, the balance is one-sided, which unfortunately I don't really believe anyone would choose a melee class over a magic class. Magic class like Seer for example got teleporting to any locations on its reach which means traps on battle field would affects it no more(melee classes all have to walk, any tangles and traps in a hex can slow them down). while it has the ability to do mass healing and still being able to learn magic that can do powerful healings. A melee class like Warlord for example, doesn't' have a huge gap of HP than Seer while with limit amount of mana, it can only heal itself and the army by learning magic. And Warlord needs more skill points on its class specific, mostly combat skill related, which means less points on nephilim skill tress, so skill like in incorporeal and higher chance of evasion would be difficult to learn in an early stage, while magic class like Seer gets teleport to locations freely and heal the ally units around her while damaging the enemies with a single or two passive skills. This is significant different when you play higher difficulties like hard or brutal. Because the enemies hit everybody very hard, survive in battle within a turn can be crucial to lead a victory. Honestly, it isn't a place for a melee class to walk around, while easily getting hit, with few healing tricks. less support skills for its allies. I think the developer should have looked into the class balance much careful, it could be a different story.Units and the companions. It's the same thing. In a difficulty like hard for example, generally range units & companions are much better than melee units. Not only because enemies hitting a lot harder than your units can do, but also there are variety magic, creatures' abilities  etc. could make a melee units can't attack anyone. For example, immobilize. Also, some creatures's attack leaves traps on hexes, that by walking on them, melee units will take damage. There are also units has thorn ability which will reflect some damage to its attackers while melee. So range units have mess advantages on several situations across the battle field on hard or brute difficulties, I found myself have only one melee units in my army while battling Hard, which I believe drastically reducing the fun part of building different units to test different strategy when playing the game on these difficulties.OverallAll in all, these are all minion flaws and will not cover the facts is- Disciples: Liberation is still the best Disciples game so far which none of the past titles can compare. I've played all disciples games, this is the thing I can safely guarantee. I also think they've done a great job generally regarding to the gameplay part.These small flaws would not led me to a recommend, if not for this serious conversation loop bug. I am not saying a game should be 'bug free' which is likely impossible, but for such a gameplay reducer still out there not being fixed yet, I'm afraid there is no way I'd agree this is also should be OK.Though I do understand bugs can be specifically a rig thing. It happens to me, might not for you. I'd still advise either waiting for a low price meanwhile waited developers to fix the game hopefully for safety or buy it, play under 2 hours condition, see if it triggers to you or not, then decide whether to keep the game or not. Choices are always yours

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game from the steam sale and review is belowCost: I would not buy this at full price and I would wait for it to go on saleThe game play overall is very traditional hex based combat, but it does get a bit boring after a while. There are a limited number of units and the greatest diversity comes from the spellbook abilities rather than type of units. Where there may be 5 (or 4) different types of units you can buy from each race, there is at least 10-30 different spells for 4 different spell groups. There is an "auto battle" feature which lets you skip a great deal of battles, but it's use definately needs an expansion.  There is also some issues with unit levels and areas that match your characters level and etc that can cause issues. There isn't really a "pre-set" path the game will warn you of which can make things difficult.One feature I love is the fact that you can steal companions or enemies and recruit them to your side. The downside to this, is that you are limited in your ability to outfit these special or named units and they often are very similar statwise to other units. If there was a way to buff their power or make them seem more important than it would be fun trying to collect them or feel like a legitimate loss.The added launcher and inability to skip the logo is strange for a modern game as well. There is a "kingdom management" feature but it's painfully limited. rather you build just two buildings and upgrade them with resources gained over time. Overall it's a fun game I would recommend to someone who enjoys a hex based repetitive combat game and not lore. The disciples world seems like it would be fascinating if it had a greater expansion it it.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting blend of genres such as Heroes of Might and Magic, King's bounty and early 2000 2.5D RPGs but not at full price... there is way too much fights which are unavoidable and animations are way too slow to my liking even though you can speed up the game to 300%, the game also drain the steam deck battery likes crazy but it works fine. Difficulty is alright.I love the background of disciples which is mature dark fantasy type, it has beautiful sceneries akin to what you can find in HoMM 3 but in full 3D, fun races, fun mature dialogs with choices (a bit dumb sometimes but still okay), the game has a good vibe with good turn-based combats. The blending of genre really shine here and i think it is good althought not perfect.Maps are small but there is many fights here and there that makes you feel maps are bigger. If you enjoy the fights then it is alright but it is very repetitive after a while.The game has a RPG vibe with an alright feeling of exploration, the story is long, pretty much likes if you played a single hero in Heroes of Might and Magic on a single big scenario albeit a bit more simplified (without the map strategy level), you level up, add points to a three branch skills tree, equip stuff with various degrees of rarity, upgrade stuff, discover other heroes, manage a city, upgrade buildings with resources to unlock more units and train them, find scrolls so that you can get more magics, you can even trade resources, equipments and units. You can go back to your city almost anytime if you are on the map.There is some annoying bugs on the inventory UI and i also had a blocked turn bug (which freezed a fight) but overall it works ok on the steamdeck, just draining the battery likes crazy. There is some amount of backtracking where you unlock skills for your characters that are useful to unlock stuff on earlier maps.So yes i enjoyed this slightly "innovative" game although it gets very repetitive after a while (it is just fights, a bit of exploration and some events / choices here and there), slow fights doesn't help, it is still alright to discover the cool maps, gain power and equipments and continue the story since there is many choices on events which will determine your allies and stuff.Great at low price (let's say ~20$ ?) and if you have time ahead!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm leaving a negative review for now simply because the developers think it's a great idea to put up an annoying 'leave your review here' message every single time I login to the game. Furthermore, even after leaving this review the message continues to show.Edit: I decided to leave a positive review after finishing the game but hopefully the dev team will review my feedback.Summary: If you're a big fan of turn-based tactical combat games like Heroes of Might & Magic then you'll probably get your money's worth out of this game. There are many different spells, abilities, factions, units, companions, gear, and story choices to make. It entertained me for 100+ hours.Pros* I like the frontline / backline mechanics of the game and how you can configure your squad to meet the different challenges the game has to offer* The tactical combat is well done - the animations, the power ups, the different map layouts, etc.* The music that they implemented is good, and thematic based on the enemy faction you're fighting, but I just wish there was more of variety.* There are four factions with lots of companions, special units, and normal units to work with* There are four classes you can take, which adds some replayability. However, they all boil down to either a fighter/mage class and a pure mage class.* You can easily update your class and skill points as you progress through the game* Decent story - enough to keep me interested while I play* The game was very stable for me - no crash to desktops or game breaking bugs.* The "Liberation Mode" for the second playthrough is pretty interestingCons* The AI is highly predictable and lacks optimization [e.g. enemies with AOE buffs will always use it before moving regardless of who's around them]. AI sometimes doesn't know what to do [e.g. if they're blocked by obstacles on the bottom of the map they won't go around them]* The reputation impact for many choices makes little to no sense at times. Because of this, it's difficult to get more than one faction to a 'revered' status in your first playthrough. You often have to save scum just to figure out the reputation impacts because they're so illogical.* There's a lot of busy work in this game [e.g. back and forth with quests, can't upgrade all your units or equipment simultaneously, merging shards, phasing buildings in and out, etc.]* There aren't enough building slots in your city - at least two more slots should be added to prevent phasing in and out nonsense. At least let the player buy new slots or something.* There's not nearly enough battles that allow you to "conquer" or bypass them. This leads to a lot of boring combats that you have to slog through.* There aren't any maps for indoor zones* You can't trade resources for gold, which is sometimes a bottleneck, depending on how you play* Not enough quick / auto saves [should be able to get 15+ of each]* Can't name manual saves - they're all labeled 'manual save' so you have no idea what they are* While there are multiple classes, the casters are far more powerful once you get access to T4 spells compared to the martial classes, and the dark caster is superior to the light caster. More effort should be spent balancing the classes.

_childDocuments_.review: Glad to see a new Disciples game coming out. Loved the series even the third one.But about the game.It's a mix of RPG with TBS with more emphasis on story building, which is new to the series.The game play is relatively easy  you move on the map with your hero and engage in battles with your army.Unlike the previous games you have a single base where you build army's from all races , well all that are available at lunch which are Empire, Demons , Undead and Elfs ... no love for Darws (might appear later in game am ~10h in and 3 maps down).Since the narrative is the main focus throughout the game you get just one hero and you find companions throughout the world.The hero can be customisable as he levels up and has the option to switch class from fighter to mage and hybrid classes.The companions are like units you recruit but with personality that you can interact with and deploy in battles but you are limited at how many come in battle at any given time. The game gives you option to swap in and out when on the map.Gameplay is ok not revolutionary but ok if you played Kings Bounty Heroes of Might and Magic or Disciples 1/2/3 you pick up really fast. There are some features that are missing, from more modern games in the genera, like autobattles when you have unskippable battles and against really low level enemies also the game speed in battles even om max speed feels slow.Spells are cast in battle unlike previous games where there was a mix of either world spells and/or battle spells. This are gained through quest and missions, the blueprint I mean you still need to research them in your Keep.Graphics are ok for this type of games but not last gen.Interface is a bit on the controller side, yes the game is out on Xbox to, and sometimes holding a mouse button to interact and cast is weird for a PC gamer like me used to click.And the interface could use a bit of stream lined it feels like you need to may windows to get to a desired place.  ConclusionThere are some reported bugs, that my brake the game please keep in mind, so far I haven't encountered any and the dev's seam to work on them and also on improving the game, which is a plus. Overall I'm enjoying the game the story and decision making focus gameplay, some decisions make ponder from time to time and it has consequences on the story evolution and access to units etc. If you like the genera give it a go. If you are hesitant you can wait a bit for the game to become more solid and try it then. Or wait for a discount, although 40$ is a good price from my point of view, to feel more inclined to buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed the game. 7.5/10. It is like Kings Bounty with Disciples setting.Units are quite different from previous games. Liked art syle from previous games. It makes special atmosphere for the game. But it depends on perception. — Did not see Ents and Griffins in Elves race. — Empire units are good. But it is strange to see Dragons in Empire. No Angels or cavalry.— Demons does not have gargoyles. Demons were more stylish and scary in previous games. Check Abyssal Devil or Tiamat.— Undead melee units remind of typical Zombie trash movies and not scary. Check Zombie or Skeleton warrior pictures from Disciples 2-3. They are quite ominous. Example Reaper from Disciples 3 with 6 scythes is scary and I did not want to fight him. Or compare dreadful Archlich (D2-3) and fussy Lich with nails instead of eyes (Liberation). Werewolf does not have physical immunity :( Ghost does not have paralysis spell. It made Undead quite a unique race. You can build houses from any faction in it + blacksmith and market. You can buy equipment for your companions in market.Pity that city does not change because of your main faction reputation. Like a red sky with a high Demon reputation. Or black sky without any sun with Undead. No unit upgrades. One of the best parts of Disciples series is unit upgrades progression. Apprentice can become Mage and then choose between Elementalist and Wizard. For example here Arcanist could become Elementalist and then Archmage. It would make the game more interesting.  — Good story line with different endings and a lot of companions (you can romance them too).— A lot of eqipment for your hero. Beautiful armor sets.— You can play as mage\warrior\assassin class.— Enjoyed to explore maps, details on maps are also good. — Liked new battle system. Backline units is a good innovation. — You can not load in battle or restart battle. It is very frustrating to go to Main menu and then load game.— No hotseat, wanted to play with a friend on one computer. Or play against computer. — Spellbook in battle has only 8 spells. I played as mage and it was not enough to me. Second tab will definitely help. — Another thing - did not find auto-battles as in Disciples 2-3 and Heroes. It saves a lot of time.— Micromanagement - all resources from mines go to your warehouse and you should manually take resources from there. It will be more convenient if they added directly to your resource pool, without any warehouses.— Demons\Dragons\Titans are kind of small, they should be huge (several hexes) and have much more health than units from the same Tiers.—  Summon spells have weird conditions to summon. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, it's not a bad game. There is good stuff in it, but these flaws require too much for my taste to overcome and I'll stop my playthrough here.Even at 300% speed, the Combat is slow and annoying because you wait for UI animations, that do not get sped up, as well as ingame animations that take control away from you after every action. And when there are 20-25 units on the battlefield (which is standard after a certain level), this becomes a farce.You can only cast a single Spell from your storygiven Book of Spells. The book will let you bring 10 spells into combat at a time but there is no need for that as you only get to cast one spell per round anyway. You are supposed to use these special spells, because that what your speciality is, but you only cast one and then either move somewhere or don't. Super slow and boring.Some Combat Encounters allow you to Retreat. But a lot of them also don't.Once you are in Combat you cannot load a save file. You cannot Surrender the fight. You either sit through the entire fight or quit back to the Main Menu.The interesting part about this game is that you can not only bring 2 companions with you into battle, but also up to 10 Units. These (Trash) Units can be recruited in your city for various resources and get more expensive the higher your level is. When these Units die in combat, they stay dead, so you have to spend resources to hire them again. Your Companions get ressurrected with a sliver of hp if they fall in combat.Where this gets annoying:Once you and your squad are above a certain strength to the enemies in the combat encounter, you get the option to Capture them. This button is a welcome sight because it autowins the battle and gives you full xp and rewards. Which is a blessing considering the slow and frustrating combat.But some combat encounters are forced even if you are 10 levels above the enemies. So you have to endure that slow and unresponsive combat against enemies who are not a challenge. It just wastes your time and I'm not talking about combat encounters with bosses. And the best part is that the enemies will sometimes just focus all of their attacks on one unit and kill it which then also wastes your resources.The game lacks a Tool to properly check out what's going on. Effects are just symbols, sometimes it'll give you a number if you hover long enough with your mouse, and sometimes it won't. In Combat you don't even see all the Effects on you or your enemies and what these do exactly.You gather Resources by capturing Sawmills, Mines, etc. These then generate you Resources in real time and only while you are ingame. Which is absolutely ridiculous. You need these Resources a lot because once you do the upgrades, and get better units, things start to get expensive really quick.Essentially, you would just have to afk for literal hours (no joke) and wait for your stockpiles to fill up, then gather your Resources. Why does it work that way? That is such an unintuitive and frustrating way to go about this. I want to play and enjoy a game, not leave it running in the background so I can stock up on resources. How did this not raise concerns during development?You either play 6h sessions minimum to pile up on resources or you let it run in the background. This is dumb.You cannot transition between maps via the map you are currently in, but by teleporting back to the main city, talking to your friend, telling him to open the map, and then selecting the map you want to go to. Quests markers do not appear on the map, so you don't know where a quest might take place until you visit that map.When you have completed a certain story milestone on certain maps, the main story will tell you to go back and talk to your friend to look at the map. If you want to go to a different map you have been to before to finish a sidequest or remove an obstacle that you couldn't remove before, tough luck. That Map Friend of yours now only gives you the option to go to the new map that has opened with the main quest line.You travel to the new Main Quest Map, go through the dialogue, teleport back to the city, talk to your friend, open the map and then travel to one of the old maps where you still have some loot or sidequests open. Unnecessarily complex and unintuitive.

_childDocuments_.review: Disciples: Liberation pulled me in with the Heroes of Might and Magic-esque battles and HoMM3-like castle, but I stayed for the story and the characters. Try the demo and see if you are hooked like I was. My main complaint with the game is that it becomes almost too thin at times.I played through the game twice (normal and Liberation, the New Game+) and found the story to be very enjoyable, with interesting plot points and characters that interacted with each other. I have never played a Disciples game before, so I was thrown into the lore pretty much blind. It was interesting to explore the world, and I felt rewarded most of the time. The game world is advertised as dark, but there was always a bit of reality and hope tied in (depending on your choices). There were dark themes that were explored without being unncessarily overdone.The battles were fun at first, but did become kind of dull after a while as I became much stronger than the opponents I was facing. The AI seems to lack planning, and can be easily beaten if you set up the battlefield correctly (The dev has since updated the game to be more in tune with you if you have completed all of the side quests). However, there were some balancing issues that came to mind during my two playthroughs: 1) the main character could get spells and the spellcasting classes quickly became 1-round 1-shot matches. 2) The companions felt very wildly balanced. The companions are based upon other units, and the units have tiers. Higher tiered units have better stats, but more importantly, higher tiered units have better abilities. Companions have better versions of those abilities. This means that some companions were just more useful than others.In the end of the story, it kind of became noticeable that the choices you were making in the background didn't seem to matter, except if the person in question came up again. There was a particular side quest person I saved, and she appeared later in the game and that was a cool nod, but alternatively, I had saved a bunch of people and became a queen of a land and it didn't seem to change anything at all. On this vein, some of the companions really stick out, but some just fade into the background.Lastly, there is a faction system, where when you complete quests for certain factions, you get reputation with them which changes what units of theirs you can recruit and their morale in your army. I noticed that some factions are really, really easy to please and others are not. Not for lack of trying, but because it seems the quests tend to be skewed.Overall, I recommend the game if you like RPGs and strategic combat, but play it in sections. The maps are huge and take multiple hours to beat: mostly because combat can take 30 minutes, but also because you need to run from place to place to complete quests. I was hooked by the story, but I did find myself spending a lot of time in the combat wondering when it would be over.

_childDocuments_.review: I was gaming for a while before the first Disciples game came out and have played the first 3 multiple times.  This will be a comparison to what I recall as it has been a while since I last played the older games.  First, I liked playing the story from different points of view as you could in the first three.  Here, you are stuck playing the main character and then choosing which faction(s) you ally with or not.  The talent tree is something you get access to immediately, but you don't pick your specialization until much later.  While the tree is divided into 3 parts, I had no clue class specialization was coming and would  have talented more appropriately had I known I had to specialize.  You can re-do your points, but by the time you need to you have already gotten used to a certain play style that may not fit the specialization you want.  Frustrating, but minor.  Quests were much easier to follow in previous games, but the map is of near zero  help in this regard and the journal descriptions are bereft of pertinent info to guide you.  It's like you have to remember what the quest giver told you instead of using the journal.  There is also an assumption that you can remember places on the map that aren't named on it and sometimes you aren't able to get back to the area you need to be for some time (and at a certain point, the maps change and you can't complete many of the quests).  I enjoy completing all the quests, so this was frustrating.  This also brings up the map issue.  You can only be in one area and if you change areas, you cannot go back to previous ones until much later in the story.  That is highly frustrating.  Also, this game does not like multiple monitors.  Sometimes the Kalypso launcher appears on my second monitor for no reason, but at least the game remains on my primary monitor.  Further, I periodically change music or want to look up hints for the quests and the camera locks permanently to the right and won't reset to default view.  Nothing short of quitting the game entirely and going back in will fix it.  Similarly, during combat you cannot inspect the full battlefield.  This is frustrating when you are trying to use in-line attacks and some of the targets are out of view, but still within range of the attack.  That is my biggest frustration with the game.  I also miss the guard setting where you can move one of your forces to a spot and if anything comes up to them or passes by, they get the remainder of their turn saved to actually do something compared to not at all.  The second most frustrating thing is that the Kalypso animation when starting the game cannot be skipped and IGNORES THE VOLUME settings of the game, so with the sub-woofer it is extremely annoying when it is late or early.  As for the positives, the game still has some roots in the turn-based styling of the first three Disciples games and does it well for the most part (see  the guard omission above).  Is it worth the price?  Sure, when it is on sale.  It is still fun and can be played with frequent interruptions because of the turn-based style.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR. If you are Disciples 1 and 2 fan (like myself) - this game is a pass. If you are looking more into experience similar to Kings Bounty, HoMM, or Age of Wonders, it's pretty good. My first impression is more on the negative side. The game has very little to do with the beloved classics - Disciples 1 and 2. Even less so than Disciples 3. I do miss the stationary large dark fantasy units in particular. But at the same time it pains me to write a negative review, as the game is not bad by all means.  Definitely there is more features now. They added companions which are basically somewhere in between regular units and heroes. There are dialogue options and some role-playing choices. The writing and voice-acting are both pretty weak imo. There are multiple (3) skill trees per hero, spell-casting in combat, in-combat abilities for all units, equipment grades. Looks like it's possible to hire units from all races as we are playing for a neutral faction. So far feels like a weird and overwhelming cocktail I'm having difficulty digesting. The combat is actually pretty satisfying and tactical. I quite like different types of action points used. The downside is imo the HP to DMG ratios and overall time to kill is pretty high, you need to keep bashing the remaining 1-2 enemies for a few minutes before they day. Maybe include an option to auto-play / quick-finish the battle when you have a large advantage. Not sure that I like the fact that all units can basically restore some HP in battle. Just unnecessarily extends the battle time.

_childDocuments_.review: First thing you should understand - this is not the sequel of the original “Disciples” series. It is not even a strategy - it is a RPG with turn-based battles and some strategic elements. The closest analog would be the “King’s Bounty” series.I am not familiar with the original “Disciples” series, but I assume this game shares its lore and world history with it. But that’s all.Here we travel around an open world, interact with its inhabitants, complete quests and so on. But unlike the most such games, while fighting enemies the hero does not do it himself, but instead he commands a small army, which jumps out of the pocket. So the main gameplay aspect is a tacticals turn-based battle. And it has been done well enough.Game has a nice combat system, where each unit has regular attack, special attack with cooldown and passive ability. There is also a rear line, where we can put a unit to gain some passive effect over the entire squad. All these features produce a good variety of tactics and combat schemas, making the battles quite interesting.However, there are some absurdities in unit properties: skeletons and ghosts can bleed and can be poisoned. How it can be possible, while such creatures do not have a bloodstream? Some imp-archer constantly yells “I will bathe in fire”, but has no resistance to it and burns like everyone else. And so on.During the gameplay we will fight the giant bosses, which requires special tactics. This provides additional diversity for the battles.However, only Avyanna can cast spells. You will not face any equal challenge: an army led by a hero with a spellbook and the same abilities.The game has a good variety of units, coming from 4 different factions. During the game we have to pick sides in the world events, improving relationships with some factions, but losing it with the others. So it is hard to remain friendly with everyone, which limits the available units list per each playthrough. Thus the game provides a good re-playing potential.Also there is a “game+” mode with a twist. I do not want to make a spoiler - you’ll see it when you get there. There is no automatic healing after the battle. We’ll need to find a healing spring in order to replenish the unit's health. This leaves us running circles around the map: fight with the enemy - go back to healing spring, return to fight the next enemy - go back to healing spring and so on. Also there is no way to heal the squad at the home town.The game takes too much time to apply the unit's passive effects during battles. Hit a succubus and wait a few seconds while she casts a backfire effect on the unit, hit her again and wait for another few seconds… Such things are better to speed up.The game does not contain cut-scenes or cinematics (actually it has 3 or 4, but I would not count them). The entire story is presented via text descriptions and partially voiced dialogs, in which we can see only the characters’ faces. Such game appearance is very disappointing, as it does not channel emotions and drama behind the story events. It looks like an interactive book - not a video game. If we were talking about a strategy game with some story campaign presented in this way - it would be fine. But this is a story-telling RPG!The game already has character models with enough detailisation used for the tactical battles. These could be easily reused in cut scenes, which should not be necessary implemented in very high detail mode. Just remember the “Spellforce” series for example. Of course, someone may say this is a “classic” or an “old school” approach. But I think this is simply “end of the budget”.One more thing related to the story-telling: it contains a lot of sexual encounters. At some point it seems Avyanna sleeps with everyone she meets, including demons and undead... Perhaps this is how authors define the term “dark fantasy”. Nevertheless, without any cut-scenes or other visuals for it, all these sexual stories look rather stupid then lustful.Story itself has a lot of holes in it. For example: we find the home town, which is an “abandoned ancient city” in a livable state with some buildings producing modern units in “ready to go” mode. There is no rebuilding, no seek for the builders or workers - nothing. There is no formal requirement for the castle advancement, just - “you need to advance the story”. How does, for example, the emperor’s death relate to our town building? It could be justified better, like we need a specific schematics, a special resource or artifact, but…Same thing appears for the Avyanna character class. She starts the game as a “mercenary” and can pick another class only after a particular story event. For an RPG it looks stupid: she should be searching for a mentor or something to master a new profession.Graphic is basic. Can’t say it is bad, can’t say it is good or realistic. For the game, which main feature is tactical battles shown from the height, it is acceptable. There are some glitches like collisions in clothing (elven robe in particular).Music and sound is unremarkable, but suits the gameplay well enough. However, the sound sometimes freezes right in the middle of the dialogue phrases. It looks like a disk swap. Although It may be just my local machine’s problem.Overall it is 6/10. If you like turn-based battles, you will probably enjoy this game. But its other aspects appear unfinished, which is a pity. I think the game could appear much better without much extra effort.

_childDocuments_.review: This one here is a decent game, and I think it's worth it's asking price.It's an dark fantasy RPG game featuring tactical combat and many hours of content to go through in my case (doing everything) it was nearly 80 hours of playtime.Features one difficulty setting which I can classify as welcoming to new players in tactical games to not say "too easy". Difficulty picks up after chapter I but only to get easier again.Visuals and Music are really on a great level for a small studio game, and it runs very well too so it won't be a slouch on lower end machines. I have to commend devs for adding such a rare visual thing as "sharpen filter" to make blurring caused by TAA less obnoxious. The RPG.Trade mark of any good RPG is plenty of choice during dialogue, and here you have it most of the time, from small choices that will avert or provoke combat, to deciding fate of regions in game or alliances that are forged or broken.Another strong point of this game are  the companions that you meet and get to travel with, they are strong characters with fleshed out back stories and stories developed during your journey.Characters like Necromancer Ejimar who's eccentric and possessed with lust of power, he has absolutely no remorse and is full dedicated to his quest of becoming most powerful necromancer in Nevendaar. You get to help him along this bloody and ruthless quest. Add to this his otherwise cheerful personality and womanizing, makes him quite unique and very memorable. This is topped with superb voice acting, he's one of those characters that will stay with me, darker side of me. Talking about voice acting though it's all over the place, from phoned in performances to really great ones, that are mostly reserved to few companions. Voice actor for Melindrah the Druid, is really great at portraying strong outcast angry at the civilized world and It's only a pity his quest doesn't match quality of that performance.Sebastien is another one with a good story and voice acting but unfortunately talking too much about him is spoiler territory. The Story.In broad strokes, main story is just OK, to my taste story of a hero that goes from nothing to become everything can rarely be good and could use more games, and more chapters before we reach any sort of ultimate power. Story at some point just gets high and mighty and it doesn't serve itself too well. Dark fantasy generally sticks to telling dark and grounded stories, but main plot quickly turns away from this into high fantasy realm where sky is the limit, or you could say cosmos...Game shines the most in companion stories and zone stories, bigger and smaller side quests, some of them are just 'go there do that' of course but bunch some of them are good. You get to make moral and immoral choices with a gravity.The Gameplay.Onto an elephant in the room for this game our main protagonist Avy has well designed skill tree and 4 classes to pick from, and it's absolutely great, they feel good warlord is a hard hitting tank, while witch is a primal magic wielding spell caster with great power. What's not great 3 out of 4 of those classes, as our characters progresses through the game get more powerful, so powerful in fact Avy does not even need an army behind her to win 99/100 fights. This defeats any excitement that comes with fighting in a tactical game even if you loose a unit here and there, you have a feeling that you just can't loose and I never did. Otherwise units and their races feel very nice and combat is quite balanced across the board. Every unit has their counterpart in 3 other races, but that counterpart comes with it's own abilities and passives that feel unique yet still fair and balanced across the board. It's hard to say who's the best melee unit or a caster and so on it all depends on how your party compliments each other. Each of 4 factions has 4 tier of units and every tier feels good, considerably stronger then the other unit progression is great. Unit design as well. The big bad, of gameplay beside Avy being super overpowered, is the enemy AI. It is extremely simplistic and follows same routines regardless of factions, you have defensive ai and offensive ai. Defensive AI is the support units and some casters that just runs away across the map, in what you could call random fashion.Aggressive AI, melee and ranged units all do the same thing every single time or at least 9/10 times, target weakest unit they can reach within a turn and that's all. Every fight plays the same, and it's quickly becoming boring. What unties those two is ignorance of the map often tripping negative effects or going onto aoe effects that linger on the ground.They are also eager to fire their powerful abilities as soon as they can usually round one often doing minimal damage to you, or minimal healing to their allies or if you're unlucky taking out one of your units, because they'll pile on the weakest link, without any strategy to it.They only best your units like that on chance, if enough enemies with strong single target ability spawn near enough to one of your weak units you can kiss it good bye. replay-ability.Game features ng+ mode that alters a story a little bit, so on top of that 80 hour first run it has replayablity factor to it.You can also quite freely try any unit combinations and put any and all companions into the battlefield. Reputation gains are booster and XP is boosted as well, it's ok but downside to NG+ is if you found the first run easy, NG+ is easier, pure story mode. Honestly as much as it's a great idea to have new arc to the story in NG+ and I'd wish more games would do it, its not that great here... it's just another powertrip through the game, and changes to story are miniscule. It usually is exactly in the form of Avy saying new line of dialogue and it doesn't change anything for the most part.Few quests change, and ending is a new one but not a good one, just a bland and overblown in proportions.In summary game is decent, stories can be good and worthwhile, but NG+ isn't. The choice is fun, and combat can be fun, but you will get bored of it quickly.I've had a good time overall.Edit: I forgot there's a multiplayer, feel free to forget it exists as well.Thanks to Eman for a game key.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had great potential, trying to mix it up and be "multi-genred" by taking influences from various cool games that many of us love. However, it ended up being mediocre or even less in almost all areas. Nothing has been fully fleshed out, it's buggy, unpolished, unbalanced, the story and most characters are uninteresting and the overall feeling that you get is "meh". *Why even have mana/hp fountains instead of healing after every fight making us run around?*Why make us waste so much time in long and maze-like but mostly empty dungeons?*Why have world "blockers" that you unlock with character quests if all I will get is going to be "generic randomized item #58?*Why is the story so incoherent? *Why are the fights so boring for the first 10 hours? 2 skills per character, really?*Why do I have to go through multiple unnecessary steps to fast travel to other areas? *Why do you randomly lock me out from doing that after I end a part of the main quest?*Why do we have to go back to the main area to collect resources? *Why is there no button to train all of your characters at the same time? *Why do you make me hold my clicks to do anything? *Why make us phase out buildings if there is clearly not enough resources in the game to progress quickly through tiers?*Why have so many levels when they barely change anything? Adding just some hp/power points per level..*What's the point of leveling at all if wherever you go everyone will be basically the same level?*What the hell is the point of getting 5 leadership points at some levels when everything you may add to your roster is 10, 20, etc. points??*Why is the UI made in such a way that makes me feel like I am playing a mobile game?*Why are the heroes absolute boring carbon-copies of higher tier units?Those questions and so many more really make me appalled by the decision-making process of the developers of this game. It felt like they tried to mash in as much as they could without ever thinking if they should. There's so much time you waste backtracking, going through boring dungeons, leveling everyone individually, healing and much more crap that half your playtime feels like a chore. You don't need to pretend your game is long, just make it fun. I had this game in my wishlist for such a long time, I really REALLY wanted to like it, I gave it a lot of my time waiting for it to get better, but it barely did.. The game looks nice, I liked the aesthetic, I liked the variety of creatures, the animations were great, the music was cool. But everything else? Simple mediocrity. That is the feeling that I was left with in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah man..... Been a long time since I've been so enthralled/enamoured by the storyline and the deliverance of such in a videogame. Given, there are ways the story resonates with me personally with how I observe the world around me which puts it over the top of surface-level observations which is already a deeply-engrossing faction-based dynamic conflict of epic scale. Despite some issues Disciples: Liberation delivers a stack-load of content, amazing story and lovable combat. What you see is that the plot is elevated beyond just 'yeah, I hate that guy so I'm gonna fight him' or 'they are the enemy because they do things that I work against or do not want'..... It reaches a level of the world understanding itself, of things falling into place because of all the things they have been before, of things being who and how they are because of events ingrained in the lore and world-building.... With some room for a cliche hero archetype, negated by the fact the the hero is in fact influential in the politics of the world and by the fact that you're not guaranteed to be a hero in everyone's eyes because of the decisions you make.Maybe the combat you've seen before, I concede that turn-based hex-based combat has been done before in certain known niche subgenres. And the combat has been labelled repetitive, personally I just found the end-game a bit of a slog until I realized the impact of switching Avyanna from a melee to a sorceress build very late... about 80% into the game, which stats-wise was actually a pretty good decision. The combat was an aspect I thoroughly enjoyed with minor fatigue towards the end. As others mention, the UI delivery and the hard-handed implementation of the 'base-building' aspects to upgrade your units etc seems to be the results of slight lack of forethought and laboured development cycle.Its not the worst thing, for me it meant I went the whole of the game playing with the 'starter' units and shop mercenaries because you're supposed to phase out one building and build another to get access to the new units, but then you lose access to the old units, which goes against the grain of your implemented battle strategies and the units you've recruited up to that point no longer having support. And you can literally not see what new units you can get until you destroy the unit building....Anyways, yeah, the story, I loved it. In a psychopathic way you can say that your choices don't matter because the story will happen and there is no wrong choices per sé. But personally I found a lot more meaning in the story by associating the factions in the story with things I observe in my own life and the dynamics thereof. I'm not a Disciples veteran like some others complaining here, so I dont have that benchmark. But I looked at the old Disciples games and they look like **** soooo.......Listen, I can talk a lot about this but who has the time right, so recommendation is as follow...10/10 For Myself8/10 As a general gaming experience7/10 For price being a bit high, not for lack of content but the quality of delivery and for the game's annoyances There is not a single director I believe that will successfully capture this story in a film or television media adaptation at the same quality and scale as delivered in this game, even if you sometimes have to use your imagination to fill in the blanks. And you have to be in the mood for this. Like you should know you're gonna sit down for two hours and you might do five battles, although the story advances quite a lot in between that as well.*Received as a gift It plays slightly into my assessment and comments on the price. I sincerely want others to find joy in their purchases but understandably knowing your worth is also a good thing*

_childDocuments_.review: Disciples is so close to being a good experience, but just grinds you out of it. The pacing is absolutely abysmal. The whole game length should have been half of what it is, and maybe that extra budget should have been put into making unique models for, you know, these *unimportant* npc like gods, faction leaders, legendary figures... which instead are just color-swapped companions (sometimes even standard units!) with a visual effect plastered on. This is a problem in a heavy-narrative experience. And the thing that really sadden me is that the story part, albeit a bit generic in some of its aspects, it's actually good: more than once I've found myself enjoying reading through the subquests, the discussions with the companions, the lore and so on. But the combat wears itself thin too soon, unlockables are way too slow, and as I've said, the whole experience just drags out way too much. I really hope for a sequel that addresses these problem, because the potential was there.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game.What it does well is story , the world building is very very good, the companions and chars you meet in game are interesting both in story and their designs.Even the fetch quests stand out because ..well the characters you are fetching stuff for and the stuff you are fetching is not your usual three rat tails for a generic innkeeper I tell you that much.The artwork I like, especially the character designs and models are really nice and so are the animations.It´s not AAA levels cinematic motion captured stuff ofc but for what it is , it is very solid.Voice work is another high note (haha) both for the main chars and the units in combat. The combat is fun, it´s not super deep or complicated but there´s still room for enough thought on tactics and lineup to keep it interesting, combined with the steady supply of new units featuring new skills and great designs plus your ever growing book of spells  it´s not bored me yet (about 30 hours at time of review) enemies go "sploof" or "splat" in rewarding ways.I like that it is pretty straight forward  , each unit only has a limited number of skills and the stats are very easy to understand. there are certainly many QoL things lacking atm and some features are IMO doesn´t work to well. For example you can use fountains to heal between fights , these fountains recharge on a timer which is longer on higher diffs, where you will more often need them. But there is nothing stopping you from riding around the map until you find one that is full or even  teleport to another map refill health and teleport back again making the whole thing just a time waster.You have limited slots to build buildings to produce units but there´s no glossary in game as to exactly what skills every unit has. There should be,at least for units you have encountered.Honestly when I started playing this I felt it was "Meh mediocre",but it was good enough so I kept playing and suddenly it just clicked with me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is compelling, which I really didn't anticipate. It features tactical combat which takes place in an environment suitable to the zone you are in at the time. The story is good and has some surprises, there are companions and units representing each of he four factions. You can gather resources to add or replace units and this is all paid for with HOMM-style resource gathering (and even though the nodes can be defended, there is no danger of losing control once you are the owner). Good voice acting, choices that matter, varied and fun unit and companion abilities and so lots of options for the way in which your army is assembled--so should be considerable replay potential. I am just level 20 now, and I think level 60-80 is attainable, so obviously a lot of game left on this first playthrough. Recommended 8.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I am really enjoying Disciples: Liberation.  It is a good step forward in the series.  Have played all the Disciples 2 & 3 games.  This one is similar to the Disciples 3 series.  Better graphics and replayability.  Your main hero has 4 classes to choose from.  There are 4 of the 5 original races all involved in their own racial hatred and wars.  You can build your troops from one race or have a motley crew from several of the races.  Lots of choices.  The combat is on a small grid.  Sometimes there are chock points.  Sometimes there are exploding crystals that have timers.  Sometimes you are ambushed from 2 sides.  Lots of battles.  These games always have lots of battles.  Sometimes only one or two of your troops have a high initiative and you can over expose them if you are not careful.  So... different strategy for different battles.    You can have reinforcements.  Can't bring them on during a battle to replace your loses.  You can use them to replace loses when you have to fight multiple battles in a row. The story line is good.  There are cameo appearances of heroes and villains from the previous games. If you liked the Disciples 3 games you should like this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Disciples: Liberation is largely what fans of King's Bounty were hoping for with King's Bounty 2. It's a return to form for the Disciples franchise, and a temporary refuge for fans of Heroes of Might and Magic as well. disciples returns to the tried and true isometric exploration formula with tactical turn-based combat and some mild choice elements thrown in. It doesn't do any one thing perfectly, but it does most of what it sets out to do very well. Recommended to anyone who is interested.

Maps, dungeons, Yllian, gear... really satisfying.- The big story is kind of déjà vu. No spoiler : you decide who is the bad guy, you have 4 choices and in the end you crush all of them anyway to become the champion of the gods of god champions. And nobody cares ! Look : when you take the highway from Lisboa to Vladivostok, ALL THE WAY you are fully conscious that your destination will be Vladivostok, right ? So if the big direction is 300% predictable, the good part is the quality of the journey, the details :- Every encounter has its background, dialogue, or little story. You will meet a lot of people, they all have something different to tell. Well, yes, in the end you crush them anyway, but at least you may compose yourself a reason why you smash that specific demon and not his friend. A lot of lore everywhere- Rich rich combat system, in middle/late game you build your army with 50 unit types, each of them has animated buffs and spells and moves... Great !- I played the french version and enjoyed the voice actingCans Cens Cins Cuns :- You're on the highway for 73 hours so don't imagine you will turn right or left. Tutto diritto, immer gerade aus, straight on straight on. There is an effort to give some variation in combat (terrain, obstacles) but somehow it's  a bit repetitive. Doesn't matter, as long as you enjoy the landscape- With deluxe edition tou have 5 skill points, this is very strong already. And gear... no balance anymore, try a sledgehammer to smash a mosquito. Don't use them, with that sword and that armor you're ready for fights until level 55 at least- Some mistakes in french translation, not many, not at all. _childDocuments_.review: I love strategy turn based RPGs, so I hoped this game would be good for me even though it had mixed reviews. Unfortunately, for the following reasons I'm stopping playing this game:1. The way you get more powerful is absolutely pitiful and completely uninteresting. "You found new armor, it will increase your damage resistance to one of the damage types by 1%, hurray!" Every piece of gear I found in my 10 hours was 100% irrelevant to any battle outcome. Literally every piece of gear would grant maybe 1-2% passive bonus. Finding gear in chests, getting new spells, it all felt horribly underwhelming and this is actually the main reason I stopped playing the game. Nothing ever seemed to really change about how I played the game, Acquiring spells, getting gear, leveling up, had 0 impact on how I actually played battles. Everything you can do is some kind of mild buff or debuff that just makes regular attacks do more or less damage. This leads to the second point. 2. The combat system is overly simple and extremely repetitive. Battles are very similar to each and there is basically no variety in approaches to combat. You do the same thing, the same way every fight. And as others mentioned the fights simply take too long. I was playing on the hardest difficulty, which seemed to me to be reasonably difficult, I can't imagine playing it on an easier mode.3. Finally, I felt the storytelling just betrayed me as a player. The game pretends you have choices, but you don't get to decide what kind of motivations your character has in the slightest. For example, I want to play as a good character motivated by liberating people and lessening their suffering. Yet, I am forced to have a psychopathic necromancer as my companion and give him a high position in my base. As others have pointed out, the game has a strange tone of "this is a videogame and nothing really matters isn't that funny" the whole time while somehow also depicting atrocities and pretty interesting situations. I just felt the tone was all wrong and the player freedom was bizarrely curtailed.For these reasons I'm done with the game. If these things are important to you then I highly doubt you will like the game. However, if you don't mind the sound of that and enjoy simple turn based rpgs then you may enjoy it.Edit: I'd like to add that this game's steam description says that it's a "mature, dark fantasy game." I think this game is indisputably immature. I challenge any single player to leave a comment on this review telling me how this game is mature. Everything about how the story and characters are written screams teenage melodrama with cynical humor layered on.

_childDocuments_.review: For older fans of this series that were hoping to get to play an old beloved series, they will be saddened to know that it's nothing like its predecessors. It's not the original, turn-based, version where you commanded a chosen faction, mained a special hero then built your party and rose to power through conquest. It's a simplified knockoff that has a lot of positive praise for not being even a blurry shadow of what its predecessors were. I find it questionable that "reviewers" from influential sites gave this game such high scores. I'm assuming they are easy to impress?Disciples: Liberation has a below average level of story and voice acting, with lots of content and a large dark world to explore. In comparison with the previous versions of this game (in my opinion) it fails to leave a lasting impression or even give the urge to come back to play some more.You play as a girl who fails to kill off her target and conveniently gets teleported into an ancient city where she can recruit her army that she can build out of various factions, store her companions in a big room where they can chat later, and launch small invasions on the world when all dialogue options have been exhausted for now.The game engine gives off a hefty cartoon vibe, making monsters and characters seem unimpressive. Compared with the art design and models present in Disciples II and Disciples III, this version of the game offers nothing substantial or memorable.

And I have to say: it feels nice to explore the maps in real time, you get a lot of unit variety in the game and not starting every map from scratch is removing the grind, which is a good thing.A lot of systems have changed and it's all to make the players experience better. _childDocuments_.review: NOTE: At the time of this review, I have completed the game twice, once in original mode and once in its New Game+ Liberation mode. This review was also conducted before a major rebalance promised by the devs in a November dev post.In short, this game is a great RP masquerading itself as an old-fashioned tactical battler harkening to the late nineties. Despite the depth of its combat system, it is not without flaws, and unnecessary, time-consuming repetition bogs down an otherwise great foundation  That is not to say that it is game I would not recommend playing - if you are longing for a fun well-written mature fantasy romp, you will love it, but expect to work for it by doing the same thing over and over and over... A solid 7.Onto the full review...----This game can be summarised as "it is what you make of it". Your first experience, with all of the battles and quests on the map, will total 65-70 hours - unless you decide to rush through the game and skip optional content which will make it substantially more difficult but clock at a steady 30-50 hours. Expect it to be a timesink as, despite an enjoyable exploration filled chock-full of side quests and content, you will be battling for most of it... While the map stays static, there is tons of choice in side quests and a deep roster of party members and units to play around with which adds to replayability.However, it is impossible to talk about game length without talking about its LIBERATION mode. Essentially a "New game+", it also acts as an extension of the story and adds extra options, choices and gameplay mechanics that wholly enhance the experience. In fact, it does it so well that I would say Liberation mode *is* the main mode for the game, but you will have to work through the standard mode on the first go-around. Looking at both combined, you are looking at a game of close to 100hrs of runtime by the time you can put it aside (I breezed through my Liberation run in 25 hours).NOTE: This time is likely to increase as devs ramp up overall difficulty, but may be offset by choosable difficulty options in the menu.While there is technically no difficulty choice at the time of writing, this section will be outdated within weeks of writing as the devs are aiming to implement new options. As it stands, the game is not inherently hard but it is grindy and will require time and experimentation to go through. If you enjoy that in a tactical game, you will not be disappointed, but it can be a bit overbearing.The Liberation mode, however, is the inverse of what you would expect a NG+ to be. It is a breeze in terms of difficulty once you are familiar with the mechanics but it is very fun to play and the added story content makes it worth your while.ROLE PLAYING[/b]	Disciples opts for a more classical isometric RP experience, combining Heroes-like overworld exploration and townbuilding with conventional roleplaying. In a way, it feels very reminiscent of Heroes of Might and Magic 4 when it comes to the overworld, townbuilding, resource management, etc. That said, in terms of exploring, you are not doing much aside from collecting resources, and townbuilding feels pretty barebones, leaving me wanting, but it is a nice change of pace from constant battles. Where it shines, however, is its roleplaying. The writing, the story and party member banter is impeccable. Despite the occasionally hit-and-miss voice acting, I never thought I'd like having a necromancer in my party so, so much. Love you Ejay, you old fiend. Choices you make feel impactful due to an in-depth reputation system making you juggle relations with different factions of religious zealots, demons, the undead and elves. And trust me, the choices really matter and affect how you play the game - and often result in unintended consequences. The only downside is that it feels a bit restrictive when it comes to unit variety as you are inherently restricted by your relations to get stronger units.TIP: One thing the game does not tell you is that you can switch out your existing unit dwellings for others from the get go. I went through 40 hours of my first game before I realised I had that option from the get go. Phase out a building - you won't lose out - and pick your poison.You cannot talk about one without talking about the other. The hexagrid-based combat allows you to pit 10x10 unit armies very reminiscent of Heroes 3, solely limited by your "leadership" in terms of who you bring on. Gone are stacks in favor of single unit health bars, but ultimately that only makes the fights feel grindy as you progressively get to add more units in your army. All in all, the combat feels fun, but a bit limiting as it boils down to who has better AOE attacks by the end. And do not get me started on the system that allows to move after attacking, allowing enemy ranged units run away farther afield that you cannot reach OVER and OVER again, and the battle animations move at a snails pace. THAT repetition can be excruciating. Now, the "Conquer" button allows you to skip battles against opponents deemed weaker than your army, but it is not trustworthy, and there are plenty of unskippable battles that feel like "I've done this 400 times by now, please let me just see what's next".Now all of that could be ignored IF the unit variety made for interesting combinations. Alas, while it feels new at the start, by the end it feels like most units are just reskins of one another with the same single unit/AoE attack dealing damage in a different element. This is where Liberation mode changes things up. While you are limited to Avyanna and two trusty comrades in the main game, Liberation allows you to use all of them or however many you want. And that feels great as they are not only more powerful than base versions of the unit, but also fun to use and combine together. However, it does feel a bit wrong as most standard units become redundant by the end.If you enjoy CRPGs, tactical RPGs and strategy games like HOMM, this game will do you well. Fun, engrossing and improved by a colorful cast and a mature existential storyline, it feels like a throwback to a bygone area updated with some modern sensibilities. That said, it does not come without flaws, and the sheer grinding you will have to endure will likely hamper the experience at some point. But for what it is worth, it is a sure-fire recommendation, especially at the current price tag.P.S. It is impossible not to compare this game to a similar game called King's Bounty 2 that came out a few months prior. These two games are like two sides of the same coin and act as a foil to one another. Both stand on their own, both are solid 7's, but each of their strengths is where the other game fails. While Bounty offers too few fights and an average story, this game offers too many, often distracting from the narrative. Wish someone would combine them, you would literally get something astounding.
