_childDocuments_.review: Townscaper is beautiful, a very lovely experience and something I dont mind having in my librar. In terms of gameplay it is very shallow, though, and I would have wished for a bit more to sculpt, trim and explore my Towns. That is why I dont recommend it here as it is not really much of a game.If you are aware of what this title contains and dont mind the price - then feel free to make the purchase. I would feel 2-4€ to be a fair price.To go a little more into detail: Townscaper is great in that it generates nice and cozy looking buildings with very little input. You tell it where you want something to be and where you want empty space. The rest is generated by the 'game'. Flooring, walls, windows, stairways, gardenspace, doors, lamps ... you could place a toddler in front of the computer. It is impossible to make anything ugly, really.At the same time Townscaper lacks in this very regard. There are no tools to grant districts more character. Everything looks more or less the same. Big Seaside walls and Castles will always have the same types of windows at their sides. There is no way to connect districts with bridges that dont look like quays or houses.Townscaper offers some "secret combinations", though, which could help with giving certain parts of your town an individual feel. Spaces fully enclosed by houses turn into gardens, for example. Overbuilt gaps will shape into archways - and more. These are nice to discover when playing and do keep everything as simple as possible. They are way too few, though. I would recon you will find most of them within a few hours and not all of them are very big and noticeable. It would have been nice if more styles and elements could have been added by modding, allowing a potentialle endless repository of Doodads to allow for more individual Towns.Lastly, there is a lack of Immersion as well. I find it hard to understand why I cant walk in my city and just experience it like the townsfolk would. Why not have some random folk spawn in doors to make their ways somewhere, sit at benches or feed some birds? We can change the time of day - why is there no day-night cycle or changing weather to experience?

_childDocuments_.review: Townscaper is a solid sandbox building game about erecting little coastal villages. It's a neat game to mess around with different town designs. The look of buildings like the roofs, additional hooks, windows, doors, clotheslines, and greenery changes based on the way you place adjacent buildings. The game is set on a wonky grid allowing for more 'natural' and uneven shaped structures. While messing around with the limited color pallet and the different designs that come from placing these buildings can be fun and suck you in, there are several things missing from this game which stop me from recommending it for many. I found the game disappointing because there wasn't really any soundtrack aside from one song in the credits, and while the splish-splashing noises and other sound effects in the game make it not totally barren I found the soundscape to be lacking. The game also felt pretty lifeless. There are some birds that flock atop your buildings but there aren't any fish or people to populate the rest of the game. In addition the game is aimless. With no objectives or challenges to complete there is not much to do except make your own fun, and for most there's only so long you can mess around without a goal before getting bored. A final aside; I couldn't figure out how to make the floating islands which was very frustrating. While the building component can be enjoyable it could be more fleshed out, the game lacks music and a more lively world, so all in all the game is about a 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Townscaper is a mobile app that's been dumped on Steam as if it was a real PC game (it's not)... it's a cash grab from greedy mobile devs.  This mobile app isn't even a game, it's, well, like a playpen or a fidget spinner, I guess.  You click around on a small 3D rendered map and buildings pop up.  Depending on where and how you click, the buildings may take various different forms like a tower or something.  You can choose what colours the buildings will be from a palette on the side of the screen.  That's all there is to this.  Visual bubble wrap. For those unfamiliar with what actually makes something a game, a "game loop" describes the interaction and feedback a gamer has when playing a game.  Tetris, for example, has a game loop where a random block appears, the gamer interacts with the block to position it, and then the game decides if that finishes a row or not, increases the players score if any rows were completed, then gives the gamer another block to position.  Counter-Strike has a game loop where a player seeks another player, tests their skill against that player by shooting them or being shot, the computer rewards the player if they win, and then if the player survives, they repeat that loop.  There's no loop here, no true interactive feedback.  It simply is not a game, it cannot be "played".It can be "played with", but then you can open up Excel and use your arrow keys to make the cursor move around in amusing directions if you really want... does that make Microsoft Excel a game?  No, it doesn't (except for the version of Excel that had that hidden flight sim easter egg... which is more of a game than this is!).   See what I mean?There's not much else to say about this because it's not a game, which disqualifies this for recommendation to gamers as a game.  I suppose it's worth noting it looks nice... which just means it's a waste of effort that could have been spent more wisely on making an actual game.  This could have been the foundation for a charming Sim City style game or something... but no.  There's also some technical defects that should be addressed if anyone still wants to go ahead and buy this non-game mobile app on Steam. From a technical perspective, as a mobile app, this doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.There's no options to change the resolution for the mobile app and not many meaningful ways to customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this mobile app is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this mobile app will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.Because this is a mobile app, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the iPhones that the mobile app was designed for.  These are unfortunate handicaps and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was an afterthought for the iPhone developers who are to blame for this.  The mobile app is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for mobile phones forces upon a game.  Once more, mobile devs have made gaming worse for everyone.  I didn't spend thousands on building a gaming rig just so I could pretend it's an iPhone.These technical defects push this mobile app below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Townscaper has the preposterous price of around $6 USD ($1 more expensive than on the app stores, so that's a poke in the eye to PC gamers from these mobile devs), it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Townscaper is, without a doubt, the most relaxing video game I have ever played, and at the time of writing this I've been playing video games for almost 23 years. I jumped in and before I even knew it, hours had passed. First, its beauty is in its simplicity. There are no directions and you don't need them. You just start building using your left mouse button to build and the right mouse button to delete. There's no punishment for making a move you didn't want to make or for adding a building or land piece you didn't want to create. You just right click and it's like the move never happened. You don't have to spend fictional money to create buildings, and there's no winning or losing outside of your own satisfaction with the town you've created. There's no complex system of traffic or electricity/power or civil services. You just build buildings. If you're looking for an intense city sim like Banished or Frostpunk, this just isn't for you. Second, this game is beautiful. Whether your creation is tiny island with just a few small houses, or a massive sprawling city, it's hard to make a bad looking town. While all buildings look very similar, there are definitely some really cool hidden surprises depending on how and where you create your  buildings. Seeing clotheslines extend from two tall close-by buildings or a point sitting atop a tall tower, I time-and-time-again found myself trying to replicate some of the special structures and details I made.Overall, Townscaper is just a great way to relax after a long day or week and allow you to be as creative as you want without being overwhelmed by a myriad of options or complex mechanics. Even if it wasn't in Early Access and this is all it will ever be, Townscaper would still get an easy thumbs up from me. If you just want to shut your mind off for a bit and create something beautiful, do yourself a favor and pick up Townscaper.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I'd like to start by saying that I love city builder games. Ive sunk many hours into C:S and Tropico and all sorts of other games. If you're looking for a complex city builder with any kind of management aspects, this is not the game for you.HOWEVER, if what you are looking for is a great little time killer that is as satisfying as it is relaxing to play, then you've come to the right place. This game allows for hours of mindless messing around without any greater thought. However, if you'd like to really think things through, it'll allow for that as well. I think the pictures on the store page do a good job of illustrating the variety of what you can build in this game, as does the community hub, so if you're interested check those out.One of my favorite aspects of the game is something that I've always struggled with in other city builders; giving my creations a natural look. Due to the irregular tiles that you build on and the procedurally generated items that appear while you build, these cities have a very organic look to them that is very difficult to achieve in other games. This comes at the cost of detailed manipulation of the environment, as you can't decide what shape each tile will take, but the end result are fantastic looking towns or even bigger cities that just look real. If you're looking to kill time, relax and find a creative output for your free time, I can't recommend this game enough. I hope it continues to get updated as time goes on, as it is limited in its scope, but even in this current stage it is a great little game.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this a very simple game? Yes. Is this a fun and surprisingly addictive game? Also Yes.I'm not exaggerating when I say it's a simple game, so don't expect too much when you spend the $7 for it. It consists of being in the water, with a small colour palette to choose from, and you place down blocks (can't choose blocks, it will auto change to either street/building/etc) to make a town, that is all. That being said, it is still a very relaxing and chill game to play. I like building games like this so this is very much up my alley. The art style is cute and I really enjoy the different animations that play out when the houses change depending on the structure. You can make a lot of different things with the small palette you have to work with, from small villages to giant mansions.I've seen it said in reviews before and I also agree, that it'd be cool to have people roaming around the town as you're making it, would make it feel more alive, all we have right now are some birds on roof tops.I think another thing that could add a lot of fun to the game would be different town starting locations, not just water, although it is fun to build ocean towns.Overall, it's a cute fun little game, and if you have 7 bucks to spare I'd recommend giving it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely fantastic tool for d&d town creation, i honestly couldn't recommend it more right now at the price tag.Wishlist for the future:- Other templates such as grass, desert, snow etc. rather than just water.- A black and grey colour pallet for structures.- I would absolutely love a tool for placement of featureless walls instead of buildings, this allows for walls around towns without the bottom floor looking like its part of a house with doors, windows etc.- Inclines & declines feature in the form of ramps etc- More building styles such as rustic, medieval, victorian, gothic etc. or at least workshop support so that others can make these themes.- A brush feature for highlighting certain areas of the town as districts and ability to make them nameable.Dev: Keep up the excellent work!

_childDocuments_.review: After 6 hours and 3 townscapes, I really like this "game", and the price is a steal. I love how the grid adds a natural dynamic to the outlay without being too restrictive. If you have something particular in mind, you can just find a place on the grid that will fit.Of course there are a lot of elements you can't really control, for instance "street" width. I think the game strikes a wonderful balance between what you can and cannot control, and it does what I need it to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Just an honest to goodness chill time. No time commitments, no goals and no real deep mechanics make Townscaper one of the purest sandboxes I've ever had the pleasure to spend some time in.There is an easy joy in placing random blocks on the grid and seeing them develop into houses, buildings, towns while discovering new shapes or special interactions in the process.Pricetag wise, if 5€ seems a little steep to you or you're not sure if you're into the whole idea, then definitely wait until a sale comes around.I'll end the review here because, well, there really isn't much else to talk about. But to Townscaper's credit? That's not a bad thing at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Cornish Venice Simulator 2020When I was at school I used to doodle towns and cities and make them flow organically, without really knowing what building would come next or how it would interact with the previous ones I had just drawn. It was so fun and my only limitation was being bothered to draw more with a pencil. I remember wishing for a PC game like it that would allow me to create more.My wishes, after many years, have come true with this game. It's extremely simple in concept, and there really isn't much more here than clicking. But, do you know what? It doesn't need it. The detail in the buildings and decorations is impressive and no matter how complicated you make things, it always turns out looking smooth. The pastel colour shades are beautiful and you can zoom out after half an hour or letting your creativity wander and be truly surprised at what you've created.Above all, this game is incredibly relaxing. Like I say, it's a computerised version of city-building doodling I used to do when younger (and still do).Maybe they'll add more features, it would be interesting to perhaps see people and different categories of structures, but to be honest, the whole needs system you get in advanced city building games generates a level of stress that is pleasantly lacking here. This game is highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Super simple procedural game where you left click to place a tile and right click to remove. It uses wave function collapse to generate buildings, roofs, roads, gardens, etc., procedurally. It is super cheap, and I enjoy using the built in OBJ export feature, so I could print the model on a 3d printer; I have also tried to import the model (a flying town) into Blender and use it as a base for a small VRChat world, but still struggle to do so. I believe the developer made this more for a demonstration aid of wave function collapse, but I still find it amazing :D

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a digital artist who mainly does character art, but has recently been trying to get into full illustrations with backgrounds. For city backgrounds, I always need a reference, but I often can't find one that fits what I'm thinking. This is a great tool if that's an experience you've had, I use this to make references for all my city backgrounds now. There are different ways to view the builds you make (with textures, without, you can change the lighting a bit, etc.), and if you play around with the camera enough you can view most any angle of your build. My only issues as of the build I'm using are that the camera as I said takes a lot of playing with to get it where you want it. I like to get very specific shots and it's kind of a pain to get the camera right where I want it. Some sort of camera/posing mode to make positioning the camera easier would if that kind of implementation is possible would be really helpful in that regard. My only other note is since the houses kinda get built automatically you can't disable the bushes that appear. Which I would like to be able to do since I don't really want bushes in my backgrounds all that often, but that's a very subjective thing. And the last and my personal biggest issue is having to individually place landmasses. I'd like to be able to make a big map I can reference more than once, but it doesn't really feel worth the effort when you have to click each individual box to place a piece of land. It's not as bad with the house pieces since I don't group them all that much, but if you do you'll probably notice it there, too. If there's already a way to mass place landmasses and I just missed it somehow, then you can ignore this point entirely and that's my own fault. If not though, one of those could be useful. Those three things are my only issues, I otherwise really enjoy using it and I love how easy it is to customize. The different color options are fun to work with, and it's overall been super useful for as cheap as it is. I highly recommend it to artists who need background references because it has helped me a ton.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love it. Its not more nor less than I expected - the creator explains it the best - Townscaper is more of a toy than a game at this point. You have an empty sea and have to fill it up with buildings, as if you were stacking LEGO blocks. Townscaper lets you get really creative with its block combinations and I ended up building a Venice-inspired town complete with town squares, palazzos, a Doge Palace, an arsenal and garrison. I would be hoping for further combinations in the future - nothing that would change the character of the game mind you - but as rooftops spawn birds I would hope that big town squares would spawn market stalls and shoppers, parks would spawn people relaxing, long thin stretches of ground would spawn boats etc. Townscaper would also greatly benefit from a "proper" save system, rather than copying the seed to the clipboard.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great, calming, purely sandbox city-builder. I've said that I wanted a game where I could just build a city and not worry about infrastructure or strategy, just design, and this game lets me do that. There's no rules. You can build however you want and it adds little touches like doorway lanterns and rounded windows, octagonal towers, lighthouse tops, gardens with pathways, and balconies. There doesn't seem to be a limit to how high or how big you can make your city though it does start to lag a little once there's a lot to draw in. I would like to have some templates or starters to build off because sometimes my creativity isn't up to par. It'd be nice if there were both templates and the option to freestyle it. Some more textures for the streets and building would be nice as well.Overall, I love this game and play it any time I need to wind down or be casually creative.

All of these games give you an objective or some sort of end goal.This game gives you nothing other than to click anywhere on what I guess is a randomly generated algorithmic landscape and you build your town/city/metro however you please. And there is no objective. I love it. I don't have to stress myself to please townsfolk, manage garbage, or water sewage. I just make a few left and right clicks and boom! My place is made.I can see other skins/EPs into the future, so hopefully there will be more support for this game/toolbox.

_childDocuments_.review: The concept seems cool, but is very limited. Particularly, the controls are not intuitive at all. (Note: 24 likes for this review were before the edit at the bottom.)- The steam trailer very clearly shows a drag-to-build function that is not available in game, so building larger areas is slow and annoying. This is the main reason I refunded.- Having building and panning the camera both bound to left click is a huge mistake, and makes the gameplay feel very awkward and janky. I'd enjoy playing this game much more if the controls made any amount of sense.- There is no potential variety for style of building your making, and the game just throws in some small random things occasionally that you can't recreate. At one point, my town got a small dock/pier tile with staircases leading down, which looked really cool, but I couldn't make another one when I tried.I'd also really like to see a randomized color option.It seems like this is basically a proof-of-concept for a larger game idea, so I doubt the devs will update this or change any features listed. I think it's much more likely they're working on a larger game with more content.If the things above are changed, I would definitely recommend the game, but not in it's current state.Edit: so I ended up cancelling my refund and giving the game another shot. All the issues I mentioned above are still present, but I got a little more used to the controls. The controls are still janky, and makes zooming / tilting / placing lots of tiles at once very annoying, but the gameplay is pretty satisfying. I'm gonna change this to a tepid recommend, since the price is so low. The only real appeal to this game is the low pressure. I enjoy putting this on for a half hour when I don't have time to do much else. I don't think I'd be playing it much/at all if I was excited for any other games right now, but I'm mostly waiting for D2R and Deathloop.

_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: After 7 hours of playing sickly and obsessively, I can say that when I close my eyes I see the constructions I made. When I go to sleep, I dream of myself walking across the cities I built. And when I see buildings in the real life, I realized  most of them are made of imperfect cubic blocks, just like in Townscape.Is like a combination of Cities Skylines, playing with your childhood blocks, and european cities like Bruges or Vernice in a subtle combination... but without problems. You can't lose the game, but you can't win either. I shared some of my cities in the not so much populated Townscaper sub-reddit .Well. I haven't found the "Save City" option yet. Would be a good aggregate. I've had to destroy my creations to build new ones. Only the vanishing memory (and a couple of screenshots) remain of my first cities.I recommend this game. You'll relax or become mad. Or either both.

There're potentials of the variety in types of buildings like the churches, houses, bell towers and assembly halls in this game. But right now I'm good and fulfilled. _childDocuments_.review: A simply fantastic game. I can't believe it's only $6 either. I found myself up till 4 am, slowly creating my own town, and thinking about story lines to go with it. I love the little details the game auto adds, such as the birds, clotheslines, park benches, etc. I found myself wanting to try out crazing shapes, to see how the game would auto generate it.Three ideas I hope/wish the developers would add in the future. 1. Have the game have a starting option of either starting out in the "water" or a "land" option. Perhaps if there is a land option, you could remove areas to then make water areas such as small ponds/lakes. 2. I wish there was a tool or a "click and drag" option for auto creating or deleting mass areas. I found creating the foundations can get tedious as times, especially if you want tiered layers, and wish there was a way to quickly add them so I can move onto building creation. (If there is a tool for this, I have yet to find out how or where in the game). 3. Different color roof options, just for aesthetic reasons, and I can see it being helpful for bird eye views if you are using this for maps. This game is also has amazing 3D and mapping tools for those who would like to use it for DND. I don't do 3D printing, so I can't make a review on the files you can export, but I am going to convince my Dungeon Master start using this program for cool town/city concepts.

_childDocuments_.review: Unless you're some sort of sadist, this isn't going to be the sort of "game" you'll spend very long on. Simply by the fact it's not a game at all. Rather, a sort of point and click island building simulator. There's no goal here. Just place a block of pavement and stick houses of various heights on top of them. It does a very good job of handling various architecture scenarios (eg building over water) which keeps your interest that bit longer.Honestly, it's daftly satisfying and worth the price of a large coffee. I have some initial thoughts on the interface:1, Can we have a button hold (eg Alt) that allows you to drag around and create the pavements without having to constantly keep clicking.2. Can you let the user define the grid style. At the moment it's this wavy sort of quads. And although this makes for an interesting creative process, it doesn't account for a scenario perhaps where you have an idea in your head. So please. A square grid option.3. As others have mentioned, the island looks so lonely, except for a few birds on the roofs. Some people would be nice.4. Also, some way to add character to the houses. Perhaps be able to add a sign to make it look like a shop.I could see this becoming a game by adding achievements of some sort. Creating enclosed areas, having 100 houses etc etc. I dunno. This has weird potential this one.

_childDocuments_.review: There is no game here. It's simply a virtual stress toy which is fine to some, but not me. Although the game is clearly all about creativity, there is no form of progression which essentially locks the player into a small box of choices, rather than expanding slowly and inspiring the player to think outside of said box.. Unlocking new building types and being able to choose what types of buildings are placed would make this game way more enjoyable, encourage different flavours of creativity and increase it's longevity tenfold without hindering it's focus on relaxation and avoidance of a set goal.At 7 minutes I feel like I have seen everything that this "game" has to offer, that is probably a new record.Notice though that I haven't said that it is bad though, because it isn't. It does what it set out to do quite well, the issue is that what it set out to do is incredibly lacking in content and ironically creativity,since it entirely relies on the player's. On top of that after my 7 minutes of playtime and watching the trailers I really don't see any increase in possibilities, nothing stood out as "that looks cool, I should build that", I've literally done everything.The only downside I would say is that it bizarrely doesn't allow for player freedom, which inherently is an issue in a creative sandbox game with no goal. Want to have some stairs that go up to this other block? Nope, that's now a house.Want a long tunnel under a bridge? Nope, that's now a long solid block.Want to separate these to roads that are next to each other with a railing or gap? Nope, they are now attached and there's nothing you can do about it.It desperately needs a feature that allows players to alter a block's type or shape. The game would keep it's simplicity and flow, but will allow players to build what they truly want to. I would argue that this is the primary reason that 7 minutes was enough playtime for me to think I'd seen everything, because the blocks always play out in the same manner.It really gives off that feeling you would get while playing Minecraft where you're trying to build something but the blocks are just slightly too big for that thing you wanted to build, so now that thing needs to be twice as big as planned. And even Minecraft has started to fix that with the addition of different shaped blocks, fences, walls, windows and other decorative blocks.Again it isn't necessarily bad, but for a game that does so little it has no excuse to be anything other than perfect, which it just isn't.It's fine for players that just want to click and build blocks but there really isn't anything more to it than that. Personally I think I wouldn't have an issue with it if it was free as it comes off as a tech demo for something that might be bigger and better in the future, but right now it is a glorified fidget toy and not worth any amount of money.

Obviously, the distinguishing trait is that it is just about creating, the only game-play per say is figuring out what combinations of blocks do what: how to make stairs, terraces, gardens, towers, spires, etc.Visually, the game is utterly precious. The buildings are charmingly rustic, the birds are fat, the bushes jiggle, and there's lots of little objects that pop up with the buildings to give the towns you make some life.The towns you can make have a very... _childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, do you like making landscapes, purely out of buildings, in the middle of a nonspecific ocean?  If so, Townscaper, is the game for you.  Complete with absolutely no music (so you can play jazz in the background), Townscaper is an immersive experience, in which you create insane stacked houses, because anything else is boring and not what I like.  If you're like me, which none of you are, you enjoy sitting and doing nothing for an extended period of time.  Townscaper is like this, but with houses, which makes the experience 5000x better in every way, prove me wrong.  I've already made a stranded island of houses in the middle of the ocean, and I will surpass the size of the United States in five months.  My stack of houses is already higher than the Empire State Building. You've probably felt less power of your life in the past several years, but with Townscaper, you can BUILD it, MAKE it, CONTROL it.  You are your own president, and landlord, and house colorist, with a touch of a God's omnipotence.  Buy this game do it now.  I rate 10.

While limited in scope, there is enough content, refined to a playable level that can be enjoyed for a number of hours.Townscaper is a very enjoyable creative building toy.  Perfect for those five year olds looking to break into learning to navigate a three dimensional space.  And, it's fun for adults too.  There is plenty to discover in play.The content is very limiting though.  For the completed game I'd love to see some more animations.  Trains, hot air balloons, sailing ships, and sea monsters interacting with the environment.  Weather events would be fantastic to see, and even witnessing the effects of the the passage of time on player creations could deepen the player experience. There also needs to be more architectural variety to play with, but that is the obvious.As it stands the simplistic style and approach to play is elegant (and probably the real art to behold in any finished product).  From the mechanics to the sounds incorporated, Townscaper is a brief but hot bundle of joy to wade into.

_childDocuments_.review: Townscaper is a simple game about scaping your town. (go figure)The core gameplay is simple, you click on the ocean tiles to raise the level, first being a street or sidewalk and every level above that being a story of a house.  There is a decent range of colors to make your town vibrant.  The tiles are mostly randomly shaped, so your town wont be just a bunch of boxes, but feel more natural.  Add on little details like windows, patios, flower pots, clothes lines, etc. that appear when you connect buildings in certain ways (mostly up to the tile shape).  Beyond the "place building in cool pattern" there isn't much gameplay-wise.Graphics wise its not "ULTRA 4K HYPER REALISM" but a nice laid-back cartoonish style that just looks pleasing.Audio is nice.  There is some nice relaxing music that plays in the background as you place these colorful residences. Play time varies from person to person.  To the average person you should get at least an hour out of it as you test town layouts and building ideas.  To the more creative person or those who love this kind of gameplay will get virtually endless gameplay.Overall opinion is this is a nice game and fair priced.  It's great for relaxing after a stressful day, just boot it up and plop down my colorful abodes while listening to that soothing background music.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has no end. As the devs said, this is more of a toy box. perfect for just doodling around. If building a city of penis towers is your calling, go for it. Do note that camera movement is severely limited and very finicky when entering an enclosed area (it just becomes stupidly hard to control), and that you cannot edit the color of existing building blocks (you have to delete them first and replace it with the new color). I hope the dev can improve the camera control to be more sensible than what it currently is now.There are also some things that could be improved. of one particular annoyance is the lack of ability to mass-place blocks. that means if you want large landmasses, you need to INDIVIDUALLY PLACE THEM one by one. You can quickly see how this can get incredibly tedious when you want to build large islands (eg; a large island that requires more than 100 blocks. my hands are still hurting from that). The grid system is also confusing since the squares aren't actually showing where the block will be, but the crosses in them determine how the block will be shaped (and therefore the actual position, in a very painful to calculate manner).i would still recommend this game, but it's very tough for serious players that really want to be invested on this game, to actually be invested on this game comfortably.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok. This is the cutest thing I've seen in months. Plop, plop, plop, and you have a little village. All sorts of colors and shapes.And I'm pretty sure every one is made of pure ticky-tacky.But then come the towers! And the bridges! And other things more surprising. Wait. No! Startling! Yet, as exciting as the adventure gets, everything is fine in the end. Everything resolves into a beautiful, soft order.The story is left to the player to create. The combat is purely PvE - mostly involving birds. And the world is open and easy to navigate.( Which is good, since there are NO mounts or fast-travel points. )I do miss having any character customization - or any character for that matter. The tower I just built could really use someone cheerfully waving from the topmost window!Anyway, I recommend this very therapeutic game.Now, I need this on my iPad. ( And wouldn't it be swell if I could move my build from one to the other? I think it would. ):-)

_childDocuments_.review: My partner gifted this to me both because it's a really cute game and as a handy way for me to make city/architecture references for drawing. I love finding the tons of little surprise goodies with block combinations and getting birds to land.The only things I wish this game had are being able to put down a random color with each click, being able to conveniently put down a bunch of blocks without having to go through a clicking storm, and an ability to walk around in what you've built (and/or a more convenient way to zoom in more easily than the current camera allows). But even if the game never received another update, I'm more than happy with it in its current form.Overall, it's a super adorable game that's great for relaxing and exercising creativity in a wonderfully intuitive way. _childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this simply because it's miscategorized. This has nothing that would make something a game. Just because something is 3D, that doesn't mean it's a game. A game should have objectives or a story or both. At least any kind of challenges, achievements, or metrics to show your progress as a player. Like, highest floor built, how many meters of pavement, or how many windows in total. This has none of it.As a tool to build 3D townscapes, it's also kind of useless. Sure, you can make screenshots of what you have built, but the .OBJ file export is half-baked (it exports 3D object with broken textures). Texturing the 3D model to replicate all the shaders is not something a regular person could do with 3D Builder or Paint 3D apps, it should work out of the box or not be an option at all (like on mobile).There is one cool thing about it though - you can share your creations really easily, you just copy the state of your build to the clipboard and send it to a friend and they can paste it back into their app. So, when Wordle became viral, I was able to build a tool that converted Wordle results into Townscaper buildings So, while I have tried Townscaper on desktop, laptop, Android mobile phone, Steam Deck, and even in the browser, it's just a cute tool for me, which gets boring after 5 minutes. It feels like a prototype, unfinished.

Still getting updated, so more features are gradually being added. As is, though, it's nice and relaxing. Basically the same impulse that has people playing Animal Crossing so fervently, I suppose.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic townbuilding toy. The aesthetic is really good. No economy or management or difficulty, just plopping down buildings.Only complaint is I wish the map would get bigger but it's a good size already, I assume that's for performance reasons. Also not a complaint but I do with there was an option for like shops, just to breath a bit more life into it. Regardless of that it's a great game and well worth the asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: It sucks that I can't recommend this because it looks like so much fun on paper. Just click and watch the town build itself! It prides itself on being this "relaxing" experience, but from my experience the only thing this game gets from me is undying frustration. And it's all because of just one tiny snag.The problem is that you can only place one singular block at a time, absolutely no exceptions. Despite literally showcasing the ability to drag the cursor in the game's trailer, you have no way to place multiple blocks in a row. This makes the "calming" experience into such a tedious chore. Any building or town I can think of requires multiple hundreds of clicks just to plan. All of those giant towns and villages you see on the store page and community hub? Forget about making those.I truly cannot play this for more than 5-10 minutes at at time because it causes genuine pain in my hands in order to play properly. 200 clicks. 500 clicks. 800 clicks. One at a time, no exception. I want to play this so bad, but I doubt we'll ever get a click and drag feature because the developer confirmed that the game is "finished" and shouldn't be receiving any major updates post 1.0. It's so heartbreaking that I have to give such a cool concept a scathing review like this, but I seriously doubt your idea of fun is destroying your index finger just for the outline of a cool city plan.Apparently I'm the only one who thinks this? All the negative reviews for this game are judging it for what it isn't. You having little control over the building process is the whole gimmick, if you want to position every window and bench yourself play minecraft or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, some flaws.I really enjoy this game, and everything it offers. I like architecture and worldbuilding, so I find this game fascinating. There are a few flaws though, mostly due to its newness.1. The grid is not straightAlthough it can make for interesting shapes, the different shapes on the grid can morph your town into something you don't want it to be. Part of the problem is that you cannot control which block is which shape.2. You cannot draw many blocks at onceThere should be a shift click mechanic that allows you to draw or delete a row of blocks at a time. Since there isn't this mechanic, it makes destroying buildings difficult.3. You cannot delete savesIf you create a town you don't like, you cannot delete the save. Because you cannot widely delete blocks multiple at a time, this is very tiresome.4. You can't chose what to buildI expect this will be different later on but for now you cannot chose which types of buildings you want to build. This can be especially annoying when you place 5 blocks next to each other. This automatically creates a raised patio instead of a house. 5. There is only one styleI know this will likely change, but for now there is only one style of building. I think it would be cool later on to incorporate different architectural styles.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun, could use some quality of life changes tool though, for example : A fill tool.The option to change the shape of grid tiles, since you can't really decide what shape to make your .town, the grid is a repeating shape pattern so you're kinda at it's mercy to shape the base of your townKeybinds for switching colors without having to click on them.A way to click and drag for placement and deletion, currently you have to place each base/building down one by one.A color wheel so that instead of choosing from given colors you can customize them to construct your own palette.Workshop support so that people can add their own building skins, think like modern skyscrapers or old wooden shacks. And also for people to explore other people's townscapes.A way to place yourself in the streets of your city in a first person POV so you can see what it looks like from ground level. And also to be able to do this on workshop-downloaded townscapes. A way to construct bridges, currently you can't make high bridges because if you click on a base block it will always construct a building instead of another block which you could use to build your own custom bridges.Special buildings, like being able to designate zones for police/health and those buildings becoming a police station/hospital, not for use, just aesthetics. Also stuff like shops, clothing stores, patisseries, bookstores, with unique storefronts, etc. More street props, cars, animals (other than birds), signs, stuff like that.More building options in general, currently things are pretty limited, in order to create a park you MUST have an open space completely enclosed by buildings and sometimes that will glitch out and break if you build 2nd or 3rd layers around/in them. Let us build open parks, add it to the current sidebar or a new sidebar for special areas, pools, sports courts, stuff like that. That's all for now, obviously the game is in early access so I'm sure the dev is already thinking about and working on implementing many of these, just thought I'd put forward some suggestions that may be new to them. Overall, fun and relaxing game, I like to play it while watching other stuff on my second monitor since I don't think it's engaging enough to be played on it's own, at least not for me. It's pretty easy to build pretty settings without much, if any, thinking. Townscaper already has a very nice aesthetic, and I hope the dev can add new content while also staying true to the fundamental image of the game. I'm not going to give it a number rating since there's hardly anything to rate yet.

_childDocuments_.review: While I've only played for a very short period of time, I am absolutely in love with it. Being able to build up from the water and create whole towns/cities from nothing, coupled with the fantastic art style, gives the game an enjoyable and relaxing atmosphere. I was surprised at how well the game responded architectually when I would begin making multi-story buildings which would span over my roads. Loved the little arches and gardens which would automatically appear depending on how you placed buildings. On top of all the good, the developer seems to be very engaged with the community and cares about their feedback. I feel as though I can say, with reasonable certainty, that this is not just a money grab.With the good having been said (though there's certainly more which could be said), I do have a couple of things I hope to see in the future. For one, it would be great to have a mode where you could walk around the town you made in first person or something like that. Actually being able to explore what you've created would be a huge bonus. Another great thing would be the ability to choose where certain features such as the grassy areas could be placed. As of now, they appear automatically when you make a circle of buildings with an open space in the middle. While this is an awesome feature, being able to place these manually would be nice. And I might be the only one who thinks this, but I'd also enjoy being able to use a larger map. I found that I used all the space rather quickly.Overall, fantastic little (non)game. With how much I enjoyed it, the price seems like a steal. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game! I've only played for a little while but I'm already imagining all the cool things I can build. A few suggestions though to improve the controls of the game (without changing the game's content):1. Fix the camera by allowing it to move further away from the map constraints. Right now I have place little 1x1 platforms around anything I build so I can move away far enough from it to have a decent look at it overall. This isn't a solution when you reach the edge of the map entirely.2. Allow us to continuously add / delete blocks by holding down left and right click in combination with some other key. Like holding down shift + left click for example.3. Allow an option to only add or remove from a certain height layer. Adding to point 2, if I want to make a massive platform there should be an option that only allows me to build on that level (level 0 for example). When builds get massively tall it can be hard to tell what "level" a block is on, so there should also be an option to click on a block and have it be set to that level. Of course you can switch between level specific building and "free" building on any height level. 4. Allow a "paint" option to change the colour of blocks without having to delete then re-add them. If implemented along with point 2 and 3, multicoloured skyscrapers will be a breeze!5. Allow us to "select" some or all parts of the map to "copy to clipboard," then select a location on any map to paste it when "loading from clipboard." There should be a ghost version of where the copied material will be placed so we can see how it will look. This "select" function should allow us to delete all blocks in a selected section as well. 6. Let us change the controls for rotation and movement. I'd much rather use right click to rotate and left click to move!7. Let us completely delete maps we don't like. Now for a few suggestions about extra game content:1. Why not add some people milling around and walking? Birds are nice but people would be even better!2. More block types! Why not add grass / land blocks, cliff blocks, wall blocks, market blocks, and anything in between?3. Make the maps bigger (if performance allows it). I want sprawling metropolises! _childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings, I enjoy playing it, but the more I play the more I'm disappointed. Things don't quite snap in a way that you want them to, grass is super finicky and specific, I just wish there was more to it. I wish we could choose what tiles to put down, and just fiddle around a bit more.It's still fun to play, but it's just a bit disappointing that there is so little, and the developer is focusing on porting to other platforms, when there could be a bit more to it first.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: THANK YOU!I will start this review with this. This game is fantastic, and I have never thought I could love a simple game like this so much, but here we are. Not much to say: join, strat building, experimenting, expanding and much much much more. 50 minutes of my lunch break flew away like nothing, and I only stopped playing because I needed to go back to work You like building your fancy world, without any money, skills, levels or any kind of restrictions whatsoever? Buy this game. It costs like an hamburger, but it gives you thousands of fun. I hope the developers will add some simple stuffs (maybe the possibility to explore your town [camera only], or a train station), but this game is Hella perfect even now.What are you waiting for?Go and buy it!!
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: When I was a kid I used tom play with wooden blocks and other similar, using them to create buildings, realistic or as improbable as I could while keeping them standing.  Townscaper is like a computer version of that.It is more toy than game (as the developer calls it), and though all the blocks are the same size, the way you put them together can lead to many shapes.  You can create balconies in your tall buildings, elevated patios, arches and sky walkways, bridges, canals and more.  You can choose from multiple colors for your blocks, creating a collage of color in one building, if you want to.  This is a fun and very relaxing toy for building your towns on an irregular grid that can lead you towards making some interesting shaped buildings.It's early access and can use some things like a fill tool and a drag tool (currently we have one size blocks and a plop tool placing one block at a time).  As it is, however, it's fun and relaxing, something you can mess around with to relax, or to build cities/towns/buildings for gaming or art purposes.  It's a lot of fun, and you'll easily get your money's worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Bleep Blopp Blopp Bleep Bleep!I personnally think, the game is great. You will get a "free-building-there-is-no-right-or-wrong" game. You can freely explore and try, whatever you like to do. Obviously, there are some basic building rules, but that's all.My children, both 7 and 4, love it, because they can simple click, enhance their skills with mouse and most important, every click is a success and your city is growing / changing.For adults, I think, the fun is in exploring and detecting the matrix behind all "secrets". When does a lighthouse appear? When does a washing line appear? How to build a star shaped house... etc. etc. etc.In own phrase:5€, good investment for a simple, fun and harmonic game -  go for it!Cheers,Bleep Bleep Blopp Blopp Bleep .... ;-)

_childDocuments_.review: Thought this was a game, its not. its nothing more than clicking and it just kind of designs what ever its going to design.  I'd call it a kindergartners version of auto-cad. This is a city builder like spiting on canvas is art and bumper cars is formula one. _childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent little program to launch up in between other things and vibe making some cute little towns. The game's generator and tile grid can definitely have a bit of a mind of their own at times, so you have to work with the game and embrace the bends and quirks. In my opinion, this actually adds to the experience instead of hindering it as it prevents you from getting caught up in getting everything "perfect". You should know there is no finish line, you just build for the sake of building.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: "Townscaper" isn't a game. Well, it's not a game yet; it might be in the future. Then again, it might not; it's still in early access, and at this point is probably best described as a technology demo. Right now, though, it's a city-builder at its most basic. Click on a square, and a building pops up. Click on it again, and that building gets a second story (or a third, or fourth, or more, all depending on how many times you click). The squares seamlessly melt together into larger buildings. The goal - in as much as there is a goal - is to build yourself a pretty town. And, limited as it might be, I'm perfectly fine with that. This isn't a game (or however you want to describe it) for everyone. It's extremely sparse in features; there's no real variety in building types, and the maps themselves are pretty small. Still, the underlying tech is pretty neat and its quite fun to see structures grow out of the ground. Even with the tiny set of structures, you can still create an impressive number of unique cities too. Do I wish there was more to this game? Sure, but even if it only managed to hold my attention for a few hours, I think it well worth the price (a mere fiver) and I can imagine drifting back to fiddle about with it numerous times in years to come, just to play around - even if only for a little while - with its impressive visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is beautifully simple with loads of room for growth. Not to say that it is not a great game now but rather that I see the potential for it to become even better with a few more tools, aesthetics etc. I love the way the building forms react to various combinations with amazing attention to details, whether it is the birds exiting a roof as you build on it or the various bits of debris landing in the water, it is visually perfect. I recommend this game as a great way to explore your creative side within a beautiful architectural sandbox.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Such an imagination freeing tool!Obviously, it's a toy, not a game.I play with it to relax at the end of a day, or to actively get creative with cityscaping.As others have mentioned elsewhere, I would like to see more visual-themes for the buildings, and perhaps some enhancements in the exporting facility.All in all, very cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very enjoyable little demo / sandbox type game that is exactly what they advertise. It is nothing more and nothing less. Pleasant, mindless clicking with satisfying sounds and splashy effects.I found I didn't enjoy playing it for as long as I might have hoped to, but that says more about me than the game, I think. For example, I don't like doing intricate little coloring pages. If you enjoy that sort of thing, this is right up your alley!I'd love to see this game expand with little people and boats, or a simple unlock path to reward players with new colors or increased build height. None of that is necessary or expected, however. Kudos to the devs for delivering exactly what they said they would. Can't fault you!

_childDocuments_.review: It is more of a toy than a game, but in the best possible way. It's fun and relaxing to just listen to music and build away for a few hours, and have a nice looking town or castle or something by the end. The building system is very well made and intuitive, so it's quite easy to make good looking buildings. If you enjoy things like drawing or painting you'll probably enjoy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Townscaper is really easy to play. Everything you do feels and looks great, and there's a lot of different mechanics that you can learn about. I personally fell in love with the lighthouses in the beginning, but as I kept playing and I discovered the gardens I fell in love again. This game put me in a trance almost, it's like the video game embodiment of a habit I've had all my life... summed up, it's wonderful, and I can't wait to see what features get added next.The asymmetrical and random map structure also makes it really interesting to play as well, I found that quite amusing while starting my city. It creates unique challenges and unique shapes that are really pretty most times.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: The developer calls this more of a toy or experiment than a game and he is correct - this however does not impact the magic and wonder this very simple little procedural town builder (or painter, or creator - Im not sure what to call it) can create. The minimalist mechanics and intuitive design is amazing and what you can get out of something that on the surfaces seems so simple is a testament to how deeply creative this little game really is. A wonderful experience and I can see myself using this like I would a sketch book... if i need a few min to let my mind wonder somewhere else this will do the trick.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, this product can be called techno-demo of the features that the author strives to put in the game. I bought it as soon as I received an email about early access release. Before that, I followed the developer on Twitter, since the game really interested me at first sight.Townscaper looks like a city builder with procedurally connecting blocks of various heights. This process is meditative and breathtaking and uses your imagination. Blocks connected in a certain way turn into various special facilities, such as towers, stairs, arches, parks, etc. In fact, they are very interesting to find and combine. The process of designing cities makes me swoon, returns to the times when I had been connecting bricks from the building kit somehow and had been having a great time. I also want to praise the sound design and animations of the construction and demolition of the blocks, they create incredible feedback.The game has a huge potential for further development. Be sure to visit the forum!

Let there be light in the windows as the sun sets.It is just beautiful =)Do not have your boss in your friend list though ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Truthfully, like many other reviewers- I was bored.  I wanted something to do, but I didn't necessarily care if it was an accomplishment.I was having a horrendous day. I didn't want to use the 2 brain cells that I'm lucky enough to sometimes have functioning properly.  I wanted something I could sit, play for either 10 minutes, or an hour, and still feel like I am able to mentally unwind.For what? $6? I cannot complain in the slightest.  I didn't want something crammed with unnecessary details and decor..  The artwork itself is appealing, and isn't gaudy by design at all.  It gives off a very simplistic, animated film vibrancy.  It's quite the humble little game, and yet contains much more than meets the eye if the right creativity strikes as you use it.  I notice as you become more intricate with your designs, the more addicting it tends to become.Overall, it almost feels like you're creating a painting of a city, if that makes sense. A very amusing, serene little city creator.  Absolutely pleased with my purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's weirdly fun, considering how simple it is. Great to play kind of mindlessly, but you'll find yourself planning new cities even when you're not playing to see how it changes things. Would love to see more options that you can put in yourself. As cool as some of the random features are, it would be nice if you could choose where to put grass and parks, and maybe some other things. Still a great game, so glad I bought it.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great for being early access, it brings a special feeling of relaxation, although I wish they'd a options for extra props like people, fish etc to add a greater feeling to the game, also adding some calming ambient music or sounds. The whole building feature is simple, you place but the fact that the thing you place is different depending on where adds so many combos. I wish they would add the feature drag to place to make it easier to place in larger areas or fill as it would make the building aspect easier and therefore making it relaxing instead of being bored of placing so many buildings. But all of that may be added as it is still Early Access, even if they don't, I'm in love

_childDocuments_.review: Townscaper provides a fresh and simplistic city building experience that casts away sim game tropes leaving a relaxing, and surprisingly, in depth city builder that's great for killing a few hours or more as you find new ways to create wonderful and complex structures with ease. Perfect for designing DnD maps, or desktop backgrounds, its a toy that too can be a tool.

Even in early access I can say that this is THE game I'll play after a stressful day. It's calming and oddly satisfying. I can see it having big potential. Add some calming music, Minecraft style. I'd recommend if you really like these calm games, but at least for me it gets boring after some time. Ah, and I had to play it while watching something so that it wasn't so boring.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: This is a super fun and easy tool to build a colourful city. You can let your imagination run wild and buy as high and wide as you want to. Plus, you can even set the lightning mood and take screenshots. Just wanted to add that I found the music in select screen very beautiful and wish it was an option as a background music while building, that you could turn off when needed. I can see myself use this for worldbuilding purposes. Very cool!!
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun little sandbox, cute buildings, and do like the optional view changes (pencil drawing, fully rendered, or all-white 3D mockups).Also fun to change the lighting, from warm to cool, sunrise to sunset -  feels a bit like painting postcards of quaint little villages.Navigation was a bit tricky with just a trackpad/mouse, but if you use the arrow buttons for movement, and limit the trackpad to zooms and rotation, it's much less frustrating. Also, not much in the way of any tutorial or directions, so it's all about discovery, which can be cool, especially since it's just a sandbox, no threat of death or 'losing' anything. It's basically an etch-a-sketch for towns, if you don't like what you've put up, just shake it up and start over!
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: I literally never review games... but this game. this toy. this is worth it. this game is worth every penny. yes there is much more that can be added to the game but for the price and what you get. its as good as you are gonna have for a sandbox game. its a perfect game to turn off your brain and just let your creative side shine.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous little toy, with a surprising amount of variety despite its infancy. Oskar, the dev, regularly updates both the back and front end with little tweaks here and there, and it's nice to see a project like this be received so well. For a humble asking price, it's certainly worth grabbing and is an excellent resource with which to de-stress, wind down, or alleviate boredom. It's still in development though, and as such I'll throw my hat in the ring with a suggested feature I'd like to see, that being a "ripple" tool. I'd like a toggle option to click a point and have a little town square, or residential area, pop up instead of the individual plots. Perhaps a drag selection, or a shift click function. That's my idea.Get Townscaper now, support the dev, make little canals and apartments.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's a toy, akin to the blocks and legos from decades passed. One would wonder, "Why buy this game? It has no point!" That is the point of a toy. That person would have played with real toys when they were younger. The young of today would play with toys like this.Long gone are the days of blocks and legos. Toys like this shall reign long and well.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's important to know exactly what it is that you're expecting to get from this when paying for it. If you want more, you won't be satisfied. If, however, you just want a cozy game to play without much stress, without storyline or characters, this is worth the price, even if just as a monetary value of appreciation for this indie game.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review: Having just crossed the 2 hour threshold in one sitting, I can safely say that Townscaper is an amazing game, and an amazingly simple one at that. But the further you dive, the more complex you can get. Different shapes (based on the randomized grid) and 16 colors for buildings allow you to mess around to your heart's content. You'll discover all the varieties of special things you can build (gardens, archways, towers, etc) the more you play.Above all, Townscaper is a great way to relax. The sound of placing building pieces is soothing, in my opinion. But if you don't like it you can always turn it off and enjoy the silence or put on some music.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

_childDocuments_.review:
Build quaint island towns with curvy streets. Build small hamlets, soaring cathedrals, canal networks, or sky cities on stilts. Block by block.

No goal. No real gameplay. Just plenty of building and plenty of beauty. That's it.

Townscaper is an experimental passion project. More of a toy than a game. Pick colors from the palette, plop down colored blocks of house on the irregular grid, and watch Townscaper's underlying algorithm automatically turn those blocks into cute little houses, arches, stairways, bridges and lush backyards, depending on their configuration.
_childDocuments_.name: Townscaper

name: Broken Pieces
detailed_description: Please wishlist the game to stay up to date! Mainly created by a team of 5 people , Broken Pieces is the first game to come out of the French game development studio Elseware Experience . When Elise and her fiancé decided to leave urban life and settle near the French coast, she could not imagine that she would end up completely alone. Now, surrounded by strange phenomena in a dark, post-Cold War climate, Elise will have to investigate and unravel the mysteries surrounding the region of Saint-Exil, its ritualistic cult, and its lighthouse overlooking the coast. Broken Pieces is an action-packed investigative and adventure video game set in France. The game puts you in the shoes of Elise, a woman in her thirties who finds herself in the village of Saint-Exil in an imaginary region reminiscent of Brittany. Following an unexplained paranormal phenomenon, Elise is stuck, completely alone and out of time. Your investigation begins here… Playtime : 9 to 12h. DLSS supported. Explore the area of Saint-Exil and its surroundings in the 1990s. Choose between either a standard TPS camera as well-known in modern TPS or a completely revised version of the camera system that accompanied legendary game franchises of the 90s, aimed at providing greater flexibility and player agency. Switch between 2 camera angles in any situation or drop into a first-person view to have a closer look around. Interact with the environment to learn more about what has happened to you in Saint-Exil. Your investigation will be rhythmically punctuated by cinematic sequences, with motion entirely captured from handheld cameras. Enjoy a thriller atmosphere in your adventure to the fullest extent. Keep an eye on the time with your watch; it is imperative that you get home before nightfall. Manage your inventory capacity and ensure that you carry about what you need to make progress. A variety of additional interactive elements, such as a vintage arcade machine, is available in your main and secondary quests. Change the weather of Saint-Exil to forge new paths or solve the puzzles blocking your way. You will discover tapes from which you can draw clues to help you in your investigation. Use the tape player to fast-forward or rewind the tapes and home in on the information you seek. Listen to your tapes while exploring the village of Saint-Exil and enjoy a seamless experience of discovery. Discover the music composed by Pierre for Élise that will accompany you in your adventure. Face challenging enemies with a unique combat system using fixed camera angles. Dodge your enemies or hold them at a distance using your powers to better defeat them. Restore your health by grabbing a drink in the fridge, catching a nap on a bench or spending a night in the safety of your bed. Craft high-quality ammo and upgrade your gun to increase your fighting abilities.

_childDocuments_.review: Story is intresting and the Game is pretty stable, never met any bugs. And the puzzles are great.However the combat is at its best decent and at its worst pretty bad. (I played in Normal)Dodging isn't reliable, your character misses 2/3rd of her shots which discourages using HQ ammo and instead just spam normal ammo. There's only 1 enemy type and as the game goes on it increases difficulty by putting more of them. Worse, you cant move while aiming, which is fine but its really hard to dodge attacks by moving and some combat requires mobility which the aiming mechanics doesn't give you.Its fine during the 1st half of the game but by the end it gets boring and frustrating. Specialy when at the end you see there used to be more enemies planned but they were scrapped in development.Still, the story and puzzles make up for it, so I still recommand the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pixel hunting "find the key" adventure game.  1000 locked doors, click on everything in sight, miss the one thing you need to progress, go back through all over again and click on everything in the entire world until you find the one key.  Open the one door, gain access to more rooms and more locked doors.  Keep clicking on everything in sight and hope you find the next key. _childDocuments_.review: I have spent a bit of time debating myself about this, but at the end of the day, I just couldn't bring myself to give this game a recommendation. My main issue with this game is that it, in essence more closely relates to games like "The Park" as opposed to classics like "Resident Evil" or "Silent Hill" but has a system setup meant to replicate 3rd person horror games of the PS1, Dreamcast and PS2 era.What didn't work for me:The Story:I liked the approach that the developers went with to let the story unfold through collected tapes and recorded thoughts from our protagonist. But since you are thrown in the middle of these events with no real connection to anything, you are relying on the final scene to throw everything together, which it unfortunately doesn't. (I hear that the developers are patching the ending, but that should have been done before release)The story gets very interesting halfway through, which makes the lackluster ending all the more unsatisfying. Combat:Just bad. It took me a while to realize that you have to wait for the aiming crosshair to shrink in order to get a clear shot on your enemies. The dodge does not work well. Think of the dodge mechanic in the Dreamcast game "Illbleed" but instead of it being broken in your favor, it's the complete opposite. Thank goodness for the "Knockback ability". There is also a mode that tones down the combat, which I recommend. The combat serves more as something to break up the monotony of running around all over the place, but honestly in my opinion should have been left out all together.What I Have to give credit to:If you can get immersed in the game, the note taking system and cassette tapes do fill you in on what you are supposed to be doing throughout the day. Actually reading this stops you from doing too much backtracking.I thought the music was phenomenal!The graphics were pretty good!The puzzle tables were challenging!If I had to give this game a grade, it would be somewhere between a 5.5 and a 6, but I just found this experience too drab to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Broken Pieces

_childDocuments_.review: All in all nice game, but I'd put it as neutral, if I could, as I couldn't recommend it.It simply has too many things wrong with it. There's a good game hiding in there, but it's hiding well. And it's not worth $25Some level areas are beautifully made. Some areas like the museum feel like there should have been more, but in general, the game looks nice and has many nice details.The journal with the clues and objectives was nicely done. collected all the clues related to an area in a central place.In general, the game feels like the devs cared about it, which is probably true for many/most indie games.But with the good stuff out of the way..The story is engaging in the beginning. But it goes nowhere. At the end of the game you feel like you played chapter 1 of 3 or so, because nearly nothing is resolved in the end.What was ? Don't know. Why did the cult do what it did? Don't know. Where did the stones come from? Don't know. What are those shadows? Don't know. Why weren't the birds affected from what spirited away all humans? Don't know. Why did the water fall upwards at sea? Don't know. And so on.When the outro rolls you really think "wait where's the rest of the game? we just got started!"The handling is really cluncy. you play third person, but your viewpoint is a random location, not over the shoulder (which would have improved this game greatly). They probably went for the silent hill 'look and feel' and I can't say if they nailed it because I never played that game, but it really doesn't work. Run one way in one direction, the camera switches and it's kinda random if holding the same key will continue you on your trajectory or turn you around. Thanks to the fixed, and poorly choosen camera perspectives, you very often have to hit the "switch perspective" button so you actually see things.The combat is dog poop. It could have actually worked, as simple as it is, if the controls wern't as unresponsive. Can't remember how many times I mashed space with her just standing there. And really, Elise or what your name was, you have to take 3 seconds to aim for the dude right in front of your face?Also, there is only one enemy types. Two if you wanna count the same enemy with a red energy barrier. The outro showed concept pictures with more, why is that the only one?The puzzles.. Also were pretty bad. Most of the time they were very easy, if voice lines didn't spoil it immediately. The times they weren't they required moon logic. For example, there is a circuit box out of your reach that you need to see the contents of. It looks bolted shut. So what do you do, search a ladder? get up there and try to loosen the bolts? Nah you summon a storm because it just looks bolted but flaps open in the storm. There was actually a voice line spoiling this, but at the time it played I looked at a truck with planes over it and thought you were meant to move them (they didn't)A smaller example was once you had to lure birds to press a button, because apparently the machine doesn't work with the birds there. No, don't ask me, I don't know why either. But from voice lines you know what to do. So you throw down the lure and sprint to the button. Thanks to the awful camera you can't tell what the birds are doing.Turns out you have to throw one lure for each bird, because nobody ever heard of multiple birds fighting after the same food, right?There are 7 puzzle boxes strewn about and those puzzles were though, at least for me, but they're side content.The whole thing being time based was anoying. Do I do this now or do I go back home, sleep and try to find my way back?Speaking of annoyances, the inventory. How did "you can only carry a lever or an axe" improve the game in any way? Instead it forces you to leave stuff behind and then later potentially search for a long time to find it again.Also, plenty of machine translation.The funniest thing is that the voice actress clearly didn't give a damn about that. An english voice actress without accent prooobably knew enough english to know that "The access is condemned at the top" doesn't make too much sense. I could believe it in cases like a blocked door and "the cult condemned this door", because she lacked context, but the example with the ladder really has no excuse.Oh and a long, unskippable credit sequence is always an automatic minus point for me.

_childDocuments_.review: In short:- If you expect an RE/SH experience: You will be disappointed.- If you expect an interesting adventure mystery game with easy-to-medium difficulty puzzles: You will love this.- Expect horror?
