_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for June 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 2nd, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.X-COM Warhammer style. Battlesector takes all the Warhammer lore and puts almost all of it on a shelf, you have Space Marines, you have an alien race like the Zerg, and you fight.  The combat is done in X-COM’s style, moving on a grid and taking shots at enemies, with a lot of randomness involved, but also a lot of awesome space battles.  It’s distilled from Warhammer in a pure essence and is the most similar to the board game with those changes.  There’s a story mode here, as well as two other single-player modes, custom campaigns are available also apparently, and multiplayer. But there are two races I mentioned.  I believe there are also four others.  The problem is you don’t get those.  If you want the entire game now, you’re paying 60 dollars.  And those additional races are only for the additional modes, plus there are elites for the two main races as well.  There are no new additional campaigns involving them.  That’s a lot of money, and I know Warhammer is one of the most expensive hobbies, but does that make it ok for the game to demand double the price to get all the content in it?  I’ll answer that, absolutely not. Pick this up if you want X-COM in the Warhammer universe, the campaign is over 20 hours, and there are two other modes you can play more of and even playing online.  However, I do struggle with how the DLC feels like they should have given players a bit more for the purchase.  This is what I was afraid of when Game Pass came around, a lot of games where you get only a part of the game upfront and have to pay for more DLC just to get what feels like a complete experience. There are coupons for some of the DLC in the bundle but it’s still about 30 dollars for the rest of the game, and even that isn’t all the DLC, or all the races, because of course there’s more.   And I do have a bit more experience with this title, due to Xbox Game Pass playtime, but I can say this really does stand upIf you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings!  Today we’ll be reviewing “Warhammer 40k:  Battlesector” a turn based strategy game that I like to think is more like X-COM at the army scale (instead of squad scale).  The 40k IP has been long associated with amazing games while simultaneously associated with some major disappointments.  So, which of two is this?  Let’s Discuss.It’s a SPACE MARINE:  At the core this game is a square based strategy game of numbers and for many lacks the rush of an RTS but with that slower pace comes more focus on the tactics.  Mistakes can cost you greatly and many units are capable of wiping out other units in a single action.  Movement and action economy is massively important and understanding both your units and the opponents is the key to success or failure.  For the most the animations and sound effects are spot on, though I still feel melta and plasma weapons sound a bit off.  There is also the way the Carnifex and Trygon move that just feels a bit goofy.  I would have also liked to see the mechanics explained a bit more thoroughly, even in manual or archive of some kind.  As it is to really understand how something works you have to do a decent amount of research outside of the game.  But aside from that the game feels 40k, I love how the units (most of them) move dynamically around the screen instead of more blocky movement in other games this genre.These aren’t the Ravens you’re looking for:  The most glaring issue with this game is the lack of factions, it desperately needs more than 2.5 (no spoilers) of factions.  I’d love to see Tyranids get their own campaign as well.  The .5 faction should get fully fleshed out and their own campaign as well.  I’d also like to see some additional ways to play; there is the ‘telephone mode’ which is a great addition but would love to see larger battles with multiple players / ai.  The game could also expand on the already done factions, more weapons and other non weapon options and maybe even a no-story campaign map against multiple AI?  There are so many possibilities and I am excited to see what they do with this game.Nom Nom Bugs:  The single most annoying aspect of this game is the 20 unit cap.  At higher points (even in the campaign) this massively limits what you can bring.  Most games tend to limit the higher tier units but this one seems to do the opposite.  I have 2k points to spend and 6 of my 20 slots are spent on named characters that I must bring and still have to find a way to spend 2k points with only 14 units.  Don’t get me wrong this is easy, but it takes the flavor out when I’m replacing all my frontline troops (intercessors and assault marines) to get higher cost units just because the Thunder Hawk doesn’t have the room.  Later in the game you get access to cheaper frontline units that I really wanted to play with but because of the points I never really got to include them.This game could be a game changer for the IP and genre if given enough support and I find myself playing it daily even after completing the campaign.  Here is hoping we see more factions with their own campaigns and I will happily buy them.  Highly recommend this game.  Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector is not only the best 40k licensed game since Space Marine, it's also an impressively good turn-based-tactics game in it's own right. Combat is robust, sometimes punishing, but always transparent and easy to grasp from the get-go. The sound design is outstanding, with lots of meaty carnage, guttural screams, and heavy gunfire against a backdrop of space-gothic music and suitably melodramatic vocal performances. Fans of the X-Com series will find the tactical gameplay familiar, even if battles take place at a platoon or company scale rather than squad. The campaign itself is better likened to traditional RTS's of the past - a linear series of story based battles - but with the added strategic depth of creating a customized force of spess mahrines who slowly gain experience and die permanently if lost in battle. The story itself is nothing too ground-breaking, but it's anchored by the aforementioned voice performances and the Warhammer 40k mainstay of a war between billions being portrayed as a character drama between 7 or 8 self-serious sci-fi archetypes. It's all crunchy and I love it but it is far from memorable.The only criticisms I'd level at the game are minor. I wish I could zoom out a hell of a lot more than I can, because the current maximum camera distance hardly offers one a broader sense of the battlezone. It leaves one having to mentally construct a geography of the map from many smaller frames, like a jigsaw puzzle of a repetitive desert landscape. I know there's a "map" view, but it feels so abstracted from the actual topography that it's not much help. Also, the game does not communicate nearly so much information about the cover system as it does every other mechanic in the game, which is a frustrating but exceptional oversight.Overall I'm thoroughly enjoying Battlesector, and I'm looking forward to the upcoming faction release(s?) and new strategic campaign mode.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly a classic case of a possibly great 40k game ruined by greed.The Good:The gameplay itself has good bones, you get a decent amount of choices for both building an army and how to use it on the battlefield. Cover does exist to a degree as well.The skirmish has a good amount of customizability with freely adjustable points limits for both teams seperately as well as local hot seat which is rare to see (also great for people who want to get the MP achivements done solo). So if you want to play against a tide of gaunts with only a few Marines you could do that.MP games exist in both "realtime" and asynchronous versions.The campaign has some nice ideas and the story is servicable.The Bad:The game is way overpriced for what it is and after release has more or less become a DLC farm. Classic Slitherine DLC policy that is in my opinion worse than Paradox. The base game has only 2 factions and a 20 mission campaign for one of them. While not terrible the campaign isnt really hard even on the highest difficulty. The "hard" part of the campaign comes from the devs pulling a bunch of "gotcha" moments on you. Mainly in the form hiding a lot of artillery units that delete infantry or spawning units behind your back after you advance from your spawn. Once you wise up to it and spam armor the game becomes trivial again.You also get skill points to upgrade your army but the skill tree is littered with point traps with no way to reset them.Once you are done with the campaign you can play either skirmish, MP, or planetary supremacy. Planetary supremacy is basically like the Dawn of War Dark crusade campagin but without any special mission, persistent building, honor guard or memorable strongholds. It's just a bunch of skirmishes while the pointslimit of the armies gradually grows the more territory you hold.Balance is kind of out of whack with DLC factions ranging from bad to completly oppressive. Also the 2 base factions have DLC that reintroduce units that were cut at release to sell them back, while not necessary in the campaign they do fill roles in the army in the other modes.The AI, even on the "smart" mode, is dumb as a brick and not much of a challange in both campaign and skirmish.MP itself outside of asynchronous is kind of dead unless you search for players on a discord or similar.All in all the game could have been a lot better if the base was iterated on a bit more but it feels like the focus was more on milking people with DLC. If the DLC had at least a small campaign included I would have been more lenient on them. The base game is also not worth it at full price in my opinion. As of this time it goes down to 20 euros on a sale which could be considered ok for some people. I still had a good time with the campaign and it could be worth it to you if you like to play skirmishes against the AI or the supremacy mode. Personally I think it's still not the greatest value and there is a reason you can buy keys for this game at sometimes below 1 euro.

The core game play is wonderfully simple, using only Left Click to select your abilities, and Right Click to execute them once you mouse over an opposing unit.  The maps are just the right size.  Army generation and composition is intuitive, while at the same time informative and simple.  It will run wonderfully on the Vega 11 integrated graphics system.  I have no complaint's about the game.  The main difference between this game and Total War, is that every unit you play in this game feels special in some way.  Each unit has some special ability that it can use.  It doesn't just apply to the commanders of the army, like it does in Total War.  Each unit feels special and, in some way, fun to field and play.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. What can I say about "Dawn of War - Light"? Although, "Dawn of War - Zero sugar, zero taste" sums it up better. Pros:Looks good.Runs well. Cons:Even the most basic features for a game of this type, seem to have been forgotten or left out deliberately by the devs (see the thread "line of sight?") where they explain how it was a deliberate decision not to include any meta information to know if a unit has LoS when moving to anyone new square.Can't access map screen while deploying units... seriously, are you r*tarded? That is the basic minimum of functionality I expect of a game when I have to deploy my units. Also, allied units available on turn 1 don't add their sight to your battlemap while deploying... sorry, but at this point you are incapable of actually designing any sensible funciont. How is it a strategy/tactics game if I literally have to save/reload to get any meaningful intelligence about the mission?The campaign... is a joke, really. Starting out interesting, but gets boring and cheap really quick. Exocrenes (Tyranid artillery) which are huge, and you have zero way of knowing that they are there will regularly snipe from far into the shadow of war entire squads with one shot, which you had for ~8 missions. If you don't want to lose them, replay the last half hour of your mission. How the f*ck can you have learned so infuriatingly little from games like dawn of war or literally any other well made game in the turn-based sector? You get ZERO intelligence from the mission briefings, it's just a "hurdur, sum lore" ramblings from voice actors that sound heavily constipated. Since when have the blood angels become functionally r*tarded and are doing zero scouting?The models look good but are hilariously stupidly animated and implemented. What I mean, is, if you let your dual-assault cannon predator tank attack a swarm of small units, it is having a seizure, because instead of... just vaguely shooting at the square of the unit, it reorients itself everytime a unit dies, to perfectly line up with the next target, which - in case of firing on many small units, killing about 4-6 depending on hit% - looks hilarious but also stupid and should be something so obvious, they should've removed since beta.Sorry, but with all the glaring "this should be in pretty much every godd*mn turn-based game for a reason" kinda issue, I am not even going into the glaring QoL issues, e.g. no option to fast forward your own turn (unit animations) but only the enemies, like... wtf? Or information in general. E.g. you can purchase an upgrade for "all Primaris Units", well, haha, joke's on you, because the game never tells you WHICH UNITS ARE PRIMARIS... how can you be so flaming oblivious of your own shortcomings? Devs in the forums go: "yeah, it was a deliberate decision, so live with it". In that case: Go f*ck yourselves and don't expect me to buy anything from you or your publisher, ever again, if that is your reaction to obvious shortcomings.Altogether, I see quite some threads of people making good points about how the game is lacking in very specific, yet very basic departments for a game of this type. Devs just shoo any complaint with "this was a deliberate decision", like how TF is that even an argument? That's not making it any better! That's like admitting to the judge it was in fact  not manslaughter, since you absolutely wanted that other guy dead, so you plead murder... good job, I guess?TL;DR: Lacking very basic gold standards for turn-based strategy, devs are way too far up their own *ss to fix any of that, so even for 50%, this game feels meh at best. Another game finding itself among the ranks of mediocrity in a long line of busts in the WH40k franchise, only garnering a lot of positive reviews because at this point people are so starved for something good, they have so low expectations, that even this turd is a positive surprise. If you don't trust yourself about the pink glasses you are wearing, give this a chance if it's reduced by about 80%, no earlier. Edit: Oh, yes, let's not forget the magically appearing "reinforcements" literally next to your units. "Strategy" my ass.

They're asking for a LOT of money for DLC race packs that are only good for multiplayer, which is fairly dead even if I wanted to play it, and skirmish mode, which is incredibly tedious and plays out much the same every time. It's a pity they don't release the race packs with campaigns, as that would add so much more incentive to buy them, but as it is I'm done with the Blood Angels campaign (there is no Tyranid campaign included either) and zero incentive to pay through the nose for Necrons or anything else that has no decent use in single player.Still, get it on sale, absolutely ignore all the cash-grab low-effort DLC and have fun for fifteen or twenty hours.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is in my opinion excellent. I have recently looked into the whole warhammer 40k universe and this game was recommended when I searched for a good warhammer 40k- game and I'll tell ya - this game is awesome. (pardon me if this review is bad. My native language isn't English and I overall suck at writing large texts)I didn't expect for the campaign to be anything remarkable and I was pleasantly surprised. (Minor spoilers, but I tried to water it down a little) I had already known some lore of the blood angels, and the 16th mission had some squads of the Death Company's Assault Marines. I was very interested how that would play out, and left the mission with some sadness for the Death Company marines. The second objective of that mission required ALL of the Death Company marines to be sacrificed, or how the mission implied it: "Assist Death Company units to meet an honourable end". That and the words of Lieutenant Carleon at the start and end of the mission had me touched. I was so honoured by them, that I put one unit of the Death Company marines in my army and I was determined to get them through the campaign to a glorious victory for the Imperium. Ironically they died right after at the next mission :D.The 19th mission was great as well. The objective of the mission was to recover and defend the body of a Librarian Dreadnought named Brother Quindar, after going berserk against the tyranids. The dialogue at the end of the mission really left me quite miserable, due to Brother Quindar being my favourite character in the campaign. I see all of the dreadnoughts from the loyalists to be all these wise and competent warriors, that have battled centuries against the xenos, thus I admire them. Which makes Brother Quindar my favourite. He was very wise and comforting with his voice. Every start of the missions he was there speaking about his wisdoms and tales. Like the Death Company, I had put a Librarian dreadnought to my army to get vengeance for Brother Quindar. 20th mission was the last mission and also the next of the 19th mission, where Brother Quindar died. In the 20th mission, the objective was to kill the hive tyrant that had caused all the chaos we have dealt with through the whole campaign. If I recall right my newly recruited Librarian Dreadnought killed the Hive tyrant, which was nice revenge-moment to honour Brother Quindar.The Campaign is great overall. The other missions were great and more importantly challenging. The game is as close as it gets to the real life tabletop. The game makes you think how to deal with your enemies with your troops, and how you use their movement- and action points. I was comparing many times which way to attack was the most optimal, and when I chose and executed the most optimal action, there were always some tyranids coming out of the view range and throwing a wrench into my tactics. Which I weirdly like.There are still many modes to play, like multiplayer and few large scale modes which I have yet to try, but eventually will. I am at the moment of writing this starting to get into the tabletop and painting my first minis, also I'm playing Dawn of war 2. I'd recommend this game to every 40k fan and everyone, who are into turn-based strategy games in general. For 40k fans, only minus I can think of are the factions. There are total of 5 factions, which are blood angels, tyranids, necrons, orks and Adepta Sororitas aka Sisters of battle. I also find this a little annoying flaw, but hopefully they'll add more in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very happy to be able to leave a positive review on a 40K game lolSo... where to start with this game. It's not the most difficult game in the world, at least on normal. But it's fun. I enjoy it. The game tries to emulate the feel of the tabletop, and I think it did a pretty good job. I don't get the people complaining that the game doesn't have a leveling system, or that you can lose 100 marines and still win the battle just fine. I don't get those people.Because since when do either of these things come up in the tabletop? Never. There's no leveling in the tabletop, there's no exp system as your little plastic models are shooting at each other, the amount of models or units that die on the tabletop don't factor into the overall game, especially in 9th(unless the one or both players have a secondary that gives them points when they kill so-and-so number of units, but that's besides the point)The game isn't trying to be XCOM, it's trying to be the tabletop, and, again, I think it does a good job.Overall, the game looks pretty nice, it plays well, and, while the Blood Angels aren't my favorite chapter, I'm happy to see them getting some love. Blood Angels are interesting, and they don't get enough rep in video games, I think. I'd love a Blood Angels game where the black rage is an actual game mechanic, like Metroid Prime 3 with its corruption meter or something like that.I can't really speak much to the quality of the voice acting, I think it does its job fine, and it's not bad. I'm not a voice actor myself, so I can't really pick out the finer points or anything. It's not bad voice acting, it's just not amazing I think. The story isn't anything remarkable, but most stories in 40K games aren't. It's always just a new excuse to go to a place and kill everything, which is fine. If I wanted a story I'd go the read the books lol.The gameplay is not the most engaging stuff ever, but it has just enough going on to keep me interested. The ability to determine the length and general area of your overwatch is nice, wish more games with overwatch mechanics did that, helps avoid wasting overwatch shots on the wrong thing. And, again, on normal the game isn't very hard. You're probably not going to need to play on easy, unless you're completely new to strategy games. You're going to be steamrolling over most things once you get your bearings on the current map, and will only really have trouble against certain speedbumps(*cough cough* exocrines *cough cough*)tldr; it's a good game, which makes it better than 80% of the other 40K games out there, and the gripes I've seen some people have with this game really only reaffirmed my belief that most die-hard 40K fans are completely unpleasable.

_childDocuments_.review: I will claim Battlesector as my official entry into the universe of Warhammer 40k. Previously, I played less than two to three hours of Dawn of War and Space Marine--not enough to really get into them. Diving into Battlesector, I started with the campaign to give me a feel for the Warhammer universe. The campaign has players in control of Blood Angels clearing out lingering Tyranid forces after the Devastation of Baal to prevent things from going bad to grim dark worse. It's a focused and small story that both is and isn't of great magnitude. What's more catching, story-wise through the campaign, is just witnessing the Warhammer 40k universe play out through voice acting of the HQ/hero units before, after, and rarely during, missions.Campaign missions are enjoyable while challenging. I had fun with the turn based combat and didn't find myself saving often as careful strategy seemed to pay off rewardingly well. Each mission has enemy setups and map layouts that keep you on your toes. Level design seems to aim for providing a different type of location to do battle in for each mission, which keeps the variety going throughout 20 missions on the red moon of Baal Secundus and makes for some memorable experiences. In the second half of the campaign, I had a lot of fun with a siege mission requiring the player to get a unit(s) over fortress walls to open one, or both, giant gates to take on enemy forces.As a player essentially new to Warhammer 40k and not a big strategy gamer, it took me 34 hours to complete the campaign on normal. It should be noted that 20% of that time was spent trying to complete mission 10, 'Landing Pad,' without failing the bonus objective. That mission is the worst! The bonus objective, which awards desired upgrade points, is so dependent on RNG and constantly reloading saves that I had zero fun with the several hours it took to finally be successful. Word to the wise, skip the bonus objective because you won't even need all those upgrade points--maybe on higher difficulties. Focus your unit specific upgrades on the units you will use in your army, as you won't have space to effectively deploy all unit types at once, anyway. There's no need to pour hours into the poorly designed bonus objective of mission 10. That mission left a bad taste in my mouth but I pressed on... for Sanguinius! [That's the kind of thing you're obligated to do when you're into Warhammer, right?] Fortunately, I found the remaining missions get back to the standard set by the earlier missions with no random RNG dependent objectives.Outside of the campaign, game modes seem to aim at creating a playground for tabletop experienced players with a single player skirmish mode and two modes added for free post-release. Demonic Incursion is essentially a horde or wave battle mode and Planetary Supremacy provides an opportunity to play some skirmish battles that fit into a larger conquest. I've read that people aren't happy with how Planetary Supremacy works but I'm not sure why. Seems cool, but I got wiped out in my attempt to take out my first zone of the map, so I can't say if it delivers on the cool idea or not.You can play against other army types in modes outside of the campaign, but without purchasing DLC you can only play as the Blood Angels or Tyranid. Those DLC do not include campaigns, which is disappointing but still seems much cheaper and less time consuming than buying and painting minis. So, I'm cool with it and hoping some additional narrative driven campaigns are added to the game later. The Blood Angel and Tyranid Elite DLCs each add two units to the game. The Blood Angel units can be used in the campaign, which is cool.I imagine multiplayer is the best place to spend your time after finishing the campaign. Live, tournament, hotseat, and I love that there's an asynchronous multiplayer option where you can play at your own pace and receive emails when it's your turn in a match, or in several matches that you've joined concurrently. Turn-based games are such time suckers and both finding and playing a real-time match may not be realistic, so I'm excited to dive into that.Overall, Battlesector seems to be a solid presentaton for Warhammer. Voiceacting is good. Graphics are cool for turn based strategy and this is one of the few games with a 'photo mode' that I actually used. Soundtrack is great with some fittingly dark orchestral sounds. From what I've read, this is one of the games that comes closest to the tabletop experience. I can't say I would know but since this is fueling my exploration of the Warhammer 40k universe, maybe I will soon enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to claim this is the most sophisticated strategy game, or possessing the best balance.  Many of the abilities and weapons you can unlock aren't really worth it and some units just struggle to justify their cost.  But thankfully that doesn't stop it from being a lot of fun.  I have a soft spot for Blood Angels and Tyranids both, perhaps because Space Hulk was one of the earliest Games Workshop games I progressed onto after Heroquest.  This game gives you the chance to deploy the awesome might of the Astartes and leverage it to push through a much larger enemy force.  The kind of slightly lopsided strategy game which just makes you feel like you're the all-powerful conqueror of worlds.And then there are the occasional moments where you really need to pay attention, divert firepower to take down a big threat, present the enemy with targets of opportunity who can take the beating and actually wage war.  A little more polish on the game systems and unit abilities and it could have been like this throughout... I'm just not sure that would have been an improvement.My only actual gripe is the main menu, which is clunky and far too old-school.  Once you're into the game proper though this drops away to a much better UI, so this really is a minor complaint.Well worth getting if you are a 40k fan.  If you're simply looking for good strategy it can't compete with XCOM or Gears Tactics (or even Mechanicus) but is still worth the price of admission.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best 40k games released Since Dawn of War 2 and Space Marine.Battlesector has huge potential I can see how implementation of more units and factions will work. If we had a map making tool that would be the icing on the cake and provide endless possibilities.There are only two factions right now, with a Third one on the way in the form of DLC.A whole new faction with great quality models - what's better is that you can still play against the faction without having to pay for the DLC, just in case you are not interested in playing as them.Ultimately, the number of DLCs may be off putting to some people but I can safely say that if each faction is as well crafted as the base game and are getting new campaign modes it would be totally worth it. The game itself is not even charged at AAA prices, yet I feel like Battlesector might be approaching that.The audio mixing may have to be tweaked a little bit. When being shot by an enemy squad it is a bit annoying to hear the target unit repeating itself or moaning, especially since it tends to be louder than other effects even though I have adjusted the sound settings. The music is not fantastic either, it's not as grand or intimidating like other 40k titles.All in all, Battlesector is a good turn based strategy game with a good campaign which can be challenging. It stays true to the universe and the models are incredibly well made. Is it perfect? No, but I can recommend this title with out a doubt. If you are a fan of Warhammer this is the best turn based strategy on the market right now. If you like strategy games in general, I don't think you'd be disappointed.8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I was among the lucky ones who got to play the beta for Battlesector, and I liked it from the very first moment. As soon as I jumped in, I was brought back to the times of Warhammer 40,000: Squad Command - the first Warhammer 40,000 videogame I ever played. It took me a little to get used to the flow of the action, but after the first few missions, I was completely captivated.The campaign runs as a turn-based strategy game and, a bit like tabletop Warhammer, you get to create your army list before each mission. Once the mission starts, you can check your units once again, choosing the weapons they'll carry, where to deploy which unit, and which units to leave outside of the game.Each gun has an optimal firing range - a feature that, if used correctly, allows you to be much more effective - and several units can swap between different guns, opening up several possibilities. Personally, I like to shoot fewer times and deal massive damage rather than shower the enemy in bullets.During the campaign you will have several HQ units that you can upgrade with Tokens earned after each mission - the upgrades are permanent and the tokens limited, so be careful with what you invest on. As you progress you will also unlock new units to bring along, so you can experiment with new strategies.Multiplayer (both live and "play-by-e-mail") and Skirmish modes also exist, and although I'm not much into them, those are very fun to play too. Skirmish mode lets you replay the same maps as the campaign with a different army for you or the enemy, and you get to customise them in every detail, which is perfect if you wish to give yourself a challenge or you want to test something out.The game looks and sounds great. It's a turn-based game, so it's not like you end up looking at things close-up that often, but all units and scenery pieces have plenty of details to admire. Units could use some more customisation and variety (which I already pointed out to the devs), but overall I don't really have any complaints on this regard.I wish there were more corpses on the ground when you begin certain missions (especially the first ones, given the background to the game's campaign) but I see that would become too chaotic as all units leave bodies when they die.Perhaps a few more animations could be added as well, but I'm sure the devs are already working on that.BlackLab developers have already stated in the FAQ that the game will receive further support, including both free and paid DLCs, and new races. Given how well the gameplay flows with both races currently available, I'm pretty sure we're going to get at least a couple new campaigns as different races at some point in the future (if I had to wager, or implore the devs, I'd say orks and imperial guard).During all the time spent in Betasector, BlackLab and Slitherine were always there to answer our questions and listen to our feedback, so I can't possibly imagine things being different after the game launches. These guys know what they're doing.So, if you people love Warhammer 40,000 and like turn-based games, I would absolutely suggest you get Battlesector.

_childDocuments_.review: It's...okay. Strategy-wise it's kinda laughable, since the AI has an infuriating habit of just spawning enemies in and using them against you on the same turn - which makes a mockery of any tactics you might try to apply. In fact, everything about the mission design seems to focus on keeping you rushing around to ensure you don't get to be very strategic. Marines are also frequently outranged by units like the Exocrine, which results in yet more charging towards the enemy to close the distance and hoping not to die - hardly Sun Tzu. The whole 'it's easier to shoot bad guys when they're far away than up close' deal half your units have seems wildly illogical but does work quite well in terms of adding a bit more depth to the gameplay. There's no real way to effectively use cover without blunting your attacks, I guess again because they want you constantly on the hoof and not turtling. Basically, they seem to want you to play Marines like tyranids.Most of the unlockable abilities aren't very inspiring or useful, or even tied to the lore very well, and some of the unlockable weapons seem to be straight downgrades. And yet, it's fun in small doses. Not really what I was hoping for, but pretty enjoyable, for a 40k game at least.

_childDocuments_.review: Update:  After about another 10 hours of gameplay I wanted to provide an update.  Still very much enjoying the combat, voice acting, and graphics.  The battles are strategic and you can get wiped quickly if you are trying to pull a LJ.  I sincerely hope that the devs can flesh out the unit recruiting and death mechanic.  This would make this game a 9.5/10 if it had Xcom's unit recruitment mechanics.  In Battlesector, when a unit dies it's no big deal outside of the current battle/map you're in.  If that unit of intercessors you've been running for the last 5 maps dies in your current mission, no biggie.  Just recruit a new one when you complete the mission and get back to the mission select screen.  Having read a lot of Black Library books, Night Lords, etc. I know that in 40K lore units are not "that" disposable.  They are battle brothers, they know the names of the brothers fighting beside them.  With the way unit recruits currently work, it's pretty meaningless to lose units in a battle.  I realize a lot of people probably want to see additional factions or chapters as DLC, but I personally hope they will flesh out that unit recruitment part to give death an impact before they do anything else.  It's my biggest complaint with the entire game.  It takes what could have been a 8 or 9 and puts it at a 6 or 7 out of 10.Very fun game still and after 20 or so hours I'm still much enjoying it.  But lack of impact and meaning when your veteran units are killed in a massive and critical  battle with a hive is a huge let down.  You should be able to name units and see a log of those who have passed in battle, like a rememberance log or something.Original review:  Best turn based 40K game in recent memory.  I know that may not be saying much in that context but if you're a 40K fan you should not pass this one up.  Art direction, graphics, and sound are all spot on.  The turn based combat has some nice tweaks that actually speed things up a bit and keep things fresh.  The command point system is also a nice boon for the combat.  Being able to call in an artillery strike is just flat out awesome (though be careful as it does friendly fire).  I'm about 12 or so hours in and am really digging it.  The UI is fantastic in some areas but also lacking a bit in some other areas.  Oh, and it's only $40?  $35 if you pre-ordered?  Done deal.  All in all I think this is a fantastic 40K game and one of the best in recent memory.  Probably my fav 40K game since DoW2.  I really hope the devs service it with some other factions via DLC and I hope that they will make some minor improvements to the UI.  Fingers crossed that this sells well and the devs will continue to support longterm.To the folks saying it's too slow.  This is a turn-based game.  Ala Divinity Original Sin, XCom, Mechanicus, etc.  I find the turn based combat in this game to be much more involved and flows very well compared to some others.  I love the fall back, facing, and overwatch mechanics in this game as well.  Actually, this game's action point system in general is very refreshing.  For less than a box of primaris intercessors you can purchase this game and get countless hours of enjoyment and hopefully support what proves to be the first game in a successful IP/series.

_childDocuments_.review: My Friends, my mission to explore the mysterious world of "Warhammer 40,000" continues as I enter the Sector of Battle to update you on my discoveries. Last time I checked in, there were some pastel fellows with wolf sidekicks who were battling the Word Bearers, a group of space marines who turned evil because the God-Emperor of Mankind was pissed they wanted to worship him as a God. As a hint, GEM, maybe don't call yourself "God-Emperor" if you don't want the worship? Just a thought. Anyway, here, we have a group of people named Blood Angels (...Angels, Gods, Crusaders, YOU SEE THE CONFUSION GEM?) who are going to war with the Xenomorphs from Alien, who have painted themselves white and purple in hopes we don't recognize them. The plot is... Sadly somewhat questionable. And I've honestly mainly been playing the Planetary Supremacy mode, so as far as story, I can tell you that the plot of this game seems to focus around the fact that there are a bunch of space nuns who keep making extremely poor strategic decisions because they're more invested in checking out their cool upgrade tree than they are in winning, and then they get murdered by a variety of green-colored enemies. And in that world, there are not only green robots (called Necrons) but also some yellow-orange robots (called Necrons) who are, presumably, not the same robots, but it might just be gamer lighting. Anyway, apparently Necroranges lived on this planet a long time ago, but then a bunch of Helluva Boss characters showed up, and that was all a long time ago so nobody can remember much of it anyway. This time, there are only GOOD space marines, so I haven't been able to learn what other factions of evil space marine exist, aside from the Death Guard (a bunch of dudes with questionable immune systems lead by the King Emo named Mortarion) and and the Word Bearers (Some guys who thought that just because someone is borderline omniscient, capable of destroying entire armies and mind-controlling people, and goes around being accompanied by dudes called "Angels" that he might be a God). Nor is there much said about the good marine factions, although I can now confirm that some of them are called "Blood Angels," and said angels are red. More on this story as it develops. Meanwhile, let's talk about the game as a game. It does a good job translating 40k's nature as a turn-based tactical wargame into, well, a computerized one. There's a lot of stuff in any normal turn-based wargame that doesn't translate onto (or off of) the compute,r and Slitherine clearly know which parts to keep, which parts to move,e tc. This is a high quality game, and frankly, I wish they would expand the planetary cnquest mode a bit more. They clearly have the ability to make an interestiung game on the strategic as well as tactical level, and I'd love to see that worked into this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Best TBS 40K yet, just needs more factions and some UI tweaks. I put about 8 hours into a pirated version, but had to buy this to support the devsThis one ticks all the boxes for me, outside faction diversity. I'm on mission 7 now, and they keep expanding our army size while introducing more units and skills. They've been slow to usher in different enemy types too, but I'd much rather they mix in another faction.It's still awesome though. I have to start recording things to show my buddies how epic some overwatch/battle moments can be. It's a light show!In any RTS/TBS I like splitting my armies and playing defensively/turtling with a large chunk, while having a quicker/smaller force to advance to various objectives, and divide enemy forces.Unless I have to defend a specific point, I'll slowly move that chunk towards enemy groups, using overwatch-like abilities with half of it to punish anyone that comes near.Weapons are very punchy, so when you have 8 unit groups unleashing hell in overwatch, it's a glorious thing.With jetpacks, and vehicles, you can get around quickly, so you can make a devastating blitzkrieg force, also using your commander for air supportAfter some updates and DLC's, not to menion mod support (do it devs) this is can be one of the best TBS of all time.Pros-nails the 40K aesthetic-voice actors are awesome!-while tile based, you can move diagonally.-You can move, attack, and move again if you have the move points left over.-you can establish a control zone and go into quasi overwatch, even if you didn't select it-so long as you're being melee attacked from the direction you placed your troops, your units will defend themselves.-as you move a unit, you can move others and give them commands before the other unit reaches its destination, really promotes more action/less waiting. It almost feels like an RTS-enough skills for your hero units, with pros and cons like Fallout perks-weapons feel badass-While we only play as Blood Angels in campaign (I don't care about MP with only two factions) there are quite a few units to deploy, with lot's of weaponsCons - Needs more factions-UI needs some tweaking in army selection, can't see proper unit details-mini map needed

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to recommend it at this price, but it's a decent game and I wouldn't feel too bad paying around 20$. I don't get all the positive reviews. I really don't get all the positive reviews considering some of the issues. The game is just extremely confusing. Nothing is outright game breaking or pathetic, but I expect more at this price point. The game feels like it's in EA. They recommend a GTX 950 and whatever older CPU. I have a Ryzen 2600 / RX 480 / 16GB / Samsung M.2 and it just runs funky. No matter what settings it hovers in the 25-50fps range and becomes pretty choppy at times. Rounds tend to be pretty boring and take a while. You can speed up the enemies turn, but not your own turn. Sometimes it takes a while for them to walk from point A to B and wish you could speed it up like you can do for the enemy. When you have 10 enemies and 10 characters each turn has a whole lot of animations playing out.I've been playing turn based games since X-COM: UFO Defense and this has to be one of the most confusing games in recent years. It's just not very intuitive or smooth moving thru the characters and doing things. I prefer some sort of confirmation system. In this you select ability and right click once to cast it. It just doesn't have the polish a 40$ game should have. The graphic settings are severely limited and audio takes some tweaking to get the right balance of music / sound effect / voices.Unfortunately it took me about 3 hours to realize I didn't want this and now I'm stuck with it. I will only play it some more because I'm stuck with it, but if I could return it I would much prefer this, but now I am at 5 hours in. One of thing is that you can customize the weapons they use, but so far I don't get any new items to equip and would think after several missions I would have something. Doesn't seem to be any sort of loot and not really sure what is causing new characters to unlock, nothing is clear in this game. Even when you are messing with attacks it's just kind of trial and error, then simply remember. Not sure about mod support, but it could potentially save this game and make my investment worth something. The visuals and sound effects are nice, some of the skills / characters are cool, it's an alright game that's worth maybe half the 40$ price. I'm not even sure what the point of the game is or what's going on. So you don't seem to have any sort of progress other than the game says play this map and it's the ONLY thing you can do. The main screen of the game has 3 things to click on. One brings you to the available units, the other is the skill tree and last is the mission name and it's always those 3 same things. There are no secondary things going on like you see in something like X-COM or Battletech. No choices to make, no stores, nothing to interact with.It's sad this new trend we have seen over the years. You get games that truly should be in EA, but they are dropped as final products. The only thing this game excels at is being mediocre across the board. It's like they just wanted to milk the name and gave this to programming students working on their first game and on top of that they don't play TBS games at all.Apparently this game is known for performance issues and making graphic cards run warm. Thought it seemed odd because my system always runs really cool, even running much more intense games, but this game pushes it too hot for my liking and does get worse as you progress. Game actually ran good the first mission or two and then after you have a couple hours in the game it changes, you would think they allow a return considering this is a known thing, feels misleading like they made changes so people wouldn't experience GPU issues at the start of the game and be able to return it.*update*Wanted to give this game one more shot so I updated all my drivers just to rule it out for performance issues and the game still runs like total garbage. The worst part is that if I go play earlier missions it runs really really good. They should be forced to give refunds because it really does seem like they altered the levels some so that you get good performance at the start and forced to keep the game. Complete waste of money, game is literally unplayable unless you can play on low settings with the game being choppy between 25-40fps.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the very best 40K  Games out there. In a skirmish on easy mode you can pick forces to the points limit no restrictions exactly like the table top game but with no chance for cheating like front to back movement to gain extra distance, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dice, or players quoting different rules.Limiting availability numbers of powerful units in campaign games on harder levels (via limited requisition points) and momentum penalty for breaking maximums means that you can still use horrendously unbalanced armies if you really want to. The fact that you can tell how effective your attacks are going to be before you make them (it tells you the percentages) means more scope for tactical thinking and less on luck of the dice gods. The Planetary campaign also includes Strategic Decisions which you don't get on the tabletop. On the tabletop enhanced skills and better weapons are just paid for in points but here they have to be unlocked first just like every other computer game. There are BETTER Strategy games sure, but they are all more complicated. Battlesector is dead simple and easy and fun to play.2 OG Armies Aeldari and Adeptus Militarum still need to be introduced however.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game. It's like a light version of the 40k tabletop game. The Blood Angels story campaign is decent, story is decent and full of all the lovable 40k fluff, and the voice acting is incredible. The different units are very well done as far as their different attacks, abilities, and appearances. Love the models. It would be neat if you could custom paint your army, but whatever. The gameplay is enjoyable, weapons feel good and destructive (especially the plasma weapons), the maps are a manageable size so battles don't take forever (one thing I dislike about some turn-based games is when the map is so big that it takes an hour of manoeuvring just to make first contact with the enemy). For a turn-based game, the action is fast. A couple gripes I have are that sometimes the missions objectives are kind of unclear and it can be hard to tell exactly what you have to do, or if you need a specific hero unit to complete a task. It can be kind of frustrating at times. Another thing, which seems to be pretty common from other reviews I have read, is that they should've just included all of the different factions from the beginning, or maybe just have one cheap expansion pack with all the factions, and they should've added story campaigns for the factions as well. The money-grabbing tactic to get the different factions seems lame: $20 for a single faction with no added campaign? Come on now... should only be a few bucks if anything. If there was a campaign, maybe $10-15. I got the game on sale. I think it was like 50% off or something. Definitely having fun with the game for that price. I feel like they could've done a lot more with it, but what is there isn't bad or anything. It does seem like they are still planning on releasing more content, I just hope they don't keep overcharging for it unless it's something big. Bottom line: I find the game chill to play while I'm waiting for friends to come online to play other games or while I'm watching TV or something. I was super into it when I was just playing the story campaign, but aside from that it gets old kinda fast. Needs more story! More factions! More faction campaigns! This game could be huge. The core is good. AS LONG AS THE ENEMIES OF THE IMPERIUM STILL DRAW BREATH, THERE CAN BE NO PEACE.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game. It's a lot more stable now and it's a lot of fun especially if you're a fan of any of the armies that are available, which I am. I have three problems though, one is somewhat minor and nit-picky so I'll start there. You cannot disable auto-save, and this may or may not lead to the game crashing. It autosaves constantly which while great, floods your save files with multiple sometimes redundant auto-saves. Also you have to delete them individually by selecting the file, clicking the delete button and then clicking the confirmation button. This is an annoyance but it may not bug you. So grain of salt.My big issue is I really really want a planetary supremacy like we got with Warhammer 40k 2. The RTS one. This is not that, and that's okay. I understand this mode is a work in progress too, so hopefully we get a more robust version with a bigger map allowing for more factions as other faction(s) release. My complaint is that the AI can cheat in one way specific to the AI, and in another way that can be exloited by you as well, but is non-the-less problematic.1st. There are unit caps based on your held territory, starting at a base value of 1500 and going up as you claim more territory. I really enjoy this gameplay loop. Take territory, improve/reinforce army, buy upgrades and repeat. My issue is the AI can ignore the unit cap for an unfair advantage. I have watched the AI take it's turn, reinforce above it's army point cap and then attack a territory and that feels unfair. Even if it's obeying other rules the whole mid to late game is ruined because even if you are taking their territory and should be weakening your opponent, it doesn't matter. They can always reinforce as much as they want and hit you back while your weakened even beyond their armies point cap. You could hypothetically cripple them round after round taking all their territory and dropping their point cap to 1500, and they can still counter attack with a 2500 point army and push you right back to where you were.2nd. Buildings may or may not actually be cover. You won't know until you lose an entire squad hiding behind a Steel bunker only to discover the AI can target you through the bunker and it doesn't block any of their shots. Don't worry, small imperfections in ground terrain will however block shots. You can't see them from overhead mode but once you start shooting you'll find them. Bunkers, buildings, defensive emplacements and the like may in fact be illusory though, and there's no way to know until your enemy shoots you through it. This is my biggest complaint because it makes the actual gameplay in the core system of battling armies an absolutely miserable guessing game of whether or not you are going to get shredded positioning your troops behind a structure. (THERE IS a UI element that is supposed to indicate when something is cover, but it may only work in the campaign.)As a whole it's great and I recommend it. The campaign is fun, if not a bit short, but the longevity is going to be in The Demonic Horde Mode and Planetary Supremacy. The problem is if the AI continues to be able to cheat one of those modes has no legs.

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps the driest WH40k game ever release, Battlesector is one of the better Warhammer (40K) games on the market, but is a great example of wasted potential. The campaign, while lengthy and varied in both mission structure and unit types, offers nothing more than static painting and slowly delivered lines of lore and generic military talk--and not even during the mission, only before and after! The lore, for all the major loreheads, is only somewhat interesting with it being the first game to introduce the enhanced and now-standardized Primaris marines, but nothing really comes of it. At least, I don't think it does. Once again the presentation was so lackluster and borderline unfinished, and the story so rote, so that I started skipping expository scenes just to get to the next battle.But damn if that gameplay doesn't hit. Missions that once felt imbalanced or impossible challenges suddenly become adrenaline-pumping, skin-of-your-teeth victories that beg for a do-over to try and get a cleaner victory. Each mission begets an exciting turn-based fog of war battlefield that often rewards tactility and smart positioning, yet often throws a wrench in your plans in unexpected ways. I heavily enjoyed unlocking new units, new weapons, new abilities, and tinkering with my new toys to see what I like, what fits fits my playstyle, and what needs to go back in the box. Each unit is lovingly modeled and really taps into to that desire to simply admire Warhammer minis; this one is truly for the fans. But still, the game lacks in some key ways that--with it now being helmed by a new developer Slitherine Ltd.--may improve in the coming months or years. Currently, other than a campaign, you have a few additional ways to play: Daemonic Incursion, which acts as a horde mode; Planetary Supremacy, which is like a 3-way free for all; custom campaigns made by players I've yet to try; and Skirmish, a one-off battle. In each of these, you can choose your faction, which at the time of writing, has some of the all-time greats: Orks, Sister of Battle, Tau, etc. But the issue is, unless you want to forever play Blood Angels, you have absolutely zero way of knowing how a new ($15) army plays. This game is niche, so guides are very few and far between, and your $15 only gets you access to the army. No tutorials. No campaign. Nothing. Just the armies and a dream. Hopefully that changes soon. A full campaign would be fantastic, but even a mini tutorial "story mode" for each faction to get to grips with the strengths and weaknesses would be great.As it stands, I still highly recommend this game to turn-based tactics and Warhammer 40k fans, ideally both. On sale you can get a ton of content and factions which hopefully amount to more in the future, and if you have a friend, can even be a way to simulate the tabletop in the cheapest way possible.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic adaptation of the tabletop game.  It's not perfectly accurate, but it doesn't feel like a different game.  It feels like Warhammer 40K.  Graphically, it's superb!  All units look detailed and are animated in ways that feel natural and alive.  Attacks feel weighty, and special effects are great.  Sound design is very well done, voicework is pretty spot-on, and I love the way that weapons actually fire the correct number of times according to the attack dice those weapons would receive on table-top.It's the gameplay itself, though, that wins me over.  Unlike a lot of other games that rely on crazy RNG to make things tense, often giving the AI pretty silly bonuses to their attack, damage, or survivability, nothing like that happens here.  What you see when you mouse over a target is what will happen.  If you see 42% chance to hit...42% of the rounds fired *will* hit.  (This is so much more enjoyable than an "XCOM-approach" of watching 98% chance-to-hit fail 3 turns in a row.  It places emphasis on positioning, planning, and intelligent risk-taking over RNGeebus.For negatives, they are few:- It's not a very challenging AI.  You can significantly up the difficulty in terms of how much damage is given/received, as well as how many points you are given to upgrade your whole army between missions.  But nothing saves the AI from making pretty self-defeating decisions during missions.  I've seen them get one of my powerful units down to a thread of health, then arbitrarily switch targets for the next attack rather than finishing it off and gaining a large advantage.  - A few of the missions are a little cheap in the way they are presented.  Most notably, a mission where one of your secondary objectives is to save a crashed ship.  There's no actual way to do this -- the objective will fail no matter what...and trying means that you'll over-extend your army in a desperate attempt to save it numerous times, ultimately losing repeatedly before looking it up online and discovering that it's not even possible.  Why put it in the mission then?  A few decisions like this simply add confusion instead of interesting challenges.  But this is a rarity.- Things seem a bit heavily in favor of the Blood Angels as far as power goes.  I have beaten the AI as Tyranids in skirmishes, but I've never beaten a real player.  Conversely, I've never lost an online match to the Tyranids, either.  There are just too many ways for Space Marines to completely annihilate multiple, healthy Tyranid squads in one turn.  Giving Tyranid players a points handicap seems to be the only way to balance this...and it's very easy to tip the scales too far in the other direction as well.  Tricky, but I see this potentially being a major issue with new factions being introduced.  Tough one.Definite praise to the game overall, though.  It's well worth the full price for what's there.  The thing I like the most is the potential this has to build on the beautiful foundations that have been laid here.  Totally recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: The game has some UI issues that initially made me refund when I first tried it around launch. It improved somewhat on that regard, and now I managed to push past that.The skirmish AI seems a bit too weak, at least on the control point objective modes - I imagine it's slightly better on the deathmatch mode.The story campaign is well made so far, unfortunately there is only one. The procedural planetary conquest campaign seems too barebones. I haven't tried the Daemon Incursion wave survival mode yet.One thing I really like about the game mechanics here is the Momentum mechanic that rewards constantly pressing forward instead of the usual "crawl-and-overwatch" that tactical games often devolve into. Really good alternative to the time pressure that other tactical games like XCOM 2, Phoenix Point, Daemon Hunters, etc. uses.

I don't want to change the settings for one game). -CRASHFEST (haven't got through tutorial without crashing. I've wasted half a day trying to get to running). _childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: A very good turn based tactical WH40k game. Feels a lot like the tabletop, in a good way. Campaign is a bit short but enjoyable. On the downside, there's only a handful of factions: Blood Angels and Tyranids in the base game. At the time of writing this review, Necrons are available as a DLC and sisters of Battle are planned. Devs promise more to come in future but not much was said in terms of release schedule(and so far it was fairly slow TBH).Given the amount of content in the base game, full price may be a tad bit high but certainly worth getting it on sale.Edit: to clarify: single player campaign itself is long enough but there's only one proper story campaign following Blood Angels. Neither updates not army DLCs contain any campaigns for other armies. Nor there are any plans af of now for bringing in more story campaigns as separate DLCs. There is a planetary conquest mode currently being tested, which allows to play a sort of non-story campaign with any army you own, but that's not quite the same(no story, random missions).
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, this is kind of fun-ish, but don't spend good money on it.It is pretty empty and a touch clunky, and the Blood Angels army list is not complete, requiring purchase of a DLC for the 'elite' units.Aside from Tyrranids, all other armies require DLC to access, meaning that the cost you see for the game is nowhere near what you will end up paying for all the armies.It doesn't really bring anything new to the genera, and what it does bring is implemented in a rather mediocre way.Player created campaigns are not of great standard, based on the top rated ones i checked out (some of which i could not play as i did not own the army list for it).It does have a nice army development system, which is a plus.-----------------------------------------------------------------So, some cost data as at 6 Oct 24, and using Aussie dollars.At 50% off, the base game costs $30.81To complete your Blood Angels and Tyrranid armies will cost $4.94 (total)That is not a lot, but why the hell are we paying to finish off our army lists?!As for the other lists, they range from $6,50 if you want Khornite Demons (Who doesn't want BLOOD FOR THE BLOOD GOOODD!!!).$15.36 each will get Tau and Necrons.$17.55 is the price for Orcs and Sisters of battle.Further, the lack of Eldar or Dark Eldar suggests more DLC on its way, most likely at the $17.55 price or higher. At least I hope so, Eldar being my favourite, and most neglected, army for W40K.Total price is going to be $107.55, at special prices, for a pretty mediocre game.Of course, you can pick and choose, not everyone wants to play orcs, or sisters, or whatever, but for someone who likes to have access to the lot, this price is way over the top compared to the mediocrity of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a pass, but despite offering a good looking and relatively faithful adaptation of the tabletop wargame, the extremely disappointing singleplayer offerings along with an absolute graveyard of an online community make Battlesector hard to even get a sense of, much less sink your teeth into.Mechanically, Battlesector is pretty sound, though a few glaring bugs still remain. For example, on multiple occasions, when attempting to board a transport with my HQ unit, overwatch from enemy squads unfortunately killed said HQ unit. Despite this, the transport registered the HQ unit as having successfully boarded, even showing her icon as being carried by the transport and allowing me to attempt to disembark her. However, when I actually attempt to disembark her, the transport doors open and nothing comes out (because she's dead). This would be a funny and harmless bug EXCEPT that disembarking a phantom unit burns that transport's EXTREMELY important Action Point for the round.Unless you have a group of friends that you play with regularly that are all jazzed about trying it with you, Battlesector isn't worth your money. Your only options for play beyond the underwhelming singleplayer campaigns (in which only a handful of the available factions are featured as playable) are joining Discord servers where you will promptly have your ass handed to you without learning anything about the game over and over by the same six-to-ten 1000+ hour players that are still haunting the game.This one stings more than most because the bones are good, but the meat is all rotten. Battlesector COULD have found a small but dedicated following in the style of Dawn of War before it, but just couldn't find its way to crossing that finish line and instead joins the legions of forgotten licensed Warhammer titles you see pop up during Festival of Skulls.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend this so badly, I really do. But I can't.On the surface, it's everything a tabletop 40k fan has missed for years: a well translated tabletop-to-VG experience. The points system is familiar, the units do what you'd expect them to do in the right/wrong situations, it looks and sounds phenomenal, and is an obvious love letter to the franchise.Until you've been playing awhile. To take today as an example: I have had, in under 1 hour, three separate occasions where the AI simply refuses to end its turn. I've waited minutes, I've waited hours, and the only recourse is to reload or quit. I could almost understand if this were a rare occurrence, but three times in under an hour, is not a rare occurrence. It's a  occurrence.Some digging around has revealed that this exact issue has come up in prior titles, and while apparently resolved there, they are not resolved here.I don't know. Maybe I've just gotten impatient in my older years, but when my time is so finite (both from a mortality perspective, and from available free hours in a day), it hurts to load up a game and have it bug out this frequently. If this bug is ever fixed, I'll come back and revise this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I was able to get acces to the Closed Beta and until release i played 50hours in the game und cant wait to play it more. :)First to say, dont Expect High End Production like Starcraft where you have high end cutscenes behind every door. Battleseactor is clearly an AA game (to an AA price) and miss all that things.Also you should know a lot about the current Lore of Warhammer40k. I recommend to read the Novels Dante and Devastation of Baal prior to play the game to understand everything. The Devs try there best to inform the player but to be honest, if you have a situation like this„Baal is the homeworld of the Space Marine Chapter Blood Angels. There where massively attacked by Tyranids which overhwelm the Blood Angels and all other present Chapters and whipe out 90% of them.While that happens, a crack in the warp opened over Baal and released a lot demons which start to mess up everything.While that happens, the Warp ripp the universe in 2 Sections which one is cutoff from the empweror lightWhile that happens, the imperium create a complete new form of space marines.While that happens, a primarch of the ultra marines awake from death and lead the primaris marines on a new crusade.ect. ect.„You cant explain that  all in a cutscene. As i said the devs tried there best but if you only think „yeah i knowe Ultra Marines from THQ games, what exactly was a primarch?“ i think you would have problems to understand what happens.  If you are familiar with the lore go ahead.Back to the game. For me Battlesector is like Terminator: Resitance. An AA Game with AA value but  where you feel in every way that the Devs love the source material. There are allways easter eggs and small hints to the lore that i would not expact from the game. For example that the marines coming from Baal, called Baal Secundus Baalfora. Description of weapons ect. Ect. That guys now there stuff!Also the game is very fun to play. It feels at the same time like tabletop, but is also able to create that epic moments i know from the novels and other games. The optic has lot of details. I just can recommend, use the photo mode to go very close to models, and look at the details, at the blood, the animations. Its just great.So at the end, if you are a warhammer fan, you know the lore and you dont expect AAA Quality for a 30€ game you are at the right place! And as long as i know Slytherine and Black Lab, we will see a lot DL'cs with additional storys, factions ect. Ect.At the very end just a small warning.In lore small Tyranid creatures which are out of range of leader-creatures get a lot thumber and act unorganised and like animals. That is something the devs considered when creating the Ai. So on the first few missions, where you only face the small creatures without for example warriors, the Ai act a lot thumber then in later missions.Also i recommend to start on the 3. or 4. difficulty. Then the Gants are still thumb animals, but they come in masses and your simple cleaning mission get to a fight for survival where you try to reach the mission opjectives why you are surrounded by Gants and don't have enough shots to kill them all. When you paint the map red with blood, filled the streets with corpses and they dont stop coming... then you dont bother over the AI anymore. :D

_childDocuments_.review: 4 out 5.  There are 2 great things about this game and 1 issue.Greatness (1) - The Base Engine.  This is a 40K game in its truest form.  It is a well polished and professionally made turn-based game.  The graphics, and interface and animations are all exactly where they need to be to permit you enjoy the experience of commanding your badasses to krump them bugs in the Name of the Emperor!  Tactics, unit positioning and strategy are important and allow your battlefield choices to be meaningful.  The game strikes a good balance between making your space marines feel like the greatest warriors the human race has ever produced yet still allows the Tyranids to feel like the apocalyptic biomass devourers they are.Greatness (2) - the Potential.  Oh boy the potential!  Gives me flashbacks to Dawn of War at it's height, a cornucopia of races, units, weapon types and strategies all engaging in Glorious Melee Combat (and ranged too) This game could ultimately go there, allowing solo or multiplayer battles of godlike proportions.Issue (1) - Lack of Content.  at this stage I can only give the game a 4 out of 5.  Whilst I have thoroughly enjoyed it, it is a bit of a bare bones affair at the moment.  2 playable races is the absolute least a game can ship with, and 1 campaign, which is again the absolute least that could be provided.  I am excited to see the devs are feverishly working at the content, but I kind of feel like I paid for it, but it ain't here yet.  I was particularly annoyed when I went to have some EPIC battles in skirmish mode and discovered you cannot use Sisters of Battle units?  WTF??  Did I pay for dembitches or not?  Also the 20 unit cap kinda restricts my wild skirmish ideas,  I can't field 2000 points of bolter noobs.  Why not?!!SO.  I feel like I paid premium game price for a game that will likely be truly awesome in due course, but isn't quite there yet.  As long as the devs continue to support the game then I will be happy with my purchase.  I loved the game, loved the campaign, enjoyed the units and the blasting and the screaming... Then the game ran out of content.  If I dare compare it to  the SPLENDID Mechanicus game of recent years, there is no real replayability here beyond playing the exact same missions, only on harder, or dreaming up different variations of Blood Angels v Nids in skirmish.  I think the devs should have had at least a Tyranid campaign (could literally have been the same maps, just in reverse) and allowed sisters to be used in skirmish.  One final wish would be for a more in depth end game stats counter.  Probably just the Nerd in me, but I want to know a little bit more than just who died...!

_childDocuments_.review: For avid enthusiasts of Warhammer 40,000, Battlesector emerges as a truly immersive and faithful rendition of the beloved tabletop experience. From the meticulously crafted graphics that adorn both the environment and character models, to the enthralling soundtracks accompanying each level, the game truly excels in providing a visually and audibly captivating journey. The melodies interwoven into the gameplay proved to be an unexpected delight, with some tunes so alluring that I couldn't resist humming along while commanding my forces.Delving into the core of the gameplay, Battlesector offers a fresh take on the Warhammer 40,000 universe, albeit deviating slightly from the exact mechanics of its tabletop counterpart. Nonetheless, the alterations implemented in the game remain effective, offering an engaging and enjoyable experience for players. Throughout the campaign, I undertook the challenges on the Lieutenant difficulty, and while it proved to be a gratifying endeavor, I must admit that I didn't venture into the Captain difficulty. My hesitance stemmed from my impression that the enemy AI could have presented a more formidable opposition to truly test my strategic acumen. It's possible that the developers aimed to intensify the difficulty on the highest setting by imbuing adversaries with an air of resilience and augmenting their reinforcements, a common tactic to enhance challenges in games.Let it be known, though, that Battlesector does not lack in content. With an array of enticing extras, such as the exhilarating survival mode pitting players against Khorne daemons and the Planetary Supremacy mode that hosts encounters with the formidable Necrons, Orks, and Adepta Sororitas, the game ensures a diverse and captivating gameplay experience. Despite this wealth of additional features, I found that, over time, the allure of the game waned slightly, leaving me with a faint sense of monotony. However, given the reasonable price point at which I procured the game—around €15 or so—I cannot help but deem it a truly worthwhile investment, offering a generous return on entertainment value.All in all, Battlesector emerges as a commendable addition to the Warhammer 40,000 gaming universe. Its visually stunning presentation, accompanied by well-crafted soundscapes, makes for an immersive experience that will resonate with fans of the franchise. While the gameplay may not perfectly mirror its tabletop counterpart, it remains a satisfying and enjoyable endeavor. With ample content to explore and engage with, the game undoubtedly stands as an enticing opportunity for players to venture into the unforgiving battles of the 41st millennium.

_childDocuments_.review: In a world of so-so Warhammer games, Battlesector is a slow-paced, beautifully sound-designed turn-based approximation of a Warhammer 40k tabletop match. It's not for everyone, but it's worth playing for fans of the franchise and fits in very nicely with the storyline of the Devastation of Baal 40k novel.Every squad feels like a group of gigantic transhuman walking tanks, every mission feels like it could end with your force being dropped into a meatgrinder, and the game leans heavily into the lore of the Blood Angels and their chaotic neutral superhuman vampirism. No destructable environments though, which seems like a missed opportunity.If the game has a flaw, it's that it only allows you to play or fight Blood Angels, Tyranids, and now Necrons--which is a tiny minority of the available forces in 40k. Fighting Tyranids is like fighting the ocean, and fighting Necrons is like shooting ancient Egyptian terminators who just glow more instead of dying when shot. There's a lot of potential for some great DLC here--this game is screaming for a Waaaaaagh! of Orkish Boyz.
