_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Just replay XCOM 2.Honestly, I like this game... or at least I want to like this game but, by the Blood God, is there some clunky af game play and design choices (or lack thereof) that just wrecks the experience and makes you want to flip the tabletop, sending little Blood Angel models flying across the room.* Pros- It tries to be XCOM 2. It fails, but at least it tries.- Once you eventually figure out what's going on (about halfway through the campaign), it's fun. You know... not take acid and stare at the stars fun, but fun.- Uhhh, it's W40K and you want to like it so bad, so you'll keep playing it.*Cons- The tutorial missions are whack and leave you with more questions than answers. Particularly because the second tutorial is bugged and broken. Not off to a great start.- I hope you're  up with your W40K canon, otherwise you're going to be scratching your helmet and wondering wtf they're talking about. - Really unclear mission objectives. You'll really enjoy reaching an objective with your HQ unit only to realise it has to be a particular HQ unit that completes it, and they're on the other side of the map.- You'll spend an agonising hour at the end of each mission trying to find and mop up the last of the enemy squads that're in one of the far flung corners of the map. Usually the opposite corner to where you are.- You'll retry a mission 3 times before Googling 'wtf is this mission' only to find out that the MAIN OBJECTIVE CAN'T BE COMPLETED AND NO MATTER WHAT YOU DO THE OBJECTIVE WILL FAIL. Like, it's literally a feature of the mission that you fail the main objective *table flipping intensifies* - Which leads me to this... No Autosave or Quicksave. In a poorly designed turn based game? In 2022? Really?- The upgrade system lacks any clarity whatsoever and expects you to just know certain things. In particular, what upgrades affect what units is really vague for a lot of upgrade. Like, you're just supposed to know which units wear Mk X Gravis Armor (this is never explained), or which units are which type (Primaris Infantry vs. regular infantry, Librarians, etc.), or how to actually equip the weapon upgrades you've acquired (hint: there's a tiny i-toggle next to the weapon box in the unit info in your army management tab. Duh.) and you won't be told these weapon upgrades cost campaign points to use.- You cannot reset your HQ upgrades when you realise later in the game that you've wasted points on useless upgrades, or eventually figure out which units are which and wish you'd picked their upgrade.- An infuriating lack of camera tilt/zoom control. You'll want to be able to tilt up and zoom out just a bit more the whole game.- Last, but certainly not least... Considering half the enjoyment of W40K is customising your army, THERE IS NO UNIT CUSTOMISATION. Wat? Even just a basic colour scheme change would be something. But nope...As with most Warhammer franchise games I've played, it always leaves me wishing a more competent (or at least a better funded) developer would take on the franchise. Gods... the things Firaxis could do with this game. You just want it to be so good, and to have all the things, but it just leaves you feeling sad and disappointed... like that time you were 4 and Santa brought you a NES but no TV to play it on :')
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: It's a 40k turn based game - space marines (Blood Angels) vs. 'Nids.Multiplayer is fun - online and hot-seat on the same machine, with plenty of army options.  Various weapon loadouts and army sizes are available.Single player is a fun (if sometimes very samey - kill this then this then that but you know....40k) romp with bolters, plasma and chainswords.  A good variety of units for the 'Angels and various abilities to use for your HQ characters (along with more to unlock as you progress including new units).Hopefully, soon, there will be more factions to play as and against.A nice addition would have been an army painter for multiplayer (like Dawn Of War's) and some generice SM quotes for the multiplayer.  The voice clips can get very samey very quickly, and the voice acting isn't the best (but by no means in the realms of "Metal Bowkses").All in all a decent 40k game, with hopefully some promise for the future.  Would love to see more chapters and some differing xenos to fight - along with some nice new missions.Runs great on my Ryzen 5 with a 1650, and 8gb RAM at highest qualities.

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector - A Grimdark Turn-Based Blast! (Review)Just finished purging the heretics (or getting purged, depending on the match) in Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector, and here's the deal:For the Emperor (or Whoever You Serve!):  Command iconic Warhammer 40,000 factions like the Blood Angels or the Sisters of Battle in brutal turn-based battles.  It's a great way to experience the grimdark universe without needing a mountain of miniatures.Tactical Depth, But Not Overly Complex:  The combat is challenging but rewarding. You gotta position your troops wisely, use their special abilities, and exploit enemy weaknesses.  But it's not so complicated that you'll get bogged down in rules.More Than Just Shooting:  There's a lot of strategy involved. You gotta manage cover, abilities, and momentum to win the day.  It's like an epic chess match with chainsaws!A Faithfully Grim World:  The game captures the dark and brutal atmosphere of Warhammer 40,000 perfectly.  The environments are suitably gothic and war-torn, and the voice acting is suitably grimdark.A Few Squiggly Bits:  The campaign can be a bit short, and there aren't a ton of factions to choose from at first.  Also, the user interface can be a little clunky at times.Overall Verdict:Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector is a fantastic turn-based strategy game for fans of the Warhammer universe or anyone who enjoys tactical combat. It's got deep strategy, a great atmosphere, and it's perfect for a quick and brutal battle.  Just be prepared for a shorter campaign and a slightly clunky interface, but the core gameplay is a blast!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely brutal. You really feel like the Tyrannid threat is very real as you watch your men mow them down leaving behind a gory mess and a battlefield littered with corpses and yet they keep on swarming towards your marines. The voice work is top notch too and all the story missions are very well acted with the over the top and campy dialogue you'd expect from the 40k universe. You hear the roar of your holy bolter rifles as their rounds crack through the air and the distinct rev of your assault marines' chainswords is followed up with the ripping and tearing of xeno flesh that is a gory and outstanding sight to behold. So much so that even DOOMGUY would blush. You watch as your aggressors hold the line outnumbered 10 to 1 as they fire rapidly into hordes of xenos and watch your mighty war machines make quick work of the largest beasts that the Tyrannid have to offer. You hear your men howl in pain as they're overrun by xenos as they fight to the last man and you clench your teeth as you watch your battle hardened marines fall one after another as your line begins to falter after countless waves crash against them only to call in a desperate, danger close air strike to wipe out the xenos in glorious fashion. The game may not be at the strategic or customizable levels of Dawn of War 1 and 2 or XCOM, but this game truly is an outstanding addition to any fans of strategy/ turn based games and Warhammer 40k. I STRONGLY recommend this game to any and all fans of said genre(s). This game seriously makes me want to start a Blood Angels army on the table top game.And do be careful when you charge up those plasma rifles :P

_childDocuments_.review: Played around 40hs on Microsoft Store where I got an offer with all the DLCs. So far a couple of things I noticed:- First and foremost, for someone who haven't played any 40k game before I had my fair share of fun, the game is intuitive enough not to feel frustrated and allows you to build an army that matches your playstyle. There is some replayability with the custom campaings, maps, planetary supremacy and multiplayer but we'll get to that later.- Now the campaing: story easy enough to follow even for someone who knows basic bits of the lore, still it suffers that most missions end up being the same: secure x objective. Now kill all remaining forces. If I have to end up killing them all, then why don't we skip me having to rush to certain point just to discover it doesn't change anything at the end, save leaving me in a rather stretched position? - On the same page, I've read on reviews about people savescumming to get through the missions... while it's certain difficult to fanthom what you will need for each mission (and fog of war tends to mislead you on where to send your troops), I've found that once you get the tanks every mission gets easy enough as you become a wall (go intercessor - tank - intercessor for the first line, then battle priests with techmarines, hellblasters for the third line. Finally get some jetpack boys with a liutenant and a librarian for rushing/flanking priority targets and you're good to go). At the end with three tanks and the composition I proposed you have enough units to go 3 ways and even mobile teams to support them. Early missions on pletary suppremacy with the sisters of battle against the demons of khorne were harder than the final campaing mission.- Planetary supremacy: nothing much to add here, adds replayability while letting you contend with 2 other factions for the plannet. Only 2 actions allowed per turn (be it claim a tile, upgrade your faction or restore your army) and unfortunately it's only against the AI. Which honestly sucks as you can't play with more than one friend at the same time, and that's only in pvp in multiplayer.- Multiplayer: similar to the tabletop experience, you can already imagine what's here- Custom editor: not a lot of variety to customize really, you can't change the models, add custom sounds or cinematics which honestly would give custom campaings a much needed inmersion since even on the oficial campaing is only a pic with a background dialog and not much else. Overall:Pros:+ Entertaining gameplay+ Plenty of factions for the multiplayer+ Good quality and runs fluidly+ Intuitive interface+ There's some level of replayabilityCons:- No coop mode, neither a chance to play with more than one person at the same time.- Campaing missions are all the same- Custom editor not complete enough (it's debatable since... well it's a wargame based game, not an actual rts. Same with the campaing complain)- No mod support- Plenty of factions bought via dlc, which can be expensiveOverall: 6/10. Has the potential to be a 10, but runs short in a lot of aspects and can be very expensive for what it can offer. Adding mods could become an easily 8/10 or more, since that could fix most of the problems.

_childDocuments_.review: I would prefer a Neutral review for this game.. but there is noneWarhammer Battlesector began with a singleplayer campaign but the game was always tailored towards becoming a cash sink towards multiplayer online gaming. If your purchasing the game for the single player campaign then look below since I dont play multiplayer:1. Game design - Good enough graphics with nice little shiny models. Turn based strategy that makes you pick and choose different unit types with different strength/weaknesses for that strategic advantage. Engaging for ~5-7 hours? Maybe more2. Unit Unlocking Tree (HQ Upgrade) - Not really explained properly since game was released. You need to play the game once to know what you will get down the line of campaign so that you dont sink points into one tree and then realize something far more worthy pops up the immediate next mission3. Game Lore - This is where the Tyrannid campaign falls off a lot. Enemy tyrannids are super intelligent AI. If you overwatch they will try to not enter your overwatch zone or run over the length where your not looking at/facing towards. While this makes the campaign challenging,... is this really warhammer 40k? Aren't tyrannids sort of like Zerg from starcraft with swarm/large numbers tactics? So how exactly do they attack in large numbers and with decently strong weaponry. Im no warhammer expert but should tyrannids hold little guns? XD ... other than the most basic line troops, every other tyrannid has both range and melee weapons and their flying units take out ranged accuracy by 30% in a game where base accuracy is at 80 and sometimes at 85% accuracy... So yea.. until u get some veterancy or have accuracy booster units (mid to late game) you can watch how battle ready, battle born soldiers of race with superior technology geared towards war sucks at shooting... sort of like storm troopers. Kinda kicks you out of immersion. If they had instead just made the game to swarm you with tyrannids it would have made for a much more immersive play instead of the constant - 'omg for f*** sake another gargoyle?'... oh and lets not forget the poison damage enemy attacks do randomly, taking out a massive 20 HP the next turn from each model in a squad. Conclusion:Im definitely not buying any of the DLCs since their all for multiplayer and thats where the unit balance makes sense.. So buy the game for its turn based action, multiplayer etc..  but not if you want to immerse yourself in the warhammer etc. series and/or lore... atleast not versus tyrannid faction

_childDocuments_.review: This is for me the second W40k game happening after the fall of Cadia (after Mechanicus) and the first encounter of new Primaris marines. It is turn-based tactical game, fairly fluid (more units can execute commands at the same time) and with a host of quality of life improvements. The momentum mechanics is quite interesting and it motivated me to be agressive and not turtle in overwatch. There is no high pressure to finish side goals before the primary goal, because in the final phase of the mission you are tasked with is elimination of all enemies, giving plenty of opportunity to finish everything. Some people find the extermination part annoying, but I was OK with it and it makes sense in the story. In the final missions the enemy turns might drag on, but that is a price to pay for seeing what is happening.  The story is pretty interesting and working well with lore of Blood Angels and sudden imposition of new Primaris marines. There is fairly diverse mix of units that are progressively unlocked during campaign, mixing heroes, old style Astartes, Primaris units, mechanical units (old style) and even some Sisters of Battle. These units can be customised and upgraded in limited way. This allows for creating an army that fits well to chosen fighting style. The enemies, Tyranids, present quite a set of creatures, ranging from hordes of gaunts to veritable kaijus like Tyranofex or annoying Exocrine. Some of these I have seen for the first time as well. It is very satisfying to purge them with flamethrowers or concentrated bolter fire.  The graphics looks good. Units are detailed and well animated. The terrain is mostly blasted post-nuclear desert, but there are various towns, fortresses, and factories that liven it up a little. Sound and music in battle are working well to create atmosphere of 40k combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's way too expensive for what it is.You get a rather lengthy (but also rather bland) campaign, exclusively against the Tyranids. Given the nature of this foe, the turns take forever, since you're constantly being swarmed, slowly inching your way towards your objective. I think I'm about halfway done, and should have unlocked most if not all of the units, since I'm already up to tanks.You also get a short "horde" mode vs. Demons of Khorne, which I haven't checked out yet, and a "planetary domination" kind of "campaign" where you fight against 2 other factions for, well, domination, i.e. a set of skirmishes, nothing curated.If you want to play as anything other than Tyranids or bloody Space Marines, you better fork over an excessively high amount of money... up to 17 bucks per faction, which is insane for a few units and a tech tree with upgrades.The campaign is voiced, that's it, but the story meanders, and is certainly nothing memorable. The fights are, again, pretty much just skirmishes with predetermined enemy units. Sound and voice design is good, presentation is okay, animations are ... mid, but the big issue here is the balancing. If you have a turn based game that is based on hit percentage and damage calculation you can get screwed over pretty hard when your enemy has units that can ONESHOT an entire squad from halfway across the map. In a skirmish that's one thing, in a continuous campaign where your units get plus accuracy and critical chance PER mission they've survived on the battlefield, that's just a no go, especially because you can (and will) just save after every turn, because the game has no fixed calculation. Just now a reload was the difference between my Hellblasters being all but obliterated in one shot by an enemy I had NO way of seeing, since he was 20 tiles away in the fog of war and you can't simply rush units blindly into battle (you're always immediately beset by a large number of enemies), and the dude totally missing his shot, doing exactly ZERO damage. That is not good game design, sorry.Better to make hits more reliable and tweak the damage instead, so you at least have a chance to react and/or save a squad. In the same mission a Trygon came out of nowhere and killed most of my Assault Squad... it's useless now for the remainder of this mission. And the only way to counteract this is saving and reloading constantly. That sucks. For some reason the game also doesn't tell you how many shots a unit fires in game when hovering over your weapon of choice, only when you're on the army screen. Instead you have to hover over the enemy to see a potential damage calculation.Apart from that, like I said, it's just too damn expensive, but they can do it, because it's WH40k and us idiot fans will buy it anyway if it's halfway decent. I get that it takes resources to develop and "balance" these factions, but for real, I can get 1 to 2 WHOLE indie games for that price. Make it 8 bucks or so and that's fair for a DLC.And, of course, there's multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: *3 hours in*Action has started to heat up.  Fought my first monstrous Tyranid.  Battle is a bit of a nail biter.  Not that Blood angels can't chop up swarms of termies and hories,but you can't stack when there are so many AOS poisens sprayed by tanky things.Now with a variety of inceptor weapons and plasma weapons, the flexibility is making it more fun.* 1.5 hours in *  Very preliminary, as I'm only on the 3rd mission and haven't gotten any special toys to play with, and have only encountered a few types of enemy units.  Will update with game progress._____If you're a 40K player and know the basic sketch of what the current lore is, this will make a lot more sense to you.  If you don't know what a Primaris marine is and why that's significant, you'll lose out on the fluff.  Lore knowledge will also give you a hand up on how different troops are utilized.Graphically, I like it.  It's definitely a turn-based strategy game, but the models are well done and the shooting is simple but effective.  I think the hero unit should visually appear more "heroic" when doing their actions, but that's nitpicking.Story, too early to tell.  At least it's a notch down in the LOUD PROCLAMATIONS that seem to plague every 40K game.  These space marines can get sleep when back at the barracks.Gameplay is decent, with good mechanics to encourage you to play in the "Blood Angels style" (again, lore knowledge helps).  You can still be an advance under overwatch player, but you lose out on potential buffs if you do so.Cons:<Added 3 hrs in:  Some other UI quibbles:  You can't find the range and stats of enemies?  I can see the first engagement or two, but by the third engagement SM should have an idea of the actual capabilities of enemy units.Also, on the deployment screen, unless you have a weapon choice, you don't get to see weapon statlines.  So why would you know if you should take a squad with bolers or plasma guns? (If you don't know lore)>*There's some definite annoyances.  On a game with less technical complexity than Xcom (at least early on), some things are difficult to see.  I know where the action points are, but you have to mentally read the statline for it (data is arraigned almost like those codex sheets).<There is a next unused unit button, but it's the letter P default, so you have to take your hand off the mouse of the left side of the keyboard to use.  Nothing major, but hmmm.>It's easy to send troops tromping off into the face of the enemy when you think you've selected to shoot at them.  Against Tyranids, that is a bad thing.<I think if you use a melee weapon, you enter the space you attacked; whereas shooting into the space doesn't make you advance, pulls you out of position in a defensive position, but cleared that up anyway.>Overall, this is a decent game.  GW tosses licenses to their games to developers of all levels of skill and passion, which makes their games something of a crapshoot.  Like most Slitherine published games, this one is a B title, but is a solid niche title for particular players.  Worth playing, especially if you're into 40K.  If you're not on the GW wagon, it probably shifts this into a decent TBS, but held up against say, Xcom, I'd recommend Xcom to the general TBS gamer.

_childDocuments_.review: Replaces Sanctus Reach as the closest you can get to the tabletop experience.Games with overwatch tend to incline players to sit back and let the enemy come to them. To avoid that, those games punish the player for inaction by setting an arbitrary time limit on missions. Momentum instead rewards players for pushing into the fight, by giving extra actions and empowered abilities for kills and the like. I found this made the game a lot more exciting.On standard difficulty the game was just the right kind of challenging: low fail risk, but you have to really pay attention, and be flexible as the situation changes.There are lots of modifications for units, but you add them to each unit individually, at a cost of army points. This is a lot more like the tabletop, and means you can have a dreadnaught that hunts swarms with a heavy flamer, and one that hunts heavies with a multimela. It means you can take a hand flamer off a single assault squad if you're a few points over the army limit for a mission.There are tons of units to choose from, and lots from the newer age of 40k. This gives you a huge amount of choice going into each battle, from battle sister seraphim and death company assault squads, to interecssors and agressors.The graphics are solid and the sounds are great. Animations are crunchy and powerful. The music (with the exception of one awful pipe organ track) is really good and fits the theme.The UI is a bit lacking, but my main complaint is that it isn't at all colour blind friendly: range is shown as coloured eyes or targeting rings, with optimal ranges being shown as a changing shade of the orange colour used.There's a bit of a lack of info. Very few tooltips, and although you can see what weapons enemies are equipped with, you can't see those weapon's stats.After the initial tutorial there's no more guidance or information. A quick guide to army building would have been good, and it took me a minute to figure out how upgrades work (select a unit, click their weapon listing, toggle different weapons.)Some sound files seem to be missing. Tanks have no engine growl, gargoyles have no wing flap sound, landspeeders make no whine as they fly...There's an upgrade for gravis tank units, but there are no gravis tank units.

_childDocuments_.review: Regardless if you know the WH40K Lore or not, I think if you have any interest in tactical strategy or war games, this is a fantastic title to pick up. I am impressed by the game on all fronts. It has a great campaign, different map objectives, lots and lots of bugs to kill and awesome units to deploy.What I like about this game is it is kind of like playing a tabletop campaign of WH40K. You get requisition points per mission to add more troops to your reserve and get a point limit to build a squad out of units in your current barracks or reserve. Picking up different units have different costs, and adding different armaments to their models increases their effectiveness (in most cases) but also increases their cost. You can make some very different squad and loadout builds for every mission and adapt to the ever changing threats that the Tyranids began to deploy.The game starts off with very basic stuff and gradually opens up. Newer and tougher enemies start to appear in missions, and you will need to have a squad capable of handing multiple threat levels and priority targets. You will learn to love certain units as you play, and as they keep surviving they gain veteran status which gives them bonuses to accuracy and damage.  I have two squads of Intercessors (your basic bad ass Marine squads) that have survived for 12 missions, and they are some of the best units I have in my squad, even though they're a tier 1 unit.This is probably one of the best Warhammer 40K games I've played. The attention to detail in this is great. The voice acting is your typical grim dark space opera stuff but it fits this setting and lore so well. The music is also very good and adds a lot to missions. I am very excited to try planetary supremacy and the developers are introducing more factions for skirmish and potentially more campaigns down the road. It's a game that will have some good content to come. It's worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: From my understanding this game is trying to imitate the tabletop game, which is cool, but also left a lot to be desired. The more I play this game the more I thought about games like X-Com or Dawn of War 2.1. Bad UI: For lack of the better words, the mission overlay UI is horrendous. In the army screen before mission and especially on the deployment phase. Since they often give you more point than your deployment allowed. Painstakingly scroll down pages of huge unit tab to plus minus them is always a headache. Dawn of War 2 manage this and customization far, far better. X-Com also let you know whether you can hit something at a certain position or not, there's none of that here.2. Exocrine and stuff : I think whenever dev wants to add difficulties to the players they want to make sure the players realized their fault and recklessness and learn from it. In a sense Dark Soul and XCOM does this really well. This is why I think that Exocrine really has no reason to be this one-shot, out-of range, run and gun weapon(and boy can it run). Don't get me wrong you can deal with them just fine. But they feel cheap, artificial, like NPC facing you simply harvest more resource per turn. And that in a strategy game is just....well...cheap. I think they would have a more designated role if it can barely moves and shoots scatter shots among a area or a powerful 1 shot towards a single model to force engagement. Not a explosion that wipes out a team WITH PLAYER UNABLE TO DO ANYTHING ABOUT IT. It's just bad design.3. Cover: The cover system can really use some work, unlike Xcom, your team don't actively lean against wall and turn a corner to shoot. They would just shoot at the wall, with a serious face. I know this is meant to imitate the tabletop, but it pulls one out of the immersion really hard. It would be nice if cover can actually be used.4. Disappointing customization: The army customization left a lot to be desired, and by that I mean even Dawn of war 2's 4 squad limit customization without gear selection has a lot more variety than the whole blood angel army in this game. venerate plate, veteran armor, prestige helm, noticeable change when upgrading armor, force your HQ to obey common sense and wear a ♥♥♥♥♥ HELMET. There's none of that.That's my main gripe with the game, like I said it's a fine game, but it could have been so, so much better and epic.Some miscellaneous things:1.We have a really cool animation when dropping a assault marine. I don't get why we don't have that on the deployment phase. Things are just...there, instantly. I get sometime we get ambushed but heck I like the animation when thunder-hawk swoop in.2.If all of the above is added, tyranids are due to a big buff, perhaps double the number/spawn rate in the campaign.3. A random spawn in a strategy game is not exactly fulfilling, I often have some flyer swoop in from where I just passed and pick off my basic units. Which again, feels disingenuous. That's why people don't use Sister of Battle.4. some sync animation would be nice, great build-up animation before mission launch would be cool. A simple 3d viewer on the army screen would be great.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game especially if you like Turn Based Strategy and Warhammer 40K, a great game if you like either.The Blood Angels are my favourite 40K Space Marine Chapter for many reasons (suck it, Ultramarines!) and I really recommend getting the Blood Angels DLC as it gives you access to the Sanguinary Guard, which can A: use Jump Packs (fly greater distances, over obstacles and other troops). B: excellent in Close Combat and C: not too bad at ranged combat (but come at a points cost to match, but worth it) as well as the famed Blood Angels Assault Terminators with Lightning Claws which can tear most things apart in close combat (they can be equipped through HQ Management to Deep Strike and I believe be equipped with Thunder Hammers and Storm Shields.New units and characters are unlocked as you complete missions, making your army more varied and your tactics more flexible, choosing which you want to take on a mission can mean success or failure, some focus on close combat, some on ranges and they have different weapons reflecting the capability of them against different enemy types.Overall, this is one of the best Turn-Based games I've played, and I own a few, and definitely one of the best 40K Turn-Based games (Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters is brilliant too, but Grey Knights, my second favourite Chapter). Both games have solid character customisation through progression rewards to make your troops more effective. Battlesector is a little more on the large-battle, points-based side, like the tabletop Warhammer 40K, whereas Daemonhunters is is more skirmish-sized.I'd happily pay full price for this, but if it's on sale, I highly recommend picking it up if it seems like something you'd be interested in.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Warhammer 40K and you like turn-based strategy, this will scratch that itch.It's different enough from existing WH40K strategy titles so that you feel like you're playing something fresh.To sum the game up, Battlesector has that Dawn of War combat feel combined with the satisfaction of army management from Warhammer table top while introducing digital turn-based combat similar to Warhammer 40,000: Gladius and Mechanicus with unique unit abilities and skill trees.It's similar to "Warhammer 40,000: Gladius - Relics of War" in that it's turn-based, map tiles can only have 1 unit per tile, and units have unique abilities that have cooldowns, but Battlesector focuses on individual battles where as Gladius focuses on an entire map with cities, resources, and an economy to worry about.Battlesector is purely strategic play revolving around your unit composition and maximizing their strengths while minimizing their weaknesses vs enemy units, and maps have cover and terrain features like choke points that can be exploited.Instead of an economy, you get an Army Management screen where you build your own army using a unit limit and a point value system (similar to Warhammer table top). Each mission will have its own maximum point cap, and you have to configure your army so you don't go over the cap but still have a balanced unit mix (meaning you can't just load up on dreadnoughts).Added to this is a skill tree where you can spend command points you've earned from completed missions to boost various skills based on what your army makeup is.If you focused on melee units, there are skills to bolster melee combat, and visa versa for ranged.A skill line also exists that lets you call in off-map air support from Thunderhawks with available weapon upgrades if you go further down the tree.The combat is satisfying, with fully voiced units and audio and visual fx that fit the 40k bill. There is no "queue" of units performing actions, meaning if you're quick enough you can have all of your plasma rifle units firing on the giant, high armor Tyrranofex at the same time and enjoy the light show of awesome firepower.A helpful UI tool that allows you to speed up/skip animations lets you control just how much animation realism you want.The campaign has fully voiced characters talking back and forth to each other, with some monologue here and there from your Sergeant as he apparently talks into his digital dictation device and conveys his thoughts on current events instead of simply writing it down.Most of the issues I've found are largely UI issues.The biggest glaring UI issue is the Army Management screen gives you ZERO information about unit weapons. You can see unique unit ability tooltips and info, but if you're trying to compare damage, armor penetration, and optimal weapon ranges for unit A versus unit B....you can't currently.A workaround is getting all this weapon info from a different pre-deployment army confirmation screen that only pops up right before a mission is launched and write it all down on paper or a spreadsheet. It's honestly a huge flaw that was somehow overlooked during testing and quality assurance.Other minor issues include the game not doing a great job of showing you optimal ranges of weapons unless you mouse over the weapon's hotbar icon and the game will then display which tiles surrounding your unit can be targeted using the weapon, but even then the optimal range tiles are highlighted with a bright gold symbol, and as the accuracy falls off the symbol gets dimmer and dimmer, with extremely subtle differences in the intensity of the dimming.Other quality of life changes that could be made would include a way to tell where you unit has to stand to inflict the maximum damage/accuracy of a weapon/skill against an enemy unit before you actually move your own unit.Currently you have to read the range info on the tooltip, note the optimal range, count that many spaces away from the enemy unit you want to attack, and then figure out if you have enough movement points to get to that spot.I think it's a solid enough strategy title that is worthy of the WH40K brand. It could definitely be polished more and improved, but it's a great start and lots of fun if you're into customizing your units and fielding your composition creations during scripted campaign or skirmish missions against Tyranids (the developers have stated more factions are coming).

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics are excellent with great rendering and animation of the different units. The voices for the Blood Angels troops are the usual devout and bombastic declarations of battle mottoes and faith in the Emprah.Scenarios are interesting and engaging. The Sisters of Battle (only an ally of Blood Angles, not a whole faction - yet) voice overs are clear, shrewd and cynical. The reason I keep playing this one is the action system for your units. You have movement points (used for moving - no surprises there) and Action Points (1 for most units, 2 for command units) which are used to shoot, attack in melee, and power some abilities. these points are completely decoupled. This means you can move & shoot, shoot & move, move some then shoot then move the rest, or even shoot move and shoot again (if your unit has 2+ action points). This makes for very flexible deployment of your troops in exactly the way you want. Every weapon has both a max. range and an Optimal Range - at which you are most likely to hit. SO even if there is one position clearly favourable to fire from, multiple units can shoot from there if you carefully consider how they can all move through that one spot and away again after firing.  I think this flexibility allows me to run my army in groups or detachments  in the way i "expect" detachments to work and its very easy to strategize as you can usually find a way to do what you want.If you prefer more of a "warriors charging into glorious combat" approach, you are rewarded with Momentum Points for kills or certain actions with each unit. When these hit 100 you can  or  your unit.  gives you an extra Action Point that turn.  gives you access to a "beefed up" version of one of your abilities. I don't try super-hard for the surges, preferring to get the right position and use a good mix of units to do the job. ALso the main way to conserve momentum is to use all your moves. When a unit has 4 movement points to burn and only one open space to move to, it looks like a school kid who needs the bathroom. There should be a command that lets you "burn" leftover movement points as long as you have one open space around you. But that's a minor gripe. At the end of your turn, the game does prompt you to put all units that still have Action Points into Overwatch (this reduces Momentum loss from 20 to 10).The Necrons have been announced as a new faction coming soon, along with a new campaign mode where BAs, Nids and Necrons try to conquer a planetary map by pushing the other two off. If its done as well as the current game, Black Labs will have increased the replayability of the game significantly for the enthusiastic one-player fans.If you enjoyed Dawn of War or Sanctus Reach, this deserves a good look.TLDR: it looks and sounds pretty, easy to manage your whole force and quite entertaining. If you're a 40K fan  its definately worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: Best digital version of 40k tabletop. Great SFX & VFX, great fidelity for models, maps, and animations, and has a few different ways to play that were not there on release!Firstly is the campaign, play as the Blood Angels after the universe gets ripped in half with the Primaris against the Tyranids invaders on the moons of Baal alongside the Sisters of Battle. Surprisingly great VO for the main characters that you'll control and have narrate throughout the campaign.Second is player-made campaigns that you can download and supplement for the other races which didn't get a campaign.Third is a world-conquest mode, generate a hex map overworld to conquer and manage army composition & upgrades, and then fight in randomly generated battle maps that feel VERY close to what you'd actually run for 40k tabletop (including the first turn being mostly charging).Fourth is the standard Skirmish mode, make an army of a certain point value for two sides, pick a map, play!Fifth is Demonic Incursion, a last stand type mode, build a starting army then survive indefinitely against the Daemons of Khorne as the progressively wear you down! Between waves you can reinforce your army so as to not make the battle too short for the skull throne.And finally is multiplayer, which is like Skirmish, but meaner and more heretical.All the different factions are fun to play as and against, though I feel like just one extra unit for each race besides the space marines would be a nice addition as everyone else's roster feels just a little too short. Overall though great adaptation of 40k!

_childDocuments_.review: Battlesector is a great example of a solid tactical strategy game.  In the narrative campaign you play as Blood Angels against Tyranids.  It took me about 20 hours to complete on the default difficulty (Astartes), and I only had 2 battles during the campaign that gave me any real trouble, so if you're decent at these kinds of games you might want to consider upping the difficulty for more of a challenge.  The story in the campaign is solid though not remarkable, but the voice acting is excellent, if mostly isolated to vignettes before and after missions.  The map campaign (which was added in the DLC but which is accessible to anyone who owns the game) lets you play as Blood Angels, Tyranids, or Necrons.  Necrons are only available for play if you own the DLC, but they'll still show up as adversaries.  The soundtrack is ok, and if you get it in a bundle it's nifty to have, but I probably wouldn't buy it separately.  I'm not a big multiplayer guy so I haven't really delved into it, but the Skirmish mode is a lot of fun.  All in all, if you're looking for a game to scratch the tactical strategy itch, then this is a good game to try out, and if you like Warhammer 40k, it's a great game with the license.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game for tabletop 40k fans.Although it doesn't follow the rules of the game completely (no movement phase, shooting phase, etc), it does a great job at adapting turn based gameplay with the core functions of the tabletop game. I just finished the 20 missions in the campaign with 30 hours on the clock, and haven't even touched the other two modes yet. This could very quite a bit depending on the campaign difficulty (I did mine on 2nd or 3rd highest difficulty). If there's one thing I love about this game (so far) is that all units feel balanced and important. As someone who has played Tyranids, unbalanced units suck in that army. The same could be said about the blood angels, but I haven't had much practice with them on the tabletop.If I had to critique a few aspects of the game, the graphics and amount of detail in the maps could use some work. The last half of the campaign featured some really great maps, but nothing that blew my socks off. Some camera tweaks would also be nice, but that's nit picking a bit. With that said, I plan on playing more on the skirmish and multiplayer modes available and can't wait to see the more units, factions, maps, and other DLC they will add to this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Battlesector is a well designed tactical game in the Warhammer 40,000 universe featuring the conflict between Space Marines (Blood Angels in particular) with Tyranids. _childDocuments_.review: Conditionally recommended. If you want to know if this game is for you, read on!This is a game about small battles in the Warhammer40k universe. It´s strictly turn-based. The videos with seemingly many things happening at once are misleading. This is actually good: you can take your time and work out the perfect order of moves.What you get with the bundle is: 3 army lists (Necrons, Tyranids & Blood Angel Space Marines) with about 15 different units each. A unit is either a 3-5 men squad or an individual monster, vehicle or hero. 2 campaigns and 11 skirmish maps.The presentation of this game is great: Units. maps, animations, voice acting, music- I like all of it. Most importantly, the presentation adds to the gameplay and doesn´t distract from it. Nor does the interface. It is functional, which is all that it needs to be.Multiplayer skirmishes are chess with fog of war and army building.  If this is your niche, it´s your lucky day: Buy the bundle immediately! My recommendation is for you and ONLY for you. I can´t think of any other game that does this small skrmish/army building combo so well. The units are all unique and come with one or more special abilities each and usually with a few alternative weapon loadouts to choose from. Tinkering with the army building alone will keep you busy for many hours.The skirmish AI is not terrible. It can´t replace a human opponent, but to learn the game and as a sparring partner it is ok-ish. However, if you are not interested in pbem or online play at all, I am not sure if I would recommend this game to you. In the long run, the AI is no match for a player who knows what he is doing.Campaign play is the weakest part of Battlesector.  I do NOT recommend buying this game for the campaigns. There is only one story campaign for the Blood Angels, and it´s not very good.  It is totally linear with not a single decision point. Don´t bother about avoiding losses, either. You move from one scenario to the next, regardless of losses. The campaign scenarios are boring as hell: Waves of Tyranids are sent against you, and you dispatch them, like in a tower defense game. There is no scripted campaign for the Necros and Tyrants, and that´s just as well. There is a random campaign, which they honestly admit is a work in progress, and, like the AI, it is ok-ish but not great.So there is my recommendation: Absolutely get this game, if you are into MP and army building, but it´s not a must-have if you are interested in SP only and particularly in campaign play.[Edited slightly after 60 hours. My opinion on the random campaign has a little improved and I do not totally recommend against buying the game any more if you are playing SP only.]

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is really good! But, only get it if you've been wanting a tabletop experience on pc for a while. Here's why: The Good:- Tabletop likeness: Battlesector bears striking similarity to the tabletop game in how it plays.- Graphics: The graphics are spot-on. looking vibrant and satisfying, but not so much so that it would harm immersion with the Grimdark- Sound: The voices are very similar to those in the Dawn of War series, which in my opinion is somewhat of a gold standard for voices and sound design in the Warhammer 40k franchise.- Gameplay: The gameplay is satisfying. The planar levels with mild height differences serve to make the game feel similar to the tabletop, which I love.The Bad:- Jank: Battlesector is very immersive between its sound design and voice acting particularly. This makes short moments of jank with poorly registering cover, immersion-breakingly bad aim on plasma cannons, and the camera clipping through terrain much worse. Particularly the last occurred only about four times in my playthrough of the story,  but each time was a real stinging pain.- Balancing: Balancing is generally good, but there are some issues, particularly with the Prime. Now I don't have experience with the tabletop game, so this might be a common issue, but a unit with enough hp and armor to survive three squads of space marines with high hit chances, along with three action points, high damage double melee attacks and increased movement range every turn is not balanced. Spoiler warning: The two primes in the final mission were a far greater threat than all other Tyranids, including the Tyrant, together.- Unlocks: Throughout the story you unlock unit buffs. They are honestly pointless, and really just add an element of frustration. I guess the army customization needed to be fleshed out to give a break from battle, and the set amount of slots in the army, which completely denies the good old fun of strength in numbers by the way, just didn't offer enough room or reason for customization. I'll add to that in the next segment.The Ugly:- Content: I want to see this gameplay framework with other factions. The Gameplay itself offers a great basis for games and the two factions in the game are nicely fleshed out. So why give it the shortest, least replayable campaign I've ever seen? The missions all play the same, with two major elements of objective: 1. "eliminate the Xenos" and 2. "activate this field", with the former requiring strong slow units and the latter favoring mobile units. If your army is built with some Aggressors and Dreadnoughts, some marines as DPS and one or two assault Intercessor squads in case the objective is hard to reach, you never have any reason to switch it up, so any visit to that screen is only to replenish the dead.  Other fun strategies include:1. The stompa: get a bunch of heavy storm boyz and stomp on gitz. Also very punishing because they die very quickly. There's no victory like... actually, theres just no victory. The Waagh won't save you. Also. you're not orks.2. The low baller aka. Adeptus Sororitas: Since you only have so many slots, fill them all up with Battlesisters! You will never exceed the point limit again! Or use abilities for that matter. But anything for waifu Verity!3. Mecha Mekka: Give Techmarine Croginax a stiffy by using only Dreadnoughts. Side effects may include tiny armies, ineffective damage and friendly fire.4. Double take: Librarians get a second turn. Their abilities aren't fleshed out a lot, but that second turn sure is fun. Totally not disappointing.My point is, that there are many possibilities, but they usually can't beat a large group of space marines behind a wall of Aggressors and Dreadnoughts. At least during the dreadfully short campaign you're punished for anything that isn't slowly advancing a giant army and putting objectives on the backburner because there aren't really any punishments for failing objectives, so long as you end up eliminating the horde.This game is really fun and I love it to death, but it just needs more content. I want to see more factions, and a system where each unit has something that makes it special. Especially the Sororitas offers no benefits or fun mechanics other than haha girl can pray brrrrrrrrrr - or give it numbers. Having both a point limit and unit limit makes sense from a pc resource standpoint, but is very redundant, especially for people like me, who enjoy large armies over diverse ones.If we get campaign expansion dlc, and/or more factions, then I will recommend this game for really anyone to play. That said, I really like this game. It does mostly everything it tries to do very well. If you really want a Warhammer game similar to the table top, this is that game.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who plays Blood Angels on the tabletop I was absolutely stoked for this game. But it has some problems that I just cannot overlook.For the impatient, TLDR:Buy this game on sale only if you:- Love Blood Angels- Are interested in playing with Primaris in a PC gameIf you are interested in an actually good strategy game in the 40k universe buy and play Sanctus ReachLong version:This game has a very similar feel and mechanics to another 40k game by Slytherin themselves: Sanctus Reach. That game is quite a few years older so the graphics (and voiceovers) in Battlesector are better. But in every other aspect Sanctus Reach is just a superior strategy game. Here is a list of things that Slytherin managed to implement years ago and for some puzzling reason are not in Battlesector:- A clear way of visualizing line of sight and the amount and direction of cover. Also, being directly behind cover and shooting OUT OF IT penalizes you exatly the same as if you were shooting at something in cover. So your guys can be inside a building shooting out of the windows and will just regularly hit the walls of their own building. I just... cannot.- The ability to exchange the position of one unit for another in the pre-game deployment. You have to move unit A to an empty square before you move unit B into the square previously occupied by unit A, which is just unnecesarily tedious.- A pre-game mission breefing showing the map and zones of interest on it. You can't even look at the map while deploying. This is just baffling, especially in the context of the campaign you are playing. These are Blood Angels cleansing their literal home planet on which they have been fighting against this very enemy for the past months and you go into every.single.mission... blindly.- A clear way of showing units stats. This is so aggravating, especially because the stat improvements you buy during the course of the campaign are just never shown in the army selection screen. If an upgrade gives +10HP to your intercessor, the army selection screen still shows you the base HP. Armor is another basic stat that is just... not shown.  (not even the pre-game deployment will show you) to see all the stats and their improvements implemented live on the units.- Friendly fire is just not a thing. Or shots landing somewhere else and thus hitting other units on adjacent squares. Bullets either hit their intended target or dissapear into the aether.- A help page or even a clear explanation of half the things that happen, especially around close combat. There are 3 tutorial missions that cover the absolute basics. After that you can figure out on your own why some of your guys get a pistol reaction shot and others not (hint: surprisingly, it is not tied to actually being equipped with a pistol)Then there is this design choice, a thing that Battlesector just manages differently than Sanctus Reach (in my opinion, for the worse): Individual unit advancement and abilities tied to it are gone. Instead, Battlesector has advancement trees in a separate screen "emanating" from the comanders, where you buy improvements for tokens you get for completing missions and individual units increase in veterancy (with a fairly neglible bonus) for being deployed on a mission. What it means in practice is twofold: 1) The best improvements specifically for your heroes are deep in the tree. And if the choice is improving the whole army or just a single dude, the best choice will always be improving the army. While in Sanctus Reach your heroes felt actually heroic and their heroic deeds allowed them to be even cooler, in Battlesector your heroes are just... kinda hangig around. They are free so at least you are not actively punished for bringing them, but they just feel so bland (except the Librarian Dreadnought, because he is just a god out of the box).2) if a particular unit dies, you substitute it and just move on. There is no real sense of connection or narrative. Their improvement is decoupled from their performance. This is intercessor unit 3, it has been with me for 6 missions and they might have done the most heroic ♥♥♥♥ during them or maybe they were in a corner staring into the distance. There is no difference. If they die in the next mission I will get another intercessor unit and rinse and repeat. It feels less like a story that you are developing and more like what it is: a game where you move (poorly shown) statblocks around and fight against other statblocks.The game offers some fun and some missions have interesting designs, but overall it is just a worse game than what Slytherin has already shown they can do. If you want to play an actually good strategy game and don't mind playing with the wolfi-wolf Wolvelord McWulfen Marines, just get Sanctus Reach.

_childDocuments_.review: [x] Good gameplay loop[x] Missions don't last too long--------The Joke: 0/10 they play this completely seriously--------[x] Tabletop with a lot less dice rolling[x] Good showcase of the new "Space Marine Space Marines" in the Primaris[] some units just sorta stop being used[] Few hints of mission objectives/map layout - reloads may be needed--------This game is both Dawn of War and  Dawn of War at the same time.  It's not Dawn of War in obvious ways ie a turn based tactical game much closer to tabletop mechanics than Relic's largely-conventional RTS, but at the same time both worked as a showcase for new units.  Dawn of War was released 1 month after 4th Edition came out, and Battlesector was in the middle of 9th (iirc Angels v Tyranids was the 'starter box' at the time).  For people that didn't touch the tabletop, this is probably their first regular experience with Space Marines in almost 10 years since Retribution (there was no game after Retribution, what are you talking about).  Gameplay is straightforward.  Units have move points to get around and action points to spend shooting or on various abilities, there are also free abilities that may come with a cooldown or some other cost.  Units cost points (like on tabletop, buying better/different wargear for them makes them cost more) and there is a points (and unit) limit for your deployed army.  There is a reserve of units that you can't take with you to the deployment screen, but there's absolutely nothing stopping you reloading back before mission select and swapping out units as necessary.  Units also cost nothing to recruit between missions (besides perhaps a timer for elites), so replacing all those assault marines that died by jumping into a bad melee is quite easy.  The real balance is making sure you have enough mobility and the right mix of trash clearing and armour piercing, since AT units will prefer to overkill one model in a larger squad rather than spread their limited shots around.  In conclusion, it's a fairly good intro to the franchise for newbies, also tackling a non-ultramarines force is nice.  I wouldn't have minded a ranged army in the regular mix though, it's not the greatest to send a melee-oriented force to fight tyranids....

_childDocuments_.review: Right, this game feels more like a proof of concept demo than a full release. My suggestion is to wait about six months to a year then check back to see if the developer has made any progress.But to go farther into why I feel this game is underdeveloped: First, there are only two playable factions in this game right out of the box. The Blood Angels, and the Tyranids. There is a third faction in "The Sisters of Battle' that is only present as an NPC faction used during the new Planetary Supremacy mode.Only the Blood Angels have a dedicated single player campaign, the Tyranids are playable during multiplayer and planetary supremacy only. The Blood Angels campaign is also very limited. pretty much a linear path of missions which always ends the same way. Then they have the nerve to charge 5 dollars for two elite dlc packs. Each adding a small selection of units to the Blood Angels and Tyranids. Oh, wait, you want a third playable faction? Well, instead of the Battle Sisters already programmed into the game have these necrons which will have an annoyingly broken mechanic which makes them overpowered in multiplayer. And of course they don't get a single player campaign. Multiplayer and Planetary supremacy only.Honestly, if the devs do read this, I am sorry that this comes off as harsh, but I only state this because of how solid the gameplay itself is. This plays and feels like a good adaptation of the current table top Warhammer 40k experience. But I feel like you guys launched this way too early to call it a full release. At least mark it as a pre-release build and assure your customers that the game will have more content added in the near future. Do that and I will change this review to a glowing recommendation. But as a full release, I just can't recommend this to anybody.EDIT: So yeah, quite a bit has changed since I first wrote this. The game has had a number of updates and has seen some free content added. Now while I would recommend this game I highly suggest waiting until Battlesector and all of it's paid DLC are on massive discount, at least 45% or more.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a fan of Games Workshop's settings. Warhammer Fantasy, Age of Sigmar, Horus Heresy, and 40k each have expansive worlds with much to enjoy. The video games are not nearly as expensive as tabletop, and they are far more stable. I generally find them to be the better experience for play/relaxation. This game was loads of fun for a turn based strategy fanatic like me.I didn't have to buy any DLC or play any online multiplayer to complete 100% of achievements. I actually enjoyed it so much I wrote a guide - .The user interface is pretty clean. The graphics aren't too intense. Multiple units can follow commands at the same time. There is a surprising amount of depth and replayability. It's pretty intuitive if you know anything about the units, and if you don't, the information is easily accessible. I can actually recommend this at full price, but there are good deals on it regularly because it came out in 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: This is pure and glorious Space Marine wankfest, and I love it. Definitely a decent 40k game in a sea of abysmal shovelware. If you don't care for Space Marines as a faction then this game probably won't be for you, since that's all its about.Updated review: I still recommend the game, but it lacks depth and variety as well as any real sense of challenge or weight to your decision making. I will compare it to a small tactical RPG title called Battle Brothers where you slowly and meticulously develop a band of weak fighters into a much larger and more powerful professional mercenary force. If a powerful unit dies it is a catastrophe, but units ARE going to die, so you have to play carefully and also utilize cannon fodder tactics with less developed troops. Basically, there is nothing like that in this game. Sure an 18 veteran rank space marine squad is nice, but they really aren't all that more potent than a base rank squad. Landspeeders and tanks and dreadnoughts and every other unit can be stockpiled in your infinite size reserve army to replace any losses you incur, rendering their 'cooldown' requisition period irrelevant. You can, in theory, lose every single unit in your army except 1, finish the mission, and then instantly have an entire full army of the exact composition you want the next battle. This is clearly the intention and meant to represent the available forces of the chapter supporting your important mission, but it still feels sort of whacky and removes any sense of danger or urgency from battles.Speaking of battles, due to the way the game is designed, you will almost always be bringing the full force of your deployed units down onto a much smaller number of enemy units almost every time. The 'trickle in' enemy forces present more of a shooting gallery than a real WH40k tabletop battle might go, with a 2000 point army squaring off against a 2000 point army and both poised to fully engage the other.The most fun I had with the game were the very rare moments where a truly large number of enemy forces appeared and seemed primed to bear down on my guys, but the number and type of tools the game gives you to quickly pare down trivial enemy units is excessive, so these encounters only superficially appeared to be dangerous.I would like the game to be more complex, faster (watching every single slow motion overwatch shot and enemy move gets old really fast), more challenging by default, and to have a sense of continuity. The devs are working on more content for the game and I think it has some really great growth potential that a lot of 40k fans are hoping for.As I mentioned in the beginning of this review, it's all about space marines and it provides a great fantasy in that regard. The game could just be more than it is now, and here is hoping their coming DLC/update manages to do that.Allowing for a modding scene for this game would blow it wide open and fast.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't pay full price. This game is currently worth about £15 in content. It has all the foundations of a potentially great game, however the devs phoned it in and half assed it. Graphics - Good, not greatMechanics - Lacklustre, very basic compared to X-ComSetting - Amazing, you get a real feel for the Warhammer 40k settingOther Notes -Absolutely zero repercussions for losing squads and don't be surprised to have 1 or 2 men left out of a whole army when the missions are over on high difficulties. Next to no RPG elements. You get a very boring upgrade tree for your named characters which affect the rest of your army. However individual units have zero 'experience tracking' and restart every mission as new. Such a shame, allowing each unit to upgrade on their own and earn new weapons and stat improvements would of gone a long way to making this a solid game worthy of the price tag. This would also give an incentive to 'save' squads as at the moment they may as well all be guardsmen with how replaceable they all are. When this is supposed to be showcasing the blood angels space marines, expecting even half of them to die each mission is completely against the lore and setting.As with all games utilising the Warhammer 40k IP at the moment, this game pulls you in with great graphics and the promise of scratching that 40k itch before letting you down just like the rest. Final verdict:5/10 - Flawed game, great foundationCould be a 8/10 game with more content and a altered progression system.

_childDocuments_.review: Battlesector is a solid game  and a breath of fresh air compared to the usual shovelware games that somehow end up with the 40K license. It has a lot of complexity to it, a reasonably compelling single-player campaign, and a myriad of ways to play online versus your friends.I think it's an excellent foundation and I'm excited to see what the devs intend to add on to it. If you like turn-based strategy and/or enjoy the tabletop game, this is a reasonably faithful recreation of that rendered in good graphics and surprisingly good VA. Whether the online play and 20-mission campaign is worth $40 is up to you, but it has the legs to go wherever it wants from here.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? YES! Turn-based battles do not get much better.Control your squads of Blood Angel Space Marines in a deadly fight against swarms of ugly Tyranids. As Sergeant Carleon says, "Their death is our only option". You can command the Tyranids in multiplayer, other races are not included (yet).The main game consists of squad-level combat on various maps. Your squads use movement points and action points for their attacks or special actions. What I absolutely loved is that you can give orders to the next unit while the first unit still executes it's orders. You can examine the levels from all directions, zoom out or down to a close-up view of your units. Enemy units are of course covered in the fog of war, but there is an overhead map for extra convenience. Between the missions you can buy new units in the army management screen or spend HQ tokens to unlock new abilities and weapons for your hero units - there are large tech trees to unlock.Quite a few of the (often good) strategy titles published by Slitherine are ugly and with a cumbersome user interface. This game looks amazing and has a user interface that even I understood after a few minutes. In addition to the good looks and polished UI, it comes with professional voice-overs between and during the 20 missions of the campaign.The Emperor is always the truth! As long as you don't suffer from a Warhammer 40,000 allergy, this is one of the best squad-level turn-based combat games you can play.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first; if you are a 40k fan, you definitely should buy this game. Further, if you're a Blood Angels fan (like I am) then you NEED to buy this game. This is objectively the best 40k game since Mechanicus, easily among the best 40k games ever, and I personally enjoyed it more than Mechanicus, though that is probably just the Blood Angels fanboy in me talking.Pros:- Very 40k story that was written by 40k fans. You can tell that the developers love the setting and have an understanding of the material they are working with. Nods to Commander Dante and the level of detail that they've put into locations like Angel's Fall show that these people know their ♥♥♥♥ when it comes to their 40k lore.-  Great gameplay. Nothing feels without purpose, and every unit feels like it is point-priced fairly. Force multipliers like Librarians and Sanguinary Priests are expensive, but their buffs are valuable. Units like Intercessors and Sisters of Battle are cheaper, but are great for clearing chaff or just doing that last sliver of damage to take down a big bug.- Variety of gameplay. Lots and lots of options for how you want your Blood Angels to play. Being a Blood Angels purist, I leaned heavily into a highly aggressive, highly mobile force with a focus on close-combat, and bringing one or two iconic heavier Blood Angel units like the Baal Predator and Librarian Dreadnought when I needed the extra firepower. However, it is just as possible to build a gunline army of Intercessors, Battle Sisters, Hellblasters, and Aggressors, or to build an army that leans heavily into Hero units.- Probably the best representation of the tabletop game to date on a digital platform that isn't a mod for Tabletop simulator. Right down to the point values of the units to the additional wargear options.- DEATH COMPANY! Easily my favorite unit in the game, replaced my Assault Marines with them as soon as they were unlocked. Great for clearing out chaff with either their ten attacks or Hand Flamers (when they've been unlocked), which builds up their Black Rage stacks (which buffs melee and makes their shooting less accurate) and their momentum meter, which makes them an enormous threat to even the chunkiest Tyranids. x20 attacks of +30 damage ain't nothing to ♥♥♥♥ with. If you want to absolutely annihilate something, throw a couple melee buffs from your Sang Priest and Sisters of Battle character and watch them go to town.Cons:- The unit limit can be pretty frustrating. It steadily rises through the campaign and then around the middle caps out at 20 units. Further, you HAVE to take all the voiced characters into each battle, which takes up five full slots by the midgame. I understand the balancing concerns, but if I'm going infantry-heavy my Techmarine doesn't really have a whole lot to do except take potshots with his bolt pistol or maybe swing his axe a couple times.- I wish there was a way to see how many points unlockable wargear added to the unit cost before you unlocked it. As it was, on several occasions I unlocked a weapon, equipped it, saw it would send my desired army over the mission point limit, and reloaded a save so I could respend the points. Thankfully, the game autosaves after each mission before you've spent your tokens and the load speed is very quick, so it wasn't a huge issue but seems like it would be an easy fix.- No Chaplains. This was pretty disappointing for me personally, as the Chaplains of the Blood Angels play a pretty important and unique role in their chapter (and successors) compared to other founding chapters as they are tasked with overseeing Blood Angels that have succumbed to the Black Rage. The fact that the Black Rage plays an important role in the story makes this extra disappointing. It would have been awesome to see a Jump Chaplain leading my three+ squads of Death Company and giving them additional buffs.What I want going forward:- More factions. This gameplay system is great. I'd love to see it applied to factions that could be added in the future like Imperial Guard, Chaos Space Marines, Necrons, or Orks.- More campaigns. Kind of goes hand-in-hand with more factions. Having additional campaigns to play such fighting any of the factions I listed above would be great fun. Really, I just want more Battle Sector.

_childDocuments_.review: GRADE A-. So i wasn't expecting much from this game at first glance and i ended up picking it up on sale since i like the IP. What a pleasant surprise to find that this is a much better game than i anticipated. I liked how it really captures the feel of tabletop Warhammer in the 40k universe.Battlesector is a love letter to the tabletop game, capturing its tactical depth and unit variety in stunning digital form. Each squad feels distinct and has a specific tactical purpose. And The RPG-like skill trees add a layer of satisfying customization, letting you forge your own band of grimdark Squads and customize your tactics.I thought the story was good but it does contain some deeper references into the VAST lore of the 40k universe. And it might be hard for some to follow. But the Voice acting brings the narrative to life, and even if some details might seems obscure to casual fans of the IP, it's stil a FUN tale of heroism and sacrifice in the face of galactic horror.My only REAL gripe? It could really have used more playable factions with their own stories and missions. The Two it launched with were well balanced and excellent, but the 40k universe begs for more. And even though the online community is still pretty active the limited  army choices means that fans of the IP, who would love Battlesector, might give it a pass since their favorite armies are not represented. Expansions or multiplayer modes offering more factions would be a big plus. But once i finish my current play through and a few online matches, i don't know if ill re-download this in the future to check out the new content unless its a NEW full campaign with a new story.Overall, Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector is a a FUN game and a pleasant surprise. It nails the tabletop feel, offers strategic depth, and delivers pure, grimdark fun. If you're a fan of the franchise or turn-based strategy, this is worth checking out. Just be warned: you might end up wanting to paint some miniatures by the end of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great tbs game. Don't expect too much in the way of deep narrative as even in the sole sp campaign the story comes across largely as throwaway gibberish. Despite this, Battlesector's primary strength remains its campaign as each map is well designed and interesting with new army upgrades and/or new units being awarded at the end of each. This progression gives the campaign a satisfying and utterly absorbing feel. There are 3 other game modes one being a fairly standard skirmish mode which can be played against AI but I'm certain is primarily there for the inclusion of PvP; a survival mode where you just try to outlast wave after wave of enemies, and the other is a new hex map conquest game called Planetary Domination and it's quite fun.Regarding DLC - unless you intend to play lots of skirmish and multiplayer there is currently no reason to buy any of the dlc beyond the Blood Angels Elites one - which is a great dlc. Sadly, none of the other dlc add any campaign content and you can't run the main campaign with anything other than those it offers you as standard and those that come as part of the Blood Angels Elite pack.The game is still actively being worked on and improvements to all aspects of the game (including the new Planetary Domination mode itself) are evident. A future new campaign is also in the works. It's a shame the devs haven't (yet?) found a way to let you take your dlc units into the main campaign as this would have greatly added to both the value of the dlcs themselves and created a lot more replay value for those not too interested in PvP or survival mode.NB: Keep in mind that creator content IS available through a weird in-game interface rather than through the external workshop and that you do not see this until you agree to the online part of the EULA via the "custom" menu.

_childDocuments_.review: It's turn based, so just be warned if that's not your bag. Otherwise, this might be the most enjoyable and most Warhammer40k of the WH40k games I've played, and that includes the entire RTS series of Dawn of War, Space Marine, and the other turn based WH40K games, which I have here on Steam or other services.   That said, this is more along the lines of a budget to mid-range title, as opposed to AAA. There are only Blood Angel space marines(and some Sisters) and Tyrannids in the campaign, no other races or even other chapters.  I got about 20 hours out of the campaign, and I was taking my time. 20 Missions total?  There are some rumors of the developers making a more open ended campaign with a map, which would be amazing, but currently you just have the single path of missions campaign, just vs Tyrannids.  It feels like some of the upgrades for single units (Warhammer for your main NPC, for example) are WAY too expensive, 65 points, when plasma marines are 110 points and are 10 times more useful.  The Pistol and Melee weapon upgrades for most of the HQ units should be far cheaper, that's really my only gripe.  I  would like a way to upgrade the regular marines (Intercessors) and Sisters to have plasma or something, because late game they are basically useless against higher level enemy troops, but that's game balance for you. It's true to the lore, I'd assume, but shooting armies are far better than trying to go melee vs the Tyrannids, especially later in the campaign.  I dropped all my Librarians and even Dreadnoughts for just tanks and plasma troops, and wiped the floor with the highest level enemies.  Missions design was overall very enjoyable, with only 1 mission where you're designed to lose surrounded troops really annoying me, as I could not figure out how to save all 7 surrounded troops!@#!  It's okay though, lore wise; humanity is always getting slaughtered by the xenos, until overpowered Space Marines show up.I would love to see this game added to with additional campaigns and races, the core engine here is great, and the voice acting and writing was even acceptable, which I was not expecting, hehe.  Additional DLC campaigns with more races, get to it, Developers! :)tl,dr: If you enjoy turn based games (on the slightly simpler side) and enjoy the Warhammer 40k universe, pick this up.   Also, plasma is your friend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is certainly not a AAA title. It's not bad. But it's not great. It's snugly right in decent territory. The campaign is so-so. It's honors the Warhammer 40k aesthetic really well. Everything looks good. Models are good. It's kinda cool seeing it on the screen in 3d. I really like the presentation. Angels look great, the Tyranids look great. Although, hive fleet leviathan isn't the coolest color scheme. But good god the callouts, and the Tyranid roars sound awful. "They will fear to tread close" is an awful sentence, and I hear it ♥♥♥♥♥♥ constantly. It's only in there because of the Sanguinius book Fear to Tread. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate that. There are like 3 tyranid pain roars, and they play on repeat, and are shared between creatures. So a Trygon sounds exactly like a hormagaunt sounds exactly like an Exocrine sounds exactly like a Warrior. It's awful.Some of the music is ok. But some of it is AWFUL. The Astropathic Relay map has teh worst music hands down. I turned it off. The AI is ok, but sometimes it is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid. I had a Trygon crawl just far enough into my bolter battle line to activate every single Overwatch. Then it burrowed 3 spaces back, then forward to. Why did it do that? I had an exocrine walk between 3 of my melee guys triggering Zone of Control and taking a lot of damage. Then it burned it's AP to take one more step. It didn't even attack. This leads me to my next complaint. I'm playing on Hard (Lieutenant) difficulty. And so far the grand strategy is to just pile up all your Blood Angels into a Big Blob of Bolters and just march across the map. Sprinkle in a few jet pack dudes to close the gap between you and the artillery. That's all you need to do to win every mission. The tyranids have such ♥♥♥♥ ranged weapons that they pose zero threat to you. Just keep marching forward firing with all your bolters and you'll win. There's not much tactical skill required to be successful. It's really difficult to recommend this game, but given that it's only 40 bucks, it may be worth it for you if you love Blood Angels. If they add mod support in the future then buy this for sure.
