_childDocuments_.review: First impressions were good, it had an appealing monochrome pixel art style that gives it a nostalgic charm, and it managed to communicate the story without dialogue, just visuals and minimal controls, using just the spacebar and left/right arrow keys. Visually speaking, it's a lovely game. As for the story itself, it's a collection of slice-of-life vignettes focused on the daily lives of a handful of anthropomorphic animals. The story of the rat lady in the beginning was rather heartwarming; it had this sweet melancholic feel as we watch her live out her golden years alone in the countryside. The life of the moose kid in the fourth chapter was interesting as well, watching him grow up throughout the chapter and seeing all the troublemaking he got into as a kid. At times when it seemed like something bad would happen I actually worried for him.I just have three major issues:1: The soundtrack is annoying. It's mostly these long, slow, sentimental ballads that feel like they're desperately trying to tug at your heartstrings, and most of the lyrics are sung so soft I can't tell what the singer is saying half the time. I'm sure there's plenty of people who like this sort of music but I prefer something less dreary.2: The actual story and gameplay is incredibly boring and a slog to get through. In order to progress the story you have to move the current character around to find what they need to interact with next. That wouldn't be so bad if they didn't walk slowly and half the time you have to keep walking for an agonizingly long period of time to progress. At most you'd be holding down the arrow key for maybe one minute at times, but it feels like ten minutes. As I said before, the first and last chapters were alright. The chapters between those, however, were just really dull and uninteresting, including the interlude scenes with the elderly gator who worked at an antique shop. It feels like they were all going to be connected somehow but aside from it all seeming to take place around the same city it never comes to a head. In the end I was left saying to myself "That's it?" and "thank god its over", which is never a good sign.3: None of the characters have tails. That's really the most minor nitpick I have but it's something that always bugs me when it comes to animal character designs.Overall it was pretty disappointing. I normally like these sort of minimalist, narrative-focused games, but this one just didn't leave an impression on me, and the incredibly slow pacing keeps me from going back again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Is it still a game if we only have to push right or left and press A every now and then? Comparing a game with a movie and thus denying it its ludic nature is the lowest blow of game criticism. And yet we have to ask ourselves: How much is still left to reduce here? Chunky pixel graphics, no text or dialogues, only accompanying music with vaguely fitting vocals. The actions we "control" for the characters are inconsequential, but at the same time so specific that pressing the A button doesn't do them justice in more ways than one. So does The Longest Road on Earth fail because of the input device? Perhaps putting water on in the kitchen would be more exciting if we could perform the action in VR with our hands.  Maybe five minutes of staring idly in a subway would be contemplatively stimulating, if there were something like a sense of presence. Then perhaps the everyday stories would also be fascinating, as they certainly have their heart in the right place.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I've been isolated in a room and away from my family following a positive covid test and this game (not really a game, more of an interactive experience) made me tear up, made me contemplate loneliness and how life is passing us by. All in all very sad and poignant experience, with a great soundtrack, that I recommend strongly.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this game, and I felt compelled to immediately leave a review. Sure, it's unusual. Sure, it's very slow, and fairly minimalistic in terms of gameplay. But some of the sequences in there are absolutely beautiful, the music is gorgeous, and if you've already stopped once to wonder about what makes us humans, you'll connect with the stories that are told. Also, the greyscale pixel art is stunning. Very much recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I approached this title without defined expectations, seduced by the prospect of an original concept based on intriguing retro visuals and a narrative without words. That much is true.It could have been compelling if the pacing wasn’t so deliberately lethargic and less of an exercise in patience. I would have enjoyed the sensitive nods to everyday life if there was a common narrative thread tying them together in a meaningful way. It just comes and goes.This narrative experience doesn't really tell a cohesive story as much as capture disparate snapshots in time. It carries no connection between the characters and ends without a satisfying sense of purpose or accomplishment.Enjoyment boils down to whether you appreciate sitting down to take a breath and relax to this acoustic indie pop soundtrack, while everyday events unfold as in a decelerated black and white video. Wait. Walk. Pause to look at mundane items. Find the one interactive spot. Wait for a prompt to show up. Walk. Wait more.The music is somewhat pleasant but also kind of sameish, without any outstanding part from song to song. For a game built expressly around its soundtrack, I didn't feel the songs particularly connected to depicted scenes, especially at times when I couldn't always hear or focus on the lyrics properly.This game will probably be enjoyed more by a specific audience with measured expectations, an abundance of patience and a distinct appreciation for the more subtle side of storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I think the best way to view The Longest Road on Earth is a series of music videos. The songs are mostly decent and sometimes even good but they do run into the problem that most double albums have. It’s difficult to make 20 songs feel memorable and varied enough to not have your overall project feel too long and bloated. The visuals and interaction in the game don’t really do the songs much of a favor either. Everything is subdued and mostly open to interpretation. Although, I have a pretty good idea what The Longest Road on Earth is trying to say (Life is long, sometimes mundane, and that it’s ok to not know what we are doing), it’s not saying anything loud enough to feel lasting and impactful.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: The music and art are nice but I honestly don't know why it's a game. The user seems to be  part here. You move very,  slowly, you can't make your own choices, you can't even impact the world in the game. Everything is predetermined. All you do is click the left or right arrow (and space once in a while!) and listen to music. Sorry, but I prefer Spotify to listen to music, not Steam xd This story should be made a film, where the storyline is told just with lyrics of the songs. I think it could be great. As a game, it's just not enjoyable. My first refund on Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so... the message of the story is great. It has an amazing art direction and even better musicHowever, this is the clearest example of... not everything needs to be a game. Not even an interactive experience. Literally all the pros of this "game" are about the non-interactive areas. This should absolutely not be a game. This is not the right media for it. Staring at the screen for 5 minutes (not an exaggeration) without doing anything? Go watch a movie insteadLast but not the least --> An interactive experience doesn't even allow me to sleep, and this game truly needed it lol
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I was pretty excited to purchase this game for a while when I learn it would be following the story of multiple anthropomorphic animals that leave you to interpret what their stories are all about, plus having a highly detailed pixel art style is a must-buy for me. But, I didn't anticipate how slow it would be, gameplay-wise, and I like to think I'm quite patient for these sorts of games, but apparently not for this game as most of the things we do are quite mundane like changing the laundry, going for one place to another slowly. Maybe, something a little more dramatic like a high-speed chase or something to help with the gameplay, but it wouldn't have worked in this sort of game, so forget I said that. Speaking of gameplay, I wish this game wasn't a 'game' per se, but just a short film with the lyrics in the background, it would help people like me who find it difficult to focus listening to the lyrics whilst doing something else at the same time. I feel it would have been a better experience to digest with only the soundtrack to explore isolation, passion and love that got me feeling all teary-up and goosebumps. No matter what, I'm planning to purchase the soundtrack to support the artist. Anyone who doesn't want to purchase this game should do the same.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: The game… it's really what you make of it. It's definitely best to go into this not expecting to understand the point of what your doing and what you're seeing. If you're expecting to understand why the game is showing you the things it is showing you, you may not enjoy this game. This game doesn't "exactly" tell you a story.Conversely, if you are someone who likes people-watching as a way to pass the time, you will probably enjoy this game.The second story with the fox kinda made me think about my own life, about my own life ambitions amid being a cog in the capitalist machine, a part of society while apart from society. The last one made me think about my parents and what they did for me growing up, despite the trouble I had caused for them.I think the first story is kind of about saying goodbye and venturing out into the unknown.It didn't move me to tears, but it did give me some time for personal reflection. I'm a hard guy to get to cry though, so your mileage may vary. Not everyone can completely relate to every story, but I feel like there's something here for everyone. I do recommend playing this with a controller; my hand got cold after awhile holding down the movement keys. In retrospect, having the volume turned up while playing may help the soundtrack really have impact (so I do recommend turning the volume up and/or wearing some nice headphones).
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely not for everyone, especially if you find it hard to sit still mentally and everything moves so slowly.Which seems like the whole point of the game. I wanted to love this game and enjoy slowing down, but the whole thing made me so impatient and angry. It was like a special kind of torture, and the music made it even more torturous. _childDocuments_.review: Boredom isn't always bad.The Longest Road on Earth is a very slow and deliberate "game." In 4 chapters, it takes the player through multiple loosely connected slices-of-life, conjoined with an folk album performed by the artist Beícoli. The game is the result of a successful   funded in early 2020.This game will not be everyone's cup of tea, and you might even struggle to call this a "game." Even the store page calls it an "experience" and it's pretty much the definition of a 2-D walking simulator. All of this said, I still appreciated the art, music, and the exploration of more mundane aspects of life, and it definitely was worth my time.Like other "walking simulators," The Longest Road on Earth is very gameplay light. There are only three buttons involved in controlling the characters in each chapter, left, right, and interact (spacebar). The interact button might bring up a still life image, or might make your character perform an action, such as putting heat on the kettle. I would say that almost anyone can play this game, although there is a section that involves rapidly pressing the interact button that I'm not sure absolutely everyone could play, but maybe they could.The developers describe the game as free from the "punishment" of failure-states, and "untarnished" by challenge. I wouldn't go as far to celebrate these features of the game - I don't think they make the game better, necessarily - but these aspects of the game are certainly tolerable as long as you go in expecting them.In a game like this, you might expect this to carry the "game," but it is very hands off with the story (especially since it relies on no written text), so it allows you a lot of leeway in interpreting the behavior and emotions of the characters. The game, I will say, is bold in the stillness and boredom present in the stories. The only other game that I can think of that effectively communicates these ideas is "The Longing." But the most important aspect of the stories, I think, is that each character's story is believable - you believe them enough to put yourself very squarely in their shoes, and empathize with them. My interpretation is that each character is a different animal to emphasize their uniqueness. But beyond believability and triggering empathy, the art and music might be more essential to the experience.As mentioned before, the game moves back and forth between pixelated environments, and more detailed still life images. I really liked the stills. The game has a deep streak of black and white still life running through it, a bold choice matching the other decisions to represent banality. If you don't appreciate still life, you probably won't like this game. But if you do, there's a lot to appreciate.I'll also add that the graphics are another choice that make the game accessible. It's black and white, and lo-fi. You can play it on your phone, and you can play it colorblind.Running underneath all of these aspects of the game is a good folky soundtrack. It wasn't the best or most affecting folk music, but it also wasn't bad. It was good enough, calling to mind the emotions of being confused about your direction in life, or being confident. It did occasionally dip into corniness, I felt. Here's one of the songs I thought was good not great, to give you a taste of what you might find:  The vocals are sung in English - perhaps the game would have been better served by leaning more into ambient music to make the game even more accessible. As it stands, though, the game probably sounds good even if you can't speak English.As I have mentioned in the other sections, many features of this game add up to accessibility, the lo-fi graphics, wordless storytelling, and simple gameplay mechanics. This "game" is a paradox. It is very accessible, and yet I anticipate that only a narrow audience will like it for what it is, a slice-of-life experience intertwined with a folky album and a set of still life images. I did like it, but you might not. I hope this review helps you decide on which side you fall!

_childDocuments_.review: I am not entirely sure how to feel about this game.As others have pointed out, this isn't much of a video game, but more like an interactive music video. There is practically zero gameplay. The music is gorgeous, the art is well done, but the rest is just lacking, to be quite honest.The point of the story, I think, is to have the player reflect on their own life while observing the lives of the characters in the game. Except, I found myself getting utterly bored in the first two chapters, even to the point of falling asleep several times while keeping my hand on the walk button, and wondering if I should continue playing or not. There wasn't much reflecting to do there, since the "story" felt too mundane to put a mirror up to. I guess the two characters were lonely because they got separated? But I didn't feel like I could connect with them at all, even if I can very well understand that loneliness.The third chapter I think I related to the most, because it felt like dragging yourself through the days, going through the motions without really thinking about it. And before you know it, months have passed, and then suddenly years of you doing nothing to realize your dreams, and you're still in the same spot as you were last time. The thing is, this theme has been on my mind a lot recently, so I'm not so sure whether it's meant to evoke this feeling or if I'm just filling in the gaps with my personal and current circumstances.The fourth chapter starts off really slow. I couldn't really relate to the main character either, but at least it was a bit more interesting than the first two chapters. It's the ending where I shed a single tear, because the lyrics were very reassuring: to know that nobody really knows what they're here for and they're just going with the flow. At the same time, however, it's a very depressing reality. I wish people knew what they actually wanted in life, and chased after it, like I am doing right now. And that they could find that something that fulfills them and makes them feel like they have meaning and belonging in this world.All in all, even though the story is meant to be interpreted by the individual, it remains incredibly vague, and doesn't convey its message loudly and clearly enough. It might as well have said absolutely nothing.If you want to give this "game" a shot, I recommend getting it on a heavy sale. I would not have bought this for the full price.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more of an art piece than anything else. It watches the lives through the perspective of different characters in everyday situations. I enjoyed the music, and I respect the art it's trying to embrace. That being said, it's personally not for me. That doesn't mean somebody else won't enjoy it. It's a very zen, minimal interactions game. If you want to relax, not think about game play, and just enjoy the "vibe", this is a good one to play. I prefer more game play myself, and that is why I would not recommend it for people who do need that extra engagement.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not get bamboozled by all those reviews saying this isn't a game or complaining about the lack of story. This is a game and it has a story, it is called pure, unadulterated communist propaganda. These "furries" (I'm 99% certain the little boy deer is none other than Josef Stalin himself), mask the true purpose of this game. The devs don't call themselves the Brainwash Gang for nothing. It's all in there if you pay attention and look closely.This "coming of age / life cycle" non-verbal narrative is really a stinging critique of our capitalist system. Just look at the worker's going about their day. Taking "mass transit" to work, then toiling all day, while the "owner class" checks on them & their every little move. Karl Marx "Das Kapital" was more forgiving of capitalism than this low-hanging fruit narrative on worker's unionizing and scheming to overthrow the owner class.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like an interactive screensaver.  The focus is really the music and pixel minimalism.  And when I mention minimalism, I am referring to the actual "gaming."  The "gaming" aspect involves intermittent clicking and button pressing to advance the screensaver.  Aesthetically, it feels like it wants to be a silent film without subtitles (the marketing pitch being that you create your own story), but fundamentally, it is a chill interactive screensaver with music.  If you find that you like the music, you'll probably like this product.  If you don't like the music (generally finding it to be a grate on your soul) and opt to turn off your speakers, this will feel less like a "game" and more like a trial by torture. Game Play: MinimalVisuals: 10/10Sound: ...depends if you like the music...Difficulty: ...depends on your level of ADDFinal Verdict: I'd say go for it.  I bought it, it has pixelated furries, and if I wasted my money, misery loves company.  That being said, maybe wait for a sale.  It feels like a solid $3.99 USD title. Or if you are from Canada, buy this game with a bunch of Canadian pennies, just to stick it to the developer.  In the US, Canadian pennies infuriate Americans, I can only imagine what they would do to someone an ocean away.  :3

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant short story with appealing pixel art, supplemented by the amazing music of Beicoli.It’s not a game, It’s more like an interactive movie. Seems most of the negative reviews stem from people complaining about a lack of deep gameplay mechanics in something that features “stripped down mechanics” as a selling point. Got it cheap on sale and I’m happy with it so I’m sure you will be too. Plus, even at full price it’s cheaper than a movie ticket, lasts about as long as one and comes with a great soundtrack. Consider the value of your money and support good developers, guys.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect to empathize so much with this game. A lot of the scenes expect you to fill the gaps of the stories, but while you do so, you somehow feel certain emotional connection with each character. The meal time at the office, waiting at the bus stop, or going to visit the doctor are spaces that even though may seem mundane for many, they meant the world in certain moments for us. These are spaces where significant realizations in our lives took place. This game is about those moments, and it's been beautiful to remember them through its stories.

_childDocuments_.review: Walking simulator meets the flaubertian idea of a novel about nothing (which by the way he never managed ou actually tried to pull of). Literally nothing happens, the most significant actions you take are waiting for the right time to cross the street ou looking at your on shoes for as long as a song lasts (I guess its nicer if the soudtrack is to your liking, its not particularly my style, though it isn't bad). But honestly I just found it boring.Update: I'm updating this review about a week after having played and written it, considering only that the game kind stuck with me and gave me oportunity to think a lot - not particularly about life in general as seems to be the case of many positive reviews here (honestly I believe I already give that a lot of thinking, specially in critical moments of life) - but about games, how they tell delicate stories, and about stories without a plot, with twists and turns, adventures etc. Think I just came to be glad that this game exists and that I have played it, a little like a De Sica movie or the Tree of life, by Terrence Malick.

_childDocuments_.review: Saying so much with so little is an art form in itself and this game excels at it. As people we find ourselves not drawn to the stories of the mundane, since we are already drowning in it this makes us seek out the amazing, the incredible and the exceptions, then something like this comes along and reminds us what life is. Life is the longest road on earth with all its ups and downs with its mundane and exceptional. This game drives this idea incredibly well and the soundtrack complements it in the best way possible. Of course no game is for everyone but I can confidently say this is one of those where you owe yourself to see if its for you or not, since you may find somethings long forgotten or sadness or warmth in every one of these stories. Life is the longest road on earth and it's always great to see games like this. If i start to gush over the soundtrack this review may look like a novel so I got to keep short. Definitely worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I’m walking into this game at a good time as it is described as a “walking simulator”.  And to be very frank, I don’t think it’s a very good one.  It just so happens I played this off the back of another walking simulator.  Dear Esther, which I find to be a very good…  Well, thing.  Here I want to explain why Dear Esther works as a “walking simulator”, or at least a good example of it, and why The Longest Road does not.Let me preface this by saying it’s always nice finding something I don’t understand.  I will, unfortunately, be talking fairly negatively about this but before I do I want to say I understand this is a passion piece.  This isn’t meant to be enjoyed or played like your conventional game.  Going even further than most games to a point where it genuinely confuses me on some of these decisions.  Though, just because I don’t get it doesn’t make it the wrong choice.  It’s just different.Anyway, both Dear Esther and The Longest Road (TLR) follow a character through some point of their life.  While TLR is focused on a few different perspectives, Dear Esther focuses on just one.  Obviously this allows for a more focused experience.  Having one central figure for the player to get attached to instead of multiple.  Of course, having multiple characters isn’t necessarily a bad thing if they all connect together somehow.  There has to be a reason for jumping between perspectives or they should interconnect in some way.  Have a central theme.TLR vaguely does this in theming but not much else.  Every story is self-contained (for the most part) and don’t affect each other.  It makes you wonder what was the point?  Going off these vague assumptions and leaving everything up to interpretation does not make the game deeper, its themes more complex, or its message more understandable.  It bogs the whole thing down and leaves the player confused, and not in a good way.Dear Esther stays consistent in tone and makes it fairly clear what the intention is.  As you follow his story you pretty much already know the ending.  A journey to the end, his longest road is the final ascent up the mountain.  He speaks of his grief, his life, his loss.  It’s spelled out for you.But, as you listen the scenery changes with his mood.  They reflect his thoughts, his tribulations.  The music swells and quiets with his turbulent thoughts.  It makes each step that much more impactful.  It’s the fleeting nature of life, the climbing and falling, the deep dive into the human condition and the beauty of the most basic of feelings.  Even the lack of being able to interact with most things leaves you feeling helpless against the storm that is life.  The more you grasp onto the harder it is to let go.  All this can be extrapolated thanks to its central theme and story.  It knows exactly what it is and what it wants to do and it executes it almost perfectly.TLR almost does this in the end.  Where  you play the young moose who constantly gets into trouble for expressing himself.  You might think this will tie into a greater theme of loss of innocents, or maybe how our society often crushes the artistic spirit of young people.  But then it just goes into something else.  One story just has you riding on a train for half of it, looking out the window.  There is no real interaction with the player.In Dear Esther all you can do is walk and look around, but this is central in understanding his mental state and seeing the landmarks that act as his emotional tether.  Despite having very little interaction it all helps us understand the theme better, the general ideas and makes us feel a part of the world rather than just looking through a window.TLR would have made a much better short film than a game.  The fact that it is a game doesn’t add anything to the experience.  Your interactions are very few to begin with but even when you do they feel menial and unintuitive, almost forced.  The gameplay does not add anything to the experience but toon out the player.  It disconnects us from the world.  The only time I was really invested was with the toy minigame where you had to fight the dolls with a well timed button click.That was something.  I felt a connection to the activity, like I’d done as a kid.  It gives me a deeper connection to the character.  And then it ended and I was back on the grind.  Video games are so unique in their artform, in what they can make you feel and see.  When the creator understands that the gameplay plays into the themes as much as the writing and the story you begin to get some of the best media there is.4/10 - A game that tries too hard to be an artistic expression.  It’s like a song with no sound.  If you make such a tune, is it really music?  Who’s to say.

_childDocuments_.review: There is no game.This is some nice music tracks playing with almost no pause on some cool pixel art, but it is not sufficient to make a game, in my opinion.No interaction besides making your character walk very slowly in a corridor and sometimes zooming on a particular object on the decor, and that's pretty much everything, for an hour and a half.No story, no choices to make, no narration to draw a common thread between each character, and the scenes presented all along are so depressively ordinary that they only inspired me boredom instead of nostalgia or melancholia.If the point was to show some "hidden beauty in common things", it just didn't work for me at all.Yet, I'm usually fond of games that can be qualified as "interactive movie", but there, it in fact  seemed to me that in the end I just listened to a folk music album while watching a pixel art landscape scrolling, with my finger constantly pressed on one single key of my keyboard.Why so many characters presented without any real connection between all of them ? With only 90 minutes of playing, you cannot relate to all of them as a player, nor feel invested in their personnal stories.It seems to me that you should have sticked with only one of them, and dig deeper into his daily life from his childhood to his old days, like you tried to do with the moose in the end, but extended so that the player can really feel for him/her.The constant music with vocals not always matches with the things we see on the screen, and sometimes I felt I needed a pause in the soundtrack so that I can breathe, because in the end the music never stopping becomes like a white background noise and you don't really enjoy it anymore.So this was just my immediate reaction after playing and I hope it doesn't seem too harsh to the developpers because they clearly put effort into it, but for me it just didn't work well, whereas I was expecting the release of the game for months.Some good ideas though, and you should consider a career in music.

_childDocuments_.review: Most game's I've played tend to utilise music more as a supplement. Not exactly significant- easy to forget about at times, but improve the experience nonetheless. The Longest Road flips the script in that respect as the music literally makes the game in a distinct and brilliant way.One of the first thing's you'll notice while playing The Longest Road is the lack of colour. Visuals are monochrome, and in a way so is the plot. Revolving around more mundane scenes rather than more typical ones of conflict. Normally it would sound like a criticism, but its these aspects of The Longest Road that make it so memorable, even if it can feel overly sluggish at times. With that aforementioned mundanity creating a poignant experience that really makes you think about life- even reflecting on your own life as a whole. These visuals works in conjunction with the game's biggest element, its wonderful sound track. Beicoli's music, both parts haunting and soulful fill the entire game and create what I feel is an unparalleled vibe. The Longest Road would not be what it was without this absolutely amazing quality. Its a joy to listen to, and its emotional nature fits the game perfectly Not everyone will agree with the game's extremely 'Walking Simulator' nature. Particularly how it makes you more of an observer rather than a player for its entirety. But regardless, its an artful experience I'll always recommend. Its different, its touching, and its beautiful. Make sure you bring a decent pair of headphones too.

_childDocuments_.review: The Longest Road on Earth can be finished in an hour and a half's sitting, I've now completed it twice and I've probably spent twice as much time as that just thinking about it.Slice of life stories really tap into something in my head and my heart that makes me tick. Finding something special in the mundane everyday, observing and cherishing those small moments in life that can resonate in unexpected ways - it can be very poignant in a subtly beautiful way. The Longest Road on Earth is a series of vignettes following the lives of an unrelated set of different individuals, where the greatest dramatic plot twist happens when the two POV characters of one chapter meet for a fleeting moment and exchange glances as practical strangers. It doesn't contemplate on life's big questions or try to weave some form of extra meaning of how everything is connected in unexpected ways: it's just snapshots of moments. The only increase in stakes is the growing scope between each chapter, from a simple two-location jaunt to a sprawl in the city, then the afore-mentioned double-POV chapter and at last the final chapter where the personal narrative grows over years.That alone is like crack to me but what makes this special is the soundtrack. There's no dialogue or sound on The Longest Road on Earth: the characters speak but you're never told what they say. The only source of sound you do have is the soundtrack, and that's the big "gimmick" of this game specifically. It's all written and performed by Beícoli, one of the developers who sadly doesn't seem to have done anything else: her wistful, beautiful indie folk and voice are a constant presence leading the stories onward. The lyrics never narrate the plot but can punctuate particular moments in a way where you wonder whether it was intended or simply a great coincidence, and the mood her songs craft really lead the tone and emotion of each scene. It's such a beautiful soundtrack and honestly about 50% of the reason this game hits me so much. It's not a sad or "deep" game but that's where I find its beauty. It allows its quiet moments of other people's lives speak for themselves and for the player to find the moments that they view as poignant for themselves (for me it's the last part of Chapter 4 which is just such a wonderful mini-narrative, with the game's fantastic title track providing the emotional push).It's not a game I'd recommend unless you really just like walking around absorbing the ambience but it scratches a narrative itch well enough that I keep coming back to those little moments I've witnessed and imagining how everything else played out afterwards for those five unnamed characters whose lives I've been able to peek into.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to really call The Longest Road on Earth a game, at least in the conventional sense. Relative to others, gameplay is pretty sparse, relegated to arrow keys to move from one location to another, and pressing spacebar at various intervals to advance the scene. It is hardly an active experience, but I think that was the point.The Longest Road on Earth's strength is in its introspective look into the daily lives of others, all set to a beautiful soundtrack by Beicoli. Spanning four chapters across various points in time, the game follows different characters as they go about their lives, told through the framing device of belongings at an antique store. Although it may sound banal, the game makes each vignette poignant, dealing with themes that leave you reflecting well after they end. It revels in its slow - nearly glacier - pace, and eschews dialogue or narration in favor of letting you come to your own conclusion about your experience. Admittedly, the game's pace is at times its weakest area, assuming you were willing to overlook it's general lack of conventional gameplay. There are some points in-game where I found myself sitting for well over a minute waiting for the vignette to move on to the next scene while the sprites looped in animation. Just as I was starting to worry that my game may have bugged out trying to load the next scene, something would happen, and I'd realize the game was taking its sweet time. Perhaps this was intentional, though, as the game so very much wants to you take joy and find solitude in the little details of existing. Ultimately if you're looking for a short experience with a lot of heart, I highly recommend checking out The Longest Road on Earth. I am truly impressed by Brainwash Gang's ability to capture the small realities of different lives and foster a sense of care for them all without words. The Longest Road on Earth's strength is undoubtedly in its empathy and understanding. If Brainwash Gang can replicate such insight in future projects, I have no doubt that they will have a long and successful future ahead of them.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A short film rather than a video game, there's not much you can do except move the characters left and right, hit Space on items. 1/2 time is to control random working class characters walking around town/shop/home, the rest 1/2 is about their regular life about work and family. This reminds me of a story when I was told when young:In poor areas in the country, middle schools hang a straw shoe and a leather shoe at the school entrance, to stimulate the students to study hard so they can go to college in a big city to restart life - to wear leather shoes. Otherwise, wear straw shoes and be stuck in the poor area.It's cruel.I don't recommend it because it is not a game, and a bug kept me on a train for nothing, I had to quit the game and try again to pass.

_childDocuments_.review: Right, so. I love artsy games. They're some of my favorite digital products. Dear Esther changed me profoundly. Everybody's Gone to the Rapture was a weaker effort, but still good. Night in the Woods is another game which left an indelible mark on me. I love high-concept games with minimal gameplay and extremely dense or emotionally resonant plots, and I recognize the pretentiousness inherent in such. So when I saw there was a period walking simulator which billed itself as an emotional journey involving animal characters, I practically leapt out of my chair with joy. However, what is on display here is a lump of raw nonsense. I wish I could be more charitable, but I genuinely struggle with articulating my thoughts in any other way. As far as high-minded concepts go, this game has one in spades, but that concept is so bogged down with nonsensical, boring, and frankly insipid game mechanics and messaging, and doubly so because its soundtrack is unbearable. Allow me to elaborate.This game has no named characters. It barely has a coherent plot beyond slowly moving from one end of a pixelated house or space to the other, and often requires you to sit and wait for minutes on end as nothing at all happens. If there is a plot, I am, by the grace of God, unable to suss it out. Precisely what the developers were going for is beyond me. On the one hand, we follow several different characters as they make their way through their lives. A stoat (?) woman who is cycling a lot and who apparently misses someone. There's memories of travel in her narrative. I couldn't identify much beyond this. An alligator man who runs a shop of some kind, albeit what he sells is dubious, and we see him wander up and down said shop, inspecting himself in the mirror. A commentary on bygone youth and old age perhaps? No idea. Maybe the stars can tell us. This lack of substance is bolstered by what I would classify as exceptionally poor pixel art. Broad and wide angle scenes look great, but the moment you zoom in, you're met with a cryptic mash of pixels which leaves you fumbling for meaning. Is that a tea kettle? Is it an Italian coffee kettle? What on Earth is it? Maybe it is once again the stars we need to ask.I am not the easiest person to get along with. Broadly speaking, I am a woman stuck in the 1950s in so many ways. 95% of my musical listening predates the year 1970, and about half of that 95% predates the year 1960, with most being focused on the 1920s and 30s. I find the overwhelming majority of contemporary music to be dull or simply uninteresting and have never engaged with it. And when I saw that this was a period piece, I was excited! Finally, something historical, and hopefully with a soundtrack to match?No, what we get instead is what I would generously classify as soundcloud mumblecore folk, the likes of which I was never interested in even in passing, and whilst taste is one thing, quality is another. Whoever is doing the singing sounds even more sloshed and breathy than Marilyn Monroe singing "Happy Birthday Mr. President." Most of the songs sound the same, and I could not, gun to my head, distinguish between some of the tracks. The lyrics are unintelligible, and with no written plot, I was hoping they'd shed some light on what on God's green Earth was happening, but not so. There are lyrics, but without subtitles, they're irrelevant. The game developers have addressed this, and have said, no joke, that this is the intended experience. To read the lyrics you need to buy them. Extra. For money.What the hell.I am glad this game moved some people, and that they got something out of it. All I got out of it was a headache and a desire for an actual plot because the visuals were interesting, but nothing is underpinning them. Just slowly walking from one end of a scene to the next, pressing a button, and squinting as I try to figure out what I am looking at, often to no avail.I am glad I got this game for very little money, because full price is downright absurd. If you want a structured narrative, and you're not a fan of someone exhaling overtop the dullest indie guitars imaginable, look elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: The game in an interesting idea, but ultimately it's a flop. I'd recommend buying the soundtrack, it's a lot better.PROS:Good musicNice pixel artCONS:Gameplay: While the premise of the game isn't bad, it's brought down by having the world's slowest walking speed. I get wanting to have a slow pace, but this makes walking across a room an extremely tedious chore. Don't even get me started on how long it takes to walk across a city block. Story: The game follows four characters as advertised. Conclusion:This is a game with good music and pixel art that is dragged down by exceptionally slow walking. It shows exactly why you don't make a movie about a random boring guy who works at a gas station.

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are nice and the music is fine if you like that breathy kind of singing where sometimes its hard to understand the lyrics and other times its just speaking softly and not really singing. It wasn't necessarily my cup of tea and after awhile all of the songs sounded the same but It was still pleasant enough. I think probably the game is just a vehicle to show off the singing because unfortunately there really is not much else on offer here.  Game play consists of slowly walking left or right and interacting with a point of interest. There are also quite a few sections in the game where nothing is happening and just the music goes on playing for a couple of minutes and then it eventually fades out to the next scene.There are 4 chapters in the game which show snippets from the lives of a handful of characters. I think out of the 4 chapters the last chapter is arguably the strongest and maybe the game should have just been that chapter sold on its own for a fraction of the price.To be honest I struggled to finish this. Overall I don't think I could recommend the game at least not at the current price point as I think that would be considered somewhat of an insult to other Devs who've actually constructed a proper game with a connected story and actual mechanics for less

_childDocuments_.review: I'm neutral on this, but going with Yes since there's no middle ground.  I guess this publisher is trying to be like AnnaPurna, but this game is not very intuitive.  I spend a lot of time watching the screen, waiting, and from the very beginning, you're expected to hit buttons to progress the story.  But there's no indication onscreen that you need to do something.  I was constantly being pulled out of the experience, waiting for something to happen, then I hit a button and the game proceeds.  The very intro went on for about 5 minutes before I hit a button and the credits began rolling, and you have to hit a button to have each credit move on to the next.  This is more like work, not relaxing playtime.  I'll struggle to get through this for the sake of getting my money's worth, but it's a chore.  I'll give it a Yes because I'm trying hard to be good about this experience.

_childDocuments_.review: After powering through the longest and most horrifically boring intro on earth, I shut the game down because the music was insufferable and the gameplay is made for sloths. It takes 10 business days for the character to walk from one end of the screen to the other. I've never been this disappointed by a pixel-graphics game in my life.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: 'The Longest Road on Earth' sounds like a post apocalyptic thriller where the protagonist must travel across the country on the remains of a desolate and crumbling highway, fighting zombies or mutants or cannibals or something.This game is not at all like that.Actually it's not really a game. I wouldn't even classify it as a walking simulator. It's more like an only slightly interactive art project.There are no puzzles to solve, no enemies to vanquish, no achievements to unlock. There are no names. There is no dialogue. Over the course of traversing The Longest Road on Earth you will:Mop the floor.Serve coffee.Fill out invoices.Tend to an antiques store.Ride on a crowded subway.Eat cafeteria food.Engage in water cooler chatter.Get lost in the crowd of a large city.Possibly make a fleeting connection with your soul mate without either of you knowing it.Experience the way-too-fast progression of the life from crawling baby to new parent.In short, it's a game about life. The mundanity of it. The beauty of it. The special moments. The long stretches of nothing of particular importance happening. The solitude compared to the loneliness. The companionship compared to the crowding out.None of this might sound particular enticing, I know. But trust me on this: The hauntingly beautiful soundtrack by Beícoli makes everything work. Every song is written to fit the corresponding scene (or maybe every scene was written to fit the corresponding song? I dunno). If you do decide to take the plunge and get this game, I highly recommend the soundtrack as well. The experience *is* quite short. But I'm not sure that's a complaint. At 2 hours the length of The Longest Road on Earth is perfect. Any longer and it would have bordered on repetitive and the theme would have been diluted.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: No, no and no. I don't mind the pixelated graphics.I like the song. But the gameplay? it's mashing keys that are obvious, backtracking on your steps with nothing new to see at the speed of a salted slug, and overall has no replay value, or even entertainment value.If this was a music video for a band, I could understand the concept (Bjork messed with something similar in the past). But in this context, the other way around, it simply doesn't work.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I wrote this review while I was waiting for something to happen in the game. The Longest Road on Earth is essentially a 2D walking sim where nothing happens. There is zero compelling narrative or gameplay, this game is quite literally a waiting sim. If you ever play this game (god forbid) you will find that there are several parts of the game where you are left wondering "am I supposed to be doing something right now?" only to find that you were literally meant to just wait for the game to move on to the next segment. This game is literally just meant to be a vessel for the soundtrack, and the soundtrack isn't really something I would listen to, so there's really nothing good in this game to find.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game. It is a slightly interactive short film. As a short film, it's great. As a game, it's a waste of time. Most of the positive reviews I've seen are correct EXCEPT that this shouldn't be packaged and sold as a game. It's not. If you wanna watch something while making the characters walk in one direction and occasionally pressing the action button when prompted, this "game" is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: The Longest Road on Earth   Casual Game Relax with beautiful music and simple gameplay. The game has no words, There is only the music driving the player into it. The developers haven't said much about the simple plot of the game, We have to think over and interpret the story ourselves.   If you want to immerse yourself in beautiful music and a simple, relaxing, and comforting story.The Longest Road on Earth is the game that deserves for you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: The Longest Road on Earth isn't just a game; it's a deeply moving experience that left me utterly captivated from start to finish. As I journeyed through the lives of various characters, I was struck by the game's ability to evoke a wide range of emotions, all while accompanied by a mesmerizing soundtrack that elevated the entire experience to new heights.Let's talk about the music first. From the moment I started playing, I was entranced by the hauntingly beautiful melodies that filled the world of The Longest Road on Earth. Each note seemed to resonate with the emotions of the characters, adding depth and nuance to their stories in a way that words alone could not. Whether it was the gentle strumming of a guitar or the melancholic hum of a piano, the music had a way of drawing me in and immersing me completely in the game's world.But it's not just the music that makes The Longest Road on Earth so special; it's the way it intertwines with the storytelling to create a truly unforgettable experience. As I guided the characters through their everyday lives, I found myself becoming deeply invested in their hopes, dreams, and struggles. Each encounter felt like a window into their souls, revealing the complexities of the human experience in a way that felt both intimate and profound.And then there were the visuals. The game's minimalist art style may seem simple at first glance, but it's incredibly effective at conveying emotion and atmosphere. From the subtle expressions on the characters' faces to the evocative use of color and light, every frame feels like a work of art in its own right, adding an extra layer of depth to the already immersive experience.In conclusion, The Longest Road on Earth is a masterpiece of storytelling and music that deserves to be experienced by everyone. With its mesmerizing soundtrack, poignant narratives, and stunning visuals, it's a journey that will stay with you long after the credits roll. Trust me, you won't want to miss out on this unforgettable adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: If you're alright with a game that MAYBE should have been a meditative short film / music video series, this is exactly for you. While I think it's successful in the way it portrays and expresses the themes it's trying to convey, I don't think it was interactive enough for me to say "yeah, I'm glad I *played* that." But I was glad to have watched it, to have experienced it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant slow burn story about melancholy and the quiet moments of everyday life. Not particularly ground breaking, but that isn't the point of this game. If you are looking for visual ambiance to go with Beicoli's amazing music, I would recommend this game. If you are looking for thrills or a stunning story, look elsewhere. That is not to knock the game, the point is to make your own story from what you see and feel. And given the first sentence of this review, I'm certain you can figure out what you will be feeling.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: "I found out: no one knows. Everyone just goes with the flow."Essentially a brilliant indie album by Beícoli.  Focusing on the mundane aspects of life without heightened drama or spectacle,  with some really nice pixel art and visual direction. It's only interactive in the minimal sense but that's fine. I really liked it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a strange experience, many times it was not so clear what was happening during the gameplay, the purpose of the game was to feel things through the soundtrack in conjunction with the game but often what was being said in the music was not It fit very well with what was happening during the gameplay.The game's soundtrack and art are incredible, the problem was that they didn't mix very well, which in this case would be the game's purpose.They could add subtitles translated by region and give more context to what is happening.I discovered the game through the soundtrack, I almost cried listening to one of the songs, but during the game this feeling didn't come to the surface.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I am genuinely so torn on this game. On one hand, the narrative and visuals are beautiful. It has a story to tell, and a point to make and it does so very well. The soundtrack is gorgeous (unless you don’t like breathy indie singing lol).On the other hand, the game play is slow to a fault and has no fun factor whatsoever. I know for some people this is their jam so. Yea.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: First game I played that was completely murdered by its own soundtrack. And it is a good soundtrack, I dont think those are bad songs, but other comments are not exaggerating: the music is completely out of place and takes you out of the experience. The experience might be good, I liked the first 20 minutes of the game, but EVERY scene, every second of gameplay has a different song that is wispered, or very loud, that mixed with a slow gameplay creates something really boring. The gameplay by itself is good, I loved the fact that it is slow, and you have a lot of time to take in the feelings the characters must be feeling, it should be an experience,  but the song keeps taking you out of it, you can't think, you try to adjust the volume, but nothing fits.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short beautiful game that only needs not even 2 hours of your time. _childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interactive movie. If you are here to make choices or be immersed in a deep story, this is not the place. It’s a mood piece, 4 short stories put together. There is value to be had in this; however the game struggles to convey it’s message properly as the only words are in the OST; leaving the rest of the story to be picked up from limited interactions between the characters and the world around them. This made it hard for me personally to connect to the stories, except for the story of the moose; who’s story of growing, coming of age, and facing the world with fresh eyes I found inherently relatable. The mood from this game is dripping with loneliness, even if there are others around, but it has trouble anchoring that into a greater message.

_childDocuments_.review: Now I understand why this game get nominated for best soundtrack award. The songs are really amazing, they are the soul of this "GAME". _childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral review option, because I only disliked this as an actual game. I would have LOVED it as a short film. I just found "playing" it infuriating and couldn't wait for it to be over. I think what I was most frustrated with, was on top of the incredibly slow pace, there were far too many times I couldn't tell when one of the slowly moving scenes was over, and it was time to perform another slow moving action.I generally love casual games, and playing games at a leisurely pace, but this was too much for even me. If I could go back knowing what I know now, I probably would have skipped this one. Which is a shame because again,  it looks and sounds beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: This one really surprised me, I was expecting an hour or so of scenes mainly with some neat music. _childDocuments_.review: Try the demo first unless you're quite openminded.It was certainly interessting but more an experience than a game. You briefly take the "control" of a few characters (really you're just walking and using an occasional interaction prompt) and a bit of a slice of their life, however what exactly is going on is pretty interpretable and not that clear. The songlyrics might be a clue but then again they might not be entirely related.Since the interaction is so minimalistic it was not really clear you are supposed to hold down the spacekey whenever it shows an arrow(?) or just wait for a certain amount of time to pass to let the music do its work.In the end it was cute but didn't really have a whole lot to say. Recommended if you like the type of music and the pixelstyle, it feels calming and melancholic I did like it but it felt a bit short.Not so much if neither are your thing and you expect a click and point adventure or a story with a specific goal.

Requires a peaceful moment so you can sink into the stories. Also helps if you've gone through relationships or have kids irl.Not worth of a full price though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: What mainly grabbed me toward this game was the music and it does not disappoint. However, despite how wonderful the soundtrack is, I found myself wondering why some songs were paired with certain scenes. It almost feels like the songs came first, and the developers needed enough scenes (no matter what they were about) to occupy your eyes while you listened to the music. This was a slow paced ride and although I did not enjoy it the whole way through, the ending sequence worked in perfect synchronicity with the title song to hit all of the right notes (no pun intended) and push me to make a quick review. As I went through those final scenes I thought about my life, my parents' lives, their parents' lives, and so on. Overall this was a beautiful game about the human experience, which is ironic since you play as animals the whole time. Highly recommended for those who do not mind playing games on the more conceptual side.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: It works perfectly well considering the type of game that it's ment to be. A collection of situations that do connect emotionaly with the player together with the melancholic and overall beautiful songs that form the soundtrack. It transmits, which I understand is the main idea here.There's no much interactivity or any kind of playability anyway, beyond clicking and tapping keys until the action is finished. So I guess I could say that it would've worked fine as a collection of videos on Youtube, one for each song in the soundtrack... that this is not really a "game"... but it would be false. It IS a game. A simple tap is already connecting you to the action of the character. There's no real discussion here.It's just a certain type of game for a certain kind of person. If you enjoy slow paced, melancholic and minimalistic games, this is a must.

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult to put this into words, really. This isn't a game in the most conventional of senses. It's more-so an interactive bundle of stories, where the meanings and motivations are up to you and your own perspective of life and the way you interpret the music accompanying each piece. I truly don't believe this is for every single person out there, as it is slow and the interaction is nothing more than a couple clicks in-between the music. However, as an art piece and form of expression not just from the creators, but for a way for the viewer to express their own thoughts and feelings into the art and music, I cannot recommend it enough. Each of the four stories has many outlooks you can see it as, and it all really depends on how you analyze the visuals and music cues. That's special, if you ask me. I can't tell you what it's "about", as that would only be my own opinion, but I can tell you that somehow, without dialogue and complex 'gameplay', I still felt a personal connection to each character, through projecting myself through them. Loss, gain, the burden of existing and growing. It's unique, but I feel only certain people will truly appreciate that, and that's just fine.Go in expecting more of a music album with visuals than a true game. You'll enjoy it more and analyze it better without wondering what the game is 'telling' you. What its saying is up to you, entirely. I have a lot of respect for that, and I became incredibly emotional by the end of it all. Short, but enjoyable, like a film.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: I really really had high hopes for this one to be honest. Was expecting at least a comprehensible story with subtlety, but the presentation is too vague: it's a slice of life with not enough context to form an understanding of what the creators wanted to show. Except Chapter 2 and Chapter 4, I am almost completely in the dark..and the game has  What this is in essence, is a long interactive music video that unfortunately suffers from over pretentiousness. I get it, the longest "Road" on earth is life itself; but making me literally walk a character for hours is not the way to show that.The songs are good, I most likely will also get the OST later on.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A good experience of a game.  Not much too it, but that's fine. Pros- Good pixel art.- Amazing music.  The game IS the music.  Like, actually somewhat literally.  The gameplay is sort of restricted by the music that is playing.  And that's fine.  The game is really just an OST that provides an interactive narrative w/o any dialog.  - A good reflection on life, its mundaneness, how it changes, how we're all ppl living our lives and can come into each others' lives w/o really any thought (think of the movies Crash and 21 Grams). Cons- Brainwash Gang is super minimalist in their style based on this and Nongunz.  The gameplay is simple, just has a prompt icon and you press a button.  Which is fine.  But sometimes the game isn't progressing and you do not know why.  But it is because the music has to finish.  This is nitpicky, not really a big deal, but it may throw some ppl off.Overall, a good experience for the price, especially if you like narrative games.  Can finish in under 2 hours.  And the OST is great.  Props to Beicoli.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is heartbreaking(In a good way), I haven't gotten that far, but I already feel emotionally impacted. I am in a place where I need to allow myself to cry, and this game does that. However, it can get so intense, that even I need a couple breaks. But that is a good thing, because it encourages me to slow down and really enjoy the emotional journey that The longest road on earth takes me on. I truly encourage anyone reading this review to buy it just to take that time, and allow themselves to just FEEL. Don't think, just let your mind meld away and tell you your own story as you enjoy this experience.If the devs are reading this, I want to really thank you, this is the type of experience that I really need in these times of crisis, and it would be amazing for the game to get more. I know that might be asking a lot, but this is an amazing experience, while 3 hours can really be expanded when I take my time, I know it will be over sooner than later, so basically, I'm just asking for more, either way this is a great experience, and I recommend it to all, except for those youngin's who haven't gotten far enough in life to truly understand the importance of this game yet. But yeah.

_childDocuments_.review: Mesmerizing, overwhelming, right in the feels. This experience is imbued with melancholia and takes you to a trip with you emotions. You don't drive here : you are taken to a journey, staying on the passenger seat. On rare occasions I was moved by a game which guided me through what it wanted me to feel.No dialogue or text to set the atmosphere. The soundtrack is enough to give you a powerful storytelling. You have to be in the right place to play this game. The game is pretty quick, even if there are some length (the section on public transports). Still a beautiful piece of    arts !

_childDocuments_.review: Best described as an interactive novel, 'The Longest Road on Earth' is a pixel-art tale told in four chapters, each from the perspective of a different character. The game is an auditory and visual experience, with the story told through images and songs, rather than words. Each chapter focuses on aspects of everyday life, from strolling to work, to learning your first steps, to riding a bicycle. The simple things many of us take for granted, or rarely stop to think about.  The chapters are contained within an overarching narrative featuring an elderly crocodile who runs an antique shop. Items from his shop trigger moments from the past featuring the different characters. Without words, or any real context, the four stories are solely down to the players’ interpretation.  Since finishing the game, I’ve spent some time ruminating on what it all means. It’s certainly the type of game you’ll want to talk to others about.  The game explores universal themes we can all relate to – particularly with regards to time and its passing. For better or worse, things change, people grow up and grow apart. The four chapters are tied together by this thematic unity.  Special mention must go to the soundtrack of the game. The 20+ songs that feature were written specifically for the game by Beicoli, who also performs the songs which lyrically link to the text-less narrative. And these atmospheric songs are just sublime, many featuring euphonious swirling choruses that, like the story, provide a timeless quality.  The game does have some draw backs; it’s a short experience, lasting between 90 mins to a couple of hours. The player has little to do, other than move a character left and right and occasionally interact with items. And everything is deliberately slow paced; expect to spend minutes walking a street, or sitting down on a train waiting for your stop. But that’s life! And that’s what the game captures so well.  'The Longest Road on Earth' is a unique game; a transcendent gaming experience that will stay with you long after the credits roll. Each player will interpret it in different ways; perhaps in relation to their own lives. It’s also a prime example of the creativity that comes with indie games – and a great showcase for games as art.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a story about you or about seeing yourself reflected inside the special moments that the characters show. The OST masterly underlines every passage of their lives. These bits of life are perfectly featured through the curated pixelart. All these elements are properly combined to deliver a different narrative experience. Totally recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: NOT A NARRATIVE GAME. Already my #1 all-time favorite small indie pixel-art game ever. Steam has refund, so why not give it a try and make up your own mind?Long version:Most importantly: again, not a "narrative" game. I think most bad impressions about The Longest Road on Earth come from trying to interpret it as "telling stories", in the way narrative games usually do. Looking at the game through this lens could probably result in a frustrating experience. But NOWHERE within the game itself is a narrative experience promised. I mean "narrative" in the sense of "this is a story made of words" - whether directly, or indirectly translated into words from images or interactivity. A "story" like A wants to B therefore they C but D happens so they have to E which takes them to F etc. There's no such thing here, at least not at the level of the whole game as perceived by the player. And if such plots do form, they form intuitively and _very approximately_ in the player's mind. They're anything but spelled out, or meant to be deciphered like some code. Instead:- your ears are flooded with lyrics-heavy music and no other sound at all- the on-screen stuff contains no text (except a newspaper title and a few fictional brand names and such) - the one-button interactions are as minimalistic and non-story-driven as I've experienced in possibly any game except mobile hypercasual ones, with which this game has otherwise nothing in commonI think, for lack of a category, people are automatically classifying it as "narrative game" - and the devs/publisher seem to be somewhat using this as a selling point (still there's no mention of narrative or story in the Steam tags, and I think that's a good thing). In my opinion, selling it as "narrative" could be a mistake on their part.It's definitely an art game. There is _narrativity_ to it, both cinematographic and ludic, if we think of these concepts in a very academic sense. But it doesn't necessarily amount to what we usually mean by "stories", particularly in games. At least not in my immediate perception as a player. It's much more of a poetic piece.It has a reference to THE RED STRINGS CLUB, of all games (among others).The Longest Road on Earth feels extremely artsy and even pretentious - but somehow pulls it off in a very self-aware, satisfying and meaningful way. It often feels like the video game equivalent of a good European arthouse film. For furries.Not fitting any genre. I think this is the most important point.Not technically a game, I we need to be old-school purists about what games are - but do we? Also one of my favorite games ever. Probably my absolute favorite small indie pixel-art game from all I've played so far.And the most aesthetically mature game of any kind that I played. By aesthetics I don't mean just visuals. I mean the aesthetics of the actual game, the entire thing, the experience.I dare say it's low-key redefining game design with its minimalistic, discreet excellence. But the point of this can probably be missed if you enter the experience with a lot of game-literacy and expecting gamer's game conventions to work they way you know they work. The game does away with all that, and sets off to address a different audience.100% must play if you like the trailers.Also, as far as I know, Steam allows refunds, right? So why not give the game a try, despite some negative reviews? The reviews for such a game can only be HIGHLY subjective.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

_childDocuments_.review: A thoughtful and deeply personal title with stripped-down mechanics. The lack of dialogue or text allows you to create your own narrative through your time with four characters. Each short story will allow players to be swept away by the haunting lyrics of over twenty original, nostalgic songs.
_childDocuments_.name: The Longest Road on Earth

name: The Mortuary Assistant
detailed_description: Having completed your degree in mortuary sciences, you have taken on an apprenticeship at River Fields Mortuary. Over the past several months you have logged many hours aiding the Mortician in daily tasks along with learning the ins and outs of the embalming process as well as how to properly handle and care for the deceased. Late one night, you are called into work to handle some embalmings. Death doesn’t keep day time hours. But there is something different about these bodies because there is something different about you. The phone rings with the Mortician on the other end. The rumors are true, and you can not leave. Perform embalming tasks while keeping demonic forces at bay Practice occult rituals to identify demonic entities Piece together clues to banish the demon and save your soul Uncover the gripping history of Rebecca Owens, the haunting past of River Fields, and a sinister secret that lies just beneath the surface… Ground breaking system makes every playthrough unique, guaranteeing you will never feel completely safe. A story that unfolds through multiple playthroughs. Each demon you banish is just a piece of the puzzle 10+ hours of content with more to find for inquisitive eyes Perform embalmings, handle the various jobs around the mortuary, and exorcise demonic forces. All in a day’s work.
