name: Forgotten Fields
detailed_description: Check out my next game! About the Game Sid is a writer struggling with writer's block, attempting to recapture the feelings of inspiration he felt when he was younger. In order to pay the bills, he needs to think up a story and apply for a grant - the deadline is today - a lazy Sunday in the middle of summer. On this Sunday, his struggle is disturbed by an invitation to attend an unavoidable family obligation - the place Sid grew up in is about to be sold, and his mother wants him to come home for a small party so he can say goodbye to it. With the deadline approaching and his creative juices having frozen, this is not something he's looking forward to. Talk to old friends, run through the fields, swim in the ocean, and solve relaxing puzzles in this warm, slice-of-life narrative about nostalgia and the passage of time by the developer that brought you Rainswept. Features: A warm, slice-of-life narrative about nostalgia, appreciating the present, and the passage of time by the developer that brought you Rainswept. Take part in Sid's creative process as you play through a parallel story set in a fantasy world - right out of the book that Sid is attempting to write. Simple, relaxing puzzles that keep gameplay interesting without slowing down the story. A friendly and supportive cast of characters with deep histories and fleshed-out personalities. Cinematic presentation accompanied by a beautiful soundtrack by micAmic (Rainswept, The Cat Lady, Lorelai, Downfall) An atmospheric, warm, and cozy world to lose yourself in as you get immersed in Sid's journey back home.

short_description: Forgotten Fields is a cozy narrative game about Sid - a struggling writer who travels back to his childhood home one last time before it's sold off. Visit old friends, relive memories, solve puzzles and play through sections of Sid's book in this warm game about nostalgia and the passage of time.

_childDocuments_.review: Brought to you by the same developer who made Rainswept, Forgotten Fields is an atmospheric, narrative driven, cinematic experience, chronicling the events of one Summer in a quiet town. The inspiration gained from the developer’s own home town near Goa, India. Alongside these adventures we also witness the struggle the protagonist experiences writing his latest book and even have the opportunity to influence how the story progresses. Sid is a fiction author who is currently experiencing a creative block. It used to come easy to him in his care free days but now he feels like the magic has disappeared and he now questions his ability.A deadline is fast approaching and he has hardly any ideas to present.Meanwhile, he receives an invitation from his mother to attend an important family gathering. His mum is selling the family home. She wants him and his friends to say goodbye to the house for the last time before the move.Sid returns to the home he grew up in. The visit stimulates memories of his childhood and we watch as his family and friends spend a last evening in the house.. I was completely captivated by its charismatic and cinematic outlook. The game is paced wonderfully. There is quite a lot of text to read but it does a great job of interweaving you into the story. We learn about his friend’s hopes and dreams as well as his own and travel the journey with them. You care about what happens to them, and their back stories and experiences are carefully planned so you know exactly where everything fits in. The conversations range from everyday mundane issues to deep and thoughtful relationship talks. There aren't that many characters in the story but each one gets a decent amount of story time to showcase their personalities.The story is told imaginatively through some amazing art direction, different camera angles and interesting asides. We experience flashbacks of his childhood, interactive mini games and even get to watch and participate in his novel. The story is presented so cleverly that you never feel like you are being bogged down by text. The environments are very immersive. They are beautiful, colourful and detailed in places, oozing Summer vibes. The interactions with the characters are often pointless but they make you feel part of the story which is clever. The music is astounding and really emphasizes the emotional pull of the story. It does sometimes end abruptly which can feel irritating when you are enjoying it so much. I’m sure it could be refined to fade in and out of scenes a bit more.You may experience the occasional graphical glitch or anomaly; Characters walking in mid air or swimming oddly, for example. They seem to occur now and again, but don’t distract too much.Navigating can be a bit annoying using a controller. Often, you get hampered by furniture when moving around as the controls feel loose, and the camera angle doesn’t give you a good perspective of the room. When climbing stairs or entering rooms, the camera can be tricky to navigate. Outside, trees and buildings often obscure your view. I was disappointed when it finished. I just wanted it to continue. There were a few loose ends but I understand the game can’t go on forever, even if I wanted it to. Most of the game is narrative driven, talking to characters and performing basic tasks. There is no voice acting. All discussions are text based, displayed in different coloured speech bubbles above their heads. There is quite a lot of text to view but the fonts are easily readable and I never felt it was a chore.Occasionally, you get the option to make a choice that can change the story.There are also opportunities to interact in mini games to immerse yourself further. They are usually silly things like throwing stones to get a football out of a tree or collecting washing that has blown off the line. They’re all really simple but a welcome distraction from the text-based dialogues. Running alongside the narrative storyline, we also enter the mystical world in Sid’s novel, and get to play as a different character called Ciradyl. As Sid gets bursts of inspiration, we watch as the story in the book develops and even have a couple of opportunities to influence how the story progresses. There are also numerous flashbacks depicting memories of Sid’s childhood and special events that have shaped his personality. Often, in these dream-like states, you will have to perform very simple tasks to advance. For most of the game however you are a passenger, watching events unfold in the life of the protagonist. We get to unravel and learn about past relationships, reminisce about old times and hear about the plans of his friends and family. There are two endings, which I highly recommend viewing, so make sure you save regularly especially at your mother’s house and reload afterwards.Some of the graphics are impressive and incredibly atmospheric and immersive. I loved watching the waves on the beach and the trees swaying in the wind. The art direction was wonderful. It felt like such a cinematic experience with different camera angles and attractively framed shots. Even watching cut scenes with Sid driving in his car were attractive, and along with the excellent music, it just felt pleasant to watch.However, on occasions you are brought out of immersion by some graphical glitches like running in mid air or swimming out of the water. The music for Forgotten Fields has once again been made by Micamic, who also made the very well received soundtrack for Rainswept. It is absolutely amazing and does a brilliant job of creating extra emotional prowess. It truly is spellbinding. It’s a shame the crowd funding didn’t reach $15000 as this would have included voice acting which would have been very interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields is yet another narrative masterpiece from the developers of  It features a heavy focus on self-reflection and the passage of time, as well as the importance of family and friends. The story is told seamlessly, and I was captivated from start to finish. Despite not having a high budget, Forgotten Field's manages to make up for it with its atmospheric soundtrack and brilliant ability to express a story in such a creative manner. Similar to the developer’s previous game, it is a real treasure to all story lovers.+ Captivating and evocative narrative that is communicated brilliantly, without the use of voice-overs.+ Superb character growth and development.+ Colourful, vibrant scenes.+ Coherent and interesting incorporation of a fantasy world, countering the main plot that is centred around an ordinary yet realistic man’s life.- Extremely buggy camera angles with constant invisible walls and collisions inside inanimate objects.Once again, Frostwood Interactive has successfully created another narrative gem. Interestingly, it delves away from the more serious themes as shown in  and instead focuses on memories and life as a whole. Admittedly, as someone in my early 20's this does not seem like the most appealing subject and I was doubtful it would have the same impact on me that I had heard from other older friends. Gratefully, this is not the case at all, and the narrative is told in such a way that it does not matter your age, nor your life experience, I feel like most people will be able to relate in some form to the main character, Sid.The protagonist, Sid, is an author who specialises in creating fantasy worlds and is passionate about the idea being transported into another realm, losing oneself in the mystery and excitement of the unknown. An excellent getaway from the tedious nature of day-to-day life. Yet, despite having a major success in his previous project, he has now befallen to writer’s block and is struggling to find that creative spark he once so easily had. The frustration of worrying about meeting a fast-approaching deadline has made Sid isolated and feeling unproductive, never getting anywhere with his book. Luckily, preparation for a family dinner gives Sid a bit of a reality check and helps break the monotonous cycle. The game does take a more unique approach and there is a secondary plot around the fictional characters and fantasy story from Sid's writing. The two stories are cleverly tied together and often switch seamlessly between each other. Avoiding spoilers, the fantastical narrative centres around a magical girl who is discovering the true nature of her powers and sets off on an adventure, determined to change things for the better, but is afraid and unsure of her path.I noticed Forgotten Fields is adequately described on the Store page as "cosy" and I could not think of a better word myself to describe it. Everything about the game is comforting, secure and evokes a deep level of reflection and realisation. There is just something unique about the writing that the developers have fine-tuned to near perfection that I just cannot pinpoint. Whilst there are some minor puzzles scattered throughout, mainly consisting of fetch quests of nearby items, Forgotten Fields is predominantly a cinematic experience. The gameplay elements were enough to keep me interested and aware that it is indeed an adventure game, as opposed to a visual novel, but the puzzles themselves are exceptionally simple.Some examples of puzzles include finding scattered laundry around the town, minor QTE's and following verbal instructions to correctly setup a washing machine. These examples are typically what can be expected throughout the game and I quite enjoyed this. I believe the narrative is constructed to be cosy, atmospheric, and relaxing. If the puzzles were frustrating, difficult, or just annoying, this whole vibe would be ruined. I also greatly enjoyed the change up between mundane realistic life and being transported into this fantasy world that Sid is creating. It gave a nice perspective and complimented the main plot, allowing players to delve into a whole new universe. Switching between this and completing simple tasks like setting up the dinner table, washing the dishes and preparing the drinks, really gave a nice juxtaposition. Furthermore, the inclusion of these ordinary tasks established a family atmosphere and helped demonstrate Sid's memories of family events, whilst also conveying the message that family time should be cherished as nothing is permanent. Unfortunately, Forgotten Fields is plagued with awful camera angles and colliding objects. It soon became commonplace to me to expect to be able to walk through almost every wall in the game. Sometimes, interacting with objects would also not correlate and  for instance, when I tried to pet the dog, I was suddenly transported inside the house (when standing outside, separated by a wall), the character leaned down and was petting absolutely nothing. This would also disturb the already semi broken camera angles, usually showing the roof on buildings when inside so I could not see where I was going. Understandably, it is an Indie title with a small budget and thus sacrifices must be made on certain elements within the game. Obviously, what the developers do exceptionally well, is the storytelling. Which is the main aspect of the game and is something I cannot quite fault. Although the awful camera angles and colliding objects are bothersome, it did become something I could overlook, and my experience overall was not ruined due to this but is something I believe prospective players should be aware of.There are many colourful environments in Forgotten Fields and the character model is more customizable which is a great improvement from the developer’s previous game. The vibrant, sunny nature of the town is quite eye-catching. Even the simple drive scene feels cosy. However, I am not a fan of the character models with expressionless faces, no mouths, and stick-figured bodies (also seen in ), but the environment has a certain artistic approach that I appreciated.Whilst there are no voiced characters, the beautiful narrative is expressed through the equally stunning soundtrack by micAmic. The studio responsible for the audio in some of the most poignant titles including  There are many scenes in this only 3–4-hour game that come to mind as particularly memorable, simply due to the atmospheric music that creates such a genuine tone, truly bringing memories and nostalgia to life. Forgotten Fields is a must-have for story lovers. The developers at Frostwood Interactive have such a creative talent of transporting players into their world, captivating them from start to finish, in such a way that I cannot seem to pinpoint. Although some of the more technical areas could use some improvement, the narrative can hold its own and make players feel as if they are a part of the journey, evoking feelings of self-reflection and reminiscence. Despite being a short 3–4-hour experience, I highly recommend this to all fans of the genre, particularly those we have played  , but with a price tag of $AU18.50, it may be best to wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely little story game and i enjoyed every tiny bit of it. You're playing a guy called Sid (and partly also his fictional character...No spoilers!) who's spending his time doing basic daily life things, reliving old memories and gathering new ones.Meeting friends, helping neighbours, meeting family members.  All regular stuff, and doesn't seem to be so interesting, but what made it really intresting for me was the way of storytelling and the really beautiful artstyle.The developers played around with colour contrasts and added tiny details everywhere and i'm a real sucker for those.Music in the game is pleasant and relaxing. About the story,... well, i don't wanna spoil anything, so i'd just like to say that it made me think about how much more we should enjoy and appreciate every moment we've got, with all the people around us, how much more we should should try to memorize places we visit, because nobody can take these memories from us, and they make us who we are. Even the most trivial and random looking thing or moment we experience today, can look wonderful when we look back, someday in the future.After the poetic thoughts, back to the game to talk about some things i didn't like:First of all, the game (I've played in 4K if that matters to anyone.) had quite a few visual bugs or glitches, like people walking through objects or standing in them, flickering textures when i swam back to the shore at the ocean and when i drove the scooter and the yellow car in 3rd person.My second problem was the camera.  There were many situations where i just didn't see where i was going, especially inside the house(s).  I wish we could freely move the camera, that would also give TONS of more opportunities for fantastic screenshots of the game. There are really so many impressive artsy things, but you can't really capture them properly because the camera angle, or items blocking the view, won't allow it.The controls sometimes show wrong prompts on the screen when you play with keyboard and mouse, for example getting back with glasses at the beach, showed me RMB as prompt, while in reality i had to press Q, as before.  And tbh, the controls overall feel a bit unresponsive, and need work.Not a negative thing per se, but i have to admit that the game would be in my top 5 if it had voiceactors instead of text.Sometimes reading takes a bit of the immersion, so if it's somehow possible, please get some voiceactors into this, it would make the game AMAZING!And as always, when i love a game: I wish it was much longer!

_childDocuments_.review: engages the audience in a lot of self-reflection by the interactions between the protagonist Sid and his family and friends. It involves careful reading of the dialogue to get the most out of this title, and there is no voice acting. There are some gameplay elements with some running around, doing fetch quests, tackling mini-games, and just player-interaction with the surroundings to move the story along. But all in all, the meat of the game is in the play-esque flow of the discourse among the characters.The main theme of the story revolves around major decisions at the crossroads where every step could significant impact one's life. This is true for the protagonist Sid, his friends, his mother, and also the story-in-a-story protagonist Cyradil in Sid's new novel outline. Sid uses his self reflection to drive his novel plotline as he is dealing with writer's block, trying to come up with ideas after his relatively successful first novel, in hopes of not becoming a one-hit wonder.We learn about Sid and the other characters through their interactions with each other during the events of the single day that we can effectively call Act I of this play and Act II involves the following day's major decision making that will alter multiple storylines. So it's not entirely a play in two acts, because there are different outcomes possible. There's no right or wrong decisions here, just decisions that affect how we live, the same decisions we all face at one point or another ourselves.Whether you work the same shift doing the same thing, or your life is filled with fun and exciting adventures that seemingly never repeat, the game/story reminds us to live in the moment. I do not think that the message is lost on anyone who ponders on the dialogue, and I appreciate that the game allows us to think on this from multiple perspectives as we progress through the story. I am thankful I still wake up on this side of the ground every day. Life events, good or bad, shape our lives and make us who we are today. We fondly reminisce the past in-part because they define who we are, but also because we know that we cannot go back. The majority of the story takes place in one day, but we share glimpses of a lifetime. What a nice way to tell a story.Keyboard and Mouse is the way to go for this game in its current state. The controller feels rather clunky in places. There was one or two places that I lost control of my mouse cursor and had to use the controller to regain control, then the mouse started working again. The game really doesn't need the quick-time events or the charge and throw mechanics, I wish these could be made optional. A view of the control page can be seen here:I really enjoy the presentation of this game. Sure, I would have enjoyed it more with more photorealistic models, full expressions, etc. but that is not easy to achieve for any indie team. It seems that the developers made the best use of the resources available to make this game look nice.Some places the game offers a natural frame for some nice screenshots, such as here:The music is really fun and there are a couple of nice vocal tracks in there as well. The sound effects are good for the most part, some places I did feel that there were a bit more noise than necessary in the background undertones.Too bad there is no voice acting, I would have liked to experience this story from a completely passive perspective except for the decisive choices and soaked up the sights and sounds along with a running vocalized dialogue.For those who want a good story who don't mind a bit of reading and dealing with the clunky controls in some places. This game definitely will not appeal to everyone.Base price is $12.99, making it a bit on the pricier side for a game that lasts about 3-4 hours. Even though there are choices in some dialogue, they do not affect the story (or minimally so) except for the final big decision, so a save toward the end is all you need to see both endings. There are also some achievements that you may miss in a first play through that you would need to play again to get, unless you kept some timely saves that would save you the trouble.Hopefully some of the issues that affect the enjoyment of this narrative can be fixed. Aside from some bugs, there are also some really clunky-feeling controls and difficult navigation. Some of the player-interactions really feel unnecessary so it would be nice to make some of this optional--such as the QTEs, the Charge & Throw mechanic (used once), and all of the small actions that the player needs to carry out mindlessly, especially at the dinner party. I just feel like I want a passive option for experiencing this story. has some rough edges, perhaps too much in places, but the overall story is worthwhile for an experience and some deep contemplations. I do feel that the gameplay can be significantly improved with some bug fixes and QoL changes. The technical issues currently do rather hamper the overall enjoyment.Score overall: 6/10 (written April 18, 2021).

_childDocuments_.review: For some of us, creativity is like a candle. You light it up, and the flame burns bright, lighting the entire room around it. You revel in said light - I mean, how could you not? - and you feel motivated to do everything there is to be done… up until the moment the light burns out, and you’re left in the dark, trying everything you can to light the candle again. This is a tale as old as time, one that is unfortunately all too familiar for quite a few of us who actively exercise our creativity, including me. Perhaps this is why I was drawn to Forgotten Fields and its slice-of-life tale about a writer that has a severe case of writer’s block.—---------------------------------------------------------------The steam store page description for the game says “Sid is a writer struggling with writer’s block, attempting to recapture the feelings of inspiration he felt when he was younger”, and I feel like this sentence captures a lot of what is special about Forgotten Fields.  - yet, as a guy who loves to write and has not been able to do so for years, yearning for my teenage creativity that pumped out dozens of chapters for many different stories, Since publishing his first book, Sid has been unable to even write a story summary for his second book. This shouldn’t be a problem, but unfortunately, writing is Sid’s job, and our capitalist society demands him to pay his bills, so he has to submit a new idea in order to receive a new grant and continue writing full time. The kicker? It is the day of the deadline, and Sid still can’t bring himself to write anything. While he struggles with this problem, his friend drops by and passes along a message from Sid’s mom, who wants to have one final dinner with Sid and his friends before selling the house the very next day. Despite being reluctant to go due to his deadline, the protagonist decides to go anyway, embarking on a nostalgic adventure home. The writing does try too hard to be philosophical at times, but it brought me some new insight into an issue that has plagued me and countless others for a long time. The issues, struggles, fears and hopes that Sid has are mostly shared with me, and I could clearly notice that the developer’s own heart was poured into this game. It really feels like a personal experience, an insight into his mind, which provides a very unique opportunity for introspection.While Sid is on his trip to his mother’s house, he meets up with his old friends, and manages to slowly develop the story he has been stuck on for ages. Basically,  These story developments are both a narrative and gameplay device, acting as a very interesting way to develop Sid’s tale. These story developments work as a narrative device because there are plenty of parallels to be drawn from Sid’s story and Cyradil’s story. The fairytale world develops in direct response to Sid’s real life experiences, often mirroring things and dilemmas you just played through as Sid. In turn, watching things unravel in the fairytale world allows us an unfiltered insight into the protagonist’s mind and innermost thoughts. As for the gameplay device, it comes in the form of the occasional switch between the “real” world and Sid’s imagination. The fairytale world also has a bit more liberty in terms of themes and gameplay, as demonstrated by a basic stealth section and even a 2d section.Story aside, the game also excels in two other very important departments: the art style and soundtrack.  At one point, we have the warm colors of a sunset and the sounds of waves crashing against a beach, giving us a sense of relaxation and a feeling that everything would be alright, while Sid himself had a moment of introspection. At another point, the game used blues, whites, purples and yellow colors to convey the feeling of magic and safety in a certain location, with the ambient sound of birds and crickets to further collaborate in the construction of the environment.So the story is good, the soundtrack and artstyle are awesome… but what about the gameplay? There are some deviations from this, such as segments in which you play in first person, but those are unfortunately not very common.  I take good care to not call them puzzles because really, you are told what to do and you basically have to go and do what you’re told. The minigames aren’t too great either, mostly revolving around quick time events or specific movements (like flicking the mouse to throw a rock), but they do serve to stop the game from being dialogue after dialogue.The main problem with the gameplay, though, are the  There were a few sections in the game that genuinely made me frustrated, as I was unable to properly do what the game wanted me to. The main offender here was the rock throwing minigame: for some reason, I could never get it to throw properly, instead either barely moving the rock from the ground or just yeeting it off camera, with no middle ground. And while we’re on the topic of issues… There were two main issues that I found. One of them, that you can easily replicate, is related to the space bar. If you press space, you skip your current text. However, if you press space bar while the game is controlling your camera angle (for example, when the camera focuses on the shower when you’re showering in the beginning of the game), you can move your character, but the camera angle gets stuck in the wrong angle and is unable to be fixed except by reloading an earlier save. The second one was that my character just… refused to move properly at some point. He basically walked in one direction till I paused the game, then unpaused and quickly pressed another direction, which would prompt Sid to eternally walk in that direction. If you run into this second issue, just open the clothing menu and it fixes the problem. Overall, I was glad to have played this game. It made me think about a lot of things, but I think the main takeaway I had was that maybe, just maybe, trying to re-light the same candle that was put out in the intro to this review is not the way to go. Perhaps what I should instead be doing is lighting new candles, and looking forward to the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Rainswept so I had high hopes for Forgotten Fields.  For me, it fell short in a few areas. You control Sid - a 20-something guy with a deadline and a case of writer's block. His mother is selling the family home and he is at that cusp  in life where each of us recognizes that we are going to have to be a grown up.  Much of the story and dialog is between a set of friends who are about to step out into 'real life,' each in their own direction.In parallel, Sid is writing a story about a princess in a fantasy world. About half the game is controlling the princess within her own adventures. There are definite tie-ins between the choices facing the princess and the choices facing Sid.Like Rainswept, Forgotten Fields has spectacular art and a lovely sound track. The cut scenes are put together beautifully, with cinematic effects that one might expect from a major motion picture. There are no voice overs and there is a lot of dialog to read throughWhere the game stumbled for me was in the camera angles and the controls. I struggled with both throughout my time playing and encountered a couple of bugs that required a restart from a prior (manually) saved file. There were scenes that became jerky, rooms that spun, objects out of synch, and walls/doors that could be walked through. At times, I missed potential interactions because some require perfect positioning before they are displayed. I could not rely entirely on either my keyboard/mouse or my controller. So, I played using a combination of both. The camera angles drove me crazy as often, I could not see the character I was controlling when objects in the environment would get in my way. My recommendation is to save your game (there are 3 slots available in addition to the auto-save) frequently.I would recommend Forgotten Fields. It is an interesting study of character relationships and does a good job of capturing the angst most of us feel as we transition to adulthood. My hope is that the development team will continue to fine tune the code and make the mechanics more enjoyable.Added Note: The developer is extremely responsive and is actively working to fix reported items. I really appreciate it when development teams join the community and interact with players like this!

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields is a good story and an ok game.  The game discusses the topic of our past vs our future, and does a decent job, although the writing is clearly done by a non-native English speaker, if that matters.The game itself has some definite problems.  The camera is awful, whether in the story or the story-within-a-story.  The controls and object hitboxes are not good.  The inventory system is not well designed (and can't be rebound).  There are a number of graphical issues throughout.  There's no reason for the 1st person sections (there are 2 of them).  Even the quick-time events are shoehorned.  And there are no puzzles whatsoever.  Why do 3 characters (of 6) in 1 scene all have green dialogue text?  This is a narrative-only experience, but the narrative is the best part.  Or the audio, for the most part; the songs are chill, although there are multiple areas with no music and minimal sound effects....  or there is the beach scene where the waves are so loud you can't hear anything else (including yourself).  Pick this up if you want an interesting, reflective story.  Don't pick it up if you want a smooth gameplay experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields is a fairly relaxing walking sim where you play an ennui-ridden twentysomething with writer's block. He's all wrapped up in nostalgia and sadness over growing up and not quite ending up in the life he imagined. During the course of the day you visit family and friends in beautiful surroundings and reminisce about the past and ponder the meaning of life. None of it is super-insightful, but it is familiar - they're emotions that most everyone has experienced at some point in their lives.Throughout the thread of the game, the main character also starts to come up with a new fantasy story to pitch to his publisher, and to be honest that's the weakest part of the game for me. I could identify with the main character's anxieties, but the heroine of the story-within-a-story just seemed a bit flat and uninteresting, full of typical tired old high fantasy tropes. I would've enjoyed the game a lot more without those shoehorned interludes.The controls are incredibly janky and sometimes it's difficult to get the camera in the right place or click on the thing you're supposed to be clicking. Fortunately there is hardly any clicking to do - the majority of this game is just reading dialog and doing the occasional small "fetch quest" (if you can call things like setting the table for dinner a fetch quest). It's not the greatest walking sim that ever came out, but it's definitely worth playing if you like the genre. The humid, tropical setting is charming, the dialog is reasonably believable, and it feels like an honest slice of life.

_childDocuments_.review: is not something I particularly relate to, but I appreciated what this game was trying to do. It's short, it's sweet, it has a clear point of view, told in interesting ways.Now, to some particulars: The environments, especially the outdoors, and just the general atmosphere are remarkable. One of the best visual representations of the ocean I've ever seen in a videogame.   The human characters are a little too nondescript. It's absolutely an aesthetic choice, but one that I feel ultimately didn't serve the game too well. The style works great for the environments, and at times even does an okay job with the human characters in the wide shots, but then you have full closeup scenes intended to be relatable or emotional entirely acted out by stiff ghoulish unblinking mannequins. The story is good. It's well thought-out and well paced. The dialogue is not bad, but it isn't great. _childDocuments_.review: I recommend Forgotten Fields to narrative fans who don't mind a shorter experience.Forgotten Fields is the second game from Frostwood Interactive, coming on the heels of Rainswept, a murder mystery that was less about solving a murder and more about celebrating the lives and stories of the victims.  Like Rainswept, this game is a game about people and their stories more than anything.  The game uses a vibrant, nostalgic palette and has a good soundtrack to help sell the story.In Forgotten Fields, we play a young author who suffers from writer's block.  He learns that his widowed mother plans to sell his childhood home to downsize to a smaller apartment.  He goes home for a final visit before this happens, to see some old friends and have one last dinner in the old place.  We experience frequent flashbacks as he walks down memory lane.  Meanwhile, he begins getting ideas for his next book, a fantasy, and we play short sequences in this imaginary world as the ideas take shape.Nothing much happens in Forgotten Fields - that's the whole point.  This is the kind of game where two characters idly gaze out over a beach, sipping beers and chatting about nothing - the kind of game where doing the dishes after a meal counts as a dramatic beat.  Characters primarily reminisce about the old times, and talk about their current life situations, and getting older, and getting married, and settling down.  It's very relatable.  I would not classify Forgotten Fields as a point+click.  There's no puzzles in the game.  To control the game, I used a mix of mouse+keyboard and controller.  I found that each option worked well in some circumstances, and less well in others.  There is an inventory, but it only gets used a handful of times.  There are also a few QTEs, but there's no penalty for failing them.  The game is largely a third-person game, but there are a few short sequences where you are in the first person.  For such a small package, there's a lot of experimentation with perspective.Playing a release build, I did experience a few bugs with the game.  I expect most of these will get ironed out over time.  At the top of the game, I managed to break an interaction and had to restart.  There are one or two walk-through-able walls, and some visual clipping in places.  The most serious bug I encountered was on-screen button prompts clipping into the game's environment, rendering them unreadable.You can expect 2-3 hours of playtime, and two endings to explore based on your choices.  This is a short game, but I am glad that I backed it and helped it get made.

The story of the main character and the character in the story he is trying to create throughout the game. I enjoyed the little journey the main character went through in this game. _childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields, created by Frostwood Interactive, invites players to embark on an emotional journey through nostalgia, creativity, and the passage of time. This indie game, with its delicate storytelling, touches upon the complex feeling of being neither entirely happy nor sad.In Forgotten Fields, players assume the role of Sid, a budding author grappling with writer's block. An invitation to a farewell dinner with old friends at his childhood home sets the stage for a poignant exploration of memories and the present. Sid's journey takes unexpected turns as he encounters familiar faces along the way.What makes Forgotten Fields unique is the parallel narrative of "Sid's Story." Players step into the shoes of a fantasy character who, like Sid, seeks to rediscover a time and place long lost. This secondary story initially introduces an interactive story-creation aspect, but it wisely evolves into a more immersive narrative, allowing players to fully engage with the story and its symbolism.Visually, Forgotten Fields opts for simplicity, with subdued graphics and basic character models. While not highly detailed, these visuals effectively convey the game's core elements and facilitate meaningful interpersonal moments. Nevertheless, some scenes, such as a sunset beach and rustling leaves in the wind, showcase the game's true visual beauty.The game's music, featuring songs by Portland-based singer-songwriter Altadore, plays a crucial role in crafting its bittersweet atmosphere. Altadore's music captures the melancholic yet contented emotions central to the game's themes. The combination of visuals and sound helps convey the nuanced sentiment of appreciating the present while acknowledging the nostalgia for the past.While Forgotten Fields excels in emotional depth and tone, it falls short in terms of gameplay. Controls are basic, offering little more than running, talking, and interacting. The game includes a few mini-games, such as knocking a football from a tree or assisting with a boat, to break up the dialogue-heavy sections. However, these activities often feel unfulfilling and occasionally repetitive, although they may serve to emphasize the importance of embracing ordinary moments.Ultimately, Forgotten Fields' quiet poignancy outweighs its minor gameplay shortcomings. Its message resonates with those who hold nostalgia close or possess a creative spirit. The game's bittersweet hopefulness lingers, making it a compelling experience that invites reflection on themes of growing up and appreciating life's fleeting moments. While the impact of its message may vary from person to person, Forgotten Fields has the potential to become a beloved favorite for those who connect with its sentiment.

_childDocuments_.review: -Beautiful artwork and lovely, colorful environments. The ocean waves particularly, at the beach scene, are drop dead gorgeous, some of the most lovely I've ever seen. Unique art style in the game. -No voice narration, but as long as you read the easy-to-view dialogue boxes you'll be fine. Actually having no narration makes one pay attention MORE, I think. -The control scheme (and I'm playing only with mouse/keyboard on a desktop PC) is functional, but awkward; to me the controls are the only poor mark in this game. One can rotate the camera-view if needed, but even then the running and walking in certain directions leaves a bit to be desired. You'll run into things and have to either back away or re-adjust camera view. Still, with this being said, it's only a minor inconvenience IMHO. -Music score is also stellar. Gorgeous, lovely songs. There could have been more ambient audio added here and there, but even that didn't bother me. The musical score is a perfect accompaniment to the lack of spoken dialogue.-Lovely, angsty storyline about a young writer trying to get along in the world. Nothing too preachy, and his interactions with other characters are believable and mostly enjoyable.-The game for the most part leads you by the hand (through dialogue trees) but there are some things you will need to figure out. It's not difficult, so don't go looking for a challenge. But the storyline is more than interesting enough, the music score utterly enjoyable and the environments are uniquely gorgeous from the various perspectives you encounter.-Very good price-point for the game.-Finally: multiple save slots (four,apparently) and the game auto-saves! This is a welcome plus in most games nowadays.-Game is perfectly optimized for me at max settings (I am running the game on a new-ish desktop PC, so can't comment on how it would run on lower-end PCs).-For an indie game?  A superb effort and well worth the price. ENjoyable, lovely to look at and an interesting storyline to boot, especially I would think for millenial players (heck, I'm an "old guy", and I'M enjoying it!)-I've not yet finished the game, and I've only found one minor storyline "bug" which the DEV has already patched a fix for. Perhaps there are more, but I haven't yet encountered any. -EDITED: I finished the game, and it took about 3.5 hours. Every minute worth it. Found no more bugs. Lovely ending. Just a pleasant game throughout; truly enjoyed the storyline. I made good use of my 4 save game slots, and will go and re-visit these areas for their lovely scenery and enjoy the game further...I'd guess exploring every nook and cranny and slowly progressing through the dialogues would bring one about 4 hours of gameplay. Still a good price for such an enjoyable game.Support the DEV!

_childDocuments_.review: A narrative story about an author with a bad case of mind block, reliving his past nostalgia of home in between deciding his own future and that of the heroine of his upcoming novel facing the same dilemma.Pros+ Interesting blend of real life situation and fantasy intertwining for a narrative+ Nice colour palatte and whimsical feel+ The nostalgia angle was nice, but under-performed (Try Venba for a better take)Cons- Very linear story line, without any real major developments- The horrendous art style and graphics, mix of 3D with shaded art, the people model without eyes were right out from a horror story.. The waves crashing onto polygon rocks and 80s background graphics were cringe. At least the tree animations were good.- Very little world building to anchor in your interest, spent my time wondering where this took place and setting of the story, was it India. the US, some Pacific Island? May not matter but as it hinges on nostalgic building and empathy the visual models and setting detracts from the people within- Your choices in decision making doesn't really matter or make nay difference to the story.- The bugs, had so many bugs from misplaced people models, book jackets not appearing properly, characters swimming on land, etc.- The crash model and navigation was horrible, visual clipping saw objects cut into each other, some camera angles were truly unworkable, an odd first person swimming sequence was so out of place. Many times walking into an invisible wall cuts the immersion- The visual UI was bad, the colours on choice selection makes it hard to see which choice you were actually selecting, and the backpack object use was really not something you'd think you'd find in a completed game.- Achievement didn't pop one time had to replay to get it.Don't recommend this game at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is very pretty. The ocean particularly was very breathtaking. However, the rudimentary animations and plethora of errors that resulted from them broke my immersion way too much to enjoy. The story is great, if a little text heavy at times. For the rest of the gameplay, sometimes knowing what to do is difficult if you missed even a single box of text. There's nothing reminding you what your task is, and especially in the house scene towards the end, its almost impossible to find the one interactable that you're supposed to be using. Played it once to get the achievements but I wont be revisiting it.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: While this game has an interesting storyline, a pretty visual style and a nice soundtrack, the execution is really sad.The characters keep clipping through objects and walls, controlling the characters is not smooth, the camera sucks, the models are many times hovering above ground, render issues, no facial animation, very basic character design, etc. There are loads of glitches in this game, and the puzzles are not very interesting either. Thus, this could have probably made a better film than a game. Honestly, while playing this game there were many times I could not wait for it to just end.One thing I did enjoy was seeing an Indian context for the story. I look forward to what the creator of the story (not the developer, mind you) makes next.Overall, this game is definitely not worth your time. Maybe watch a playthrough video on youtube, so you can skip forward the boring parts, and experience the story, which is decent and uniquely structured.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: You've been through school. You've made and lost friends. You've worked a career for a number of years. As time marches relentlessly forward, you begin to lose touch with yourself and who you once were. is a game about choosing whether to look ahead or back, self doubt, and ultimately navigating the uncharted waters of your 20s. It's a touching story with presentation that's a little rough around the edges.F̵̺̒u̵̧͘ṇ̴̈n̷̤̐y̶͔̿ ̸̞͝g̴̠͝l̴̬̈í̵̼t̸͍̐č̸̯h̵̫͆ ̸̯͛g̶̨͒a̶͔̐m̵̳̈́e̸̠͌Let me get this out the way first. Forgotten Fields is very amatuer in its design. It's ridden with glitches and animation errors, abrupt music cuts and more. It's unpolished chaos, and I'll admit that I definitely got a kick out of it.The time that my friend phased through the world to take the optimal route to the garden? Wonderful.The time the music forgot to stop playing only to abruptly realize it had missed its cue and shut off halfway through the next scene? Classic.The time my character got stuck in a fetal position but could still slide around like he was moving on ice, then I dropped him into the ocean so he could trawl the seabed moving like that ? Masterpiece.I don't think the glitches hindered the game in any way, instead  the experience.Sadly, everything else is just as clunky or unpolished, just like your grammar, try to fix that, bud.Overall, I'd say this is a very soft recommendation. Forgotten Fields tells a story that will likely resonate emotionally while at the same time having absolutely numbing gameplay.6/10
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game purely based on my last experience with Rainswept. It was one of the most immersed experience I ever had with adventure games. Rainswept packs full of amazing cinematic moments, a crime story has a fine twist, a solid plot, very plausible, mature and relatable story. It's a truly mesmerizing experience. Although the graphics was extremely simple; just match stick characters, that actually plays an advantage to the game, it push players more focus on the story side.Unfortunately Forgotten Fields is a huge let down. Although the graphics has been a big improvement, that's the only positive side. The creator wants to create an relaxing experience but I don't feel that at all, in fact the opposite. Because the story and conversations are not captivating or entertaining, most of the time I feel very random with the game. There are some tasks with controls but they don't feel relate to the story. I much prefer like Rainswept, the control was basically going from one place to other but the story kept me going, it doesn't feel like an effort. I actually wanted to go there to watch how the story unfolded. As for Forgotten Fields, everything feels like a chore.First, I found it really frustrating that there is no objective text to remind me what to do next. When I load the save, I am lost already. If the story is not gripping, players will forget. Next, I don't know why the creator chose a fantasy story that the main character having writer block, it feels extremely off. I honestly cannot care the fantasy side. Third, the controls feel very off on the Mac. I try to like this game but I just can't.I truly believe the creator has great talent on crafting an immersive story with gripping dialogues , as he proves it in Rainswept. I hope the next game will put back the focus on the storyline.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields is a nice little interactive novella. A few points of choice are scattered throughout, but it's otherwise a linear progression of the main character's store interspersed with embedded smaller tales.I really enjoyed playing through this. It was relaxed without the usual pressures of a game, save for a few quick time events.I don't know that I'll play it again, but the overall stories here may stick with me for a while. Definitely worth the few hours I spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: The twilight of youth and the uncertainty of the future.  Forgotten Fields meditates on those themes through the eyes of a young man, his friends, family and hometown.I thought it was beautifully observed, the writing was of an excellent standard and the framing of the scenes really worked for me.There are moments of pure sunset joy, some very cinematic montages, some insights into the creative mind that flesh the themes out beautifully.  It's a joy to experience.The visuals are nice and the Unity-look is well suited, I'd say.  The "alternate" story is especially lush and well designed and I loved the idea of the parallel journey; it really worked well.I played most of this game through the Linux Proton compatibility later (7.0.4), it played fine but there were a few graphical glitches and one sequence failed to fire at all.  It all worked perfect on WIndows though.If you're after something a little meditative, definitely give this a run through for it's roughly two hours of playtime.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible narrative marvel at a low price!This game is exactly what it looks like, a simple Unity Game, driven solely by its direction, artstyle and narrative. And it does not disappoint at that!Now obviously this game isn't perfect, so if the above mentioned sounds interesting maybe keep some things in mind. This game has a lot of minor issues, like dialogues skipping too fast, spelling errors, clunky camera movement at times, being able to walk through objects and so on, but none of these are game breaking and didn't ruin my immersion either. If you've played games at this price-range before that's all stuff you should be used to by now.Now the story and the way it is presented to the player is really to be praised, it is very linear but very well written with minor choices here and there and alround likable and relatable characters.There are some personal issues I have with the narrative, like some choices being completely useless, or outright contradicting the narrative presented by the game, or the fact that there are several points at the end where a (in my opinion) more impactful, open ending could have taken place, but the ending is still great and wraps everything up nicely.All in all, I would definately recommend this game, and it makes me wonder what this team can bring to the table, if their next game is one price range higher and more polished, but no matter what it will look like, I'm excited for future projects!
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields tells it's story of adolescent nostalgia and creative crisis in a very meditative, quiet manner and the landscapes bathed in warm lighting emphasize this melancholy beautifully. While the character models look a bit rough and doll like, the lush landscapes are really something that transported me into the mood of the game. And I liked the idea of mirroring the journey of the struggling writer with a game within the game - a formulaic, but nice little fantasy story. The writing is overall well done, never gets overdramatic and finds the right tone for the topic and that was for me, what transcended the stiff character animations and made me feel for the protagonist. Gameplay wise there are a few minigames and (unexpected) quick time events, but overall it is a  very calm and even cozy experience that is centered around the dialogues and is concerned in setting the mood. There are a few smaller bugs though. At one point I had to restart the game, because I got stuck in a landscape. But overall this is a nice game. It is not very long and can be easily finished in one sitting of 3-4 hours. But to me it was fully worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields is a really emotional, contemplative game. It's...it's hard to describe what it's about. Change, and loss. Nostalgia and hope. _childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game because I was a huge fan of Rainswept and I'd definitely say that Frostwood Interactive has done it again! This is a wonderful game for anyone who appreciates a good, emotional story. The characters are relatable, as are their struggles and the game does such a great job of showcasing their experiences. I can't comment first hand on the graphics because I was playing on the minimum specs and needed to use the lower graphics setting, but it was pleasant to look at and I'm sure it will only be better on the higher settings. This game is a new release and an indie game, so it is definitely not bug free but the bugs I encountered didn't detract from my enjoyment of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgotten Fields

_childDocuments_.review: Finally got around to this, and it did not disappoint. This gorgeous narrative game is a worthy followup to Frostwood Interactive's previous work, Rainswept. This game is raw and heartfelt; it's a deeply personal experience that will connect to those of us having a "quarter life crisis," or anyone who is embarking on the next big chapter of our lives. The characters are well developed and interesting, and they have the kind of camaraderie that I crave to see in games, but rarely find. But as I found with the developer's previous game, the real thing that captured my attention were the sweeping cinematic sequences that carried the story along. Beautiful foliage and environments; low-poly and picture perfect. While there are definitely some technical errors when it comes to the animations here and there, they did not distract me from the story, and I was able to complete the game without any issues. I'd recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a warm nostalgic experience. Can't wait to see what the developer does next!

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely game. If you liked Rainswept you surely will like this game. The quality of the text improved and it is interesting to follow the story. _childDocuments_.review: Forgotten Fields is a cozy narrative game about Sid - a struggling writer who travels back to his childhood home one last time before it's sold off. Visit old friends, relive memories, solve puzzles and play through sections of Sid's book in this warm game about nostalgia and the passage of time.

name: The Shore
detailed_description: Our Upcoming LoveCraftian CO-OP The VR version About the Game THE SHORE is a game about the mystery of the unknown, set on a forbidden island filled with horrors. Based on the works of H. P. Lovecraft, the story features many of his best-known creations and more. Players will see the world through the eyes of Andrew, a father in search of his lost daughter. Players will experience The Shore through immersive, atmospheric gameplay and encounter the most nightmarish Lovecraftian entities, all while solving mind-bending puzzles. Try to survive as Andrew as he endeavours to save his daughter’s life and, perhaps, uncover the secrets lurking within his own sanity. Presented with a Lovecraftian style, As players dive deeper and deeper into the mystery, they’ll face overwhelming odds, Andrew's moments that will make you question his sanity, and a series of slow-burn scenes. It’s only by mastering the artifacts of the old gods combat mechanic that they can stay one step ahead of the darkness that tries to swallow the world of his, but will that be enough? With the ghost of an action/mystery/horror play style and the mind of a psychological thriller, The Shore's dramatic atmosphere, deep and multilayered story, and exceptionally tense, horrific combat sequences provide players with an overwhelming and stunning gaming experience. KEY FEATURES • stunning art design • immersive exploration experience • Breathtaking enviroments, with every one of them a unique story to tell • Challenging exploration, enter into unknown dimensions and come face to face with horrific entities that will try to stop you from gaining knowledge. • Chilling atmosphere and tension, what can a human do against the fear of the unknown. • Main storyline and a lot of background plot to be discovered by players • self made story inspired by Lovecraftian Mythology

_childDocuments_.review: Bought and played the game in one sitting, although it is a walking sim with some not too polished combat mechanics, the art and music design alone would make me want to play this game again, seeing Lovecraftian Horrors brought to visually amazing feats and a soundtrack that will be loud at times but also sets and keeps the tone of the game in check with every note. _childDocuments_.review: The Shore is probably one of the finer examples of a "Walking Simulator" I've played in a while. It grasps you from the first second with it's alluring music and iconography, and manages to keep its grip for most of its duration. I have some qualms related to the inclusion of its action set-pieces, but I suppose the creator wanted to add some tension to the Eldritch proceedings. You did not read that wrong either - that is THE creator. This little gem is the work of a single individual, apparently. Intense imagery, atmospheric sound design and a total duration that does not outstay its welcome, The Shore is a fine Cosmic Horror journey to spend your evening (or even better, night) experiencing. - FiOth

_childDocuments_.review: Although the game is called "The Shore" and you indeed begin your journey at a beach, however, this episode is only a short part of your wandering, which quickly grabs you into other Inter-dimensional places.First 30mins I was like "oh hey, another walking simulator". Then I turned to "сraр-сraр-сraр, run faster!!1".Wouldn't be a proper Lovecraftian game w/o "ewww" moments. Ever wondered what it's like going in a hands tunnel? Or... spinal, veins pulsing cave?Ever craved to be chased by numerous gnarly creatures? Ever dreamed of ripping hands of petrified humans, because you need them for a puzzle?Oh my Elder Gods. The sound in the game is great! Ambient: vibrations, voices in a head, footprints when stomping meaty corridors, oof!Creatures: they SCARY! they LOUD! I want to run away from those horrible beings! That Dagon though... what a roar and... the climb afterwards XDFrom a slow paced daily landscape gazing "yay, another sea shell" to a fast chase "I see nothing!" sequence and hold your breath moments.

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore has what you would expect from an H.P. Lovecraft story.  The protagonist is an insignificant human that finds himself in the middle of a major cosmic event while searching for his daughter.  If you're a fan of H.P. Lovecraft and cosmic horror, this game is a must-buy, as long as you can overcome a few caveats.  The things this game does right, it does wonderfully, but it has some technical problems, and some pacing problems.The graphics are great, especially considering the island is little more than a desolate, rocky reef breaking the surface of the ocean.  The creature design is fantastic and their animations are fluid, bizarre, and organic.  The audio and music really stand out and sell the atmosphere and mood of the game.  The voice acting is decent enough.  Overall it's a well designed game.There's a few problems with it though.  First is that the controls are hard coded, including the mouse buttons.  This made it extremely frustrating during the escape sequences in the second half of the game because I could not rebind my keys and mouse to my typical, comfortable control scheme.  This is something that I usually refund a game for right away, but as a Lovecraft fan, I really wanted to experience this game so I made a go at it.  Second, the optimization is not great.  Although I had a decent enough framerate at 4k resolution and max settings, there were problems with sound crackling and stuttering and I had to turn down the sound quality in windows as well as close pretty much every background program and process that I could to keep the sound from going bad.  Last thing, the game could be longer... it took me about 2 hours to complete going at a leisurely pace, but that would have been at least 30 minutes shorter if I'd had my own control scheme to use.  There are a lot of mythos deities and beasties in this game, as well as a lot of connections to other mythos stories, but the game is too short to really delve into each of them properly.  The narrative escalates too quickly and could easily be expanded to a 15 to 20 hour game to really flesh everything out.

Any music or interesting visuals fall flat when you've scoured and searched the same room five times over, getting more frustrated with each new pass through the area. _childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, there is no Tie option for recommendation, thus I must choose "No". Why so? _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the atmosphere. There are sooooo many excellent references to Lovecraft's mythos. From Dagon, Cthulhu, Nyarlathotep to Azathoth . It was a game that in my opinion is the most faithful  to the original source material and i appreciated that experience. Having said all that it was at times frustrating due to the glitches and game crashes. I had to play through the first 3rd of the game at least twice because the game would crash during a cut scene and I had to start over. Eventually I had to uninstall and then reinstall the game to get it to work.  Regardless of the game's flaws I still had an excellent time exploring the world the game developer created. _childDocuments_.review: I've bought this game upon release since the STEAM algorithm recommended it to me after playing several Mythos-style games. The trailer made it mostly seem like a walking simulator, similar more to Conarium than Call of Cthulhu, and as such I was very interested. Unfortunately the game disappoints in every aspect.Technical:At times choppy framerate and really bad low quality textures which sometimes are wrapped beyond the object size and stretch in bizarre or unreadable ways are weird in a game as small as this. Furthermore, the game doesn't pause when going into the options, the menus are barely readable, the inventory is a 3D-space that forces the game to rerender the environment once the player closes it and there's no meaning to it since nothing requires interaction with it. Finally, the options menu is extremely bare and almost unreadable since it hasn't got a shaded background and looks like some sort of bad steam cheapskate shovelware menu. Subtitles aren't very readable, presented in entire text blocks and similarly don't pause with the menu. Furthermore, the entire thing is full of bad english, missing or simply wrong spelling.Gameplay:The game throws the player into the role of, as becomes quickly clear, a sailor in search of what we learn is his daughter after the death of his wife. But no emotional connection is ever built up to this, or those two persons aside from two throwaway moments that last a few seconds at best. My emotional investment was basically nil. The game features a variety of simple puzzles relying on putting the right item at the right place or using an item on another item. All standard and okay, if a bit unintuitive. What isn't okay are the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrible chase sequences. First, only seemingly stunnable monsters, bad level design and the fact that the game doesn't telegraph this well makes them unbearable. Not to mention the Self-Breeder-Bossfight. If you played it you know which I mean, and if you don't, don't buy it for that. Basically there's a boss fight with infinite spawns and your gun is ♥♥♥♥, its unclear if the hits are registered, range is unknown and your character moves like an asthmatic 90-year old. Yikes. Also, the sound is extremely wacky, with voices being far too quiet while the music and ambient sounds are far too loud in comparison, even after being tuned down 90% to 33%.Finally, following in the vein of a lot of bad Mythos games, this game throws you into the face of Cthulhu, Dagon, Nyarlathothep and ...well, that's silly and BAD, especially once they start talking to you. This is cosmic horror done wrong on sooo many levels. Basically they look and act like silly monsters, more akin to Godzilla, than unknowable, alien entities to whom man is but dust. Basically the game is all "Show monsters, you scared now?". And...well, No, I'm not. With the story as weak as it is and the silly monsters, this simply isn't a good showing.2/10 stars, stay as far away as you can, even if you're a die-hard Cthulhu fan. Trust me, it's not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nicely created and put together environments, monster designs and animations for the most past, especially initially. Working out how to progress with trinkets and reading the demise of the many others stranded on the island was pretty good, it being a short game is fine and I also think the full price is right for it. I really wish it was a progression into madness however; A lot sadly just felt like the set pieces pulled out of love craft stories and just put into each area, monsters included. Having the initial landscape changing into horror or creeping in as you progress - Introducing the crystalised people, jittering heads / landscapes, having to put things back together in a pretty horrific room was interesting and so was the 2 final activation sequences with maybe one area as a completely grotesque point to a final build up before the ending would have been fantastic.  It would really help to give a sense of manipulation and question the sanity of the character with no final full story dump at the end. The monster chases, ease of killing them, jumping straight into one strange areas that all looked very similar to the next really broke this game and just made it frustrating all the way up to the end. I'm really sorry, the game is a huge amount of work especially for one dev and is an achievement in its own right. I will probably point friends and family that are really into lovecraft at it, but would have to point out how to progress quickly through certain points.

_childDocuments_.review: Little bit disappointed to be honest, the ending felt way too abrupt, is there going to be a sequel? also did the developer remove the hand to hand combat that was present in the demo when fighting those sea creatures but here those creatures weren't even seen other than in the picture you find.Overall I enjoyed this, would recommend this for hardcore Lovecraft fans like myself but for people who aren't I suggest waiting for a discount
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a way to not give this a neutral score, because i can see that it is trying so very hard.There are several good ideas here, but the execution is lacking. It is a cool visual trip, but that is all you are getting.Positives: * The visuals are nice.* The first part of your first play-through is mysterious and creepy, even with a few successful jumpscares.* The game is a fine whistle-stop tour of the lovecraftian mythos.Negatives:* It suffers badly from "walking-simulator-itis" Your movement speed is abysmally slow, especially in the first section. And in general the controls feel clunky.* There is zero replay value. Going back to fetch achievements that you missed the first time is a chore.* After you leave the island the eldritch suffers from over-exposure. There are still cool vistas, but it becomes a bit over the top.* The plot is practically irrelevant. It does not matter, you do not matter. Who are these people? A guy and his family and a big revelation, that bears little impact. There is a mystery, but the resolution is lacking.

I actually requested a refund it was such a disappointment.Visuals aren't bad, soundtrack is OK. It really is quite annoying and boring though....not a good combo.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, if you are a fan of Lovecraft, you must experience this game. But, on a sale.The art team is the saving grace of this experience, they nailed the weird, cosmic, surreal feeling and aesthetic that is needed when you're dealing with a genre like this. This is one of my favourite games visually in a very long time, perhaps ever. I cannot stress enough how incredible this game looks. It bumps up a average story with a fantastic musical soundtrack to something truly special. Unfortunately, that's where the pros end.I honestly would've preferred a straight walking simulator than what I got. Long stretches of corridors and land where I spent 15+ minutes wandering around figuring out where to go next. The level design is appalling at showing where I am needed next or where I can go, where you consistently hit invisible walls. This includes crucial story items that almost entirely blend into the environment at times. The "puzzles" scattered throughout these areas boil down to arbitrarily clicking or spinning things and interacting on an object that looks like scenery or a random set piece. These are coupled with enemy and chase sequences that include running in a straight line and shooting a couple times. Gameplay sections are bookended with dialogue that posses voice acting that is maybe good 50% of the time. Just to add, I can right click to bring up a "modify text" box on the pause menu. Really guys?Saying all this, the art team and lore 100% carry this experience, and at only a couple hours in length it is well worth your time (on a sale). Especially Lovecraft fans.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: As an HP Lovecraft fan, I really want to like this game more. The visuals are killer, the controls aren't bad (its survival horror, so things might be kind of rough), but late game is trash. I understand that some ambiguity is important for a Lovecraft game, but damn, gimme something to work with. The cavern areas had a killer atmosphere, but I couldn't make out where to go for ♥♥♥♥. I released Dagon and Chthulu, but both areas and the silly ass focus point things should have some sort of guide. That ♥♥♥♥ is surface level in regards to figuring out what to do next. Anyway, my game glitched and I stopped playing, but altogether I'd give this a 7/10. I like the atmosphere as a survival horror game, it just needs to have the bugs worked out and a little more guidance.

_childDocuments_.review: Very short, but visually stunning. if you enjoy Lovecraftian horror and need your fix, this game will please in some aspects but upset in others. like i mentioned, the art is beautiful, the idea is there, but some executions weren't 100%. in some places this even felt like a interactive art piece more than a game, but is all still very impressive in terms of being made by 1 person. some places i could see improving would be:-not making simple things locked until needed. not being able to jump till mid game is kind of an odd choice, but to each his own.-some things just seem to be added for the sake of it. im not 100% well versed in all of Lovecrafts pieces or lore, but the fleshy level just seemed out of place, as did the obelisk and orb at the beginning-no prompting for very important things. it tells me how to jump when needed, but when a fleshy monster trying to kill me starts coming at me, there is no prompt that i can now attack when i previously couldntoverall, for what it is, 7/10, like i said. this feels more like an interactable art exhibit, seeing as it only took 2 hours to complete.

_childDocuments_.review: A wasted potential and a mess of a game. The first portion of the game around "The Shore" is a walking simulator and a little bit slow but does provide a bit of a built up and I found quite enjoyable. But there are just some awful gameplay decisions. You get chased at various times and it's just bad. Then you get a pseudo weapon and just gets more (bad) combat focused.This doesn't know whether it wants to be narrative driven game, a puzzler or a shooter and it suffers from this lack of clarity. The puzzles are either incredibly easy or ridiculously poor. One puzzle has you matching patterned grey stones on grey plinths but one of the stones is missing. You can "find" it on the beach with all the other identically grey stones by scouring the beach one footstep at a time for a stone that is a very slightly bit greyer than the others.  Another room is full of 100+ heads and you have to walk around examining them all to find the "right one". No sense of achievement for doing either, they're just frustrating time wasters to block you from progressing the story.Some of the animations in the game are fine, others are just poor. Creatures slide up from  the (otherwise well animated water) like their in a pop up book that just grates with the rest of otherwise ok animation.The change of game style from walking sim to (bad) fps doesn't do it any favours. I got frustrated with that terrible combat and needless chases sections and despite being close to the end just couldn't bring myself to finish it. It's not a bad game by any means, but it's also not a good or even average game. On a scale of 1-10 (10 being the best) this would a 4/10
