_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this game, but not whole-heartedly.  It has some problems....it also has some really great aspects too.  The Shore is a Lovecraftian (boy, is it ever!) first person horror walking simulator with some light to medium combat (it's technically light, but it is difficult to get used to mechanically {for me anyway}, and very little of it is explained, so it's harder than it should be).Positives:-Graphics-  Bloody incredible!  Seriously, there is just some phenomenal creature modelling and environmental design/texturing, especially when it comes to depicting a wide assortment of Lovecraftian nasties ranging from Deep Ones to Nyarlothotep to Cthulhu himself and quite a few things in between.Meh:-Storyline/Writing-  Starts out strong but then just goes all over the bloody place and I'm not sure the pasta all sticks to the wall (if you know what I mean).  It tries to be coherent, but I can't help but think that English isn't the first language of the game-maker, and it really shows, not just for clumsy phraseology but for a meandering, not entire cohesive narrative.-Gameplay-  It's largely a walking simulator, with some definite failure states if you don't dodge some attacks or use the "weapon" to destroy the appropriate creatures at the appropriate time (or at least delay them long enough to get yourself closer to your goal....get used to running while shooting backwards).  So, it's sometimes press right to win, and other times a little bogged down in clumsy "shooting" mechanics.  Not awful, and only moderately detracts from enjoyment, but it's not exactly a 100% pleasurable experience either.To sum up, I am recommending this game because I love Lovecraftian horror/cosmic horror themes, and seeing the world brought to life was highly enjoyable (and some of those vistas......dayum!), but it is absolutely not without some flaws.  Caveat emptor and all that jazz.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about this game?  I like the Easter eggs from the Lovecraft stories (Colour out of Space, Dagon, etc).  The story seems nice and well within the genre.  Some of the puzzles can be frustrating and very little help is given which is fine; you shouldn't expect to be held by the hand in a game all the time.  It is very linear and there seems to be only a few achievements you can miss (chess game, secret ritual, coins).  The story needs more depth and choices.  There is so much more that could be added to this game and it seems a shame to be limited to only one path and one ending.  Overall buy it on sale or just watch a playthrough on youtube.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Hmmm....probably not the response the developers were hoping for, but there you go. Followed by ehhhhhhh??This is clearly meant to be an epic, mind-blowing take on H.P. Lovecrafts Cthulu mythology, with awe-inspiring scenes and tense game-play sequences. Whilst it does do a pretty good job visually, and is quite atmospheric, I don't think it succeeds with its narrative or the parts where its more action-packed.And that's a shame, as it does have some excellent design and fairly impressive technical prowess. There are some combat elements and chase sequences, but these fail to rack up tension and fear. You either just have to run away from an indestructible creature, or can shoot the enemy with an artefact that never drains out of power, making it somewhat redundant. If they had limited the energy of this device and you had to wait for it to recharge whilst avoiding enemies, then it could have been more frightening. Instead you can just keep blasting away and the creatures will quickly die. They still can't find that sweet spot between being making you feel powerless (like most games in the genre do) and giving the player some agency within the world.To be fair to the developers they're far from the only ones to bodge up these elements, and it's pretty rare for this type of game to actually succeed in being scary or involving. Often there's a lack of substance, and 'The Shore' is no different to all the other failed 'Amnesia' wannabes that include these simplistic challenges. I wouldn't say that Frictional (developers of Amnesia rebirth / SOMA etc) do anything massively different, but they do know how to squeeze out terror from these sequences in a way that the developers haven't managed here. The final nail in the games coffin is that I have no clue what the story is about, with it having some confusing elements introduced right at the end that don't make a whole lot of sense.Now, part of the Lovecraft mythos is that these entities are beyond the comprehension of mortals, but here it just seems that the author of the plot has invented some gibberish nonsense and then hand-waves it away with "who can explain the un-explainable?" In some ways this is pretty ambitious, and for the spectacle I would applaud them, but as a game, and a story....not so much.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Game is by no means a survival horror unlike some teens said in other reviews (Have they even played a survival horror lmao.), game is Dear Esther with blue tint all over and insane Lovecraftian visuals. Voice acting is insanely bad, story is just funny, game sometimes simply does not work at all (Sprint doesn't work and you have to just try again and again until game decides to work), however very solid performance and insanely beautiful Lovecraftian visuals. Get this game for the wow effect and disregard everything else i'd say, especially the voice acting at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: If you're intrigued by the premise and can find this game EXTREMELY cheap on a Steam sale, maybe give it a try. Definitely don't pay full price though, it's not worth it.Long version:Pros:-Engaging story/premise-Genuinely creepy and disorienting imagery in multiple places-Pretty graphicsCons:-Riddled with technical issues. A few hours of playing this game gave me more headaches than any 30+ hour game I've played all year. Fortunately these issues can be resolved pretty easily by quitting/restarting the game, though.-Bland puzzles.-A bit TOO pretty in some places. The underwater sequences look very nice, but they're not creepy. Fallout 4 had creepier underwater environments, and that one's not even a horror game.-Some parts of this game are just flat-out poorly designed. The monster chase sequences are more aggravating than tense or scary. They pretty much shatter the eerie atmosphere that the game has managed to build up to that point, and make the whole thing start to feel like a chore.-When you think of Lovecraft's work, do you think of artifact laser beams? No? Well, apparently the game devs did!It's too bad that so many aspects of this game were so poorly executed, because there's a fantastic idea here with the story and some of the visuals. Near the beginning of the game especially, it feels very otherworldly. The Shore does a better job than a lot of other titles at nailing scares and bizarre imagery that feel truly Lovecraftian. I wanted very badly to like this game. But sadly, despite all is has going for it, there are just too many issues with the design for me to recommend - at full price, anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoiyed this game depsite me not beeing a big fan of horror games. But my urge to play everthing Lovecraft and Cthulhu related was bigger than the "fear" of jumpscares.The Game itself is a rather short one (took me about 2.5 Hours) and some of the story elements aren't very clear as to what and why excactly this and that transpired. But in itself you understand the story the game wants to tell you.The Atmosphere in the different locations is great. I loved the other-worldly areas with all it's details and sounds. It really gave me the chills here and there.The Entities in the game a absolutly amazing. Without spoilers: I really didn't excpect so many of them ;) Although i sometimes didn't quite understand who is in allegiance with one another. The Enemy creatures are quite fair when it comes to the difficulty of the various encounters. Took me some tries with a few of them, but once you get their pattern and your goal it's absoulty doable.The Puzzles are mostly easy and obvious. there are some, that took me a while as they weren't very obvious but hidden in plain sight though. All in all they were pretty fun and really gave the player a feeling of beeing in control.Alltogether this game was really fun, but left me with some questions. But I recommened it to everyone, that likes Lovecraft and his Mythos.

The atmosphere is really good.On the other hand it's very slow ( it's a walking simulator and the running and jumping mechanics will be unlocked further in the game ) and it was a bit hard to keep up to reach the ending.THE DEVELOPER HAS A REALLY HIGH POTENTIAL, waiting to see some other game.

_childDocuments_.review: It starts out with the typical mystery and lore hunting of a Lovecraftian walking simulator. That was its charm. Then it spirals down into chase scenes (some you can fight back, some you cannot) while navigating dark tunnels where its easy to get stuck on a wall or object. Not fun at all. The visuals were great, but even the implementation of Lovecraft's various entities felt thrown together at random. No real consistency between each one that you meet. It sort of gets put together at the end but it felt empty. And yes, there are strange audio issues as some have mentioned. Best to have subtitles turned on.I got it on a really great sale so I'll give it a thumbs up. I'd definitely stay away from the VR version of this, considering how clunky this one is.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: The atmosphere and visuals are great, gameplaywise not so much.It's a walkin' sim which in my case is fine, I like to chill back a bit and listen/see a story unfold from time to time. The issues I have with the game are that there's really clunky 'combat' mixed in alongside invisible boundries that are set way too far away from your linear corridor path (you can climb onto rocks but no further then 30cm where it feels like you should be able to get over em, just set the invis wall nearer to the path then).There's a final 'boss' which you even get an achievement for which is laughable compared to some of the run and stun sections.I'd say watch a playthrough on youtube and forget about it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a few flaws but otherwise it was an interesting experience. There are a few puzzles and items you need collect which can be really frustrating. The world also has invisible borders which stops you from walking to places you thought you could reach which is also very irritating. The enemies are mostly annoying but they were actually not that bad, I liked it. The voice acting though, it was horrible, it sounds like someone is talking into a crappy mic and the voices themselves does not fit or are just too bland. The story was alright but everything just seemed like a mashup of different ideas, plus the fact that the cosmic horrors were portrayed in a very non-horror and non-powerful way which was disappointing. Overall, it was an alright experience but I definitely wouldn't recommend it unless you like Cthulu mythology and get this on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like a gorgeous portfolio piece more so than a completed game. Absolutely stunning visuals, creative ideas, and good voice acting, but the lack of clear direction or interaction, for completing objectives made me feel like I was walking in circles and stopped being interesting after about an hour.There wasn't really a personal satisfaction to any puzzles being completed. Maybe a purchase to support an indie dev but this isn't really game and shouldn't be charged or labeled as such. This is more of a showpiece of incredible creative talent.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRRequested a refund.Long(er) version.The start of the game shows potential with a nice atmosphere and interesting narrative. After about 30 minutes you get a laserbeam and everything goes down the drain. You have to solve some puzzles, which are literally just clicking on some artifacts (no brain required), or you're supposed to "run" through dungeons followed by some immortal monsters which you laserbeam until they stop so you can run in circles until an exit appears....rinse and repeat.The game would be way better without the laster/puzzle crap. Just a good vibed walking sim. But as is, it's just too broken and boring to even finish. And having read some other's comments...I am pretty much at the end. But no, not worth the time.

_childDocuments_.review: THE GOODThis is a VERY good H.P. Lovecraft Cosmic Horror game. There are MANY mindblowing experiences with . And I mean... MINDBLOWING up-close moments!One of my favorite aspects of this game, is that it isn't the typical... "You are a detective that needs to solve a murder, or take down a cult" type tropes, which you usually see in EVERY cosmic horror game out there. The creatures in the game are amazing, and if you are a "H.P. Lovecraft geek" like me, it will fulfill some fantasies that you won't see in other cosmic horror games. Make sure you investigate and read notes to get the best experience possible. :)THE BADWhile the game itself blows my mind and is my favorite cosmic horror game to date, it does come with some "quality test issues" hehe...You will frequently encounter floating assets (like the seagulls), and awkward invisible walls, to the point where it makes you wonder if the developer had anyone play test his game. And some textures look VERY low ress compared to other high ress, which makes you constantly go... "wow the game looks beautifu.... nevermind" hehe. ':D Essentially my point is that it feels like the last 10% effort wasn't put into the quality of the game and to fix obvious bugs.The water in the game has some weird visuals from time to time. As well as having a weird "line" at the bottom of the screen when the player stands in the water.The default audio in the game is extremely unbalanced. Voice acting is VERY low, and I recommend turning it up in the options.The voice acting of all characters are top notch! Except for , who is EXTREMELY ... and I really mean it... EXTREMELY bad compared to the rest of the characters. ':D I'm usually not very critical about voice acting, but this person stuck out like a sore thumb... It kinda felt like professional voice actors were hired for all the characters, except for this one character who might have been a "non-voice actor" the developer knew and did a favor for... The main menu and options look VERY "indie game"... Or "prototype'e".(Not a "bad", but just an observation) Screen recorders have trouble capturing the game.CONCLUSIONThis is a unique experience that ANY cosmic horror fans should play! While the game has some technical issues, they won't in any way outweigh the positives. :) Even though I might have written more "negatives" in this review hehe, it still is one of my favorite indie games of all time! :)

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game despite the negative reviews, and I was pleasantly surprised. The art and sound design in this game is at times very beautiful. The size of the level and the absence of a map means you will probably backtrack needlessly a few times, wasting some time. From what I can tell, the major grievances people have had with this game is that they'e missed a small item they need, and the game won't give you hints on what you missed. _childDocuments_.review: Dear Esther: Cultist Edition (AKA "Lovecraft Island")Now being serious. The Shore is a short walking simulator with astonishing setpieces and an unfortunate late game "gamification" in the form of shooting lasers to Eldritch abominations. The first moments in The titular "Shore" reminds both musically and tonally to "Dear Esther", hence the title joke, but the game quickly shifts its focus towards small sets of Lovecraftian references that will make fans point to the screen as if they were DiCaprio in "Once upon a time". This game is made with love towards HPL and his works and it shows.However, the story is a bit confuse, even if only acts as a vehicle to jump from setpiece to setpiece dedicated to each one of the most popular Cthulhu Mythos, especially in the later part. Don't be worried though, as each of those setpieces is done with astounding quality both in graphic and sound design, so you will feel like you are playing a sort of "Greatest Hits" of Lovecraftian aesthetic.I'm a big sucker for Walking Simulators and Cthulhu games, so this is a "must" for fans of both genres. And special regards towards its small and dedicated team.Pros:- One of the best, if not THE best Sound design in Lovecraftian games- "Beautiful" and unnerving scenarios and situations- Full of Lovecraft Mythos references- Smart team doing great stuff!Cons:- Too much dependence on a gamifying late-game aspect (chases and "shooting") that negates the possibility to take some sections slowly and soak in the environments.9/10. Straight to my "Yog-Sotothery" Steam folder, which only has the best of the best in Lovecraftian games.

_childDocuments_.review: It was alright. Voice acting was kind of a miss, with everyone but the main character having an eastern European accent and, if I'm honest, not the best delivery at times.Game feels pretty strong at the start but you're quickly thrown into things and it starts to feel like the game is rushing it. You see so much and go through so much before you know it.there's fan service all around the beginning area that have no point, resulting in them feeling like red herrings.what little combat there is, feels meh. No fear from them or anything. The boss fight was a joke.There's little bugs here and there. A body you need not appearing, a whale with no collision in it's tail, a LOT of spots you can crouch next to and look through the map, losing control after alt+tabbing. Tab freezes the game for a couple seconds for no apparent reason.Some puzzles are a little too confusing. Not in a challenging way. But in a "♥♥♥♥ it, I'll look it up" way. Like, how was I supposed to know I needed to look at the EYE, not the whole body until the cursor changed?It's alright for ten bucks but I would be hard pressed to recommend for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall "The Shore" is a pretty good cosmic horror game with an excellent soundtrack and tons of awesome Lovecraftian references and aesthetics which are really brought to life with incredible detail. The setting and scenery is fantastic and dimly vibrant with lots to look at and inspect as you slowly descend into insanity in a typical Lovecraft fashion. Story wise, it is basic yet incomprehensible at the same time. Many appearances and themes leave you confused and inquisitive as to what has happened, what you are witnessing, what you have witnessed and what is real and what is not real. My only gripe with the game is the combat, the only reason it is tense is due to how irritating it is. I would have much preferred more complicated and in depth puzzles instead of tedious combat scenes which just consist of beings chasing you and outrunning you while you try and find the exit, barely getting the chance to fight back. Most of the time you can outrun certain enemies, but it is just boring. It isn't a very long game and you can easily get all the achievements and complete it in a few hours or less. Definitely a good Sunday afternoon game as you don't need to apply yourself too much as most of first half of the game is just exploring. As for whether or not it is worth the price... On one hand I would say yes because the creator has done a fantastic job making the game and deserves the support. Perhaps he will eventually create a longer eldritch horror game with more puzzles and more story, as I didn't find myself too invested in the main character. So on the other hand I would say it is more worth the sale price as the combat is tedious, the voice acting is average and the character isn't very interesting.But, credit where credit is due. I thoroughly enjoyed the game

The creatures you'll encounter are chillingly unique, and every corner hides something that will make you question your own sanity. Whether you're exploring abandoned ruins or facing off against horrific entities, the game keeps you on edge while captivating you with its dark, atmospheric world. 🌒🖤If you're a fan of psychological horror with a gripping narrative and mysterious lore, The Shore is a must-play. _childDocuments_.review: I love this game, and it's coming to VR. This is a cosmic horror Lovecraft inspired walking simulator. TL;DR - it's not *that* short, per some of the more sensible reviews. I don't know if it's a $25 game, but wishlist it and when it's 50% off do NOT hesitate. This is one of the most fun and (weird to say) relaxing games for me in a long time. During the pandemic, horror survival has helped me realize it can always get worse. =)If you are into typical horror survival, this may be too slow or too obscure for you. This won't make a lot of sense, and it's not a AAA style game... this is made by a dedicated, thoughtful, passionate single developer, not some studio, about a universe of cosmic and body horror, which isn't your typical blood and guts torture porn. The concept is more metaphysical and existential. Think a version of Myst with endless philosophical dread.If you get Cosmic Lovecraftian comment, you're going to see so many delightful literary Easter eggs that you will giggle with glee, while being both scared, awed, and amazed by the game.This single dev put his heart and soul into a game, and most importantly after the release is constantly updating it with both patches and new content. I'd seen some of the kneejerj immediate launch gripes that are coloring the aggregate review score.... and it's nonsense. Look at the trend in reviews over time. What's important is the guy cares, seems that he'll keep patching, and that's enough for me. He keeps saying VR will come, and that will be sublime.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright so let me preface this by saying I have not finished the game. But, I want to review this because I have strong opinions on it and I think the game has great potential. (Also note I got this for free in the lenovo giveaway)pros: 1.) Generation of eerie environments and tones2.) Cool creatures and fun chase scenes3.) Good soundtrack4.) The homage to Lovecraft is truly doing him justice5.) Gorgeous scenerycons: 1.) I think the game is a bit hard to follow storywise. While that may be a goal, it takes away from my emotional engagement. While that may have been more Lovecraftian to be a bit mysterious and have the plot flesh out as it goes, I think there's a balance that needs to be struck. On this note, a stronger idea of what your objective is would be helpful. Doesn't have to be overt.2.) The enemies' AI is rather simplistic. 3.) A lot of typos can be found in notes and in dialogue. This seems minor, but it shows a lack of proofreading.4.) Collision can be wonky. It can be easy to get yourself trapped in weird places. 5.) You can wander very far from the objective. In a game where the objective is kind of obscure and you have to really explore the environment, this can be an annoyance when I end up very far away.I find it very hard to recommend this game, it truly deserves to be in early access. But it has such potential to be a good game. I really think this game deserves to have some more work put into it because the creators obviously put a lot of heart into it. So I'd say a solid B- grade, and a recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: "The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of repeating a horrible monster chase sequence"I had this game on my wishlist since I first heard about it last year. The game looks very beautiful, the environment toward the beginning of the game reminds me of Dear Esther, some nice screenshot-worthy moments. There are some graphical glitches like the water effects and being able to stick your head through objects, and some of the invisible walls are pretty obtrusive.The first third of the game starts promising with a nicely designed, foggy shoreline surrounding a lighthouse, examining various curios and discovering details about the islands' previous inhabitants. This segment is semi-open, while there are invisible walls and a clear order of completion, you are really walking between connecting locations. There is one teleport segment early on, but you aren't locked out of the previous, you can enter and return as often as you want, this was not a sign of things to come.My enjoyment of the gamed dropped immediately upon receiving "the artifact", your weapon in the game. What follows is a maddeningly repetitive series of teleporting from room to room. From this point on in the game there is no backtracking, no returning to the lighthouse, you actually see very little of the eponymous "Shore" after this.There are no complicated puzzles in this game, just some poorly communicated tasks that really only involve pressing interact on things. I know this is pretty much a mainstay for story driven walking sims but I expected something trickier. You perform a simple task in a linear room, and then teleport to the next room. You run from a hideous monster in a room. The monsters. The monsters are fast and you only take a few hits before dying and reloading, but you can stun them by shooting the artifact laser beam at them. I spent the majority of these segments running backwards through the winding monster rooms, because the stun I mentioned does not last long enough for you to take the beam off them, and sometimes you have to juggle multiple enemies. This isn't how a game should be played, it's a good thing the environments during these sequences are super bland, purple flesh rooms or black oil rooms, I didn't feel like I missed out on seeing anything.The story tries to cram in as many mythos deities as possible. Though I admit, it is always fun to see references to Lovecraft stories in games; in the form of artifacts, literature, engravings on coins, symbols painted on walls, or a curious meteorite. It is not so great seeing Dagon screech like Godzilla and then hitch a ride on a monolith, or Cthulhu give a super-villain monologue about destroying the world. A few more fan-favorite Outer Gods are also named. It's just too much, the plot tries to fit them in but it was unclear what purpose they served. Perhaps I would understand better after another play-though. I don't think I will play this game a second time to find out why.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly haunting and ethereal depiction of the Cthulhu mythos.It looks incredible, that's for sure. But let's take a second to talk about the soundtrack. Holy heck, is it gorgeous. It's a mix of perfectly-timed instances of unnerving, thoughtful, and triumphant music. And it's all so very well done.For fans of cosmic horror, or simply fans of story-driven puzzle/adventure games, this is very high up there.Have a double feature night and play this along with Dagon for a wonderfully Lovecraftian evening.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished the game yet, but from what I've seen so far it's definitely an experience worth trying out. If you're a fan of H.P. Lovecraft and his mythos, this game will take you on a journey through some of the more unnerving aspects of Lovecraft's brand of cosmic horror, and will leave you feeling helpless and confused in the best of ways; as one should when they have caught the countless ever-watching eyes of an Outer God. _childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore is an atmospheric sojourn into the depths of Lovecraftian horror, replete with wonderfully-crafted grotesque art, replete with writhing tentacles, incomprehensible entities of cyclopean proportions and sights to drive you to the edge of madness and beyond.  With a plot drawn directly from the works of H.P. Lovecraft himself, and featuring a tour-de-force of Cthulhu Mythos entities, The Shore is a beautifully made experience, albeit a briefly one.  I ran through it in just under 3 hours, similar to watching certain movies.  While it was heavy on the atmosphere and grotesque beauty, it was light on the gameplay.  If you're looking for intricate systems and engaging combat, look elsewhere.  If you want a lengthy game that will occupy you for weeks and months to come, don't play The Shore.  But if you're fan of the Cthulhu Mythos and want to immerse yourself in a lovely piece of artwork, give this one a try.  Especially if it's on sale, it's spectacle alone is worth the small price it has.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: It's essentially a walking simulator with minor FPS mechanics, but it's a really touching love letter to everything Lovecraft, chock full of references and nods to his writing, and probably the most bespoke deep dive into the mythos I've seen in games. A lot of things may be similar, but this felt much more open and passionate where other games lazily borrow from the man's visuals without understanding his worldview.With that said, the plot feels a lot like fan fiction, with more focus on fantastical drama than sanity-bending horror, and the ending didn't make any sense.Buy the game for the experience of the mythos, not for gameplay or story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: [waiting for the hotfix to see if i refund or not.]as of yet the games performance is mediocre and in addition to the sadly poor optimization suffers from progress-blocking bugs that require constant restarts of segments in the hope that the game logic maybe works the next time around. (portals not appearing, getting stuck on terrain, etc.)The Shore has great atmosphere, looks mostly amazing and the sound stresses the tone of the landscape and hightens the mood in a fitting manner. it offers quite some nice amount of fanservice. a multitude of references and hints to all lovecraftian and eldritch horror things imaginable. BUT maybe keep it at hints!? once again another game showcases knowledge of the lore / stories of the lovecraftian cthulhu- mythos, but fails to understand what makes cosmic horror so effective: the fear of the unknown. throwing tentacle-monsters at players is just not scary - even if the monster-models and sounds are nice and all that. it had me joyfully explore the titual shoreline trying to figure what is happening and wanting to find every tiny detail.but at some point i changed in pacing and gameplay. even hint-markers popping up all of a sudden on items from meters away, instead of letting me find stuff. INCONSISTENT is the best way to describe it.the controls feel a tad off and the lack of video-settings makes optimisation real troublesome.the poor translations and missing dialogue and subtitles do harm the otherwise oppressive atmosphere that the game builds up. a real shame.so with a heavy heart i can NOT recommend this game for the asking price. i really, really wanted to love this and enjoyed the first hour immensely, but it falls apart once it goes from confusing explorative walking simulator to combat and flight from monsters. show less and leave more to our imagination please.IF you are a sucker for everything close to eldritch horror and lovecraftian you may enjoy it - but be warned. maybe wait for a discount/sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The heavy atmosphere and constant sense of dread is what drew me in the most. It really feels like you are walking through a nightmare that you can't wake up from. The visuals are truly amazing with an awesome sense of scale, and many of the terrifying entities look like they shambled right out from the pages of an H.P. Lovecraft's bestiary. That said I enjoyed the survival horror aspect of the first half of the game much more than zapping away most creatures with the Artifact in the second half--that got a bit repetitive and lessened that delicious sense of impending doom I felt earlier. I see a lot of reviewers going on about how it's too short, but I think it's just as long as it needs to be. I like Shorter games that are able to tell a full story and take only two or three sittings to complete. I got it when it was 50% off and after playing it think it actually is worth the full price, especially considering this was a labor of love for just one developer!

_childDocuments_.review: Many people that will play this title may not understand the purpose of design. As a fan of Lovecraft, I found this to be a perfect title for me. _childDocuments_.review: Early Impression of the ShoreThe good-Amazing environmental art.Well done world assets that pulls a player in visually.Clearly understands the core stories of Lovecraft.The bad- The Cthulhu Mythos is too heavy handed right off the bat. As a player you seemingly stumble around onto horrible things but it happens way to fast and too early and all at once.Lack of game intro- The game just loads, no information to build up to the moment waking up on the shore.The music is constant and does not allow for moments between the 'scare'. No matter if you are experiencing a madness inducing horror or just standing on the beach, the music does not allow for pauses in the audio tension. The protagonist has only one emotion and that seems of boredom. They comment on the strangest things as if they are just another day for a fisherman, but experiencing any form of horror they seem to never actually comment on it.Too much of a good thing- The game so far appears to try and draw from every example of the mythos at once without really giving the player time to delve into the mysteries of any of them. Some of the mythos moments do not seem to have a reason other than an easter egg.Final verdict- For 10$ it's a fun game so far, but it needs some better audio, dialogue and storytelling tweaks to make it truly worthy of a Mythos tale.

_childDocuments_.review: Silence.Real  or not.You don`t know.Standing on a Shore, it feels so surreal.But wait, it is not as silence as it seems.Yes, there is something … around?Welcome to THE SHORE.You are Andrew and you are stranded.Somewhere.Your Daughter is missing and all you can see are wrecks and a Lighthouse in the Distance.It is time to find your daughter, but it is also time to find out whats going on in this Place.But be carefull … it is not safe out there.At first i thought THE SHORE is a pure Walking Simulator. It is not.There are also „Combat Sequences“. Yes, you can die. But the Monster Design is really, really great.All the Graphics are really amazing and i also like the Sound and the Voice Acting.The Atmosphere is really unique. It is not also like that you know that you are alone, you can really FEEL that you are alone. That gave me Goosebumps.I love the Lovecraftian Material and it seems that there is very much from it inside. I recognized much familar Content from what i have read in the Past.The Dev put very much love and Details into this Game. That is something you feel in each Corner of it. It is exciting to explore and to find out more but sometimes it feels a little bit confusing, maybe i´m not deep enough into Lovecrafts Stuff.The Game Mechanics are simpel. Normal Walking and Running Options and also examing/taking Items, at least the Inventory, which looks optically really nice. A side laying Boat, where all your items are clearly arranged.  Nice done.Well, the Running could be a little bit faster, it feels more like fast walking, then Running and believe me you WILL need the Running Option very desperatly (sometimes).That goes also for the exploring. Sometimes it can be a little bit chewy to walk/run around, trying to find out how it can be going on.By the Way, here is a nice Vid to the Game from Ajay. Enjoy.So, in the End we have a really nice Game with an amazing Atmosphere, but it is special. This is not for everyone. Lovecraft Fans will like it, they get very much, maybe too much from it.  It is also a little bit short, but i love THE SHORE.A big thanks to the Developer who dropped me into this Lovecraftian World, i really enjoyed it.Thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: This game starts as a fairly linear experience building tension through familiar images of a shore and lighthouse, but with anomalies scattered about to show you are far from any place welcoming. It's eerie, has a great grasp on immensity, looks beautiful despite some graphical glitches, and really compels you go further into the lingering madness.Then the rest of the game happens. Once I got a glorified gun and had to run from monsters while shooting them, I wondered why this needed to be included. The environments become too samey and enemies are not disturbing to me, merely annoying. Horrific creatures from a completely alien place shouldn't be annoying, they should be intimidating. Also your daughter is missing. I forgot about that. In fact, I think the player character does too unless reminded. Then the puzzles become trial and error. Sometimes you're accidentally hitting the wrong thing or you're not noticing that an item goes onto a very particular place. It slows things down too much when five minutes ago you were running and gunning. You have to ease into different mechanics so the game is cohesive and engaging. And while interpreting the ending a certain way may explain why the Great Old Ones are so personable to you, I really disliked how the player character was relied upon too much to help these gods. I think witnessing a distant force far more powerful than yourself is naturally demoralizing. Being old chums with one is less world-defying. Despite these things, I still loved the beginning of the game. I mean, I liked it enough that I got all the achievements to experience more lore. The game after the island and underwater section is simply too phoned in and hurried. New room, outrun enemy, new room, solve puzzle, new room, outrun enemy, etc. The game looks excellent when it's not just black tentacle, fleshy room stuff, but it doesn't make the gameplay any better. I'm on the fence about it, honestly. But since these reviews are black and white with no grey, I'd say recommended while on sale. This game does well, but it seems like the developer wanted to put too much into their first game and it became cluttered. If you read this, Ares Dragonis, subtlety, simplicity, and brevity can be very powerful when used right. I look forward to your next game.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is visually atmospheric and appealing, the game feels pieced together from a variety of Lovecraftian influences without depth. The parts of a good game are there, they are just not put together in a way to make an effective final product.I would like to see a more cohesive game from this game designer but I can't recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: "You, Andrew, you're my favorite."Oh, Andrew. However, while I feel for him and his journey, I won't lie: it's brilliant. This game manages to nail the ambient and unknown dread and awe that comes with Lovecraftian works. While short, this game was thoroughly enjoyable and I highly recommend it to anyone even slightly interested in cosmic horror. The journey you take brings with it interesting and jaw-dropping sights and curiosities. While this game was clearly crafted with passion, there are a few minor bumps in the road such as grammatical errors or object collision, but these are easily ignored in favor of the overall game. Really, my only complaint was the combat. It felt kind of tacked on as a way to avoid the game being solely a walking simulator, but it wasn't the worst, just a bit boring after a while. However, I'm sure this was improved upon in other releases. Besides, the unique and interesting enemy variety and monster designs more than make up for it. This game deserves nothing less than a strong 9/10.Ares Dragonis, I look forward to more from you! Now onto Eresys..

_childDocuments_.review: The only thing The Shore is good for is getting a few visually impressive screenshots of lovecraftian monsters. The rest of it is such a hodgepodge of half-baked ideas that it fails to do any one thing well. I really took my time to look at every little detail, but you could easily finish this game in under 90 minutes. If you want to see a Lovecraftian Walking Sim done well, go play Conarium. That, at least knows to stick with Elder Things and their successors rather than trying to cram in every single thing they can.  So what is this anyway? You are Andrew, a sailor whose voice sounds like he's recording in a wind tunnel. You wash up on the shore of an island full of shipwrecks and you do standard walking simulator stuff. Problem is none of that leads anywhere. Moreover, Andrew is not well characterized because the game only mentions his daughter in the first 10 minutes and then doesn't bring her up again until the finale. The first half of the adventure is about learning the fate of the previous crew who washed ashore on the island and also searching for your missing daughter. Then a switch flips and instead of telling a story, The Shore just wants you to look at all the Lovecraftian assets they modeled, including...  not even to mention the *really* crazy stuff like . They modeled as many things as they could think of without regard to how they fit into the story. The devs behind The Shore fundamentally misunderstand what Lovecraftian horror is about, which means this could never be a good game. Call of Cthulhu isn't about a big tentacle faced monster attacking a boat. It's about following the clues following mass hysteria, finding a cult, realizing that cult is truly ancient and known by every civilization, and discovering an impossible city whose very nature calls into question humanity's role as the dominant life on earth.In the Shore, Cthulhu is a big scary monster that stands around and laughs at you. He, a great old one the size of a skyscrape, takes the time to speak to you directly. Then he walks away, his monstrous 100ft tall butt swaying with each step. It's laughable. It fails to be scary. And it's why The Shore fails at even it's most basic objectives.  There's no thematic consistency here. There is a box of Lovecraft toys and monster assets and the devs want their playset to use all of them -- so you get the color out of space, cthulhu, elder things, the trapezohedron, the dreamscape, shoggoths, and EVERYTHING else you can think of. They didn't care to write a single story, so they just picked all of them. And it doesn't work. They run out of things for you to do on the titular Shore after about 30 minutes and the rest of the adventure is runnning through an HR-Giger inspired dreamscape solving really minor puzzles and shooting a laser gun at Shubniggurath. The moment you cross over to the dreamscape is where things get bad because at that moment they give up on trying to tell a single story. You start teleporting around between rooms made of meat and the beach again, but it's unclear how or how much of it is real. You're not some man who is peeling back the veil of reality, the old ones are just teleporting you around the planes of existence so you can run errands for them -- and that's not even a joke. It is thematically and narratively broken. One minute you're walking in a cave looking at cultist symbols and seconds later you're running for your life from a giant monster in a womb level. These levels are boring an lack internal consistency. The HR Giger rooms are either running from a monster in a big maze without any lighting direction or solving puzzles in small circular rooms with no doors. None of these things feel like they're progressing the story or furthering your goal of running errands for these gods; they feel like time sinks to pad out the already weak runtime. Finally, there are technical issues. Respectfully, The Shore runs like crap. My computer can play DOOM Eternal at maximum graphics but it chugs and struggles when I move the mouse in this game. It's terrible. The sound design is tonally mismatched (often using techno sound effects in an effort to imitate Annihilation (2018) and the mixing is unbalanced such that the roar of a giant monster is barely heard over music. Long story short, I'll save you some money and about 90 minutes of your time. The actual story is that .

_childDocuments_.review: Reading a review is not enough? Want to see some footage? Check the link and watch some game footage for yourself and decide if this game is worth your time:The Shore is a running simulator with most of the mandatory Lovecraft Creatures (the old ones) and a protagonist who will not die automatically by looking at them.This is the first game developed by Ares Dragonis who is entering the world of Steam with this game.Stranded hm? Hope your mind is strong for the world you are about to enter my Friend.Lovecraft theme, Why? Why me? My Issue with Love Craft? I played the Call of Cthulhu pen and paper for more than 10 years. They say you either love or hate it, I feared it and still do.You start as a guy who searches for his daughter stranded on an Isle. The Game itself is good at creating an oppressive atmosphere with the visuals and the sound. The big part in this game are that you are an actual immune sentient being and the game allows you to see one of the Old ones like Shoggoth or Dagon, even old Cthulhu. And this is the best and the worst part in one. Yes I feared it when I had to run into a giant mouth underwater and run away from a monster, no it was not scary rather more frustrating due to the lack of knowledge where to go and not much time to run away from the beholder. The runaway segments are the weakest part in this game, but the strong ones are the creatures. The Living monolith? It's there, looks a bit clumsy, let me not get to detailed to the Monsters. They are there, and they are horrifying, it's to bad it's too bright in the game. The horror is starts once you get in the darker spots and meet the beholder or the guy who tries to eat you and the level you are in. Its great and its fun to see these sizes. The End has a great twist, two bad besides the parts where you face the Monsters and watching Dagon ride the monolith, the game is lacking content. It is a straight forward game, and you get in to great and big levels, but why are you here for? You are here for to sink into the madness of the world and this happens to less, your character is so strong bond to his daughter he cares for nobody else. _childDocuments_.review: Putting aside the clunky mechanics and awkward movement, this game is incredible. Reminiscent of old explorer games such as Myst or Riven, it feels more like an art project than a game, and offers beautifully designed assets, a rich and compelling narrative, and an environment and atmosphere that rivals that of AAA games. I remember after first playing, I had to sit down for an hour and just process everything I had experienced - it remains to this day the only game that has had that profound of an effect on me. I find myself wishing to play it again for the first time, to feel that unparalleled and unique Lovecraftian atmosphere. Almost every minute of the 3 hours it took to complete was interesting in some way, which for a heavily visual-focused game is quite impressive. My only complaint is that I found some of the puzzles to be frustratingly unintuitive - having to google walkthroughs on some sections, but overall it is a masterpiece of environment art, accompanied with a beautifully written story.

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore is a somewhat short, 2-3 hour, Lovecraftian horror title that straddles a line between being a walking simulator and casual survival game. You play as a fisherman named Andrew, who finds himself washed ashore on a strange island filled with cosmic horrors and eldritch relics after his boat capsizes. You start out exploring this shore, and learning about the island's prior inhabitants, before falling down the void of the Elder Gods.First and foremost, this game has some amazing visual aesthetics. The graphics are absolutely cream of the crop, although the first half of the campaign is filled with stuttering issues even after turning on an option to increase texture cache size. These stuttering issues seem to be due to texture loading and not actual FPS optimization, as the FPS stays at a solid 60 the entire time. The sound design also beautifully captures and instills emotions such as a foreboding sense of dread, omnipresent feelings of insanity, and a sense that everything around you is much bigger and greater than your inconsequential existence. The further you continue into the story, the smaller and more insignificant you feel, as the Elder Gods make themselves and their powers known. If there's one thing this game does well, is that it brings to life H.P. Lovecraft's visions of massive cosmic entities that control not only our very existence, but the universe itself.While The Shore has phenomenal visual and audio design, it's the gameplay that will make-or-break this experience for all players; you'll either love it, or hate it. At around the halfway point of the playthrough, the entire game shifts its focus from walking simulator to somewhat survival horror, wherein you'll be fending off eldritch monsters with an artifact that sends out a lazer-beam stream. These abominations are invincible and the beam merely stuns them and slows them down, which grants you a very minimal amount of time to run ahead and find an exit before having to turn around and stun them again. Sandwiched between these encounters you'll be solving some novel, but objectively mundane, puzzles that require little to no thought to complete.By the end of The Shore you'll feel as though you started and finished two entirely different games. It's as though the developer changed his mind on exactly what type of game he wanted to create, and did a complete 180 around the halfway point. This isn't always a bad thing to do, and in most cases it prevents a game from becoming repetitive and stale, but unfortunately in doing this the developer actually introduced repetition and predictability. Taking out the frustrating fighting mechanics and instead keeping this title a simple walking simulator would've fared better by having players focusing more on the story and visuals, rather than an annoying gameplay mechanic that was implemented poorly. It's really a shame, as Ares Dragonis really captured the pure essence of H.P. Lovecraft's brilliant tales of cosmic horror. This one isn't going to be for everyone, and while it didn't quite hit the spot for me, if you can see through the poorly crafted combat and drab puzzles, you may enjoy it more.The Horror Network  |  Click for Gore

_childDocuments_.review: A stricken Arthur awakens to sand, sea, and shipwreck. Weathered igneous formations loom formidably over fields of augite pebbles that lurch down to the lapping tongue of dark water’s edge. A phantasmal phalanx of dense, twisted palm emerges from wistful mist and hectors from higher inland ground, menacingly mocking both freedom of movement and clarity of perception. A memento, a clear memory of a dear moment with young daughter Ellie, stands in flagrant dissimilitude to the unimaginable horrors ahead. Dearest readers, I bid you a solemn welcome to The Shore; leave now… if you can.Still here? How unfortunate.Steel your hearts then, readers, and humble your mere human ego and prepare to crawl as though ants among a veritable who’s who of the caliginous Lovecraftian pantheon, where friends are few and self-serving, and foes are immense and unstoppable.And butt-ugly. Lovecraft=off. BeatYourHeadIn=on!The Shore is a faithful delve into the beloved mythos. It adheres to the general Lovecraft vibe, from the towering immortals and gods, to the unwholesome bestial talismans honed with skill beyond that of human craftsmanship, and including the incredulous characters who initially and foolishly dismiss the supernatural as observed by their own eyes with deficient secular explanations, such as psychosis, madness, and somnambulism; it’s all here. Even the usual binary of outcomes for most Lovecraft protagonists who have seen too much—either a self-euthanization as an escape from the un-cope-able or a shockingly willing embrace of dark forces beyond the knowable—both seem to be in play as possible conclusions right up until the closing action. No spoilers, though, as to which way this episode turns.As a story driven walking-simulator, The Shore exhibits a potent—though not flawless—execution. Puzzles of various sorts act as barriers to plot progress; the majority are simple to solve, with a few challenging ones sprinkled about to spool up your think-noodle. The puzzles themselves are done well. Solving them indeed lends a sense of accomplishment, and they and their outcomes tie into the plot in a sensible fashion. Sensible for Lovecraft, that is; the man dreamed beyond three dimensions and five senses, after all. The progression of the story is at all times kept in sharp focus, which is fine as it is a good story, but I feel that the linear nature of the journey along the beaches represents a missed opportunity and, in my opinion, contributes to the short time in which the game is completed.Thus, the game falls somewhat short in the exploration aspect due to the extensive use of invisible walls to corral you onto the linear path set forth by the developer. This should have been addressed properly by the use of blocking terrain features such as higher rock bluffs and dense jungle thicket, and/or some sort of feedback that insinuates something like, say, dark energies that are preventing the player from traversing the open areas. It was a little frustrating to climb boulders and see places beyond only to be obstructed from further exploration by a poorly placed invisible wall. A tough pill to swallow, indeed. Even something like a dense mist with a spooky ambiance that induces such a level of fear as to cause Arthur to utter a verbal refusal to enter it would have been more appropriate. Regrettably, I’m left wondering what a more open exploration of the island setting would have played like.What the game absolutely nails is the hair-raising and unsettling experience of a Lovecraft story. I felt genuine dread of and reluctance to witness the malevolence that the plot on several occasions built up prior to the reveal. Due to active participation in the story via the gaming medium, one’s sense of fear and nerve-tingles is heightened beyond that delivered by a reading. The Shore serves as another example of how videogaming has cemented itself as a worthy component in the history of storytelling.However, I hold that reading is still superior for this purpose, as there are details in Lovecraft’s works which I am convinced cannot be rendered by 3D modelling. Passages that hint of infernal interdimensional travel like “…one night a mighty gulf was bridged, and the dream-haunted skies swelled down to the lonely watcher’s window to merge with the close air of his room…” just cannot be visualized outside of the minds’ eye. High five to all my bookworms out there!Another rock solid segment of The Shore is its soundtrack. The music shifts from hopeful but subdued operatic scores, to musical denials of certain doom that hang over scenes of terror frozen in time like a ghostly echo of forgotten trauma, to the sinister ambiance of a technological environment produced by wholly alien industry, and swelling to impactful crescendos during scenes when monumental, awe-inspiring power has been unleashed, and does so with appropriate timing. The audio is tied to the visuals in a sincere and effective manner so that the sum of the two is greater than the parts alone. The game absolutely thrives on this photo-phonic unity.So, while not being a match for the exemplary exploration gameplay of The Solus Project—an excellent walking simulator horror game made without invisible walls by a similarly sized indie developer—The Shore more than holds its own as a delivery of an immersive atmosphere. Since the price of setting foot on The Shore is one half of the cost to crash land on more fleshed out creepy-island-to-cry-oneself-to-sleep-on of The Solus Project, it means that both games are on equal footing by my reckoning. In conclusion, there is no need to wait for a sale for this game, it is more than worth the full price of admission, even though it is a little shorter than it should be. An absolute must play for fans of H.P. Lovecraft.Helpful review?

_childDocuments_.review: This game has gorgeous visuals and interesting non linear writing in the form of notes in a bottle that one finds while exploring the world, it is well put together, no bugs or glitches that I remember (Apart from the game not responding when trying to start a new game from the pause menu).Sadly that's where the positives end for me, as a story there is not much to take home, it feels more like an "H.P. Lovecraft Bingo'' than anything else, the gameplay is not innovative, I understand that not every game has to innovate, but even as a walking sim it felt really lackluster, I'm a really big fan of non linear storytelling, especially if it's in form of collectibles scattered around the game’s world, but in most cases this collectibles will be nowhere to be found until you enter one specific area that has 3 of them one next to the other, it really takes me out of the whole "explore to find clues" idea that a Lovecraftian inspired walking sim should heavily use to its advantage, the voice acting was fine until the end where some exposition is being given by a woman and you can barely hear what she is saying.I did actually enjoy this game, even if it was because I spent more time taking pictures than actually playing it, but I wouldn't really recommend it, that being said, I'm interested on what the future holds with our developer.We will watch your career with great interest!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has unparalleled art direction, fantastic atmosphere and outstanding music. Constantly eerie and odd, the game is worth playing for its aesthetic alone. Gameplay-wise, the first chunk of the game is a walking sim, but after a point you start interacting more directly with the enviroment; solving puzzles and escaping monsters. It fits the tone of the game nicely. The one big negative imo is the writing, and I mean REALLY negative. It's like bad fanfiction. The villains (yes, "villains") are so direct and banal in their manner, methods, and goals that they come across more as humans with superpowers than unfathomable beings from beyond the stars. There's no reason a star god should *need* a human's help to change things, and there's absolutely no room in proper cosmic horror for a sentence like "Your strong will can influence Azathoth's dream."The good greatly outweighs the bad though, so it's a high recommend from me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Though I enjoyed The Shore for what it was, I feel odd recommending it because if there's a chance that my review will tip you over the edge into buying the game...well...you just might want to show up to my house wearing a pair of steel-toed boots and repeatedly kick me in the groin.  As I'm wincing on the ground and telling you that you fight like a cheap little hussy, I'll still stand by liking The Shore while you get even cheaper and beat me with a hockey stick for not backing down.  This is an odd slice of Lovecraft that has you exploring an island as fisherman Andrew who happens to be on the hunt for his lost daughter Ellie.  Things start out as an ethereal point n' click style of adventure which doesn't really prepare you for the fact that jarringly and quicker than expected you'll be running from fishy sons of swordfishes and later even gaining a magical weapon that becomes your proxy to fight off even uglier monstrosities.  First things first, The Shore looks absolutely phenomenal for an indie and it sounds great too.  The screenshots don't really tell any lies.  The island itself is gorgeous and foreboding to explore as you solve puzzles, search an abandoned lighthouse, find notes in bottles, traverse to harder to reach places that reveal all manner of Lovecraft callbacks/collectibles and do the usual adventure/horror stuff.  It's somewhat standard issue but the allure of the location that you are exploring does a lot to make up for any feelings of "same ol', same ol'" in the gameplay department.  I enjoyed doing these things in the early goings of this game more than I have in some of the other recent horror offenders that I played once and put on probation from ever gracing my PC again...they're also on probation from my memory because I can't remember several horror games I've played over the last few years but this one I will.    The trippy esoteric hysteria soon gives way to the first stumbling chase and then things are a sorta mixed bag from there in terms of mechanics.  I didn't find any of it overly difficult like some players but the stealth/running is basic trodding meat n' potatoes where you either run real fast or plod along underwater SOMA-like to get away from slimy big uglies.  You can try sneakier approaches but you'll probably get beat to a pulp.  And then...just when Andrew seems like he's gonna bite the dust, the island starts changing him.  It seems to beckon him to A WEAPON.  Now, we are f'ing talking.  I like shooting idiots back in horror games instead of taking a smacking since I got my start with this mayhem back when Alone in the Dark, Resident Evil and Silent Hill were new games.  And yeah...the shooting.  Well, it's there.  It's piecemeal and sure could have used some further excitement but it works.  So, the next phase of the game has you walking backwards through tunnels, shooting a laser with a cooldown time at monsters that don't seem to die, hoping to bump your ass into the right passage and get out of wormhole tunnels into the next strange area.  The monsters are fantastic looking, even without VR and there is a certain tension to these escapades of escape but your weapon of endless power is just a straight, static beam that you've got to lean to with until you turn on your beeping back-up lights and get your rear end literally out of the mazes.   The fighting gets a little better when you can take on your enemies and walk straight into the brawl as you fight some of the bigger beasts towards the game's finale (including the final boss) but the combat feels like it should be on some n64 port of a PC game than such a modern, surreal looking graphical masterpiece.  I honestly didn't hate it but I'm not going to run around in public and tell you to buy this game for its combat, that's for sure.  Some of the combat sequences are set up as puzzles too and honestly, if I'm allowed a choice here, those are probably better than the run full speed and hold down the fire button till you can't sequences.Aside from the increase in combat, the puzzles get stranger and some of the ones that you solve will free a few of the Old Gods from their shackles.  These scenes are always worth it as these monstrosities coming into gargantuan, towering life are certainly spectacles to behold.  For everything that The Shore handles averagely in terms of mechanics, it makes up for by delivering some kind of absolutely stunning visual reward that kept me pushing forward through my roughly 3 hours of game time.  That's pretty much The Shore in a nutshell.  I don't know what else to say about as if you're coming to see what visual triumphs it unveils, those are best experienced in your own eyes as opposed to reading me ramble on at 2:40 in the morning.  I liked it but I can see someone else hating the everlovin' Dagon sh*t out of it as well.  Some of the more direct horror sequences are effective despite the so-so mechanics but The Shore is at its absolute best when it pauses, visually creeps over your mind like a hallucinogen, reveals revelations of Elder God splendor to you and leaves you with several quiet yet possibly dangerous paths to explore and see what lore you can dig up.  7/10 for me.  I'll definitely check out the devs next game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: A very beautiful game, with a confusing plot, confusing puzzles, and boring game-play. I don't know much about Lovecraft mythos but it and the art direction intrigued me enough to buy the game. The game is very beautiful (of course if you look up close at the textures it doesn't look so good but that's alright). I didn't seem to comprehend the game-play which was just a walking simulator (I thought this was just a joke but it was true), and the few action set pieces that were there failed to be fun and engaging. I also believe the story didn't make much sense as soon as the more weird areas and monsters were introduced. The starting area on the shore, I believe was perfect in a story, voice acting, visual, and suspense, however the rest of the game was a chore to work through.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little story to play through with great visuals and decent voice acting. Felt like a bunch of cool vignettes linked loosely into a plot than a linear story. Not really a criticism as it helps the air of WTF that works for a lovecraftian story. The Shore took me 3 hours because I derped on a couple puzzles and I died a lot. Definitely appreciate that I played it post patching by the developer. From earlier reviews the experience has been significantly improved. Still, best picked up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Hate to give this a thumbs down as I love the Cthulhu Mythos, but this ain't the best representation of it. The art style and models looked great, everything else was pretty meh. Felt more like a circle-jerk expo than an interesting narrative. The story was short. You could probably run through the whole thing in about 1.5 hours. Collectibles are irrelevant and don't add much of anything. _childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be frank.I'm a diehard fan of the Lovecraftian mythos. I love everything about it. What I don't love is hitting more invisible walls than a woman in the 1950s, getting hinted at a greater story but instead getting put on a rail and forcibly driven in that direction, And basically being a passenger for most of this Walking Simulator. The puzzles seem to be a bit picky where you click, the funny enemies require you to basically travel the levels backward to keep giving them that brief stun or else you get nommed quick, and half the levels were basically me having to turn up my brightness to even see.I can tell the devs tried hard. The assets look great, the animation stickiness is minimal, and the sound is pretty damn phenomenal. I cannot say the visuals or audio is lacking, at all.What I can say is this game needs a bit more polish in the gameplay department before I'm willing to give it a second go. I'm gonna get my money back and follow any updates.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore has some great set pieces (and looks great in most areas). The first half is great, with some truly creepy moments and a building sense of dread. Things kind of fall apart in the back half though. The set pieces are still great and it's very creepy, but it focuses too much on boring, mostly meaningless puzzles and horrible combat, which distracts from the atmosphere. That said, as a fan of Lovecraft games, I think it's worth checking out on sale (I got it for $11). And it's pretty short. I was just focused on finishing and it took me 3 hours. So even though the back half isn't as good, it doesn't overstay it's welcome.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Very short and visually impressive. A lot of jump cuts and the many chase sequences made everything feel a little bit clunky but overall enjoyable. _childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Ehh, I love most things associated with Lovecraft, but I can't stand run & hide mechanics in games. This took those even a step further, making some enemies spawn on top of you, move faster than you can run, and offer no hiding space. The lack of helpful guides or walkthroughs also made many of the puzzles a frustrating exercise in triial & error as the game does not provide visual or written clues that would indicate what to do. Neat idea, but I can't recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Cool concepts, poor execution. Lacks polishing, misses a few basic game design things, bad performance. Couldn't bring myself to keep going, the game's missing a lot of things that make playing a game a pleasant experience. Stopped playing after interacting with a note softlocked the game.Lots of invisible walls, no good sense of direction or progress, and what little dialogue I've come across felt bland. I might give it another try at a later date, but a game like this could've benefited a lot from play-testing and feedback.From what I understand this is a fairly new dev who's getting started in the game industry, and I do feel like he's put a lot of love into the game; but as a player, these issues stand out to me too much, and if the very few first minutes aren't engaging it's difficult to buy into the idea.As far as polishing goes, a few examples:The menu could borrow from the game's aesthetic, it's very basic and clunky. There's no pause either, which makes it weird when I want to mess with the settings.I went through a portal which transitioned me to a different area. No screen effects, just a jump between two different places. Felt like I just moved my character's position in a console or something to that effect.Huge chunks of text in the subtitles covering almost half the screen with some notes. Splitting it makes it less distracting from what should be an immersive game experience.First "puzzle" I messed with felt meaningless, just had me interact with 3 different stones in whatever order I wanted.That's what I've got from my first 30 minutes into the game. Is it a bad game? Hard to say, but I wouldn't recommend it based on my personal experience with it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Id say this game is only for die hard fans of Lovecraft. It does a good job depicting the world, but i do think it could be improved upon. Its a bit too short, and i think there could have been room for more potential within the island itself. I really enjoyed the sections in the void though. I didn't encounter any bugs or fps problems, and graphically the game was great. The sound was a bit spotty in a few spots, but overall it was fine. I think the thousand young, and deep ones should have been involved a lot more. I think if the developer made a second game it would turn out even better. I give it a 8/10. (update) I really enjoyed the new secret encounter.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: The Start was promising. Good storyintroduction, good pace and great narration. Everthings good as seen in alpha let's plays and/or demos. After that the story and game goes down the line...pretty fast. All that storytelling and great narration gone.Very weird - even for an lovecraftian game - puzzles with little to absolutely no logic, at least i couldn't think of any good clues that could've explained the outcome of mostly all puzzles.I was hyped and was looking for that game as i saw the trailer and alpha let's plays for the first time.But i was left behind really disappointed... it took 3 hours with "guessing" solutions for some puzzles and dying a few times to complete the game.In my opinion not worth the price, 20 bucks...really? Even on discount i can't recommend unfortunately
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Went in thinking this might not really be much, but damn. This was absolutely amazing. Everything used was really simple, but really nice. Did a full play in 2 and a half hours. The simple stuff put me on edge with the whole cult feel and uneasiness the atmosphere gave off was perfect. I recommend this game highly if you like short story games that actually leave you thinking more. This made me want to learn more about Lovecraft's monsters more. I knew a bit, but after this I need to do a deep dive.10/10 ride of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: Contains very minor spoilers:This game is good, but it has a lot of issues that can easily be ironed out over the course of a few updates. First, the game is too short to warrant a $25 dollar tag. Around two and a half hours of content on my playthrough, for example. I'd say to drop the price from $25 to around $15.The game is absolutely stunning, visually. I found myself just looking around the island seeing how good it could look. Unfortunately, on my decently powerful rig, I noticed more than a few frame drops. This was the most noticeable during the chase sequences and any time I used the artifact. A benchmarking tool would be a very nice addition for those who don't know what graphics they can comfortably set it to.The acting and animations are all very well done, but the subtitles use a lot of incorrect grammar and spelling. This is very apparent in the late game, as most sentences have at least one mistake in the subtitles.The controls are fine but I would've liked key bindings or controller support. Making 'i' the inventory is a very minor issue, but I found myself locking the cursor far too many times.I followed the game's progress on itch.io and I am very glad it got its full release, and I want it to be the best it can be. If the devs read this, I hope I don't come off as rude and the next project is just as amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral rating for games, but I guess I can tentatively recommend this for the right sort of person.  If you really like H.P. Lovecraft, this game does one thing very well, and that is capture the visuals and tone of his works.The plot is a bit on the confusing side and never really made much sense to me, but the journey itself is beautifully grotesque.The biggest negative is the combat.  I think this game would have been better designed like an old school game like Shadowgate where death comes from touching the wrong thing or making bad decisions in general rather than the first person shooter thing they did with this.  It doesn't really ruin the game, but if I could remove everything that involved shooting at monsters, I would enjoy it more.Also, the asking price is such that this is a game which I'd pick up while it is on sale.  It only took me about 3 hours to complete, and I got stuck at a couple points.  It is also not a game which has a lot of replay value.  Sure, it would be fun to go through it again later on, but it will only have that surprise and mystery once.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is VERY hit and miss. On the positive side of this game, the atmosphere of the island and later parts of the game do a perfect job of giving you that eerie and creepy vibe. The music and character narration do a good job too of drawing you in. The creatures look very nice too and even give you that slight chill down your spine. Overall it is just what I wanted out of a Lovecraftian world. Now for the bad. The combat for this game might honestly be the scariest part of the game and the worst combat I have ever encountered and that says a lot because the combat is literally a one button punch or once you get the artifact, one button laser beam. Moving around in general just feels very sluggish and stiff. Maybe it was just me but the game would not let me jump even once, even though in the controls it says you can. I am running the game on a i5 processor and 1070TI and with the unlimited frames option on and resolution set to 1440p, I stayed around 80ish fps which was better than I expected. I am not finished with this game yet but I honestly do not know if I can continue playing this with how horrific the combat is. I have been looking forward to a good Lovecraftian game for awhile and waited especially long for this game and I am honestly very disappointed. If this game was a little cheaper maybe I would not be as harsh on it but it is no where near worth $25.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shore

_childDocuments_.review: The first half of the game was great. The second half feels like the developer lost creativity or got lazy. Really enjoyed the first half on the island and exploring. Collecting the notes and learning about the lore and plot was fun. Environment and atmosphere were stellar. And then everything went out the window with the second half. With just randomly teleporting from room to room solving simple puzzles. And your inventory being gone. You spend your time on the island collecting little tokens and notes and by the time you get sent to the shadow realm, you can't even access your inventory anymore. So what's the point of even collecting anything if you can't see what you collected anymore? The rooms in the second half are bland and repetitive. Chase sequences over and over again. Would have loved it a lot more if there was more creativity in the second half and it followed the formula of the first half of the game
